Positive recommendation as far as EArly Access games go. It is playable and has an interesting premise. The features currently implemented are more of a proof of concept teaser trailer. They introduce novel game dynamics that once fully built out, should make for an interesting game. But as they stand they are sufficiently buggy to prevent extended gameplay.
In its current state at the time of this writing, the game has numerous bugs that, at least for me, freeze the game up constantly, requiring a restart of both the application if not the entire save game.
Buy it to get the sneak peek and support the dev. Don't buy it if you are looking for a game with hours of playability. At least for me on my system, it is little more than a brief demo before crashing. But as a demo, it demonstrates exciting possibilities.
Good job devs, looking forward to when you find an investor, quit your jobs, and stop nibbling at this game's development part time.

ARM is, even though it's early Alpha stage, already delivering a space walking experience that I have found missing in other games of the genre. At this point the game focuses on mining, and does it quite well at that. Mining shouldn't be easy and managing battery power, oxygen, fuel and heat while simultaneously trying to catch chunks of ore is ...challenging - in a good way!
Also worth mentioning are occasional debris fields hurtling through your area at dsiturbing speeds, giving you great opportunity to experience the detailed damage model and repair (EVA) system!
Pros:
Unique mining experience.
Captures the gloomy, lonely and exposed feeling of spacewalks well (compared to other games, at least).
Lots of controls available inside the MRM (the tub you're stuck mining in atm)
Basic ontrols are easy to grasp.
Advanced controls are available (full newtonian & subsystem controls).
Great potential!
Active and attentive developers.
Ingame tutorial (could be improved though.)
Cons:
Unstable (had five CTDs during the first two hours of play).
Limited content (Alpha - duh).
Manual is outdated and there is a distinct lack of "how-tos".
Tutorial repeats every time you enter the level.
In short: If you enjoy realistic, gritty space sims, keep an eye on the beauty! Well worth the price at this point!

Honestly, when I first saw this game I thought it would just be your generic beat 'em up game like double dragon. It is so much more interesting than that. It has such a large variety of items and enemies that the game never feels old and I always want to start it up after losing a run. There is great syndergy with items that create insane combos with magic or straight up melee attacking. The game also teaches that skill and patience will take you far. You can easilly kill every enemy in the room without taking a hit if you are careful and know patterns. Even the ogres aren't bad after you realize you just hit and dodge roll or move after they roar. Or you could run around the room and use magic when your bar fills up. Or a great combo is using the lazer eye with the items that gives a lot of mana on kill. It is great. It is a fun and difficult game that is just so good.
Another interesting thing is that achievements actually give you permanent buffs in this game. It is great. It's a new incentive to actually go for tough achievements and it unlocks the other classes. Particularly the Warlock is kind of too good, but so is the battlemage if you have patience. Every class has a weakness and strength.
The best part is that this game has online co-op. Simple and fun co-op. Host a match and invite over steam just like that. DONE. It is so simple. Or you can even play local.
Overall, amazing game, pick it up. Even playing alone is fun

For the price of admission imho this game doesn't offer much.
You get to choose from 6 different classes (Adventurer, Barbarian, Pirate, Assassin, Warlock and Battle Mage), which are all suitable different: The Barbarian can't wear armor and is slow but tough, the pirate uses a cannon, the assassin can vanish, the battle mage uses spells instead of dodging, etc. This is all kinda nice. Unfortunately you have to unlock all the classes first. Now, granted, this is relatively easy, since you unlock casual mode, where you can simply restart a level, pretty early on (by just dying 3 times), but there's 1 achievement I still couldn't get to unlock the Warlock, because I never get ♥♥♥♥ing cursed or find a curse removal item. Because yes, this is a rogue-lite/like. After unlocking the characters there's not really any more progression. You do not get stronger after runs. You start just like that from the beginning.
Going through the various levels takes about 1 1/2 hours to see the final boss...and then it's just rinse repeat with some random elements like traps, enemies and items of course. Since I've seen the same few weapons drop in the first 5 levels in pretty much every run, as well as the same items, I don't think there's too much variety here. Later on there are a few more, but it's no Isaac or anything like that. Items are armor, weapons, potions, scrolls, throwables and a kind of artifact you can find. Then there's various poisons, diseases and curses in the game as well. And you can definitely kill any chance of completing a run by picking up or using the wrong items. So far so semi-fun.
Where the game falls apart imho is in the combat itself. It's slow, sluggish and very punishing. You think you hit an enemy but you're 1 mm short or the enemy swings a nanosecond earlier and you take damage. Damage you can't heal, unless you find healing potions. And you can die very fast to many of the enemies in the game, especially the giants. Evading, attacking, it's all not terrible, but not great either. However, in the later stages combat becomes terribly difficult to manage imho, because the game throws a lot of enemies on you and by that time you will also have some "familiars", little creatures that accompany you. On my first successful run I had like 6 or so floating around me, all doing their own little effects. Needless to say I killed stuff incredibly quickly, but I also didn't see my screen much in combat. I got this for like 3 bucks and I'm ok with that. It was fun for like 3 to 4 hours and now I'm done with it, since I'm not really interested in the other classes anymore after testing them out a bit. I only really liked the Barbarian and perhaps the Assassin. The battle mage cannot dodge, so he's a no go, despite having nice spells, the pirate can't do a charged attack, which is incredibly important to knock down groups of enemies imho, instead he gets a reloadable cannon that does no damage and only a little pushback...and like I said I haven't unlocked the Warlock, though he does sound interesting. Nice concept, terrible graphics, mediocre execution. Wait for deep sale imho.

I can't believe I didn't write a review for this when I first played it. I love this visual novel. It teaches you about a lot of cool locations and aspects of Japan. Quite frankly you could experience culture shock just by playing this. If you want a laid back VN that's actually full of really cool trivia and facts about Japan, you should definitely pick this up.
However, if you do pick it up, I recommend getting it with the 2015 DLC. That DLC improves the game tenfold in pretty much all areas while also doubling the content. I went from 6 hours to 15 hours (and still going) because I want to do multiple playthroughs. This allows me to visit all of the locations, discover all of the CG, and read all of the dialogue. The 2015 DLC is pretty much the Brave New World of Civilization, so it's definitely really recommended to get.

This game is interesting to say the least.
To get started the story is not the best. The two female leads do not have much depth, and are mostly there to serve as tour guides and shallow love interests. The overarching story of this being a short trip in Japan is mostly just there to give you reason as a player to be going to these varied locations and, like the two female leads, only offers a shallow amount of depth.  Moving onto the games art, it is good. The characters have appealing designs and the environments look nice. The games music is also enjoyable, fairly generic but enjoyable. Each of the areas has ambient sounds which help do wonders to the emersion. As for the gameplay, the games visual novel style controls work well, though it’s hard to mess up saving and loading features..... The game offers a fair amount of information about the places you visit and even has a button that you can press to see a google maps image of the real life area. To me this was the highlight of the game because the game does offer more or less an abridged history lesson about the areas that you visit. The game does a good job of making you feel like you are in fact getting a tour and the games inclusion of background noise adds greatly to this. The biggest flaw that the game has is the length. The game is only about 2 hours long to get one of the endings and is about another 30 mins if you want to get the alternative ending, if you skip through previously viewed dialogue. This game will appeal to a somewhat small audience but those who find the idea of touring Japan with anime girls will not be disappointed.

Heads up requires a lot of hoops to get it to run on windows 10, if its even possible at all. I didn't want to put the work into making it run, but this is the solution that looked most likely to work to me.
1) Set both engine.exe and startengine.exe compatibility to XP3.
2) Set log.txt to read only.
3) Rename settings.cfg and settings.xml (i.e. I renamed as settings.oldcfg and settings.oldxml respectivley).
4) Search bar for "Windows Features", activate, then click on Legacy Components, expand and then click DirectPlay.
I did not delete any .bik files. I did not copy d3d8.dll into the directory.
But as windows 10 is standard and its a game that will run for 0% of people on said platform as is, thumbs down.
The game itself may be good, I wouldn't know.

This game. Oh, boy. Let's get started, shall we?
PROS:
-Gun disassembly is very accurate
-Firing and executions are correct
-Leaderboards to race against players
-A true "story" experience (as long as you don't go along and use your mommy's credit card)
-Large selection of weapons
-Included disections such as a human skeleton, cars, etc.
CONS:
-Part(s) of the game require a substantial basis of money (which I'm not willing to pay)
-Achievements of the guns give somewhat little EXP for their difficulties (I'm looking at you, Timed achievements. 400 EXP for my "perfection" of disassembling and assembling a Tec-9 in 1:37?)
-Random selection of when to unlock guns in the game (the catalogue will allow you to get something at any time, with a little bit of extra pricing I believe). What I'm saying is, I would've started with pistols and you would've kept expanding into higher tiers of weapons: e.g. pistols, sub-machine guns, assault rifles, light-machine guns, sniper rifles, artillery.
PERSONAL COMMENTS:
-I know a very good general understanding of most weapons, and I love expanding my knowledge to more guns and learning how to fully disarm weapons.
-I love field stripping weapons in real life, so this game really speaks to me.
-I like looking inside the mechanics and seeing how a weapon works to a full extent.
Hope any of my review helps your choice on downloading this or not, and if you're still not sure, it's a very quick DL and you can try it out for yourself.

I'm not really a big fan of anime, to be honest. 'BlazBlue: Calamity Trigger', on the other hand, looks amazing and is probably (one of) the best looking 2-D fighter game out there.
There are 12 characters to fight with (or against). Not a very big number but at least every character is unique and plays totally different. The gameplay is great, fights get your adrenaline pumping and there are lots of special moves.
There are a few modes you find in every fighter  like; Arcade, Time Attack and Story mode, so nothing special there. Also, there's no option to play vs friends online, which is something a game like this should have.
There are also a few things I did find weird, probably because I'm not into anime. Things like; a round is called 'rebel' in this game? and before every match a voice says "the wheel of fate is turning"...
In my opinion, BlazBlue: Calamity Trigger is a great game but it wouldn't hurt if there was more content. Still, if you don't mind playing story mode or have some friends to play with locally, you can still have lots of fun with this one.

Very interesting concept, very weird decision to enable Early Access on such a "Pre-Alpha" early stage.
A space game with decent simulation and an actual interesting plot which challenges you to break away from its chains? Definitely interesting.
In A.R.M. you are a (possible) criminal locked up in a Mining Barge, and mining asteroids with a mech for as long as the system tells you to is your sentence.
If you try to misbehave, they come for you. If you try to escape, they come for you.
Your mech has upgradable parts, and there's a modular damage system.
There's a really cool system by which you use the ARM tool of your mech to pick things, like bombs, wedges or other tools, and you can also activate a jet on the "hand" in order to propel whatever you're holding, or use it as a reverse thruster. Never seen that before - very interesting.
There's other simulated variables, like heat, oxygen, fuel, energy, battery, and newtonian flight.
However, this is all there is to this game at the moment.
When I first bought it, you couldn't even play for more than 5 minutes without something breaking.
Now it's a little bit better, but all you get is a very little sample of what the game COULD be, with some weird gameflow issues.
In my own, personal and honest opinion, releasing a game this early is an horrible idea.
There's not even an actual clue to where the game is going - it could become a Sandbox game, or a linear story game with open-world elements. It doesn't seem like the devs have a consensus about it, either.
ARM is all concept, no game. I wish all the best for the developers, which seems to be a brand new company. They seem really interested in making something good. And for Early Access games, the developers matter more than the current state of their product.
But, again, you can't just release something in this state. It's more of a weird Kickstarter than an Early Access purchase. And as a reviewer writing for fellow gamers, I can't just pretend it's not.

A decent beat em' up roguelike that accomplishes what it sets out to do. Difficult at first, but once you get down the patterns and item abilities, it becomes fairly manageable.
Admittedly, I don't think the side scrolling fighter aspect pairs very well with the roguelike elements, or perhaps it has more to do with how it was executed. Most weapon wielding enemy types have almost zero windup on some of their standard attacks, whereas you have a second delay most of the time. This produces scenarios where you'll get hit by an enemy, despite the fact you almost cannot predict their attack. To make matters worse, enemies that are lying on the ground can occasionally pop back up and hit you within seconds flat. The AI makes predicting attacks even more dubious, as they will sometimes not attack at all or fall back for no apparent reason.
Once you settle into the game's mechanics though, it becomes a decent veg out game. You can just boot it up and turn your brain off an play. Even better, the game saves between each area, and you can hop out at any time. Runs are usually 45 minutes to an hour long, but can be split up between sessions of 15 minutes a piece if need be. Their system is robust enough that I even had a bluescreen while playing(unrelated to the game), and was still able to continue where I left off with no penalty.
Basically, I can't recommend this game on the grounds that it breaks a cardinal rule of game design. Don't require challenges that don't reinforce the core elements of your game's genre. You'll play for an hour to get to the final boss. You finally find a strategy and set of items that works and defeat him, only to be insulted with a post boss mini-game that is completely alien to everything the game represents. A bullet hell shooter that throws your items out the window.
How... How on earth did this idea even get considered. Many have warned it in the reviews, but I simply have to reiterate how bad this is design-wise. A non-optional fight that uses a different control scheme and does not take into account any of the skills or items you had previously used. It makes me angry every time I get to the end. I've managed this sequence a few times, with some close calls, but I can't imagine having players who can't manage a bullet hell get destroyed by what is basically a middle finger to the player. Imagine playing Binding of Isaac only to get to the end, and it turns into a Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles arcade beat em up for the final boss, and none of your items count. Imagine Left 4 Dead's finales requiring you to play Bubble Bobble to escape. Imagine playing Dark Souls, and the boss in Anor Londo is a few rounds of BurgerTime.
The fix is simple, cut the shooter out or make it an optional side gag. The fact that it's mandatory is juvenile and insulting. Until then, it's not recommended.

(Review based on original non-2015 version.)
Pleasantly simple visual novel that seems either like a substitute for a vacation, or preparation for one.
Your character travels to Tokyo for a week, staying with some people he met online--he thinks he's going to stay with brothers Makoto and Akira, but it turns out they're _sisters_ Makoto and Akira. They act as his guides, showing him how things work locally, such as how to use the train system and use Suica cards for payment. Choices are mostly limited to "Which area of town should we visit today?". You'll take a tour of the area, see some drawn images, learn a few facts and history of the place. A single playthrough lets you see half of these locations, so two playthroughs will let you see pretty much anything. It's easy to quickly skip through sections if you've seen them before. There is an extremely light bit of romance plot, which basically boils down to which of two people was your tour guide on more days, so two playthroughs covers both of those bases too.
Another kind of neat thing is that since most of the time the conversations are supposed to be taking place in Japanese, it has the option of showing you the "real" text in a box above the English translation. Even if you know just a little of the language, it can sometimes be interesting to compare the two. It's also pretty funny that Akira's poor English skills are represented by katakana.

It felt fun to play through the game again seeing how fast you can the first boss with a leaf blower that blows more♥♥♥♥♥♥♥than freshmen in college while at the same time trying not to die. Again the sound track made each boss enjoyable and unique, while at the same time making me realize how good of a band Celldweller is.
Then we come to Dead rising 3. One of the huge issues veterans to the Dead rising series will notice would be the protagnist Nick Ramos failure in pretty much every sense of surviving. At one point running out of cover to yell at Spec-Ops to say "You killed that man". It took a lot of effort to not run out of my window at that point. After being forced to reinstall the game to play CO-OP with a friend, I realized how better the Co-op partner is comparied to Nick. If I say his name Steam will probably censor it. Richard feels more like Frank and Chuck from the previous games, making wise cracks when they can and not acting like a shelter child who was forced outside for the first time.
Its not hard to fail at making fun weapons to dismember and disembowel zombies with. Dead Rising 3 gives the player a great assortment of fun and good weapons to use again the countless horde of Zombies. That is however its flaw. There is way to many zombies to actually have fun with a weapon. I ended up using only the Spilt Shot gun for most of the game since it goes through Zombies like the IRS does with my Money.
The game adds Ultimate Combo weapons which require you to find all the blueprints to use them fully, Something that I will rant on further down. However some combo weapons seem like a weapon you should have trouble getting until you have all the pieces to get. The weapon locker makes these weapons as common as the billions of propane tanks laying on the roads of the city. The game did make it so you can only get two of these ultimate weapons out of one locker at a time. Its not broken or Overpowered, it just makes them not feel like Ultimate style weapons.
Driving in Dead Rising 3 is fun for a bit before you car slows down from the amount of zombies and then blows up once you run of an gas barrel that someone left outside of a Hotel. If the game didn't have these cars, it would be impossible to play. Most of the Combo Cars looks like the rejected concept art of a Mad Max Horror game.  If you were expecting more than a few combo cars and junk cars, why are you playing a zombie game? Buy Mad Max or a GTA.
Just a few more things before I get done ranting. There are more skills points and than there are levels so even if you are level 50 you aren't done yet. However you don't really need all the levels. Once you get every perk, Nick becomes the Sheltered Super Man of the Zombie world.  The spilt shot would probably be considered a WMD. Boss fights become how fast can I kill this Boss with a single Assault Rifle. The answer is fast. Paul Walker would be jealous of how fast you are going,
Boss fights become just Boss fights not scary or troubling just a thing to do during the 7 days they give you. There are only 6 side quest Boss Fights, That 7 deadly sin thing is kinda redundant if one of them is a story boss. The Boss Fight themes which use to be one of the highlights for Dead Rising are kinda bland and forgetful in DR3. Side Quest Survivors are now more Go to A to B to get 3 items to destroy an item across the map. I had trouble not giving up after one survivor told me to destroy Vans all over the city.
I promised to complain about the collectables, but I was also promised a game that I would enjoy playing. The game is fun before you realize how irritating the story, protagnist and collectables are. The final, not OVERTIME, boss comes out of no where. If it was suppose to be a plot twist, it needs to have a plot people are engaging in first. I have to say No to this game even though I forced myself to get everything in this game.
If Dead Rising 4 feels like this I may have to drop one of my favorite Series.

Casual game types? Not exactly.
Death Snatch:
Every kill counts—as long as the Blutonium vial gets picked up. Picking up the red vials dropped by dead opponents scores your team points. Deny the other team from scoring by grabbing the green vials dropped by dead allies. It’s vital to stick together in Death Snatch so that there’s someone left alive to grab the vials and score points.
Jackhammer:
Forget capturing flags. Capture the enemy’s hammer and take it back to your base while protecting your own to score. Oh, and the hammer is a brutal melee weapon. Smashing enemies with it nets more points on a successful capture. Steal the hammer -> smash people -> profit.
Extraction:
Grab the unrefined Blutonium scattered over the map and take it to the grinder bins for processing—and points. Stop the other team from scoring by killing their collector. When a collector dies, another player on the team is randomly chosen. Unrefined Blutonium is incredibly volatile when shot or thrown—watch out!
Blitz:
Capture the active control point to score. The more players in proximity to the control point the faster it captures. Taunting in the capture zone also speeds up the process—but makes the capping team an easier target. The closer a team gets to capturing, the longer it will take the other team to capture the point.
And that's not all :)
I highly recommend this game for casual players.

Before the review I have to tell you that I played the original Deus Ex:HR, not the Director's Cut (which probably won't be that of a problem because most of the content is still the same). Also, I don't want to write the whole story-thingy here because you can LOOK IT UP under "About this game" right above the review section - which leads me directly to the PROs and CONs of the game.
PROs:
+There are many augmentation-upgrades, which can give you the possibility to lift heavy things, such as vending machines. Others make that you don't take any fall-damage, or let you jump higher and much more.
+The graphics are really good looking and are mostly very detailed.
+You can choose how you want to play the level: Stealthy, avoiding or just gunning everything down.
+Through the hacking you can unlock special areas of the map, where you can find extra missions.
+You have to make sometimes quite tricky choices in order to reach your goal (mostly through talking with the main person in the mission) which also affect your later gameplay.
+The story is quite long, even if you dont do any side-missions.
Sadly there are also some really annoying CONs:
-The faces of the randomly generated people you meet on the street not only look bad (and by bad I mean the faces look as if they were photoshopped out of a potato by someone who doesn't have any skills in doing that) AND it feels as if there are only 5 differnet faces per gender in the game - I mean it really ruins the feeling if you are running around and suddenly you walk past 2 people with EXACTLY THE SAME FACE AND HAIRCUT!
-The boss fights. I mean I feel genuinly sorry for people who invested all their augmentation-upgradepoints into hacking because in most bossfights THERE ARE NO ALTERNATIVES but GUNNING THE BOSS DOWN!
But all in all I'd say it's one of the best games I've played so far and if you don't mide the CONs you should really start playing RIGHT NOW!

Fallout 2
My introduction to the Fallout world was Fallout 3, but it interested me so much that I wanted to find out as muhc as I could about the lore behind the game, and play the originals for myself to truly see how great the games are, and how far it's come from the original.
I was very pleasantly surprised.
Fallout 2 is a top down isometric turn based rpg.
The premise is very simple, years after the Vault Dweller founded Arroyo, his ancestor known only as The Chosen One, steps up to prove his worth to the Village, by overcoming the Trials, donning the Vault 13 Jumpsuit, and is sent out in search of some way to save the Villiage from famine with the Garden of Eden Creation Kit.
As far as Role Playing goes, this game is phenomenal. From metting and performing certain actions, requirements, helping people out or just plain being in the right place at the right time, you can meet a plethora of people willing to join you on your quests, each with their own personalities and styles, including the return of Dogmeat from one of the various well made Random encounters placed along the decently nice sized map of California.
From building your own cars, getting married, joining a New Reno mafia gang to exploring the Vaults, fending off Raiders, various Mutants and the Enclave, and making visits to the civilizations scattered around the wasteland, this game immerses you completely in the world, complete with iconic Cultural References and humor between the Developers and players.
This game is superior to Fallout by improving it in almost every way, and I have to say, as far as RPG's go this was my favorite game next to Fallout 3 (probably an unpopular opinion, considering I disliked F:NV)
I highly recommend digging deep into the Wiki's, and fully playing through this game from beginning to end
(and beyond for more content, and more of that Developer humor throughout the world after the end)

Fallout 2 is fantastic but very frustrating all at once, and has left me confused on how I feel about it. The game provides plenty of content, it is easily worth the price. When the game is good, it is addicting to play. I could not put it down sometimes, wanting to see all the quirks of the wasteland and how much my actions affect it. But the game has so many issues that when fallout 2 starts to show its problems, it can get rough. I had to start over from being 12 hours in because the game stopped working altogether on my pc and I had to start fresh on my laptop. Late in the game a bug took away my companions, but restricted me from entering certain places normally because it still detected them. The game is incredibly inbalanced, leaving alot up to chance and making the freedom of the character creation, feel restricted if you want to even stand a relative chance. Even my combat focused character would get destroyed, having me reload single encounters over and over again. My endings were bugged, certain missions didn't occur correctly, and there is a clear amount of cut content, which can be pretty disappointing to think of what this game could have been with more time. Fallout 2 is still an amazing game, despite all of its flaws however. The attention to detail is mind-boggling, and there is so much variety that you could play this game 20 times to its completion and still run into so many different things. The dialogue is cleverly written, voice acting is superb, and storytelling very solid. Fallout 2 is a masterpiece, just flawed, if that makes sense. With lots of patience, and I mean lots, getting through Fallout 2 is worth the time and effort, despite the extreme frustration I got from it sometimes. I recommend it wholeheartedly, just pack some talenol...

Valve first announced the Steam Controller way back at the end of 2013 and after plenty of revisions, tweaks and even feature changes, we finally saw it launch last year. However, it looks like Valve isn’t quite finished refining its gamepad yet as reports are suggesting that another hardware revision for the controller is already in the works.
This information came from a GDC presentation (via PCGamesN), which talked about the design of the controller and the future. The new controller apparently won’t guarantee any new functionality but will make changes to the “look and feel”.
“In the future, we are working on a hardware revision to the controller to improve look and feel. But we’re pretty happy with the feature set we have now and do not intend to drastically change it, or even change it at all. Maybe we’ll throw extra features in here or there, but the controller’s not gonna grow a new touchpad, or a new set of buttons, or a new major feature.”
If Valve were to add major new features to a Steam Controller hardware revision then the company would run the risk of alienating those who already bought one. However, giving it an ergonomic touch-up doesn’t sound like it would be as big a deal.

I have the steam controller about three weeks now, and due to some issues with time I haven't been able to really intensely use it.
So why this review alreadt?
Well, the fact that I haven't been able to use it intensely, doesn't mean I haven't used it at all.
Basically this is my first impression review. An impression of what it is like for a newb to start using a device like this. And basically I can narrow it down to two stages, finishing it off with a first impression conlusion.
Stage 1: the unboxing and first starting to use the controller.
The controller came in an awesome box. Immediately starting to use it, out of the box gave me a little bit of an awkward feeling; did I do right spending so much money buying this controller? It didn't feel natural, the haptic feedback was not what I had expected and most annoying:  to actually be able to use it in games and being able to perform modifications you HAVE to use steam big picture.
In my case I bought this piece of hardware especially for black desert online. I was already using the xbox 360 controller, but navigating through menu's and dialogs is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ I have already used a touchpad to play mmorpg's with, so I'd figure; the steam controller is basically a controller with a touchpad. That should work pretty well, especially in the situations when a mouse is required.
So I had to search the net for a workaround to get black desert to start from big picture to be able to use the controller.
My aim was to be able to turn on my PC, start up and play the game, only using the steam controller. I was getting close, but unfortunately the final wall I ran into, which I couldn't overcome, is the login of the patcher of black desert. So, when starting the game from steam big picture, the game doesn's start immediatley. The Patcher is started, then you have to log in through the patcher, and then start the game.
The steam controller keyboard cannot easily be opened (has to be done through the menu button on the controller), and even then the keyboard lags terribly, making it unable to provide input.
Once logged in and starting to play the game, as I said, no plug and play. Out of box the controller simply doesn't play well with the standard templates.
Stage 2: experimentation and development
So, well, got the controller, intiated the use with the keyboard template to be able to use the trackpad as a mouse function. And after hours and hours of going through the menu's I learned two things:
1. The steam controller has already replaced the xbox 360 controller as the better controller. After learning to configurate the controller I really got it to replace my keyboard and mouse. Being able to switch between actions sets and setting the automated trigger to do so when there is no mouse icon on screen and when there is, is simply genius.
Being able to map every button, stick and pad as either, keyboard, mouse or gamepad input is awesome! Really, I'm starting to fall in love with this controller. Being able to modify so much, and really seeing how much thought has been put in it. It really is amazing.
2. It is very, very time consuming to configure the controller.
Tips towards valve:
1. The customisability is really beyond this world and should always remain in place, even when future versions come out. However, it also has the risk of people not willing or able to succeed the learning curve. The advantage of consoles and their controllers is the fact that the way the controller has to be used is already predefined to a number of templates and some limited sliders for some more finetuning. The advantage for console builders is that it is done by the game developers. I'd advise valve to either seek contact with developers that are developing potentially popular games, or assigning a small team of people that develop templates for specific upcoming games. The predecessor of Red Orchestra: Ostfront 41-45 is a modification of Red Orchestra: the Combined Arms for Unreal Tournament 2004, created by enthusiasts, who later organized the company Tripwire Interactive.
Modification participated in the contest «Make Something Unreal», conducted by Epic Games, creators of the games «Unreal». Due to the subsequent victory, the command Tripwire Interactive received the prize pool and a license for commercial use of the game engine, Unreal Engine 2.5. Later it was decided to move the modification of the format of individual games, elaborating some elements.
The game takes place on the Eastern front during the Second world war and covers the period from 1941 to 1945. The player is given the opportunity to participate in the reconstruction of events as for the Red Army and Wehrmacht troops. The game is targeted primarily at the network mode, but there's a single-player game against the bots. Each location (map) is a real historical area.
In multiplayer mode, the player can take any direction - both Soviet and German soldiers. In addition, there are several types of slot classes with their own unique capabilities and skills for the use of certain weapons. There is a possibility to manage a real military equipment, such as tanks, mobile artillery, artillery guns, armoured troop carriers.
For Red Orchestra was done many custom modifications, such as the sets of cards, a variety of game content or full total conversion.
Below is a list of published or under development projects:
Carpathian Crosses - focuses on the participation of Romania in the Second world war. No longer supported by developers.
Mare Nostrum - focuses on the Mediterranean theater of operations.
Darkest Hour: Normandy 1944 - focuses on the capture of Normandy.
After-Hourz Community - includes several new vehicles, new tanks and anti-tank weapons.
Defence Alliance 2 - ported by the authors of UT2004.
Part 2.
Red Orchestra concentrates mostly on the multiplayer aspect of the game, although there is a singleplayer "Practice" mode available. Red Orchestra: Ostfront 41-45 features an advanced ballistics system for both small arms and tank rounds - incorporating bullet drop, flight time, and tanks with more realistic armor properties than most games (featuring: penetration and deflection, in relation to range and projectile trajectory angle). The player's movements are realistically modeled, giving them the ability to lie and move prone, sprint (while standing or crouching) and to deploy machine guns on objects.
Red Orchestra is notable for its emphasis on realism in comparison to other World War II-based FPS games. There is no "crosshair" for a player to aim with in the middle of their screen; instead, the player must either aim down the three-dimensional iron sights, or aim from the hip using the game's free-aim system. The former requires compensating for the breathing of the character and natural sway from holding the gun, while the latter is much quicker but accurate only at very short range. The player must also keep track of their ammo usage mentally unlike many other FPS games, most of which use an ammunition counter. Additionally, the player's health status is not represented by "health points" as many other games use, but by a diagram of the player's body with reddened sections that show where he or she has been wounded; there is no way to recover from wounds, although after a brief period of time, the player will function at 100% again. Receiving wounds will temporarily slow the player down, especially if they receive a wound to the legs or feet; receiving a wound to the hands causes the player to drop their currently held weapon on the ground. Rifles usually kill players in one shot if they connect with the torso or head.
Vehicle support is also a prominent feature of the game. The player can operate the combat vehicles as one of the crew members. Most tanks, for example, can accommodate up to three crew members (a driver, a commander and a machine-gunner) to make them fully effective in close city fighting, however it is easy to crew a tank solo and simply switch to different positions as needed. When grouped together in a vehicle, all players in the vehicle receive points for their actions and for the actions of their fellow crew members; for example, if a player is driving a tank and the tank commander destroys an enemy tank, both the player and the commander will receive the appropriate number of points for that kill. When operating a tank solo, the player can only perform one of the roles at a time; this prevents a solo player from being able to fire, move and reload all at the same time (reloading is a task performed by the commander). The game also features artillery support in some maps which can be utilized by both squad leaders and tank commanders.
The game received generally favorable reviews from critics. On the review aggregator Game Rankings, the game had an average score of 81% based on 22 reviews. On Metacritic, the game had an average score of 81 out of 100, based on 22 reviews

Not for the feint of heart, BlazBlue is truly a 2D fighter of its own kind. The game is a fantastic exclamation point, and one that pushes the boundaries of 2D fighting games. It's a hardcore game that also can be fun to the amateurs of this genre, but make no mistake; the challenge is here if you want it. Overall, this is a wonderful addition to the genre and it exemplifies why 2D fighters are still alive and kicking.
At first glance the game is a beautiful masterpiece. All character models are drawn in high-res sprites. Backgrounds are done in 3D, and the blend of both equate to a wonderful convergence of visuals. The game is pretty to say the least. Each character also has a fun and quirky style reminiscent of Guilty Gear's lineage of outlandish character stock. We have cat girls, huge breasted beauties, mechanical marionettes, and countless odd yet cool fighters. If you can find your own quirk, there is bound to be a respectable character to scratch that itch within the game's 12 playable fighters.
Sound, too, boasts a caliber of oomph, which is usually accompanied by a mash-up of heavy metal riffs and classical music. While to some this might be an irritating soundtrack, I didn't find it to be annoying and it blended quite well with the high-intensity fights on screen. The one thing that can detract from the experience is the constant yelling and yelping that accompanies each move characters make. Some are more irritating than others (Tao for example comes to mind--meow, meow, meow...) but overall, the battle cries aren't excruciating, and after a few moments you drown it out into the background.
Gameplay itself is where the meat is, and with that players divulge into two camps; the ones that button mash, and those that take the time to master the mechanics. It's totally up to you how you approach the game, but to the dedicated they will find a rich experience to sink their teeth into. There are four attack buttons: weak, medium, strong, and Drive. The first three are self explanatory, the fourth, Drive, is a special attack that utilizes a characters special ability. While this array of button layout may seem tame compared to other fighters, in combination with quarter-circles, half-circles and the like, the game opens up considerably and the emphasis of quick dash and strike attacks takes over.
This is where the depth of the game shines. Knowing what moves and attacks do what kind of damage and how it affects the opponent is the key to opening up an opportunity to create a combo string. There are also two gauges, one controlling your guard and the other your super. Combine these with cancels, grabs and others, and you have quite and arsenal to kick some...well you know.
Once you think yourself decent, take the game to its various modes. You have your mandatory training, arcade and versus mode. These are self explanatory, but there are others. Story is an interesting change to the formula for this genre, as there is an actual story to follow. Granted the story here isn't amazing, but it is entertaining and the way the game forces you to choose different paths to unveil the whole story is interesting and a welcomed change to the usual we've seen before in this genre.
Along with story mode you have Score Attack (a variation of survivor mode) and Network, its online component. Online is pretty basic with player and ranked matches and you can watch a match along with four other people. The online mode is regular 1v1, but be forewarned, there are some top notch caliber people out there right now so you might be outgunned. If you have friends who have the game you can always set up a private match for a more balanced game. As of now, the online portion is very solid without any lag and most people whom I've come across have been cordial and stayed through the whole game. Obviously this can be different in your location but I live in Scotland and I've had zero lag issues online--two thumbs up to Arc Systems.
Overall, the game is a true keeper. If you are tired and feel Street Fighter and others alike have become stale, give this a definite buy.

Getting a kill in Tribes: Ascend is hard. It takes many shots, and a lot of determination. You will rarely get the jump on somebody because of how fast everything is moving. You need to either chase down your foe and fire into their moving bodies, or aim for their feet with explosive weapons. None of your weapons or bullets feel like they have a lot of weight or power behind them. Getting a kill is a time-consuming, yet rewarding experience that is a welcome change from the “pull left trigger, pull right trigger, move on” twitch shooting of a game like Call of Duty. You also have grenades and a melee attack, but using either effectively is difficult.
Only true FPS gamers can compete here, leaving the Call of Duty "wannabe pros" rage quitting.

A fast-paced, truely 3D shooter that provides a unique take on the class-based FPS, Tribes:Ascend shows command of an immensely deep experience. From using your jetpack to soar high above the battlefield to zipping down mountains at speeds unheard of in other games, Tribes: Ascend is nothing like anything you've played before.

So I'm a huge Dead Rising fan, and I really need to get this off my chest. With Keiji and the original Dead Rising team gone, Capcom Vancouver has to develop the Dead Rising series themselves. So how did they do for the 4th installment? (I'm counting OTR and not CTYD) Oh god where to begin.
It still feels like Dead Rising, the survival horror aspect is obviously there, killing zombies in the most craziest ways possible while wearing the silliest of outfits. The time limit is there, but it's almost pointless unless you're playing Nightmare mode. You have 6 days to escape the city and that just seems like way too much time to give considering how short the game is to begin with. Since I speedran for my first playthrough (I was spoiled 2 things in the game and wanted to beat it as soon as I got it) it only took me about 4-5 hours. If you don't speedrun it, it'll probably take you 7-8 hours at the most. Some stupid additions include a weapons locker at safe houses, which really kills the point of scavenging for weapons. Survivors that follow you are now considered followers, and can be summoned and dismissed at will ala Saints Row. Special moves have been replaced with a combo system, which gives you the ability to perform one after a certain amount of kills instead of performing specials at will. None of these changes feel right at all and they don't need to be in a Dead Rising game.
Overall, I'd have to give Dead Rising 3 a
. While it's still hindered by stupid changes the devs decided to make, it's still a fun game. I recommend it, but you should play through Dead Rising 1 & 2 first. Then you'll understand how I feel about Dead Rising 3.

TL;DR: It's a frustrating masterpiece.
This is my first time beating this game and my ears are still steaming. I started it many times and never got very far.
You probably all heard how this game is awesome, the best of it's kind and what not.... and it's true, the amount of RPGs that ARE NOT FANTASY is quite small, so Fallout with its post apocaliptic setting definitely stands out as a unique game in that regard (Yes, I'm aware of the Wasteland).
The story, the setting, design, characters, dialogue (if you don't mind reading a lot), companions, choices and consequences, role playing abilities, violence, lots of adult themes, big world to explore.... this game has A LOT to offer and ways to beat the game and quests.
It's the only game where I was allowed into a porn studio and massacre everyone in there. That felt good!
Random unscripted events that I witnessed were funny and very enjoyable.
I played a character who absolutely hated drugs and when he got into "Sin City" of Fallout (won't name it), he was hell bent to kill the source of the drugs and he did that.
What happened is hillarious. I returned to the city and the guys that were making money off of the drugs attacked me. Makes sense. I decided to leg it, but one of those guys accidentally blowed a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to bits with a burst attack and her pimp didn't liked that one bit and attacked him. Next thing I know, there was a war on the street between pimps and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s vs guys that run drug business. I absolutely loved it!
When you finish the game, a narrator will explain how your actions affected each major faction/settlement.
Personally, I liked the graphic and turn based combat. Gory critical kills really made the combat felt rewarding in addition to xp gained.
So, in that regard, the game is awesome....
However...
I don't remember when was the last time I cursed and yelled at my monitor as much as when playing this game.
Please excuse my harsh language.
The game is unbalanced as f*** and if anyone says "Git gud" or any other silly "advice", use your Speech skill to tell them to go to hell.
I like challenge, I really do, I don't like hand holding and dying or failing because I made a mistake is completely fair.
But it's NOT FAIR when during fast traveling you encounter 5 f***ing slavers with assault rifles attacking you on sight while you have a spear. What the hell was I supposed to do??? They have the first turn, no option to run and before I managed to get my turn, I'm dead.
Only thing is to save before fast traveling and if aformentioned situation happens, reload that save and hope to Jesus you won't meet those slavers again. That happened a thousands of times and made traveling from settlement to settlement a nightmare.....
Get a car! Seriously! Get A CAR! It has a trunk to store items, makes fast traveling faster and it takes less action points to get to the car and escape than running all the way to the "magic" brown field on the edge of the screen.
If you choose Energy Weapons as your combat skill and didn't put points into Melee weapons, you're screwed, because I didn't find a single energy weapon until later parts of the game. Yeah, I guess they went for realism and it wouldn't make sense for a tribal to know how to use energy weapons. I get that, but from gameplay point of view, it's stupid.
The next, and probably the biggest, problem I had with the game is that it's cryptic as hell.
Is that sprite there something I can interact with or is it just a part of the scenery? I spent many hours just clicking on everything on the screen that might look important. That was not fun.
Game often throws a curve ball and change the rules randomly.
For example (I'll try to avoid spoilers):
I got a quest from a certain someone to rescue certain someone that is locked in a cage. The cage is opened by a terminal next to a cage. Logic tells me to use Science on a terminal because: A) it's a terminal; B) all terminals till now used Science skill.
Well, I was wrong. THIS particular terminal requires you to have high LOCKPICK skill in addition to SCIENCE skill. How did I found out? After hours of searching on the internet I came upon some old forum where some guy went through game scripts and found that this skill check requires high Lockpick skill.
How the hell was anyone supposed to know that?? Did the game manual said to decompile the exe to find out what skills were used in skill checks?
In another example, everytime I had to clear some rocks or destroy doors with explosives, all I had to do is to "use" the explosive in my invertory, set the timer, place it and run. Logic, right? Bomb goes off, the rocks are gone. Easy.
But not THIS time. This time I had to place explosive and LEAVE the area otherwise I could be placing a ton of explosives on this particular pile of rock and the explosion won't leave a dent.
How was anyone supposed to know that? I don't know.
I literally played the game with the game on one monitor and FO2 wiki on another, because I didn't know when I was just being plain stupid and when did the game decided to change the rules.
Ok, that's out of the way...
Some skills are very underused. I got crippled twice in the whole game, one is a scripted event and another was from combat. I had Doctor skill of 5% and I managed to heal myself with just that. I never used Trap skill nor had a reason to use it. Gambling, Barter, same. I ended with so much money that the bigger problem was to find a merchant with money to sell my sh** to.
Never used First Aid as well, because you can always rest to heal yourself.
Last thing, you CAN get stuck in a game and unable to progress. I did some quests in weird order near the end of the game and spent days searching how to unfurl myself from mess I did. You can say it's my fault, but I think main quests should always be possible to solve regardless of your character build and choices you made.
To wrap up the negativity... I tried to role play as much as possible, but the random bulls*** game threw at me really put a strain on it.
Veteran players shouldn't give advices like: "Oh, pick this skills and this traits, go here to get this awesome weapon and then there to get that super armor... Oh, you'll rock then!"... no.
This is a ROLE playing game so you need to ROLE play it, not META play it.
You should be able to make a character you want with good sides and bad sides and take the game slowly to really immerse yourself in the world.
So to conclude...
Do I recommend the game? Yes.
Is it a perfect game? No.
Will I play the game again? Absolutely!
Thanks for reading!

I have had a Steam Controller since mid November (2015). The reason I bought one is because I had hurt my right arm and it was painful to use the mouse, and it was going to take a while to heal. I already have XBox 360 controllers for certain games and local coop games, and my arm didn't hurt playing games with a controller. While waiting for my arm to heal and after playing only controller games for a while, I wanted to get back to playing games that required the use of a keyboard and mouse, so I bought the Steam Controller.
I have been back and forth on whether I to recommend this or not, for reasons I will detail below, but I can't recommended it,
. This doesn't mean I think it's a bad device or that you should not buy it. I think it is a good piece of hardware, but it is the software (A.K.A. the Steam client) that ruins it for me.
Overall I like the Steam Controller. Unlike an XBox or Play Station controller, it allows you to play games that can only be controlled by a mouse and keyboard, even first person shooters. It can emulate an X-Input controller and work with any game with native controller support, but it's not as good as a standard controller for some of those games. I still go back to using my XBox controllers for some games, for example, I received Rocket League with the purchase of the Steam Controller, but I still prefer to play it with the XBox 360 controller.
Since the controller has dual touch pads, an analog stick and buttons, it can be configured to work with pretty much any game that only works with a mouse and keyboard. It works great with turn-based strategy games, isometric RPGs and point-and-click adventure games. It's not too bad with first person games, but it's still not as good as a mouse and keyboard in a FPS.
When I got my controller, you had to be using the beta Steam client. I don't know if this is still required, but I'm still using the beta client and it frequently gets new Steam controller features which eventually make it to the stable Steam client build. This is both a good thing and a bad thing. It's good tat they are constantly adding new features, but it's also a bad thing because they sometimes change or remove features that you liked.
At first you had to use Steam's Big Picture mode to configure the controller, but once setup you could play the game from the normal Steam client, although some advanced features of the Steam controller required you to use Big Picture mode. They have since made it configurable outside of Big Picture.
You can play non-Steam games with the controller if you set them up to launch through Steam and configure the controller to use it. In the
they added a feature that would let the Steam controller work with non-Steam games even when launched from outside of the Steam client, if you had set the controller up and weren't using any of the advanced features that required the overlay. This was great because one of the games I was currently playing was a non-Steam game and the Big Picture overlay caused problems with the game. This feature was short lived though because in a February update, that feature was broken and hasn't been fixed yet.
There is now a setting to disable this.
Pressing the Steam button on the controller is supposed to launch Steam Big Picture. This feature keeps getting broken and fixed every other update, but for the past few updates it has remained broken. You can see this bug and the bugs with the overlay I mentioned above in the following videos:
I don't hate the Big Picture overlay, but I don't like it either. It's designed to be used with a controller, and it works OK if you're gaming in your living room and only playing with a controller, as I sometimes do, but it is not very mouse and keyboard friendly and is still very, buggy, unstable and crashes often. It also just flat out doesn't work with some games. The Steam controller only works like a traditional controller in the Big Picture overlay also, so you can't use the mouse functions (this is a planned feature though).
Even though I sometimes use the Steam controller to play games on my TV in the living room where the Big Picture overlay works OK, I still like to use the Steam controller with certain games on my desktop. It's nice to sit back in my chair and relax while playing some games instead of hunched over a keyboard and mouse. When gaming at my desktop, I want to have the normal Steam overlay, not the Big Picture overlay, because the Big Picture overlay is very awkward to use with a keyboard and mouse.
The main reason I can not recommend the Steam controller at this time is the unpredictable state of the Steam client updates changing and breaking features of the controller. The controller itself is fine, but this constant breaking of features in the Steam client has turned me off from using it lately, and it has mostly been sitting on the desk collecting dust. I was happily using the controller until that February update, but since then I have not been able to use it for a few games I was playing. I have posted bug reports in the proper forums, and a lot of people replied confirming them, but they have yet to be fixed.
Overall, I like the controller itself, but it seems like Steam is mainly focused on Big Picture mode since updates have broken features outside of Big Picture and ignored bugs present in the regular Steam client. I never would have gotten a Steam controller if I didn't hurt my arm, and knowing what I know now, if my arm weren't hurt, I probably wouldn't get one. I still go to the XBox 360 controller for any game that has native controller support and I'd rather play FPS/TPS games with the keyboard and mouse. Now that I have it, I will continue to use it because like I said, even when gaming at my desktop, it is nice to relax back in my chair instead of hunched over a keyboard and mouse while playing games.
I hope these bugs get fixed eventually and I can then update this review to recommended. Until then, my advice is to wait for the Steam client to be more stable before buying a Steam controller.

Got the SC in a bundle with a game so didn't pay the full price but still don't think it's worth it.
The idea of replacing the right analog stick with a touchpad-like thingy is intriguing. However it is also highly annoying, because for it to provide any kind of accuracy it had to be made very large. That in turn makes it hard to miss even if you aren't aiming for it. On the other hand the abxy buttons are positively tiny and there is hardly any room between the buttons and the pad. A large part of my frustration with the device are scenarios where I was making an upward motion on the pad and wanted to hit a specific button right after. Half the time I miss the button and hit the wrong one. Two thirds of the time I inadvertently touch the lower edge of the pad, which either throws my aim off or spins the camera. That is one in six tries that the controller does not arbitrarily kill me, not a good ratio.
The only reason  the left pad is so huge is aesthetics and symmetry of the device otherwise a smaller, more precise variant would have been preferred.
How do you actually hold the thingy while gaming?
I started out with a Ps3 controller. They fit my hands very well and at first glance the symmetry is appealing. However most games are played primarily with left analog and right buttons and suddenly the symmetry backfires: left thumb angles down, right thumb angles up.
Since Ps3 controllers and PC games don't combine too well, I got a Xbox360 controller. It felt weirdly shaped at first but after playing a lot with it, I dare call it the better ergonomically shaped model. At first the asymmetrical layout bothered me but it is actually brilliant: left analog and right buttons are both reachable in a relaxed up position.
Now back the Steam Controller: it takes the worst of both worlds and makes it worse. Left analog and buttons are low, sure. However they are very low. And I keep having problems when switching from touchpad to buttons.
If you do not have a controller at all, this might be the bees kees for you. If you haven't been living under a rock labeled WASD-AND-MOUSE-OR-DEATH for the last 10 years (aka you already own another controller), don't switch.
Regardless if the device is good or bad, it is alien and doesn't have enough of a market to make developer's stick a optimized-for-steamcontroller-in-favor-of-classic-controllers on their games. At best this is the BetaMax of controllers. Even if technically superior (and I dispute that) it will go the path of the dodo due to market shares

Having played the original BrainBread mod a long time ago, I was excited to play this. Unfortunately, it's just not very fun.
The enemies are very weak and don't do much.
Most of the enemies are walkers, which walk slowly. Unlike in left 4 dead 2, they don't seem to target players very often. Instead they wander the area they spawn in, only attacking players that wander too close. And unlike in Killing Floor, they don't spawn in numbers large enough to overwelm a group of players, or even a single player. Most of the time I can just walk away without worrying about walkling into another group of them.
The bandits are mostly the same. The only difference is that they have guns, which make them slightly more dangerous. But they can't shoot a moving target. Literally. Just strafe left and right and they won't even try to shoot you.
The runners are better, but they only seem to show up in the wave attacking game mode. They target players and run towards them. If there are many players moving around, they can get confused, and run around unsure of who to attack.
In most maps, there friendly NPCs who stand in one place and shoot enemies. They mostly stand at spawn points, which is nice. I feel they are overused, because they pretty much stop any enemy from getting near you, until the finale, when they only kill some of the zombies.
Playing as a zombie is also very unsatisfying. This seems intentional, because playing as a zombie seems like a punishment for dying. Instead of waiting for a respawn timer, you run towards the humans and die. It's very hard to get skill points as a zombie because you die so quickly, you don't get points for levelling up, and your skill points don't transfer across servers or rounds.
As far as free games go this is pretty good. Overall though, it was enough to keep me occupied for a couple of hours, but I don't think I'll be playing this again.

Fun, simplified tank combat.  Visuals are pretty nice, wish the game were optimized a bit better though. Feels like it takes more to run this at a reasonable framerate than the game is really pushing out. Controls might confuse you a bit at first since reversing actually inverts your controls. The PC version of this game is quite frustrating. It's a straight-forward, fun game - undeniably. But, it's ported from an app and it suffers as such. It requires far higher computing resources than such a lightweight program should ever demand. Framerates should be through the roof on even the most modest equipment but that's not the case. And, there are precious few settings options to help improve performance or control. Video options are limited to only resolution and low/medium/high graphics quality.
The worst are the controls. Standard keyboard left/right/forward/back (A/D/W/S) with mouse turret are offered and that is IT. You cannot customize a single key. Worse, however, is that the control's don't remain consistent. While moving forward, left and right work normally. But, if you come to a stop, they reverse. Left turns right and right turns left. This is because it changes lateral behavior when you go into reverse and it does this as soon as you come to a stop. Add to this that the tank model is very cartoonish and at times it's difficult to tell the front end from the back in the heat of battle, causing mismovement, distraction from any engagement and, ultimately, frustration. Lastly, while you're focused on aiming at the enemy and battling with the controls, don't run into a wall or a building or a tree too fast because you will flip your tank over and explode. Seriously.
Now, despite all of that, I still have to say that this is one damn fun game and it's simplicity helps it shine. It just seems that with a very small amount of additional work it could be top-notch. The tank mechanics are good, the graphics look good, play action is really fun but it can be a very frustrating experience.

This game was a suprisingly fun multiplayer experience.
I'd like to begin by saying I did not like the singleplayer experience. Its just deathmatches , same options as multiplayer, but against computers.  Computers have pretty much perfect aim so, it isn't fun or exciting.  it's just a constant uphill battle.
The multiplayer is very smooth. Best played in teams (I played a lot of 3 Vs 3, but I believe there are 4 v 4 and 2 v 2  options). The gameplay is well balanced.  After each round the winning team gets money (and maybe the losing team gets some mooney but not much). The first 5 seconnds of the round is a buying period where you can buy a gun. The more powerful guns are more expensive, adding some progression.  But after you win a round or two you can pretty much buy any gun.
It isn't unbalanced though, powerful guns take much longer to reload, so with a weaker gun you are forced to land shot after shot, but can miss some.  With a big guun you're practically a sniper / mid-range, trying to fire off one big shot then retreat for cover while you reload. With this dynamic, I found teams where one or two players chose weaker faster guns, moved upward and then one powerhouse supported from a distance. This tactic is even better because, in this game you cannot see your opponents unless they are somewhat in view. So despite the camera being up high, a tank can still hide behind a wall, so long as it hasnt been seen by you or your teamates recently. On top of that, there is a fog-of-war effect to ensure you can't see what the other team is doing all the way across the map. Even better, just bum-rushing the enemy and spamming shots is not effective. So you really have to take cover, peak when you feel safe, and flank with teamates. Constantly moving and firing with weaker guns, or positioning and providing support with bigger ones. You can even hide in bushes, or behind walls (some of which are destructable).  I found my evening with the game suprisingly fun, and a smooth expereince. It's worth noting despite it being a sort of third-person camera, you cannot aim up and  down.  Only side to side (with right click being a sort of zoom / shallower camera angle).  This means there is no elevation in the game, but I think that works in this game's favor.  iit's a simpler game, and just generally a fun time, reflexes are not tested here.

Even on 1v1 in "Normal" mode, the computer AI is very good and knows where you are straight away, which does make it somewhat frustrating (and not in a funny or a good way), and then reduces the dynamic to a battle of "who can fire faster and has a better gun".  The element of surprise or hiding seemed to be completely lost, it was like the AI had X-Ray vision and was able to find ridiculous angles through the holes in the covering walls every time.
Versus a human player, I would expect very different results and a more balanced match.
Some information on what the controls are would have been nice, maybe a tutorial as to how to aim the gun (red crosshair vs green crosshair ?!), distance to fire vs damage and reload speed etc. and how gun dynamics can affect a battle (as per my point above...a gun with a slower reload that does more damage can be offset versus a smaller gun that reloads faster, meaning that 'anyone can win' if they are skilful enough, it doesn't degenerate into a one sided match versus the AI).  Also, basic information on whether or not 'real life' applies, as in, a tank's armour is traditionally less at the rear, so does that apply here ?  Like Kelly's Heroes..."If you're gonna shoot a Tiger Tank, aim at it's @55"
Good concept, but it needs some work on it, I'd like to see some refinement / add ons, e.g. a faster tank or ways to increase speed, different camera angles (first person etc.).  I'm going to try it again versus as many PC opponents as I can, hopefully I might even have some bots to help me on my side if I do that.

As someone who thoroughly enjoyed and completed the original Deus Ex back in 2000, this one was definitely a must. I had bought the first release of Deus Ex: HR (DEHR) and the DLC, but didn't have the time to play it. When they released the Director's Cut which contained the DLC, improvements and fixes, I upgraded and am finally playing this.
It's an absolutely superb game. It's one of those rare occasions, where they did the original game justice, didn't dumb it down, but rather improved on the gameplay and graphics given the 13 years or so in between. The story is intriguing, and it is definitely one of those games that will suck you in and will keep things interesting. For instance, I absolutely do not mind revisiting a location, or combing every inch just to not miss a particular gadget, credit chip or other goodies. There are also a ton of different paths and even if the game tells you this, I will reiterate it again at this point: Think out of the box! The most direct path rarely works best. Not because you can't use it, but because it is usually the most difficult way.
An all-out assault will only do one thing: Antagonize entire factions and make you literally hide at every turn. It is far more fun to use the stealth approach and leave a location without so much as having raised any suspicion. You will also get the opportunity to augment your character with all kinds of bio-synthetic technology. Word of advice: Improving the hacking and cloaking abilities will make your life a lot easier throughout the game!
DEHR perfectly combines RPG and FPS elements, requires you to think while solving certain (security) puzzles, and there are choices to make that can affect the outcome of a situation and/or the potential reward. And, again, do look around. If you cannot get past a hack, somewhere there will be a PDA containing the code.
A brief note also on performance issues; I had them, too. It's not so much a frame rate drop, than a stutter, as if your computer is trying to load more data. Since there are no texture pop-ins, it's not a performance issue as such though. There are guides with a number of registry fixes which seem to have worked for some people, but not for me. My solution was to run the game at my monitor's native resolution. I found by chance that the game was auto set to 1920x1080 which is fine, except my screen's native resolution is 2048x1152. Once set to that, even on all settings maxed out, no more stuttering.
So, in conclusion, even if you do not know the original Deus Ex (I would strongly recommend you play it just for the sake of having played one of the best games of all time, despite the somewhat dated looks), this game is worth it. You are given a mission, how you approach it, is your call. If you want to go in with weapons blazing (providing your have the ammo for it), do so, if you want to go stealth, do that. Combine both approaches, sure. Trust me, it's going to be a great and memorable journey.
For me, personally, it sits right up there with the likes of Mass Effect and Splinter Cell. Truly epic.

STEAM CONTROLLER - FORMER CONSOLE GUY, MIGRATED TO PC
As stated, I was a console gamer for years before ascending to PC gaming. As such, the controller has always been more comfortable for me. I can objectively recognize that keyboard and mouse are more accurate, and even that people nail games like Super Meat Boy (which I feel like was DESIGNED for controller) with a keyboard, which I can't even fathom. But that being said, I just like to game on the couch, and having a controller makes every game more enjoyable for me.
From that perspective then, the Steam controller is phenomenal. It is also really, really ♥♥♥♥ing weird to get used to. I'd say that I'm at about 40% of the accuracy I would expect to be at this point, but that is only one week in. I'm actually amazed at how comfortable it has become.
It also has an absolutely asinine number of inputs. Aside from the two touch pads that can function as press buttons, touch sensitive buttons, mouse pad, trackball, or analog joystick, they each press in, there are the traditional triggers, but they can be set to partial or full trigger as separate commands, and the back paddles. You could program anything into this if you had the inclination. I personally do not. But that's ok! Because you have access to other people's profiles that have already been tweaked, and can edit them further if you wish. I do this a lot.
But where this piece of hardware really shines to me is games with no controller support. I can make them work ANYWAY. Like, for example, Shadowrun Returns. Primarily mouse based. Having a controller has infinitely improved this game for me. because I just prefer them, damnit. But seriously, like half my library just became available to me on controller, and its dope.
Tangential side benefits: I use my steam controller when on my couch to navigate my computer using my tv as a monitor. I still suck at typing with it, but it's getting better. Also, the battery life is pretty damn impressive, especially since it will be paired with my own rechargeables. And the build quality is really, really high, I'm amazed for their first piece of hardware.
I will continue to update this post as I get better and better with the Steam controller.

Nier: Automata is great in just about every catagory I can think of.
Playtime: 9/10: While I did many sidequests, I still got 37 hrs of playtime before reaching the true ending.
Graphics: 8.5/10: Nothing to complain about, and the world is large so there's a lot for the game to process already.
Plot/Worldbuilding: 10/10: World is very interesting. Development is very interesting. One of the only games that can have me play for 37 hours and still wonder if I'm doing the right thing. Well developed themes that make the player think.
Music: 9.5/10: Great althroughout. Catches your attention but somehow doesn't get annoying after 37 hrs.
Difficulty: 8/10: Subjective for me, but I like games that are not too challenging, but give you a run for your money when s*** gets thrown down. Nier was more challenging during the beginning, but once I leveled and played my stats out right, I was basically unkillable. I died once in 37 hrs and it was due to a stupid environmental hazard.
All in all, Nier: Automata is an incredible and well rounded game that I would highly recommend to pretty much anyone. The only people I would not recommend Nier: Automata to are people that are looking exclusively for challenging/competitive gameplay.

Huge disappointment.  I didn't do "research" before buying, but I expected a FUN fighting game like Bayonetta, Revengeance, or God of War.  The combat was boring.  The quests were boring.  Think of the most dull MMO you've ever played: menial tasks, pointless runnign back and forth, picking up thousands of items off the ground, grinding for crafting materials, crafting upgrades, fighting the same enemies over and over.  Thats this game, but single player.  I'm telling you it is tedious.
But I also expected a GREAT story.  People say things like: changed my life; emotional roller coaster; greatest story ever; what a twist!  So I trudged on so I could experience what a great story this video game would tell.
20 hours in, I "finished" the game and got to the credits.  The credits (and internet) urged me to keep playing.  It will get better, they said.  So I did.  I played a 2nd time as a different character.  I thought combat with the first character was pretty bad, this 2nd one is even worse!  Do you like playing Space Invaders?  Because that's the hacking game that you will have to master to finish the game.  "Keep going" they said-- the 2nd playthrough is the weakest part.
OK.  Fine.  I have a thing about finishing what I started.  So its now my 3rd playthrough.  I'd have never played this game twice, but people were raving about the story and how the game isn't finished untill you get the 5th ending...  So I race through the game, replaying all the worst parts, skipping the awful menial sidequests and trudging over and over and over the same territories.  I will say, I didn't care about the characters, the stories, or the endings. This game was flat out wasting my time.  Anyways, I get to the end, and none of those life changing emotional revelations happened.  I guess you have to be into Japanese philosophy or something to appreciate the story.
Long story short: this game is a huge slog to get through.  Not fun.  Bad gaming.  Possibly an interesting story if you can put up with some pretentious story telling.

I am using a computer that meets the MINIMUM requirement for GPU, that is it. Everything else is under what they said is required. However I can still run the game on lowest settings and get a good framerate. Since I care more about gameplay than graphics, this is fine with me.
