What sets this apart from other multiplayer co-op first person shooters? A strong emphasis on realism and historical accuracy.
The closest comparison to this game might be Enemy Territory: Quake Wars, but Team Fortress and Counterstrike are in the same genre. Basically you've got two teams and you've got to attack/defend various objectives within a time limit. But those other games are far more forgiving; if you get shot you can just use a medkit, if you get a baddie in your crosshairs just pull the trigger.
Well, in Red Orchestra there are no crosshairs for most guns, and there is no health regeneration. If you get shot even once you're probably dead. Expect to die a lot in this game. Fortunately the respawn times are short!
Other realistic aspects include significant recoil and reload times for most guns. In Team Fortress you'll be spraying bullets everywhere without worrying about aiming or ammo. In Red Orchestra you've got to make every bullet count, because there's no auto-aim and ammo is limited. Even if you end up with a machine gun you'll get much better results firing short controlled bursts rather than spraying bullets everywhere. Realists rejoice!
There's a large number of maps to choose from, all of which are based on or at least inspired by real World War 2 battles between the Germans and Soviets. A great amount of work went into making sure the uniforms and equipment were historically accurate, and even that the interiors of the tanks looked realistic.
TANKS! Yes, there's more tanks than you can shake a stick at in this game. Tanks are very hard to destroy and can easily mow down waves of attacking infantry, but they are not invincible. On many maps the gameplay will involve trying to destroy the other team's tanks, or getting your own tanks to the objective.
Tank armor is strongest in front, weaker on the sides, and weakest in the rear. So a lot of tank battles involve trying to sneak up on enemy tanks from the sides or rear. It helps that tank crews have a restricted field of view, so it's easier than you might think to ambush them!
There are some other vehicles too but they are mostly transports with a secondary anti-infantry role.
The realism may put off some players. As a WW2 history buff I know that a Tiger tank is much better than a Panzer III tank, but a casual gamer offered the choice of getting into one tank or another couldn't be expected to know that. The fact that there are so many tanks and they mostly look alike compounds the problem, although it is realistic.
Did I mention this game is complicated? There's a key to fix a bayonet to your rifle, a key to change the barrel of your machine gun if it overheats, a key to pop open the hatch of your tank to get a better field of view...need I go on? Expect a steep learning curve.
My main complaint is that teams can become unbalanced rather easily. A game with 8 players vs 6 will see the smaller team struggling to survive. I guess I got spoiled by the auto team-balancing mechanic of ET:QW and TF; I just always assumed a game in this genre would have it. On some servers bots can be substituted for people to balance teams, but bots are a bit of a wild card. They can be awesome marksmen as infantry, but they're hopeless when driving any kind of vehicle.
There is no single player component. The soundtrack is appropriate and non-intrusive. I got this game practically for free in a sale; buy it if it's $5 or less.
If you're a World War 2 history buff or you liked Enemy Territory: Quake Wars then you'll like Red Orchestra.

So let me break it down. World of guns: Gun Disassembly is a unique 'game' if I've ever seen one.
You start off with a classic Kalashnikova and work your way up to a colt, not much of a spoiler there. but yeah.
The game is all about unlocking things; Field strip your gun to unlock dissasembly, dissasembly your gun to unlock reassembly... Assemble to operation, operation to game, game to super game and super game to hardcore game. You can geuss what the first three are; Operation is using the various features on a gun, changing handgrips, firing it, attaching a silencer or even folding a stock. The games however are a test to see your memory of how to put a gun together, you get bonus points and kudos if you manage to do it without touching the wrong part or taking a hint. On super game and up its instant failure to touch the wrong part and there is no hints.
You might be thinking "okay thats easy" well... I've spent a bit of time getting raged at a gun for getting one peice wrong or forgetting what came first. A few times the game screws you over by saying "YOU NEED TO DO THIS FIRST" even though there are other points where you do the same thing and the game lets you.
Example: You need to attach two rods to a plate and put the springs back on. One gun lets you put a rod and then the string on before having to deal with the second rod. But this particular gun needs both to be on.
Its a bit annoying when some guns let you do it and doing it for real lets you do it.
On the graphics end of it. The outside of the gun, looks awesome. 10/10 texturing. On the inside though... many parts have 'brush' texturing. This means that they are all are very basic tons of grey and black. Honestly they're just shaped blocks at that point, a mere representative. No complaint unless your obbscessed with HD textures.
On the of the guns themselfves. TONS of variety. I find quite a few guns I like in their collection, however... I need to sift through alot of guns I don't cary about at all just to get to them. Sure you can buy the starter pack or the full unlock... but whats the fun of that? Well, i'll tell you: total access. Unless you got alot of time and patience, you won't get through this game without paying. Because the awarded points for working with a single gun almost never total enough to unlock a new one. Sure the points increase as you move on up... but the points needed per gun almost quadruple. So it makes playing fairly hard to do. Also you cannot earn any points through the ranges, I do not suggest unlocking them unless you really like the guns your using alot. Plus its just challenges and not free shooting; you also cannot repeat the challenges once you finish. The graphics for the range also take a plunk, going to CS 1.6 esque graphics. There is also another few ways to unlock points (two of them broken for me, reinstalling to see if it fixes it for me).
First is coming back every day. Don't laugh you get a points bonus for coming back so many days in a row; even if you only pop in the grab that bonus. But make sure you come back every day or it'll reset.
Next method is by joining the group and inviting freinds. I managed to join the group... but now it won't let me invite freinds because the button for it does not function. I have even used the other method in game and it still doesn't work. but this gives you some credits and a ton of XP to use on unlocking guns. But, I can't use it because it's broken.
Last method is the quiz (which has a high failure rate for me... figures)
Quizes test your ability to recognize the gun models, the more you get right is the more XP you get to walk away with. Get one wrong though and you lose your shot and get locked out for 2 hours.
The funniest thing about the quiz not working for me is that it will go through just fine, but it will basically not give me the button to collect my points. It will however (even though I got all the questions right) lock me out for 2 hours. Its interesting to note that is registers me as unable to take another quiz... but yet I get none of my earned points. It only occasionally gives me my points for the quiz, if not... it basically locks the game up because it doesn't give me the button. CRAZIEST THING IS... If I fail the quiz, it doesn't crash at all. I feel like they're trying to keep me from getting points... Cheeki ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
Anyways I'm reinstalling, still voting positive for this game. Even though its got a bunch of Cheeki Breeki coders.

STEAM CONTROLLER - FORMER CONSOLE GUY, MIGRATED TO PC
As stated, I was a console gamer for years before ascending to PC gaming. As such, the controller has always been more comfortable for me. I can objectively recognize that keyboard and mouse are more accurate, and even that people nail games like Super Meat Boy (which I feel like was DESIGNED for controller) with a keyboard, which I can't even fathom. But that being said, I just like to game on the couch, and having a controller makes every game more enjoyable for me.
From that perspective then, the Steam controller is phenomenal. It is also really, really ♥♥♥♥ing weird to get used to. I'd say that I'm at about 40% of the accuracy I would expect to be at this point, but that is only one week in. I'm actually amazed at how comfortable it has become.
It also has an absolutely asinine number of inputs. Aside from the two touch pads that can function as press buttons, touch sensitive buttons, mouse pad, trackball, or analog joystick, they each press in, there are the traditional triggers, but they can be set to partial or full trigger as separate commands, and the back paddles. You could program anything into this if you had the inclination. I personally do not. But that's ok! Because you have access to other people's profiles that have already been tweaked, and can edit them further if you wish. I do this a lot.
But where this piece of hardware really shines to me is games with no controller support. I can make them work ANYWAY. Like, for example, Shadowrun Returns. Primarily mouse based. Having a controller has infinitely improved this game for me. because I just prefer them, damnit. But seriously, like half my library just became available to me on controller, and its dope.
Tangential side benefits: I use my steam controller when on my couch to navigate my computer using my tv as a monitor. I still suck at typing with it, but it's getting better. Also, the battery life is pretty damn impressive, especially since it will be paired with my own rechargeables. And the build quality is really, really high, I'm amazed for their first piece of hardware.
I will continue to update this post as I get better and better with the Steam controller.

This is the way I see it:
In 1997, Interplay released Fallout, an isometric RPG built around the custom-built SPECIAL role-playing system (which was only partially derived from the GURPS system for legal reasons). This game involved a timed adventure in which the Vault Dweller would go on an epic turn-based romp through the wasteland to save his people. A year later, Interplay released Fallout 2, a game with an identical system, that utilised the features of the SPECIAL system far more efficiently, bringing more marginalised and useless skills like repair and science forward alongside major combat and persuasion skills. The plot was similar in concept, but wildly different in execution, often embracing its more absurd and comic side before dropping you into chem-reliant slums and abusive ♥♥♥♥♥houses.
Then they released Fallout Tactics and, let's face it, you're better off just playing XCOM instead. Absolutely nothing (and I repeat: ABSOLUTELY NOTHING) happened until Bethesda took over and made Fallout 3, which dropped the isometric playstyle entirely to favour a more Oblivion-esque playground of destruction, retaining nothing more than the SPECIAL system upon which the originals were built. Then New Vegas came along (by a different developer, mind you) and dethroned Fallout 3 as the best Bethesda-era Fallout, then Fallout 4 came along and... didn't dethrone anything, let's be honest.
You'll notice I used the term "Bethesda-era", and this brings me to the point I wanted to bring across. We have seen that the Fallout chronology can be divided into two epochs: the Interplay era, and the Bethesda era, with absolutely no interim or PS2-exclusive titles having existed whatsoever. You'll see that the games in these eras are completely different. There is nothing that the two have in common, save for the names and the core elements of the role-playing system on which they're built. They have wildly different gameplay mechanics, different visual styles, different combat systems, hell, even the stories are nearly completely distinct (with the possible exception of New Vegas). They're practically their own distinct franchises.
So to compare Fallout 2 to Fallout 3, or 4, or what have you, is doing both of them a severe injustice, because there's just nothing to compare. Fallout 2 is the best Interplay game, Fallout New Vegas is the best "Bethesda" game (indulge a reviewer this little circlejerk), and Fallout: Brotherhood of Steel is the best Fallout game that never existed.

So after hearing about the majesty and amazing RPG elements of Fallout 2, I decided to give it a try. Bought it in a sale, which I think most people should, since buying a 20 year old game for 10 bucks is always just... a less than economically sound idea.
Anyways, I can definitely say the controls are tragically outdated, but definitely playable and somewhat easy to pick up after an hour or two. The combat is... pretty much what you'd expect from the screenshots; you get close to an enemy, they initiate a fight, and you spend action points to move closer, run away, shoot, use items or go into your inventory.
. It should be obvious, but the gameplay in this game can be tedious,  headache inducing, and make you cry out of sheer boredom. It also has weird difficulty spikes that can bulldoze you out of nowhere, especially if you don't pay attention to your surroundings and don't prepare first. Really, I feel that it all just gets in the way of the real reason anyone still plays this game: which is the genuinely grand narrative and amount of choice the player has in the story. Got that? Great.
Now, the actual meat of the game: the story, is pretty compelling. I can't spoil much, since I feel the first playthrough is the best due to the discovery of certain quests, but if you feel at home playing a isometric CRPGs, then it should be satisfying enough going through the game, solving puzzles and making actually interesting decisions. It has a fair amount of awesome lore that I'm sure most hardcore Fallout lovers will love too.
Not the best review, but in the end I think Fallout 2 a must buy for RPG lovers and people who don't mind putting some time into a game purely for the story... but only when it's on sale. Buying this at 10 bucks is just dumb.

Fallout 2 is the sequel to fallout 1 (go goddamn figure) and improves pretty well on almost all fronts. The game features the same dark humor as the previous one though it seems to be more on the fore front than before.

***Attention***: From what I've read on the Steam Community, a lot of people have been having trouble running this game on computers with Windows 7 or later. Fortunately this game is listed at the price of $4.99, so if you want to take a chance with it the price isn't that steep. For me, this game is running on my computer (which has Windows 10) with very few problems.
SHORT REVIEW:
Pros:
This is a game that I've had a lot of fun with over the years playing both the retail version back in the day and the Steam version now. It has a decent amount of content, including an excellent "Battle For Europe" risk-style game mode. The tactical battles can become very involved and get very exciting, especially when you avoid pausing to give orders and let it all play out. It is really enjoyable to create battle formations on the fly while you are under pressure from the enemy. The game simulates basic Napoleonic warfare pretty well, and the AI is competent and can challenge you in almost every battle you fight it in. The game's graphics are really bright and look good, and the music is decent.
Cons:
Some people are having serious trouble running this game on their Windows 7 or later computers. I have been fortunate enough that it has worked for me. The gameplay has typical old-fashioned RTS problems, like unit clustering and awkward base building due to size of buildings and map terrain. Also, lack of unit collision for allied units leads to awkward situations, and the fact that units block the line of fire for other units in their army can be frustrating when they start clustering together.
Rating:
7/10
FULL REVIEW:
I will admit that this game is a little dated, but that hasn't stopped me from having fun playing it. This game is an RTS set in the
Napoleonic Wars era, featuring 9 factions: France, Britain, Spain, Austria, Prussia, Confederacy of the Rhine, Poland, Russia, and Egypt. The game has three game modes: Campaign, Skirmish, and Battle For Europe. The campaigns include one for France, Rhine, Spain, and Poland. To be honest, I've never paid much attention to the campaigns. They seem like typical campaigns in an RTS game (i.e. each mission has an objective(s) and you build a base and raise armies or work with what you are given to complete the mission). Skirmish mode is where you can set up a match pitting any of the factions against each other on a premade map. Under Skirmish mode, you can also play historical battles such as Austerlitz, Borodino, and Waterloo; as well as generic battles focusing on tactics and maneuver rather than base building. Overall, it's a decent amount of content.
Battle For Europe (which I hereby abbreviate as B.F.E.), in which I've spent probably 95% or more of my time playing (back in the day and now). In this mode, you play on a sort of risk-style board as one of the nine factions. This mode is a free-for-all, and the goal is to eliminate every other faction from the game. You can can declare war and make peace with whomever you want, and you can negotiate an alliance or non-aggression pact (which are both temporary) to prevent declarations of war and possibly team up on someone (beware though, as the computers can form alliances to bring you down too). The game is driven in a turn-based format. You have a single army consisting of platoons of any combination of your choice (with restrictions on the number of the same type of units). You can move this army across the board at a pace of one space per turn (unless a random event happens).
When entering a hostile territory, it initiates a real-time battle that pre-deploys all of the units in your army and the enemy's army on a specially designed map for that territory. Gameplay in these real-time battles is essentially the same as in the campaign/skirmish battles (with the notable exclusion of base building in B.F.E. battles), which is why I've waited until now to explain how they work. On the battle map, your units are divided into platoons of infantry and cavalry, as well as single artillery guns. You can move the infantry and cavalry in different formations that fit the tactical situation. Essentially they can be described as offensive, defensive, and travelling formations. The artillery simply move, get in position, and fire. Tactics on the battle maps generally revolve around capturing/holding towns which provide resources. I find that there is always something to do, with very little downtime. When you encounter the enemy on the battlefield, this is when the most fun of all begins. You will find yourself scrambling to position your troops in the best ways possible while taking into consideration terrain, chokepoints, angles of attack and defense, formations, reinforcements, strength of your troops and the enemy troops, and so on.....ALL AT THE SAME TIME. Yes, you can pause the game and give orders, but I find it much more exciting to resist the temptation to do so and to let it all play out uninterrupted. And when the battles feature approximately 15-20 platoons per side, it starts getting really intense. Managing to create well planned and executed formations and tactics on the fly really creates a sense of achievement at the end of a battle.
The AI does a decent job with its tactics and formations as well, and understands and executes basic maneuvers rather well overall. It is also great at micromanaging and can attack you effectively on multiple fronts all at once. The game also simulates Napoleonic Wars era combat pretty well at a basic level, allowing you to order your troops to fire by line or as a whole formation; having different ranges of effectiveness for firing; ordering bayonet and cavalry charges; and the feature that morale is what mainly makes or breaks the unity of a formation, rather than trying to kill every last enemy soldier.
When the battle is over, you return to the B.F.E. strategic map and the results of the battle are applied to the map, armies affected, and resources gained/used. This process is continued until all factions are eliminated from the game. Overall, I enjoy the Battle For Europe mode the most and I recommend this game mainly based on this mode as it is that good in my opinion.
The game does have some flaws though. As with many old RTS games, units in a battle often tend toward clustering together. Even though I've explained how you can set up well planned formations, when the fighting begins it more often than not devolves into a clustered and chaotic mess (which is how many real life battles go, however, so I don't personally view this as a serious flaw). It is in this clustered mess, though, that some of the goofiness of the game shows. Namely, there is no collision detection in the game engine for units in the same army, so they can walk right through each other as if they don't exist. This leads to awkward situations where platoons can stack on top of each other; and it's even more awkward when your cavalry charges straight at the enemy right through your soldiers without trampling them, which for gameplay reasons is a good thing, but it does take away a lot of realism. Also, while there is no friendly fire, units also cannot fire through allied units, meaning that you can inadvertently block your own shots and leave your troops vulnerable with empty firearms. Also, the fact that artillery consists of only single cannons means that they are often woefully ineffective, and quite frankly whether or not they are even worth the space in your army is seriously questionable. This is unfortunate because artillery was an extremely important part of Napoleonic warfare.
Overall, this is a good game that I have had a lot of fun with, and I really hope it runs properly on your computer if you do take a chance on it.

A real masterpiece, I have no idea how to write a short rewiev about this game without giving away too much information about this game. This rewiev turned out to be pretty long, but hey..I tried my best ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ . It has a really solid 98/100 score in my opinion. I'm not giving any higher scores to any games (at least now), because there has to be room for improvement for better games in the future, if there are any xD
(Everytime you'll see a 99/100 it's because I think it's as close to perfect as it can get...but I think there could be better games in the future in that category)
Let's start by saying that this game made it in my top 3 games of all time, and that's because of:
-The music:
....oh the soundtrack of this game is perfect! The way the music describes the mood of a character or the area you're in is just breathtaking. And the transition between quite music without vocals and dramatic music with vocals always happens just perfectly based on your situation. Best OST I've personally ever heard.
-> 100/100 for that, if I could give more than that, I would do it...the soundtrack is just perfect.
-The story:
Without trying to spoil anything, you are not done if you play through the game once...you can experience the story through the eyes of another character in your 2nd playthrough and the 3rd playthrough is like the end of the story. And it is really well done...even though the 2nd playthrough is just like the 1st one through the eyes of another character, it still has a lot of new things to show you. I can only say that the story has a lot of moments you simply don't expect. Sidequests also show you a lot of things about the characters and they give you a little bit of insight, so they are not so meaningless as they might seem (most of them anyway). After finishing the game it is a whole other experience to play through it again. There are so many hints towards the feelings of characters that you simply don't realize...and it's amazing how much the developers thought about that.
-> 99/100 best story I've seen in a video game so far, really well structured but you might miss some story elements if you rush through the main story, so be aware of that
-The gameplay:
It's mostly a "hack and slash game" with you playing as 2B or other characters most of the time. But this hack and slash element of the game is sometimes in normal 3rd, sometimes in a top-down perspective, and sometimes it's a sidescroller. Even though this seem odd, it is really fun and the transitions are actually really well done. There are other gamemodes which happen a lot less frequently, like the "bullet hell ship" or the "hacking game" which are kind of similar. With both you steer a ship/arrow and you try to dodge bullets while shooting your enemies/objects or cores. Even if it seems simple and weird in a game like this, it isn't and it fits well. You mostly hack as 9S, who is specialised in that area, and you mostly fly as 2B, who is a combat model designed to fight. Both other gamemodes have their own challenge and are a lot of fun. Overall there's nothing bad in the gameplay, it's just that the game doesn't show you all mechanics. You have to find out most mechanics by yourself, which can be annoying for one person or fun for another person...I enjoyed not knowing most of the mechanics, because when I figured something out, I had a reason to be proud of myself (like figuring out the POD throwing mechanic to get to certain building which you can only reach by doing that)
-> 99/100 for me, nothing that wasn't fun, everything was enjoyable and after getting used to it it became kind of automatic and intuitive
-Difficulty and enemies:
Well... this is MY opinion, everybody has a different opinion on difficulty.  I think normal is way too easy...while hard is too hard. I'm talking about the tutorial right here, because certain moves are one-hit kills in hard while you only lose 20-30% HP on normal against that same attack. And also the tutorial should be the best place to get used to a difficulty setting, but in this game it gets easier from here on out...like a lot easier. But I think it can get really challenging if you don't do sidequest or don't kill every enemy on your way to a quest. Because being underleveled is the worst thing that can happen in this game. You always want to be at least on the same level as your opponents. If you are more than 10 levels lower than an enemy most attacks are one-hit kills in hard mode
-> 90/100 there really is no perfect difficulty setting for me in this game..it should be like the hard difficulty, but easier in the tutorial and harder in the rest of the game, the difficulty curve is not that well done in my opinion, there is room for improvement
-The atmosphere and overall design:
Although the pure graphics may not be on the very top of todays standards, the atmosphere of the game is astonishing. Without trying to spoil anything right here...the way you return to certain areas after a quest is done is really really well done. The areas are changing and you do experience the change a lot when you return. You get to know the areas and you get to know everything first hand, but after the area changes there is so much more to explore. While some might call the returning to the changed area bad level or game design, I call it genius. Also the different areas have a unique feel to them that no other area has. Overall the areas all have different OSTs that all give a unique impression
-> 95/100 because the world is overall very good, but the desert might feel too empty, and the forest might seem unimportant, because you're almost never there
-The characters:
Not saying anything in particular here, because of spoilers. You might think a certain way about a character during playthrough 1, but after the last playthrough most of what you think IS most likely going to change, because that is when most of the background is going to be revealed. Every character has a "thing" that drives them to do "things" (best statement ever) and it is really well structured
-> 99/100 you can emphazise with all of the character really well, there are unique characters, weird characters, funny characters and many more
All just fits together so well in a package and it is my favorite game of 2017. I am glad that Platinum Games released this game and I hope to see more video game gems of them in the future!

One of the strangest and most satisfying games I have every played. Nier: Automata plays on your expectations in the first twenty minutes, and never seems to let up on the new ideas that it presents the player. The gameplay consists of a hack and slash, (in similar vein to other Platinum games), hacking, bullet hell, and so much more. I never thought that all of these different types of gameplay would mesh together into a cohesive hole, but they do wonderfully. Soundtrack also deserves a mention, as it is one of the best soundtracks I have ever had the pleasure of listening to in a video game, ever.
(Mild spoilers from this point on, read at your own risk, no major spoilers)

I love the first two dead rising games but held off on playing this one because of various reasons. Now that I have time to try it, I'm pleasantly surprised. It does a lot of things different. It's more weighty, like every swing and movement has a realistic delay to it. Once you get used to it though, I found this game to be much more immersive than the previous ones. It gives you that desperate feeling of trying to avoid zombies, running through the streets looking for supplies. Wherever it can though, it doesn't sacrifice fun for realism.
It's less colorful than its predecessors, but its got character. It controls better and you have a good dodge move from the get-go. Boss battles still come down to trading blows, and running away to eat food for health. Some gamers might not like that, and wonder why bosses survive an assault rifle to the head.
All in all, its a unique sandbox zombie game and I wholly recommend it. I have not experienced any technical difficulties, and a youtube video shows you how to unlock the framerate.

A fantastic Free 2 Play title that helps to gain insight in guns.
The GUI is minimal, the models are really accurate and the textures are well made (except for some matte-black internal part).
You can also operate the guns to see what happens when you pull the trigger (and whan you flip the selector/safety, when you remove the magazine and so on), thanks to the X-Ray view and to the cutoff view. You can also slow down the simulation up to 50 times.
Disassembling and reassembling procedures are "simple" and clean thanks to the assonometric exploded view of the disassembled parts. "Simple" is between commas because you still have to learn and remember the disassembling order.
There are hints (in case of you really can't see that tiny pivot holding up the entire safety lever), but don't rely on it too much if you want to achieve a good score.
By completing tasks related to a model, you earn XP that you can spend to unlock further models. There's also a Quiz feature, where you get to recognize the gun by its silhouette.
You can also try out some gun in shooting ranges, but I think they don't worth the cost.
You can buy the sport cars pack or even the skeleton model pack. You can also buy the whole pack of models (98 models!!) for 36€, but hey, where's the challenge if you already unlock everyting by the start?
If you know guns you'll like this game, and if you like this game you'll start to learn something about how a gun works.
(Fun fact: I own a deactivated Desert Eagle .50AE, so I already knew how to disassemble it. Guess what, I got the best daily score with that gun. I already knew what to do, and the big work was only about clicking faster and faster.)

Aura Kingdom is a majestic new MMORPG published by Aeria Games. From the developers of popular fan-favorite MMOs like Eden Eternal and Grand Fantasia, Aura Kingdom uses state of the art graphics and a detailed anime art style to depict a sprawling fantasy world for players to journey through. Guiding a hero from humble beginnings, players will soon discover a menagerie of loyal companions that will prove to be invaluable in their journey. With up to 14 classes to choose from i'm sure that playing Aura Kingdom for the first time you will find you time enjoyable.
Guilds in Aura Kingdom make the community come together and fight at the same time; a guild is a sort of team of users that will stick together to help on quests, PvP battles or Monsters. Guilds can be really handy for newer and less experienced plays to get a helping hand from higher level users whether it be on a simple tast or crinding to get a stable level.
Crafting in Aura Kindom can make a big difference between you being a strong player or an overpowered user with max equipment and armor. Crafting makes the smallest and weakest items stat balanced, easy to use and all around higher quality. There is not much more to say other than without crafting everyone would be roughfly the same in stats, the game has thousands of options for different enchantments, stat boosts and options for you to make your own unique custom layout.
Fishing in Aura Kingdom can provide a stress relief mini-game that users can play whilst on a break from defeating, conquering and exploring. Fishing can be tough at times though; with up to 70+ fish types a user can catch you can be sitting there for hours waiting for the next bit, all fish have different catch difficulties, rarities and skins. Fish you have caught can be sold on the market to buy yourself some new armor, weapons and or some new fishing gear.
In the hands of a Guardian, armor and a shield are as much a weapon as a sword. These steel-clad strategists can withstand the mightiest of blows, keeping enemies busy while their team goes all-out.
Duelists shine brightest when launching an offensive against strong single foes. Their defense lies in their acrobatic evasion, and their ability to quickly unload a flurry of high damage makes them a powerful force.
Ravagers are known for their take-no-prisoners philosophy. They swing their gigantic axes in arcs so broad, and with impacts so powerful, that many of their strikes damage not only the target but surrounding foes as well.
Brawlers live for the thrill of close-range combat, their blades turning their arms into deadly weapons. With superhuman reactivity, they pile on heavy combos to lock down enemies. Darting and weaving in and out of the fight, Brawlers will carve up any foe who can't keep up blow for blow.
A Ronin uses blade skills and observation to destroy enemies in a flash by striking their weaknesses. The unique skill of the Ronin drains the souls of enemies and collects them in the blade. Souls stored in the Tachi can be released in battle, destroying all that stands in their way.
Those who hold the Holy Sword should have strong convictions and a brave heart, and be able to show righteousness through sword fighting. They can transform their faith into Divine Energy in battle, and use the Holy Sword to punish all evil hindering their beliefs.
Attuned to the forces of nature, Wizards focus power in their elaborate staves to call upon elemental magics, often damaging several foes at once. Their access to a broad range of elements allows them to capitalize on enemies weaknesses.
Sorcerers draw their shadowy magics from ancient tomes and grimoires. Calling forth the spectral power sleeping within each page, they conjure up dark spells to raze and torment foes, leaving them weakened and vulnerable.
Far from shy harpists, Bards dive into the thick of battle, making magic with their music. They can attack with potent sound waves, but can most often be found strumming rousing songs that heal or bolster their allies.
He who wields the scythe marshals unrivaled destructive power and ferocious attack speed. When the blade falls, heads will roll. He signs contract with minor devils, and summons them in battle. He is also versed in various kinds of powerful magic, which he uses to inflict heavy damage on the enemy.
A tremendous power sleeps within the Lance's mark. It is capable of harnessing the elemental powers of fire, ice, lightning, and darkness. Once awakened, these ancient powers will suppress all those who stand against the wielder.
Grenadiers are known for their trademark weapons: massive cannons that convert magical energy into missiles and plasmic discharges. Not content to simply blow foes to smithereens, they also engineer turrets and other gadgets for support in battle.
With a pistol in each hand, Gunslingers bring enemies to their knees with a hail of bullets. Lacing their shots with magic and employing fiendish traps, their battle is a high-stakes game of keep-away, with victory the likely outcome.
Warbow turn to the bow, a noble time-tested weapon as deadly as it was in ages past. With their long-range assaults, Warbow can drop many foes before they get a chance to attack. The arrows they fire are not only as damaging as any blade, but a fine vehicle for enchantments as well.
Shinobi are an ancient and mysterious group that live between the light and shadows. When good and evil are aligned, they will reappear to claim their rightful inheritance.

An excellent commentary on the school system and on the toxic social structure everyone has experienced in school. Rockstar always has been great at creating a living, breathing world for their games, and this one is no exception.

A good, solid game with a lot of charm. However, just like it's protagonist, it's rough around the edges and lacks what is needed for it to be great. When people say it's kinda like GTA in school enviroment, they're right. It's kinda like GTA. Unlike GTA, you're somewhat limited by the school system and time, because you can only do certain things at certain time, but the time flies by quickly and so does the tempo of this game. You're constantly on the move, doing a lot of smaller missions and try to fit them to your daily routine, which is not a bad thing, but a lot of missions are really primitive, especially compared to GTA. Many of them are creative, so you won't be getting bored, I just wish we perhaps had less and more fleshed out ones. You can of course slow down, doing less every day and just fart around, but it can be frustrating, knowing you have to commit truancy to finish a mission, when you want to go to class so you can get a nice upgrade (passing at least some classes is adviced, others give you crap like different clothes you'll likely never wear out of embarrasement).
Bully has a lot going for it, but it has some drawbacks, making it somewhat difficult to recommend to everyone. First off, the obvious - poor PC conversion. You will not have a good time playing this with keyboard and mouse. A gamepad is a must. Second, the controls are sometimes very loose and inprecise, plus the autoaiming system when you fight somebody is downright broken, on multiple occasions it targeted an ally, or target that was much further than the one I actually wanted to attack. Also, I really had an issue with a camera, not only it likes to fly around like crazy, but the default view is almost sitting on the ground, not like in any GTA, where it flies over your shoulder. Here, I found myself constantly battling against it.
The game has a decent lenght, but it pales compared to GTA. It's by no means short game, but I couldn't help wishing for more - spending more time with certain characters, longer missions and better main story, which is rather weak to be honest, not that it's bad, there are many great moments, but it's somewhat overshadowed by smaller and isolated encounters with weird inhabitants of Bullworth. You meet a lot of hillarious characters once or twice, and then they just fade away, or maybe you'll bump into them randomly, and that's kinda it. Not that it's dissapointing, once again, I just wish there was more, because this settings has so much potential. The main protagonist is kinda underdeveloped, he doesn't have that much character going for and sometimes does questionable things without questioning them at all, when just few seconds before he was pretty vocal about it.
With that out of the way, Bully is worth your time. For a great price, there is every school steteotype imaginable, it's all filled to the top with great humor. Dialogues are fantastic, characters are fantastic (although you spend way less time with those that are really interesting, and there is very little character development, again, probably due to the more arcady nature of the game), the atmosphere is fantastic and despite you being limited to much smaller area than San Andreas for example, it's packed with stuff to do. I've especially liked that weather changes as you go through whole year and so does appearance of everything. I don't think there are many games from school enviroment, but I'm willing to bet there aren't any that have open world and are this funny. It is a miracle that we even got this game, and even though it's flawed and lacking, it puts an evil grin on my face.
// Also, outdoor graphics are strangely muddy and blurred, there is some rather unfortunate effect applied there, and it doesn't happen indoors. Because of that, when you first start the game, you'll immediatelly feel like something is wrong, and that perhaps you have a wrong resolution. No, it's the game, either a weird design decision, or another bug.

Okay. So this review will be derived just under 2 hours of playtime. I did this because I was not sure at all if I would like it. So this review is ultimately for those people who played the three Dead Rising Titles, or in the very least one of the Dead Rising Titles. I have personally played 2, which I enjoyed, and a slight deviation of 2, Dead Rising 2: Off The Record which I mostly didn't enjoy even though I've heard it's superior. The reason I didn't enjoy it was because whilst there was a minor amount of new content, I didn't actually enjoy due to the fact I had already played the original version of 2.
Moving on to the review.
Starting with the game for the first time.
The options are fairly standard. You have resolution which on display supports up to 4096x2160.
Originally the game apparently did not support 16:10 but only supported 16:9. Based on the resolution options available. I'd say it now includes 16:10 Support as well. But I've got nothing I can say on 21:9 Support unfortnately.
Game Quality is an option which allows you to change which resolution the game renders at, which is for some reason seperate to the actual resolution. You can choose between 720p, 900p, 1080p or Full (Full being what ever resolution you set the game to. Meaning you have the option to put the resolution to 4K, but render it in 1080p..)
Level of Detail which seemingly does nothing despite it's obvious name, but to me the difference is so minute that I can't tell the difference even at 3840x2160 with Game Quality set to full.
Other than that we have a fairly standard set of options. I only bothered with the options which stood out as either being pointless, or strange.
Moving in to the gameplay.
We start out in the tutorial, finding food or drink to heal ourselves. As is the standard in Dead Rising games. Finding a weapon to break down a couple of gates. Doing some other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to complete the tutorial and moving on.
After the Tutorial of sorts you're introduced to a couple of characters - Through the cutscene which activates - whom will repeatedly pop up often through the following chapters, Characters who practically immediately make cheesy, stupid mistakes which shows you how and why to dislike them.
But it's o-♥♥♥♥ing-kay mate because two of the most annoying characters in this very first cutscene; Panic, and run in to a crown of zombies, only to be chowed on by said zombies moment later. Well that's good. Because the, now literal, dead weight has been dropped. I'm sure that'll lighten your load as a player a little more, considering one thing I had trouble enjoying from previous Dead Rising Titles was the A.I. and Survivor mechanics. Which were bloody awful, right.
Anyway. You have to escape from a diner following your arrival there during the aforemention cutscene. Making your way through some zombies towards your objective having to occasionally help the two NPC's who've been grabbed by a zombie, unfortunately smacking said NPC(s) in the face with what ever you've found on the floor. Warranting them to request you stop doing that. So if you want to avoid this. You can just ignore them and they'll get out of the grapple themselves easily enough. (Personally I refused their requests because one of the characters is an annoying whiny ♥♥♥♥♥ so I hit her at every chance I got with my 2x4).
Making your way to an SUV. You then drive to a chopshop for safety. Where you're introduced to another character, and then told to go and explore for a bit whilst Whiny ♥♥♥♥♥ McGee needs to for some reason mess with multiple wires just to get a DIGITAL TV working, not even an ANALOGUE TV, to get a signal. Like that even ♥♥♥♥ing works somehow.
The gameplay like previous Dead Risings is tank-like. There isn't a sprint but you can roll to dodge things though, Combat gives you two basic attacks with any melee weapon. Light hit, and heavy hit. You can also throw your weapon with a single button pression, or alterntively aim and throw you weapon.
Some weapons are only used for Throwing. So be aware that the basic light and heavy attack buttons will likely do nothing for you with these weapohns, but it's fairly easy to tell which are normal melee, and which are used for throwing.
You can pick up firearms around the game which are used like just about any other shooter in existence. You press the expected Aim Button, and you press the expected Shoot button, and they aim and shoot. Doesn't get any more complex, and I can't explain it in a more complex manner even if I tried. And I shouldn't need to unless you're like 12 and possibly broken.
All you do in this game, as in other Dead Rising titles. Is Kill zombies. Earn PP (XP, basically), save random survivors. Play the story, complete optional sidequests if you feel like it. And so on. Not exactly complex.
The performance.
Now for my specs: I have an Overclocked Intel i5 6600k @ 4.2GHz
Gigabyte Windforce G1 GTX 980 @ Stock Speeds
16GB of DDR4 RAM @ 2166Mhz
Game is installed on a 1TB Seagate SSHD @ 7200RPM
(Those are the important specs really)
Now to achieve what I consider a playable of framerate with those specs. It wasn't hard honestly. But my computer in total costs over £1000 even now let alone when I bought each important component which makes said computer functional at the time that I did.
So my settings are 1080p, Game Quality Full, Motion Blur Off and every other setting at absolute max. They are the highest they will go on each option. I get 60FPS just fine.
The game however is by default Capped at 30FPS. Meaning you need to make your own user.ini file and put in a specific line so as to uncap the framerate. There are multiple guides on Steam, YouTube and just the internet in general which will tell you how to uncap the framerate.
To me, this is perfectly playable. But I'm sure for some of you this might be unsatisfactory.
I don't however get a playable experience at higher than 1080p. 1440p chugs the game down to about 45 FPS, and 4K takes it down again further to 30FPS or less. Sometimes dipping as low as 5-10FPS. Not good.
Pros:
+ Kill ♥♥♥♥ing zombies. Hopefully not literally otherwise that'd be disgusting.
+ Fun with a friend in Co-Op, silly little things like wearing women's clothing and wigs, and costumes. Can really spice up the cutscenes when they're portrayed in a cheesy but serious manner.
+Loads of weapons, quite a few vehicles. Most if not all of which can be combined thanks to the many blueprints you can find.
Cons:
- Performance does reach a standard for beefy high-end computers, but just barely. Even if your computer meets the recommended specs you might still be stuck at 30FPS regardless of which settings and resolution you choose. Even with Uncapped framerate.
- Atmostphere, Gameplay, Story. All inferior in most ways compared to Dead Rising 2.

Honestly speaking, I don't have much to say regarding the third entry in the Dead Rising series, I was a huge fan of the previous titles, in fact Dead Rising 2 Off The Record is one of my personal favourite games from the seventh generation of consoles, as I put well over 50 hours into it on the Xbox 360, and Dead Rising 3 from a gameplay perspective is really just more of the same.
You can still kill zombies with a variety of different combo weapons(the flaming dragon head is a favourite of mine), the vehicles still don't handle very well but it's not like they did in previous installments either, there are still a number of crazy psychopaths to fight against throughout the story, such as vomit-spewing segway riding fat lady and a man who uses a phallus-shaped flamethrower to kill you....so it's still as over the top as always.
In the place of Frank West or Chuck Greene, you now control Nick Ramos in this game, a skilled mechanic who is somewhat cowardly but has a heart of gold. He's a decent character as Nick is probably more relatable than Frank or Chuck due to him acting much less badass but I don't feel he has as much character due to this. He's just always kind of afraid or skeptical and only shows glimpses of pride or badassery unlike Frank or Chuck who were more endearing characters in my opinion.
The visuals are pretty good considering this game is almost three years old now and the port runs very well for me almost always maintaining a solid 60 FPS on high settings. The game does lack some of the charm and colour of Fortune City from Dead Rising 2 with an overall grimier and darker look to everything, but I'd be lying if I said the game looked bad.
Before the port was updated the game did run quite poorly for me and textures took much too long to load and the frame rate was dire, but thankfully these issues have been resolved.
There is a nice wealth of content to find in this game with about 30-40 hours worth of missions and sidequests in the story itself, and another 8-10 hours of free DLC content as well, so this game offers quite a lot of bang for your buck.
Dead Rising 3 isn't my favourite entry in the series but it's still a solid game and I would recommend it to anyone looking for an open-world game with a large amount of content as Dead Rising 3 delivers on that front.
Just to save people the trouble of looking it up, to have the game running at 60 fps you need to create a text document called user.ini and open the notepad and type the following: gmpcr_unlock_frame_rate= True and then save it. The game will then be running at 60 FPS.

It's taken me some time to get used to it, but after putting in a few hours with Dead Space and Dark Souls  and modifying the controller configuration to suit my own needs, I can say that it's really hard to go back to an Xbox One controller now. The addition of the grip buttons on the back of the controller (the ones you can hit with your middle or ring fingers) makes a HUGE difference in Dark Souls, because now you can adjust the camera as you run, or heal without taking your thumbs off of the moving and camera controls.
And in Dead Space, I downloaded a controller configuration that makes it so you can do a left-trigger soft-pull to aim your weapon, and then pull a little more past the threshold for the 'click' on the left trigger to fire the weapon. It feels really weird at first, but now that I'm used to it, I can't imagine going back - having to use both triggers for aiming and firing is what seems weird to me now.
The only negative things I can say at this point are that the giant right touchpad is tough to get used to as a replacement for a right analog stick, and even after hours of play, sometimes I accidentally move the camera too much, or not enough. But I've been using dual-analog-style controllers for over a decade now, so I expect it'll just take time to adjust.

(UPDATED REVIEW FOR OB64)
Paladins has been my favorite game of the last year, and still is, and I first played it on xbox console to level 70 and then am now level 19 on PC. My total hours are over 600. It is very deep with a high skill ceiling.  I am giving a slight positive review (JUST CHANGEG TO NEGATIVE - SEE REASON AT END) for the state of the game at at ob64, but it would have been an enthusiatic review at OB63 (Open beta patch number 63).  Overall, the the choice of hero, the gameplay, the five on five matches, the in-game adds, and now to a lesser extent now because of 0b64) card loadouts allow for endless replayabilty and challange.  The game is still worth playing for free, and  most will find it prudent to spend $30 to speed up your initial progress once you get a feel for it.
THE ELEPHANT IN THE ROOM - IS IT NOW PAY TO WIN (P2W) WITH OB64?
Yes - Ob64 also introduced the fact that you can make your cards stronger with real world money. Currently this is available only for legendary cards, but the path seems clear for them to implement this for all cards. I hope they do not do that.  There is now an endless progress grind for an overhauled 'unbound' card system. So they definately did introduce p2W, but only for the unbound mode.
DO I HAVE TO PLAY THE P2W UNBOUND MODE?
However,  there are ways to completely bypass the  p2W aspects by playing a 'bound' mode where you cannot use any card upgrades. This mode is in fact used for competitive play. They also gave us at OB64 all the cards unlocked which saves tons of time that it took at OB63.  New players have all the abilities in bound competive and casual mode that experienced players do.
WHAT DISADVANTAGE DO NEW PLAYERS HAVE?
New players havent yet learned how to play the heros, and this is where the $30 purchase comes in that I recommend. Rather then grind out the gold needed to unlock all 34 heros, get the $20 founders pack so and a booster pack so you get all the heros unlocked. THe booster pack agets you extra XP and cards/gold for a few weeks to jump start your progress. That is all the money I would say you should spend.
IS THE GAME STILL CUSTOMIZABLE AND BALANCED AT OB64?
The heros are constandly being balanced through patches so dont ever think you wont play a hero just becuase he is bad today. To get all 34 would take time or gold (in game currency) though. You can be very competive with about eight unlocked. Ideally, play them all at least to level four to learn their abilities so you can counter them with your favorite hero, as well as to get the chests to champion chests to unlock the cards for your favorite heros. At OB64 Hi-Rez trashed the popular and unique idea of a custom 12 pt balanced card loadout system, and by doing so ruined a really nice aspect of making it a custom experience. All cards now have set pts assigned. The cards variously affect the power of the four abilities each hero has, as well as other things like speed, hit pts, or anti healing against opponents. This also resulted in a unbalanced mess and many heros who were good are worse, and many who were average are better. Movement playstyles are gone, but new damage ones are possible, and additional legendary cards that focus on added damage were added as an option. Basically it is a completely new game at OB64.  Overall there are horrible balance issues though right now. The good news is that in future patches these should be more easy to fix since the ability to favor cards over others has been removed by loading htem with pts has been removed. Although HI-REx completely ignored its fans by removing the 12 pt system, they do have a good history of trying to balance cards. I feel they will balance the decks in future patches. However, I do think they should have kept the 12 pt system in place and instead just made that more balanced rather then trash it altogether. Regardless of how much Hi-Rez says this is hard to do, I agree with the community that they did not listen to us and did not try hard enough to make a 12 pt system work.
IF YOU CHOOSE TO PLAY UNBOUND HOW BAD IS THE GRIND TO UPGRADE CARDS FOR FREE?
Unbound mode right now against humans is pretty much even, as most folks dont have cards with advanced pt spreads yet. This will change and it wil be chaos soon. Occasionally I see someone with an 8 or higher card but that is about every fourth match. It is basically the same as bound mode, and the vast majority of players have level 4 cards or less. If you do decide you want to play unbound 'pay to win' mode you will want to upgrade your cards though, as you will get left behind. I fear a bit for new players in a month or two and have no idea how what they will think. You can currently get cards for free in a predictableand daily grind through 4 minute almost guaranteed win of the day matches against bot players. They better keep this shortcut in place or I am definately not recommending this game, because right now the grind to level up cards is insane by playing 50/50 win percentage ~12 min games against human oppenents. At least  the daily bot matches give you the equivalient of 34*7500 gold for free for 34 unique champion chests (if you played each champion once a day), including alot of legendary card upgrades as well, which seem to have a normal drop rate.  These champion chests give you cards only for the champion you just played with, so they are not as RNG as the Radiant chests, which give you random card upgrades across all 34 champions. So although the grind is bad, and especially bad for new players, you should be able to get all cards to around level 6 (out of 10) using this tip and be competitive without too much effort if you grind against bots, especially at least if you do it for your core heros each day.
HEROS AND TEAM COMP AND IN GAME ITEMS:
There are 34 heros and each match is a five on five match. You also have to learn the pros and cons of each hero and how they both compliment your team, but also counter your opposing team. This all has to be a bit relearned at OB64 due to the balance changes. There are obvious bad and good hero picks that are situational, as well as for the map itself. You should have nowledge of which card deck you want to pick once you see the others teams compostion. You can only do this once at the start of the game. Then, during the match, as it progresses you choose to further develop your character's abilities to run faster, or take less direct damage, or regen abilities faster, etc. Through a choice of four in-game items. Turn off auto purchase but remeber to try to buy extra in game items when you die. A sure sign of a noob is someone who doesnt buy in game items or buys the wrong ones.  There is little nuance here although not as much as in Smite.
CONCLUSION
I am giving it a positive even tough ob64 hurt it alot. Based on past attempts to balance the game, I feel Hi-Rez is committed to continue to balance the heros in future patches. Although they introduced some P2W aspects it isnt that hard to get the cards if you play daily against bots, and at least by  keeping an unbound free and compitive mode non P2W mode they allow everyone to be on 100% even abilities on day one.  The optional cosmetic skins are good and the core  gameplay overall is fun. Matches often can change momentum and a team losing 1-3 comes back and wins 4-3, so never give up.  You really don't have to spend anything to have a blast and be competive. You do need to commit a lot of time to learn all the heroes and play styles though. It is more challenging and deep than you might think at first.

Masterpiece. This is my personal game of the year for 2017, and it was a STACKED year for games (seriously, you should have a nice big to play list of 2017 games if you don't already.)
This game has a generation defining OST (It won best Score at the Game Awards as well), Combat is fluid; If you have played Platiunum games before (IE Metal Gear Rising/Bayonetta/etc.) Itll feel right at home. And although its combo heavy/a beatem up, the enemies are not easy unlike games like Dynasty Warriors. There's a fair difficulty curve here. It can be an easier experience or a challenging one based on difficulty. Lots of endings to unlock (including troll ones), great characters, and although the story gets really out there in left field at times, that is a Yoko Taro trademark and gives the game charm. Its by no means a bad story; on the contrary its a very good one. Just don't be surprised if you find yourself getting confused at times. You don't need to play the original NieR to understand this game or not miss important plot points (I didn't play the original). Rather, there are a lot of homages and things like "Ohhhh so THAT'S why this background point/etc. is like that" and Easter Eggs you'll only catch if you played the original. But don't be afraid to jump in if you are new to Nier: the game does a great job of getting you right into it without losing you.
Buy it. Buy it. Buy it.
P.S. The "end" of the game isn't actually the end. You need to play through the game multiple times.

This game is a great RTS game if you like challenging but fun games set in the 18th century. You will be able to make squads of 120 troops with or without an officer, drummer or banner carrier to help with Morale and fatigue. The game has you build a town like an rts but you have to build at least 120 musketmen to have a squad. Having a squad is more effective then individual units and comes with great benifits. When you have a squad (Or lines) you can give them differant formations such as Box, collum or line. Line is the more traditional fighting style, putting your men into three rows and having either one fire at a time at your command or having them all fire. Next is collum which has your men form a collum to march in. This game has fatigue and morale, using collum and having them go on a road helps them with these. For example a squad in line thats marching takes more fatigue then a squad going in collum formation. The last is the box formation which you use if you are either surrounded or have cavalry charging. The combat is very interesting and somewhat challenging as it has you either hold formation and fire when they are close, or you move forward and fire when you are close to them. There are three ranges, green (Long), yellow (medium), and red (Close). As these are muskets, green does the least amount of damage and the least morale damage. Yellow is the second highest and red is the highest as it will go. Keep in mind that firing at the wrong time can and will infact screw you out of a squad. One good volley and your men may break. Your infantry can also "entrench" positions. This is not exactly like digging entrenchments but they are seen crouching and kind of preparing. In this form they do more melee damage if charged at, have a higher morale and can take more of a beating. Melee is used if you know you can break an enemy squad quickly, some are better then others so watch out. Treelines and forests can help/hurt your infantries accuracy, as it gives an increased chance of missing their targets. The next thing is the Artillery. Artillery features cannons and for the British, rockets. Cannons and rockets have an OK accuracy hit rate but can definatly miss completely. Cannons can use either round shot (Default) or scatter shot which can be used for up close combat or a charging enemy. Cannons when they hit deal massive damage to both troops and morale, causing them to break easy IF they hit. They are also slow to deploy so you can make a type of carrier for them to go faster, those these are somewhat weird as they may just freeze in place and not mount the cannons at all. Cavalry is great at melee and ok at range as you would've guessed. The AI is challenging...If not a little stupid. Sometimes the AI will charge you, using massive amounts of squads, some artillery and cav. But sometimes they will march straight infront of your line only to have their squad get shot and break with ease. It is a very challenging game but its very fun to play. As a newcomer to the series, I had no idea what to expect from this title, and I was certainly surprised how deep this game went in seemingly all directions. There’s so much more than what you might see as a just another shooter with stealth mechanics. There is a very open-ended spectrum to how you can play this game: from core mechanics, to how you approach the levels and scenarios, to what decisions you make along the game’s satisfyingly lengthy narrative. Will play it stealthily or with guns-blazing? Will you go under, over, around, or through your enemies? Will you take your enemies down mercifully or lethally? Will try out all these things, whenever you feel like it? With this game, you certainly can, and I chose to use variety as I played through on the game’s Hard difficulty setting. And unlike many RPG-type games, you can play with variety and not really feel penalised for it or pidgeon-holed into a certain play style.
Although I did focus mainly on the stealth and hacking route, I was never afraid to pull out the guns when things got hairy, and I never really felt the need to choose the powerups relating to guns and the brute-strength approach. At any rate, it was highly enjoyable going into each of the games encounters, figuring out what approach I wanted to take and then using the right tools for the job to execute my plan. And when things didn’t work out as planned, it’s still fun enough to weasel your way out or simply re-load and try things differently.
I would insist people try to play this game more as a stealth game where possible, as that is what makes this game stand out. Most of the weapons feel quite good, but other, more high-profile and dedicated FPS games do it better than what can be found here. So if you’re looking for a gun-toting blast, this game certainly has elements of that, but it shouldn’t be the reason why you should play this game. A second qualm I have with the game would be the sub-par graphics, which are likely by-products of game development sprawled across a variety of platforms, but as a trade-off I guess you get a lengthy game with still quite detailed environments. Lastly, there are a couple signature moves the game has which the game doesn’t really capitalises on nearly enough, or provides enough obvious and enticing opportunities to use.
At the end of the day, when it comes to this Director’s Cut, you’re left with a great package with excellent value. This sci-fi romp delivers an experience which is far greater than the sum of its parts, and it’s all tied together with strong characters and a fantastic story that isn’t afraid to ask the big questions of humanity and progress.

Okay, first of all, whoever came up with the "sniper" achievement should burn at the stake, because that achievement is absolute bull, and it only gives you 400 XP, which is only pocket change, really. Now that THAT's out of the way, let's get on with the game. The gameplay itself consists chiefly of disassembling and then reassembling guns, which is a nice way of researching guns or training yourself on how to do gun maintinence, and has some shooting range levels thrown in. It's a nice concept, but where does the actual game begin? When reviewing a Free to play game, what is arguably the most important part of it, is the business model, and this model is corrupt, and almost certainly too far gone. Now, granted, the achievements can give a major boost in XP, but later on down the line the achievement awards for each gun altogether cannot "pay for themselves", let alone turn a profit like they should be. Fiddling around with gun internals is nice and all, but even still, the amount of grinding you have to do is very, VERY evident of an obviously corrupt business model, it's basically the same concept as waiting 6 hours for a new floor to be added to your skyscraper, but with THIS one you actually have to put in the work to do it. Alternatively, you can put down some money for credits and bypass the grind, but I strongly reccomend that you don't pay a cent and leave now, chiefly because the money would be going into the hands of the sick and twisted developers of this game, who deserve to be starved out of cash. Overall, if you are obsessed with guns and can therefore justify throwing yourself at the grind or selling out for credits, then you probably can find a decent experience in this game.
This game also has an "elite club" feature that requires you to invite 5 friends to the game, which, being the equivalent of a ponzi scheme, is just the developer's way of using you as a tool to rake in more hosts to suck blood(money) from. If you do play this game, I ask you don't pay the developers anything, AT ALL. They're not worth your money and they certainly don't deserve it.

AdVenture Capitalist is an idle game in which you buy different investments and hire managers to keep them working, meaning that the game pretty much plays itself, with minimal input from you, other than running the first investments before you can buy managers, and resetting your progress here and there in order to earn Angel Investors, who boost your money-making. So, in principle, it sounds like a very boring game; and that might very well be true. Even then, it's a good time waster for when you're waiting for something, and you wanna launch a quick game.
Something that makes it stand out, in my opinion, is the huge amount of easter eggs and references this game hides, whether in the name of the upgrades or the managers themselves, who, most of the time, are a mix of two or more characters, or even real people. Also, the music, while playing on a loop, is nice, in my opinion; and the game offers three different stages, or planets, in which to play: Earth, Moon, and Mars. It also has special events, one per month, centered around a holiday from that month, and the events have their own special rewards and mechanics.
All in all, while it's not that great of a game, it's still decent enough for a time waster, and seeing your cash increasing surely feels great.

With only a few days of use despite the learning curve associated with the design this  is by far a mostly superior alternative to console controllers.  Mostly.. and not without its faults.
Positives
Whether you use this as a KB/M mode  or Gamepad mode device the right track pad offers superior analog accuracy that you cannot get with an actual analog stick.  It also doesn't have the same downfalls of your run of the mill laptop track pad, suitably rotates the camera about as well as a analog stick.    Of course the only negative is if you want to spin your camera in infinite circles but I am sure most people would choose accuracy over something silly as that.
As for the left pad, I will only offer an example for FF14 Players out there.  You can set the left pad to be touch sensitive, but then have a click action like Left Mouse, or A on the game pad.  What is the benefit in this? say you are using shadow flare or sacred soil you can select it from hotkey then click into the dpad to drop it down.  Basically it functions like the type of macro most people desired for target spells.
The Left/Right triggers have a good analog action and a hard stopper/click button at the end of it.  Allowing you to have a good feel of when you've maxed out the trigger, and giving you an additional action  at the end of it.  If you were to say, play final fantasy 14 with this you could tap the left trigger, bottoming it out to the button press for Left Set 1 hotkeys.  And then hold down and click the button to get LT + RT to gain access to Left Set 2.  This is just an example of how it can be used.  You can pretty much configure the button and trigger to function  as you wish it to.
The configuration software in Steam, just basing this on its merits alone.  You can do more with this controller then you'd ever think possible by looking at it.  You can tweak how the touch pads act (are they only buttons, do they have touch sensitive options?), how the triggers act(hair pin triggers.. and more). What every click or action does.  Multi key functions ect ect.  Its overwhelming how many options you have to customizing this controller and making it do things you'd just not think is possible at all just by staring at it.  I don't know how else to put it, you'd have to try the software out yourself to understand the vast amount of amazingness that it is.
Negatives
No global configuration software, you need steam overlay active in every game that you use this with.  This reason alone nearly got me to return the controller.  Its a bit cumbersome to have steam big picture mode open + overlay in every game I want to use this in.  Also means that any game (non steam, or steam) that has problems with the steam overlay will also have problems with this game.  If you are a normal PC user you probably already know big picture mode is a mess that's less efficient then the normal steam UI.
Left/Right Track pad push buttons, they are not bad and I am functioning fine with them but they are a bit rigid and tough to press in.  Unlike the face buttons which are minimal force it feels like I have to exert a bit of effort to click into their axis.  The center push is fine though, its about as tough as most Left Stick and Right Stick buttons.
Ergonomics are something you get used to, but  I am in the camp that finds the x face button to be a bit too far from the  tip of my thumb.  While even with small to average hands you can reach it, it feels like a bit of work to do so and sometimes triggers a reaction to touch the grip buttons since you're tightening your muscle to extend.  Shoulder buttons are a bit weird in their  angle and actuation position but the triggers and grips are what you'd expect from a normal controller. Right stick button requires a bit more force then other controllers to me.  Other then that holding the controller in my hands, palms cradled on on the curve of the outside grips.  You can hold it like a traditional controller almost~ but cradling your palms is important to give you  stability without the normal death  grip you'd give a traditional controller.  You need a bit of finesse and a lighter touch for most parts of this controller even if the buttons seem to follow the opposite ideology =P
Edit:
I've decided to part with the controller, but my review still stands.  For the goods, its still a highly customizeable controller but for games that fit its purpose its still far too cumbersome to be  used  reliably.  For games that prefer gamepad input,the DS3/4 are much better options due to controller design and the fact that you don't need the extra customization or inputs the steam controller offers which just confuses things.  The buttons on a Dual Shock 3 for example are far more comfrortable to press, perfect size and distance from your finger.
I could only fully suggest this controller if you plan on playing heavy KB/M games far from your actual KB/M.  Doesn't make it a bad controller, it is just a jack of all trades master of nothing.
