It sucks to not recommend this game because I really liked Dead Rising 1 and 2. But in the apparent rush to improve the graphics and get this out as an Xbox One exclusive launch title, Capcom sacrificed a good game.
The core elements of a Dead Rising game are here. You're trapped in an open world zombie apocalypse and there are dozens upon dozens of weapons at your disposal, lying around everywhere. Combo crafting new, wacky types of weapons also make it. You'll follow the main story, save survivors by either clearing zombies near them or escorting them, and kill psychos. You gain experience points (Prestige Points, or PP) and level up, gaining new abilities, more health, inventory space, passive buffs, etc. One nice addition to the game is a skill tree that lets the player decide, through the early and midgame, how they want to specialize. You can level up forever though, and they even keep giving you skill points after you've bought every available skill in the game. Come now, that's got to be a few lines of code at most... Anyway, Dead Rising 3 occurs on a bigger scale than the previous two, you've got a whole city now! It should be great, right?
But I think it's simply lost its self-aware charm. The city, Los Perdidos, is as bland as it comes. The way roadblocks snake through the city seem artificial. Instead of funny moments, there are little Tragic Endings. There are only 7 Psychos in the game, plus main story bosses. The psychos are based off the Seven Deadly Sins, which sounds cool in a boardroom design meeting, but there's an absurdity missing from most of them. Dead Rising 3 might be trying to be a little more serious, but at the same time it does try to be silly at times too. The whole balance of the game has been destroyed by Safe Zone Weapon Lockers, which, I♥♥♥♥♥♥you not, let you load up a full inventory of miniguns at level 1, and just mow zombies, human baddies, and even bosses to a pulp with zero effort. The old weaknesses of Dead Rising are present. Movement is sticky, it's often difficult to target the item you want to pick up, and survivors are morons. Nothing new or interesting is really brought to the table for the franchise. The graphics got a sizeable makeover and the zombie hordes are impressive, at the cost of a 30fps cap.
The lack of love in the game really comes to fruition in the DLC packs, which are good examples of the ♥♥♥♥♥iest game design I've seen out of a AAA game studio since whenever the last Dynasty Warriors game came out. Take most of the grindy collectible activities you do in the main game: pick up statues, destroy surveillance cameras, and drive from Point A to B to C to D. All right, now do that with a different character in four separate stories. The collectible activities are just reskinned: pick up WHISKEY, hack INTO cameras, and of course, drive from Point A to B to C to D, oh and some roads are now closed, making the drives even longer and more pointless. To top it all off, the only rewards in the DLC packs are more experience points (PP). Just more PP, here have some PP! I hit way past max level playing the base game, the rewards are completely useless. You're also essentially a god at max level, and you need to try to die in order to lose a fight, even against bosses. So what's left here? Nothing really. Just a chore.
So, then we get to the PC port itself. There's a 30fps cap which you CAN disable with some .ini editing, but that's a mark of a lazy port right there. Unlocking it can cause issues. The game has a few CTD bugs. The Co-op experience is nothing short of a ♥♥♥♥ing nightmare. If you're LUCKY, you'll only get CTD when you host or join another game. The unlucky will have their game hang the whole computer, sometimes requiring a restart. You pretty much have to do alchemy with your game settings until the co-op experience works... MAYBE. I managed to get a single co-op session going after about 2 hours of trying. And although this didn't happen to me personally, there are even higher frequencies of CTD bugs while playing co-op. Woo, zombie slaying with a bud has never been easier...
Just kidding. Get Dying Light instead. It's not comical, but at least it's properly fun.

If you're a fan of previous Dead Rising games, you'll absolutely love this game. It takes everything about the previous titles, and perfects them. Weapon crafting has never been better, just open you inventory and make a weapon on the fly. There are FAR more combo options available, and almost all of them are fun too use, and will level you up very quickly if you spam the hundreds of zombies on screen.
The game feels like a kind of RPG hybrid, with tons of side quests, far more then before, and a unique upgrade system not seen in previous titles. You can unlock the ability to create weapon combos with multiple different items instead of the one on the blueprint. What this means, is say you can't find a Baseball Bat, if you have unlocked the ability to use random parts, you can use a 4x4 instead and create the combo without the Baseball Bat. There are tons of survivors to rescue, and the ability to form your own posse. Which is basically where you choose a set amount of survivors from your base to come travel the game world with you.
Firearms feel more useful, and actually do damage to the zombies instead of just sponging every bullet you fire at them. Co-op is awesome, and seem's to work perfectly at the moment. Also, I've owned the game for over a year now, and haven't seen a single performance issue or any of these glitches people keep whining about. The game seem's to work with no faults from the technical side, I have everything on high with only a mid range PC build.
Overall, this game is definitely worth the cash. A must buy if you love zombie games.
EDIT: This game doesn't run poorly at all, ran it on multiple different rigs, both AMD AND Nvidia, it ran exactly the same. Max settings, zero frame drops except during explosions. Here's the thing about PC gaming, you can't use a PC built in 2012, and expect it to run this game. If you can't afford to game on the PC and UPGRADE YOUR PARTS, GO BUY A FREAKING CONSOLE.

This game is fun, but it needs more options to configure and customize the instances. It would be great to be able to apply different settings to a game instance (e.g. a "custom game" that allows you to pick enemy types, drop types, chest types, etc.) and it sorely needs an option to DISABLE FRIENDLY FIRE. For what is kind of supposed to be a friendly "couch game" it is incredibly annoying (after it stops being funny the first few times) to constantly hit your friend down holes or knock them down as they are trying to escape a hit. How this simple option eluded being implemented is beyond me. It also wouldn't hurt expanding supported players up to 4. I realize that requires rebalancing, but this is not a competitive game that should require a lot of balancing thought - maybe just bump up the amount of monsters and spawns? I don't know, I'm sure the smart people who designed the game can facilitate that.
My final takeaway (TL;DR): A good game to play casually with friends and hack and slash your way through levels, but it can be refined. I would tell the developers to have some more fun with the game and don't try and make it such a try-hard game like Isaac.
- Add options to mess with the game instances
- Add the option to REMOVE FRIENDLY FIRE
- Potentially up the supported players to 4.
Regardless, a decent game in it's current state - hope to see it get better so I can justify playing some more.

NieR:Automata is an open-world action RPG narrating the wonderful and emotional journey of 2 soldiers forced to live and fight in a very peculiar circumstance and cause, later on used by the game to touch upon a couple eternal philosophical questions about humanity and our lives.
The world is fascinating and beautiful; lots of interesting characters, side stories and in-game lore archives that help build it. The pleasing sceneries are accompanied by one of the best OSTs in gaming.
The gameplay is fun and fluid but maybe too simple once you get the hang of it, unless you turn on the 1-hit death mode. It's typical platinum game fighting (somewhat slower than usual) with just a little bullet hell mixed in, which has been pretty fun and offers some variety.

Go! Go! Nippon! ~ My First Trip to Japan ~ is a cute little visual novel, where you explore many of the most famous landmarks in Japan, in the company of Two sisters you befriended online and whom you stay with during your weeklong visit. Awkward situations arise, giving this game the feel of an anime, and as you explore more of Japanese culture and learn about it's history, your relationship with your new friends develops as well. All in all, it was a very cute game, with some funny dialogue and a couple of situations that gave it an anime feel. I thoroughly enjoyed the game, even though the playthrough was very linear. You can make some choices as to where you want to visit; However, a large part of the playthrough will be visiting specific areas in Japan, such as Kyoto. I don't regret picking this game up in the slightest and would like to see a sequel even, to further explore Japanese culture and history, as well as to continue to character development and relationship between the Protagonist, and the sister.

I was actually pretty excited about trying Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~
The premise sounded interesting, the fact that it would tell you facts about Japan was also interesting, and I thought perhaps it'd be a fun little story that would give you some knowledge of culture and such as you played.
First, what I liked:
The part about Japan facts was interesting, not everything was new to me, and half of the stuff you'd already know if you ever opened, you know, a brochure for Japan or watched an anime... but it was still interesting.
The graphics were nice, background as well as characters were well drawn.
I loved the idea for the VN, and loved that you could actually have it with Japanese text too.
The idea of having expenses added was interesting, but badly done and underused.
I guess if you're getting ready to visit Japan this would be cool.
Now, what I disliked:
While the graphics were nice, they were poor. Half the time you had sky shots with music/sound/text that would be like "Oh, the train arrives~! Let's get on it!" like they couldn't find the image of a train or something, which was slightly annoying. But I could overlook that, or could have, if the story had been actually interesting.
It wasn't.
So you play as this guy who realizes is life long dream of going to Japan. Only unlike any normal human being, he makes no research whatsoever of who he's actually going to be staying with ("friends" from Japan whom he never exchanged pictures with and he thought were guys but are really girls. Yay, score for him, right?... yeah), and just hops on a plane. Lets assume I can suspend disbelief enough to think this really smart guy couldn't have found out before hand that his "friends" were really girls.
We move on in the story and find out that the guy whose long life dream was going to Japan has apparently never even watched an anime (or read about the place he wanted to go to), or even stepped foot outside his own home back in his country. He knows none of the basic things an anime fan would know, or that someone who cared about the place they so wanted to see would be aware of, or basics about the culture. Basically: he's highly unprepared. He seems to even be amazed at the dumbest things (train, shopping mall, everything! Ooooooohhhhhhh, I've never seen a shopping mall before! - I grant you Japan ones are probably impressive, but probably not like this.)
Then, you spend most the novel on invisible trains. I say invisible trains because, as mentioned, you get most the time a sky view as the girls proceed to explain everything about how the train system works while you travel to and from places. And it's not a lot of places.
All the while you're supposed to "choose" one girl for the love story that's behind all this... only you don't really know which you're picking (each girl shows you a different place out of the few that are to be seen, but you don't know which girl will show you which until you've picked it).
Do I recommend this VN? Well... no.
If you want this for the culture shot - don't get it, watch any anime instead.
If you want this for the hentai/ecchi - don't get it, there's none.
If you want this for the story - don't get it, there's also none.
If you want this for practicing Japanese - go ahead and get it if it's on sale.

Ok so first of all before i start this review just a real quick disclaimer, do not pay attension to my hours on steam, iv played atleast 12+ more hours offline and i thought i should clear that out of the way first.
So first thing first Rampage Knights is the best indie game i have played in the last 2 years. It combines all the elements i find essential in a video game and i will now list all the pros and cons so that you can see what it does right and what wrong.
Pros:

+Really neat art style

I dont have many cons for  this game, but i will still try and list some.
Cons:
-Game can be unfair at times (you might get so powerful with all possible gear and powers, and then just in a brief second you dont pay attension and fall down to a pit leading to your death.)
-The game is not rewarding enough (after you finish a run, all your gear resets and you dont really feel like you accomplished anything which is frustrating.)
-You need to unlock achievments in order to play certain game modes (and i know some people may find it fun but i just think it's really annoying cause some achievments are really hard to unlock.)
So overall Rampage Knights is a very solid game, with elements suitable for both casual and hardcore gamers and a smooth gameplay that will keep you at the edge of your seat at times.

It is a decent game, though it's a bit of a upwards-downwards journey.
It's ALL about the action on screen. And I do mean ALL. The story is virtually non-existent.
There is an attempt of sorts, but it falls into a category of 10 year old writing a sci-fi after playing through the original DOOM. And if you want to get even that you have to do it yourself - scavenge notes and manually read through pages of fluff text. But there is no one to blaem there, as to expect a coherent story from a DOOM game, well, no one considers it even.
The gunplay is really just that: no relevant strategies, no cover shooting, just run-and-gun. And tbh it's the game's forte among the lines of Serious Sam and Wolfenstein (I will come back that one in a moment). But that sadly you really have to span it out to short play periods as the brain quickly notices the repetition: came into a room, ran around, killed everyone, next room. Rinse. Repeat.
Don't get me wrong it's fun, it's gory, it's SATISFYING as all HELL (wink wink, anyone?), but after you quench your daily thirst of mayhem, it's lacklustrer as it's the core gameplay element.
Last boss was a complete let down. Almost worth a not recomended in of itself.
The collectibles are a nice touch but, really, just prolongs your experience with an hour or two of unnecerssary prop-hunt if you're a completionist like me.
So, final verdict, it's a decent game, awesomely satisfying in dosages of 30min\a day, as prescribed by Dr. Vee. Other than that - MEDIOCRE. I would suggest picking up Wolfenstein: New Order (created and released by the same company) or maybe even the newly announced Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus (finger's crossed for that one) for a truly awesomeness like you never thought would be possible done with a FPS game (the final boss still was a letdown, but the whole package just tickles my fancy that much).

Thumbs up to Hyper Hippo Games, they've done something completely unexpected. On paper, this seems like the most boring idea for a game to ever exist. Your role is to literally click buttons to watch numbers go up. Occasionally buying modifiers or mulitpliers, but still with the single goal of making large numbers. Sounds mind-numbing, right? Well, it's somehow kept me hooked for 16 hours. 16 hours over at least half a year, though. This is one of those games you play for about 2 minutes a day and put away. In fact, the game encourages you to quit and leave it alone pretty early into your game. So, it's probably best experienced on a phone when you've got a few minutes to burn, but the PC version works fine. I'm not sure how it's got so much time out of me, or what that says about myself, but it's worth giving a shot.

I don't review things often, but when I do it's a doozy.
The steam controller is an unnatural abomination, an experiment from the mad scientists at Valve. It's exactly the kind of controller PC gamers need.
This controller has two trackpads. Depending on how you set them up, they're extremely responsive. So responsive that I dare never to use a thumbstick for the camera, ever again. It supports profiles from gamepads, Dinput and Xinput. If you have a game that supports a gamepad, the Steam controller is supported using a generic config. Maybe, there's a nice soul out there who's made a dedicated, custom config for your game.
It supports Keyboard and Mouse configs with some rejigging around. If you have the patience, you can make this controller work for every single game, if you so desire.
Seen a bad review? They've not given the controller enough time. There is no downside to this controller. It doesn't feel cheap. If there's a single thing that bothers me, it's the glossy part on the front, that'll get fingerprints pretty fast. It uses batteries, which both offer a good trade off between longevity and usability. Wireless, chargable controllers have lithium batteries that eventually lose their charge. The batteries also give the handles a bit of heft. AA batteries aren't even that expensive. You have 6 back buttons. Two shoulder, two triggers ( nice, analoggy triggers) and two clicky back buttons. These feel a little stiff at first, but you get used to them.
I recommend this controller as both a PC gamer and Modder. The endless customisability is something that we gamers dream of. How you use this controller is up to you, the player and not the developer who made the game. Don't like the official profile? Use a user creation. Don't like those? Make your own.

I enjoyed this visual novel. It gave me a taste of what the different districts of Tokyo are known for, and provided just the right amout of interesting history behind them without getting lost in details.
This story is about a teenage boy's first trip to Japan to spend with two friends he knows online, Makoto and Akira - but, much to his surprise, they are attractive teenage girls, not boys. Their parents are away, so he spends the week touring various parts of Tokyo with them.
There are six districts to visit; you can choose one to visit on each of the first three days (meaning that you can only see half of them on a single playthrough). Depending on which district you choose, one of the sisters will come along with you for the day (there's no way to know which until after you choose). Days four and five are an overnight trip (via Shinkansen) to Kyoto with both of them, and then day six is spent with whichever girl joined you more often on the first three days, So there's a light romance plot tacked on here that ends up with you falling for whichever sister you spent more time with; there's no real way to choose which one to love, but since Makoto will come with you to three of the districts and Akira to the other three, a second playthrough will let you see the other three districts and the other sister's ending. You've got more say over a few other choices long the way (like, what do you want for dinner: pizza, Japanese pizza, or sushi?). I spent about four hours playing through the story twice (and making liberal use of the handy "Skip" button the second time through).
One of the story's strengths is that every line is displayed in English, with the Japanese translation of it displayed in kana - very handy if you're learning. Also handy is that the text is displayed in different colors depending on who's speaking it. (No voiceover here, unfortunately.) An odd feature is that it asks for the current dollar/yen exchange rate and then displays your running expenses, so you have an idea how much your trip is costing you. One tidbit I stumbled upon by luck: while there are many ways into the game's menu, the only way out is to right-click. Until I discovered that, I was frustrated at being trapped in the menu.
The only really unfortunate thing about this story is that you'll walk in on one sister bent over in her panties, and the other sister (tastefully) naked. That alone kept me from recommending this to a neighbor's kids before their trip to Japan, and it's a shame, because the rest of the content here might really have interested them.
All in all, "Go! Go! Nippon!" is the next best thing to taking a tour of Tokyo with somebody who really knows the place and can point out interesting stuff along the way. (And this visual novel is much, much less expensive than a trip to Japan, too.)

For anyone interested or planning to go to Japan, "Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~" is a fun, hilarious yet simple visual novel that will teach people about various locations throughout Tokyo, riding on the train or shinkansen and also other things pertaining to Japanese culture.
For those who purchased this game in hopes for nudity or sex, no, this is not that type of game.  While it has two scenes of fan service, this game is primarily about a foreigner who comes to Japan and has two sisters showing him around.
There is replay factor in the sense that you won't visit all locations during the first play through, so if you want to open up all the other artwork, you will need to play it again for the second time.
Also, choosing the cities and making sure who introduces you to locations the most, will determine whether you will be with older sister Motoko or younger sister Akira.
But overall, I enjoyed this game for it's dialogue and while I wouldn't call this an educational game, it is educational but in a more fun and perverted way.
It's simple, straightforward and an entertaining visual novel about one going to Japan for the very first time and learning key facts about various locations around Tokyo.
Recommended!

Mods included are 'Mare Nostrum'; based on the Desert War and "Darkest Hour"; based on the Allied invasion of Europe (D-Day) as an integrated part of the steam purchase.

I never thought this game would actually be so much fun!
This pretty much sums it up.
You will hear so much swearing, cheering and laughing playing this game the way it's supposed to be played - with your friends.
TL;DR
Here is my shortcut; the hole in one for this review.
Positive	Mediocre	Negative
+ Pretty maps	~ not even a handful yet	- Not optimized
+ Different ways/paths to hit
+ Custom Modifier
- No Steam Integration
~ The UI could use an overhaul
+ Zooming in and out is possible		- No free camera
+ Relaxing Soundtrack	~ some might find annoying
The Levels
Currently, there are 4 different levels: Forest, Desert, Moonlight Park, Spooky Mansion. An additional 2 are supposedly planned.
Each map contains 18 holes and at least in the forest level you can finish it with 18 shots - but this will take you a lot of practice.
The design is really neat and most of the time you can take more than one approach to hitting the ball.
With to the many possibilities comes a big part of the replay value and the whole fun of the game. If you manage that one insane hit, none of your friends even thought about and you leave them wondering how you managed the hole in 2 strokes when they are on the 7th.
The Gameplay
It's Golfing - as easy as it gets - you hold the mouse button, move the mouse to change the strength and direction of your shot and release to hit the ball.
You can also zoom in and out to get a better idea of the location of your goal, but sometimes it is obscured by obstacles so you won't be able to see where to hit at all - I really wish there was a free camera so you could inspect the level beforehand.
Multiplayer
Creating and joining a lobby is super easy, as well as setting up modifiers.
Another big part of replaying this game will come from setting up different modifications - such as 'random ball shapes'. When the unlucky one with the acorn hits the hole in one - a ♥♥♥♥♥torm will be unleashed :D
However before even going into multiplayer, I advise you to paint your ball under 'Customize' - so you can be recognised by your friends. Just don't take the same colours.
On the downside: you can't join a game through steam yet, which is a shame since you have to leaf through a few pages of games to find the one you are looking for.
The Visuals
All the levels are really neatly designed and have a really cool air about them, to match a certain theme and bring you in the mood.
The Forest, for example, is an all outside map, with a timber mill and saws and rolling logs around the place.
The Desert features a pyramid theme with a sphinx and switches from an open-air level to an indoor level around the way.
Moonlight Park is the currently only night level which has a really different feel from the other maps, it's quite magical.
Last but not least in the mansion you will play all indoors and have ghosts spooking around as well as weird statues and trophies as well as cobwebs all over the place.
However, in the current state of the game, some locations will just eat away your framerate - so you might have a look at your settings.
The Sound
I really like the sweet melody in the background, my friend, however, turned the volume way down because he couldn't stand it - so it's really a preference thing.
The Verdict
If you have friends willing to play this game with you - by all means you can have a good time.
However, there isn't that much content in the game yet. Of course, you can aim for the hole in one on every map (if this is even possible; I don't think it is), hone your skills by trying new hits and playing with funny settings but it depends on how long you and your friends will stay motivated together - because if the first one loses the interest, the others will probably follow.
Also: always play with Collision - on. HateThank me later.
Note:
If you have read this far - thank you.
I hope this review helped you in deciding to buy this game and if it did, I would be grateful for a 'thumbs up', if you didn't like it, you can give me a 'thumbs down' but I would be glad to hear your opinion on what you didn't like.

I don't get where all the hate comes from.
Sure, it's not your traditional arrangement of buttons. It's not the regular amount of them and there are lots of new elements introduced.
But this is a fantastic controller, very optimized for PC games. After getting used to the buttons, which took a while but isn't a negative thing for the controller, I could play any game I wanted. I played The Witcer, Dark Souls and Borderlands 2 without any issue. The trackpads work wonderfully and provide tactile feedback on how much you're rotating, and every button input and trackpad sensitivity is configurable per game.
Steam will remember these configs for each game and adjust them accordingly once set.
The gyroscope functionality is amazing, too. Much better than any other controller, including PS4. And the buttons on the underside mean you can reload while aiming without removing your finger from the trigger or drink a much needed Estus Flask while rolling away from danger, impossible on a regular controller.
Once I got used to these, I could explore new possibilities and play using unique movements and stratagems.
It won't beat mouse aiming for FPS games, but it does a damn fine job at keeping up.
Do NOT judge this book by it's cover. A marvelous piece of tech.
It may take time to get used to; but once you are. GG.

Set in the dark, dystopian future of 2022, ‘Deus Ex: Human Revolution’ is a fantastic blend of the First Person Shooter (FPS) | Stealth | RPG genres and a testament to gaming as both an art form and sublime story-telling medium.
Released by Eidos | Square Enix in 2013, the world of ‘Deus-Ex’ is a bleak near-future where Corporations are increasingly more powerful – and Biotech firms vie for control of the Human Cryogenic Augmentation market. These increasingly high stakes result in a growing focus on corporate espionage and security – enter Adam Jensen – an ex-SWAT Commander hired as head of security for Sarif Industries. The opening credits detail Jensen’s brutal execution-style killing during a break-in at Sarif Industries, his resurrection through cryogenic augmentation and drops you into the shoes of the Part-Man, Part-Machine, to piece together the fragmented memories of the past and uncover the cause of the attack. An engrossing, deep campaign takes you around the world, on sprawling open world levels where the broader storyline is broken up through the distractions of a richly atmospheric world, numerous side quests, and lots of collectibles and readable background lore scattered around the maps.
Gameplay is aligned around the game’s 4 pillars of FPS based-combat, Stealth mechanics, RPG elements (of character customization) and Player Choice in story-telling direction – and the game seamlessly switches from one mode to another. You are allowed considerable breadth of choice in approaching every situation – Frontal Assault, Stealth or even Smooth-Talking your way past the opposition - building in replayability into the title as well. Several different situational outcomes, great graphics with a trademark orange machine-hue, a brooding pulsating score, responsive K&M controls and controller support round out a well polished title.  Note that this review is based on the ‘Director’s Cut’ version of the game which includes all DLC integrated directly into the overall campaign – resulting in close to 75-80 hours of gameplay to complete the campaign, track down all side-quests, see through multiple endings, read all the lore etc (but your mileage may vary).

Minor quibbles with the game include the occasional scripted boss battle that while serving to move the broader narrative along, tend to stifle the freedom otherwise celebrated throughout the game. Other issues include longish load times, an inordinate disk space requirement (of 20+ Gigs) and being particularly resource heavy, resulting in some framerate drop issues.
Overall however, ‘Deus-Ex: Human Revolution’ is a triumphant blend of story-telling and disparate game genres. A visually stunning and immersive world, a deep, layered campaign, large open world levels, multiple endings determined by player choice, and very good replayability make this one of the best story-driven titles of recent memory. While the game’s broadly Sci-Fi / Cyber-punk theme will admittedly not be to everyone’s taste, for fans of the genre and classic sci-fi flicks such as RoboCop and BladeRunner, this is essential gaming and overall, a shining example of Gaming Evolved. Very Highly Recommended – Rated (9.5/10)

Disclaimer: these are only my first impressions of the game and not really my final thoughts.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a dense bomb that appears like a simple game with not much to offer to the player, but once you use it, you'll see that the explosion is that of a nuclear bomb. Essentially this game is a - mainly - story-driven game that mixes some story elements from the Crysis-series with Fallout 3/New Vegas.
It's a new era where the ethical questions of mechanical implants in humans are top discussions, naturally, this leads to protests.. sometimes to the extreme. You're Adam Jensen and you work for Sarif Industries which is the leading research company for these implants (augmentations, in-game), however, there's a terrorist attack by the anti-augmentation group and you almost die, however, augmentations to the rescue, you live! However, as you're sent off to an investigation to find out what/who was *really* going on behind this terrorist attack, you find out some things that were never meant to be found out. Either way, story so-far is fantastic and really interesting!
If you're the type of person who always prefers shooting and killing, well, you can do just that! You can also go stealthy through the entire game - marvelous. It does blend the two very well, and I find myself to prefer being stealthy because it's smoother and better implemented. Guns feel as if they're not really meant to be the primary choice of the player, and do feel somewhat dumbed-down, because aiming is a little difficult and the only real weapon with good accuracy is the standard pistol. Other than that, it does work quite well and it's different, so I won't complain. Ammo has to be bought and sold which adds some challenge to the game, so you can't really "run-and-shoot", you have to keep your strategies organised, which I definitely like, and the Fallout-aspects really shows off here.
Animations are buttery smooth and they really do a cool thing here. Instead of making the speech-animations (body animations) generic and stale, they have several to fit in with the situation and feelings and loop them which gives it all quite a good variety and more natural than you'd expect. Not to mention the stellar voice-acting. Voice acting is seriously top-notch. Doesn't get much better!
I really enjoy this game and feel as if more people HAVE TO own it, those who enjoy Fallout 3/New Vegas & Crysis 2, 3, in particular! I can't believe I've had it in my library for so long without giving it a glance.

I'm not usually one for fighting games, having only really played Super Smash Bros Brawl, but I was totally hooked by this one! Intuitive but deep is the only way I can describe the combat, and the small but diverse roster and good backstory helps a lot as well.
Core Gameplay:
Pretty solid, with moves that fluidly turn into combos; I'm playing with just a keyboard, which is probably not the recommended setup, but I'm still doing fine. The simplicity of the game is really helpful; no enviroments to get in your way, just two combantants duking it out. The seperation of the "drive" - one of the most often used abilities - into a seperate key is the cornerstone of the easy to learn, hard to master fighting system in the game.
Character Roster
Twelve is a pretty small roster for a fighting game, but a fantastic point is the game's favour is that there are no clones; each character fights in a totally different style befitting their personality and powers. My favourite, Jin, keeps his opponents at a short distance using ice projectiles before freezing them and moving in for the attack. Carl, on the other hand, uses his robot sister as both a shield and a catspaw to catch an opponent off guard. You're sure to find the one right for you!
Aesthetics/Graphics
The designs in this game are some gorgeous 2D stuff, no mistake, but if you have an aversion to anime and anime-like designs for backgrounds and characters this game will turn you off; it subscribes to many, many anime conventions. However, the bold stylistic choice results in a very diverse group of character designs; they look distinct, in both clear and subtle ways. For example, Taokaka,  Iron Tager and Arakune look totally different, coming from various backgrounds. On the other hand, Noel and Jin wear similar uniforms (both belonging to a military called the NOL) but are easily told apart on the battlefield due to minor but well placed differences in how they wear it, no mean feat.
Story and Story Mode
As with the designs, the story is very anime-ish; it is presented piece-meal, but after playing through several different perspectives (which, incidentally, is a good way to become familiar with the roster) you start to get a handle on it. Really, the powderkeg personalities of the roster are the key here. I found myself liking even characters like Taokaka and Bang, who I initially thought ridiculous, because their individual stories are told with humour and pathos. Of course, not everyone is guarenteed to be likable (I can not bring myself to bear Noel and her constant whining) but odds are you'll find a horse to back in this very confusing and at times incomprehensible plot.
The best thing is how gameplay and story co-incide! Characters will offer voice clips when they fight each other relating to the situation and how they view the other person; this is amazing for building atmosphere. It can range from simply recognising the opponent as an agent of a rival faction like Sector Seven or the NOL, to calling them a pet name, to swearing at them or giggling psychotically at their pain.
The bosses (by which I mean the two "hidden characters", who you will likely face on your first runthrough of any story) can be very difficult, especially if you're using someone you're not familiar with. However, they never feel impossible or super-cheap.
Conclusion
I've still got a lot to do on this game, and I hope they add acheivements and maybe even steam-supported netplay, but for its low price tag and taking into account single player and local multiplayer, I encourage you to give it a shot, especially if you're interested into starting out in fighting games!

This is a Rogue-lite beat-'em-up with online multiplayer. Wait, what? "Rogue-likes" are games that where you navigate a procedurally generated (that is, randomized each time) dungeon without saving, each attempt starts from scratch. A "Rogue-*lite*" game like this lets you unlock better starting abilities based on progress from your previous attempts.
You're an adventurer returning from a successful dungeon raid, when an evil wizard steals all your loot. Time to march to the wizard's tower and have a word with him about that. You'll just have to use whatever you pick up along the way.
I started with the keyboard, but ended up buying a gamepad, since a fighting game just doesn't feel right to me otherwise. The left analog stick is used for movement, X is attack, A is jump, Y to activate things and grab items, B to use items, LB and RB cycle through inventory slots, LT and RT are for dodge-rolling. It was very responsive and worked fine for me. You can use the direction pad for inventory, dropping items, and emotes, but you only need drop and emote in multiplayer.
It plays a lot like side-scrolling beat-'em-ups like Golden Axe or Final Fight. You can move in any direction, but only attack left and right, except for things like magic and some special attacks. There's a life bar that you replenish by eating food or chugging healing potions, and a magic bar that restores itself over time. You only start with one extra life.
Your inventory has a spell slot, a throwing weapon slot, a scroll slot, and potion slot. You can only carry one of each, so use them instead of hoard them. You can carry plenty of throwing weapons but they have to be all the same type.
Most spells have a big magic cost to start, but a slow magic drain as you continue them, so it's better to hit a group with a long blast of magic than to use it sparingly. There are lightning bolts, fireballs that set the enemy ablaze for damage over time, ice storms that freeze them in place, and more oddball stuff like a "Dwarven Contraption" with many uses, from crushing enemies to cracking locked treasure chests.
Throwing weapons are pretty important to your survival. You can chuck a simple stone at your enemy to stun them, fling throwing daggers, knock down a row of them with a throwing axe, or lob Zelda-style cherry bombs at them.
Scrolls are single-use magic spells. There's a wide variety of these. Some grant powers, some remove curses, some freeze monsters in the room, etc. There's even one that instantly builds a floor over all the bottomless pits in the room.
The potions are mostly healing or powerups. There are some that give a huge amount of healing but also give you a random disease. Of course, there are also potions to remove curses and diseases, and some to increase your strength.
The main challenge of the game is collecting a combination of abilities that works well from what you have available. Many of the sources of powerups (like the demon's card-guessing game) can give you random curses and diseases. Some powerups have inconvenient drawbacks, but then some curses and diseases actually have useful side-effects! A classic example is the Mighty Foot, which tries to stomp you every few seconds, but can also stomp enemies near you. There's also a mechanical arm which lets you do constant spinning attacks, but you can't use the dash attack anymore.
There are lots of weapons, armor, and other gear available along the way. Some you get from chests (solve a simple lockpicking minigame) or you can find shops to buy them with gold pieces. You can also pick up familiars who follow you around and zap your enemies or help you in various ways. Altars give you random powers, but some are cursed or have other costs.
Combat is quick and frantic, with lots of enemy variety, hordes of minions, nasty little fliers, and fearsome giant bosses. There are different special attacks you can perform depending on which direction you're moving when you attack, a stomp for prone or crawling enemies, and jump and dash attacks. Some enemies use shields which can only be broken by jump attacks or dashes, or by weapons with the shieldbreaker ability. The dodge-roll helps when fighting giants, because they get temporary stagger resistance after they get staggered; knocking them into bottomless pits is sometimes an option. Kick enemies across the room, toss them into the air, and spin them around to hit other enemies! The game gives you lots of ways to handle large groups.
Critical hits (a slim chance that any hit does lots of extra damage) are a thing, and some magic weapons have extra effects on criticals. Status effects like getting frozen, set on fire, poisoned, etc. are also a thing, but there are ways to become immune most status and damage types.
There's quite a bit of platforming, that is, jumping over pits and spikes. Most of it is tough but fair. Fortunately there are also jump boots, levitation scrolls, flying carpets, and the like which can be useful there. A double jump can be unlocked in various ways, and this is very handy for both combat and platforming, but it needs to be unlocked again every run unless you're an Assassin.
Losing all your lives (or finishing the game by reaching the castle and killing the evil wizard) sends you back to the beginning to start all over again. There are "challenges" that track your lifetime stats over multiple runs, which unlock new abilities and character classes. For example, breaking 200 shields makes your shield-breaking create a shockwave that damages everything nearby, inflicting 100,000 spell damage gives you a spell damage bonus, and opening 200 locked chests makes lockpicking much easier by making the lockpick minigame shorter. Some challenges also unlock new hats for your character, and many different player skins are available from the start.
Aside from the starting Adventurer character class, there are unlockable classes. Some of them change the game in significant ways: The Pirate uses a cannon instead of a dash attack, the Assassin can become invisible briefly instead of dodge-rolling, the Battlemage can teleport, etc.
I didn't play any multiplayer yet, so I can't really review that part. It's two-player only, with an online server browser.
The sprite art style and funky music give the game a fun arcade feel, and there's lots of bizarre humor in the game. There are some cute shout-outs to other indie games: The "Serious Bomberman" powerup gives you a Serious Bomb for a head, and the "Fish Warrior Lady" player skin might look familiar to Undertale players.
Overall I was very happy with this purchase. I'm not that much into Rogue-like games, but it was a nice change of pace.

I never thought this game would actually be so much fun!
This pretty much sums it up.
You will hear so much swearing, cheering and laughing playing this game the way it's supposed to be played - with your friends.
TL;DR
Here is my shortcut; the hole in one for this review.
Positive	Mediocre	Negative
+ Pretty maps	~ not even a handful yet	- Not optimized
+ Different ways/paths to hit
+ Custom Modifier
- No Steam Integration
~ The UI could use an overhaul
+ Zooming in and out is possible		- No free camera
+ Relaxing Soundtrack	~ some might find annoying
The Levels
Currently, there are 4 different levels: Forest, Desert, Moonlight Park, Spooky Mansion. An additional 2 are supposedly planned.
Each map contains 18 holes and at least in the forest level you can finish it with 18 shots - but this will take you a lot of practice.
The design is really neat and most of the time you can take more than one approach to hitting the ball.
With to the many possibilities comes a big part of the replay value and the whole fun of the game. If you manage that one insane hit, none of your friends even thought about and you leave them wondering how you managed the hole in 2 strokes when they are on the 7th.
The Gameplay
It's Golfing - as easy as it gets - you hold the mouse button, move the mouse to change the strength and direction of your shot and release to hit the ball.
You can also zoom in and out to get a better idea of the location of your goal, but sometimes it is obscured by obstacles so you won't be able to see where to hit at all - I really wish there was a free camera so you could inspect the level beforehand.
Multiplayer
Creating and joining a lobby is super easy, as well as setting up modifiers.
Another big part of replaying this game will come from setting up different modifications - such as 'random ball shapes'. When the unlucky one with the acorn hits the hole in one - a ♥♥♥♥♥torm will be unleashed :D
However before even going into multiplayer, I advise you to paint your ball under 'Customize' - so you can be recognised by your friends. Just don't take the same colours.
On the downside: you can't join a game through steam yet, which is a shame since you have to leaf through a few pages of games to find the one you are looking for.
The Visuals
All the levels are really neatly designed and have a really cool air about them, to match a certain theme and bring you in the mood.
The Forest, for example, is an all outside map, with a timber mill and saws and rolling logs around the place.
The Desert features a pyramid theme with a sphinx and switches from an open-air level to an indoor level around the way.
Moonlight Park is the currently only night level which has a really different feel from the other maps, it's quite magical.
Last but not least in the mansion you will play all indoors and have ghosts spooking around as well as weird statues and trophies as well as cobwebs all over the place.
However, in the current state of the game, some locations will just eat away your framerate - so you might have a look at your settings.
The Sound
I really like the sweet melody in the background, my friend, however, turned the volume way down because he couldn't stand it - so it's really a preference thing.
The Verdict
If you have friends willing to play this game with you - by all means you can have a good time.

I'm an old broad (51) and have been gaming  since before there were even console games. You now, like pinball machines and those big arcade machines where you could play Pac Man and such. Over the last 10 years or so I've mainly played pc games requiring a keyboard and mouse. I've recently started playing console (Xbox) and games on steam requiring a controller. I'm not so good at the controller/gamepad thing and have had a hard time getting used to it.
So basically, I'm a total n00b at conroller games.
I figured I'd give the Steam controller a try and see how I could do. I ordered it on Monday and it was delivered on Thursday. I've been using it for the last 2 days and although there is indeed a learning curve to it, I find I'm able to get used to this style of controller easier than the traditioal gamepad like an Xbox 360 controller.  I wish I had just bought the Steam controller straight off when I started playing more games requiring a controller because I wouldn't have had to unlearn all the stuff I got used to with other controllers.  If I had gone from keyboard and mouse right to the steam conroller it would have been a less painful process for this old gal.
I like it because it really is a good combination between mouse/keyboard game play, and controller game play. It's hard for me to describe, but it just makes more sense to me than using an Xbox 360 style controller. I've been able to intuitively adapt to this controller just by trial and error. When using the dual trackpads for typing, think of how you text on your phone. You use two thumbs, and your two thumbs usually only strike the buttons on their respective sides on the keyboard. A few minutes of practice will do.
The only difficulty I'm still having is the dual touch pads. I really love them btw, especially the left one because I play Deadpool a lot. On my old controller I was all the time hitting that in game and inadvertantly switching my weapons. Where it is on the steam controller completely prevents me from doing that.
The trouble I have with the right touch pad is when I'm trying to look around as is normally done with the right stick. You really have to practice placing your thumb in the right place, and using the correct pressure so that you don't make yourself dizzy panning all over the place. Gentle touch and gentle brushing with your thumb on this touch pad is key. I'm used to being rather rough on my gamepads, in fact I've deveoped callouses on my thumbs as a result of how stupid I get with the right and left sticks. So, granny has to be gentle with her new toy in order for it to function properly. All it really needs is gentle pressure and brief brushing with your thumbs on either touch pad.
So now I'm going through and adapting my new controller to each of my games that will allow me to use it. I've found the user created configurations helpful, and easily accessible. You don't have to worry about where to find these configs, because once you get your steam controller going, and go in game, there will be instructions that will pop up for you on how to set things up.
Also, this controller works for basic navigation in a web browser. You can use it exatly like a mouse when going here and there on your own computer doing funcions unrelated to Steam. You ust have to learn which control acts as a mouse click, and which controlls scrolling and whatnot.
I would definitely recommend this controller to eveyone. I would suggest if you are a pc gamer and are used to a mouse and keyboard style of gaming, instead of allowing a traditional controller ruin you as you move to gamepad style game play, you get a Steam controller and get used to it first.
Right now I'm figuring if it can work with games like WoW. So far it can. Just working through a custom configuration and it seems to be working great! I haven't played Wow in a whie (got bored) but I may give a go for a while again.
Heck, I'm a granny. If I can learn it, anyone can. ;)

Hi,
ich finde den steam controller super, initiale idee war für mich spiele die man mit pad spielen kann bequem von der couch zu spielen auf dem fernseher auf dem ich ohnehin schon viele sachen via stream angeschaut habe. Ich hatte mir irgendwann witcher 3 gekauft und es auch gespielt, fand das game super aber ich war total schnell so müde das ich mich lieber auf die couch gelegt habe und einen film zu schauen. Am liebsten hätte ich es gerne weiter gespielt aber die komfortable haltung in verbindung mit meiner müdigkeit war mir dann doch wichtiger.
Deswegen habe ich mir den Steam Controller sowie den Steam-link geholt. Die ursprüngliche Absicht mit dem Controller alle Spiele, auch die man bisher nur mit maus und tastatur spielen konnte, an einem Gerät zu bedienen geht meines erachtens nur bedingt auf, es gibt spiele die man mit maus und tastatur spielt und auch weiter so spielen sollte. Man kann zwar viel emulieren mit dem Pad (die Konfigurationsmöglichkeiten sind unglaublich), allerdings erreicht man nie eine Geschwindigkeit die man per Maus und Tastatur hat. Spiele die nicht direkt Pad Titel sind und wettbewerbsorientiert sind wie zum beispiel ego-shooter multiplayer kann man vergessen, single player ist es schon spielbar macht aber mit maus doch mehr spass. Games wie witcher sind dann perfekt für ein pad, es gibt strategie spiele die super mit dem Controller harmonieren wie zum Beispiel XCOM 2.
Wenn man keinen Controller hat und einen sucht für den PC denke ich ist man mit dem Steam Controller im Moment am besten aufgestellt, Maus und Tastatur ersatz ist eher als notlösung zu betrachten, dafür bin ich aber mit dem controller viel flexibler wie mit irgendeinem anderen Controller. Die Touch-Pads finde ich super und sind so viel präziser als ein zusätzlicher Analog Stick, ich könnte mir vorstellen das andere Peripherie Hersteller in Kürze nachziehen mit so einem Konzept weil es einfach besser ist. Die Verarbeitung ist gut, er fühlt sich gut in der Hand an und mit den Wippen unten an dem Mittel/Ringfinger hat man nochmal eine sinnvolle Möglichkeit Befehle abzusenden die normale Kontroller nicht bieten.
Die Konfigurationen für den Controller werden zum Teil von den Spieleherstellern angeboten, in der Regel kann man aber auf einen guten Pool an Community getriebenen Profilen zurückgreifen. Sprich ich habe in kürzester Zeit eine sinnvolle Belegung für den Controller für einen bestimmten Titel.
Wichtig zu erwähnen ist noch das man auch Spiele die bei Steam als Fremdspiele eingebucht werden damit spielen kann, für diesen Fall gibt es sogar Datenbanken die Konfigurationen für Steamfremde Spiele als Datei bereitstellt. Es ist also möglich den Controller für jedes Game zu nutzen das man auf dem PC installieren kann, nicht nur für Steam Titel.
Der Preis mag höher sein als der von anderen Controllern, dafür bietet der Steam Controller allerdings auch mehr. In Verbindung mit dem Steam-Link habe ich jetzt die aller allerbeste Konsole bei mir im Wohnzimmer, mein Steam mit meinem Power PC.
Über Big Picture und den Controller lässt sich Steam komfortabel bedienen und ich nehm einfach das pad in die Hand und alles läuft automatisch. Steam Link fährt meinen Rechner bei Bedarf hoch oder weckt ihn aus dem sleep modus, sobald Steam dann erreichbar ist startet der Big Picture Modus und ich kann zocken was ich will.
Ich nutze das W-LAN für die Übertragung, das funktioniert auch in der Regel, ich hatte es erst einmal das ich bei Dark Souls 2 ausgerechnet in einem Boss Kampf dann Aussetzer/Lags die durch die Übertragung zum Steam-Link bedingt war. Alternativ kann man auch das Steam Link per Ethernet anschliessen, aber ich finde dann brauch ich auch kein Steam-Link wenn ich da die Kabel zum Wohnzimmer legen muss, dann kann ich gleich den Fernseher als Monitor registrieren und nen Funk Pad benutzen.
Selten gab es auch mal Probleme mit Big Picture, zum Beispiel bei der Spiele Installation, ab und an ist dann der Steam-Link einfach abgeschmiert und ich musste dann doch aufstehen und ins Arbeitszimmer gehen und nachsehen was jetzt das Problem ist.
Mein Fazit, der Steam Controller ist meines erachtens der geilste Controller den man an einen PC anschliessen kann.

It doesn't even have any gameplay or choices that would require you to remember any of the information presented.
The game seemingly pretends to involve some kind of money management simulation, but actually contains no such thing. All the money you "spend" is shown on screen, and the girls will explain
the different options for train tickets and whatnot, and where you can go if you need to withdraw cash, but none of it ever comes to anything. There was exactly one time where I had to choose how to spend money (on a restaurant meal), and zero times where I needed to concern myself with topping up my prepaid train pass, or visiting an ATM, or... well, anything else the game beats you over the head with. If the intention was to teach practical information for prospective tourists, shouldn't that be, like, incorporated into the game somehow? I probably would have remembered it for more than ten seconds that way.
There are two girls to choose from, and by choose I mean you can save scum while blindly picking which area to visit, and hope the right one is the assigned tour guide for that region. After three days whoever has guided you the majority of the time is apparently locked in as your waifu, but you are forced to slog through two or three more days of information about random crap until you get to the end. I assume if you opt for the twelve-year-old tsundere, you just go to prison instead of living happily ever after, but I'm not going back and playing it again to confirm.
There are many spots where a well-placed dialogue choice could have steered you towards one or the other in a logical way, but instead your character just has a mind of his own. There is even a scene where the girls ask you to pick out costumes for them, and emphasize how seriously you should take the choice... and then there is no choice. Another where the older girl, a terrible cook, wants to help prepare dinner, and her sister doesn't want her help. Your character just gives his opinion without your input. The mind boggles at how such obvious opportunities could have been missed.
If a visual novel can't be bothered providing meaningful choices, then at least it should have a compelling story. If all else fails, it could at least, I suppose, give you something to fap to. This game has none of the above. Its sole use lies in streaming it and sharing the misery with friends while making jokes at its expense.

"Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~" is yet another title put out by MangaGamer (That's right, the eroge guys) and OverDrive. Unlike OverDrive's previous production, this is much more...educational. Learning about Japan with hospitality provided by two kawaii sisters sounds like quite the ideal visit, right? That question will determine your enjoyment of this game, and whether or not it warrants your investment.
Of course, you are a "filthy gaijin", for lack of political correctness, and your objective is rather simple: Go around Japan. Learn some history, and have copious amounts of fun while at it. Throughout the duration of your week in Japan, one of the two sisters (or both) will take you around notable places of the country, and intrigue you with some history and other facts about the place or landmark in question. A lot of the things in this game are basic knowledge that most people might have learned in high school or college, but OverDrive does make the effort to squeeze in some facts or speculations that you probably are not familiar with, and I commend them greatly for that. Added to the charm of the two sisters that will be embellished during the course of the game, it makes for a familiar, yet amiable experience that I think most VN fans will get a kick out of.
There is a bit more context to this game though, and that is the light romance that starts protruding from the main backdrop around the final third of the game. It isn’t very elaborate or urgent like in a true romance visual novel, but it’s concise, sweet, and serves as a little refrain that love triumphs cultural differences. It’s well written indeed, but to some extent the circumstances are not realistic. Unless you are one hell of a weeaboo that believes he is fated to meet his true lover on the other side of the world, the notion of being involved an intimate relationship in a completely foreign country within ONE WEEK will be questioned. After all, I think it bears stressing that this is just an ordinary traveler’s story other than the fact you are temporarily living with two cute girls you just happened to meet on the Internet. (
). That doesn’t mean this game does not have a plausible change of pace, which it definitely does when it starts shifting its gears upon learning more and more personal things about the two siblings. Despite the small nitpicks I have, the romance is well-done overall, and honestly, I couldn’t think of a more satisfying ending.
Should you ever spot a sale on “Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~”, I recommend you to not hesitate to pick this one up and give it a try as it is a charismatic yet adequately informative visual novel that satiates the need for a quick kawaii fix. There's a chance you might learn a thing or two along the way.

I beat Nier: Automata a month ago and it hasn't left my mind since. I still go on youtube to rewatch the most memorable scenes, I listen to some songs from the (
)
daily, and I generally can't stop thinking about the themes it presented and the mindbreaking twists in the story.
The story and the music are the main draws of the game. I haven't ever played a Yoko Taro game before so the way the story is structured is unlike anything I've ever played. After I saw the end credits once, the game tells you that you should keep playing to see everything Nier:Automata has to offer. I'm not usually the type to do New Game+ runs so I did some looking online to see if it's
necessary to keep playing after you get the first ending. The answer is
. If you stop playing after route A or even route B you're missing out on the best part of the game. Though, with how route B ends, I'm not sure how anyone can possibly think to put the game down at that point.
I would also recommend to everyone to think about every line of dialogue as you're playing. I'm not going to spoil it, but there was one line in particular that I thought was a pretty funny throwaway line at first but after completing the game I realized there was a specific reason for it that ties directly into the story. Everything ties together. I'm looking forward to replaying the whole game just to pick up on more little hints along the way that I was completely oblivious to the first time around. This is an extremely well-written game.
Despite how much I like the game I can't exactly recommend it to everyone. I've seen some people claim the gameplay is bad; I would disagree with that because I think it's about average for an action RPG. However if you only play video games strictly for the gameplay you're probably safe skipping Nier: Automata. I got to the point where I put it on easy to make the fights quicker because I didn't find them all
engaging. Plus I really wanted to see what happened next in the story.
This review probably sounds pretty vague but it's hard to write a comprehensive review without spoiling something along the way. When I bought the game, all I knew about it was that it was a JRPG and 2B was the protagonist. I think that's the best way to go in.
I don't say this lightly but if you're into story-driven RPGs this game is essential to play at some point. This is a totally unique experience (especially if you're like me and haven't played any Yoko Taro games before) and it'll stick with you long after you complete it. This isn't just a typical "good" JRPG - it's the highest opinion I've had of a video game in a really long time.

TL;DR: I can understand how pay2play and friend-nagging stuff can be off-putting, but the alternative is to pay $1.00-2.40 for each gun (earlier business model, still available BTW). And I will explain why they're worth it (for some).
I've played Gun Disassembly 2 (base of this game) for many years, and saw its library of models grow, and be regularly updated when the old models began to seem crude or low-poly. I know from the source that every model like this needs at least a month of work by several people, not including the research phase (you need either the full blueprints AND an engineer to convert them into working 3D mechanism; the actual gun on hand; or preferably both). So earlier, Gun Disassembly 2, which is the title World of Guns is based on, featured purchasable models, or a lifetime 100 bucks subscription. Which, to put it in perspective, is about 50-70 DLC's (to date) for $100.
Anyway, this game is an indispensable learning tool and instructional aid. I am a serious gun enthusiast, and if you ever wanted to really delve into the intricacies of firearm design, its history, and trends, and incredible elegance, I heartily recommend it. Of course, it is also an ultra-cheap way of illustrating a TV show or video about gun design. And if I was a teacher for gunsmiths or shooters, it would be my very special "save hours of tedious explanation without guarantee of understanding" magic wand. Even for US gun nuts, the luckiest ones on the planet, many of these firearms are still out of reach due to price, rarity or destructive potential (artillery pieces and BMP-3 are fitting examples).
I really can't speak from a normal gamer's perspective. But I wanted to point out the enormous deal of labor that went into each model, and the seriousness of approach. The menu design or spelling errors may at first give off the impression of something wonky and cheap. It isn't. World of Guns (and Gun Disassembly) is the Microsoft Flight Simulator of gun-disassembling games. Ugly in places, but can't be beat in realism and attitude.
Of course, until another hardcore gun-disassembling sim gets around! =)

Hi,
ich finde den steam controller super, initiale idee war für mich spiele die man mit pad spielen kann bequem von der couch zu spielen auf dem fernseher auf dem ich ohnehin schon viele sachen via stream angeschaut habe. Ich hatte mir irgendwann witcher 3 gekauft und es auch gespielt, fand das game super aber ich war total schnell so müde das ich mich lieber auf die couch gelegt habe und einen film zu schauen. Am liebsten hätte ich es gerne weiter gespielt aber die komfortable haltung in verbindung mit meiner müdigkeit war mir dann doch wichtiger.
Deswegen habe ich mir den Steam Controller sowie den Steam-link geholt. Die ursprüngliche Absicht mit dem Controller alle Spiele, auch die man bisher nur mit maus und tastatur spielen konnte, an einem Gerät zu bedienen geht meines erachtens nur bedingt auf, es gibt spiele die man mit maus und tastatur spielt und auch weiter so spielen sollte. Man kann zwar viel emulieren mit dem Pad (die Konfigurationsmöglichkeiten sind unglaublich), allerdings erreicht man nie eine Geschwindigkeit die man per Maus und Tastatur hat. Spiele die nicht direkt Pad Titel sind und wettbewerbsorientiert sind wie zum beispiel ego-shooter multiplayer kann man vergessen, single player ist es schon spielbar macht aber mit maus doch mehr spass. Games wie witcher sind dann perfekt für ein pad, es gibt strategie spiele die super mit dem Controller harmonieren wie zum Beispiel XCOM 2.
Wenn man keinen Controller hat und einen sucht für den PC denke ich ist man mit dem Steam Controller im Moment am besten aufgestellt, Maus und Tastatur ersatz ist eher als notlösung zu betrachten, dafür bin ich aber mit dem controller viel flexibler wie mit irgendeinem anderen Controller. Die Touch-Pads finde ich super und sind so viel präziser als ein zusätzlicher Analog Stick, ich könnte mir vorstellen das andere Peripherie Hersteller in Kürze nachziehen mit so einem Konzept weil es einfach besser ist. Die Verarbeitung ist gut, er fühlt sich gut in der Hand an und mit den Wippen unten an dem Mittel/Ringfinger hat man nochmal eine sinnvolle Möglichkeit Befehle abzusenden die normale Kontroller nicht bieten.
Die Konfigurationen für den Controller werden zum Teil von den Spieleherstellern angeboten, in der Regel kann man aber auf einen guten Pool an Community getriebenen Profilen zurückgreifen. Sprich ich habe in kürzester Zeit eine sinnvolle Belegung für den Controller für einen bestimmten Titel.
Wichtig zu erwähnen ist noch das man auch Spiele die bei Steam als Fremdspiele eingebucht werden damit spielen kann, für diesen Fall gibt es sogar Datenbanken die Konfigurationen für Steamfremde Spiele als Datei bereitstellt. Es ist also möglich den Controller für jedes Game zu nutzen das man auf dem PC installieren kann, nicht nur für Steam Titel.
Der Preis mag höher sein als der von anderen Controllern, dafür bietet der Steam Controller allerdings auch mehr. In Verbindung mit dem Steam-Link habe ich jetzt die aller allerbeste Konsole bei mir im Wohnzimmer, mein Steam mit meinem Power PC.
Über Big Picture und den Controller lässt sich Steam komfortabel bedienen und ich nehm einfach das pad in die Hand und alles läuft automatisch. Steam Link fährt meinen Rechner bei Bedarf hoch oder weckt ihn aus dem sleep modus, sobald Steam dann erreichbar ist startet der Big Picture Modus und ich kann zocken was ich will.
Ich nutze das W-LAN für die Übertragung, das funktioniert auch in der Regel, ich hatte es erst einmal das ich bei Dark Souls 2 ausgerechnet in einem Boss Kampf dann Aussetzer/Lags die durch die Übertragung zum Steam-Link bedingt war. Alternativ kann man auch das Steam Link per Ethernet anschliessen, aber ich finde dann brauch ich auch kein Steam-Link wenn ich da die Kabel zum Wohnzimmer legen muss, dann kann ich gleich den Fernseher als Monitor registrieren und nen Funk Pad benutzen.
Selten gab es auch mal Probleme mit Big Picture, zum Beispiel bei der Spiele Installation, ab und an ist dann der Steam-Link einfach abgeschmiert und ich musste dann doch aufstehen und ins Arbeitszimmer gehen und nachsehen was jetzt das Problem ist.
Mein Fazit, der Steam Controller ist meines erachtens der geilste Controller den man an einen PC anschliessen kann.

More than anything I am happy with how damned configurable this thing is. There are a considerable number of settings and options that can be tweaked to your liking, making the controller overall very versatile. It is also very quick and easy to remap keys in-game with the press of a few buttons through the steam overlay.
I've had the controller for about three weeks now. I was skeptical at first but it grew on me quickly. The trackpads are great in most games, especially those designed for a mouse and keyboard. It almost completely eliminates the need to get up and go over to the mouse and keyboard when I'm on the couch playing on my tv.
The XYAB buttons seem awkward and tiny at first, but once you get used to it you can press them more quickly than on a 360 controller because your thumb can rest between them while still touching the edges of all four buttons. The addition of grip buttons and the ability to hold a button down to make the controller behave differently (ex. Change joystick to a mouse, map additional buttons) was a stroke of genius. The only areas that the 360 controller outperforms it are in fighting games and action games (though these can be played effectively on the Steam controller) and in theory racing games, though I haven't tried one yet.

Seeing as we are nearing the end of development of this title with v1.5 (which is not a bad thing!) I feel like I should write down some of my thoughts on this amazing sim and thank Reiza for the fantastic work they put into this.
What has Reiza has achieved with Automobilista (AMS) on such an old engine is nothing short of amazing. While many sims have already moved on from gMotor2, Reiza managed to squeeze the best out of it and a little more. They created a spectacular simracing title, with many features that many modern sims don't have.
Perhaps given it's developed on a old engine the visuals might not be the best out there (though I personally like them, I understand that not many people feel the same way) and VR support in non-existant which might a deal breaker for some. It also lacks any weather outside of sunny/cloudy which is a bit of a shame.
What AMS excells at and why it is loved by many in the simracing community is simply the variety of the content available. AMS is centered around motorsport found in South America, which makes sense since Reiza is a Brazilian studio. If you are looking for yet another sim with GT3s.. well AMS isn't that. And thats what makes it great. I does have plenty of European and North American circuits, but most of AMS' track repertoire consist of tracks in South America.. tracks you probably never heard of! The same thing goes for cars. While there are some series which are clearly inspired by various overseas series, most of the conent is centered around South America. You can find some series which are inspired by real ones (V8 Supercars, modern and historic F1s, Porsche Carrera Cup to name some) but you won't find much official licensed content. There is some licenced content like the Brazilian Stock Cars or Formula Truck, but there are only a few of those. Some people view this as a negative, but having this sort of variety is what makes AMS stand out in my opinion. Learning new tracks in fun, exploring new series I've never heard of and trying out cars I also never heard of is simply a blast. It is worth noting that AMS has a full mod support, so if you don't find the content attractive enough, there are always mods :) The CART Extreme conversion from rFactor is just superb for example.. the same goes for some of the tracks you can find online.
The physics is consistently good in all cars. I honestly don't think there's a single bad car in AMS.. all of them drive differently, which makes each car unique in its own way.. The FFB available is top notch and they even have a full support for the Xbox controller with haptic feedback and all.. AI is also very good and since multiplayer is not very active in AMS (outside of league racing and
club races which I highly recommend) the AI does a great job. You also have tools to create custom championships with custom rule sets to keep you entertained if you're interested in offline racing.
Thats all that comes to my mind currently about AMS..
As a closing note I would like to thank Reiza for all their hard work they put into this title. I loved the way you guys communicated with the community - each month I was looking forward to read a new development update and see whats new. You offered us with a Beta to try out new things before they were pushed into the final build (oh how I loved Formula Classic with 4 bars of boost!!) and gave us high quality content for a fair price. You've done a fantastic job with AMS and I can't wait to see what you guys will come up with after AMS.

Set in the dark, dystopian future of 2022, ‘Deus Ex: Human Revolution’ is a fantastic blend of the First Person Shooter (FPS) | Stealth | RPG genres and a testament to gaming as both an art form and sublime story-telling medium.
Released by Eidos | Square Enix in 2013, the world of ‘Deus-Ex’ is a bleak near-future where Corporations are increasingly more powerful – and Biotech firms vie for control of the Human Cryogenic Augmentation market. These increasingly high stakes result in a growing focus on corporate espionage and security – enter Adam Jensen – an ex-SWAT Commander hired as head of security for Sarif Industries. The opening credits detail Jensen’s brutal execution-style killing during a break-in at Sarif Industries, his resurrection through cryogenic augmentation and drops you into the shoes of the Part-Man, Part-Machine, to piece together the fragmented memories of the past and uncover the cause of the attack. An engrossing, deep campaign takes you around the world, on sprawling open world levels where the broader storyline is broken up through the distractions of a richly atmospheric world, numerous side quests, and lots of collectibles and readable background lore scattered around the maps.
Gameplay is aligned around the game’s 4 pillars of FPS based-combat, Stealth mechanics, RPG elements (of character customization) and Player Choice in story-telling direction – and the game seamlessly switches from one mode to another. You are allowed considerable breadth of choice in approaching every situation – Frontal Assault, Stealth or even Smooth-Talking your way past the opposition - building in replayability into the title as well. Several different situational outcomes, great graphics with a trademark orange machine-hue, a brooding pulsating score, responsive K&M controls and controller support round out a well polished title.  Note that this review is based on the ‘Director’s Cut’ version of the game which includes all DLC integrated directly into the overall campaign – resulting in close to 75-80 hours of gameplay to complete the campaign, track down all side-quests, see through multiple endings, read all the lore etc (but your mileage may vary).

Minor quibbles with the game include the occasional scripted boss battle that while serving to move the broader narrative along, tend to stifle the freedom otherwise celebrated throughout the game. Other issues include longish load times, an inordinate disk space requirement (of 20+ Gigs) and being particularly resource heavy, resulting in some framerate drop issues.
Overall however, ‘Deus-Ex: Human Revolution’ is a triumphant blend of story-telling and disparate game genres. A visually stunning and immersive world, a deep, layered campaign, large open world levels, multiple endings determined by player choice, and very good replayability make this one of the best story-driven titles of recent memory. While the game’s broadly Sci-Fi / Cyber-punk theme will admittedly not be to everyone’s taste, for fans of the genre and classic sci-fi flicks such as RoboCop and BladeRunner, this is essential gaming and overall, a shining example of Gaming Evolved. Very Highly Recommended – Rated (9.5/10)
