This game is really strange. It puts on this facade of being cartoony and goofy, and just your average rogue-like beat em' up. What you don't see in the first few playthroughs is the potential for this game to force you to refute the comfort and consistency of a normal gaming experience, and make you deeply question what makes you keep pressing on in the face utter madness and unfairness.
The answer to that question can be broken into two parts.
1. Your skill.
The player actually has a pretty big influence in their success. There are no dice rolls, this game is a pure and simple beat em up, with a surprisingly fluid combat system.
2. Beating the game. And once you get to the endless dungeon, more importantly, killing the ever-loving christ out of Rolf Ironbutt.
Do you think that's a funny name? DO YOU THINK IT'S A FUNNY NAME???? I'M SURE YOU WILL BE LAUGHING. I'M 100% SURE YOU WILL BE LAUGHING WHEN YOU MEET HIM, AND IT'S NOT BECAUSE OF ANYTHING FUNNY.
You will spend hours in the dungeons amassing countless curses, learning to fight rooms of at least 20, 30 mobs with a giant foot creating a steady breeze running up your back from crashing behind you every 5 seconds, as you run FRANTICALLY, in the DARK, TRYING TO LIFESTEAL YOUR SIGNIFICANTLY LOWERED, CONSTANTLY DRAINING HEALTH, ALL THE WHILE AVOIDING A SINGLE STRIKE ON THE EXPLOSIVE BARRELS RAINING FROM THE SKY EVERY ROOM, WHICH CAN LEAD TO MOST OF YOUR PRECIOUS HP DISSAPEARING, OR JUST ENDING YOUR RUN FOR NO REASON, BECAUSE MORE THAN LIKELY A *GIANT ♥♥♥♥ING FOOT* WILL COME DOWN AND REMOVE THE REST OF YOUR HP ONCE YOU GET STUNNED BY ONE OF THOSE BARRELS.
And then... you wil meet Rolf. You will step out of the shadows into floor 25 bloody and disheveled, and face this boss. You will then embrace and appreciate the nature of this unstable game, and realize how his death rests timidly upon the precipice of true lunacy and obsession.
You have to deal with a fresh hell every run. Your character will become increasingly grotesque the further you venture into the dungeons, as will your thoughts and feelings. You either accept the madness or fight it, but your efforts are in vain if you do not make it out alive.

I am a first time player of AK.
I've read alot of the negative reviews to get a good insight of what to prepare for when I got into the game.
1st. You must realize this is not really pay to win, but like a lot has said, it's pay for convenience. ESPECIALLY in regards to inventory space. There are a few quests that will grant you a few more spaces. BUT in the end, if you want to seriously play the game, with PVE vs PVP, you will need bank space and inventory space.
I shelled out money to buy Aura Points or AP as they call it to buy 20 slot bags to create more space. I had to buy 5 of them. That's 26$ with a bit of tax.
Once that was done, I found that the collecting of crafting goods and etc was not so panicky. You realize as time goes by space becomes a premium and you have to start stripping out stuff. That sucked.
But that 26$ investment was a wise one. So if you can't spend up to 26$ on this game JUST for space. You may NOT want to play it for the PVE aspect. I don't do PvP so I couldn't tell you if you will need to spend more than $26 on the game.
2nd. There is crafting in this game. There is gathering too. And unlike some other games, they don't completely shaft you if you don't pay more to buy 'better' crafting gear. Surprisingly, even if you fail, you still can keep crafting.
3rd. The rules of crafting kind of is clunky. In the sense that it's not easy to do. I had to use Wiki's alot to figure out what the heck was all the goods and materials I was picking up to use and what good was it for? Super annoying. But once the Wiki explained it, I was ok. Thank you wiki nerds.
4th. Fishing rules in the games was rough to understand. I've been playing video games since Pac Man was cutting edge. I've probably played thousands. I've had fun with hundreds. I can think of dozens that have truly made me think. I can even think of a scant handful that have coaxed a genuine emotional reaction from me.
But Nier hit me in a place deeper than all of that; somewhere cold, vast, melancholy and eternal. This was as close to a legit spiritual experience I have ever had with a videogame. The only other game that came anywhere close to invoking that reaction was maybe Xenogears back in the 90s.
Incidentally, the game is also ridiculously fun. The combat is fluid and challenging. The characters are unique and interesting. The world is gorgeous, the music is gorgeous, and the women are gorgeous. Playing this game at my humble battlestation instead of in some opulent home theatre feels kind of like drinking expensive champagne from a plastic beer pong cup.
Is it perfect? No, because nothing in this sorry, dying world will ever be perfect. Does it scrape against the ceiling of those limitiations? Yes, and with unforgettable results.
tl;dr - Do you have a brain in your head, a heart in your chest or a dong between your legs? Did you answer 'yes' to at least two out of those three questions? Then this game will mean something special to you.

The game's story takes place in 2241, 80 years after the events of Fallout and 164 years after the war. It tells the story of the original hero's descendant and their quest to save their primitive tribe from starvation by finding an ancient environmental restoration machine known as the Garden of Eden Creation Kit(GECK).
The player is free to move at will until they enter into combat. Combat gives them a number of action points to move, fire, check their equipment, reload and the like. When a player uses up all of their action points, they end their turn and enemies start theirs. Combat and completion of jobs or quests rewards the player with experience points with which they can level up their characters and apply beneficial perks to become more suited to the dangerous post-apocalyptic world. General gameplay consists of traveling and interacting with local inhabitants and organizations to complete goals and aid or inhibit the NPCs. The player's actions dictate what future story or gameplay opportunities are available. Mature themes such as alcohol consumption, drug usage and sex are present. Organized crime, prostitution and slavery are major elements of the setting. Character creation is based on the SPECIAL roleplaying system.
The Fallout games both allow you to create truly individualized characters, which you can then role-play essentially as you see fit. In the Fallout games you can choose to play a righteous avenger, a nonviolent scientist, a self-motivated bigot, an evil sociopath, a jinxed moron, or some personalized variation of these character types, and you'll experience the game quite differently depending upon your character's attributes and actions. While other role-playing games boast of "dozens" of available player character types, your experience with any of those characters will often be almost identical to all of the others except you'll use different weapons in combat. No game does a better job than Fallout 2 at actually giving you opportunities to act in a distinctive manner representative of the role you choose to play with your character. A smooth talking, highly intelligent character may be able to persuade other characters to reveal their secrets, while a dim witted thug character may be unable to express anything other than basic intentions and risks being manipulated and sold into slavery. Fallout 2 is the real deal when it comes to roleplaying, and its open-ended nature makes it far more replayable than the average game of the genre.
In Fallout 2 your character can be accompanied by a number of computer-controlled nonplayer characters. Unlike in Fallout, nonplayer characters can now wear armor and gain proficiency in skills as your character does, making them more consistently useful during the course of the game.

Performance issues aside I really enjoyed Dead Rising 3.
I've never been as impressed with the amount of zombies on screen since Left 4 Dead came out and blew us all away. This game has hundreds of zombies on screen at one time and they seem to have refined the zombies, their animations and AI. Zombies are zombies. They're slow, dumb, react to noises, light, movement and shamble towards you. They're not very threatening unless in a large group and in confined spaces. They may as well have been ripped straight out of a Romero movie which is fine by me as it oozes atmosphere. It just feels satisfying to see a hundred zombies between you and your objective and watching them slowly walk or crawl towards you from all directions and then to try outrun them or face having to kill a swath of zombies just to carve a path out. Overall the zombies are really impressive and the amount of them on screen at one time is equally as impressive.
While I really liked the zombies in this game on the other hand there's the human enemies which are terrible. They seem to only really take damage from guns but they dodge bullets as if they've come straight from The Matrix. It feels like only the first bullet you shoot at them actually does anything while the rest go through them or deal zero damage even if they don't dodge. I found the best way was to either get a shotgun to the face(Which only worked 50% of the time if even) or to shoot once, wait two seconds and then shoot again until they died(Which would generally take three headshots). Some human AIs would dodge constantly which made killing them very frustrating and completely detracted from the game as a whole. It simply wasn't a good mechanic to allow AI to dodge bullets and be able to spam dodge. Terrible concept altogether. Give them armour, sure but leave out the broken bullet dodge. On that note your companion AI were just abysmal. They hardly ever attacked, took forever to get into vehicles with you and just took damage. The entire game I ended up ditching companions because of their terrible, inexcusible AI. Zombies are a 10 out of 10 but humans are definitely the polar opposite.
The game itself is actually rather interesting. Unlike Dead Rising and Dead Rising 2, games which were a bit too tongue in cheek, this venture into the franchise was surprisingly more serious but counter balanced by a nice bit of silliness reserved only for combo weapons and combo vehicles which proved to be extremely fun. The weapons and vehicles weren't too over the top a la Dead Rising 2 but a nice medium; fun, easy to use and highly effective. The story and characters were serious, had more going on and were quite likable where most of the silliness came in the form of optional side bosses which were a nice distraction and good for a chuckle. I really enjoyed the pace and humour of Dead Rising 3 which had me hooked playing it for some hours straight.
The interiors and the open world of the game were disappointing for a "next gen" title. There was only a few houses or places you could enter fully and explore. Most of the stores were single rooms and little more. The major inside areas themselves felt relatively small but did prove to be atmospheric and entertaining. The police station for instance, while short, certainly was done well. Collections and blueprints were nicely added. All of that optional stuff around the world was well placed. The majority were easy to get it with a handful of locked away or not so obvious ones to get to. It was enjoyable to actually spend the time hunting each zone for these collectibles.
Side quests and the Untold Stories DLC were a mixed bag. The side quests in the main game weren't annoying, drawn out or overly complicated. They were actually pretty simple things to do and weren't very tiring or taxing in the grand scale of things. They do add to the game so i'm glad they were there as opposed to being cut from it or just wanting them removed altogether like the horrible side missions in Dead Rising 2(Hand holding AI and babysitting them from point A to B). The Untold Stories DLCs were terrible. Episode 2 made no sense, it was extremely frustrating to play through and added nothing to the original game at all. It basically tells of what happened to the illegals which, turns out, wasn't much. You're given no reason to care about them in the main game so why would you care them in a dedicated DLC? Episode 1 was okay... a bit repetitive but it did add a decent amount to the game itself in terms of story. Episode 3 was enjoyable except for the side mission(It's just one but it's very frustrating) but it adds virtually nothing to the game at all. Episode 4, however, tells the story of what happened after you left. Each DLC is 1-2hours long depending on if you get the collectibles or do the side missions. Worth doing one or two of them but Episode 2 is a recommended "SKIP!"
I would definitely recommend this game on sale. If there's a Dead Rising 4 and it's released on PC with better optimisation I would definitely buy it full price.

Let me clear up something first:
You don't play through the game a zillion times! It's twice.
First playthrough is roughly 12 hours. It's "Side A", one perspective only.
Second "New Game" can be done in just a couple hours and is "Side B". A and B are just different character perspectives.
Third "New Game" is not a replay at all, but is Chapter 2 and continues the story. It's all new stuff.
The other important endings are simply picking a different option right at the end. Chapter Select exists.
All other 20 endings are joke endings. They're not anything serious and you may come across one depending on how you play. It's hilarious when it does happen but you aren't replaying the game over and over for them. Again, Chapter Select exists should you want to find them.
Anyway, so to get the main experience, you only replay the game twice, really. The third is not a replay and instead is a direct continuation of the story. It's just the Director's style of game.
It's a neat a game. Not Platinum's Gold Standard combat, but they certainly make the flow feel infinitely better than the first Nier game. The music is pretty good and relaxing, and the story themes are decently thought provoking. A little anime cliche here and there, but it's serviceable. There is something missing from the game making it a must play for me, but I can't quite figure out what! Either way, I did enjoy a fair bit of it.

In all seriousness, this game carries a lot of parallels with Grand Theft Auto, making it a spiritual spinoff of sorts. Fortunately, it shares the characteristics that make us love GTA with a passion, with a twist of youthful innocence (relatively, at least) that lets it stand on its own. Bullsworth Academy is set up to be the worst school in America in the same way Liberty City was called the worst place in America. There's the warring factions (cliques instead of legit street gangs) with their scheming leaders, and the authorities who overexert their power to bet the snot out of anyone they can (while there are legitimate police in the town, prefects will chase you around the school).
The seemingly unique thing about Bully's mechanics in practice is that you are not necessarily encouraged to be a rampaging jerk. Your rewards mostly come from doing well in class, helping people out, giving flowers and chocolate to girls, and standing up to bullies. Dan Houser, creative director at Rockstar Games, has compared Jimmy Hopkins to Niko Bellic, in that they come the closest of all of Rockstar's protagonists to try and maintain a moral compass. His comment can be read in full on the Bully Wiki page on Jimmy Hopkins.
For me, at least, Bully is to Rockstar is like what Barry Lyndon is to Stanley Kubrick: a cult classic that has mostly taken a backseat when compared to a great creative's other works, but is still worth your time. It's obvious that the developers are very proud of the work being done (though the original studio, Rockstar Vancouver, is long gone), since it's referenced once in a while in GTA (Bullsworth Academy on TV in IV and the Hopkins jersey in V come to mind).
Oh, and you can kiss boys and/or girls, with one of its characters being implied to be gay or bi AND is sympathetic and kind.
In conclusion, Bully is worth your time and money because its a unique take on the sandbox gameplay we've come to expect from Rockstar, blending those elements with the young mischief we associate with high school for an underated piece of master work.
And for $15 + tax, the experience can be yours.

For my sim racing friends: pick this up with the season pass while it's on sale. It may look oldschool but for a proper driving simulator it's actually really fun. Physics and force feedback are up there with the best in class... but there are plenty of sims that can say that. This one beats them by providing the full package out of the box - the stuff you actually enjoy in driving games, and lots of it. This is particularly the case if you miss a quality single player experience. (There's MP too but I haven't tried that.)
It has a fantastic comprehensive library of cars (including some unique classes) and tons of tracks and variations, which all feel very different. Every class has a full championship available, some several. Racing against AI is actually pretty good, with convincing 3 wide stock car action, an ai spotter on the radio, and real safety cars and flag rules. Glorified lawn mower 1 gear rental carts feel like rental carts, 70s muscle cars feel like they should, modern stock cars (particularly the aussie and brasilian formats) are especially satisfying. The insane open wheel and dirt cars, even trucks! are all convincing. This is also the only sim I have played where they sixties formula 1 cars drive like a modern evolution of the punishing GPL engine. As for F1, no licenses, but you can drive representatives of major format from the sixties onwards on historically matched track variants. Awesome. :)
I'm kicking myself for having bought it a few days ago for full price, but after putting a few hours in I can see it's worth every penny. If you are an even occasional sim racer you'd be nuts to pass this up during the sale given the value here. I can see the thirty or so championship seasons on offer being my go-to offline racing kick for some time. :)

Look I know that you're gonna think I'm wrong that I don't like this game but please let me explain, and I'm sorry if you don't like my opinion of this game but I'll try my best to explain why I don't like it.
I've given this game a very reasonable 15 hours, and everytime I play I just end up not liking it and not having any fun. I really am at a loss for explanation as to why I don't like this game, since I loved Fallout 1, I loved it so much. I figured Fallout 2 would be even better than Fallout 1, many many people say it is the best RPG ever and constantly makes top 100 lists everytime. But for some reason it just always makes me hate it, and I try every single time to like it but I just can't force myself too.
Listen I'll be one to say it might've been good, maybe even a masterpiece back in the day but for me this game comes off as... a piece of garbage. Now again, let me explain my reasoning.
First off, I hate the combat, I find it the most atrocious thing about this. I played Fallout 1, with practically the same system but I don't remember missing nearly every single time I clicked on the enemy, and when I do hit, I expect to do suffecient damage, but to no avail. My best build I put so many points into unarmed but even then the game was stupidly difficult in how I could deal with enemies, not even Dark Souls level hard it was just ridiculous in how tough these enemies were being. People say it is tactical, to which I disagree, combat for nearly everything feels the same, at least for the enemies I've been fighting throughout these 15 hours. Everytime I try and kill something, I die, even with a good amount of points invested in my stats. It's just not fun.
This means that everytime I try a playthrough of this game, I eventually die so many times that I just can't get into it and the run is over. The first cave/enemy infested area you go to you can't even complete, the enemies there are stupidly difficult and I tried it with a combat focused character to no avail WITH a party member.
The first time I played this, and this might sound pathetic, I had to look up a walkthrough. You wanna know why? Because for some reason almost every 90s game back then pretty much required you too know everything about the game, which doesn't make sense because well...how the hell would I when I've never played it before? I had to use a walkthrough many times. Once for getting past the very very first place you start in the game because I didn't know you could use dynamite on an inpenetrable door, yes an INPENETRABLE door. If a game requires you to practically look up a walkthrough then it has failed, it does not provide clear help and it just isn't fun to look up a walkthrough since it makes the game feel lazy at not teaching you this stuff beforehand.
The soundtrack as far as I can tell is awesome, but it recycles a lot of stuff from Fallout 1, which I find to be a little lazy, but neverthless it still is very good to listen to. The atmosphere of the world is also very good, and I think it is a step up from what Fallout 1 had.
I've looked up guides on how to play this game right and enjoy it, but they just don't work. When I get told to save everytime I speak to someone, that just isn't fun, and it severely kills any need or want for interaction with any character in the world, and it just shows how broken this game can get if you push it far enough. When I get told to seek out an OP armor set or to try and work my very soul off for a car, that just isn't fun, and ends up being a waste of time in the long run. When I get told to make a specific and "perfect" build to get through the game that doesn't allow roleplaying at all, and for being called the best RPG of all time that just doesn't make sense to make one build to simply progress through the game normally. When someone does all that and tells me to follow very specific rules to enjoy the game, not only does it inhibit the whole RPG aspect, it makes the game feel cheap when I am playing down one path. When I get told to just "get better" it never works and it always makes me hate this community more and more if you just can't accept that some people need help or time to adjust to this game.
When I see people who play the game and see that they have the same problems as me, they always, no matter what, get ridiculed for being "bad" at the game, and that kills the sense of finding help when you just get bullied for doing so. Why do we not like that? Because it's not helpful and if you do that to us players kindly asking for help in the game it will make us quit playing not just because of the inability to find help, but the pure fact that we have seen the true face of this community who flat out refuses to acknowledge or hear anything bad about their "best" RPG of all time. I know getting your favorite game♥♥♥♥♥♥on sometimes is not a good feeling but when you say our opinions are unfounded or we are just bad at the game or just be an outright d**k about it, you're just gonna make us angrier and more knowledgeable to the kinds of people you are about this, refusing to accept the bad aspects of this game.
For giving this game 15 hours to try and interest me, it has utterly, and miserably failed to capture me in its grasp. In the end this game just brands itself as a waste of time and not that fun after all is said and done. I don't know maybe I just need to play this game in an updated format like in the form of an enhanced edition like the other Black Isle games got but that doesn't make sense when I played the original Fallout 1 without any trouble.
I wouldn't reccomend just downvoting this out of pure disagreement, because it won't help my impression of the game and it's community, it will just drive me to further dislike the game for what it is. That being said please please tell me how to properly enjoy this, because I want to, and I think I can enjoy it if someone can give me exactly the right tips on how to properly play the game.
Unless someone can tell me how the game should be played it will be one of, if not my most hated game of all time, which I never thought I would say to something that's been hyped as the best RPG of all time, as this is my favorite genre and I have liked many other classics from the 90s.
Again, please tell me how to enjoy this game, I don't want to see myself throwing it away without giving it a really really good try. If you've made it this far, thanks for reading, and for not just downvoting this out of pure shock to see someone hating on something that is honestly kind've overrated. "You can play as a porn star! Oh man!" Yes and what more? Be helpful and say why this is truly the best RPG of all time. Because I am tired of people just saying how incredible it is without explaining why.
I'll keep trying to play the game as best I can but as long time progresses and as this review goes unanswered, I likely won't pick up the game ever again. For now I say Fallout: New Vegas is the best Fallout, with 1 being a very close second.

Coming into this game, all I knew it was about is you shot stuff. What I experienced is some of the most fun shooting stuff I've had. In this game, everything but having fun takes a step back. The story? From what little bit of it you have to experience, all I could tell is people wanted to use Hell for energy and it backfired for some reason (Reason is told to you ofc). But there's very few cutscenes, maybe 10 minutes of gameplay where you are forced to view story related stuff. There's audio log type things you have to stand still to listen to, or you could click them and leave to go kill more stuff. The majority of the story is told by voice comms from two people. The original half life has more character models than this game does story characters, which means not counting the demons you kill.
But, they took the shooting aspect and made it as fun as possible. Reloading? Not fun.(Okay, the super shotgun reloads and that was my favorite gun, but it's dope) Running out of ammo? Not fun. Shooting demons? Fun. Non stop shooting demons with metal music? Super fun. It took me roughly ten and a half hours to beat this game and I never got bored. Demons explode, you can glory kill demons where the doom guy rips them apart in some fashion depending on where you initiated it, and this game is chock full of secrets and easter eggs. There's probably about ten guns in this game, a chainsaw, and a BFG. Earlier, i hinted that you don't run out of ammo. In the first hour when you only have two guns, you'll probably run out a few times but a glory kill usually gives you enough. After you get about three guns, running out of ammo is rare especially once you get the chainsaw (A chainsaw kill drops tons of ammo, but it uses fuel which does not drop from said chainsaw kill).
In all, this game was amazingly fun. More fun than I expected. If you like shooting stuff, this game is great. If you like story, I've heard you can read about it but don't expect to experience it like The Last of Us or Firewatch.

My thoughts on this controller can be summed like this:
I've been using game controllers since before I could walk, and the last controller that felt like this much of a game-changer for me was the original Dualshock for the Playstation One.
Since the dualshock, almost every major controller has followed the same basic principles -- dual analog-stick setup, two triggers, four face buttons and a d-pad, and rumble feedback.  For nearly 18 years, that's all we've had to work with, and (aside from some meager attempts at motion control) there really hasn't been any big revolution in gamepad design.  The Steam Controller is the first legitimate leap forward in game controller design that I've had the privilege of experiencing.
The haptic feedback is amazing -- pressing buttons gives you a nice, satisfying "kick" which makes it feel that much more responsive (It's almost comparable to the "clicking" feeling of a pressing buttons on a mechanical keyboard) -- and I wouldn't be surprised if every controller from here on out adopts a similar technology.  The touchpads are extremely responsive and capable of being fine-tuned for every game you play.  In fact, every aspect of the controller is extremely customizeable, from the amount and type of haptic feedback for each type of input, to the deadzones of the analog stick and the responsiveness of the dual-stage triggers.
To address some of the criticisms I've heard about this controller:
To those who say that the build quality feels "cheap," I really don't get that at all.  The triggers and buttons don't feel as solid and smooth-pressing as the Xbox One controller, but it's not a huge difference and it certainly doesn't affect my playing experience.  In fact, I really don't get how people are comparing this controller negatively to any existing console gamepad.  The customizability and compatibility is lightyears beyond anything else available on the market.  Changing the controller settings is more than just the ability to change a few bindings -- you can basically program the thing to act like half a dozen different controllers from game to game.  With a traditional gamepad you're at the whim of game developers to implement compatibility or forced to use external software like Xpadder to try to make your controller emulate a keyboard.  The steam controller and Big Picture Mode basically does all of that work for you, and it works extremely well -- I haven't run into any major compatibility problems yet.  Community bindings are also great, especially to use as a starting point for your own personal profile for each game.
Basically, if you don't mind tinkering with settings to get *just* the right setup for each game, then I couldn't recommend this controller more highly.

I prefer using gamepads whenever possible. Typically I use either my DualShock 3 or Wii U Pro. I picked up a Steam controller so that I could develop for it (someone has been working on making cool stuff for HaxeFlixel that integrates with it), and because Steam suggests making your game Steam Controller compatible.
I spent a couple of hours trying to 'break it in' when I got mine, playing all kinds of games - 2D, 3D, etc.
The problems are:
It's unwieldy, very big, and the contours just don't feel comfortable.
The button placements are just weird... L2/R2 are like on the bottom of the thing?
The L-stick is too 'tall', so it feels really awkward trying to use it with any precision in, say, a platformer game or something, but the circle pad things are way too big, so trying to use the left one as a Dpad is gross... Especially in a 2D game - I want to be able to sit my thumb on the D-pad, and 'rock' it around to move. This doesn't work on this controller since there's no resistance to your movements, and you realize your thumb is all the way on the edge and have to quickly change direction...  and the right one is a touch-pad thing that is supposed to be used as the R-stick, but, unlike a 'real' R-stick that requires some pressure to do something with, just accidently brushing it sends the camera spinning wildly (in a 3d game with a camera).
I feel like Valve looked at all of the existing gamepads out there and intentionally tried to make something as different and as unique as possible, while ignoring the practicalities that led to the designs that currently exist.
I absolutely DO NOT recommend buying one of these.

This is by far the best controller I've ever used. It takes some time to get used to it though, (just like any other thing you're trying for the first time) - in particular, the fact that the action keys (a,b,x,y) are at the bottom right rather than the top.
What I really like about the controller though, is the ergonomic placement of the common controls (i.e. the touchpads). It might not be immediately evident, but with regular controllers, your thumb are always in a contracted, and slightly stressed position. By placing the touchpads at the top, the thumbs are able to sit in the rest position and effortlessly glide across the touchpads, all while having the unique feel of the haptic feedback beneath them.
Another important thing to note here as well, is just how accurate you can get with those touchpads. They're so accurate, you can actually replace your mouse with it. It's just like the touchpad on your laptop...only better.
The main event however is the gyro aim. As far as I'm concerned this is it the best thing to happen to controllers since the introduction of the analog sticks. It adds a whole new level of precision control - something you could never hope to achieve with any other gamepad.
TL;DR This gamepad i seconded only to a mouse and keyboard

The controller feels great, works great and is a unique piece of hardware. It feels comfortable to hold and use, the buttons and triggers feel just right and it has these new additions -- a pair of touchpads, grip buttons and a gyroscope. The grip buttons are easy to adjust to and are convenient, but the main addition of the touchpads may need some time for you to learn and adjust to use. The gyro is a rare, if not odd case, but that also takes time to getting used to.
Valve's software support for the Steam Controller is superb, and it grows better every day. It's a plug and play experience to a Steam Link, or any PC that has Steam running in it, and games work on it in ways you can customize. The degree of customization for the controller is very high as it covers what keypresses it should follow, which modes it can perform, and more. It's even more detailed with the touchpads since they emulate either joysticks / analog sticks, a mouse, a touch menu or stylus-like input. You can customize how it performs as you scroll towards the outer ring, the deadzone and when you press it and many others.
With an update, the Steam Controller also provides the benefit of personalizing it to your needs (with a name and beeping tones when you turn it on) and it actually stores your controller layouts to particular games. It's convenient when you're moving across PCs or friends and you want to bring back your controller layout just like at your PC.
I highly recommend the Steam Controller, but only to those who are willing to experiment, to learn and to tweak minute details on how they play their games. This isn't great if you just want to pick up a controller and start playing. It takes getting used to, and it'll feel sluggish and slow at first and may want to go back to KB+mouse or a traditional controller. But once you get over that, you'll be able to make your gaming experience that works comfortably on a couch or off the desk on games where it couldn't on a controller.
(Reviewed after three weeks of use, with the following games: Cities: Skylines, Crypt of the Necrodancer, XCOM: Enemy Within, XCOM 2, The Witcher 2, Trails in the Sky SC, Spelunky, Tales of Zestiria, Civilization V)

This game..... THIS GAME!
Where to begin.... I've mentioned this before in my reviews about racing games/sims, I'll say it again, I primarily play racing and sim type games on PC and console, if there's been a racing game released on either in the last 30 years I've likely played it. In regards to sims; Assetto Corsa, Project Cars, rFactor 2, R3E.... you name it, I own them all, and play them all. Automobilista has to be my favorite out of all of them!
Here's why;
Automobilista is a fantastic racing sim. Reiza has taken rFactor 1 and built on that to the point that it feels like a new experience. Essentially what we have here is rFactor 1 with all the best mods included and updated, plus many little tweaks here and there to bring one of the best racing experiences available on the PC at this time.
Sure the graphics may not be on par with something like AC or PCars, but this is a DX9 title and for that era of game engine, the visuals certainly do more then enough to appear convincing and many of the car models included as well as available via modding are faithfully reproduced inside and out. The full daytime spectrum is available when racing from dawn till dusk and overnight, unfortunately weather is currently not an option but I dont find I miss that too much since the simulation is so engrossing in other ways.
By default the game ships with some of the most diverse racing series available in a game and this is great as it allows you to dip your toes into something you may not have otherwise tried. From stock cars, to Porsche GT3 cars, to nearly EVERY era of Formula 1 cars and Trophy Trucks to Karts, this game has it all. Oh yeah.... The Formula cars.... Automobilista has a car from nearly every era of Formula one, and this is awesome! Im a big F1 fan, so its really cool to be able to drive all the diff car styles throughout the history of the sport when you please. As far as track content goes the included list is lacking.... it's mostly made up of random Brazilian tracks that no one really knows or cares to know.... There are a few highlights thou, particularly both old and current configurations of Hockenheim and Imola (both of which I love), It's super cool to take a modern car down the original 72 layout of Imola!! I also love the addition of the Montreal GP circuit from Canada (I'm a Canadian eh!) so i can relate to that track IRL.
Reiza has also released some great DLC in the form of new locations, all of which are faithfully recreated.
The physics are some of the best in a sim game, even with all the other aforementioned heavy hitting sim titles I still find myself coming back to this game time and time again.... It's just the most fun, and I find the driving model to be spot on with most of the vehicles both included and mods. The FFB is great and the AI is really really smart, probably the best of all sims I've seen yet.
Then there's the mods.... This game, like AC and many others available is made exceptional through the mods. In particular there is a track pack with 24 additional circuits by a guy named Patrick you can find on The RaceDept website that is so good its basically considered an official part of the game. It has a lot of the tracks you'd expect to see in a sim such as Monza, Spa, Laguna Seca, Nurburgring, Road America, Road Atlanta, etc. They are all made to the same level of quality as the provided Reiza circuits as well. Simply a must have. Then theres the available cars and series addons..... GTS, WTCC, Formula 1 (skins), CART, it goes on and on. Not the largest mod pool available yet but its growing and the quality of many of them are really really good.
BOTTOM LINE; If you love sim racing, do yourself a favor and grab this game! It is hands down one of the best. If you can, try and grab the DLC as well in a bundle, it goes on sale at times.
11/10 would buy again.

Summary: Good, hardcore fighting game with barebone features.
I don't play many fighting games so I appreciate a good tutorial, which Blazblue unfortunately lacks. You've got the standard modes of Story, Arcade, Versus, Training, Score Attack, and that's about it. I heard that the game used to have online multiplayer through Games on Windows Live; it's a shame they haven't added new support through Steamworks yet. I'm sure the hardcore players will be upset that they can't thrash noobs online.
Despite the lack of additional features, the game is gorgeous with solid mechanics, so fighting game fans will love it. For the casual player who needs more help to get into the genre, start with a game that has a strong tutorial like Skullgirls or King of Fighters XIII.
I still recommend the game itself because it's freakin' cool and fun. :)

None of these relate to DOOM.
After acquisition of id Software, Bethesda started to make remakes of classic id games - Wolfenstein, Quake and Doom. Somehow, they managed to distort formulas of fun in at least two of these - Quake (with character skills) and Doom.
Development of DOOM started with Doom comic -
. Somebody really liked the RIP AND TEAR page, so he decided that new DOOM should be about ripping and tearing. Therefore, shooting became a necessary mechanic to let player rip monsters. Players are given health and ammo for tearing, but you get almost nothing if you shoot enemies without ripping - a subtle way to move away from the core doom gameplay.
After choosing the main game theme, developers discovered that some players still chose to shoot monsters avoiding melee contact. More limitations were added such as RPG elements. Now Doom guy is a weakling, who can carry 10 shotgun bullets without any upgrades. He also cannot wear armor in proper quantities, his health is 100 out of possible 200 - he is crippled in any way possible. Lack of ammo boxes almost forces you to rip and tear - as intended.
After crippling the main character, developers found out that player can just run around looking for supplies to shoot monsters and avoid ripping! So they decided to place you into tight multilevel arenas without exit - just like Painkiller, but with more jumping and ledgegrabbing.
Game also has a plot with missions. That's right, doom guy is a mission guy now. He has a mission to do, with someone else above him (which is total heresy). He is not a free independent marine anymore, now he needs to save everyone. Of course Bethesda tried to hide that via character's actions - like constantly destroying important stuff. And yet he still follows the orders.
Guns are somewhat nice, but without ammo upgrades they feel underwhelming. Not to mention the amount of upgrades - weapon tokens and argon energy balls for ammo (maybe something else? Too many upgrade categories to keep track of). Was it really necessary? Doom needs no feeling of progressing aside from getting new guns and meeting stronger monsters. Now player is faced with decisions - do I need more hp or armor or ammo (protip: you always need ammo)? Acceptable for any shooter, but not for the shooter with DOOM in title. Not to mention that game ends like a level after you feel really powerful. Of course there is an arcade mode with all upgrades, but why not make it the default mode without RPG crap?
Monsters are fine, they do monster things and do them as they should.
Graphics are fine, nothing bad about it either.
Music belongs to the garbage bin - wubs are not music. Occasionally there is some guitar - when a strong monster enters the arena.
Bethesda and remains of id Software managed to make a good shooter, good enough to be a proper Painkiller sequel. Unfortunately, it has almost nothing similar to original Doom in gameplay terms aside from Hell setting and weapons. Sonic-speed running marine was replaced with jumping ape, who has shotgun without ammo and forced to rip and tear. Get it for 75% off and play arcade mode, avoiding campaign. And please ignore DOOM in the title.

NOV 17, 2017 UPDATED REVIEW:  Just a heads-up, i needed to polish this review just a bit since i forgot about the multiplayer... I'm sure we've got a few triggers around here... Whatever, i just realized i forgot the MP and needed to nitpick it for a bit when reviewing a game which is overall amazing despite the MP.
Doom is nothing short of amazing!  The controls are precise and sharp.  Movement is great as well.  The entire game is bloody beautiful as well as the incredible soundtrack.  Simply put, Doom is one of the best games i've played in this generation *right there with Disgaea 5).  The Campaign is the highlight of DOOM with some of the greatest aspects that any FPS can and should dish out.
If i do have to point out the only fault with this game, it'd be the multiplayer.  Don't get me wrong, it's not bad and I'd much prefer this over "cough" Gaylo 5 "cough" any day.  However, it's a bit lackluster compared to the phenominal campaign.  But in al honesty, this doesn't damage the game in entirety, it's just something that needed to be better.

My Score: 11/12 (130/144)
It's close to being near-perfect.  While the multiplayer is the game's weakest point (which is just a bit lackluster), it does not keep this game from being admirable.  If you're looking into DOOM in this day and age, it's definitely worth picking up for PC.

Ahh, another great tongue-in-cheek humoured game from Rockstar, what more could a GTA fan want? How about giving it the twist of the main character still being at school, but not just any school, Bullworth Academy...
I love this game because you feel almost like you're playing a parody of the GTA franchise where instead of machine guns and grenades, you have slingshots and stink bombs! With the classic amount of adult humour thrown in, it's crude-er than ever when put into a school environment. The story is about Jimmy Hopkins being moved into this notoriously crummy academy, and after making acquaintences with the psycho Gary, it's soon on Jimmys agenda to take over the school by winning favour with all of the stereotypical school cliques, whilst solving their problems, going to class and dodging the prefects catching you from skipping class if you decide to do so.
Despite it's age, the Scholarship Edition adds a couple of new classes to go to and a few more missions, not to mention the graphics upgrade, makes buying this game a worthwhile re-visit to the classic.
8/10

In Go! Go! you will be playing as a Weeb that met some dudes in a chat room, and you go to vist them in Japan but SUPRISE they were girls now you have to live with two hot chicks. These two gals will be showing you around Japan as your tour guides, "Hot Tour Guides". They will take you to the hottest tourist locations in Japan such as Akihabara and Mt.Fuji. Along the journy you will learn little facts about Japan, and what day-to-day life is like there.

I recommend this controller. It has a bit of a learning curve, but nothing too big. You can use this controller for pretty much every game on PC.
The trackpads are the biggest part of the controller, and they work well for the most part. The right trackpad is good enough to be able to make large sweeps, simulating the large surface area of a mousepad. It also has lots of customization for the options, like on a mouse you can adjust the smoothing, sensitivity, you can make it work like a trackball (which I really like), and there's lots of other settings which I won't go into great detail about.
The left trackpad has inlays to suggest that it can be used like a D-Pad, and it works pretty well as a dpad. In platformers it works well, just remember to set it so that you don't need to click it to activate it. I tested it with Super Meat Boy and I had no issues. I'd say that it's better than a normal dpad, since it allows you to play for longer periods of time without your thumb getting fatigued.
There's a gyroscope, which is good for driving games and FPS games. In driving games you can set it to work like a joystick, which does a good job of emulating a steering wheel.
In FPS games, you can set it to work like a mouse which does a good job and is really accurate, so accurate to the point where it is technically more accurate than a normal mouse (however this doesn't mean that it is necessarily better than a mouse, it can just detect very small movements.)
In FPS games, there are different ways that you can set it up. You can set it up so that the trackpad is used for turning around, doing large sweeps, flicking etc, and that the gyro is used for precise aiming. Or you can set it up vice versa, where the trackpad is the one doing the precise aiming and the gyroscope is the one doing the large sweeps. Both work well in my opinion.
The joystick is pretty good, it has a nice grippy texture and it feels nice to use.
The triggers are good, not much to say about these really.
The bumpers are really stiff, but they're usable.
The ABYX buttons are a bit small, but I found that easy to reach and usable to the point where the size doesn't matter.
The back paddles work great, I have no issues with these.
The actual shape of the controller is really comfortable, it's not digging into my hand like other people say, and it's relaxing to use.
Overall, it's a good controller.

The RT and LT buttons don't have very much travel compared to an XBOX controller, which is limiting in a game like Rocket League.  I'm sure with some time you can get used to it but the reason I'm not recommending it is because they don't have free returns.  It cost me nearly $20 dollars to ship it back to Valve.  I was willing to give it a try, but I never expected a company as wealthy as Valve to cheap out and stick me with the insane return cost.  And that's with USPS, not UPS or FedEx which are more expensive.
Thanks for screwing a guy who took a chance trying your new product, Valve.  Shameful, absolutely shameful.  I'll never buy any of your hardware products again.
Edit: And I'm not sure why it says 0 hours used, I used that controller for a week, around ~10 or so hours in games like Rocket League, Tomb Raider 2013, and MGSV.  It was fully updated and used in Big Picture mode.

This game is a little bit of a depature from what made the original games so fun and popular as graphics improve in general. They've strayed away from rescuing people and some of the sillier moments in previous games. This game isn't by any means bad though, and I think it's a good thing that finally firearms are somewhat useful in the game. Don't let some of the negative comments sway you and this game is not as "short" as some people suggest. This game isn't set like the prior two where the timer is always working against you. See, the other games give you a sense of days within the game. What I mean by that is certain events MUST happen within certain time frames or you must WAIT until it is that day and hour before they will begin. This game takes that mechanic out and you have a set number of days to get through the story (plenty of days to go exploring and save people). So in some ways, the better you become and the higher level you become you can progress through the story VERY quicklky and could easily finish this game in about an hour and a half at level 50 and knowing exactly where to go to hit each story line mission. (You could easily do this in the prior games if you weren't  forced to wait) Anyways, you will like this game, there is much to explore, and it is fun crafting weapons. I hope that if they make a Dead Rising 4, they include some more of the silly story lines and I like saving people and bringing them somewhere. (lots of people actually hate that aspect from the first 2 games and maybe it should be adjusted but I do like it) The ONE downside to this game is the fetch quests. I hate fetch quests where you literally drive around the city looking for stuff, totally lost, and then have to drive back to the original quest starter. That's the weakest part of the game and reminds me of lazy MMORPG quests.

Background: Big fan of the original, love stealth games and the Bladerunner cyberpunk genre.
The Good:
* Interesting plot and missions

* Interesting powers change gameplay

The Bad:
* Bland character models and stiff animations
* Stealth sections are far too easy with obvious routes and dumb cameras
* Weapons and upgrades lack impact
* Buggy quests make completion impossible
* Hacking mechanic is boring & characters ignore you stealing from them
* Sandbox play makes for nonsensical conversations
* Map system is oddly weak in a technological future
* NPCs speak as if you aren't standing there and totally ignore you doing awesome feats
Impressions: I really liked the experience despite some terrible lack of refinement and  buggy gameplay. The stealth options are a blast even if the enemy is really easy to predict.
Recommended for: sci-fi stealth fans.
Conclusion.

Great game, as was the original. Nothing I need to say about that that hasn't already been said. Mostly here are my thoughts about the changes.
The good: 2 energy bars that perma-regen (except on hard mode), some new items that add a few more possibilities but are mostly trivial, the additions to the boss fights (turrets and other items added in expanded environments), the promise of a New Game+ mode. The Missing Link DLC mission was odd to start but ended up being very enjoyable and adding to the game well.
The bad: The look of it. I guess it was a huge complaint with the original game but I liked the orange/gold tint on things. Seems like there were several other small graphical tweaks that I think made it look worse as well. Also, the NG+ mode doesn't carry over items or money or really add any new fun to the game. I read some incorrect info that lead me to believe that NG+ would carry over everything and I was looking forward to the cheap fun of blasting through the game with my hilariously OP weapons and not having to spend extra time finding all the upgrades and ammo and such again. Instead, all you get are augments, which are still fairly gamebreaking (pacifist and other achievements are 50x easier), so why not go all the way?
The REALLY bad: Game ran like absolute crap until I found a registry fix online. It seems to be an uncommon problem that only NVIDIA (read: most people) card users have, but the game was just running terrible, even at the absolute lowest settings (which made it look worse than the old school Deus Ex). After the fix, it still didn't run as well and still looked worse than the non director's cut version, but hey it was playable. This is with me using a GTX760 I might add.
All in all, still a great game and worth buying if you haven't played HR at all, and still worth buying imo if you want to play HR again with a few additions, especially if you catch it on sale. I'm pretty bitter about the graphics problems and the crap version of NG+, but I'd still reccomend it.

Pros
+Level 1-60 is simple and gets you used to the basics of the game.

Cons

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a Cyberpunk first/third-person shooter with some RPG and stealth elements. This game executes all of these ideas wonderfully making a fantastic game to the point where it's one of my all-time favorites. A single playthrough would probably be 25-30 hours and you are likely to replay it because of the large amount of secrets and achievements.
The gunplay is pretty polished and enjoyable. While there isn't much weapon variety most of the enviroments seem to be designed so that a player can clear a level reguardless of their arsenal. You can play lethally or non-lethally; Lethal weapons have the advantage of killing your enemies but they reward less XP while lethal weapons only knock opponents out until one of their allies wakes them up. The stealth is good but the AI can be pretty bad sometimes (sometimes they won't see you switch cover in plain sight). Resource conservation is a major part of the gameplay. There is only so much ammo in the game so you have to use it carefully.
The augmentations add some variety and replayabillity to the game. You can get the abillity to jump 3 meters high, throw heavy objects, takedown two enemies at once or even turn invisible. However, some augmentations are much more useful than others.
The levels are very well done. There is virtually always multiple ways to complete an area or a mission. You even get bonuses and loot for exploring the levels thoroughly.
The cyberpunk atmosphere is very well done here. The cinematics have a nice look and have a very unique style. Everything looks pretty good even with low graphics settings. My computer is pretty weak (as of writing this review) but it gets a decent framerate with some occassional stuttering and FPS drops.
The Director's Cut fully integrates the expansions into the game making them stick out less. The missing link expansion now carries praxis points over into the base game and you no longer start with an arsenal and 10k credits. Some other interesting features include New Game+, which carries you augmentations over into a new game and you can find more of the DLC weapons scattered in the world. Making the Director's Cut superior to the base game with all DLC.
Perhaps the biggest problem with this game is the boss fights. All of them are pretty easy and simple, especially with the new ways to beat them introduced by this version.
I would reccommend this game to anybody who likes shooters, especially the more "hardcore" shooter games. You'll get your moneys worth no matter how much you pay for it. This game gets a 9/10 in my book.

Deus Ex: HR is a really good game for the most part, and the improvements made to the Director's Cut, like the alternate means of fighting boss fights, definitely add to this. Whether you want to run and gun or you want to sneak around and not be seen by anyone in the entire game, or anything in between, there are a lot of ways to play the game. And it's pretty fun, though you may find that some parts drag a bit.
Only two minor annoyances:
1.) The switching between FPS and 3PS as you move into and out of cover can be jarring. Honestly, I rather wish they'd made the whole game 3rd person, or at least offered it as an option.
2.) Character animations are often weird and jerky during cut-scenes; it's like they were trying to have the characters make emphatic gestures with their dialogue but just didn't pull it off very well.
Other than those very minor things, everything else is pretty good. The story is enjoyable, the environments can be interesting, the combat is solid, the voice acting is acceptable. A game worth getting. Or, in the case of those who already own the non-director's-cut version, worth the few bucks to upgrade to this version.

If Steam had a "recommended with massive caveats" button, that would be an appropriate way to sum up my feelings toward this game, because for everything it does right or well, something else comes along that's either poorly done or is a bad idea altogether.
The concept is solid--take a guidebook of Japan, its history, and some cultural/tourist hotspots, and deliver it in the form of a fictional story as a visual novel--but everything that isn't explicitly focused on educating the reader feels like a waste of time.  There really is no story.  The foreign protagonist, your canonically nameless player character (PC), fumbles around in the company of two cute sisters, and his "tour guides" don't really get much character development until the very end of their respective stories, when the time comes for an obligatory and bare-bones romance.  At least the sisters don't completely feel like stereotypes; while innocent and sweet, the busty Makoto is not particularly gullible, and the younger Akira maintains a gruff exterior but is usually friendly, intelligent, and observant of the world around her.
That being stated, even the game's few attempts to develop its characters have their downsides; for Makoto, despite her being gorgeous, she just happens to be very naive about red-light districts.  Take a wild guess what happens, and take a wild guess who has to "save" her.  This also looks really weird in reverse, in an unrelated scene where the protagonist doesn't trust Makoto to go out alone at night in a quiet and completely different part of town THAT SHE LIVES IN AND KNOWS MUCH BETTER THAN HE DOES.  For Akira, her sometimes abrasive personality leads to unnecessary, contrived drama where she cynically overanalyzes everything that's said to and around her.
(This sums up far too many of the main character's ideas about Japan.  I've seen worse protagonists in games, but I've rarely wanted to slap one so hard as I do here.  The 'hero' is incredibly childish, becoming overly excited about everything to the point where he causes a distraction and embarrasses one of his tour guides.  Never mind when he suddenly starts looking, or trying to look, at adult magazines in public, with said guide only a few feet away.  He is a consummate "weeaboo," who loves Japan for no real reason and doesn't so much as understand the convenience stores or the toilets, let alone the nation's complex history.)
The actual educational segments are much more interesting.  You receive a guided tour not only of Tokyo but of various other areas, and the game does merit a lot of credit for providing a nice variety of settings and for not promoting an image of Japan as some sort of universally modern tech haven.  The "Show Photo" feature found in some scenes is a game-winner, as it actually loads up Google Maps in your Internet browser and shows you a real-life photo of whatever you're looking at in the story.
Then the production values start becoming unpredictable.  The music is very hit-or-miss, sometimes being low-key and utterly beautiful, and sometimes being inappropriately excited when the exposition is tragic or depressing.  Building interiors work the same way; you get to see the insides of some temples and plazas, while others are simple and pointless fade-to-black transitions.  One museum is explored completely and instantly off camera.  The same goes for various characters, such as a sumo wrestler and a geisha who are mentioned but not actually shown, and this and the few varieties of character expressions make the game quality feel cheap.  (The player character also lacks eyes for no clear reason in the few scenes where he's actually shown.)  On the other hand, much of the dialogue is rendered in both English and Japanese, which is a really nice touch, and the game at least does a great job of making Japan look like a place well worth visiting and appreciating, especially since several background scenes such as the Ikebukuro district's are really well done.  Besides, you can hardly go wrong with delicious pictures of food.
Some of the "facts" you're given are actually wrong, however.  Matthew C. Perry --
-- did help open Japan's borders, but he did part of this work in 1853, not 1863 as pictured (
).  He wasn't even alive by 1863, and to the best of my knowledge, he was a commodore at the time, not yet an admiral.
One of the game's neater features is that you can manually enter the real-life exchange rate for yen to and from the American dollar or the Euro, thus having prices reflected in a currency and at a rate of your choice.  There's little sense in counting each penny you spend on foreign food, however, as your prices start skyrocketing when you begin riding the advanced trains.  It would have been nice to keep an eye on a set budget for food and travel expenses as an actual tourist would, since the game isn't designed to let you visit all of its half-dozen destinations in one playthrough as is, but your purchasing decisions are generally made for you.
The attempts at non-educational writing--comedy, drama, romance--largely fall flat.  Much of the dialogue feels horribly bloated, especially with the constant use of ellipses (......................... ................ ......) and parrot exposition ("Parrot exposition?  You mean where one character repeats something that was just said?"), to the point where it can become tempting to skip through long sequences of nothing to get to the next historical exhibit.  Despite this, the game is not long: my play time encompasses two playthroughs as well as time I let the game idle while I was checking facts or generally web-surfing.  The still-image fanservice is of the cheap and tacky walked-in-on-someone-dressing variety, and the protagonist's tendency to linger and ogle completely ruins the "gentleman" characterization that he and the game desperately want the reader to believe.  At least he has the decency not to ride the women-only trains, but other than his tendency to listen respectfully, I have no idea what the girls see in him.  Scenes like these and various suggestive or perverted-humor references scattered throughout, while not explicit, make me question claims of this being an all-ages VN.
(People who complain about "spaz" references will want to be aware of scenes like this.)
The user interface is full of uneven decisions.  A corner of the main game interface contains intrusive save/skip/load buttons that could easily have been left to hotkeys or the pause menu.  Being able to fast-forward through dialogue using the scroll wheel can be handy or annoying, but since the conversation archive only stores text and doesn't actually rewind scenes, you may find yourself reloading earlier scenes if you want to revisit a certain piece of art, especially if you wind up skipping several lines of dialogue by accident.  Still, there is a requisite CG gallery, and the remarkable sightseeing album contains plenty of distilled and informative commentary on the various sites and places you visit, even as you might be better served by checking out an actual guide or history book from a library.
In short, there are a lot of decisions you should make on your own before deciding to buy this.  Can you deal with writing that vacillates between being decently entertaining and frustratingly boring?  A main character who acts like he's never been taught to behave in public?  A detailed but somewhat cluttered user interface?  Music you may find yourself turning off, and art that feels like incomplete potential?  The links to real-life photos are amazing, but I won't say they justify the price; the product is short yet still drawn out, and it needs a lot of polish.

Great controller honestly.  It's still taking a lot of practice.  Essentially i've learned that touchpad FPS is lame, but with the gyroscope my accuracy is better than it ever was with a thumbstick.
One thing you have to realize is that if you've been using a 360 controller or a mouse and keyboard for over a decade than it's going to take a LOT of practice to get your muscle memory to coordinate the controls properly.  I think i've played about 20 hours and I still have to stop and think about what i'm doing, but it's getting better.  With gyroscope-enabled aiming my reaction time is slower, but my ability to hit moving targets seems easier than it was with a stick.  Now i just have to get good at coordinating strafing with the left stick, rough-aiming with the right touchpad, and fine-tune aiming with the gyroscope.

so i have had allot of time to get to know this controller. when i saw the pictures of it for the first time i thought it looked dumb. i didn't have any interest in it at all. then i tried it out at pax on a whim and it felt immediately intuitive. much more accurate then trying to use a joystick. so when it came out and i bought one and it didn't click with me the same way i was a little put off. what i came to realize is the one i used at pax was calibrated set up and fine tuned to play the demos. what i mean is; like all things in the pc world, it took some tinkering to get it to work the way i wanted it to. the first game i tried was tomb raider. the preset that came out of the box was a bit slow and clunky. i messed around with it for about an hour and i got it set up so i could play it but it didn't really click perfectly the way it had the first time i used it. so then it was on to assassins creed rouge which had no controller support natively and i ended up defaulting to the keyboard and mouse. the next game i played was deus ex human revolution. it took me allot less time to get it set up. maybe 10 minutes to start and a little tweaking here and there. this is where i started to not notice so much that i was using a different controller. it was starting to just become second nature as my fingers learned where the really close together abxy buttons were. i played through several games with mixed results. i didn't run into too many issues but it really didn't work in project cars. that game had a hard time using the trigger as a peddle instead of an on off switch. do not recommend for racing sims. the game that really planted faith for me in the hardware was when i played rise of the tomb raider and realized how good a pre setup was. a popular title that came out after the controller with official support. it worked perfect right out of the gate. no set up. no tweaking. this made me relies that this controller may not be the quickest thing to pick up for older title especially ones that people don't play much anymore but on all new titles from here on out, it will likely run smooth as butter. i vastly prefer this to a normal joystick. Valve's promise was to bring the almighty power of the PC to the living room. Did they deliver? You bet they did. This controller is truly a 'passport from the PC to the couch'. It works with virtually any game in your steam library. There is no feeling more joyous than loading up a rickety, twenty year old, keyboard and mouse only game and playing it on the sofa effortlessly. It cuts out the to and fro troubleshooting and clunky, archaic remote viewing software. It sits comfortably in the hand and blends the familiar feeling of a laptop trackpad with the comfort of a controller.
This controller is not without its issues however. The controller is designed to be moulded around the user's preferences, which requires varying lengths of play by ear fine-tuning. As I finished configuring the controller to a comfortable setting for Valve's golden boy and posterchild, Half-Life 2, it immediately crashed to the desktop, taking Steam with it. Playing FPS titles and competitive games such as Counter Strike and Insurgency requires practice and patience, as you abandon the familiarity of pinpoint precision aiming from a mouse and a dual-stick layout controller.
However this doesn't set the precedent for Valve's promising newborn. Software updates and controller customisation options are continuously being developed and improved by the day. The gyroscope feature is a godsend and adds a whole new level of depth to PC gaming, especially in racing titles such as Burnout Paradise where the controller can act as a steering wheel. The gyro feature can be utilised for an alternative to trackball aiming and provides a well deserved alternative to a mouse.
One surprising feature is that the controller emulates a multi-button mouse which can be very useful if a game happens to crash, eliminating the need to liase with the host PC in person. You can browse the net, your files and do anything a mouse can do with this controller, even without big picture enabled. Nifty touch, Valve. This controller eliminates the need for tedious typing as the dual touchpad layout allows for easy typing, making it once more, enjoyable rather than a task. This controller coupled with big picture mode essentially turns your PC into a console. For those who enjoy taking your hands off the wheel and reclining on your bed or sofa, this is quintessential to your collection. This really is the bread to your butter.
Pros

+Multi-function capabilities
+Vast array of options for personalisation
+Comfortable and stylish design
+Excellent price
+Lengthy battery life
Cons
-Unsound for some titles
-Steep learning curve

-Sometimes confusing to use

Fallout 2 is a retro RPG with turn based combat set in a futuristic nuclear post apocalyptic America. The player is tasked with finding a piece of old world tech that was intended to help survivors rebuild but the plot soon becomes more involved with the players actions determining the fates of the wastelands inhabitants. There are numerous styles of play, from a smooth talking swordsman to a kleptomaniac explosives expert to a sharpshooting doctor and the games well written quests offer multiple solutions catering to various character types. Making an int 1 character is a viable build and results in hilarious new dialog as everyone takes advantage of your stupid character. The wasteland is much bigger than in the first game and the design team thankfully dropped the time limit from the 1st game, so there is ample opportunity to hoon around the wreckage of civilization in your tricked out ride, looking for action. I'm not able to offer an unbiased opinion of fallout 2 because I loved this game as a kid and I can't even talk about it without getting nostalgic but the story, RPG systems and game world are very well built and the combat is tactical and fun.
-the seminal fallout experience. Forget the FPS RPG's and that 3rd person rubbish, this is the title that made the fallout name
-that rush of adrenaline when marcus pulls out his minigun (nonono I took that off you where did you get that?!?)
-the Vats system is awesome and combat in general is very enjoyable
- the games characters are well done and memorable
-putting a damn bullet or ten into myrons dumb face
-easy to break the game wide open
-glitchy and it's probably worth installing the community patch. No fun finding half your car missing
-hard on the eyes. Some of the death animations are still great though
-some of the wacky encounters feel kinda dumb (the bridge keeper for example or the "buffy" thing)
-the censorship and the fact that some quests seem unfinished (the giant talking mole rats for instance)
My opinion on fallout 2 is that it's a bit crusty in its old age but the RPG under the hood works very nicely and if you're a fan of RPGs its worth the time to experience the story and world. A legendary PC title

When i was first introduced to fallout in 2012, I kept hearing that Fallout 3 was amazing. When I played it, it didn't have a good story but it was enjoyably bad for me. I tried Fallout New Vegas and I found it better than Fallout 3 and played it death. A side note here: I played both games on the Xbox 360. Now 2017 Sept 13, I tried out PC gaming and had fun with it but wasnt dedicated to it. When Fallout 2 was on a discount for 2 dollars I said hey why not, it's a Fallout game that I never tried. Needless to say I was impressed.
Fallout 2 was made in the late 1990's and had a completely different style than 3 and New Vegas. It is a turned base rpg developed by Black Isle Studios. From what I heard, this game was rushed and was in development for 1 year. 1 YEAR!! I haven't finished the game yet but there's already plenty to do. This is more challenging that 3 and New Vegas and it's the challenge that keeps you invested than leading to you ripping your skin off. This game had me use my brain more than any other game I played. You actually had to strategize in combat than just mindlessly shooting. When ever I kill anything It is satisfying, especially when their guts explode. This map isn't the biggest but every location you go to feels unique, in my opinion atleast.
The story at first sight looks simple. Go to a trader, he will tell you where the G.E.C.K is, collect it then go to your village Arroyo. Before we talk about the story, let's talk about how it's handled. You're going to actually how to use your brain to complete the story. Fallout 3 had a bad story becuase it basically did everything for you. New vegas kind of did this but you felt like you were the main character. In Fallout 2, you feel like you could change anything. You actually felt like someone who had an influence. Now lets talk about the story. In one of the tasks on saving Arroyo, it expands to something more. In your way to find the trader that will help you, you find a town with things to do. I don't want to spoil much but at some point your involved in a gang war and your able to become a slaver. You went from finding a trader to being involved in slavery.
The characters aren't the most memeorable, in my opinion, but you certainly remember  them more than Fallout 3. Most characters don't have voice actors but that's okay becuase the dialogue they tell you is great and beyond the time it was made in and holds up to this day. You have many dialogue choices with them and they are all interesting, including theirs. There are talking heads, characters with voice actors and are typically important in someway. When I listen to them, the voice actors do a great job at keeping you invested in what they are saying.
What can I say about this game? I didn't finish it yet and I nearly wrote a whole essay. The game will keep you hooked at the cost of you thinking more. If you played Fallout 3, New Vegas, 4 as one of your first fallout games you will likely not enjoy this game. However, it is different and has the enjoyment of the modern Fallout Games
but you have to use your brain more and challenge this ruthless wasteland. Get this game on discount and prepare for the different style of gaming you don't see often to truly enjoy this game. I will post a full review on it when I have finished the game.

Christ was this game an experience. This game made you feel like a badass, especially after you defeated the end-game. This game has balance of seriousness and just silly. When I looked back on it, there were many pop culture references that went over my head. Throughout my experience I've done and seen so many things from murdering children, driving a car, associating with mutants and a deathclaw, finding Chinese ripoffs of Star-Wars, to becoming a ♥♥♥♥ing pornstar. This game is absurd yet also has a mature edge to it. In my opinion, when serious moments came I felt threatened.
