Originally, I down-voted this game. I really did not enjoy it.
And, I still don't.
However, after discussing the matter with the Fallout 2 loyalists, I cannot deny that this is a really good game.
It is a bigger, louder, and mechanically improved Fallout experience.
It's everything a sequel should be, and for the pricetag it delivers an insane ammount of new content to explore.
My sole issue with this game, and what effectively ruined it for me, is the game's tone.
For some reason, it drops the headier more serious text that filled the original masterpiece in favor of MUCH lighter dialogue. Jokes abound in this sequel, as do wacky side-quests, and more often than not they are based around now-dated references to 90s pop-culture. This has not helped the game age well. Additionally, the game allows you to team up with a veritable entourage of colorful companions, making this trek through the wastes feel more like a buddy-comedy road trip than a post-apocalyptic fight for survival.
And, maybe everything I just described sounds great to you. That's fine.
I found the game to be a mess of conflicting ideas that could never decide on what it wanted to be. But my preferences should not lead me to deny the fact that this game works fine. The price is a bargain for how much content you'll get. And, there is a surprisingly active modding community constantly improving upon it to this day.
TL;DR: Great game, not so great plot, groan-worthy dialogue. IMHO

Like many Fallout fans, I started with 3, played New Vegas, and eventually 4, and also like many fans, once I played 4 I thought to myself "man this really isn't much of an RPG, is it? Doesn't really feel like a Fallout game". Now that I've gone back and played this and the first one, I kind of can't help but feel that way about 3 and New Vegas too. Not that they're bad games by any means, I greatly enjoy them both, but this, #2, feels like the true Fallout experience.
I know a lot of fans who started with 3 or NV or 4 are going to look at this game, see how primitive and dated it appears and think "i just don't know if I can go backwards like that", it's what I thought too, but take my word for it, after the initial 30 minutes or so of working things out, you're gunna enjoy this goldmine so much. Is it less immersive than the 3d games? Yeah, that's inevtiable, the 3D games are great at creating a fun world to explore, but in about every other aspect #2 shines brighter. I especially enjoy the turn and hex based combat much more than I enjoy the live combat of the others.
If you're one of the Fallout fans that was disappointed with the lack of RPG elements in #4, and want to see more New Vegas-like content, #2 is a must play. Trust me, it's a cheap game, just give it an hour, dont be afraid to use a starting guide so you're not overwhelmed by the differences, and you'll be hooked. Such a gem.

This is, simply, a brilliant RPG. Lets start with the story and presentation.
The story is one of the best I've seen in games, up there with Bioshock Infinite. The story is about Adam Jensen, a man hyper-augmented against his will to have a voice that seems to be constantly crying out for throat sweets. He must uncover the story behind the attack on his workplace and a global conspiracy. The graphics aren't great but the visual design is. The cities all look very Blade Runner-like and the art style has a clean, scientific look about it which I like a lot.
The gameplay is very good, an FPS/TPS with RPG elements in big levels with multiple pathways. The stealth is the best I've seen in a non-stealth game (I'm looking at you, Burial at Sea), but the combat is also ridiculous amounts of fun.
Overall this is a brilliant game if you like RPGs or Sci-Fi.

This game is a creative masterpiece.
Everything in this game is interesting, well-done, and amazing; the concept, the art and design, the voices (JP), the story, all of it. Other than the visuals of this game being great (both graphics-wise and art direction-wise), the gameplay is an interesting mix of hack-and-slash and bullet hell and at any point in the game it can and will smoothly trasition between the two as well as be a mix of the two at the same time. The more bullet hell-like sections aren't limited to a 2D plane and can feel more like 2.5D to even more 3D-like.
Another thing I'd particularly like to point out is the soundtrack. It's not every game where I feel like the soundtrack is absolutely gorgeous and fits all the scenes perfectly. The music in this game isn't something that woud be fitting to listen to like it were some band's album (though don't let that stop you) but the music will be left in your head even when you're not playing and I mean that as a good thing.
Now one thing I've seen people complain about is the lack of depth in the fighting mechanics, and well, there really isn't a whole lot. However, the fighting never bored me with its flashy visuals, not to mention there are multiple weapon types (and support weapons) that you can mix together to create different combos and fighting styles (for 2 of the 3 playable characters). So if one fighting style starts to bore you, perhaps try another.
You will play through this game multiple times as different characters and it was an intersting way to tie the story together and an enjoyable experience. Despite just recently "beating" the game as one character, I was eager to still go onto the next.
All in all, this is a superb game and there's not much for me to complain about, In fact, there really isn't anything for me to complain about. Just a warning, you will need a powerful system to run this game. There is a fan-made mod that helps run the game on lower spec systems but even with that mod I could not run the game still on my previous PC.
Anyway, NieR: Automata gets my full recommendation. Avoiding any spoilers, I have never been so emotionally moved by a game, particularly at a certain part which I've never seen any other game do before.

I didn't care for Nier: Automata. After playing it for 16 hours, I ended up quitting due to boredom, frustration, and irritation over being railroaded into idiot plot choices that were inconsistent with what the characters knew in-game and how they had acted in previous scenes. (Also, the fanservice got irritating after 5 minutes.)
In particular, this game does't seem to be set up for those of us that identify the main plot, then strive to do everything BUT the plot (ie, all the available side-quests) before moving on. As such, I ran into the following problems:
1. Side-quests that were visible on the map, yet were not reachable until the main quest line had progressed. I probably spent 3 or so hours, total, trying to get to navigation points that were simply impossible to get to at that point in the game. It got so bad that I stopped even trying to figure out what was going on, and just looked up what I was supposed to do in the wikia - and half the time it was "yeah, you can't actually do this yet. Continue on the main quest for a while."
1a. On a related note, the fast-movement ability unlocked too late for me - I was already well into "this is a stupid slog" mindset with the amount of travel time in the game, and realized that there probably SHOULD be some way to unlock fast-travel, but didn't realize it was tied to the main plot line.
2. The main-line has plot points whose cut-scenes seemed to assume that you hadn't done certain side-missions yet. Or at the least, didn't have the sheer amount of experience in doing the side missions.
In particular, there were a number of times that the cut-scenes had the main protagonists discussing the non-sapience or inhumanity of the robots, even though I had just spend literally HOURS talking with the robots and doing quests for them and saving them from a number of other (more violent) robots and generally learning about how sapient and emotion-filled they were. As such, each time I touched the main plot line, it felt like the protagonists were going handed the idiot ball, and/or were being forced to ignore most of what I had learned and the choices I had made up until that point.
3. In a similar vein, the game has required game-play elements that contradicted the underlying theme of the work.
That is, it was pretty obvious within 5 minutes of playing that the robots weren't intrinsically evil, and that as such I shouldn't be killing them without a good reason - but the entire game is set up to advance your character by killing robots. But even in-game that's a questionable thing to do, so I stopped doing it. Which means that I was skipping over a good portion of the advancement aspect of the game by trying to not be a psychopathic jerk....which made me realize that the only valid way to be true to that conclusion was to stop playing the game. (Ie, there didn't seem to be a meaningful or interesting "pacificst run" option.)
4. In addition, I found the fan service and camera angles to be pandering and irritating - I don't care to stare up the crotch of any characters for hours on end, much less those stylized as adolescent girls. As such, I ended up having to manually hold the camera up in a more "above the shoulder" normal 3rd person position, as opposed to the Spielberg "up from behind" that seemed to be the default.
So, I suppose had I played this differently, I may have enjoyed it more - but I didn't,  (Note that in 15 hours, I didn't even get to the first ending - I got up to the "break into the castle and try to kill the baby king-leader robot" mission, before I got fed up with a game that was unsubtly trying to get me to commit infanticide while simultaneously trying to make a comment about violence in video games and and/or the emotional capacity of inanimate objects via Shintoism - So, I quit.)

I've been playing the browser version of this game for a couple years, and have gotten into the Hall of Fame twice. I've also assisted Sid Meier with the two online Civ games so I'm very into this genre.
Ways of History is the most advanced Civ-like MMO currently in existence. The devs have solved a number of very sticky design problems related to running a game like this with over 1000 simultaneous players. Games can run long, up to a year. Players are dumped into the center of the map if they join on server day 1 and as time goes on they arrive further from the center where competition is less fierce. The social aspects of the game are amazing, and this (along with excellent economic design) is where the game shines the most.
On the business model side, the devs have done an industry-leading good job of making the game competitive and F2P but not P2W. You can boost some of the gameplay aspects by spending, but no more than 30%. Wonder development and troop movements cannot be affected in any way by spending. Build times for most buildings are fairly quick, this is not a game where you get lots of resources but have to pay to speed up construction. You have that option on non-wonder construction, but the need for this is really low.
Combat used to be tremendously fun but the game recently went from "instant and abstract" to "real time 3D". This added a lot of complexity that the devs are still trying to sort out, so right now this is the weakest area of the game. Mixing squishy units like slingers (speed 85) and tough units like macemen (speed 50) will cause the slingers to run out in front and get pasted before their meat shields arrive. So being aggressively offensive is going to have a very steep learning curve. This is good news for carebears, of course, and static defenses in this game are quite good at discouraging all but the most determined attackers.
The weakest area of the game currently is actually in the Terms of Use. Section 3i of the rules states that "...extremism, terrorism, Nazism, hate or disrespect for any culture, race, nation, language, religion, politics, political regime, ideology, or social movement is prohibited." It's been pointed out to me by the devs that this does not include any sort of protection against sexism or gender shaming so I've seen misogyny run rampant in the WoH community with the okay from the dev team.
I think Ways of History is hands down the world's best, and fairest, massively multiplayer strategy game. It is my hope that an influx of Western players will make it even better. Be warned that it's not an easy game, even though it starts you off gently. Ask questions, make friends, and don't ever underestimate the Russian players who in some cases have been playing 5+ years and know you haven't.

Dead Rising 3 is a fantastic zombie game, that acts much the same as DR2. Awesome combo weapons, crazy psychopaths, and a nearly endless hoeard of zombies to slaughter til your hearts content.
However, with everything great that this game offers, I can certainly see where some of the criticism lies. The area is rather bland. Compared to the interesting and different locations of Wilhomet and Fortune City, Los Perdidios is just a bit...boring. There are a few interesting stores here and there, but outside, there's not all that much that makes the place stand out. I'd much rather be in a mall of a Vegas-esque area with cool casinos and restaurants, but oh well.   Plus, there's no fear of a need for zombrex, so that danger isn't here. However, all of that matters very little in a game where you can use a flaming scythe to burn zombies dressed as Ken Masters.
Also, the game's psychopaths mostly a lot less interesting and a lot less tough) than those of 2. However, I will say, Darlene is by far one of my favorite psychopaths in the entire series. A fat lady on a Rascal that projectile vomits all over the place, while wielding a giant spork. What's not to love?
Overall, this game is a lot of fun, even if it's not as good as DR2.  I definately recommend DR3. If you're looking for a good zombie game, this is a great choice.

Dead Rising 3 does take a lot of liberties with changing established gameplay styles (7 days, no real sense of urgency, saving on the fly, an unlimited armory.) and at times it appears incoherant. Your milage may vary on whether or not this would work for you. But as a long time fan of the franchise I can tell you it doesn't dissapoint in one department: being fun. New and returning combo weapons like the Mini Chainsaws, the Grim Reaper, and the Super Massager guarantees absorbtion into the game for hours on end.
Dead Rising 3 isn't perfect, but really none of the games in the franchise have been. But I do find its 'Mixed' review status rather undeserving.

The Steam Controller is a good idea. In practice it's not as good as one would hope. The primary problem lies with the button mapping and the much touted "high precision technology", i.e, the touch pads.
I should first state that the controller comes with no configuration software at all, which is pretty standard for PC controllers these days and a glaring ommission. Without any such software there's no way to intuitively change the settings on your pad. Don't like that the shoulder buttons are right and left click? Tough. Want to set it so that the stick uses the arrow keys instead of WASD? Too bad. Want to play any game that doesn't use the standard Valve control layout? You're hosed, son.
In practice this isn't the Steam Controller, it's the CounterStrike controller, and I wouldn't even use it for that. Trying to play an FPS with this thing is like trying to play basketball on wet ice. The "precision technology" slides all over the place, and you have to swipe several times over the pad to move the mouse over the length of the screen, when ideally you wouldn't have to remove your thumb from it at all.
As it currently stands, if you really really want a controller for games, just buy a PC controller or use a last-gen console controller like everyone else. But really, why not just use a wireless keyboard and mouse? Oh, and it works even worse outside of Steam's Big Picture Mode, so why would you buy a controller that's LESS functional than a normal one? I might change my mind if this controller gets a MAJOR overhaul, complete with software and even some firmware tweaks, but right now it's NOT worth fifty bucks.

The worst part is, the USB dongle fell apart! The plastic cover seperated exposing the circuitry. OVERVIEW- Bully is one of those games that is incredibly underrated. However, despite releasing in 2006 & being graphically remastered for newer platforms and expanding to multiple systems in 2008, this game is still receiving support from gamers and critics alike, unlike most games where they're left to rot two weeks after release! Let's cut to the chase, I ADORE this game, it's hands down my favorite rockstar game to date and I LOVED Jimmy Hopkins as a protagonist. In spite of it being titled "BULLY" you are not at all a bully unless the player desires to be one as you do have complete control of Jimmy's actions and how he interacts with school faculty and other students present at Bullworth Academy, Jimmy is more of an anti hero, stands up to bullies ranging from spoiled rich brats to greaseballs still stuck in the 50s to even school dropouts!
PROS:
Excellent Gameplay- Jimmy controls smoothly and isn't limited to a single move set or a single defualt outfit
Unique Story- GTA titles usually involve a criminal searching for work in a fictional city rising to the top of the criminal underworld. Bully on the other hand involves a struggling teenager with a messy past with a mother constantly being remarried. Despite Jimmy's bad behavior, he does have a soft side and is willing to be friends with those he trusts, a perfect example being Petey. Great story and throws dull moments completely out the window! Funny writing and great story telling.
Soundtack- Bully is no stranger when it comes to music pieces, ranging from chill to intense chase music, honestly the musical variety is fantastic and I highly recommend listening to the soundtrack! Great music on Rockstar's end
Setting- Bullworth Acadmey feels like an actual boarding school, riddled with mischievous students all across campus, though sometimes It does feel barren and not very alive.  Being sent to the principal's office and doing slave labor for breaking various rules at once is definitely a must and the devs hit it right on the nail with this feature. The seasons change as well, making each chapter unique in it's own way, something the GTA series lacks!
CONS:
Mission Difficulty- Okay, let's be honest, Bully has next to no challenge, each mission is unique and special to each chapter but most missions can be completed with ease and sometimes requires zero skill, while I did enjoy each boss fight, they were relativley easy and It felt like I was fighting a normal student. Hopefully in a possible sequel the difficuly gradually increases with each chapter! Loved the mission variety but sometimes ya gotta crank up the difficulty.
Lack of WIN10 support- Bully is a great game jammed pack with features and I love to play It on my PC! However, If you are a Windows 10 user like me, say hello to constant crashing and freezing, this is an extremely fatal flaw that needs urgent fixing, It's an immensly large annoyance when I'm half way through a story mission only to be greeted with a freeze indicating that the "application has stopped working". To add insult to injury, it's even more irritating when this occurs after a large gap of not saving in between a string of missions because you're forced to restart at square 1!! Please FIX THIS IMMEDIATELY! I highly recommend saving at all times, as these crashes occur at complete random. Thankfully save locations are scattered amongst the map.
Conclusion and Verdict- I HIGHLY recommend this game to anyone looking for something new or enjoy the GTA series or any other rockstar title! It's jammed pack with with hours of fun and mods make it even better thanks to
, they house several modifications ranging from beta content recreations to even custom missions all coming in as free downloads for all users! It's fantastic! As of now, despite this review being "recommended" I actually do not, unless you own a Win 8 machine or below, DO NOT purchase Bully, trust me, the crashes will drive you nuts and as of now, no current fix exists! Purchase at your own risk! I DO adore tthis game and have been praying for a sequel but this constant crash issue is a major turn off for this game, I really hope it's fixed soon. My final verdict for "Bully: Scholarship Edition" is an 8/10 (Great!)
I hope you enjoyed reading my thoughts on this game! More reviews to come!

Originally, I down-voted this game. I really did not enjoy it.
And, I still don't.
However, after discussing the matter with the Fallout 2 loyalists, I cannot deny that this is a really good game.
It is a bigger, louder, and mechanically improved Fallout experience.
It's everything a sequel should be, and for the pricetag it delivers an insane ammount of new content to explore.
My sole issue with this game, and what effectively ruined it for me, is the game's tone.
For some reason, it drops the headier more serious text that filled the original masterpiece in favor of MUCH lighter dialogue. Jokes abound in this sequel, as do wacky side-quests, and more often than not they are based around now-dated references to 90s pop-culture. This has not helped the game age well. Additionally, the game allows you to team up with a veritable entourage of colorful companions, making this trek through the wastes feel more like a buddy-comedy road trip than a post-apocalyptic fight for survival.
And, maybe everything I just described sounds great to you. That's fine.
I found the game to be a mess of conflicting ideas that could never decide on what it wanted to be. But my preferences should not lead me to deny the fact that this game works fine. The price is a bargain for how much content you'll get. And, there is a surprisingly active modding community constantly improving upon it to this day.
TL;DR: Great game, not so great plot, groan-worthy dialogue. IMHO

Like many Fallout fans, I started with 3, played New Vegas, and eventually 4, and also like many fans, once I played 4 I thought to myself "man this really isn't much of an RPG, is it? Not that they're bad games by any means, I greatly enjoy them both, but this, #2, feels like the true Fallout experience.
I know a lot of fans who started with 3 or NV or 4 are going to look at this game, see how primitive and dated it appears and think "i just don't know if I can go backwards like that", it's what I thought too, but take my word for it, after the initial 30 minutes or so of working things out, you're gunna enjoy this goldmine so much. Is it less immersive than the 3d games? Yeah, that's inevtiable, the 3D games are great at creating a fun world to explore, but in about every other aspect #2 shines brighter. I especially enjoy the turn and hex based combat much more than I enjoy the live combat of the others.
If you're one of the Fallout fans that was disappointed with the lack of RPG elements in #4, and want to see more New Vegas-like content, #2 is a must play. Trust me, it's a cheap game, just give it an hour, dont be afraid to use a starting guide so you're not overwhelmed by the differences, and you'll be hooked. Such a gem.

updated Oct 2017: I've now raced this sim for over 1300 hours on Steam (the beta version) and well over 2000 hours before it made it onto Steam.
I'm updating this review to say that the latest game updates are making this the BEST AI I have seen in any recent/current race sims.
The work that Reiza have put into the AI in the past few months are now showing amazing results. The cars will now leave the grid on their formaiton lap, and drive in single file, then form up efficiently in their grid slots when they get back to the grid. If you lke race sims, the extra atmosphere this gives before the race even starts, is superb.
The starts are better than ever, it's tight and close, with some rubbing of wheels, but the AI are now clever enough to fight for a place, know when to give in & try again, and generally get themselves through the first few turns in one piece.
Reiza are still polishing this and it has got better with each update lately, but if you still haven't tried this sim, I definitely recommend it for it's offline racing.
It is undoubtedly the best all round racing sim for me.
I'm unsure why some reviews have said there is not a lot of official content - there are loads of different cars to choose from and lots of tracks from all over the World. Plus the best support, development & updating in any game I've seen .
It's close to the end of it's development now, but even more new cars have been added (Touring Classics most recently with Golfs, Passats, Beetle/Fuscas, Polo, Uno in the mix).
And there's still a great selection of modded tracks available.
This has been excellent value for me, my most played game of all time, and it is still a great buy.
The latest AI improvements have given it a massive shot in the arm, & ensured that I will continue racing it much longer now. It will take some beating.

I've played a lot of Assetto Corsa, but this sim is now my equal favourite. Going to compare this into AC since I know AC very well after hundreds of hours in it:
- Damage is better. Cars come apart when they smash together, with pieces flying through air and in worst case whole wheel coming off. This looks very entertaining, when AI (rarely) has huge accident, and several cars get totaled. There is punctures, and cars can even set on fire. AC damage model is very basic compared to this
- Sounds. AC sounds have improved lately, but Automobilista sounds overall better, cars have raw aggression and lively detail to them. Recorded from real cars, and it sounds like it
- More tracks. However not laserscanned, and not many famous F1 venues, but South American tracks bring interesting flavor. There is also European tracks like RedBull Ring
- Graphically doesn't lose to AC when you put settings on Ultra and extra Anti-Aliasing. There is quide in Steam how to do this. Performance is good, I get nice FPS and with same amount of cars, better FPS than AC. Actually while cars don't look as good and detailed as AC (Assetto  has insanely detailed cars), I would say tracks, trees, sky and environments look actually better. But you need to do steps in this guide:
If you try to use the default AA in the game, it will look like crap and also kill your FPS. Use the Steam guide to set up your graphics!
- Safety car and proper racing/flag rules. Rolling starts, even formation laps and off-laps, timed races. All can be enabled/disabled
- Night racing. Although it hurts FPS quite a lot, because there is more light sources
- Dirt racing. Same, quite heavy on FPS because of all the dust I guess but you can dial the Dust Effect setting down. Not many dirt tracks yet, but it's really something different
- Interesting racing classes like Super Trucks and dirt vehicles, crazy "you've never heard of it but it's awesome" Brazilian racing series cars, endurance prototype car, variety of formula cars. Even karting cars and separate karting tracks for them
- Engine stalls and ignition button, launch control in some cars. Pit limiter on/off
- In-built race engineer, that talks to you on radio. Spotter can be enabled or disabled. CrewChief mod is available for both AC and AMS and is probably overall better and more detailed pit radio. But the stock pit radio in Automobilista isn't bad at all. If he gets annoying, you can of course turn it off.. also change how much he talks (essentials vs. chatty version)
- Famous official brands like Lamborghini, Ferrari, Porsche. AMS has Porsche cup car, but it's not officially licensed and has different name (Boxer). In terms of feel it's very similar to AC official car
- Wider selection of cars, and wider selection of street cars. AMS is mostly about racecars
- Laser scanned tracks
- App overlays are cool system. AMS has customizeable HUD but it's more clunky system, which requires you to launch external editor and do some research on how to use it. Not as flexible. Default HUD in AMS doesn't suit triple screen setup
- Both have real good FFB. Both also requires you to own FFB wheel to be worth it. With only gamepad don't see point of getting these games (while gamepad works). Both require some settings tweaking, to get most out of your wheel. If someone says FFB in Automobilista sucks, he either 1) hasn't driven a real car, or 2) didn't use correct settings
- Both have good AI. Automobilista used to be better, but AC update finally fixed the bad AI
- Both have lots of good quality mod tracks, so you don't have to settle with just default tracks. I downloaded the Mega Pack from
for Automobilista, most of the tracks in it were of great quality and easy to install (just drop into Locations folder.. done)
- Both games have no rain. As far as I know, not coming into either of them
- Both have crappy UI. Automobilista is slightly clearer and easier to use, but still not great

The Deus Ex Series has had tremendous ups and downs over it's lifespan.
It began with the critically acclaimed Deus Ex, but that was followed by the widely panned Deus Ex: Invisible War.  A straight up FPS sequel was under development at the time of Invisible War's release named Deus Ex: Clan Wars, but was retooled and released as Project Snowblind.
It wouldn't be until 2011 that Deus Ex would finally see a worthy sequel in Deus Ex: Human Revolution, well...actually it's a prequel, so the wait's still going on in that department.
The Director's Cut isn't a tremendous upgrade over the original, the largest difference is the inclusion of "The Missing Link", a challenging DLC for the original game.  With or without The Missing Link however, this is still a tremendously fun game.

Relatively realistic portrayal of a week's visit to Japan. I was informed and quite amused. The characters were certainly very lovable, and the art is beautiful.

This seems aimed at an audience much younger, probably around 13 or so. The novel is 1/2 story and 1/2 information with a sightseeing backdrop. There are extremely few choices, and it's advised to save before you choose your first destination, else be forced to click through the lengthy prologue again just so you can check out the other three options, as all 6 destinations can't be visited in a single playthrough. Even if you save immediately after the prologue, you'll still have to cycle through the joint destination before being given one of the two final destinations.
The details given while sightseeing are interesting- different history and cultural elements. That's this novel's real strength. The story, on the other hand, is fairly bland, and almost seems like it was written by an overly-emotional pre-teen with little concept of how people interact. The parts that seem to have more thought put into them, as few as they are, tend to be drowned out by obvious railroading down a predictably forced plot and quickly forgotten. There are a couple points in the plot that try to be controversial but fall flat due to the intended audience being younger, so they feel needlessly preachy and feel rife with projection. Further, it's difficult to connect with the protagonist, which is supposed to be you, since so much of "your" dialogue comes from an easily excitable 13-year-old who is supposed to be somewhere between 17-21.
Overall, I'd recommend this for a much younger demographic, the lower end of the T-rated spectrum, although parts will still seem contrived to them. As for people 18+, the only real reason to get it would be for the info on a couple tourism hotspots in Japan you might not of thought of visiting if you made the trip, but that really only pays off if you aren't already into researching Japanese culture, history, etc.

This game is a gem that you should play. On the other hand, the port is not as good as we'd like, so don't forget to install FAR mod (Fix Automata Resolution) to polish a big part of the problems the PC version has.
Finally, if you are new to this saga, I really encourage you to learn about the previous games' story, specially NieR (Gestalt or Replicant, they are the same game). You will enjoy a lot more of Automata, because is filled with references that make the game a much more complete experience.

K I'm gonna just lay it all out on the table, this might be my favorite game of all time (given my other favorites are Fallout New Vegas, Shadow of the Collossus, Dark Souls, and Silent Hill 2). Imma give a list of Pros and Cons to describe how almost perfect this game is.
Also as an important note: I highly recommend anyone that's interested in playing this game to at least look up a walkthrough of Nier 1, because it gives more context to the story of Automata. There's a lot of really amazing moments that you'll miss out on if you didn't play/watch Nier 1. I recommend the Nier Lp by the SuperBestFriends
Pros:
+Fantastic Combat that's simple on the surface but with many layers if looked a bit deeper. This is an overall huge improvement from the first game since Nier 1's combat is overall not great.
+Segments that shift the gameplay game, making it more and more fresh all the time. Every now and then the game will change from 3d action game to a shmup (Shoot em up) to a twin stick shooter. Nier 1 also had these shifts, which helped it quite a bit given it's mediocre gameplay.
+Amazing fully realized and thematic story that would be impossible to tell in any other medium. This is not an exaggeration, anyone that disagrees straight up didn't finish the game.
+Fantastic English dub. Everyone gives their all in this one, especially whoever played 9S.
+Great amount of customization. While it isn't Dark Souls levels, there's many different weapons to choose from, many different plugin chips that give abilities to your character.
+Tons of (mostly)Fantastic Side Quests, often giving insight to the world of Nier along with fun banter between the main characters.
Alright, now I'm gonna get into the bad stuff. Don't worry, this won't take long.
Cons:
-I can't ignore this issue. The PC version isn't great overall. If you're interested in getting this game, I'd honestly recommend getting the PS4 version over this. However if this is your only choice, or you don't care, there is a few work arounds. Specifically a mod called FAR, it's more or less the DSfix of this game. If you want the game for your PC, I highly recommend getting that mod, as it fixes a lot of the problems the PC version has.
-There's some sidequests that are really gimmicky and not fun to play, which can especially be annoying for the completionists.
And that's it, honestly those issues are so minor (except maybe the pc issue for some people) that I can't imagine anyone having any actual issue with the game because of it.
Overall, I'd highly recommend it for anyone that likes video games. To some, it just might not be the type of game you like, and that's ay-ok, but I really hope you give it an honest try before judging it. Because this game is something that holds a really special place in my heart, and is something I will be playing for years to come.

11/10 Single-player game done right.
I knew that this game would be good but never realized how in-depth and amazing the story would be. Each quest is so well made and some (like wondering couple quest) have twists that you don't expect to happen. I also love various endings the game offers, some happy, some funny, and some meloncholy and perplexing.
Pros:
1. Visuals. It's absolutely stunning how good it looks. When I first saw this on steam front page, I simply wanted to get it all because of visuals.
2. UI and controls. They are well organized and sooo smooth to work with. The movements of avatars flow seeminglessly, unlike many other games that have clunky animations.
3. Story. I came for the visuals and stayed for the story. The complex plot and the backstories of characters make this game extremely enjoyable. I originally thought this game was just cheesy due to ending A, but when I started to play route B (and especially, routes C,D, and E), I realized I was totally wrong. Also, like I mentioned before, the side quests, although somtimes time consuming and fraustrating, are incredible; you will be missing out on lots of extra stories if you don't do them. The stories make you think and give you so many different emotions as well. Not only that, you play as different characters to experience their own part of the stories, which I absolutely loved!
4. Open World. Done right, that is. You can, if you are good enough, can almost go anywhere as long as the map allows it. There are still so many places I haven't been yet because I either wasn't skillful to get there, didn't find them yet, or didn't get missions that allowed me to get there.
5. Voice Acting. The voice acting in this game makes me immerse myself into the conversations the characters are having. It's not akwardly scripted or overly dramatic to make me cringe (well, most anyway); rather, it feels like they are actually having conversations and are reacting accordingly.
6. Music. ABSOLUTE MASTERPIECE!! It's always enjoyable to listen to the OSTs even when I am not playing the game. The vocals....so mesmerizing
Cons:
1. Bugs with some missions. For example, I couldn't complete YorHa Betrayal quest in my first run because there were no enemies spawning. I could do it in my 2nd run though. Also with Machine Examinations; I couldn't talk to the machine in my first run.
2. alt tabbing. This game hates it. It immediately goes to small windowed mode, and I always have to press alt+enter to make it back to full screen.
Neutral:
1. Camera angle while fighting. It is sometimes hard to see what's going on because there are so many enemies, lots of dashing around, and light particle effects everywhere. So it does get quite confusing sometimes as to where you and your enemies are.
2. I wish there were a way to get alphabetical listing of places you go to whever you want to teleport. I
3. Also, there you be like a search box for items you want to buy or sell. I don't want to scroll all the way down or up hundreds of items in my inventory or shop.
4. Open for interpretation. Because this game ends with multiple endings, there are lots of theories for the purpose of andriods and machines.
5. I wish there would be more backstories for those who don't know much about Nier and how it came to be. I had to watch Youtube videos to understand few references (not many though).
6. I wish I could raise my fps limit to 144, but it seems like the game has a cut off at 60, a bit disappointing.
tl;dr: It's a game you won't regret buying at full price.

None of these relate to DOOM.
After acquisition of id Software, Bethesda started to make remakes of classic id games - Wolfenstein, Quake and Doom. Somehow, they managed to distort formulas of fun in at least two of these - Quake (with character skills) and Doom.
Development of DOOM started with Doom comic -
. Somebody really liked the RIP AND TEAR page, so he decided that new DOOM should be about ripping and tearing. Therefore, shooting became a necessary mechanic to let player rip monsters. Players are given health and ammo for tearing, but you get almost nothing if you shoot enemies without ripping - a subtle way to move away from the core doom gameplay.
After choosing the main game theme, developers discovered that some players still chose to shoot monsters avoiding melee contact. More limitations were added such as RPG elements. Now Doom guy is a weakling, who can carry 10 shotgun bullets without any upgrades. He also cannot wear armor in proper quantities, his health is 100 out of possible 200 - he is crippled in any way possible. Lack of ammo boxes almost forces you to rip and tear - as intended.
After crippling the main character, developers found out that player can just run around looking for supplies to shoot monsters and avoid ripping! So they decided to place you into tight multilevel arenas without exit - just like Painkiller, but with more jumping and ledgegrabbing.
Game also has a plot with missions. That's right, doom guy is a mission guy now. He has a mission to do, with someone else above him (which is total heresy). He is not a free independent marine anymore, now he needs to save everyone. Of course Bethesda tried to hide that via character's actions - like constantly destroying important stuff. And yet he still follows the orders.
Guns are somewhat nice, but without ammo upgrades they feel underwhelming. Not to mention the amount of upgrades - weapon tokens and argon energy balls for ammo (maybe something else? Too many upgrade categories to keep track of). Was it really necessary? Doom needs no feeling of progressing aside from getting new guns and meeting stronger monsters. Now player is faced with decisions - do I need more hp or armor or ammo (protip: you always need ammo)? Acceptable for any shooter, but not for the shooter with DOOM in title. Not to mention that game ends like a level after you feel really powerful. Of course there is an arcade mode with all upgrades, but why not make it the default mode without RPG crap?
Monsters are fine, they do monster things and do them as they should.
Graphics are fine, nothing bad about it either.
Music belongs to the garbage bin - wubs are not music. Occasionally there is some guitar - when a strong monster enters the arena.
Bethesda and remains of id Software managed to make a good shooter, good enough to be a proper Painkiller sequel. Unfortunately, it has almost nothing similar to original Doom in gameplay terms aside from Hell setting and weapons. Sonic-speed running marine was replaced with jumping ape, who has shotgun without ammo and forced to rip and tear. Get it for 75% off and play arcade mode, avoiding campaign. And please ignore DOOM in the title.

TL;DR : It's not as bad as everyone says, just look at it like a puzzle game and don't expect it to move too fast.
I play a lot of FPS, or at least I used to, and in that time I always wondered a bit how the virtual guns I was using to pwn all the noobs in town actually worked. Being financially challenged and completely unmotivated to get the permits to own these guns, this wonder was set aside.
That's when I saw World of Guns. "A gun simulator where I can take apart guns to see how they work?" I said. "What's the catch?"
The catch is that it's free-to-play, and that comes with all of the normal trappings of free-to-play games. Several other reveiws have been comparing this to a Facebook game for a good reason; lots of grinding, lots of repitition, lots of soft paywalls, and there's even incentives to invite your friends to play.
The game itself is rather enjoyable and novel, and is about what it says on the tin. You disassemble, then reassemble, a firearm. The amount of guns there are is staggering. Name any gun from any modern-military FPS you know of; it's in the game, and you can take it apart, and even see how the parts work together while it's firing. You unlock the first few guns quickly, but the cost of guns later on increases, and the only way to gain more currency is through repetition. If you're looking to shoot actual things, there are firing ranges, but they're far from the main attraction and probably shouldn't be what you're spending your time looking at.
The repetition itself isn't too terrible. By the time you're forced to start repeating builds to get more currency, you've a decent selection of guns to play with, and each gun has it's own set of achievements to complete that help you earn currency. These achievements are repeateable, but subsequent completions don't give you as much cash as the first. The achievements range from simple completion to speed-run awards, and even reward you for having the best time on the ladder for the day.
When playing, it may be better to see the game as a thematic, informative speed puzzle centered around guns. I've gotten quite a bit of enjoyment with this mindset and have killed several hours of time this way. However, as the cost of guns rises, it may become less and less feasible to continue playing, but it depends on your level of involvement.
I reccomend only to people who think guns are neat and/or like to do fast-paced puzzles.
As a F2P it could be a lot better. Very limited access for no money, and for full access, costs an arm and a leg. Would not recommend this game to anyone.

Japanese propaganda! The tag says "nudity", but it's a trick to getting you to learn about their country! I've been deceived, and now I've been indoctrinated!
Alright, so I cracked this game open on a whim; it was part of a bundle, so why not? What I got was... well, that's what this review is about.
Go Go Nippon is a visual novel. You loosely decide a few things throughout the story, but mostly you sit and read. While it looks like it's going to be a dating sim, in practice it's a lesson about Japan that happens to have anime girls thrown in. The entire novel focuses on learning about Japanese cultural norms and everyday life, as well as classic traditions and history. In short, it's a lesson in common knowledge about Japan for those who have never been and lack the aformentioned common knowledge. These are the kinds of things that aren't taught in a classroom - you might learn about the Edo period in class, but a lot of people wouldn't know everyday things like what a Bento or a Kanbini is, or how a conveyor-belt sushi place worked unless you looked it up yourself.
The game even has a few features to help further understanding. When one first opens the game, they are asked what the current exchange rate is between your country's currency (well, dollars and euros anyways) versus the yen, and the game uses that information to give readers an idea about what things cost whenever a purchase is made. When sightseeing, the game will even offer a "photo" option in the bottom right which conveniently opens up your web browser to the Google Street View of that area, allowing you to look around the area that the characters are taking you through (that's kind of a brilliant little feature, actually).
In a sense, this game is sort of like Age of Empires: at heart it's a game, but it will happily introduce to you characters and concepts from other parts of the world, letting you learn a thing or two about history while also enjoying yourself. Go Go Nippon tends to pride itself a little more on the educational bit, but it still remembers that it's a game and retains its light-heartedness. In fact, I wouldn't mind if more educational games, or games in general, took this route - it's kind of fun to casually learn about somewhere without being drilled or quizzed.
Unfortunately...
The game suffers in that, at the end of the day, it caters to a very, very small group of people. Your protagonist is stuck as a male character in a semi-dating sim (complete with 'accidents'), and the cutesy style is intended for a younger audience. As such, this will appeal best to males in their teens more than it will anyone else, despite that the game has the potential to be very informative to a wider demographic.
As well, although it is kind of nice to have text both in Kanji as well as English, I would have perhaps liked an option to have the text in Romanji so I could sound out what the characters are saying. This game is otherwise a good intro to Japan for foreigners; it would have been nice if we could have learned about the language a bit more as well.
Don't expect anything too deep, but it can still be entertaining.
In sum:
-Informative!
-Entertaining!
-A bit too cutesy
-Meant for younger males
Now if you'll excuse me, as a man who is too old for this demographic, I'm going to have to get rid of any evidence I had of enjoying this game. And then I think I'm going to buy myself a new toilet...

This is one of the greatest games I've ever played. I consider myself a hardcore gamer so I don't use that lightly.
Nier is not just a game Nier is art. This game has an amazing compelling story that most developers have been too lazy to do for years and it raises the bar above the ones that were not too lazy.
The gameplay is fluid and exciting. It is easy to pick up but has enough depth to keep seasoned players coming back.
The game has no autosave. This is NOT the developer being lazy and leaving it out as the reviews from people with 1 hour playtime will tell you. It is a very important gameplay mechanic which is critical to the games story. Death in this game has some very interesting mechanics. I advise you save often though. The game has some bad ending and there are ways to get game over. I can't tell you why that's so good without spoilers.
When you finish the game it feels a little short, until you realise the game is designed to be episodic. It autosave on completion. Then you load it up again and it starts with a new story. The first one eases you into it playing the same story over from a different characters perspective with some small gameplay changes. The the 3rd story starts with.... ..... with..... I can't do that to you it would be too painful. All I should say I'd that the 3rd story story (and all of them really) is a hugely moving emotional rollercoaster right from the start.
You will see some complaints that the PC controls are terrible. I never used them I played gamepad but given how the combat mechanics work I think it would be impossible to make them work well with keyboard and mouse. You NEED 2 joysticks for it to be fluid. There isn't really a way  to make that smoother  with keyboard  and mouse. Seriously get an Xbox wired controller. They install automatically in Windows 7+ Trust me it's worth it.
Some users have reported buggy graphics. I never had that problem.

DR3 is a much better game than I expected, if not without its quirks. I never played DR2, but was a big fan of DR1, and DR3 builds upon the strengths of the original game while mitigating some of its weaknesses.
Pros:
+ Open world/free-roaming city environment, densely packed with a lot to do. It’s not an especially huge or varied open world, but it was very satisfying for the purposes of the game.
+ Tons of zombies onscreen at once, especially in the late game.
+ Fun combat. Obliterating a sea of zombies with overpowered weapons and combos is every bit as satsifying as you would hope.
+ Tons of interesting weapons and vehicles. Collecting and crafting the hundreds of combination options and discovering your own favorites is fun, and they did a good job offering a lot of variety.
+ Fun characters. They’re stupid, but they serve their purpose and the off-beat atmosphere of the game well.
+ Survivors aren’t nearly as irritating as in DR1. They hold their own pretty well and kind of auto-keep-up with you and/or will find their own way back to base, depending on the situation. It’s even occasionally useful to have a couple along for psycho battles, to help distract the psychos as you fight them.
+ Atmosphere and general gameplay: I always thought DR3 looked like it had abandoned the fun, weird sensibility of the earlier games in favor of a “grittier” more realistic vibe, but that’s actually not true, which for me was a plus. I love the game’s weird sense of humor, multiple-playthrough/mode structure, bizarre unlockables, goofy costumes, over-the-top weapons, etc. – all the things that made DR1 so interesting and fun when it first came out.
+ Less time-pressure intensive than DR1, though there is still a timeframe you have to keep an eye on. Don't expect to get every collectible or combo blueprint the first run through.
+ Rewards multiple playthroughs with multiple endings, unlockable modes and costumes, etc.
Cons:
- Pretty hard to get ideal performance out of this one, even on high-end PCs. Quite good-looking at highest settings, but poorly optimized, with an FPS cap of 30 and no ability to take advantage of SLI configurations. At 2560x1440 and maximum graphic settings, I was happy just to hover around 25 fps, and I have a moderately high-end rig.
- Frustrating play control. Not so bad that it isn't still really fun, but it can be maddening on occasion. I used keyboard/mouse, but I have a feeling it’s an issue regardless. My biggest frustration was constantly “accidentally” picking up items and weapons other than the ones I intended to, and accidentally “throwing” some weapons away from me, by hitting the wrong button. In general, the button combinations are not well thought-out and you will often do things you didn’t mean to do, which can be very aggravating when you’re in the middle of fending off an onslaught of zombies.
- Kinda sludgy movement in general. Even after you max out your agility, the response times and fluidity of Nick’s movements leaves something to be desired. This doesn’t stop combat from being fun, but it does make navigating the environment tedious at times.
- Horrible vehicle control and too many arbitrary blockades. These become very tiresome to navigate in the latter half of the main game.
- Inability to teleport in any way makes for a lot of tedious re-tracking/back-tracking/looping through the same routes in the latter half of the main game.
- Inventory is too limited for my liking, even after you level up to 50. I hope future installments build towards a more RPG-sort of feel that allows you to carry and manage and do more with loot.
- Level 50 cap / max attributes is pretty easy to reach if you know what to do. It was a little disappointing to have nothing further to do with my PP before I even got halfway through the game. Future installments should let you reach higher highs in terms of what your character can do (cf. Saints Row IV, Crackdown).
- A tad glitchy. Not really too bad, but there were occasions when I dropped weapons – on purpose or accidentally – they would just vanish and I would be unable to retrieve them until I went back to a safehouse.
- Kind of easy, certainly compared to DR1. As long as you have a few super combo weapons and/or some DLC in your locker, the boss battles are mostly a cakewalk. This didn’t bother me, much – super difficult boss battles aren’t really what I was after, here – but sometimes I was surprised how readily I was able to breeze through some of the major confrontations. Then again, if you really want them to be challenging, just don't bring along overpowered weaponry (which I always did).
General verdict:
Awesome, super-fun game that is totally worthwhile, but poorly optimized to take advantage of PC hardware, with some frustrating idiosyncrasies to the play control. While I listed a good # of cons, they're mostly nitpicks with respect to the overall experience. Definitely not perfect, but 100% recommended for the many things it does well. 8/10. I wouldn't (and didn't) pay $50 for it, it's too console-porty for that price -- but if you can grab it on sale <$20, it's absolutely worth it.
Performance tips: Like I mentioned, this game is limited to a single GPU, so no SLI here. If you’re using an Nvidia card, turn on “triple buffering” for this game in the control panel – it noticeably helps the game run more smoothly. You can unlock the framerate cap if you want, but I found doing so caused crashing, and I couldn’t seem to break 30 FPS by much anyway at max settings. I don’t think I crashed once, as long as the cap was left in place. There is also a FOV fix that will place the camera  a little further back from you than it is by default, which I do recommend, though the difference won’t be huge.

Being someone who played Fallout 3 and New Vegas before trying this out, I can say that the beginning of the game will be rough, very rough.
The interface is very different. The combat is more XCOM than modern Fallout. And it's not as pretty or immersive as Bethesda's 3D world. If you stick with it, though, you will find a lot to like. One thing you should know is that a lot of the great elements from this game never made it to Bethesda's games.
You can find encounters where two opposing groups will be fighting each other, and you can either leave them alone, take a side, or engage both at once. What do Bethesda's games have? Just the same group of enemies that respawn in the same areas after a while. I suppose in Skyrim you will occasionally find a fire mage fighting against an ice mage, but here we're talking two small armies engaged in battle.
The companions in some ways aren't as fleshed out as the excellent ones in New Vegas. They don't really have their own extended storylines. You pretty much do them a favor and they'll tag along with you. But they make up for it by having a bigger impact in fights. I loved my companions in New Vegas, but they rarely make a noticable difference in fights, you might kill them by accident, and most of the time I'd rather leave them at the Lucky 38 to take advange of a Perk that gives me a damage buff when alone. In Fallout 2 though, they are a big help in fights, and some of them have VERY special behaviors - do you prefer a Deathclaw that will always charge ahead, or a Robobrain who's really good with guns? Note that neither is humoniod enough to wear Power Armor!
When it comes to story, I'd say it's about on par with New Vegas, which is a very high praise. You actually get to make decisions unlike Fallout 3 and 4, and unlike NV, if you don't have the stats to choose a certain route, you wouldn't even know it's there. So if you set up your character differently at the start of a new game, you will be very surprised at how different your new playthrough can be.
Bottomline - it's a great game, but it can be difficult to get into at first. If you enjoyed NV and want more of it, you will have better luck with Fallout 2 than Fallout 4.

Woah. What a blast from the past.
You like Fallout 3? New Vegas? 4?
Well, sorry to bring it to you. But you most likely won't like Fallout 1 and 2.
I don't say this because they are bad games. They are not. They are one of the best turn based RPGs I have ever played.
However, Its extremely difficult to get into those games from a todays perspective. Horrible graphics, clunky GUI, doesn't run well on modern systems (even with patches installed), a weird turn based combat mode, a difficulty level that forces you to save all few mins. This alone will be enough turn off for most modern players. Honestly it was even for me for some time.
But at some point I gave a damn about all the modern Fallouts. I just wanted to play the classics as others experienced them in 1997-1998 and I think I came close to such an experience.
The game really opens up once you learned to overlook the "bad" aspects of the game from a modern standpoint. I got used to save all few mins. I did usually anyway since I tried every approach in the game. I wanted to get as much lore from the game as possible.
What I got was a great oldschool experience. This is one of the few pre 2000 RPGs I was able to get into. On a second look, the game didn't age as bad as you would expect. It still has many of the things that the modern Fallouts have too. Ok, maybe not Fallout 4, not saying its a bad game but the RPG and dialogue aspect of the game really were lowered to a minimum, sadly. Fallout 1 and 2 had Interesting dialogues for example. I often just laughed reading the lines in those games. I don't wanna spoiler anything. But having for example, a low intelligence, makes a whole different game out of it. It is really funny. New Vegas was similar actually, which is no wonder since many of the same devs worked on it. Fallout 3 is a mixed bag when it comes to RPG. It had some of those moments but not as much as the classics.
Another really interesting thing is that you can do EVERYTHING. Yes, you can kill everybody you want, including all characters and even children (I think the Steam default version doesn't have children, use the unofficial patches). I found it interesting that you can do whatever you want but be ready to face the consequences. Hell, you can even have sex in the games and the nudity is not really censored. There is even a perk for having the best sexual intercourse possible. Now that are things you don't find like that in modern games anymore, without mods at least. Especially not in the modern Fallouts, which is REALLY a shame. Yeah, Bethesda made it more commercial and casualized and therefore removed such features because many probably would have been confused or felt offended by its content. Plus having to deal with worldwide censor cuts like in the EU. Both Fallout 1 and 2 were censored in the whole EU. Only the US versions really were 100% uncut. I really miss such content.
Can I recommend it? Hell yes. But only if you are able to overlook all its non modern aspects. And this is difficult. But if you do, you gain access to one of the most beloved RPGs ever. Just make sure to grab Fallout Fixt and the Unofficial Patch +  latest Sfall. They are mods with bug fixes and small improvements, especially to the technical aspect of the game. This makes the game really playable in my eyes. Still, the game suffers from many modern system problems. Crashes, graphic problems, blackscreen, color pattern problems, you name it. Its usually all fixable but honestly the experience is really meh sometimes.
I should note that Fallout 2 feels a lot more polished and has more content. If you ask me, this is probably the best RPG ever made. Especially when it comes to the role playing aspect. You won't find a deeper experience anywhere. The possibilities and the replayability is endless. It also improves on many of Fallout 1s blemishes. But don't let me fool you, Fallout 1 is definitely a great game as well and should definitely be played. Then you honor Fallout 2 even more. In comparison Fallout 1 feels like a Beta version. Not even kidding. They took everything people loved about the first game and improved and extended it further. The only feature they removed for some reason was the "Tell Me About" feature. You could ask all NPCs for some words and they might respond with something useful or a note. Honestly this rarely worked but it was still amazing seeing such a feature in a game in 1997. When it worked, it was really mindblowing. Hell, which game has this nowadays?
Now those are really games which would DESERVE a remaster. I see games from like 3 years ago getting remastered so why not this? Really Bethesda, consider this. The franchise was never so successful and many would love getting to play the originals but optimized for modern systems and with modern graphics. Maybe also some small adjustments like autosave, etc. I don't even need a FPS experience. Even if you make it top down view + turn based combat again. Just do something with it. If you don't have the resources or will for it, then give it to Obsidian! You can't tell me that New Vegas wasn't successful. Hell, it was the best RPG + FPS Fallout experience yet. Just give them some other Fallout game to develope or let them remaster the first 2 games. Would be a shame having to wait like until 2025 when there might be a Fallout 5 from you, which hopefully reintroduces some more RPG aspects again.

Try the 1975 F1 car, called 'Formula Retro'.
Try the 'Test day'.
Pick you car and pick 'Johannesburg' as your track. This was the old Kyalami race circuit.
Remove the 'Electronic aids' listed in the garage, and do so again in the 'Options' menu.
Reduce the tyre pressures to 17.8 for the front, and 18.3 for the rear.
Alter the camber to '0'.
Now go and drive...
Remember, the tyres are cold for the first lap, so don't push too hard yet.
Hopefully you'll be getting a 'feel' for the car, and it should bring a smile to your face...
After a while, you may feel confident enough to post a time on the 'Time trial', and you'll soon realise how much you want to do better...  ...and you get another go in 1m 13 seconds or so! Exhilarating isn't the word!
Once I'd realised where all the 'Electronic aids' were in the menus, and removed them, I began to live.
Even some time in the tardy Formula Vee helped my understanding of weight transfer.
It's easy to over drive the car, and you need to control yourself to get the best out of it.
And then there's the circuits...
OLD Interlagos, with its fearsome double-apex first corner. I was taking the first part at 163mph! It takes your breath away.
At Brasilia you'll begin to learn how to deal with the lack of grip. At Cascavel you'll have yor breath taken away again.The first corner is a full 180 degrees in fifth gear, ultimately leading into a VERY fast 4th gear left hander before you have to anchor it for a slow right. It's awesome!
At Kansai, which is in fact Suzuka, you will be seriously challenged by the lack of grip. It's literally rally-driving a F1 car!
Imagine taking a car like this to Britain's Cadwell park? It's a motorcycle track after all.
Imagine no longer! Hanging on to this car at Cadwell requires your bravery as well as your judgement.
Then you watch the replay and think, "Wow, this is also fantastic to watch!"
Having played 'Grand Prix Legends' in the past, now being able to drive the Brabham is fantastic, nothing less.
My frustrations are with the dreaded 'understeer' on everything, but it's easily controllable on the Brabham 'Formula retro', but I'm trying to engineer it out, which is quite a challenge.
Having learned some set-up lessons from the Formula Retro, hopefully I can apply them to the other cars should I choose to try them.
The graphics are fine by me, and anyway, it's the feel of the car that matters.
I use a cheap Thrustmaster (Non-force feedback) steering wheel, which works very well.
I'm really pleased with this game.
It's frustrating but very rewarding trying really hard to get the best out of that old Brabham.

Firstly, I loved the original Deus Ex (DE1) and it is the best game I have played so far. Thus, if you don't mind old graphics, just start by DE1 :) However, Deus Ex Human Revolution (DEHR) is also a great game and it is the worthy successor of DE1 … after a "fair / easier / simplistic" Deus Ex 2!
As each game of the series, you will move in an awesome cyberpunk environment, which is as complex and consistent as in the best SF books. Cyberpunk games are usually really interesting because they often deal with a lot of interesting concepts such as transhumanism, bioethics, economy and law.
DEHR is the prequel to DE1: no nano-augmentations, only mechanical ones (e.g. strength, mega-jump). You play as the security guard Adam Jensen who works for the biotechnology company “Sarif Industry”. You will discover a world in which there are 2 factions: people who are for the augmentations and those who are against them. You will obviously discover benefits and problems linked to the progress of technology … and you will have to regularly make important choices that will influence the subsequent chapters!
### Pros: (most of them are shared by DE1 and DEHR)
- Good story and great cyberpunk environment involving corporations, secret societies, and charismatic characters
- Fun and addicting gameplay (immersive FPS with 3rd-person cover if desired)
- Inventory management, physical augmentation upgrades, a huge variety of weapons …
- Large number of side quests (you have to speak with most NPC to find them)
- Play as a stealthy ninja or Rambo since you can choose your game style
- Your choices will have major consequences on the subsequent missions
- Game with some difficulty in realistic mode
- You will not finish it in 10 hours and it has good replayability (see below)
- Great graphics, musics and good dubbing for a videogame (English version)
### Good replayability:
There are multiple ways to reach the main objectives [ "how can I get in the police station ?" ==> you can choose at least between the 1) main door 2) roof 3) sewers ]. Thus, it can be fun to replay a chapter using another tactic (especially if you upgraded other physical abilities). Besides, all achievements can't be unlocked in only one go. To date, I played DEHR 3 times:
1) I played "as usual" (tactical rush, killing most enemies)
2) I played as a ninja to unlock the hardest achievements (Factory 0, Pacifist, Foxiest of Hounds)
3) By starting with my augs & skills (NewGame+ mode) to quickly unlock remaining ones
### Cons:
- Use the hardest difficulty since the AI can be improvable
- Voices are pleasant but badly synchronized in the French version
### Conclusion:
- You like killing people with guns or using slow-motion animations? DEHR is for you!
- You are a real pacifist? DEHR is also for you since it can be finished by killing only bosses!

I just finished the game after 29 hours and all I can say is that this game is unbelievable.
First of all the story is just amazing. You will try to learn everything in every place and its done so beautifully that you don't even get bored or you just don't want to continue without wondering around. Different endings and being able to somewhat change the story is a huge plus.
Soundtrack is pretty good too, it really makes you feel the game. I still listen the soundtrack in youtube, what else can I say? If you play the game you will understand it, it just suits perfectly. Brilliantly created. You will not be upset if you care about the soundtrack.
Gameplay is also good. Skill system and inventory was well done, it made me think carefully before I change anything or pick a new item or skill. Upgrades to weapons are also very good, they change the game dramatically. Combat was challanging too and I loved the finishing moves. The game can be played by either stealth or pure combat styles. I loved the stealth action but sometimes the finishers were not good. For example when your character kills a guy silently, it should drag his body back but instead it sometimes just throws it away and it results in a bad situation. Overall if you enjoy stealth or fps games, I believe you will enjoy the gameplay. Being able to focus on pure combat instead of stealth makes the game also good for players who wants action. It is good that game gives you a choice depending on your style.
There are a lot of, I mean a LOT of places to wander around and tons of hidden places to discover. I didn't expect that when I started playing but you really feel the freedom while playing. Game doesnt just force you to play it linearly, it gives you many options. Lots of side quests, places and things to find and play styles to choose will definitely keep you excited about the game. 29 hours felt like 9 hours. If you are like me and want to explore every corner, you will not be disappointed.
Unfortunately there are some things that I dont like about the game. Sometimes game just makes you feel like it's wasting your time. And as I said there are many places to investigate, you want to explore every corner but it makes you exhausted.

Have you ever questioned what games are and what they can be?
This is the best game to release in 2017, arguably the best game to come out this decade, and in my opinion possibly the best game I have ever played. People look at Zelda or Mario 64 and see them as games--while not perfect, as games that managed to set the standard and define what great games can achieve in the late 90's to today. Nier Automata is the game that will define both story telling and gameplay from 2017 and beyond.
NieR:Automata defies expectations in both story and gameplay, combining them in ways I personally never thought to be possible. This is done by either straight up changing the genre of the game, hitting you with a heart-compelling character interaction, or a combination of both. The game plays the way you want it to. If you are feeling like it's too easy after setting it to hard mode you can remove HUD elements, increase damage taken, or dive into the combat system and learn 15+ weapon combos by combining your 4 equipped weapons and your pod. The game is meant to have you experience it the way YOU want to. If the game is too hard you can equip as many chips as possible and set the game to easy, basically having the game play itself by healing and fighting for you so you can experience the story the way YOU wish to.
In order to experince Nier:Automata fully, the game is designed to be played multiple times. After initially beating the game, you replay the game from another perspective. After that, the game opens up even more in a way you wouldn't ever see coming in a blind playthrough, opening the world up even more (quite literally). This idea of story telling may throw people off initially but can only truly be accomplished in this form of medium--as a game.
I never really saw video games as an art. Video Games have defining artstyles, music, atmosphere, themes, and so on...yet I never considered them as an artform, just something that is there to entertain me. NieR:Automata showed me the light. The atmosphere is truly something else. When it wants to, Nier makes you feel part of it's universe, and then a moment later you are catching your breath and you feel something off. You then remember that you are playing a video game. This is done intentionally and happened to me multiple times. As someone who enjoys phycological elements in entertainment, while questioning the motives of characters and diving into the meaning of character interactions, cutscenes, and atmosphere, I ended up questioning what I was doing as a player experiencing Nier:Automata.
As I was questioning myself, I was also wondering what made me want to question myself as a player. I have no idea how to describe that feeling other as looking into your heart. NieR:Automata is a game meant entertain your heart and make you feel something. It will likely be different for you, but I ended up feeling something amazing inside me up until the end of the game and past the credits.
And this feeling is something I wish for you, a potential player, to pick up and experience yourself.
Please play this game.

I can't help but notice that I haven't left a review for this great game yet, so let me do that here. This review will contain minor spoilers about the enemies, weapons, and mechanics.
There are a few different class types, and all play differently, so variety seekers this is a treat for you.
Rampage Knights is a fantastic beat 'em up game that features procedural generation. Now, let me talk about the mechanics of the procedural generation and the game.
PG (procedural generation)- There is a set pool of weapons on each level, I believe, or every two levels. The starting level basically teaches you how to play the game, while the very first combat room of the second stage offers you a glimpse into the power ups and weapons. There are 3-5 weapons available on the second level, and they go from a slower club that stuns on critical hit, to a poisonous sword that poises enemies (not skeletons though, look out!), and my personal favorite in the form of a dagger. It's short, so your range is limited, but it's fast and does +50 critical damage on hit. And that's just a few weapons on that stage that CAN pop up.
At first, I said "oh, so I'll either get A-D on this level, meh, I want it to be random." After completing the game multiple times (look at my hours in the past week, insane mode is hard, man), I can safely say that the system is a wonderful one. If every weapon in the game was able to drop on the second floor, I'd be incredibly overpowered, and then later severely screwed.
This is because modifiers exist, such as curses. On Insane mode, you get a new curse every floor. On the other modes, you don't, unless you are forced to trigger a demonic statue. This can happen only once per run. What does a curse do? It varies! The most tragic one, to me, is "Animated". All the barrels that you've been smashing for gold pieces and health pick ups? Yeah, they are enemies now. And man, there are LOTS of boxes, statues, barrels and more in this game to smash.
Which brings us to the mechanics- Your standard attack is mashable to create as big of a combo as you want. You won't be doing that though, as in instead you'll hold the attack button and dash forward. Why? It breaks shields, and man do you want to break the shields of the enemies, trust me. If you press attack and up, you launch enemies in mid air. Follow it up with pressing attack, and you do a neat combo that ends with them on the ground. If you're close to an enemy, you do a punt, which also ends up with them on the ground. Once there, you can stomp them for a lot of damage, but be careful, you become very vulnerable to any attack while stomping an enemy.  For defense, you have an excellent and easy to use doge roll that becomes incredibly difficult to master when♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan.
The variety of enemies is good. We've got knights, demons, goblins, undead, giants, trolls, crazy chickens, Halloween looking ♥♥♥♥ers with swords that throw pumpkins at you, and more.
There is one final boss who has a very cool final form (won't spoil that one), and a mid point boss. Actually, the midpoint boss draws from a pool of I believe 5, so it will be different each time you play.  They are tough, but very fair after you learn what you need to do to defeat them.
Potions range from hilarious to useful, but not a single one feels pointless or tacked on. Diseases, such as being poisoned, can be cured with a variety of potions, but do you really want your character to be drunk, making movement difficult for a few rooms?
Overall, I really enjoyed my time with Rampage Knights, and I'm excited to go back to it. The developers put their own unique spin on a classic formula, threw in some humor, a doge roll and tons of love.
And I, for one, am very thankful that they did so.

Coming into this game, all I knew it was about is you shot stuff. What I experienced is some of the most fun shooting stuff I've had. In this game, everything but having fun takes a step back. The story? From what little bit of it you have to experience, all I could tell is people wanted to use Hell for energy and it backfired for some reason (Reason is told to you ofc). But there's very few cutscenes, maybe 10 minutes of gameplay where you are forced to view story related stuff. There's audio log type things you have to stand still to listen to, or you could click them and leave to go kill more stuff. The majority of the story is told by voice comms from two people. The original half life has more character models than this game does story characters, which means not counting the demons you kill.
But, they took the shooting aspect and made it as fun as possible. Reloading? Not fun.(Okay, the super shotgun reloads and that was my favorite gun, but it's dope) Running out of ammo? Not fun. Shooting demons? Fun. Non stop shooting demons with metal music? Super fun. It took me roughly ten and a half hours to beat this game and I never got bored. Demons explode, you can glory kill demons where the doom guy rips them apart in some fashion depending on where you initiated it, and this game is chock full of secrets and easter eggs. There's probably about ten guns in this game, a chainsaw, and a BFG. Earlier, i hinted that you don't run out of ammo. In the first hour when you only have two guns, you'll probably run out a few times but a glory kill usually gives you enough. After you get about three guns, running out of ammo is rare especially once you get the chainsaw (A chainsaw kill drops tons of ammo, but it uses fuel which does not drop from said chainsaw kill).
In all, this game was amazingly fun. More fun than I expected. If you like shooting stuff, this game is great. If you like story, I've heard you can read about it but don't expect to experience it like The Last of Us or Firewatch.
