As a big fan of the Guilty Gear franchise, and Persona 4: Arena, I had...somewhat high hopes for this game. I'd heard what I'd heard, and little of it good, but still...a 7.5 wasn't too much to ask, was it?
This game is, in a nutshell, Guilty Gear if it was trying too hard. For someone who has played this, GG and P4A, it's so easy to see this as the middle child, with neither the love and care of the former, nor the time-tested wisdom of the latter.
The character designs in this game are atrocious. Each character has been over-designed to the point of becoming completely generic and uninteresting, a feat which I'd've thought impossible. Ragna the Bloodedge, a main character with a name somehow stupider than Sol Badguy, looks like an anime character merged with a matryoshka doll. You could shuck ten layers off this character and still not get to the actual man beneath. Every anime trope is piled on these characters in order to make them memorable, and a similar concept has been followed with the game's combat.
The Drive button is an interesting idea. I can see how it evolved into the P4A persona attacks. But here, it creates a combat system that is equal parts chaotic and clunky. I fully admit to scrub status; I am not particularly GOOD at Blazblue. But that is irrelevant here; I'm terrible at 3rd Strike, I'm terrible at P4A, I'm terrible at friggin Skullgirls; but it doesn't impact my enjoyment of the game.
With only local co-op available, the AI's gotta stand up. And it just doesn't. Set it to highest difficulty, pick Officer Moe, and spam Down+D. Oh, look what happened. PERFECT.
Is it? Is it
Main takeaway? People like to play fighting games for a lot of reasons, and the big two for me are the feel of the combat, and the design of the characters. And in both cases, Arcsys seems to have taken the approach of "throw stuff at a wall and see what sticks."
What they didn't realize is that the wall was sticky. Very sticky.

Essentially the GFWL version now without GFWL, the Steam version now lacks Online and apparently still suffers from the same issues.
Being the first entry of the series, Calamity Trigger is a bit simpler than the other combo heavier sequels and revisions (characters being given more move set options) but all 3 main entries in the series try different balance mechanics that make them play a bit different. With Dashes, a Parry system, Barrier blocking, a simple "revolver" combo system (A > B > C > D move links) and Cancel options, the pacing can get pretty hectic in BlazBlue.
Aside from the PC versions (Steam and Windows 8 Store), I've only played the PSP version of Calamity Trigger and the Steam version appears to be a port of the home console versions meaning that it lacks the addition of Legion mode from the PSP port and the BlayzBloo Shop (there are still unlocks from the shop available.)
If you don't mind having to restart your PC to get rid of the framerate issue that appears after a while of PC uptime (fps sinks to a capped 30) every time, the PC versions of the BlazBlue games have almost instant loading times for matches (you can skip the matchup screens not long after they pop up) which make them my preferred versions, having played the latest 2 installed on the PS3.
The included OST appears to be the one from the console's US Limited Edition as 320kbit mp3 files.

Red Orchestra is an fps which immerses players in reality based gameplay that is visceral and exciting. Can you survive WW2's Eastern Front?

While it is a very hard game in the worst ways possible, Red Orchestra is still fun. The controls feel like you're wading through mud, and you'll be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off that you can't kill anything half the time, but the sheer size of the maps, along with the ability to play with somewhere around 80 people in one server, makes it an interesting play nonetheless. I give it a very tentative buy, because many may not want to take the time to get acquainted with the.. 'interesting' controls.

If you're a hardcore WWII simulation fan, then this game is for you.
I recommed playing with a group of friends.

Solid gameplay I haven't seen in a long time. The only downside is its terribly dated graphics - I'd hold out for RO: Heroes of Stalingrad running on the UT3 engine.
Unlike other WWII FPS games that rely heavily on automatic weapons, RO goes back to basics with bolt-action rifles for about half of each team and they have a distinct advantage over SMGs at about more than 10 feet. It sounds dull but makes it really intense. Tanks, artillery, and machine guns weren't left behind either.

I'm not a huge fan of music games that don't let you import your own music (Guitar Hero, Rock Band, Guitar Hero World Tour, The Beatles Rock Band, Guitar Hero II, Rock Band II, etc.) but Red Orchestra is a winner in my book because you just conduct an orchestra playing classical music, which I really enjoy. It has all the classics (that was a pun!) like Tchaikovsky, Mozart, Bach, Beethoven, and (unfortunately) Wagner, and it also has some more snappy modern stuff like Shostakovitch, Mahler, and stuff Mozart wrote when he wasn't 12. I feel like this would have been better as a Wii game or a Kinect game or something, because using the mouse to conduct feels weird, but it does support joysticks and frankly it's so well done that I don't see why anyone would complain. A must for fans of music games who, like me, want something other than Coldplay or Freezepop to listen to.

"GOOD IF IT DETACHES ITSELF FROM THE NAME BRAINBREAD"...
edit: SO I had a review here bashing the game. A lot of people didn't like my review.
Allow me... to retort....
I am a BrainBread 1 (and Public-Enemy) player who enjoyed both mods since their inceptions, through their peak player surges, until they dwindled down. I must've put 2, 3, maybe even 400 hours into BreanBread itself? I loved that game. That game, was one of my all-time favorite HL1 mods. With the funky tropical + suburban + whatever the hell maps, with it's awesome "beta Resident evil" style zombies (who you could blow body parts off of, including their faces), all the way to the 500 guns and weapons (including everything from a lever action rifle to a propane tank, to a man carried minigun to a set of dual Uzis), this game was the premier zombie killing mod of it's day IMHO. I just basque in the memories of running into a mall as a mime, jumping in a shopping cart and hatcheting away at zombies while my teammates wage war against a giant muted zombie roaming the mall wearing jean overalls...
Flash forward to today... BrainBread 2 comes out. Now I've followed the development of BrainBread 2 for quite some time, since it was announced, and I believe it was being made by some of the original team before but got handed off and whatnot and then became a "spiritual sucessor". Heed my warning, BrainBread players - this is not the BrainBread you knew and loved from before. Oh no... no this is much, much different. The voices - all Britishified... I mean hey, I'm ok with that, but it seems SO strange to hear all these voices as European people who can't get a good American accent going on. Now this is not a big deal but listen - this game takes place in USA... so shouldn't the people at least SOUND American? Not to mention, but also missing: the awesome maps, the tons of awesome weapons, the zombie hit detection/and damage setup.. and MANY many other features the original BB1 had. And the zombie hit detection is ♥♥♥♥E (for my EU friends out there, trying to spit some of your lingo). 8 shots in the head to kill a zombie? I remember in BrainBread where 1 Desert Eagle shot or 2 M4 rounds would put a "zed" down. (More EU lingo eh)
So I'm left wondering, with all these features missing and this feeling like a completely different game, why is it still called "BrainBread"? It feels nothing like BrainBread, the original game I played, which evolved from Public-Enemy as a futuristic neo-noir cyberpunk Japanime type game where cyber ninjas fought on futuristic battlefields - which evolved into BrainBread the game where you run through these futuristic battlefield, but as if they were turned into malls and shopping centers and suburban neighborhoods. With zombies.
BB2 feels nothing like what I remembered.
edit: There, is that a better critique? Or will I still have 50%+ of the people reading this click "Not Helpful" (because you probably are a dev for this crappy "remake". Just throw away the name "BrainBread" and I would love this game! for reals)
tl;dr: Good if it detaches itself from the name "BrainBread". Otherwise, for actuall original BB players, you're left with a huge gaping hole in your gameplay experience wondering where the BrainBread 1 is at?

I originally gave this a negative review. I did so out of frustration. Frustration at how infuriatingly bad the controls were ported. The bullet hell and hacking sections of this game were translated to the mouse and keyboard with what seems like no consideration or oversight at all, which for the most part produces a game that is floaty, imprecise and slightly irritating. At one point, around 30 hours in, however, it because literally impossible. Fortunately the game does provide some god-items on easy mode that essentially allow the game to play itself as long as they are used, which got me past that sectioin of terrible design.
Like I said, initially this exerpience led me to give the game a negative review. Upon reflection, however, the reason I was so infuriated by this setback is simply because it was preventing me from progressing in what may have been the single best game I have played this year, and one of the best I have played ever. Would I have been so displeased by this series of events if I weren't 30 hours into a game I was absolutely loving?
The game itself is tremendous. Truly. Do beware, however, that the port is competent and playable, but not especially good. Controls are janky, and the resolution needs to be fixed in a third party mod unless you are already playing it at 720p or lower.
The story though. I don't fully understand what happened or the order of events, so I have to replay again (and that's in addition to the five playthroughs the game warrants anyway). Couple that with an amazing soundrack that really gvies life to the entire atmosphere, I cannot say enough positive things about this game. I just wish the PC controls were more than the afterthought they were.

I am strictly a PC gamer, as are most of you steam users out there. Using this controller is definitely a new experience with me, but im proud to say it was a good experience. This controller is amazing for any game really. Massively customizable for any need, also is customizable in game for menus and gameplay. You don't need to set up your own bindings as you can grab someone else's binding from online (Which is easily accessable because its right there in the binding menu). The touch pads are tricky to get used to, but it doesn't take long if you are a gamer ready to explore new ways to play(via Steam Controller). Long story short get the darn thing; 100% worth the money.

Bully is an open-world crime game that playfully twists the formula of its Grand Theft Auto cousins. Set in an unforgiving private school, you’re tasked with taking down the school’s feuding social cliques as a bully who fights bullies using any means necessary. Instead of firearms, you’re given the arsenal of a traditional schoolyard prankster (itching powder, stink bombs, slingshot, etc.) and follow a series of diverse missions that have you racing bikes, winning boxing matches, delivering papers, painting graffiti, and even playing rhythm games. This variety extends to a surplus of optional content in the surrounding town. The game favors density over volume, as the relatively small world feels expertly crafted. Most notably, every single student has a unique name, face, and voice, which helps the game succeed at building the “living world” that so many open-world games aspire to. You can watch these students go to class, kiss in the hallway, hang out with their cliques in the evening, and bully each other using the same pranks you pull on them. Bully’s attention to detail and gameplay variety make it a charming and unique open-world game.

Dead Rising 3 has received quite the negative reputation over it's course of existance. The only thing is, I can't agree with it's negative feedback.
From someone who enjoyed both Dead Risings 1 and 2 on the Xbox 360, the transition over was very nice if I do say so myself (from Xbox to PC). People claim this is a very "poor port" but yet this game runs flawlessly on my rig without a single issue. Before I mention anything else about performance, please realize that I DID unlock the frame cap and I enabled Vsync because this game suffers pretty badly from screen tearing. I might also add that my system is pretty beefy (I'll add my specs at the bottom of the review).
I guess since I'm already talking about performance, I'll start off straight away with that. This game DOES have a frame lock at 30, but you can download and add a .ini file from a website (I'm too lazy to get the link) that offers the file. Other than that, the game runs very smoothly without any real major dips in framerates. Users have complained about frame dips, but like I said, I didn't experience a single dip. Zombie hordes do lower my FPS by about 5 or 10 FPS, but it usually kicks right out of it and by the time it does that it's almost completely unnoticable. Regardless, the game can hold a 60 FPS very nicely. Some people have also complained about crashing- in the time I've played it, I haven't experienced a single crash yet.
My only real complaints for this game are the controls and it's lack to sometimes render small objects that are mere feet away. The controls feel very poorly done, especially with the camera. The manual mouse movement feels slow and laggy almost. Using WASD to move around also feels like it's delayed or something. Using a controller would probably feel better, but as far as keyboard/mouse, I think it just needs some getting used to. I haven't played a Dead Rising game for a couple of years, so it might just be me getting used to the controls again. Regarding the rendering with some objects, notice that I stress "sometimes" because this only happens very seldom. Most of the times I forget about it- in fact, I'm actually editing my review after I wrote this to add this in because I completely forgot about it.
Compared to other Dead Rising games, you're not stranded in a god forsaken mall. You're set in a fairly open world environment with lots of backroads and the sorts. Lots of areas in the map are open and are accessable. I read somewhere that "90% of the doors are locked in the game" but yet I've only seen two locked doors- and they were apart of a mission where they were SUPPOSED to be locked... DR3 takes on a nice and new approach and I think they did a great job with it so far.
DR3 also added in a better (imo) crafting (or 'combo' system as they call it) system and way more vehicles. They added in craftable cars and combo-cars as well. You can combo weapons and things found through blueprints, just as in Dead Rising 2. Blueprints are scattered across the map, along with PP collectables and more, all of which are located on the minimap in the corner (which is nice). Unlike DR1 and DR2, the time system is MUCH more leanient. I still have a few missions from when I started the game that I haven't even touched, yet I still have over 75% of my time remaining.
While I haven't delved much into the story yet, . Overall, the story seems to be very well written and it's as quirky and stupid as the previous installments. It's a lot like the other ones where you're getting rescued in a certain number of days, except the government .
Overall, I'm very happy I decided to pick this game up on sale for $14.99. This game seems definitely worth the retail price and/or sale price (as long as everything works fine for you).

The third game with the Deus Ex title has a lot to live up to on both positive and negative ways. Firstly, it has the name of expectation, to be something grand, one of a kind, stylized, distinct, and memorable. And on the other hand, there's Invisible War. You see, Deus Ex isn't just another game with another sequel, much like Doom 3, there is such a history, that the expectation is to overshadow the past and not relive the mistakes. With Human Revolution, it feels like both aspects exist, but leans more on the good side of things rather than being a blunder.
The majority of the story revolves around a thinly veiled and, for me anyways, a predictable plot line, but then again, Jurassic Park was predictable, yet that doesn't necessarily take anything away from the movie and nor does this fact take away from the game. It does give the sense that something greater is driving the pieces in play and you do get the feel that you are part of a much larger world that is on the brink of a revolution that will, for better or worse, change the course of mankind. The acting staggers depending on which character you interact with, some are superb, while others are pretty dull, but in all fairness, that could be attributed simply to the way the game's chat mechanic works. The characters truly shine during the more tense, though I wish were more common, 'choice/decision' making moments where your actions determine how the future of your experience will be, from convincing an old friend to help you, to deciding to get something fixed or not. My favorite of these are the ones where you have to 'monitor' another character's vitals in order to get what you want and asking the right questions and reacting in the right manner, an ability you can unlock should you choose to do so. Speaking of game mechanics, Human Revolution does a fantastic job of mixing both the HUD with the theme of the game, as if you were merely looking through the eyes of Adam Jensen, the character you play. Many other graphics follow suit such as the ability to see through walls, health bars, and info pages.
Just like with the first Deus Ex, this game has some RPG elements, but as Zero Punctuation bluntly pointed out, Deus Ex is an RPG game with action elements and Human Revolution is an action game with RPG elements, thus the skill tree is severely lacking and some of the skills are rather pointless, such as the hacking skill that gives you more info on a particular node, though the standard info is sufficient enough for the player to make an informed decision. Some other skills though come in handy, which in my experience I wish I would have taken up sooner rather than later in game, like punching through walls, but like in all RPG's, such decisions have to be balanced between a survival skill or an advantage skill. The other thing that Human Revolution does particularly well is its non-linear exploration, something every other first-person shooter these days seems to forget how to do. Often times, I was so in tuned with exploring that I accidentally got to where the main story wanted me to go and ended up missing some side quests. The side quests, too, carry their own weight and consequence as well as advantages. Some give you insider info on a person you may need later, a personal revelation, fancy toys, or just a comfort to a person in need, which is a nice distraction from the action sequences. Human Revolution also builds an organic environment with the NPCs as you interact with them peacefully or, if you choose, violently. You can, for instance, subdue a clerk, steal the good from his store, and be on your way. Just don't expect him or her to be so friendly the next time you decide to visit, unless of course you choose to simply drop them like yesterday's laundry, but be warned, killing civilians may alert the authorities who will come searching for the suspect and if they see you, they will be on the look out for the rest of the game. Stealth is definitely a prized skill, since your resources are limited. When you're hacking a door or sneaking into a vent, if the wrong person sees you doing it, you can end up in deep trouble, even with allies.
Combat in Human Revolution can be very intense and can match the likes of any modern action shooter, but on the flip side, one can go through the entire game without a single conflict, shot fired, or death, barring boss fights. It is extremely comforting to be able to have such options and not just going in guns blazing, and trust me, doing that all the time will have consequences later on, most of which lay upon resource management. You will find yourself buying more ammunition for your weapons instead of on health packs and other tools you would need. On the flip side, being stealthy may cause you to miss out on important information that certain characters are carrying, such as secret compartments, passwords, and codes. Speaking of codes, there are certain things you can hack if you are at an equal hacking level (This can be upgraded by using praxis kits). When you use a code or password to access a terminal, you gain no experience, but you also have a lower risk of being detected should your hack attempt fail or you're spotted while doing so. Depending what praxis' you choose to spend where, this can hinder your journey or become very advantageous.
A majority of Human Revolution is also quiet, running from one person to another, leaving big action scenes a good distance apart, a pacing I did enjoy more the second time around. If you're not used to actually having to search for something in a free roaming environment, especially in a first-person view, it can be quiet a drag actually having to run from one side of town to the other, but that just added to the immersion for me. The cites are big, alive, and imaginative, yet they seem like they could be real. That is what shook me the most was that a LOT of the ideas are beginning to sprout up here and there today. How do we handle sports or crafts that require learned skills? What becomes of art, music, and talents? Should we be so integrated with our technologies and to one another?
Of course, this is not a perfect game, though it is pretty close, there are some very BIG, glaring problems. The first being the boss fights. That being, they are ridiculously simple and involve none of the skills you've learned and acquired along the way. It is truly a missed opportunity to have some very unique fights especially within the FPS genre and instead becomes very run of the mill, the ending being notorious among gamers. Although, with a new "Director's Cut" coming in October 22nd, 2013, this issue, among others are (hopefully) resolved[1]. The second issue, isn't really an issue, but more of a critique on the cinematic team. I'll just say this: When making pre-rendered cinematics, make sure they are better than the in-game graphics' highest setting, not that they're bad, just that some instances are better than others. Part of me even wonders why the cinematic team didn't just make the movies in the style of some of the trailers or the "ending," but I could just be jaded because of Blizzard's cinematics.
All in all, Human Revolution is a fantastic game with a moral compass that surpasses every other game in its genre, which comes as no surprise, with Deus Ex, you're kinda pin holed in a good way, into certain ideas, concepts, and views that puts you above the warfighters and modern warfares. There is NO multiplayer (What a concept) and one above par DLC called The Missing Link. It in itself is worth picking up, contains its own plot line and challenges, I recommend it. Deus Ex lends itself to exploration and growth not just as a game, but as a way to think, it gives the chance to do things differently, you become a part of the world, but just like with augments, only if you choose to do so and that is what the game does best - giving you a real choice.

This game's narrative is told in 3 major parts. While the first part might be a little of a slower start and hard to understand the first time, it really starts going in the second part and finally, without halt will charge attack a player in the third.
Since this is not your typical popcorn action game story, it requires you to focus on many things that are not told by some voice audio. There are many things a player won't be able to understand without collecting and reading additional information hidden throughout the game world, talking to characters as well as finding hidden chests will provide these bits of additional storytelling. Before calling this a grind for collectibles, think of it as an enhancement of narrative, due to the great addition of even more depth to the story that it's cutscenes and story based conversations provide.
I will not go into detail about this games mechanics, you can basically see those in the Store's gif animation above, it felt like a unique basic RPG (skill distribution is nicely made and I can't remember a game with something alike this) with Hack and Slash gameplay mechanics in an open world scenario. Also I will not risk any spoilers by going more into the game's story, if you like a game that perfectly merges several genres (like top-down, bullethell, sidescroller with kind of platformery style to it and the typical 3rd person RPG adventure style), simply play and experience it for yourself.
The game's soundtrack needs to be mentioned as well. The songs are so incredibly well made for where they are being used in the game, that i even felt like i wanted to write a review for this game just because of the soundtrack. I will talk about it a bit more later, but i thought the soundtrack should also be mentioned in my objective review, after all it also got at least one soundtrack of the year award already.
The last game I remember to have enjoyed like this might have either been Witcher 3 or Journey. All 3 games have at least one thing in common: a beautifully crafted and precisely to the situation fitting soundtrack. However, I can definitely tell which soundtrack i like the least, that is Witcher's in this case. Compared to the other two, it's just too repetitive, listening to the songs without playing the game feels boring. This is not the case with NieR's soundtrack. Every song has it's own characteristics and feel to it. It's like knowing exactly where I walked in the game when I heard the stage of a soundtrack, what I felt when playing the game at different parts with this soundtrack and so on. It's like the soundtrack of Journey, where the soundtrack was made to be one with the game, you can't play the game without the music, it will just lack a part.
which makes this my most favorite soundtrack to a game experience so far (in about 18 years (no, that's not my age, I'm older than 18) of playing and growing up with all sorts of different games).
As I already wrote above it's told in 3 major parts. I, for myself, didn't really understand what all the stuff at the end of part 1 was about, so i thought "okay, lets just wait before being disappointed, and continue playing" (it really made quite little sense to me). Then, playing part 2, which many call "repetitve",
the skeleton from part 1 gets it's skin, that was extended with eyes, hair and clothes in part 3, still missing its deep personality. This is where the additional information come into place. While you get a really nice piece of story with just playing through it, listening to the soundtrack, watching cutscenes and playing parts where you talk to main quest people, then listening to the soundtrack some more, the additional info just adds so much depth and personality to the game, that I can only recommend everyone to just gather and read them! I for myself never did so in a game before, also I never enjoyed to read what a game wants to tell in archives before! Reading those archives, those separate stories within this universe, all created another additional feeling, addint to what the rest of the game already did. Thinking about what all I read meant without even playing at a time, recreated and even further increased the whole experience like adding fuel to a flame and providing it with oxygen at the same time to create an everburning inferno.
This was the most expensive game I got for this account so far (28,49€) and I would say it deserves every single cent I spent on it. I can definitely say, that the value of Time/Cost is much higher than I ever experienced or even expected in a game so far.
The Soundtrack is a mastercrafted piece of incredible music and feels like telling it's own story every now and then. If you asked me, this is probably the best soundtrack I have ever heard while playing a game. For me, it even beats pieces of Hans Zimmer.
For Gameplay, I really enjoyed how smooth it felt, even if it doesn't have any ridiculously hard combos you need to train for several hours to get into, they just weren't there but still didn't feel necessary, it were even without those a bunch really satisfying combat situations.
This game provided a totally new experience to me, and I loved it!

I pre-ordered the controller a while ago before it came out and was excited to start to use it, but I was in the middle of moving. So I moved and didn't realize that the controller was shipped to the wrong adress so I was paranoid that someone just took it and then found out that it was sent back to the post office awaiting pickup. So I emailed valve stating my issue and they sent the controller a day later from the post office to my new home. It was fast and a reliable effort on their side.
I am strictly a PC gamer, as are most of you steam users out there. Using this controller is definitely a new experience with me, but im proud to say it was a good experience. This controller is amazing for any game really. Massively customizable for any need, also is customizable in game for menus and gameplay. You don't need to set up your own bindings as you can grab someone else's binding from online (Which is easily accessable because its right there in the binding menu). The touch pads are tricky to get used to, but it doesn't take long if you are a gamer ready to explore new ways to play(via Steam Controller). Two extra buttons on the back of the controller are easily accessable and makes customizing great, and gameplay easier for the games with a lot of buttons. Honestly at this point you're better off just buying one and play around with it yourself. It's amazing.
Also one more thing that is really neat, is that you can customize the sounds the controller makes when it wakes up, and turns off, as well as assigning a name to the controller to know who's controller is who's if you get more than one for the family. You can also set the brightness of the main button. OH there's also a gyroscope inside the controller that you can use to do whatever you want; great for steering in racing games like Distance, or The Crew. It's super light and battery life lasts months, for me atleast. It feels good in your hands, AND you can boast about how customizable your controller is to your XBOX restricted friends. (Also the track pads have haptic feedback and makes it very convienient for playing FPS.)
Long story short get the darn thing; 100% worth the money.

World of Guns: Gun Disassembly is a good game in my book.
But first of all: What is World of Guns: Gun Disassembly?
World of Guns is a simulation. Not the "Surgeon Simulator" kind of simulation but a rather realistic one. The developers of the game took their time to good use finding information and blueprints on different weapons. They then created and animated the parts. What you do in the game is disassemble and then reassemble them in varying detail. You start of with two weapons after the tutorial. The AK-47 and the Colt M1911. You can partially assemble them (Field Strip), fully disassemble them, assemble them, watch them shoot in great detail (X-ray Cam, Cutout, Slow Motion) and finally "Play" with them. There are 2 game modes. The simple one, where you disassemble and reassemble the gun as fast as you can, which can be done competetively against others via leaderboards and the "advanced" game mode where you do the same only that when you try to assemble/disassemble parts that can not logically be moved it restarts completely, forcing you to remember how to correctly assemble each of the guns. It should be noted that you only click on parts to interact with them. You will not use any tools or choose where to put the parts yourself, that is something that the game does for you.
The game features an unlock System. You can unlock new weapons with XP. XP are gained by earning achievements for each weapon (Finishing each game mode / disassemble and reassemble in a certain time etc.) or simply by "playing." It is not all that easy to unlock all achievements and it will make you grind to unlock most weapons, which is totally reasonable since that is what the game is there for. It teaches you realistically to actually disassemble and reassemble those guns. Learning their parts and the process of assembling them by heart.
This naturally should tell you that this isn't a game for anyone but gun enthusiasts. If you have no interest in guns or disassembling them, not once but over and over again repeatedly then this is not a game for you.
Now that you know what the game is about, is it any good?
It's a good game in my book. As a long time german shooting club member (implying I already did disassemble some of the handguns also in the game) I can, at least for some of those guns, tell you that they are very detailed and correctly represented.
My only concern is that the developers seemingly weren't all that consistent when creating some of the guns. Sometimes removing a single bolt is an action you have to perform and sometimes the bolts and the part that they hold in place are handled in the same action.
Lastly, the game is free to play. You are free to try it and if you actually do get sick of unlocking you can also buy the guns.
So, if you think that you are within the target audience of this game, feel free to try it. I enjoy it a lot.

AdVenture Capitalist is a clicker game. This is a revised review. Doesn't take much to run the game so no need to worry about hardware. I've also had a long, rather mixed or bad history with this game but this review is going to appraise it as it is now, rather than how it was starting out.
Pretty simple the way the game works. You buy properties with money you earn over time, even when the game isn't running. There are 3 main planets you can play, Earth which is the longest. The Moon and finally Mars which is the shortest. There are also seasonal/holiday events that pop up every now and then so you can earn extra stuff such as real money currency to use toward in-game store purchases. There are also Mega Tickets and Mega Bucks you can exchange in-game money for to boost/guild your properties.
In the past it was impossible to beat Earth and get all the achievements. But the game was re-worked and now it is possible, which I'm thankful for. Though it still takes a lot of time and planning so that you don't waste Gold and Tickets.
As far as clicker games go this one isn't much to look at but it was enough to tick all the boxes that trigger my OCD. If you're into clicker games, check it out. If not, ignore it completely.

As a lover of the Fallout franchise and its lore, I have to say I enjoyed playing Fallout 2, but it's age shows greatly. Now that it's been demystified to me, and I now know what people are referring to when they talk about it's level of freedom and player choice I have to say it's left me feeling a bit dissapointed. I fully take into an account that this game is nearly twenty years old, but games have made great leaps within that time, and Fallout 2 just feels archaic. Maybe it's because I've played the more modern Fallout games, New Vegas being my alltime favorite of the franchise, but it just leaves me feeling unsatisfied. When playing, the highs are high, and the lows are just mediocre, not bad, but nothing special, and most of the game was just the latter. I feel I must admit, I didn't wish to talk to every single npc in game, and due to this I probably missed out on quests, or information I couldn't obtain otherwise, but I just couldn't be bothered especially as I was playing more as an outcast than anything else, for this reason I wasn't able to figure out what to do at certain points in the game, and more often than not, just had to roll my way through until I got lucky or looked up a guide. The ending boss left little impression on me, in fact the final section as a whole left little impression on me compared to the Master from Fallout 1, Horrigan just feels rushed and missplaced, we barely know anything about him and he's now the final obstacle in our quest? I won't even go into detail about the bugs the game still has, despite installing the unofficial patch.  Is it a good game? Yes, of course and it's one of the games that established what Fallout is today, yet it's one that shows its age a little too much, so is it worth seeing it to the end instead of just reading what happens on the wiki? In my opinion, no. To be honest I prefered when it was mystified to me.

--- I use the mod to control my companions in combat**.  I find it more fun that way.
- Some game dynamics can make you waste or spend a lot of time (like most games I guess; less than in Fallout 4 :P).

Not without its flaws but a step-up (in terms of physics and immersion) from the likes of the GT franchise.
Pros:
- no grinding for credits as all cars and tracks are available from the off
- great handling
- dynamic track conditions (including evolving racing lines)
- dynamic tyres (including visible dirt pick-up)
- nice sounding cars
- decent range of cars/series to choose from (several eras of F1 cars through Super V8s and the Marcas series)
- competitive AI, which also makes the odd error from time-to-time
- growing Mod library
- great service from the devs who take the time to listen to the opinions of the community and even integrate some of the suggestions
- customisable DynHUD (using DynHUD editor)
- probably the most authentic sim racing experience outside of iRacing
Cons:
- somewhat tame AI (in terms of AI-on-AI action) means its usually a case of simply 'follow the leader'
- lack of both an introductory 'training school' feature and a Career Mode
- no hover tips for the menu options (some of which may not be self-explanatory to the non-hardcore sim racer)
- lack of more popular tracks as stock content (such as Spa, Nordschleife, Zaandvoort, etc.)
- a somewhat small (though growing) online multiplayer community
- essentially, just a rehash of rFactor (although this does show how talented the devs are, given the game engine is about 15 years old)
To get a feel of what Reiza can do, try their totally free offering (Copa Petrobras de Marcas) first. If this impresses you (as it did me) then you'll get along with AMS just fine. The lack of more popular tracks may put some off making the investment, but there are quite a few Modders out there who have added a decent amount of additional content, which is still growing thanks to some good work from dedicated (and generous) enthusiast-level fans of the game.
In my opinion, AMS is a stepping stone to bigger things. It's enjoyable as a sim in its own right, no doubt, but it's more a precursor to what I see as being Reiza's main project, which I understand will get underway in 2017. This I look forward to very much. For now, though, AMS will do just fine.
As a side note, it's probably worth getting the season pass (especially if you can get it at a discounted price) because there are quite a few more DLC packs on the horizon, all of which (so far at least) seem to me to be worth making the investment.

There are driving games, and then there is Automobilista. For anyone who played the original Deus Ex back in 2000 this really is a worthy successor to that game and is scrupulous in its attention to detail and fidelity to the original's lore and universe.  The in game graphics although not up to 2014 standards are good (not 1080p good but good enough to enjoy). I read a number of reviews claiming FPS problems but I've encountered none on a medium range system (Dell Inspiron 17r SE 7720 with Nvidia Ge force GT 650).
The game's story is brilliant, its controls are fluid and switch dynamically if you want to use a Xbox 360 controller AND keyboard at the same time (a number of newer games can't do this - I'm looking at you Arkham: Origins). That said for a Deus Ex fan there really is no innovation in terms of game mechanics. In fact thus far I think there's actually less flexibility because you can't choose augmentations to install you choose which ones to activate from Adam's pre-installed augments.  Also the sneaking/combat mechanics of “locate the air vent, sneak through it and then avoid/take down/surprise enemies is exactly the same as the original game's.  That's not necessarily a bad thing (why fix what's not broken) but at some points the game could have done with having a true third person camera option. The camera will switch into third person when the player takes cover but it would have been more immersive to have a third person option the whole time. On the improvements side, the game's social interaction controls (persuasion, intimidation etc) are better than the original's, but like most choices and consequences games the choices are fewer than it may initally seem.
All in all I recommend this game. For new comers to the series this is a great jumping-on point, and for old hands like me how played the first two games this is an excellent prequel worth of the name Deus Ex. 4 out of 5

I'm absolutely floored by the engineering and effort that's gone into the production of the Steam controller.  It's incredibly well-made, Valve has a crazy level of support for it, and it features some absolutely ingenious designs.
But as an actual gamepad to play games with?  I hate it, I think it sucks.  This seems to be how this gamepad is - you either love it, or you hate it.  I think it's part of it trying to be a traditional gamepad AND a mouse surrogate.  I got the trackpad to function decently in Dark Souls 2, almost as good as my little Logitech gamepad's stick was working... but not quite as nice.  Using the trackpad-type thing for the d-pad was an exercise in mounting frustration, and I actually don't know why they felt the need to make it a semi-trackpad rather than a traditional d-pad.
The cherry on top were the bumper and trigger buttons.  I imagine they're quite wonderful for shooters and many other games, but I'm playing on a computer... I have a mouse and keyboard for games like that.  For Dark Souls 2... ugh, I couldn't get used to them.  The bumper buttons felt WAY too damn big to function effectively as my R1/L1 buttons, and the triggers didn't feel right even after I reversed them with the bumpers and turned off analog inputs.
I think some of this is learning curve - this gamepad DEFINITELY has a learning curve - but also... it just don't feel right.  In the same way that some people could never get used to the N64's gamepad and the Gamecube's gamepad, I just can't get the Steam controller to feel right, so it's on its way back to Amazon first thing tomorrow.
I still think the Steam controller is an amazing piece of tech and while I thought the REQUIREMENT to use Big Picture mode was a huge and completely unnecessary pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ I'm sending it back because it just doesn't feel right, not because it didn't work right.
I recommend people give it a try if they're in the market for a new gamepad.  Just... make sure the folks you buy it from have favorable return policies (Amazon's is fantastic!  I got an instant refund in the form of a e-giftcard, they deducted the return shipping cost from that, and since it was instant I was also able to immediately order a little Logitech F310 to replace the one that died on me, which the Steam controller was meant to replace.)

* Difficult but Fair Brawler with a New Experience Each Time *
Rampage Knights is a game I can recommend to most beat-em up fans.  It is truly Nintendo Hard with only 2 lives in a single player mode to fight your way to the final boss, with extra lives being a mechanic available to a single class (which starts out with none in reserve) or pure luck.
Despite the scarce resources and brutally punishing difficulty, I felt 99% of my deaths were fair -- I could have prevented them by dodging some other way, positioning myself better, or using an item earlier.  Even the small percentages of deaths that were almost beyond my control could have been within it if I had just done something a little differently.
The luck element still plays a factor, but not to the degree of Binding of Isaac where the RNG can make a run nigh impossible or incredibly easy.  Despite the curses, diseases and odds, each class has the tools they need to win with just their base abilities -- afflictions only limit how many mistakes you can make, and there's always a way around them (although this is luck based).
In the standard game, the right gear can make you nigh invulnerable with even serious mistakes being easily recoverable in the next room.  The standard game provides four difficulties, from Casual (which will allow you to see the ending eventually with perserverence) to Normal (NES hard) to Hard (NES Ninja Gaiden without the ability to continue hard) to Insane (even harder).  Casual can be beaten in under 30 min if you know what your'e doing; and even Insane has a few items that will allow you to turn your disadvantages into overwhelming power.
For those looking for a bigger challenge, in the Endless Dungeon game you can't rely on luck -- just about every additional edge will be stripped from you eventually (although by that point if you're still alive your skills are so great that the only chance the game has to kill you is waiting for you to make that one, fatal mistake).  You can plan for this eventualities but other than that, your tactics and reflexes are the only things you can count on.
I haven't even unlocked the Shadow World.
Despite my talking about how difficult the game is, I have to stress it is FAIR.  There's nothing stopping you from using every dirty trick in the book against your opponents and you're encouraged to do so.  Knock the giant off a cliff, endless combo your foes, use fallen enemies as projectiles, toss them into the abyss, throw everything at the room at everything else, abuse the hell out of your magic.  The room will kindly drop your rewards in safe areas so you never have to worry about being unable to claim your power-up just because you tossed a guy into a pit or killed him so his body is lying on a trap.
The base combat itself is simple but entertaining.  You have an almonst-invincible roll, a shield-destroying power-slash, a shield-destroying, staggering jumping attack, the ability to giant-swing fallen enemies to harm everyone around you, and the ability to throw most things at other things, which is a lot more useful then it sounds since throw enemies tend to knock each other down.  You also have a higly damaging air-combo, best saved for isolated or well-grouped enemies.
To this, add slots for magic abilities you can find in various points of the game (not super-common but common enough than you will have the luxury of choice), very common projectile weapons (common enough that it's a good idea to always use them as appropriate; you will find more), a single-use scroll slot, and a potion slot.
Your equipment consists of melee weapon, armour (if available), belt, boots, and gloves, all of which confer various benefits to help keep you alive.
You also can have various familiars to assist your quest -- as many as you can find in the standard game, and up to three in Endless Dungeon.  Some of these stack beautifully and can utterly destroy your foes, while others can accidentally kill you due to the area effect -- but their nature is readily apparent and you shouldn't need more than one experience to know what to pick up and when.
Finally, you have a wide variety of passive items that will increase your abilities -- to possible game-breaking extent in the Standard Game (but limited to 1 of each type in Endless Dungeon).
All these factors create a unique dungeon brawling experience, and best of all you're allowed to simply skip past all the enemies in the first two "floors" of the game -- so vetern players looking to get right to the meat can do so.
If you like brawling games but hate how repetitive they can be, then this is the game for you.

AdVenture Capitalist is a clicker game. This is a revised review. Doesn't take much to run the game so no need to worry about hardware. I've also had a long, rather mixed or bad history with this game but this review is going to appraise it as it is now, rather than how it was starting out.
Pretty simple the way the game works. You buy properties with money you earn over time, even when the game isn't running. There are 3 main planets you can play, Earth which is the longest. The Moon and finally Mars which is the shortest. There are also seasonal/holiday events that pop up every now and then so you can earn extra stuff such as real money currency to use toward in-game store purchases. There are also Mega Tickets and Mega Bucks you can exchange in-game money for to boost/guild your properties.
In the past it was impossible to beat Earth and get all the achievements. But the game was re-worked and now it is possible, which I'm thankful for. Though it still takes a lot of time and planning so that you don't waste Gold and Tickets.
As far as clicker games go this one isn't much to look at but it was enough to tick all the boxes that trigger my OCD. If you're into clicker games, check it out. If not, ignore it completely.

Automobilista is the result of Game Stock Car Extreme and rFactor having a baby.
Automobilista has very realistic physics that resembles rFactor and iRacing. Although the force feedback is a bit rough, it is overshined by Automobilista's F1 and Racecar physics. In my opinion, AMS' best physics are in the karts and single-seaters. Automobilista has a different feel than other racing titles which means you will have to get used to it.
The best part of automoblista's gameplay would be the online and hotlap modes, where the optimization and hard work is mostly spent. The AI in this game sadly is very poor and imo needs some work. For example if you are slower they will stay behind you until you fully get off the racing line and litterally get out of their sight before making a move, Which means having multiple car classes at once can be a probem in singleplayer.
The fun part of having an outdated graphics engine is that there is no lag. For people like me who have a poor system this can be a life-saver. Even if the engine is old, the game is suprsingly very nice looking on ultra and is about equivalent to the counter-parts iRacing and the rFactor series. If you are a real sim racer, graphics should not change the way you drive or see a game.
Sadly, the game crashes at this aspect. For the price, Automobilista should have double the variety of racing cars and most importantly, TRACKS. Although there are more than 12 tracks in-game, about half of them are mexican/brazilian tracks that the average sim-racer doesnt even know. Racing on Monza, Nurburgring, Spa or Paul Richard  is only acomplished with Mods.
Even sader, the upcomming content will all be sold in DLC packs which are way over-priced imo.
Overall:
physics: 9/10
Gameplay: 8/10
Graphics: 7/10
Content: 6/10

Do you like great fighting games? If you answered yes, then go get it. It's a good buy.
BlazBlue: Calamity Trigger is a 2D fighting game, and the first entry of the BlazBlue franchise followed by Continuum Shift and Chrono Phantasma.
Calamity Trigger features 12 fighters, each with their unique gameplay, strengths and weaknesses.
As a fighting game it's important to mention that the game can be played excellent on keyboard without any trouble. The combos are fairly easy, and you will always find new ways to chain them into better ones.
The controls are responsive and there's no delay at all. Graphics wise the game looks gorgeous: the 2D sprite models are looking good, and blend well into the 3D background, while animations are smooth and beautiful as well.
Aside from the usual story mode, there is an Arcade mode for every character, mini-games and tons of unlockable artworks to keep you busy for a long time!
However like most games, Calamity Trigger has its' flaws too: first off the Developers removed the multiplayer, though it was part of the game for the Games For Windows Live release, and second the game tends to have 30 FPS limit sometimes due to a bug. To fix the 30FPS limit you have to restart your PC, aside from this issue, the game runs smooth with 60FPS cap.
Overall Blazblue: Calamity Trigger is an amazing fighting game. I can highly recommend this to anyone, whether you're new to fighting games or a veteran in the genre.
And as a Guilty Gear/Blazblue fan is a no-brainer to buy, since it increases the chance of seeing more recent games from the developers on Steam!
- Graphics are beautiful. The 2D sprite models seemlessly blend into the 3D background.
- Animations look smooth and polished.
- Soundtrack is amazing.
- The game features 2 different language voice acting: Japanese and English. Both are solid.
- Controls are responsive. The game plays smooth. Combos are easy to pull off. Can be played with keyboard without any difficulties.
- Lack of multiplayer.
- Occational 30 FPS cap bug. To fix the FPS limit you have to restart your PC.
- Steam cloud doesn't work, though it's shown on store page.
Love it :O!

People told me not to buy it, because it seemed horrible because of its 2D sprites and practically no one I know has heard of it. Didn't care, and I bought it.
Money was worth it.
Interface/Menu: 5/5 - The menu was original and was layed out very well. There's not much more than I can say about it, because the menu is pretty self explanatory, you've got your training button, arcade, story, exit button, score attack, and gallery. The music is very well made, thanks to Daisuke Ishiwatari. The circle layout in the select character screen fits the way the game works. I like the part where the random select is in the middle, which wasn't that self explanatory, I had to figure that out.
Gameplay: 4/5 - The gameplay is fluid and pretty simple, yet hard in some ways. You've got your weak, medium, hard, and drive attacks (A,B,C, and D), just like Injustice. Combo stringing is very open, as practically anything goes (An A,B,C will work for most characters). The mechanics are kind of hard to learn, such as the air recovery, ground recovery, barrier break, throw escapes, negative warning, and the barrier bar underneath each character's health. However, every character, except for Tager, has a double jump and air dash. This is one major part in the game, just like ground hits. There's also distortion drives and astral heats or finishes. These are moves that take 50%-100% of your heat bar. They perform stronger attacks, and your astral heat, always taking 100, will do a finisher, which is a nice touch to the game, adding some variety to the characters. For instance, with one character, you slice them with a scythe and then stab them with a sword, or on another character, you put them in an ice cage. Some characters have special distortion drives, like pushing you and your opponent, or even causing firey attacks, allowing you to go into a more powerful mode.
Story: 5/5 - The story is solid. However, in some cases, it doesn't all make sense. The stories intertwine with each others quite nicely, and even I haven't finished all of it. The cutscenes are nice, however not very fulfilling. The dialogue is very funny. Also allowing customization for the textbox is really neat.
Soundtrack/Music: 5/5 - The music is amazing, and gives BlazBlue the feeling that it needs. It's also included in the BlazBlue folder, allowing me to listen to it in the best quality.
Sprites/Animation: 3/5 - The sprites are good, and every detail is included into them, however the animation isn't all that fluid. However, it's probably the best you can get from a 2D game. However, some animations are fluid, like Rachel ducking and sitting on her cat. Don't complain people, it's the way it works.
Misc: 3/5 - To be honest, multiplayer isn't a BIG thing to me. However, it should be in some fighting games. GWFL's port of BBCT to Steam took out the multiplayer, so it's a singleplayer game, but there's still some hope that this will be added. There's some other bugs that I've heard about, like FPS locking at 30, or sprites disappearing, but it's fixable, so I wouldn't really mind.
OVERALL: 9.7/10 - This is a recommended game. You should get it. Or you can wait for a sale, because that's what I did.

The haptic feedback, This is one part I expected it to shine over my cheap huawei phones haptics, but for some reason, they just don't feel right in some instances they work great and others fall flat. you could compare it to what an audiophole would say about flat tinny cans over a quality set of cans. : If you can race with a controller, you can race with this controller, there is barely any difference other then he addition of using gyro if you want to.
: No idea yet, Havent been brave enough to attempt yet, but if its as awkward as using the desktop, It won't be pretty until vast amount of more experience and learning has been done.
: This is a mixed bag, If I was to say that a controller was a 2/10 and a mouse was a 10/10 I'll say that the steam controller is a 5/10. you'll spend a lot of time tweaking the controller to get the satisfactory results you want, and then there is the learning curve, do you keep the trackball effect, do you combine the gyro aiming (Got to admit, that is pretty awesome for precise movements) do you assign aiming and shooting to the trigger and the "second trigger click"? That's all down to you, I went with attempting to combine them all and found the trackball to be quite annoying so had to tweak that a bit. The trigger aiming and shooting is a mixed bag, If there was more travel distance between the trigger and second trigger click I think it would of been fine but in its current state you have to be actively aware of how far you are pressing on the trigger which just takes away from the experience.
Right, that's a wrap for now. Will update this more and then in a month or quarter of a year will add upon this.

Right I've had this controller since Christmas and I thinks it's time I gave my opinion on it.
Being someone that moves between a controller and M/KB on a regular basis when PC gaming I was really excited about getting one of these, I never expected it to be better than M/KB but I thought it would at least slide into the gap between M/KB and a controller..... unfortunately (for me) this has not been the case.
Starting with the negatives the two main gripes for me are the trackpad and the YBAX button positioning.
One of if not the biggest selling point for this controller is the trackpad, but having tried to get used to it numerous times I simply can't describe it as being anything more than a gimmick, it moves your mouse pointer or camera movements etc around as promised, but the level of precision is behind both M/KB and a right analog stick which for me renders this facility useless.
Secondly I think putting the YBAX buttons underneath the trackpad was a mistake, moving my thumb downwards from the trackpad just felt really awkward and only added to my dislike of the trackpad in general (as per above).
Now for a few positive points, the overall feel of the joypad was pretty good albeit a tad too bulky for me (I have small hands for a 37 year old man), secondly the left analog stick and trigger buttons are pure perfection for pressure and sensitivity making it my first choice for driving games like Dirt Rally.
I hoped my final verdict for this controller would be that it is a genuine alternative to M/KB, but I'm afraid it's more like M/KB > XBOX/PS Controller > Steam Controller which for me at least has made this purchase nothing short of dissapointing. My advice would be to stick with your current controller and use a program like X-Padder instead.
I really want to like it, but after four weeks trying to use it every day I just can't get around using trackpads for a first person shooter. I'm probably going to sell it to recoup the costs.

Let's face it, this game is THE forgotten master piece by Rockstar. You don't have gore in this game, although I would not recommend it for kids, since it does include violence. You go to school as Jimmy Hopkins who has been known as a Bully and has been to several schools, by whom he has been kicked out. Now he is at a Boarding School in New England and whilst you can go to class and do a lot of fun minigames there, such as Music, Biology, Sports, etc.. (I am not kidding they are actually really fun!), you can also later on explore the town around the school and unlock several unique and funny save locations.
Even when you complete the game, which has quite a lot of missions, there are still so many things you can do! You can either collect all the Rubber Bands, Trade Cards, or just do some Boxing and Races, win some prices at the carnival, or do whatever pleases you!
I have an Xbox Wireless Controller, and it works great! Also the English Language is fully supported, even though Steam says otherwise. Even though some argue that this game was better on the Play Station, for me it is quite the same experience and if you play with a controller, you can really get into this game!
Graphics: 9/10 - This Edition is basically the HD edition of the old games, which still has pretty good graphic even though it came out several years ago.
Keyboard/Controller Support: 10/10 - I have had loads of fun playing with my controller, and keyboard/Mouse works also.
Story: 9/10 - A very good story, which is sadly a bit predictable (taking over the school and stuff)
Minigames: 10/10 - A lot of satisfying minigames, which you can engage several times and still have fun with!
All in all: One of my favorite games of all time, which for me is even better than most of the GTA Franchise, and for this small price, it is also more than definitely it's money worth!
PS: I am still hoping for a Sequel, Rockstar please make it happen!

This remains as one of the greatest games ever made. A masterpiece of interactivity, with one of the most doubtlessly tangible and mouldable worlds yet created.
Though it's combat and systems may seem primitive by the modern standard, they are but the gatekeepers to the stories and dialogues of deep complexity and intrigue that demand to be experienced by all who game.
Despite the fretting of others over it's lessened philosophical aspects that defined it's predeccesor, I believe that the pop-culture references simply overshadow those aspects rather than outright replace them, and if one is to examine then one can still find such things; for example
or
The only significant issue I have with this game is a Steam version specific frame rate problem which occasionally occurs when entering an area containing a large number of NPCs
, however this is not game breaking and can be fixed simply by saving, exiting the game completely, restarting it, and loading that save, the complete process of which takes no more than a few seconds on modern hardware. Whilst this may put some people off the purchase, I implore you to fight through this as it would be a shame to miss out on so go a game for so trivial a malfunction. If one is elsewise adamant even after hearing this, one can try the Good Old Games version, however I am unsure as to whether that comes preinstalled with the high resolution patch like this one does.
To conclude in a line: A great game worthy of purchase despite minor technical issues.

BlazBlue output by the same team that has given us amazing titles such as Guilty Gear and Persona was my first delve into the realm of fighting games and I was immediatly hooked myself being an avid anime fan and emerging otaku. at first it seemed hopeless as I was being used to mop the floor by my friend and coach Nick, but there was something about it that just kept me going, I have always had a love for arcade styled 2D games and especially ones simialar in style to those found at game sites such as nitrome. after playing it on his PS3 i figured it was cheap so i gave it a go on steam, this was by far my favorite buy of all year and the best 8 euros spent on any game i have ever had, its graphics are beautiful and fluid due to the use of sprites, and best of all its a low resource using game so you can play next to forever while using your battery if on a laptop (i did a check and it uses around 25% more resources than chrome).
Gameplay:
very smooth and beautiful graphics, well designed menu's, if you have never played a fighter before like me it does a wonderful job of teaching you the basics giving you a training dummy with more features than an android smartphone from blocking op's to weather you want it to stand still or you want the AI to completely hammer you. in general gameplay is very very fast paced and there are plenty of characters to shoose from such as my personal favorite Taokaka, who is light and fast but lacks defense, or Tager who is hugely powerful but isnt the fastest one out there, learn to utilize each one strengths ans weaknesses and you will be sure to find yourself evenly matched in character strengths all the time with your friends. the one thing that this game is lacking that you will hear everyone complain about is a good netplay section, netplay is a big part of fighters as it can be hard to share a keyboard or your away from friends. the game used to have it but it was lost when games for windows live was shut down and it was transfered to steam, however in the menu you see that displayed underneath versus mode it displayes offline: 1-2P, giving me the feeling that a netplay is in the future works (fingers crossed)
Story:
Normally in fighting games the storyline is rather lacking, for example the most common thing to happen is "you're in my way, so ill fight you" or for some other rediculous reason, Blazblue: CT helps remedy that by providing you with an intense and enveloping storyline that has twists and shocks at every corner, depending on if you win or lose or get what is called a distortion finish, you can get the origional endings or the non-canon endings which sometimes end in sorrow, but also are pretty hilarous in some storylines, (Taokaka has my favorite non-canon ending). Despite all this awesomeness in the story it will lead you around in circles if you are looking to get 100% completion to get the full story, a game guide is importent here if you want to get your endings right, most likely the main ending for most of the characters is a distiortion finish win for each battle, but you are going to have a hard time finding the others for example: Litchi has only one canon ending and 5 whole non canon endings, this would be nearly impossible to complete withought the aid of a guide.
Verdict:
BlazeBlue: CT is a great game graphically and storyline wise, it lacks in the first time player ease and if you dont have someone to help you out you are going to have a hard time, read the forums and find out the terms such as dragon punch standing C and dial A to get a understanding of how to play before starting as fighters may seem simple to the untrained eye, but they are by far the most complex type of game out there as you have to think watch and react and execute in a very small amount of time, consider yourself good at FPS? you may have the reaction time but try thinking through which special you should execute while in a j9 (forward jump) all in a fraction of a second, and you soon begin to see why these games are considered to be the most difficult type. however this has an upside, almost everyone in the community has a large amount of respect for one another because they all know how hard it is and are always willing to lend a hand to the newbs out there. And when you become good too you will be able to replay it again and again against a friend or in the storyline for years and years to come.

There are two things I like about Arc System Works (who made Guilty Gear and Persona 4 Arena): all of the bgm in their work is kick♥♥♥♥♥ and their games are so good that I actually postpone reviewing them to play them more, much like BlazBlue: Calamity Trigger.
BlazBlue: Calamity Trigger is the first installment of Arc System Works' BlazBlue series. Taking Place in the 13th hierarchical city of Kagutsuchi, Calamity Trigger displays the city after six legendary heroes defeated the infamous "Black Beast." Ever since then, the Novus Orbis Librarium (a.k.a the NOL or the Library) has governed Kagutsuchi. Soon afterwards, the village of Ikaruga openly rebelled and was quickly destroyed. Now the Library rules with a tight grip, punishing anyone who defies them with death. Although it doesn't really explain it in the opening cutscene to story mode, Arc System Works made Kagutsuchi feel like an oppressed city through the backgrounds showing guards locking down certain stages, to even some of the characters who work for the NOL. Much other than that, BlazBlue focuses less on the big picture and more on the interactions between characters and their complicated relationships.
BlazBlue is an absolutely gorgeous game, each hand drawn sprite looks great and is animated spectacularly. The character backgrounds also play off of the characters backstories and reflects them through the stages, like Taokaka, who comes from a poor village of cat-like people. On her stage, you can see members of her village chasing chickens around trying to eat them. All of the characters special moves, distortion drives, and astral heats are smooth and stylish.
As if the story and graphics don't appease to me enough, the flashy yet simple combat system made me feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥in no time. Playing off the revolver system (attacks go from weak to strong), BlazBlue: Calamity Trigger s simple enough to pick up and start doing combos yet complex enough for seasoned vets to dish out some real damage. The crux of Calamity Trigger's play style and one best parts of the game is the "Drive" system. In a nutshell, no to characters play alike. Ragna the Bloodedge's drive Soul Eater steals health from the opponent and adds it to his own if he sustained damage. Jin's Frostbite freezes opponents on the spot, allowing for devastating combos. Arc also did a great job balancing out the characters. Now Tager, a beefy character with a large hitbox and no double jump or dash, can have a chance with his high damage output against Taokaka, one of the fastest characters in the game and deals a small amount of damage. The only thing I don't like, however, is when they ported Calamity Trigger to Steam, something happened and there is no online multiplayer, meaning you'll have to be sitting next to your friend to fight him.
Verdict:
+Beautiful graphics
+addictive gameplay
+Awesome Soundtrack
+Balanced Roster
-No Online Multiplayer
9.5 Outstanding
Even if Calamity Trigger isn't your favorite BlazBlue title, it is still fun plus you get the soundtrack to boot. Hopefully in the future, if it's successfull enough, Arc System Works will put Continuum Shift and Chronophantasmna on Steam as well (with online capability too). If you are a fan of Guilty Gear/P4A or just want to try a new type of fighting game, then do yourself a favor and buy BlazBlue: Calamity Trigger.

The gameplay is nothing short of amazing. It's a typical hack and slash with a big mix in the forumla in the form of chips bringing in an rpg element.  I completed the game on hard difficulty and it was so difficult that I loved it. I love a challenge. It's a game where you can literally see yourself grow. When I first started on normal, I sucked. I kept dying and having to restard at the begining. So much that it almost put me off the game. Gladly that didn't happen. I pushed through and got through it. Enemies that caused me problems at the start eventually became easy. Not because the game gave me more stuff to play with but rather I just saw progress in my ability. Then every time I got comfortable and though I was unbeatable the game threw in a more tough enemy and made me rethink all my strategy again. It's a difficult game but a vastly rewarding and satisfying game
The audio in the game is some of the best game audio I've ever heard in my life. Even after finishing the game months ago, even until this day I still find my self humming and singing the songs in work or other places. I found myself just standing still in new areas listening to the music at times and now I get the OST on Youtube and just let it play when I'm in the house. I've heard lots of great sound tracks over my years and this game easily places in the top 3 franchises for audio. It might even push for number one, honestly.
The graphics again are pretty incredible. Sometimes I would look at something and notice the detail on some of the most obscure things. There are a few things I would point out that's not great but you need to look deep for them and even then, you can't hold it against the game because the rest is crafted so amazingly.
Story time.Story for me is one of the most important things in a game. I will just outright say that this might be the best story I've ever saw in a game. Without putting any spoilers, the last playthrough hit me with the feels like I haven't felt in any game before. A complete emotional rollercoaster, and I don't just mean happy and sad emotions. Any game that can give me a reaction like that deservs a medal.
It'd be tough to find a game as innovating mechanically and story-wise as this one.

I gotta note that I played this game with pretty hefty breaks in between, and just finished it in my first sitting returning to it. With that noted, this review won't be the most serious ones, and mostly just my disconnected thoughts on the game. Also note that i've only played through story route A, and from what I know there are 2 or 3 other routes I can play as different characters.
So to start, lemme just sing my praises for it : Amazing soundtrack, great story, great characters and character designs, great aesthetics, and NO QTES.
The soundtrack alone is something that makes this game stand out among so many other titles, because many of the tracks are rather memorable after playing through the game, and fit the various moods of different areas so well. Basically, if you don't buy the game, atleast listen to the soundtrack somewhere, it really is great.
Now when I just finished this game, I got the same feeling I get when I just finished watching a good anime/movie. I think the ending of this route (if there are multiple endings, iunno) was pretty good. I loved the various characters that I saw throughout the game, with so many different personalities. I loved how diverse the machines were, and how they formed their own societies forming their own networks and such. There was also a lot of diversity in how these machines looked, and enemy types there were, especially since the majority of them stem from the basic design of the weakest enemy in the game.
Onto gameplay, well......I would say it's solid for what it is. One big gripe I have that I have to note is the difficulty spike between normal and hard. I played through about half of this game on hard mode, and just gave up because of how grueling it was to kill things. Then I went back to normal, and the game was fun again! I was hoping that hard mode made things harder by removing certain things like lock-on and making the AI of the enemies smarter, and while it did do that, it also pumped up the enemies hp to insane amounts and their damage to nearly one-shotting you. I just didn't feel that was fun, since at the time this was the first time I've played a 3rd person action rpg since okami. Playing on normal, the game felt *really* easy, but it also felt a lot more fun.
With actual combat, the controls felt nice, and even though there is simply "Heavy attack light attack" I found myself discovering new moves in the final stretch of the game that I didn't know I could do before. It's a simple system that can be very difficult to master if you try to use it to it's full ability. I'm just not that good, though I did make an attempt.
All in all, I think it's a game that's worth your time and money to play through. I need to mention how amazing of a man and personality Yoko Taro, the director of the game, is. Stuff like his design for 2b's butt was simply because he liked butts or not revealing his face and using his emil mask for a while was great, and he seems like a generally fun dude.

I haven't had much time to play many "current" games lately, and even at that, I struggle to really get into many titles the way I used to. Something-something-the-magic-is-gone-etc. NieR:Automata was, I think, the only one that I played that was *released* this year. I've still played other games in 2017, but mostly ones I was already playing, or ones that I've had for a long time now. There are definitely a lot of other neat games out there, and surely ones that have gotten lots more attention than this one. That said, this is one that not only will be worth your time this year, but will be worth your time next year, and every year after that. I'm not necessarily talking about replay value here, but more that the message of this game is timeless, and I have no doubt that the people who missed out on it this year that will eventually get around to playing it will still get just as much of a rewarding experience as those playing it on release.
This game can be a tough one to love, but it is well worth the effort. It takes more than just the first, or maybe even the first two playthroughs to really get the full picture. Personally, I'm a fan of media that makes you work a bit (see dark souls) to get what the creators wanted you to experience. There's nothing wrong with straightforwardness in games, sometimes that's just what you want, and that is 100% ok. Not only that, but this game is absolutely not afraid of being a game, which I think is pretty cool. Where so many other modern games drop you right into the boots of whoever you're pretending to be while you play that game, this one takes a hint from older games in that the silly little quirks and video-gamey-ness (♥♥♥♥♥♥ term, but I think it makes sense) of the way you interact with the game and the world the characters inhabit show us as that we are the *player*, and the characters are just vessels for us to experience things through. They might be the subject of the story, but WE are the subject of the GAME.
So, I might have missed out on the big hype of PUBG and other hugely booming games that made their mark this year, but if NieR:Automata was the only new game I played this year, then I have zero regrets.
PS: To make sure this game functions on PC, download the patches that the community have made to ensure that your game doesn't look/play poorly. Unfortunately, the developers seem to have left us hanging for any official fixes to the resolution bugs and such.
