Please note that all of my experience with this game was playing co-op online with a friend.
I didn't like the first Dead Rising.  I wanted to like it, but too many things irked me.  Picked up melee weapons broke too fast.  There didn't seem to be much reason for rescuing civilians, and when you tried to do it, their AI was so stupid that a lot of the time they'd die before you could even get them to safety.
Dead Rising 3 feels like it has fixed, or at least improved on, a lot of the things I didn't like about DR1.  Weapons still break kinda fast, but it's easier to stock up on them and the weapons are better.  You can get blueprints and combine weaker items/weapons to make stronger items/weapons.  At all of the safehouses there is a locker where you can retrieve any weapon you've previously picked up or built with blueprints, but you are time limited on how much you can actually pick up before having to wait for it to "cool down".
This makes the game a bit easier, but more fun in my opinion.
I have a GTX 970 graphics card, so I haven't really run into any real performance issues, but there is a LOT of screen tearing.  Like a ridiculous amount.  It's noticeable when I'm looking for it, but during heavy action I don't really notice it.
Basically I went into this game not expecting much and was pleasantly surprised.  As long as you go in like that, you may enjoy it.

is a roguelike( permadeath machine) beat 'em game in which you start with nothing and lose everything upon death. As expected from Rake in Grass the game comes with a bunch of popular references. Apart from that the game offers 6 classes, unlocks and a lot of fun gear to use... if you find it.
Being a permadeath machine , the combat will have major role in.... getting you killed over and over and over again. Combat is responsible for most time though I had cases of my character go skating while I was using Logitech f710 . Apart from that you have light/heavy/jump attack , combos and class based skills(or dodge).
Worth noting is that you can throw/push or bait enemies into the endless pits  to save you some trouble.
The game comes with 6 classes : Adventurer, Barbarian, Pirate, Warlock, Assassin and Battlemage.
Adventurer and Barbarian play similiar to each other(only difference is that barbarian is a bit slower and doesnt wear armor). Rest classes got its own playstyle so they able to keep the game interesting.
Your starting class is Adventurer and you unlock the other 5 classes by completing challenges(3 challenges per class). Now how much it takes to unlock them all it depends on RNG for some of the classes ( finding 10 books for the battlemage took me the longest).
Now this is the beef of the game. If I recall correctly Hero Siege had the same gear mechanic before they went for the generic ARPG gearing up.
So what you have here is a bunch of random items you can pick and make a playstyle with what you find. You can equip armor , helm/mask , gloves , boots , weapon , pets and some other items that dont have defined slots. Apart from that you have consumables : skill(usually a spell that uses your mana), throwable(stones,bombs,knives and poison darts), scrolls and potions(game got some really shocking potions).
You find all the gear in locked chests(that doesnt stay locked if you have the right size boots). The lockpicking game is simple yet challenging at times. You have the lockpick moving left and right and you have to hit the 3 yellow locks. Do that twice( 2 sets of 3 yellow locks) and you got the loot! Dont worry if you fail. You can try again.. and again.. and again.. and woops now you have Treasure chest phobia... Better luck next time! Now dont worry, the phobia wont mean that you cant open chest, it means that when you try to unlock a chest, the lockpicking window will be shaky.
Levels in theme are pretty generic( forest, castle, catacombs)  but you may not pay much attention to them while getting pummeled by the chef in charge. You walk from room to room until you reach the gate to the next level. Room varies from the simple room with monsters to ambushes , vault , merchants or the Wheel of Misfortune(only once I got unluck and had to fight a lot of imps but ... lets just not talk about it).
Now there isnt that much of a variety in enemies(attack pattern) but there is still something to learn while fighting against them.  There are also bosses that you encoutner every now and then(though its matter on how deep you get). Those are quite enjoyable to often you may find a cheesy tactic and defeat them with an ease.
Now this for me is the most important part of a Permadeath machine and frankly.. the devs manage to make it fair.
So your starting difficulty is Normal - once you die you start from 0 , die 3 times and you will unlock casual.
Now dont dare to think that Casual means "Braindead stops here." Casual is more forgiving because its the only difficulty in which when you die you are spawned at the start of the level and not in the starting camp.
Casual is still challenging in combat and its good to help you practice combat a bit more and complete the story once so you can unlock Endless Dungeon and Hard mode.
Difference between Normal, Hard and Insane is enemy numbers(spawns, hp, dmg) with Insane having the bonus of getting a curse or a disease at the start of every level with a slight addition of more traps.
-
is a well made beat 'em up that offers a good variety of playstyle and enemies to keep every playthrough(sacrifice) fresh. Combat is fluid and the gear you find is fun to use.

Now granted, this is the first day I gave this game a try, but I got 6 hours clocked already. Unlocked several firearms, and getting to know their inner workings is a blast! I'll try to keep this spoiler free if you're looking forward to finding out all the different firearms you can get, like I am. It's A LOT of fun, and is THE game to get for gun owners who find legitimate enjoyment in disassembling/cleaning their firearms. Truth be told, I've managed to completely disassemble/reassemble my Springfield Armoury M1911A1 Mil Spec while blindfolded without using tools within 30 minutes flat. The only things I didn't muck with is the sights, the barrel link, and the... tail thing on the hammer. That's right, I even took out the mag release spring and screw, without the use of my eyes lol Anyways, back to the game... if you always wanted to learn how firearms function, how their individual pieces come together to form one cohesive tool, this is the perfect game for you.
I've never played anything like it, but I've wanted a game like this for years, possibly a decade. The closest thing I remember is a flash game on Newgrounds that allows you to eject the mag, replace the mag, rack the slide, and fire. Not at anything in particular, just to operate the firearm. Of course this has that, and LOADS more. I'm only 6 hours in, I've unlocked a fair number of firearms, and the ones that I'm seeing that are possible to unlock I'm very much looking forward to!
Here's where some of the *SPOILERS* start to come in, but they're mild, I won't mention any other firearms yet, I'll give a warning before I have a nerdgasm on that. There's a leaderboard for disassembly/reassembly time, and there's also some shooting ranges. The firearms will behave quite realistically with mag+1, select fire, and all that good stuff. The only way I could see it being better is if you could adjust the sights, if the controls to reload were more like Receiver, and if you used individual mags instead of the typicall 'ammo pool' that you'll find on CoD and Battlefield. Alright, now to talk about firearms next, so if you want that to remain a surprise, divert your eyes now lol
You start out with the AK47, how appropriate is that? Known for being simple, it's still got some complexity when it comes down to knowing which parts to remove first. Still, VERY enjoyable learning about every last individual part and how they all interact. Next was the M1911A1 (Called Colt 1911 unfortunately. I mean it's a Colt, but it's an M1911A1, not a 1911), and other than the barrel link not dropping before coming out of the slide, as well as the way the hammer assembly needs to be strictly removed AFTER the leaf spring (which is simply nonsense), it's 100% accurate to real life. After that you get the option to unlock the MP5 or Tech-9 if memory serves correctly, and branching off those are the Beretta 92 and CZ75 respectively.
The Tech-9 is surprisingly simple, while the MP5 is DEFINITELY more complex. Now both the M92 and CZ75B are complex in their own right, but I found the Beretta to be particularly unforgiving with its hoard of tiny spring/plugs/pins. Then again, I also had to replace the trigger return spring on my 1982 CZ75 Pre-B so that kind of gave me a hand in figuring it out, came pretty naturally. There are also some historic gems, I can see the sillouette of the PPSH-41, M1928 Thompson, P08 Luger, and the ancestor that lead to the P08 which I can't remember the name. Borsharte? Something like that.
There's more to unlock after finding those out, and they apparently release another firearm at least once a month! All in a free-to-play game!!! You need to unlock experience however in order to unlock said firearms, and that takes quite a lot of disassembly/reassembly as well as time at the shooting range. Both I find quite enjoyable :P Ah, there's also a firearm quiz that you can take once every 2 hours. It lasts 30 seconds, and you have to name all the firearms you can, at 300 Exp. per model. If you get one wrong, you don't get any experience whatsoever, so be careful with your choices. Last time I played it I got 8, which is 2400 Exp. That's almost half way to unlocking another firearm for me, however they seem to be getting more and more expensive.
Performing feats of speed/precision with the shooting and disassembly/reassembly, are the only other ways to get experience at a convenient rate. Though doing the disassembly/reassembly over and over doesn't give you experience very quickly, neither is doing the shooting ranges over and over. The first time you make the time limit/hit number, you get a good amount, but every time after that is only a morsel of your first reward, so unless you want to spend money buying Exp. or credits, you're going to be doing a lot of quizes/shooting/disassembly/reassembly to unlock those juicy firearm models you're dying to get your hands on. Not that that's unenjoyable, but it does distinctly feel like grinding. Eventually doing it more for the Experience than the enjoyment. So basically what I'm saying is unless you're willing to pay, you'll need patience. I have loads of it, so I look forward to making this my go-to game for the foreseeable future :)
Anyways I think that concludes what I know so far. If you're into the mechanical workings of firearms, then get this free-to-play game right now. No hesitation. If you just like playing shoot-em-ups without really caring how firearms come apart or work, well, you'll have to earn the shooting ranges you unlock in the game. Takes Experience for those too, you see. So far I only have two unlocked, and the next will cost me 8000 Experience if I recall correctly, which is a couple hours worth of grinding/quizzing. Still really fun though, with lots of modes to choose from, and I'm hoping to get some adjustable sights/bullet drop with the longer range firearms :) Happy shooting, and remember, check to make sure your firearm is clear before beginning your field strip or disassemble ;) Safety first!

There is not much to say about this game. It's a clicking game pretty much but I'm a fan of those ever since I played a cookie game on Google Chrome (should be available for all browsers though). You click on buttons and set a timer and when the timer reaches the end you get money. You start your financial empire selling lemonade but you can go up to buy movie studios, banks and oil rigs. This game is way better than the cookie one though, it has much more content and more fun ways to keep making more and more money. There are also some references to Futurama, Star Trek and even some famous memes like The Grumpy Cat. It's a breath of fresh air from all the other games that require shooting, fighting and a lot of action. Plus, the game keeps farming money even when you are offline. There's also timed events and a good share of new content that allows you to open business on the moon and on mars. It's fun but since it's nothing more than clicking here and there it gets tiring a little fast. However it's free so I'd say give it a shot.

A few years later the humans releases their counter attack, they use an army of androids, their goal is to eliminate all machine lifeforms. The two main characters are 2B and 9S. 2B is a very serious character, she prioritize the mission over everything else, 9S shows way more emotions than 2B and acts more like a human. I really like the contrast between these two characters, and their dialogue is fun to listen to because of that.
Something I really enjoy with Nier is its gameplay variety. It’s mainly a 3rd person action RPG, but it is also a top-down shooter, 2D side-scroller and more. It changes the camera angles different places in the story, and goddamnit this is good game design.
Nier Automata is a game with multiple endings, but it’s a little different. Often in games with multiple endings, you get an ending based on your actions and decisions you have made during the story. If you want to complete the whole story in Nier, you have to play multiple playthroughs, but every new playthrough is different, with new content and new view points.

Director's Cut is a scam. The game uses an old version of the original game, which means it has all the bugs that were patched years ago in THE ORIGINAL GAME! Only handful were fixed in DC. In addition to the new bugs players have found, this version also seems to have downgraded graphics, such as low quality SSAO, broken Post Processing, streched textures, missing colors etc.
Game's forums on Steam and on Eidos site shows no one in the company - including moderates - care about this game. Steam discussions page shows at least 144 unfixed, missing features/bugs for this game.
The only "enhancement" in this version is the toned down yellow tint a.k.a.♥♥♥♥♥♥filter, which IMO was too much in some areas of the original game. It's an artistic question. I personally prefer it off just because I have finished the game and found it hiding details in otherwise dated looking game. I also like more vibrant colors in general. They could've just toned it down in the areas where it was too much, not in the whole game. There should've been at least an option to turn it back on if desired.
If you like the toned down yellow tint in DC, you are better off with the original as you get far better results by trying out different SweetFX profiles.
To people who own the original and TML:
Play those instead. You save HDD/SSD space, have the best bug-free experience with less chance to get graphical glitches. Yes, the boss battles were questionable, but you are only missing slightly more open areas in boss battles that were probably done by some trainee in one weekend anyway.
To people who don't own the original nor TML:
Find a boxed copy on your local store's bargain bin or get an activation code for Steam from a legitimate cd-key market site. Don't worry about TML (The Missing Link). It's like the fourth episode in Duke Nukem 3D. Unnecessary. Just a nice extra. TML only explains "three days in statis" and is attached to the main story in DC.
There was no need for explanation really. I didn't even notice days were passed at that point of the game. You can get a key for TML online, e.g. Amazon if you really want.

Many people disagreed with my rage-fueled review I previously posted about this game, so I wanted to try again and be more fair.
I've had extremely mixed feelings on this game while playing it for the past couple of years.  There's a lot I enjoy about it, and a lot that I don't.  My review is my attempt to let you know what you're getting in to depending on what type of gamer you are.
Whether or not you'll enjoy this game all comes down to your attitude towards the gameplay in the previous installments of the series.  If you're a huge fan of the Dead Rising series like me, then your tolerance threshold for changes to core gameplay mechanics is a huge factor.
As I've seen many other negative reviewers say, Dead Rising 3's gameplay is only half the challenge - if that - of the previous games.  It's very casual, and veterans of the series will likely often be thinking "why would they do this" and "this is too easy."
Here is a brief list of some things I did and didn't like:
-I like that you can make combo weapons on the fly, I don't like that you can make combo drinks on the fly as though Nick has a blender in his back pocket (blending with blenders is removed).
-I accept that cars are a more prominent piece of the game; I don't like the horrendous amount of barracades that render cars near useless other then traversing highways faster, especially since cars seem to be a central mechanic of this installment.
-I like the skill tree so you can pick what you level up first;  I don't like getting attribute points after I've already maxed everything out with a constant reminder to spend attribute points that I simply can't spend anymore.
-I like limited Sprinting for a quick burst of speed when you need it most; I don't like that quickstep gives you unlimited stamina instead of increasing your overall animation/movement speed temporarily, because this feature eventually becomes useless.
-I like that making combo weapons gets faster the more you level up; I don't like how you can make combo weapons with ingredients other then what the recipe calls for.  It sounds like a good idea, but it throws memorization right out the window (which I suppose is "fixed" with weapon lockers... -shudder-).
-I like how well co-op works in this game.  Playing with my friend has been flawless; either one of you can be anywhere on the map and complete objectives.
-I don't like the game's FOV - it's way too cramped for me.  I thought the FOV in DR1 and DR2 was sufficient for seeing what was around you, and now it's way too close to the protagonist's character model.  If you have the same thought, you can actually get a mod for the game to change the FOV and make it more like previous installments.  Just google Dead Rising 3 FOV Mod :)
These are just a few of the conflicting ideas I disliked about the game, but you may see them as positives, or things that may enhance your experience.  If so, go for it, what's important is that you enjoy the game you're spending money on.
New players to the series won't notice all of the minor changes done to this installment in the series and will more than likely find it enjoyable.  I'd actually like to read a critical review of this game by someone who hasn't played any of the other games in the series, just to see what they think.  But, I digress.
Overall, for me, this game was a disappointment because it really just didn't deliver the Dead Rising Experience that I wanted.  I'm hoping they come to their senses for the fourth game.  I'm not saying Dead Rising 3 is a completely awful game in any way.  But I do truly believe it failed in many respects as a Dead Rising game, leading me to post my review as negative rather than positive.  This is not a bad game in itself, it's just not very coherent with what the first two games defined as "Dead Rising."
So, for the game experience overall, I give it an 8/10 for casual players who just want to jump in and casually kill zombies, and a 6/10 for veterans of the series who actually used to appreciate the strict mechanics of the first two games.

Tons of variety with a satisfying feel!
DISCLAIMER: Just a heads up that my review is coming from a racing sim noob with a Logitech G27 Racing Wheel plugged in a "toaster". I only play offline as well. So the pros, gear snobs, sim veterans, and club racers won't find much useful information within. And probably already have a heavy opinion anyway. I will try to gear this review towards the uninitiated and curious sim noobs like myself that are stumbling about Steam reviews behind the cheap steering wheel with genuine curiosity of whats out there.
I had a very positive "Early Access" review of this title up, something I wouldn't normally do. The game was more or less feature complete though. And I gushed and fawned over the game like an eager fanboy with a new shiny toy. I've learned a thing or two along the way since and ratcheted things down a bit. But honestly, the shine hasn't worn off. 90hrs (plus more in the beta branch) of driving, crashing, learning, and even occasionally actually racing all by myself and I haven't even scuffed the sheen a bit. Its always a blast when you're on the road and even sometimes off it.
Starting with the obvious; Variety is the spice of life and Automobilista delivers that in full. I can race in an open-wheeler that I prefer on a major track I love and know like the back of my hand... Or I can take an unwieldy Super Truck I can't handle on a track I've never heard of. Karts, Super V8's, formulas of every era, Caterhams, Camaros, Lancers, and much more. With more coming still! Each vehicle series looks, handles, and feel superb AND wholly unique. The track variety contains some classics as well as the obscure. They're all worth the time to learn and race. And the user made mods have been rolling out steadily since Early Access and only add more variety and options (HUDs/tracks/cars/skins/etc).
But the real feature(s) that made it all worth it for me was the accessibility. I got my wheel for much tamer and/or "arcade-y" racing games. Then I ended up playing casual "sims" with it, towing trailers across Europe and logs through the mud in Russia. But when it came time to step up and strap in to a cockpit of something serious to really feel my toy wheel I ran into walls and dead ends at every turn. "True sim" racing is a niche if there ever was such a thing. An odd one with unique folks owning a wealth of information scattered wide and far. And with even more varying steadfast opinions filling each and every gap between. I poured hours into trying this sim or that sim. Reading webpages, blogs, and forums. Calibrating software, looking up force feedback settings, learning new terms, fiddling with in-game settings, trying to make old games work on new operating systems. And I always ended up with something that barely worked and left me thinking I was missing something. With Automobilista I read one thing, the included manual, and set things as suggested. Within minutes I was racing. And for the first time I FELT it. I felt what seduces souls the world over and turns them into sim racing fanatics. Force feedback and simulating physics is an amazing thing. Automobilista just works (granted you read a manual) and allowed me to finally start learning how to race and actually play a game rather than just how to configure things. Though, since it indeed "just worked" it did also let me learn how to configure things and know what settings should do and let me return to previous failures and succeed in trying things. In basic terms Automobilista starts you at step "1" and it sure is easier to start at step "1" instead of step "35", or "-35"!
There's plenty of other subjective stuff I could go on about like how I do think its the best feeling sim out there and technical this or tire model that or how I like the visuals plenty fine. But the subjective opinion I will stand by the most is that this is the most approachable sim for the new guy/gal. That's not to say your journey will be as smooth as mine or it doesn't take some reading or work. And no promises you'll be any good. As with anything you're gonna get out what you put in with sim racing. My hours spent learning and configuring other games and scouring the web was never wasted, it just wasn't rewarded or fulfilling until it culminated in Automobilista. But knowledge is your friend in this niche. Learn and study anything you can get your hands on and just remember most of it is subjective in the end. The world doesn't need another steadfast stone that won't flex on anything. Find what you like and what works for you and know others should do the same. But if you got a wheel (and make no mistake a wheel is highly recommended if not flat out required) and you want to see what the hubbub is all about with sim racing without subscriptions or anything wacky, I can confidently suggest Automobilista is a good bet.
Very much recommended indeed!

Don't often write recommendations but this is one of those times. Going to write it in order of 'Pros', 'Average', 'Cons'.
PROS:
-Physics are absolutely on point. (Cars like the V8 Super cars, Go-Karts, touring cars and F3), The levels of grip given to each wheel at certain times, and the way the car 'dances', like it should in lots of cases, it's completely unmatched by any other sim . EG, taking a corner, and the FR wheel hits a bump, you don't just feel it amazingly well in the FFB, the cars weight shifts extremely well, creating more lean on the LF tyre, the suspension then reacts to it, changing grip levels of both those tyres and the movement of the car. The list goes on and on about the reactions of the cars in different curcumstances.  You can also feel the effects of the downforce much more through the FFB and car control. Take the Formula 3, at high speed the car is much more planted, but at lower speed the wheel requires far more steering input as the downforce becomes almost non-existant and you are rellying on mechanical grip. Also, the suspension physics are immaculate, low speed reactions to bumps and kurbs is great.
-Force Feed Back, Simply unmatched. No other sim is even close, 'Nuff said really.
-Management... Yes, you have to manage tyre and brake temps. If you have the HUD on, you can see your brake and tyre temps in detail. Don't keep your tyres and brake temperatures up, they become less effective.
-Car list, is fairly vast.... Go-Karts/X-cross/V8 Super cars/trucks/F3 etc etc
Average:
-Now one thing that got hyped, and rightly so, was the AI. The AI is great, far better than other titles I've played in Sim's. You can change their aggression, and skill level in percentage right up to %120. They'll do pretty well to hold their own on the track. But, and it's a big but, They also still hold big features that make you strongly remember they are AI. For example, AI does not have a clue what a blue flag is.... Imagine, you get out first in quallifying, get the tyres and brakes up to temp on that outlap, then full steam ahead down the Start/finish to start your flying lap. Just to be met with %50 of the AI coming out of the pitlane, and that don't react to blue flags.... It's such a simple thing that destroys the element of the AI supposedly being 'human'. Also when you change their aggression to 'extreme', they still are very cautious about passing you and defending. I lost my wing in F3, and completely removed myself from the racing line and slowed down to around 50mph, and moved right to the edge of the track, and there was still a queue of AI behind deciding on whether it's safe to pass me or not. Also, they don't defend as aggresive as this setting suggests, they often leave the door wide open. But the plus side in that is that they do try to counter attack..... Another note with the difficulty level, is it's too easy in some cases. I had the super Karts at Spielburg (I know I spelled that wrong), and I naturally have the dificulty set to %110. Within 17 minutes practice I was the quickest driver on track by .4 of a second... I reset the difficulty to %120, and within 45 minutes practice I was still the qiuckest driver by .3 of a second.  It should be a tad more difficult imo. 45 minutes practice, without ever driving that vehicle, should have me at the back of the pack somewhere...... BUT, In general race-craft, the AI is a huge improvement, and is actually fun and difficult to race against for the most part.
CONS:
-Graphics, it's not a huge dissapointment, but at some points it does feel very outdated. I'm running Maximum detail and it doesn't look right. I'm seeing jagged lines with Full detail and 16x AA. I feel i'm mising something, and the opponents cars give that old school floaty and pixelated look at 50+ meters. Maybe that's something at my end, but it's a bit of a turn off. Doesn't reflect the fun you have while driving though that's for sure.
-Setting up the wheel. Now this is only if you are a perfectionist, like me. You may find yourself going back and forth changing the settings, but if you aren't new to sims and Race in the likes of iRacing, you may be more used to it. But it does seem to take a bit more effort. The con is only the time it takes, but it definitely returns reward when you dial the settings in.
-Multiplayer. The public servers are a ghost town, everybody who has this Sim, and races online, races in a league no doubt.
-Mods, I went searching for them on RaceDepartment. And there wasn't a huge amount. A lot of the tracks were made by 'Patrick', or something. And there are barely any quality tracks, the only quality tracks existing were the ones made by this 'Patrick'. One Gentleman said that this is down to the Devs not releasing info on the game to support modders making tracks, specifically the shaders. I don't know how much truth is in this, but it does go as a con in my book if it is truthful.
Overall, if you're a heavy sim-enthusiast get it, just buy it. You are missing out on something amazing. But you should really look to get into a online league, because the Public MP servers are dead. Also, a league is just normally far more fun anyway than the public lobby bangers.

Get this. When a controller with two track pads shows up on sale for less than a ps4 or xbone that also comes with software to fully and easily customize 1000 different options as well as provide a virtual keyboard, you get it. In fact, that's when you get two. Most pc gamers don't even realize that there is a whole range of dynamic animations in games built for controller. They put 1000 hours into games and don't even see their character do the jog between sprint and walk, let alone the animations on top of that. FPS players forget that the slower they move the less noise is made, and they only get two speeds. SLOW or bat outta hell. Slowly peaking, slowly sneaking,  are not options. It's all abrubt, jagged, and non natural movement. The trackpads are great. Really they are just as accurate as using a mouse, it's just a matter of figuring out your sensitivity pref for whatever game you're playing, or exactly how you want the track pad to act. There's different modes, you can do button combos like hotkeys, can completely switch modes at the press of a button. Lets say you were on gtav. You could have a controller mode for first person, different one for third, different one for driving and different one for flying, all toggled by the press of one or two buttons, or activated individually by hotkey. It's awesome. You can play MMOs with a controller, in their controller supported mode, and in their regular mode, you can switch between the two on the fly. It's amazing, no controller on the market is more valuable, and that's not just opinion. Two trackpads on a single controller alone puts the hardware value over anything else in the market as just a basic controller. You may say some flight simulator gear is worth more technically but that's irrelevant. It's just truly an amazing device. Comes with batteries, bluetoof thing, and wire. If you're even thinking about it, especially as your first pc controller, you won't regret it. It will redefine your gaming experience, and it's also useful for just basic computer stuff... Running netflix, browsing youtube, that kinda thing. If you're like me and have your comp on a tv, it's the perfect remote. I am sure it would even be great for complex artwork as well.

I should (and would write a longer review), but I don't know if this game is worth more the hours I wasted on it so far.
Despite its impeccable presentation, this game has to be the buggiest Shanghai clone I've ever played (and I've played hundreds of them.)
At one point I realized that they probably added the 'pendant' gimmick because they couldn't bother to create a layout generation algorithm that would ensure no 4 matching tiles would think themselves on top of each other. (Which takes about 5 minutes to think of and implement. Believe me.) The odds are so unbelievably against you that you need to use power-ups, which quickly dry out, forcing you to use up precious crystals... Wait, is that a micro-transaction system for a planned mobile port?!
It just never stops surprising me how stupid must one be to program this game in a way that's so elegantly broken.
Do you want an example?
When you get to one of many levels where the pendant itself is *hiding* one of the tiles, making it unclickable, and you can only remove it by using a power-up, *and* said level has a third star tied to NOT using power-ups, then you'll get what I mean. You'll either laugh, or cry, but in the end you'll just stop caring.
<EDIT>
Other things that annoy me to no ends:
- Game asks you to be quick at matching, but doesn't allow you to disable the veeery slow animations that hide the tile you just matched, so you need an extra second or two just to see what tile you just freed up.
- Only one song that repeats on a loop for all games... Terrible.
- Typos everywhere. Just look at the achievement list on Steam. Or, worse, those Moon tiles... "First Quater", "Last Quater". Really? Is Quater the original Victorian-era word for "dumbass"?
- Crystal icon can be clicked to refill the bar. It doesn't even ask you to confirm! Given how hard it is to collect crystals, the least they could do is ask me whether I'm okay with wasting a crystal, thank you very much!
- Scoring isn't explained, AFAIK. Whether or not you get a star through a good score is based on luck, I'm guessing. Just like everything else in that game...
- Totally unbalanced difficulty. There's a level on the second floor of the hour that's much harder to complete than everything before it *and* everything after it. Same in the labyrinth. I retried it 10+ times, looks like Mrs. Huntress wants me to spend one of my hard-earned crystals.

The game is fun, it has a storyline which is rare for mahjong games or at least ones I am able to find but don't get your hopes up. The story is pretty much your cliche fantasy with Werewolves and ghost ships with a bit of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t magic from your "Grandfather" which just copies the shrinking scene from Alice In Wonderland! Nothing feels like it should tie together and is just there for plot.
The game does so however have its own little mechanics to make the game different from other mahjong games such as taking one piece off the board so you can continue or to destroy where its other-half is hiding with your power-up.
However the power-ups are confusing at first and I feel you are given too many of them at once. If anything half of them can be removed from the game and nothing will change game-wise. I only use half of them, the other half do not seem worth it compared to other power-ups you can use.
A big draw-back for me is past level 7. You can easily do level 1-7 without losing but as soon as you hit level 8 you are hit with the biggest difficulty curve. You will lose on this level so many times and I warn you to NOT SHUFFLE THE BOARD! The shuffle power-up is broken and there is a 50/50 chance that it will break the board and give you blank tiles. Meaning you need to start over.
Many users have had this issue and we still have it, the devs have done nothing to fix this so a few users are actually stuck on level 8. So no it is not just my laptop, it is the game itself.
I love Mahjong and play a lot of it but the difficulty curve in this one is just too much and highly unfair, specially since like most mahjong games, the layout past level 7 will cause the game to load pieces to where you will not get them, grouped with other titles just the very same so I hope you like restarting the level alot. If you do happen to get past level 8 the levels are easier with 1-2 levels being complete middle-fingers to you in each chapter.
Also a level from Chapter 2 repeats in Chapter 6 and yes it is a level which forces you to use your gems and shuffle 4-7 times to complete it. Not fun developers.
Lastly, is the boss levels. I have only reached one so far but it is NOT MAHJONG. It turns into bejeweled to where you need to match up the gem on your side of the screen to attack the boss. Not so hard until you need to avoid matching up the tiles which the boss needs to attack you. This is hard even on the first boss because the board will be filled to death with the tiles the boss needs and he kills you in 3 hits while it takes you 4/6 hits to kill them. I swear they only need half the tiles you need as well to attack you.
I don't know why the boss levels are a bejeweled-clone, yes it is a nice change from mahjong I will give it that but it seems out of place for the game itself.
I wish Steam had a MAYBE option because I would recommend this game but at the same time I would not.
This game has a lot going for it with its ideas and set-up but with the power-ups able to break the board to being incompletable is a let down for any player.
Wait till it is on sale if you really want to try this out, otherwise do not buy a broken game full-price.

While the game was frustrating, it is by any measure solvable for even a young child, once they learn the rules and how to plan ahead.  How do you plan? As a bonus, there's - as nearly as I can tell - something well over 100 bonus scenarios that all give star rewards, all of which are unique in setup and bonus requirements; some have a time limit, some have special tiles, etc.
Pro/Con: As a pure mahjong game, it's... not.  You HAVE to use the bonuses to get past some of the storyline scenarios.

I don't know what happened, but after having been unable to play this version of the game due to constant performance issues and bugs, I finally completed it yesterday, and have been awash in all the feels.
First, I'm still frustrated that it took so long - I don't know what changed, if a patch came out stealthily, or if my computer simply decided to buck up all of a sudden, but the fact that upon release, this was buggier than the original version is inexcusable for a publisher as high-profile as Eidos.
On the other hand, I've sunk more hours into this game (orignal, DLC, and Director's Cut) than Dark Souls 1&2 combined. Which is a lot. I loved the music, the stealth, the writing, the voice acting, the sheer world-building and sense of scale to the game's narrative - all in all, it seemed like a complete package, and a worthy successor to Deus Ex, on of my favorite games of all time.
This edition changed that perspective. I never cared much about the boss fights, which were the big bugaboo for most people. What bothered me - and I didn't truly realize it until I listed to the DC's commentary - was the sense that much of the story was actually left out of the game.
It's notwhere near as bad as Eidos' reboot of Thief (which was a frankenstein of 9 drafts patched together without rhyme or reason), but upon hearing how much of this game was left out - from the dev's own lips - I began to feel both cheated and vindicated. The lingering sense that I had somehow missed a key part of the story was laid to rest. I had indeed missed things - because they hadn't made it into the final game.
The backstory of the game's bosses? Cut. The relationship between the villains, the Illuminati, the power players, the opening raid? Stripped to the absolute minimum, which I totally missed the first time around. The lack of resolution to the primary story arc (the search for Megan)? The devs simply didn't resolve it, because they didn't have time. The botched "press-a-button" ending? Also, by the dev's own admission, not as they originally planned.
Upon playing through for the third time, I ached at the thought of exploring upper Hengsha, Bangalore, and Montreal. Not because those places sounded great, but because they seemed to be, from the commentary, the places where all the plot-holes were filled.
So, upon my final completion of the game, I feel both immeasurably satisfied and inexplicably cheated. This game, even with its current high level of quality, could have been so much more - and indeed was supposed to be.
This is all to say that II'm thrilled for the sequel, Makind Divided. If Human Revolution is the result of budget cuts and time crunch, I cannot WAIT to see what this team does now that it has access to new resources. Hopefully we'll get the game that Human Revolution should have been - and was supposed to be - from the start.

This is what a good solid Indie game should be- fun, easy to pick up, well-executed, performs well, and it has great replay value.
It's a game that's drawing heavily from Double Dragon, the classic arcade series.  Gameplay consists of smacking, kicking, throwing and generally causing mayhem in diverse levels that have all sorts of interesting obstacles and challenges.
While I feel that the game would benefit from having a more diverse cast of fundamental weapons (there isn't the difference in game mechanics of Double Dragon's nunchuku vs. a bat, for example) the combat mechanics are solid and fun.
What really makes it work, though, is the diversity of the special attacks.  While some of these could use some balance tweaks here and there (for example, there is a power-punch attack that works great but takes too long to charge up to be practical in a big fight, whereas the Lightning Rod is easy crowd-control fun) these mechanics make everything click well.
I also wish there was a mechanic to return to the town and spend money on a new run; most times, a good run is pure RNG luck and there isn't much sense of long-term progression at the moment, other than unlocking Classes, which give a slightly different take on the core gameplay.
Replay value is excellent, and the short duration of the zones means that this is a great game for those of us with limited time budgets for video games.

Alright.  I played it again for a couple more hours.  After the "Mega Patch" that "fixes" all the balancing issues.
Devs, i'm not attacking you.  Please understand this.  You guys are talented and i'm very proud of you.  Like i've stated many times before, I am fully aware of how painful it is to make mods and games, especially with the Source Engine.  And i'm completely willing to help you guys develop this game in the graphical aspect in terms of animations, mapping, sound, (Weapons), etc.
But, come on, man.  This is just silly.
I desperately tried to enjoy it.  I really did.  Seriously.  I was trying as hard as I possibly could to like this game.  I was optimistic after the balancing, I was proud of you guys, I was like, "They listened to the community, they're doing good, they're actually trying to improve."  But then when you did the balancing patch, not only was the balancing patch pretty pointless (Since it's still pretty unbalanced), it made me see what was wrong with everything else.
To start off, the huuuuuuge cons.
There's still weapons locked behind levels.  The minigun is understandable, but why would you have to be level 5 to pick up a propane tank?  Like even grenades are understandable (Kinda), but like..  How can somebody not be intelligent enough to pick up a propane tank.  I really don't get it.  The Levelling system is still extremely unbalanced, too.  The zombies are absolutely OP because of how easy it is to level up.  Humans are just not threats as zombies.  You don't need to do any tactical thinking.  Every single map is just not fun for humans when there's zombie players.  Seriously.  Grinding raiders for that 1 point, maxing out speed and health regen, you're unstoppable.  Hell, you could even fill up speed and health regen by halfway, you're still unstoppable.  Because then you can just nitpick off humans, get them 2 points, and max them out real fast.  It's what makes me so furious.  It's like you guys didn't even think when you made the game.  And that whole arena map, the one with Fred in it.  That's not even fun.  Like, I tried to have fun.  Even when you're doing good it's just not fun.  A zombie colluseum doesn't even sound good on paper.  Plus the raiders just overcomplicate things, it's just-.  It's a massive cluster of chaos.  Sure, that could be what you're going for, but that's not fun.
And the voice acting.  It's just bloody stupid, i'm sorry.  The voice actors are talented but the writing is still absolutely bonkers and it makes no sense half of the time.  Not only are the lines cringe-inducing alone when said in proper situations, it makes me cringe even harder when they're used in PvP or when a raider kills you.
Seriously it's like, dude, it's so stupid.  In that colluseum map when the raider flood came in with the zombies, I was rolling on the floor because all I could hear was "SUNUVA, SUNUVA, SUNUVA, SUNUVA, SUNUVA, SUNUVA, SUNUVA", all over, i'd hear "SUNUVA" in the distance, it was a Sunuva invasion.
I mean, it was hilarious, I was rolling, but..  I can't say it's good.
And of course the dialogue doesn't make sense half of the time.  I still don't understand why killing a raider or another player still makes me go "You're supposed to be dead..  ♥♥♥♥♥!"
Like, it's already cringey being said in the first place, but like-..  Really?  Who thought that was a good idea?  It's just not fun.
The PvP was fun, it's pretty well done.  I like the PvP.  The powerups are all interesting, and there's nothing that makes a player too invincible.  You guys did good on that.  I have no complaints, except the kids that don't understand that PvP requires players kill eachother.
Seriously, somebody was raging at me because I kept killing them.  Like that wasn't supposed to happen.  This game is just ridiculous.  Is it supposed to be this over-the-top, unbalanced, chaotic, and just outright silly?  I sure hope not.  The only enjoyment I can get out of the game is very short-term.  I can only play it in short bursts before getting bored because it's so repetetive, unbalanced, unmotivating, and just uninteresting.  It's not fun.  I'm sorry.  And i'm going to have to keep my review negative, because I still don't enjoy it.  It still needs a ton of more work, and like I said, i'd be willing to help in the graphics department and balancing.  Because if it stays the way it is right now, it's just not gonna be good.

I will say first of all, this game surprised me that it came onto Steam. I knew very well Calamity Trigger had a PC release and I do believe that the sequel Continuum Shift also had a PC release. This is basically Wing Commander without characters.  You don't talk to anyone unless you're in the cockpit, and they are all generic wingmen and communications officers.  There are a few cut scenes that are mostly background filler with scenery - again, no people/characters.  So if you're looking for a great and/or interactive plot, this will be a disappointment.
What you will find is fun space combat (can be a bit trying sometimes with a mouse, though), many ships and weapons to choose from (as you advance), plenty of missions, medals to collect and kills to rack up.  Some missions are very challenging because your wingmen (and members of other wings) are not very good at their jobs and some missions (the final missions of both campaigns specifically) have infinite enemy spawns.
Also note this is an old game (~1998).  Don't look for spectacular graphics.
I enjoyed it.  But I was also very frustrated at times, and that was on medium difficulty.  Good luck.

Descent: FreeSpace was - for pretty much two decades - the start of the best space combat simulation ever developed. I probably spent several years of my childhood playing FreeSpace 1 and 2 and to this day there is no other game which I will get back to every few years and then play it for months on end because it is that good.
Never before have I played a game which utilizes almost all keyboard buttons, some of them even twice or thrice with button combinations. It takes days to get used to the controls and to remember all of them in the heat of battle, but after having learned them once, I never forgot them again. I can boot up any FreeSpace game after 5 years without having played it and the controls will come back to me within 5 minutes. No other game has ever managed to do that. No other game has ever managed to entertain me to that degree even although I can still remember every single mission, every enemy wave, every plot twist and all and any scripted events.
FreeSpace might not be for everyone, but every space-sim fan who doesn't believe FreeSpace to be the best space combat sim ever developed simply either hasn't played it yet or is too young to be able to fully appreciate its actual complexity and depth, as it is perfectly possible to play and even finish the game with just knowing how to thrust, turn and shoot. But there's so much more to those who aren't afraid of delving deeper into the game.
To this day, 15 years later, the FreeSpace 2 Open Source Project is still making the game better and every person even remotely interested in the FreeSpace series should check out the several hundred campaigns and total conversions available over at the
FreeSpace community. It's by the way not only one of the most friendly and dedicated gaming communities I have ever seen, it also boasts probably a score of the best coders lurking around on the interwebs as well.
I can't just recommend FreeSpace, I would actually have to literally build a physical shrine to be even remotely able to convey how I feel about the entire franchise and its modding community.

You don't have to start at the small and work your way up.  There are 60 levels for each board that you do have to work you way through to unlock the higher levels and an achievement at the completion of each board.  It's a good deal for the price and well worth it if you can snag it on sale.  And if you get stuck, there are community guides with the solutions or you can use gold tokens you earn through gameplay for an in game hint.  If you love little puzzles, this is a great game to add to your collection.

Doomster Entertainment

A casual title with obvious arcade elements,  Oh No! Bugs! is a decent enough game with a relatively simple gameplay premise: pushing certain blocks within a maze pattern. It replaces the ghosts from Pac-Man with bugs and this type of arcade action might have been great...35 years ago. Sadly, for a game released in 2016, Oh No! Bugs! doesn’t have a lot going for it in terms of sheer replay value or any other type of value (since I consider the current price tag of 4.99 euros, too much) except for having Achievements and Trading Cards. The far too repetitive 2D pixelated insect squashing got old real fast, in my case. Still the game is not without its merits. Perhaps as a throwback to simpler arcade times?

the content that is there is top notch. cars although not the hottest (except for open-wheelers since those are great) are really enjoyable to drive and many of the obscure brazilian tracks are nice too. there are time trial challenges on every car/track combination which is nice.

the BrittPack DLC is really, really good. the caterhams are crazy and a lot of fun to throw around. oulton park is laser scanned which is nice since i know the track from iracing very well. The Imola track DLC has 4 layouts including 72 historic which is totally different to the more modern ones.
a lot of rFactor 1 mods are compatible with Automobilista which is a huge plus in my book (note that AI can behave strange on mod tracks. the AI on original tracks is actually pretty good and there are options to set them up to your liking (agressiveness etc.)
it's worth mentioning that if you're an F1 fan and you'd like to find out why you'd suck as an F1 driver this is the sim for you. it has a single representation of an F1 car from every decade, starting with the 60's and they're all challenging, fun and distinct (the modern ones less so IMO). as far as i know it is the only sim that does that.
the GRAPHICS are decent enough, car models and cockpits are detailed, just don't expect Assetto Corsa levels of fidelity.
SOUND is very good in general. especially F1 and the recently released cars sound convincing.
MENUS are a bit of a throwback, but you can get use to it.
never tried ONLINE, since random races are not my thing and i'm still waiting till someone's gonna kick iracings♥♥♥♥♥in this regard (the cost of iracing is just nuts)
all in all i recommend Automobilista to those that are patient (the setup etc.) and value the driving experience/realism above all else. this is the top of the crop driving experience for a decent price.
Oh, STEERING WHEEL and PEDALS are a must for this game. playing it any other way just doesn't make sense.
***************HIGHLY RECOMMENDED******************

This review is for the Model 1001 of the Steam Controller that was purchased from GameStop locally
While it's a good start for "breaking the mold" of PC gaming from your TV - or as a general substitute for an Xbox 360 Controller or Playstation 3/4 controller, it's far from perfect. While software side can be easily updated with firmware updates in the controller and USB dongle - hardware on the other hand, can be an expensive endeavor.
The pros :
+ Buttons, track pad, shoulder buttons, dual-stage triggers. even a giant button on the back of the controller - there's something everywhere.
+ Every single button, trackpad, joystick, triggers, can be modified on-the-fly while in a game using Big Screen mode. Though limited, the controller can be used for desktop use, and buttons may be modified while using Big Screen mode.
+ USB Micro for connecting the Steam Controller directly to the computer for use without batteries.
The Cons :
- The Steam Controller - for all it offers, is bulky. In comparison to an OEM wireless Xbox 360 Controller, the Steam Controller is quite a ways bigger.
- Tactile Feedback - while using the "D-Pad", the inscribed cross barely does anything for tactile feedback. Using the controller for fighting games, getting down Ryu's Shoryuken, or even his trademark Hadoken can prove difficult as there's nothing to stop your thumb from flying off the D-touchpad, borking what would have been a ranged strike. The same goes for the right touchpad, though completely void of tactile feedback.
- While the triggers are comfortable to use, the shoulder buttons leave something to be desired. For those that use their index fingers for both the triggers and the shoulder buttons, using the shoulder buttons can strain your hand reaching up from the trigger to use the shoulder button. Using the middle finger for triggers and index finger for the shoulder buttons is more comfortable to use, however on a personal opinion, doesn't feel right and would take adjustment. However, this can be circumvented with use of the grip triggers, or changing the button configuration of the controller entirely, the bumpers can be taken off completely.
- Fat fingering - this mainly caused issue when using the "back" and "forward", I personally kept bumping the two touchpads, which in some games did not couple well by immediately ejecting me out of the menu I was accessing before it loaded fully. Could this be remedied through adjusting to the controller? Possibly. Though considering the two buttons are rather close to the touchpads, this could be set in revision for a future controller design.
- Two AA batteries. In a world where 70% of mobile electronics contains a rechargeable battery. The controller has a USB Micro slot for plugging in the controller to the PC directly for use, but for use away from the computer requires AA batteries. While those tech savvy could rig a rechargeable battery through modification of the controller, AA batteries are not cheap. Average battery life from a personal experience is about 10 hours of heavy use. About as much life as playing a Gameboy Color back in the day if one was lucky.
- The construction of the controller has a rather large flaw in its design. The grip trigger - or the battery cover, as the triggers are molded with the battery cover, leave the batteries exposed - along with the exposed contacts - vulnerable to shorting out the controller.
-- The seams on the controller are very rough in some places. Namely around the grip.
While the controller tries to be the best it can for use with almost any PC game available on Steam, it’s far from being the “end-all be-all” of PC controllers, it certainly has taken strides to get there. With a revision, the controller could be the mainstay of PC-TV gaming.

This is my first in-depth review of a game so pardon me if it's not very helpful or insightful to others.
Fallout 2, a Post Nuclear Role-playing Game, is one of the best games I've ever had the pleasure of playing.  I agree with others when I proudly say it's the best in the series, though personally I'd put New Vegas right alongside it.  Fallout 2 had great dialogue, role playing elements, game mechanics, and it has the most replayability I've seen in a game.  Though, it does have some flaws, but they are minor blemishes on a nearly perfect game.
Just a quick disclaimer, I've only played through the game once, but I wanted to write a review of it and give my general thoughts.  I think this is a fantastic game and I don't have to play it more than once to see it.  Playing more and more will only strengthen my idea that is an amazing game.  Now, onto my first point, the game's story.
I think the story in the first game is better than the story in the second game.
That isn't to say though that the story is bad.  The story is quite good, this game just isn't as story driven as the first.  This game relies more on humor and cultural references to give the player's a good time playing their game, which isn't bad at all.  If you like story more in games, go with Fallout 1.  Like cultural references and weird, over-the-top humor?  Fallout 2 and Fallout New Vegas is for you.
Gameplay mechanics remain mostly the same with Fallout 1.  I like how the menu which contains the monitor screen telling you all the details and the button that holds your inventory slots got a visual upgrade to look more metallic looking but that's about it.  I don't like how the inventory system was done though.  It takes a long time to loot a body with a lot of items on them, especially if you don't want to take everything.  But those are really my only complaints.  Everything else was done quite nicely and they took thier time when designing these mechanics.
Let me just take a moment to try to explain my love for the way role playing is handled in this game.  It's the best I've ever seen.  I love the way speech was handled.  First, you have to have a big enough intelligence for the dialogue option to even show up in the first place(and it's unmarked too, so if you go back and significantly lower your intellgence, you'll notice changes in your dialogue choice) and then depending on your speech skill the choice may or may not work.  It's brilliant!  On my playthough I chose to be a speech oriented character.  I had an Intelligence of 8 and in the end a speech skill of 128%.  I don't know if I would say this make the game super easy, I was able to breeze through a lot of sections without fighting people as I was able to talk my way out.  But that's only one way of the many you can play through this game.  You always have a vast amount of choices in encounters to choose from whether it be talking your way out, going in guns blazing, taunting your foe, or being a meakly coward.  All in all, the dialogue system and the dialogue in general is 10/10, and I don't often going around saying that.
One bone I do have to pick with this game about the roleplaying aspect is the beginning.  Whether you'd like to or not, there is the Temple of Trials you have to go through every time you begin the game.  It's supposed to make sure you are worthy since you are the Chosen One, but it can really cripple certain roleplaying types.  For instance, when I first tried to play, I made my character with 10 Luck, Intelligence, and Charisma, but super low Agility, Perception, Strength, and Endurance.  I see now how that was a mistake but I wanted to be a pacifist and try to avoid fighting as much as possible and use my wits, luck, and speech to get out of fighting.  The Temple kicked my butt because I had a 8% chance to hit things unarmed, and a -10% to hit things with the spear you start out with.  Everything killed me, I constantly had to reload, and I never made it out.  I had to remake my character with that lesson learned, but I really wish the game didn't cripple you like that.
I also thought Perks where a little spread out.  You gain a Perk every 3 levels, and some are unavailable to you because you don't meet the requirements, but Perks kept coming out of nowhere and surprising me because since they came not very often, I kept forgetting about them.  That isn't to say there were not useful, Perks are super useful, but I wish they would come maybe every other level instead, especially considering if you don't play many of the side quests you won't find yourself leveling up that much.
In conclusion, Fallout 2 is a great game.  Sure, it has flaws, but compared to other games, these ones aren't so bad.  This is a great game and I can see why most people enjoy it and label it as the best in the series.  I agree with them, for the most part(I still think Fallout New Vegas is a close second or at least a contender for the best).  The combat could have been better since depending on the amount of enemies and how many action points you have, it can really take a
time.  But it's still good in its own right.  If you've only played the latest ones, please, buy 1 and 2 and play them.  These are amazing games and they are truly what started it all, 20 years ago.

It is in many ways a sequel of it’s time.  No real, or visible changes to the game engine, but an expanse of scope from the first.  The story is longer and there are many more side quests. Fallout 2 was the second installment of the Interplay originals of the post-nuclear series. Like any good story, your character comes from bare bones origins, a tribesman, mightiest of your primitive clan, is set to find a fantastical technology to restore your people from strife, and set off into the atompunk, futuristic hellscape of Fallout's nuclear wasteland. However, you are soon to discover settlements of their own unique stripes, scraping or thriving either on benevolence or malice, and you, the simple protagonist can change them for either the good or bad of a new age of humanity, struggling to survive.
The good:
-I see Fallout 2 as the New vegas to Fallout 3. It takes the concept of its predessecor, and polishes it with better mechanics, combat, depth, and roleplaying complexity and a new story.
-The game is displayed in a top down isometric style so its easy to see who to talk to and its impossible to get lost in an area.
-Diverse locations, everyplace and NPC you visit is somewhere unique and different, there is almost no such thing as "just another settlement" in the game, except for maybe the first one you go to.
-A decent "fast travel" system where you can get random encounters and even unique, hilarious pop culture references.
-Combat is turn-based but is thankfully fast-paced, equipment durability doesn't exist in this game like the Bethesda Fallouts so looting is especially encouraged.
-The story and atmosphere are amazing, I cannot emphasize it enough, the best of the series in my opinion. Also, unless you constantly consult the wiki, you will certaintly get a different ending through every playthrough, so bonus role-play points there.
The bad:
-Character builds can be easily gimped as some S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats, perks, and skills are significantly better than others, unfortunately severing creativity.
-(Extremely well) Hidden gems: Some objectives are extremely hard to find unless you are very persistent or sharp, and some are not well instructed or specified, this can make the game long and unfun but this is thankfully not consistent in the game.
-BUGS are the largest bane of the game, making certain quests totally uncompletable and ruining certain aspects of the game, thankfully this is fixable with a mod called the restoration project which I believe is highly essential. Link here:
All in all, I love this game and tremendously reccomend it, the Fallout series has been my single franchise to where I have played all the games and I believe this one is the greatest of all.

The best Mahjong game I've ever come across.
The Mahjong Huntress embeds the classic tile matching game into a story, in which a young woman has to find out what happened to her fiance. In order to progress through the story, the player has to solve the boards which unlock hints about the fate of the young man.
Apart from simply cleaning the board of tiles, there are a number of objectives which contribute to the player's energy bar. Depending on its charge, the player is able to use certain powers which can put an already lost game back onto the path to success. Another nice feature is the combo system, which is basically a timer counting down a few seconds between each move, awarding more points if the player managed to match several tiles within the ever decresasing intervals.
The difficuilty of the boards is steadily increasing, forcing the player to sacrifice speed in favor of choosing the right tiles. Unwisely chosen matches will quickly force the player to sacrifice his energy for above mentioned special powers. But beware - once the energy is depleted, the player will have to start over with simpler boards to recharge the energy bar.
In addition to the story mode there are more than 230 so called mystery boards, which are offering a wide range of tile layouts to choose from right from the start.
The presentation is very nice, offering pleasant visuals along with a functional and intuitive user interface.
If you were searching for a Mahjong game, you've just found it. Especially with the very low price tag attached there is absolutely no reason not to recommend it.
Info: The Mahjong Huntress runs very smoothly under Linux as well. I've encountered no problems on my 64Bit-Ubuntu Linux configuration.
UPDATE:
So far I've encountered only a few bugs. Some minor graphic glitches, some spelling errors. Worst bug was a game crash after the boss fight in the mausoleum. After restarting, I couldn't progress because the game didn't open chapter 3 for me. I had to create a new player profile and start over.
A fun puzzle game if you love Mahjong! The story line is kind of cheezy, but it's nice and casual. A nice evening game to wind down with...or when you want a mental break from fast-paced life.

I don't know what happened, but after having been unable to play this version of the game due to constant performance issues and bugs, I finally completed it yesterday, and have been awash in all the feels.
First, I'm still frustrated that it took so long - I don't know what changed, if a patch came out stealthily, or if my computer simply decided to buck up all of a sudden, but the fact that upon release, this was buggier than the original version is inexcusable for a publisher as high-profile as Eidos.
On the other hand, I've sunk more hours into this game (orignal, DLC, and Director's Cut) than Dark Souls 1&2 combined. Which is a lot. I loved the music, the stealth, the writing, the voice acting, the sheer world-building and sense of scale to the game's narrative - all in all, it seemed like a complete package, and a worthy successor to Deus Ex, on of my favorite games of all time.
This edition changed that perspective. I never cared much about the boss fights, which were the big bugaboo for most people. What bothered me - and I didn't truly realize it until I listed to the DC's commentary - was the sense that much of the story was actually left out of the game.
It's notwhere near as bad as Eidos' reboot of Thief (which was a frankenstein of 9 drafts patched together without rhyme or reason), but upon hearing how much of this game was left out - from the dev's own lips - I began to feel both cheated and vindicated. The lingering sense that I had somehow missed a key part of the story was laid to rest. I had indeed missed things - because they hadn't made it into the final game.
The backstory of the game's bosses? Cut. The relationship between the villains, the Illuminati, the power players, the opening raid? Stripped to the absolute minimum, which I totally missed the first time around. The lack of resolution to the primary story arc (the search for Megan)? The devs simply didn't resolve it, because they didn't have time. The botched "press-a-button" ending? Also, by the dev's own admission, not as they originally planned.
Upon playing through for the third time, I ached at the thought of exploring upper Hengsha, Bangalore, and Montreal. Not because those places sounded great, but because they seemed to be, from the commentary, the places where all the plot-holes were filled.
So, upon my final completion of the game, I feel both immeasurably satisfied and inexplicably cheated. This game, even with its current high level of quality, could have been so much more - and indeed was supposed to be.
This is all to say that II'm thrilled for the sequel, Makind Divided. If Human Revolution is the result of budget cuts and time crunch, I cannot WAIT to see what this team does now that it has access to new resources. Hopefully we'll get the game that Human Revolution should have been - and was supposed to be - from the start.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is number 8 on my top 10 favorite games list; it isn't the greatest game ever made, but it definitely deserves your attention and a few bucks from your wallet. It takes the fantastic concepts of the first DE game, fixes what Invisible War messed up, and adds a thick and convoluted new story to enjoy.
My personal score for Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a 9/10. There are a few kinks that keep it away from perfection, particularly the less-than-ideal gunplay mechanics, but it's an overall blast to play and certainly shouldn't be missed by any fan of games with a strong story and lots of replayability.

The reworked boss fights and integrated DLC are nice. However, it would appear that they added these new features to the FIRST build of Deus Ex HR, as all of the original bugs have now returned. Including the most annoying "save file corruption" bug, which was fixed years ago.
Stick with the non director's cut version.

An excellent local and online co-op game, Rampage Knights scratches that itch to beat up your friends and enemies indiscriminately. Except your friend only dies if you knock them into a pit. Or under a strategically positioned Mighty Foot curse that smashes them into the ground. Or walk into your bomb. Or knocked down by your ghost after they killed you.
Regardless, the randomized dungeons, traps, curses, and loot add a perfect amount of variety to ensure at least a few fun run-throughs. The combat isn't just brainless button mashing, especially with its different mobs, bosses, and curses (hi, Mighty Foot!) out to get you. Oh, and of course, your friend on occasion.

One of the BEST all time space combat games i have ever played (if not simply the best GAME i have ever played).  Old school simulator(ish) style gameplay with basically everything done right.  Review will be for both Descent Freespace 1 and Freespace 2.
1) Gameplay flight mechanics and controls:  Flight is simplified to mimic atmosphere flight mechanics (Arcade style) but the controls are simulator style.  Power managment, shield distribution, ETC.  Joystick control is reccomended but the mouse can be used as well.
2) Story:  In my opinion, THE ABSOLUTE BEST STORY I HAVE EVER EXPERIENCED IN A GAME.  The story is told through Cutscenes, Pre-mission briefings, and sometimes even during your mission.  Oh...and the games intro scene is the best cutscene in any videogame ever.
3) Graphics:  Excellent if it were 1998-2000, however now the graphics do not hold a candle to current games.  However a dedicated group of programmers have created the "Freespace 2 Source Code Project" AKA "Freespace 2 SCP".  Simply explained, this project updates all the graphics to about modern day [2015 (ish)] standards.  In order to use SCP project you must have purchased Freespace 2.  Then the SCP project will allow you to play the following things with the updated graphics:   Freespace 1 (Descent Freespace), Freespace 2, as well as additional fan made campaigns.
I could go on and on about the greatness of the Freespace games but let me ask you a simple question instead.  Can you remember the last game you played where the graphics were amazing (now using SCP Project mod), you had no issues or complaints with the controls or game performance, and the story was so amazing that you can remember it 15 years later?  I can, and they are Freespace 1 and Freespace 2 (which i have replayed over 5 times now).
Oh, and whatever company has the rights to Freespace, PLEASE make Freespace 3.

I was going to delete my old review, but then thought it would actually be best to leave it up, because I don’t think my experience with this title is unique. In short, my initial impressions of the AMS were observationally correct, and yet simultaneously completely…utterly…wrong. You can read the original review below this one.
After doing a little reading, I decided to reinstall the game and give it another go last week. This time, armed with a little pre-knowledge and a more realistic expectation of the setup curve, my experience was completely different.
First, the force feedback. I own and play (PCars, AC, R3E, and rF2) and IMO, with a little bit of tweaking, AMS has arguably some of the best force feedback I’ve ever felt in a sim.  And by a little bit of tweaking, I mean simply adjusting one setting in the .ini file to dial out any clipping from the default settings. A small bit of clipping is perfectly okay, but the devs claim the defaults settings, allow about 20-30% clipping. Not sure what wheel they tested that on, but on my CSW-V2, the default gain setting for the cars in the base installation allows a little too much clipping in the high-speed corners for my tastes. Not a big deal, very easy to dial out. And once you do, the cars will feel amazing. :)
Second, the graphics. This was a big turn off for me the first time I tried AMS. Yes, I realize graphics aren’t the end-all-be-all measure for sim titles, but, coupled with what I thought at the time was poor FFB and a poorly designed GUI, the outdated looking graphics made me feel as though it wasn’t worth the time to negotiate the setup curve of the title. What I didn’t realize at the time was, AMS’ built-in graphics processing is terrible, but you don’t have to use it. By turning off almost every in-game graphic setting, and simply creating a profile in my GPU driver for AMS, and allowing the GPU to handle most of the processing, I was able to use the enhanced HDR setting in AMS, and it looks like a totally different game—very much comparable to any other modern title. When properly configured through the GPU, the outdated graphics gripe basically becomes a complete non-issue.
Third, the GUI. Yes, it appears a bit cluttered and hard to navigate, but the more time I spend with the title, the more I seem to be discovering the method behind the madness. AMS remembers the little things, like which track you were driving in each particular car and what difficulty level you were using with that particular car/track combo. The latter was a welcome surprise, considering AI difficulty often varies by car/track combo. I believe some of these little conveniences that have been revealing themselves are made possible, in part, if not completely, by the way things are broken down and organized in the GUI. And, to be honest, after a few days of play, the GUI doesn’t seem nearly as chaotic as it did on day-one. :)
So, as much as I’d like to say, “Please ignore my previous review.” I think reading them both is best, because there’s a good chance you’re going to be feeling some, if not all, of the things I felt about the game when I first tried it a few months ago. The thing to remember is, while all my past observations were indeed true, they only apply to the out-of-the box installation. With a little patience—a browse through the community forum and possibly a Google search or two—the initial installation can be transformed into a real racing pleasure that should appeal to just about any sim fan.
Verdict: AMS is a definite must have for sim fans.
