So i've just finished this game and want to give a review:
First of all it's overall a pretty solid shooter game with really nice graphics and sound. The pace of the game is fast (unlike the Doom 3 protagonist who felt as slow as a guy in a wheelchair).
What I liked:
- All the original monsters from the real Doom games (part 3 excluded) are there and they feel basically like them.
- The original weapons find a place in this game and they even put some on top.
- The gore level is what I would expect from a Doom game and it delivered.
- The pacing of the game is fast even though sometimes I was kinda missing a sprint key.
- The story is sufficient enough to give me a second motivation to kill them all (the first motivation is pretty obvious with a Doom game I think)
What bothered me:
For me Bethesda is the 80% company: They have some really nice games in their portfolio and those I played I really liked. But it feels like they are never really giving it the final polish that a game would need to become really great. I see this in Fallout and Skyrim but the fantastic modding support more than redeems that. In this game though I don't see the same modding potential and that brings me to the following list:
- The game is short. I guess there is no need to sugar-coat that fact.
- Weapon upgrades are not a bad idea in general but in this game I think it takes the wrong implementation. To REALLY upgrade all the weapons in the game you need to find a buttload of secrets or have to do special challenges with the respective weapon to unlock the highest tier upgrade.
Personally I see the necessity to upgrade my weapons as much as I can to unlock their true potential. Too bad though that I found myself breaking the flow of the game and roaming around the empty maps after killing everything afterwards. In a game like that this is NOT wnat I want to do.
The weapon challenges are especially annoying when you have to do something to a special kind of enemy that is not overly present in the current map or is surrounded by other enemy types that block you from quickly achieving this challenge.
- To the above mentions point comes that I think there are way too few enemies in the game. I played on the easiest setting after getting my♥♥♥♥♥handed by the enemies in the first maps on a higher difficulty due to their bullet sponginess and extreme damage output. I think this is very Doom-unlike.
- In my opinion there should be enemies that are as strong as on the second hardest setting but more.. way more.
- I was shocked to see how pathetic the DOOM-guy was in the first maps. Just 20 shotgun shells and you have to get really, really close to kill an Imp.. c'mon.
- In later maps (and after scrounding alot for secrets :/) I became almost godlike which made fight too easy. You don't have this in the original Doom games and it should not have been included in here.
- Calling this game just "DOOM".... I mean really. Everyone knows that MicroSoft cannot cound correctly, but I expected more from you guys. Don't listen to the marketing monkeys. I know that monkeys through feces around when they want to demonstrate dominance but that doesn't mean you have to catch it all and re-use it.
All in all I would have given this game a higher rating if it was a bit more like the original Doom games in a better graphics but i'm still willing to give it a 7/10.

I love my Steam Controller, being able to customize every control including motion controls is a something I must have now that I have experienced it, using an xbox or playstation controller just doesn't make sense anymore, the Steam Controller is a PC controller and it should be on the desk of every avid PC gamer.

I must say that I am pretty impressed with it, sure it takes sometime getting used to, it is definitely the best joystick ever. Great job Valve !

This controller has an extremely specific niche that the promotional materials don't really make clear: slow-paced mouse and keyboard games. If you are using third party crap to emulate M/KB inputs with a controller to play Civilizations, this is a straight upgrade.
For any other type of game where you would use a controller, an xbox or logitech controller is better. If you're playing an FPS or similar on a controller, having two sticks is pretty much a necessity, if only to conform to conventions that affect how people expect to use a controller to move their characters and the camera. For games that are designed with a controller in mind, quite often those games have menus that assume you have a dpad so it can be difficult to use without accidentally tilting the stick or trackpad in the wrong direction.
For games where you would not use a controller, the steam controller is slightly better using a trackpad. Not great, in other words.
Until recently, I personally had no use for the thing, but I did finally find that playing Stardew Valley on my Surface is serviceable using the steam controller. It's especially better than using the Surface trackpad.
tl;dr - If you are tired of using the trackpad to play games or emulating M/KB with your xbox controller, I recommend it. If you're part of the other 95% of people in the world, I can't imagine what use you'd have for this.

As an experienced jong player i picked this game up on sale for a few bucks. Its got a sherlock holmes esque storyline to it that you must solve some jong puzzles to solve it. Not bad for a few dollars to kill some time and play some jong.

It's a fun game with a surprising increase in difficult the further you dive into the story.
There are multiple timers that contribute to level challenge bonuses as well as in-game bonuses & power ups. Some mahjong games set up the tiles randomly, but this one obviously follows a type of algorythm where the game wont screw you on the first few steps, offering you a short grace period before you run into issues. (There's one puzzle I couldn't get more than 15% complete before having to use every power up I could, eventually resorting to using most of my crystals to completely refill the powerup bar.) As you progress through the storyline you'll find yourself needing to use these power ups more and more as the puzzles get more difficult. One of the power ups will reshuffle the board.
There's a neat feature that allows you to remove a tile from the board and hold onto it to match later, but you have to match it before being able to pick up another one. There are hundreds of challenge puzzles available that don't affect the story portion of the game.
Another portion of the game involves "boss fights" that play very similarly to games like Bejeweled or Pokemon Shuffle. The instructions for these games aren't explained very well, so it took a while for me to catch on. There are health orbs for yourself and the enemy. The bar next to the health bar shows which color orbs will give you "crystal energy" to attack. For the entirety of the first boss fight, I had to avoid matching purple orbs or I would get attacked. Each time I was able to attack, my color changed.
The achievements are buggy right now but the game just came out so it should get fixed soon.

Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~ is an OELVN (Original English Language Visual Novel) developed by Overdrive exclusively for western audiances.  Think of it as a tour of Japan wrapped in a short but occasionally sweet story.  Is this trip worth your time?  Short answer: Not unless you're really interested in learning about Japan.
Go! Go! Nippon! is not a particularly long Visual Novel but it is full of information.  And that is the main draw.  The story itself, while occasionally sweet, is filled to the brim with annoying and tired tropes and falls firmly in the weebo pandering category.  I don't think it does these things in mean spirit but I personally found it annoying.  You assume the role of nameless (and basically faceless in the two or three CGs you are visable in) western otaku who finally gets to make his dreams come true and visit Japan.  He makes friends with some folks on the internet and plans to stay with them.   Of course, once he gets off the plane and meets his kind hosts, he discovers they're two cute sisters, Makoto and Akira.  Oh, and of course their parents are going to be out of town for the duration of your visit.  Let the pandering begin.
The rest of the story takes place over the week you spend in Japan.  You will need to play through the game twice to see both endings and cover all of the locations you can visit.  Makoto and Akira will take you on a tour through Tokyo, visiting places like Shinjuku, Akihabara, and some other areas of Japan like Kyoto.  For the main six locations each girl will be associated with three.  After visiting three locations you will take a joint trip to Kyoto and then have the ending location.  The girl you end up spending the most time with during your trip will give you her unique ending.  Credits will roll and you get a little epilogue.
The character arcs are sweet but very predictable and shallow.  The real appeal in the story is actually touring Japan.  There is a lot of interesting facts and history to take in as you get a brief glimpse of life in Japan.
The art is hit and miss, sprites are well done but not varied enough for my tastes while the backgrounds and locations are pretty lackluster.  There are only a handful of actual CGs in the game but the few that are included are very well done.
The soundtrack is acceptable, some of the tracks actually being pretty good.  There is no voice acting.
From a technical standpoint the visual novel is...functional.  The font is readable, the Options are standard, and you get the usual Extra features such as the CG Gallery and Scene Gallery.  One interesting thing is that the game does feature both English and Japanese in the text box.  It doesn't add a lot to the game unless you're already in the process of learning Japanese and thus gives you some stuff to practice with.
Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~ is interesting at times but very middle of the road as a whole.  I think for people that want to know more about Japan and the culture it might be worth their time.  For anyone else, it is a lot harder to recommend.

BlazBlue: CT is a good fighting game that could have been a great if Arc System Works had only pushed the envelope a little more in terms of creativity. The visuals are nice, the controls are intuitive, and the extensive story mode makes for some entertaining reading. All of the fundamentals are in place. Nonetheless, Arcsys pushed this game out during a time when they legally couldn't make Guilty Gear games, and as a result, everything about this game smacks of a poor man's Guilty Gear. Anyone saying it isn't fair to compare the two series is delusional. Both games are the exact same flavor of fighter, but BlazBlue performs just a step below its sibling series in most regards. Every character on the roster is some transparent Bizarro World counterpart of someone from Guilty Gear. The music is the same metal style, but the melodies aren't as catchy aside from tunes that too closely resemble Guilty Gear pieces. The story is entertaining, but not as interesting. And the lack of online multiplayer in a PC port is a fault too glaring to omit. The overall gameplay, however, does manage to be on par with Arcsys's flagship fighter. Don't confuse my intentions; BlazBlue: CT is a good game in its own right. This brings me to my point: The developers didn't need to borrow so much from Guilty Gear. If you like the developer's other fighting offerings, you'll like this one, because it's almost the exact same thing. Arcsys would have done better to capitalize on the opportunity to create a more unique series, but instead, they came out with BlazBlue: Totally Not Guilty Gear, Sega.

TL:DR Game looks fun but a really bad port, similar to Dark Souls, which make this game really hard to play right with out mods/3rd party apps and a controller.
Game seems really fun, but Square Enix honestly doesn't care about PC support. If you wish to play with keyboard/mouse you will be heart broken to find out that SE doesn't know what a mouse is, and decided that camera controls are best implemented with the arrow keys. While you can remap all the controls on both controller and keyboard, you still can't use the mouse for anything. If you wish to play this game in fullscreen, then you will be heart broken as well, because it doesn't work properly and usually run what looks like 720p even though you may have 1080p or higher selected. It wouldn't be that big of a problem if the game had borderless window, but it doesn't, forcing you to look to 3rd party apps or mods just to play the game fullscreen at the proper resolution. If you wanted to enjoy the pretty visuals that the game has at 144fps, then you'll be heart broken as well, because it seems that SE just doesn't even know what a computer is and locked the game at 60fps and cutscenes at 30fps (because mechanics and animations are frame based rather than time based). Also, a lot of people have a hard time running this game at a stable 60fps, for seemingly no reason. While the game looks nice, it doesn't look like it should have too trouble running constant 144fps on high end builds let alone 60fps, but it does. It also does't seem like SE is too interested in making an update to the game to fix the problems, because these existed at launch, and still exist now. I'd say pass on this game and make SE know that they made a bad port and they don't deserve our money for a low effort port, so that they improve thier mistakes and make a better one.

This game is one of the best racing simulators on the market. But to fully enjoy you really need a steering wheel. Then you can appreciate the physics and different car handling. The sounds are really great too, especially in formula cars, when you can hear the sound of the air passing the car in high speed. I also like the graphics. I know it's not the best compared to Assetto Corsa or Project Cars but for me the most important is actually the racing itself. The tracks looks very good for me, much better then in rFactor2 where they are using  very dull colours for some reason. Also the AI is much better here compared with the other racing games. Here you can see for example more often when AI drivers make mistakes (like in real life) which I didn't see in many other racing games. The downside of Automobilista is lack of dynamic weather. There is a 24h cycle but that's it. No wet racing :-( That's the biggest criticism. I also have noticed some AI issues, for example the AI drivers are for some reason much slower on corners, but on the straight line much quicker.

All of the content is high quality both in terms of sound and physics. The ai are good enough if you're looking for this to be a singleplayer game. Multiplayer for now basically requires you to be in a league but you won't struggle to find one. Ultimately it's a complete package, and while it doesn't have a long string of buzzwords listing technologies and systems that result in the level of simulation present, playing it reveals you don't really need that.

Well, finally after finding my way back to Simracing, I checked out AMS after quite some time. It got incredibly high quality and high standards. Of course, that's why Reiza can keep it that cheap, you hardly have licensed cars, but that's not the point I'd focus on. First of all, I've driven mainly the Formula V12 and V10. They are amazing with their high speeds and at the same time it never feels too fast. Remembering other games with GT1 Cars, it always felt like they were way too fast everywhere. Here you got clear limits, great control and quite some room to play with gas, brakes and wheel. This is what you got on all cars in the game. It feels authentic, and it looks like that as well when watching the replay. The good thing is, that modders already created several skinpacks for several seasons of those Formula 1 Cars.
Next car I really love is the BoxerCup, which is basically a Porsche Cup Car. It is surprisingly well to control while it is at the same time a classic oversteery Porsche. Great fun, but sometimes maybe a bit frustrating if you're not practiced with this stuff. But it's a lot of fun.
Another thing I tried for the first time is the Rallye Cross Car. Damn! You got an awesome control over the car and it's huge fun to drift around with it.
Another awesome thing is the flatspotting of the tires. You can see them on the tires and you really feel them. The wheel and car start to shake around and it becomes much harder to drive in a clean line. Great feature!
There are for sure many more cars I could tell about, but now the tracks:
They are done very nicely with all those bumps. You really feel every single one of them. The FFB gives great feedback. Especially the Virginia Raceway shows you how good the FFB really is. The tracks are just accurate and in many layouts. Also the brasilian tracks, known from Stockcar Extreme, are very well done.
Another thing is the performance: I have a pretty old computer, just the minimum specs and it simply runs smooth at 50-60 FPS on high details and HDR.
So, if you want a very strong Simracer, take AMS. There is high potential of great mods. Seen from the graphics point of view, it might be an old game engine, but it is great to see what they got out of it. So this is also a good one for older computers.
Regarding Mods there are already a GT3 Mod and an LMS Mod avaiable at European Endurance Center.

If you want to have a stark contrast in how much gaming has evolved over the years, then place this 2016 version of
side by side with the 1993 version of this game. The differences is startling in multiple aspects not only in the gameplay and graphics, but also the hardware that is required to run this game.
Around July, 2017, the game released it’s 6.66 patch, made all the DLC free, and was on sale for $15 (USD). This was a must-purchase. I played through the campaign mode at the “Hurt Me Plenty” settings, and it took me nine hours to get through the entire campaign. Unfortunately, the campaign storyline is on the weakest part of this game. When I got to the end, it was just “the end” with no conclusion, and no satisfactory resolution.
The graphics and gameplay, however, are excellent. I was able to get consistent 90 FPS (or higher) during the game play at 2560×1440 resolution, although I think this game is an excellent advertisement for a adaptive sync monitor. What I especially enjoyed is the “glory kill” feature which, once you weakened the enemy enough, you can perform a melee attack to rip the enemy apart and, in the process, get some health and some ammo.
What insures the replayability of this game is the same reason why the original
was played for several years: community maps. These custom maps allow for additional gameplay, and many a game designer got their start from custom maps from the original game.
For this old gamer, however, 24 years has passed, and my reactions aren’t what they are used to be. I won’t even try to compete with the younger kids who play
now.

This controller over the next few iterations can become the best controller on the market, but it is held back by certain design choices at the moment.
The ABXY buttons are small and out of reach. Earlier versions of the controller reveal that their inclusion was a late decision and they feel like they were. Most of the community botton mappings seek to completely avoid using those buttons, relying on the grips to replace the two most used of those buttons for any game. It works great, but finding placement for those other two buttons are less than successful.
The left and right triggers and bumpers are awful. There, I said it. They feel cheaper than any flagship controller on the market. The triggers have a pathetic range of throw before full actuation and the bumpers are so cheap that they rattle in the controller. The steam controller can determine the difference between a full pull and a partial pull of the trigger, but the difference in force is so low that I constantly pull too hard and activate a button I did not mean to press. It desperately needs more tactile resistance.
The thumbstick is ALMOST great, but again the tactile resistance is less than would be desired. I would often accidentally actuate the the thumbstick press when trying to use the left grip button.
As much as Valve may not want to admit it, the thumbstick is the star of the show on the left side, and it is placed badly on the controller to give aesthetic preference to the left trackpad. The most popular button layouts in the games I played all use the left trackpad as a typical directional pad. Meanwhile the thumbstick I spend 95% of the time using is so far low and center that I have to extend my thumb into an unergonomic position. The right trackpad is crucial to improving on-the-couch shooting games; nobody is arguing that. I however am skeptical just how crucial the left trackpad actually is.
That leads me to my last problem. The steam controller is too big in its current iteration. This is a less exagerated example of the Duke controller from the first Xbox. The controller is too large for my medium sized hands and WAY too large for my girlfriend to use.
All in all, I don't feel like I'm playing with an ironed out product. I'm excited to see where this controller goes in the future but I am certain that if I had been given a week to try this controller before buying it that I would not have purchased it at all. It is too early to say Valve shouldn't be making controllers. For all they do wrong on this controller to make me not like it, they do a lot of things well enough that they mae me want to like it. Tey are trying to build a controller that works with all genres of games, and that is a daunting task. In some aspects they made compromises that hold back the product as a whole. I hope that in another iteration or two, I can buy a steam controller that blows the competitors out of the water. As the controller is now, I think it is not a great product.

I bought this controller to work with my HTPC/Steam box and it works great for both.  I don't have a mouse and keyboard plugged in normally.  This controller works great for launching games that have controller support but are launched via a launcher which an XBox controller doesn't handle.  Other things I like are that you are able to close the current program via the overlay menu from pressing the Steam button, useful for poorly ported games that you need to hit esc to close or emulators.  The haptic feedback is pretty impressive and I don't think the controller would be half as good without it.
There are a couple things that I don't care for though, when using the left trackpad as a dpad, it seems too big and takes too much force to click.  I changed it to not require a click but now when I hit the select button, I always catch the edge of the pad causing a misclick.  This could be remedied in a future update as all it would need is to add an option for a deadzone on the outside of the pad, it already gives you an option for one on the inside.  the XYBA buttons are small and took awhile to get used to the placement of them, I was constanly hitting Y and B when aiming for X and A.  most games I've tested so far already had controller support which doesn't require much tinkering.  I've played The Witcher 3 most and did a complete playthrough with Arkham Asylum, and tested it with a couple uplay games like Assassin's Creed: Rogue, and it works well for them.  But, I don't care for it playing First person games.  I tried it with Skyrim and Borderlands 2 both of which support controllers but neither of them felt right with the right touchpad as a mouse,  The battery drain seems higher on the Steam Controller than an Xbox controller, Took about 2 weeks to drain with moderate usage.
All in all, I don't regret purchasing the Steam Controller but it's not going to be for everyone.

World of Guns: Gun Disassembly is a really in depth firearm simulator. Mostly in the way you pull apart the guns piece by piece but there is a firing range and operation mode where you can fire the gun of your choice with different attachments such as silencers, scopes, different magazine sizes and just learn how every single component works with each other. The satisfaction you get when you pull apart and put back together a sophisticated gun with more than 60 parts without choosing the wrong components is probably more rewarding than shooting the gun itself.
The only downside to this game is that it's a bit grindey, but I guess that adds to the charm of getting to know each and every part of the weapon you are disassembling, but it's not too much of a problem for me as I don't really mind a bit of a grind sesh once in a while. Plus I get time to learn every weapon that is in the game instead of just blazing past every single gun and missing out on how they all work.
In conclusion, it's MUCH better than the Google Play and Apple store versions just because of the fact you have full control over the camera. Plus it's a stupidly fun and rewarding game if you're into pulling things apart then putting them back together just to see how they work and operate.

TL;DR - Google Japan, watch a slice of life anime, skip the game.
How is this very positive? Are people really that desperate to get their perv on with the most stereotypical characters and scenarios ever created? Unlike some here, I really came expecting to learn about Japan, see different areas and get a feel for life there. How hard could it be? I can imagine endless scenarios where this could be done right. However, there is literally nothing to do with exploring Japan in this "game" that couldn't be learned from a quick google search or watching any anime. Want to see the inside of the a Japanese convenience store? Tough, look at clouds while it gets described to you. Want to get aninsiders look into Akihabara? Tough, look at clouds while it’s described to you. Want to get a first person look at traditional Japanese food or a street corner vending machine? Tough, just read the description of how cool it is to look at. Maybe this is interesting for people who have never left the city they grew up in but for anyone who has travelled anywhere it is intensely tedious and boring. This is made even more frustrating by how cool an actual game about touring Japan or other countries would be. The things I wish I could do while playing this game would make for a far better experience. Being able to pick meals and look at each ingredient with a short write-up would have been great. Some kind of interactive street view experience at the different destinations would have also been great; how cool would it have been to pick out items from a realistic vending machine or store and have it effect the trip! I expected a game built around a first person point and click perspective of a tourist in Japan. Instead you get a crappy and tedious "novel" that tries to gag you with exhausting tropes.

I got really mad at the game recently when I was stuck on a point that I could not upgrade my weapons, and I had to switch to easy mode for a bit. Really just one section like that could be forgiven, but there will be times where the game forces you into him that you can't escape from, so if you haven't leveled up you're screwed. Also one section in particular feels like utter b******* (LOSS mission). Also, if you've read up on this game you know that you have to go through about 3 endings to properly finish the game, it was quite infuriating that one of the routes you have to do is the same as the first (like seriously, almost EVERYTHING you already did) but from a different characters perspective
I'm honestly surprised how much I care about the characters at this point.  I even like 2B, a sentence I never thought I would say. Really I hear people praising its story, and I can see what they mean. But really, at this point (I think about 30 hours in by now?) It feels like the game is kind of pulling its punches. Maybe he does get better towards the end but if you have to play a fully our games just for the final third, it's not worth it.
Ending on a positive note, the music is AWESOME, the combat isn't as deep as, say, God of War, but makes up for it with Precision and style (little hint, make sure you're always doing side quests and grinding, otherwise it will come back to bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥. The game is absolutely gorgeous, and the enemies are endlessly creative. While I am giving the story a lot of s***, it can be a little surprising at times, (the end of route one and the start of route 3) and the two leads do grow very close to each other. However, I just don't understand 9S' arc. He goes from hating machines, to working with machines, to vowing to kill every last one, that he even kills one that's just asking for help.
I guess the point of this is that I LIKE it. I don't LOVE it, I LIKE it. Unless this next portion of the game is ridiculously good, that it helps me forget 30 hours of bland story, I don't really understand why this keeps getting nomination for game of the year.

Hey everyone and this is my review about the game!
This is a Roguelike brawler game.
You can play this game in fullscreen mode or windowed mode.
It has many resolution sizes.
You are able to change the music volume. (By 5% each time)
You are able to change hte sound volume. (By 5% each time)
You are able to play this game with a xbox controller.
You are ONLY able to change the controls for the keyboard and NOT for the xbox controller.
You are able to reset your progress.
You can play this local or online Co-op.
You are playing with a character and you have to beat up enemies in order to proceed. You are able to destroy some environment which could be rewarding. You are able to dodge and jump and do some combo moves. Monsters are able to drop some coins or health potions. You are able to unlock and play with different classes if you have completed some of the requires challenges. You are able to find some equipment and your character may look different. Some items has special effects on it. You have hitpoints and lives (depends on difficulty how many). You are able to find treasure chests aswell and you need to lockpick them. You have to hit the gold locks away, but hitting the spiked ones will hurt you.
Graphics are cartoonish but it's nicely done!
Background and scenery is very well done!
Music is decently good and has variation.
There is PERMA DEATH.
It could be a little bit repetitive because you are mainly doing the same move over and over.
Game is alot of fun and entertaining.
There is pre-set character customization.
If you Continue your game, you will be teleported back on the exact same location where you have left.
There is a tutorial/training grounds.
You can play as a female or male warrior.
There is a difficulty settings and the higher it is the more punishing.
There are challenges that you are able to do.
You are able to unlock more characters with their own power.
The game is for mindless killing and doesn't require alot of concentrating.
Health potions will not disappear whenever you are entering a different room.
You are able to fall off.. from a room.. Getting Game Overs from that are always nice. Especially when your character is drunk and he really wants to fall off.. :(

As a long time FPS player who has been in and out of the competitive scene since the early 90's, the Tribes franchise, to me, represents the very best in FPS gaming. Tribes: Ascend has done an amazing job keeping the Tribes legacy alive while keeping the community thriving with a well-implemented F2P business model.
While every game requires skill, Tribes transforms skill into art. Twitchiness and map memorization will not get you as far as it will in more traditional shooters. In Tribes, skilled gameplay means using the freedom of movement granted by a jetpack combined with using powerful weapons that have relatively slow projectiles compared to most games, turning combat into a beautiful dance of timing, prediction, resource management, and accuracy.
Multiple game modes ranging from the legacy Capture the Flag mode to the now-familiar Capture and Hold mode join other standards like Team Deathmatch, Arena, and more, keep the game fun and fresh.

NieR:Automata is a really strange game. It makes sense and the story is an interesting and the charectors mostly really loveable. I hated the annoying robot, its tying with claptrap for least likeable robo-sidekick. I am happy to say that NieR:Automata doesn't have this problem and has remained fresh throughout the entire story campagin (I finished the whole thing before writing this review). The battles -while admittedly over the top- have an epic sense of scale which gives the game an anxious sense during the boss battles in particular. There are a few moments where the story was a bit predictable and the cut-scenes were a bit tear jerky but overall it made me care about the protagonists a lot more than I expected. Oh man, this story. Or should I say stories. This game has one of the most intriguing stories of any game I have ever played. The characters, although sometimes dull on the surface, have SO much more in backstory. BACKSTORY. That is what makes this games story so great; Learning about what really goes down, and then unraveling the mysteries for yourself first hand. And don't even get me started on the Lore that can be discovered in this game, its addictive. But, no spoilers here, if you are a fan of JRPG, dystopian, sci-fi, semi-depressing, giant sword-wielding android war stories, the story will not dissappoint, but be prepared to feel the feels. And yes, 26 endings.
Dash, light attack, light attack, heavy attack, shooty shoot, charged heavy attack, dash, dash, POD ability, dash, dash... That is basically the summary of combat in this game. But what it does, it does really well. With tons of weapons, abilities, upgrades... yeah, no dissappointments, BUT USE A CONTROLLER.
Lets get this straight, the voice acting and lip syncing can be off sometimes, and sometimes the delivery can be quite... cringeworthy, but if you picture this game as a dubbed anime, it'll come across better, no joke. The SOUNDTRACK though. Beautiful. There is a reason it won best soundtrack of the year. You'll know it. Oh, and when you are hacking in the game, the music turns all 8-bit and its a wonderful feature.
Addicting, fast, MANY DIFFERENT STYLES (top down, shoot em up, platformer, puzzle.. i really can't find words to describe them), very JRPG, combat is actually fun, BIG BOSSES FIGHT THEM, theres fishing(?)
In summary, this is one of the best games I have ever played. I went into this game completely blind (other than the fact I knew it won Soundtrack of the year, and I know 2B  from waifu internet stuff) and was not in the slightest dissappointed. If you are looking for a solid JRPG hack and slash, with great music, good characters, deep lore, and a huge variety of gameplay, look no further. Well worth 60$. This was my first review yay.

Reiza have continue to deliver excellent sim racing experiences right out of the box, highly recommend picking this up if you are a Sim Racing fan, the F-V10 alone is worth the purchase.
Keep doing what you're doing Reiza!
The best simracing on the market. There is no better option, Reiza is a miracle maker, what they do with this engine is amazing!

The new rFactor.
This game is what Reiza have built after acquiring the rights to use the source code for the gmotor 2 engine and what they have made is a more polished, advanced version of rfactor with far more detailed physics and force feedback. I predict this will become the go-to platform for modders. Assetto Corsa looks great, but has poor AI and strange physics quirks that lead to mod creators having to use values that don't match real-life values when making cars.
I think this will become the go-to platform for modders that rFactor was in the past generation of sims.
If you don't care about that, the stock content that comes with the game is also excellent. Now with cool features like flat spotting of tyres, and tracks that rubber as the race progresses. Excellent sounds and the new shaders make the game look quite nice, though still not as fancy looking as Assetto Corsa.
A great Sim with a lot of variety in the car and track selection with a good amount of quality mod content available that is only going to get larger.

I don't bother writing many reviews (so far) but feel this game really deserves one.
By far my favourite simulator on the market at the moment and and I have done a lot of hours in all of the competition except for RRE and iRacing due to the cost (esp in the case of the latter).
It is difficult to describe but the game feels absolutely spot on as far as simulation goes. I think much of that comes from the amazingly communicative force feedback which seems to have no lag whatsover. You really feel connected to the car and can really get in the "zone". The level of immersion is fantastic as far as i'm concerned.
If you rate a decent game engine and realism above everything else I would definitely recommend this over the other titles at the moment (although I also rate rF2). I think perhaps Reiza really understand the importance of input repsonse and feedback.

Boy, there's a lot to talk about here. This will be a long one.
First things first: this is a *sexy* device. It looks slick, the concave design feels good, every button has a perfectly firm and clean click, etc. Even the battery cover has its own little bells and whistles. It has quite a few more buttons than any other controller, all of them perfectly integrated into the design: both triggers have a two-stage pull, both touchpads can click, and there are two "paddle" buttons hidden beneath the controller that you activate with your middle and ring fingers. However, it is too big for my very tiny hands--I have to reach a little in order to get to the thumbstick and the four face buttons. Also, the four buttons are quite a bit closer together than on most controllers.
I passed this thing around a group of friends right after I got it, and one of them gave me the female equivalent of a "♥♥♥♥ed in my pants" face. This reaction was in response to the amazingly designed haptic feedback. Hidden inside the case are multiple vibrate-y-things that are configured independently--which means rather than the whole thing vibrating, your right thumb feels the feedback from the right touchpad. This is especially amusing for "trackball mode" because the vibration simulates flicking a trackball and then feeling it gradually wind down.
Which brings me to the fact that the level of configuration that you can put this thing through is insane. Whatever level of customization you think you want for the precision and sensitivity of the thumbstick and touchpads, Steam offers ten times more. You kind of have to see it to believe it. Oh yeah, and you can download other people's game-specific configurations, modify them to your preferences, and save them as separate profiles.
All this is done in Big Picture mode, and the biggest pain-in-the♥♥♥♥♥about this controller so far is that it is only supported by Big Picture mode. I hate Big Picture mode, even though its UI is actually pretty damn good. I just... come on, this is a device made for the Master Race! Don't make us use the interface that was designed to be more friendly to the peasants!
So, how does it actually feel to play games with this thing?
Well, let's just say that I've yet to find the perfect game for it.
The game I was most curious to try out was SUPERHOT. If ever there was a game that is begging for a compromise between mouse or controller, this is the one. Analog control over your movement in that game makes a huge difference, to the point that it makes the game more enjoyable. However,  the lack of truly unerring precision from a mouse is a serious loss. If I can ever manage to tinker enough to find that precision with the mousepad, then I will declare on this page that I have found ultimate SUPERHOT nirvana.
So how about a fast-paced, twitchy game as opposed to a super-precise one? Well, so far I'm not crazy about playing Nuclear Throne with the Steam Controller. Again, it comes down to trying to find perfection with the right touchpad, something that is easy to do with a gaming mouse but very hard to do here. You want to be able to whirl your crosshair rapidly around the entire screen and stop it on exactly the right spot, but that's pretty much not going to happen. I'll see how I feel after cranking the sensitivity way up. I suspect it won't be very good.
I wanted to give the "D-pad" a try, so I booted up Street Fighter V. See, the Steam Controller doesn't have a D-pad to speak of, only another touchpad with the cross shape imprinted on it. I was pleasantly surprised to find that inputting hadouken and shoryuken commands felt just fine. Charging back for a Kikoken felt less fine. Double tapping for a dash did not feel fine at all. Again, what we're looking at here is a big touchpad on which you input "right" by touching on the rightmost edge. Mind you, the pad is large enough that you could input stuff with good precision once you get used to not having the feel of a clicky, physical D-pad. However, resting your thumb on the pad is bound to cause problems. I'm not really sure when I would be happy to have a left touchpad instead of a D-pad or thumbstick.
Finally, the moment of truth: first person shooters. I didn't feel like downloading a huge game, so I went with Republic Commando. This is what "trackball mode" was made for, and it feels surprisingly good. Again, the haptic feedback really improves the sensation of flicking your aim and having it keep drifting for a while. The config I'm using has a high "friction" setting, so it doesn't go very far--if you set it that way, it'll let you really whirl like crazy. I'd hate to try to line up headshots way, but as long as I'm literally playing the next best thing to a Stormtrooper, this level of precision is fine.
I haven't tried Rocket League yet. I anticipate a large benefit from having more buttons available per hand, but perhaps a bit of discomfort because, again, my hands are too small for this controller. I also haven't tried a game in which you actually want two thumbsticks, such as Geometry Wars or... I don't know, someone give me a recommendation. Perhaps I'll see how Nuclear Throne feels when I set it to gamepad mode instead of mouse mode. I definitely anticipate problems with using the touchpads as thumbsticks.
This is a beautifully designed controller in every way, but every time I've used it, it has been a trade-off instead of a magical revelation. I don't think the Steam Controller is the one, ultimate input device for anything except perhaps SUPERHOT. After all, its whole point of this design is an attempt to compromise between two utterly antithetical input methods. Get this if you strongly prefer using a controller and want one that is compatible with anything and everything.

AMS doesn't have the visuals of AC or pCars and it doesn't reach rF2's physics, yet it's the one sim i start up while all others (i own all the big ones, old and new) just get launched every now and then to justify having them installed on my SSD.
AMS has great unique content, the cars feel and sound great and the developer Reiza is really in love with their baby and they are incredibly fast in developing this title further.

In my view, AMS is built around a very sharp observation. Around the year 2016, if you want a full suite racing simulator, you won't find one. One title offers superior visuals, but lacks some basic features even after years of development (Assetto Corsa). Other is packed with all the simulation features you want, gives you the best physics out there, but because of a lack of content and the somewhat last gen feel graphics, feels incomplete (rFactor2). The third teases you with officially licenced series, mindblowing sounds and attractive visuals, but again, fails in the features department, not to talk about robbing you with the plethora of microtransactions (RaceRoom Racing).
Simply put, AMS is the only complete package out there. Although many say it is based on rFactor 1 engine, if the car feels as good as it does in AMS, I don't care what is there under the hood. Besides the excellent physics and FFB, the visual side is also top-notch. I don't know what the magic there is, but it simply looks and feels great, better than rF2. I especially like the day-night transitions, which are seamless, and the night racing experience is probably the best you can get. If that's not enough, all the features you liked in the previous generation of sims (you remember, back in the time when there was this strange habit of publishing finished products) - finally, they are there. And a big plus is that the game offers complete series, and though I was initially full of doubts as to how interesting these series can be for me, the European simracer, it was a very positive disappointment concerning both the cars and the tracks. The range of vehicles is vast, and even me, who is not a rally guy at all, find myself driving the Lancer RX simply because it is so much fun to drive.
I had many doubts, but AMS totally convinced me - it is possibly the best, but most certainly the most complete sim you will get. The only negative in my view, is the price tag, but for the same array of content you could easily spend 60-70 EUR in some other titles, so maybe that's fair enough.

As everyone else is saying: the ffb and physics on this game are THE NEXT LEVEL. Combined with the force feedback and handling of the cars is the sense of speed delivered in the way you're virtual head moves about inside the cockpit. I set the head motion and yaw exaggeration to the maximum, cranked up "look ahead" all the way, and it REALLY adds to the sense of g forces involved in cornering, accelerating and braking inside the cockpit as it feels like the car is violently bucking and surging, as it should in an F1 car.
As far as graphics go I was about to delete the game from my system and go on a forum and ♥♥♥♥♥ about how crappy they are until I discovered that you have to DISABLE SweetFX in the initial setup screen of the game, keep Anti Aliasing OFF...and then go into the nvidia control panel and manually setup the Anti Aliasing there to OVERRIDE the game's settings.
I bumped my Anti Aliasing up to 32 supersample and now the graphics are smooth as silk. If you just install the game as is with sweetFX enabled the graphics look a bit like playstation 1, so don't delete it from you system until you follow the above.
Don't expect Assetto Corsa level graphics here but to me, it's all about the smoothness of the jaggies. The textures of the track are done quite nicely and are very detailed. The cars are modeled very well but there are a few bugs in some views, such as when looking to the rear while in the cockpit your back wheels won't be visible in the F1 car. But this is still pre launch so I'm sure it will get fixed. The terrain in general is a bit bland but on par.
The thing I'm finding with the tracks is they are all a little bland just by their nature, but a blast to drive. So again, this sim isn't about showcasing eye candy, its about the EXPERIENCE, and in my opinion this is THE game for F1 hot lapping.
I have not yet tried driving against the Ai so I can't speak about that, but my hunch is it will be intense. I've never had a game pull me so much into the feeling of driving an F1 car at high speed as this one. Just be sure to widen your field of view a bit back to get that sense of speed necessary.
If you crave a pure F1 experience THIS is THE game.

The boss fights have been reworked, so you now have the same creative freedom to fight them as the rest of the game. The Missing Link DLC has also been seamlessly integrated, and fills out the plot quite nicely. The game has also been optimized for modern machines, and runs very well on my so/so laptop. Overall, if you like cyberpunk, stealth, and videogames in general, you owe it to yourself to get this game.
P.S. Do not get the upgraded bio-chip in Hengsha 2 unless you want to make the 3rd boss unreasonably difficult.

is a 3D space craft action simulator. You are a recruit pilot who just joined the Galactic Terran Alliance in its age-long war against the Parliamentary Vasudan Empire, but the war takes a different turn when an unknown threat makes its appearance with the sole purpose of exterminating both races.
: You get to live the war and the events through the eyes of a pilot, and the whole story is detailed through mission briefings and in-game events. Different levels of success in a mission may affect the following mission, even open entire branching side-missions. The voice acting does a good job a delivering the humane yet rigid tone of a military situation, something you'll rely on for immersion as there is little to no cut scenes. Action is great, and often allows creative thinking to resolve an issue, succeed in a mission and achieve bonus goals. The missions themselves are very varied, rivaling and often surpassing classics of the genre like the
series. Control is spot-on, although optimized for mouse-less keyboard. As you progress, you get more and more flexibility in how you want to set and arm your squads.
: The game isn't opened world, but mission-based, so forget any concept of exploring or visiting space stations and planets: you jump in, do the mission, and jump out. The graphics have aged a lot: it isn't retro-style, it's actual pixelated low-resolution interface and texture.

Don't be fooled with the title, this game is not Descent, it feels more like wing commander than any of the Descent games. Descent: Freespace is a space flight simulation, you're essentially battling in open space commanding a small crew of pilots against the shivan. If you've played the Wing Commander games then you will be familiar with this game already. You are a member of the terrans and you are fighting for mankind's survival against a hostile alien threat. Seems pretty generic I know but Freespaceis mostly focused on the gameplay.
It is important to note that this game is definitely not for the faint hearted, even on the lower difficulties this game can be quite challenging. The control layout for this game is simply put insane. You will need to master all the controls before you can effectively complete missions. Luckily the game starts out with a tutiorial but the button configurations can easily be forgotten fast and it's required to re-learn them again if you choose to return to the game after a long break.
Missions give you control of a space fighter and it is equipped with two differrent weapons, usually a gun and a missile. There are also allies to command which can be handy in certain situations. The game has a habit of throwing everything at you and expects you to understand the control scheme and manage your allies. It really makes for a challenging yet rewarding experience since you are commended for your efforts with medals and other cool goodies.
There are multiple ways a mission can end based on your progress, if you screw up (either you die, fail the mission or desert) you will have to re-do the mission, however there are many differrent ways to make progress and it all depends on your performance.
With an overwhelming control scheme and mission briefing, this game can become very intense very quickly and is reccommended for people who are willing to take their time to learn and master the game. If you're looking for a quick fix flight sim, this is not the right game for you.

EDIT: Continuum Shift Extend is coming to Steam, and as is mentioned in the final paragraph, CSE has a condensed version of Calamity Trigger's story rendering Calamity Trigger obsolete. I am leaving this review up anyway, but CSE makes a better entry point into the series with Calamity Trigger being an additional purchase for those who want to experience the alternate routes.
Blazblue features a great sci-fi story told via visual novel sections interspersed with the best 2D fighter gameplay I've ever experienced.
The story takes place in a post-apocalyptic world in which society has already been rebuilt and futuristic tech that runs off magic has been developed. The lore is quite complicated, but most of it is explained in the non-canon "Teach Me, Miss Litchi" segments, which consist of light-hearted skits performed by super-deformed versions of the game's main characters. Having the lore explanations separate from the main game allows for the main storylines to move at a decent pace. However, in Calamity Trigger the "Teach Me, Miss Litchi" segments are unlocked as you play the game, so you may end up completely lost while playing the main story. As for tone, there is a serious story in the game that is told in a serious manner, but there is also an abundance of humour and gag routes in the series.
The actual gameplay seems to cater to both hardcore competitive fighter fans and unskilled casual players (like me). Combos are easy to pull off and flow together well, all the special moves have simple inputs and can even be mapped to a single button/key/analogue stick flick, and the easy difficulty is rather easy. There's more that appeals to the hardcore crowd, but as this version lacks online play, said people are better off with the console version, which they would likely already own. I had a hard time with hard difficulty and some normal fights, so there may be a challenge to be had for those who want one, but not as much of a challenge as you could have against human players.
The PC version seems to play just as well as the console versions, but lacks online play, so it's vs. computer and local play only. The included soundtrack features a lot of metal, but also has some symphonic rock. There are 42 tracks, but some short audio clips such as the "[character] vs. [character]" screen music is included, so it's more like 34 songs.
Highly recommended, unless Continuum Shift Extend is an option, as that contains a condensed version of Calamity Trigger's story complete with most of the memorable fights as well as minor beneficial tweaks, the entirety of Continuum Shift, and a few extra story routes not found elsewhere.

Okay. No doubt this game here is a pretty bad port. I can say that it has many MANY problems but it's still a lot of fun.
So the story: The story starts with Nick. The main protagonist of the game. And that's pretty much all you need to know. It's the typical Dead Rising kind of thing. Zombies, Backstabs and general mysteries one must find to get the true ending.
Here's the kicker though. I finished my first playthorough and got the S ending. Soooo... I got the best ending in the game on my first try. At least with the other games, It was a LITTLE harder. At least the game lasts though. Lots of content and lots of things to do with lots of fun even though the last standoff is annoying.
Gameplay!: So... This game is significantly easier than the other Dead Rising games. Now you'll most likely need to level up a lot to beat the game with the true ending but side missions pop up a lot, some zombies get you lots of points and going on a massive killing spree gets you TONS of points. Leveling up is pretty easy and if played right, getting to the true ending should be pretty easy.
The survivors in the game are a lot easier to manage and there aren't as many in the game as previous. Only 25 to be found. So easy easy all around. I myself have only died like... 3 times in the entire game.
So if you want a fun time creating wapon combos and killing zombies in fun ways, this game is for you.
Graphics!: So no doubt this game looks pretty nice. Characters look good, enviroments look good, weapon models look nice. Overall, not much wrong in the visual department.
I did have some problems though. Popin. There's a lot of it. Textures, items and zombies themselves have problems loading up sometimes. Other than that, everything looks nice. Especially the gore.
Overall: This game is alright. I think it's worth a sale price. Bought this for about 15 bucks and got more than my money's worth. It was a lot of fun and I'll be playing this game quite a bit more.
Just keep in mind, This is a pretty bad port and you'll need to do some messing around to get the game's 30 FPS cap off. Yyyyyep. 30 FPS cap. Not that I mind it myself but I know people like smoother framerates.

A masterpiece from a bygone age of quality RPGs. Unfortunately, the genre as a whole has been made simpler and easier to understand for the general masses. As a result, none of the new games in the series (or the genre as a whole) really deliver what a true RPG should be (there are a few exceptions, but I'm speaking generally). Sigh..they just don't make them like they used to.
To any new players who are used to newer RPGs, it's confusing as hell at first, but if you read the manual and do some occasional internet searches in order to understand the game and its mechanics, you will have a blast. (The manual is in the files for the game. Go in the steam folder, then steamapps, common, Fallout 2, then it's in the folder named MANUAL.)
If you want to have a quality RPG experience with a solid world, plenty of lore, interesting characters and limitless freedom, do yourself a favor, get Fallout and Fallout 2.
Also, quick sidenote: If you've read the negative reviews, you've probably read that the combat is painfully slow if there are >4 combatants. This is true. When you open up the game, go into the options, and find where it says "Combat Speed" and increase it drastically. You will thank me.

This game is interesting, engaging and well thought out. The gameplay itself is fun, first it teaches you the basics of each weapon, you then fully disassemble and reassemble the weapon, followed by trying out it's features (including adding silencers, grips and other addons). The 'game' becomes a real game on the aptly named 'game mode' where you are challenged for taking apart and reassembling the gun in as little time as possible, gaining achievements for doing so in certain times or by only clicking items that can be removed at that point.
The only issues I have with the game, is that sometimes parts that clearly should be able to go together at any point (like grips, or other minor parts that are not obstructed) will refuse to do so, and also cost you the 'sniper' achievement, or ruin your 'supergame'. An additional problem is the massive grind required to unlock further weapons. Whilst there is the ability to buy 'lifetime access' this gives no indication of what it actually unlocks, and is massively overpriced. If it were round £15 or even £20 I'd consider getting it, but for the moment your likely best spending your money on other games.
Gameplay: 8/10
Cost: (free 7/10 - with lifetime access 2/10)

This game has a LOT of potential. After playing for an hour and a half, reaching level 16, I decided to write a review on this game.
DISCLAIMER: I understand this is in Early Access and many things are subject to change.
My Experience: My experience with the game has been fun up until this point. I am happy with the skilltree system for both Survivor and Zombie. The weapon veriety for the current stage of the game is plentiful. With a few restrictions due to leveling but that's understandable. You don't want a level one running around with a sledgehammer, capable of wiping out several zombies with one swing, now do you? Players might, developers probably don't.
Pros: Okay, let's get to the positives of this game!
❂ Large veriety of weapons
❂Weapons being widely different from the previous
❂Not just one type of zombie, but two! The casual Walker and the Runner!
❂Bosses, one in particular made me waste too much time and thus failing the mission. (Some people may know which boss I am referring to)
❂The maps and game modes. Maps being vastly different from the others, each having it's own unique setting and missions.
❂Thugs! Human enemies that will shoot you regardless. Easier to kill... or are they?
Cons: Now to the negatives of the game :(
❂Reload animations. Some are okay such as the Famas reload, but the Barreta reload animation is sometimes infuriating to say the least. The way the player spins the gun around and taking so long to reload can define life or death for the player. I know there is a quick reload if you don't use the entire clip but if you're in a desperite need to kill the zombies and end up using all the ammo of the clip, the player just cares about spinning the dang gun instead of shooting the zombies about to kill him.
❂Death. Of course, this is a large part of a game such as this. Instead of dying (Reaching 0 hitpoints) You are greeted with a message on screen saying "You are now infected. Have a nice day". I don't mind the joke part but once you are infected, you have about 10 seconds before you magically turn into a zombie, throwing all your weapons on the ground. I personally don't like this as it doesn't seem fluent. Catapulting your guns forward when you die of a virus doesn't make sense but hey, it's a game, right? Hopefully something gets done over the death. Maybe dying fully and respawning as a zombie somewhere or giving the player the option to end his own life (Similar to No More Room in Hell.)
❂A.I. Now I understand AI programming can be difficult, but it needs some work. On the desert survival mission, some zombies were mounting the sandbags and being stuck there. I have no idea how they got there but they always got there whenever I came around. I don't understand. Some zombies may spin on the spot for less than a second trying to calculate it's path towards the player. Some of the pathing is good but some make the enemy look a bit silly. Not just the zombies, but the Military (As they are referred to in game) sometimes shoot the wall. In the first map, the two Military outside sometimes shoot the wall as the zombies are on the other side trying to get to them when in reality, the zombies are stood still on one side, the Military still on the other, trying to shoot them.
❂The Player. I understand the player has a skill tree to help develop the player with a play style but what irritated me the most was the fact that I had no sprint. Sure, you had a combat roll to help you dodge but what about a casual sprint? I'd be extremely happy if this feature were to be implimented.
❂The theme. I don't understand the theme at all. I am referring to the game thumbnail and menu screen. How does a military zombie survival game have anything to do with piano music/ sheet music? I can't say change it but please hint a theme.
Conclusion: Besides all of the negatives, I think this game is good overall and it has a lot of room for potential, I hope it doesn't all go to waste. I recommend this game if you and a friend are looking for a free game to have fun with.

I FREAKIN love the Deus Ex franchise and who can blame me? It revolutionized gaming as a whole especially FPS games and action RPG's. Naturally when I came into Deus Ex Human Revolution(which will now be referred to as DXHR because it's just way easier) I had a lot of expections and I'm happy to tell you all that the game delivered! The game takes an "have it your way" style approach with the diverse skill tree it gives you which is basically activating your cyborg augmentations(I get to that once I get to the story)giving you many challenging situations and even more ways to complete them. Are you the kind of guy who likes to go into battle guns blazing? Well then you should pick up the dermal armor and recoil reduce upgrades! Perhaps you would rather take a stealth approach, or you just want to hack a few security turrets to kill off your enemies for you, or even just punch a whole in a wall or climb through an airduct to avoid confrontation all together. This is one of the games biggest strenghts and what makes it all the more better is the fact that the developers put a ton of thought into level design and teach you the rules of the game very well that if you can think of a way to overcome obstacles there is a %99.99 chance that it could work should you execute your plan effectivley. Now right now I'm sure any of you who haven't played the game are drawing comparisons to another great "have it your way" kind of game, Skyrim. Well the key difference is that Skyrim focuses more on where you want to explore(it is open world after all) but doesn't provide to extreme variety in play styles or how you choose to play that kind of style. What I mean is that in DXHR you can be a very stealth oriented player, but not be confined to that style of play because the skill tree is very friendly to players and allows you easy access to the basic skills required for any play style. This even carries over to the boss battles,unfortunatley non directors cut players will be very limited when it comes to how you take down a boss. Rather sadly though this doesn't mean the boss abttles are great. They are by no means bad or terrible, but they can be a little, how you say, confining. As I said before the Directors cut gives you more options when it comes to battleing bosses. By that I mean it gives you 1 more option when in most other scenarios there are several options to take down the baddies. Not to mention I found the boss battles to be boring and kind of pointless other than being used for the story of course. I think I've spent enough time on gameplay at this point, how about we turn our attention to story?
DXHR packs an impressive story about Adam Jensen, Head of security for the BioAugmentation company Sarif Industries who used to be S.W.A.T but quit after being given a questionable order. He soon finds Sarif under attack by heavily augmented mercenaries who leave him for dead after brutally attacking him and scientist in one of Sarifs labs. He miracously survived at the cost of getting heavily augmented over the course of about 6 months I believe. This gives him access to every upgrade in the game, but his body needed time to naturally turn them one one at a time unlocking praxis points to spend on said augmentations as you gain expierence by completing quest, killing enemies ect. From here you follow several leads to find the mercenaries and where they fit in the bigger picture which takes you to places like, Detroit, China, and Montreal to name a few. There are also a lot of moral decisions to make through the story especially at the end giving you three tough options to choose between. Another nifty feature is conversations with branching dialouge options that actually have an effect on the game. For example early on in the game you are tasked with getting to a morgue in the local precicnt. You have the option of sneaking in, killing everyone(that strategy is not reccomended), or you can just talk the guard out to have him let you in. That's what I love about this game. It does so many interesting things with its gameplay that affect the story and vice versa. It makes the game unique and helps it to stand out from other games. In the end DXHR packs an impressive story into the mix too, but unfortunatley it doesn't show us the worts of it. When we hear about all of this gross things like harvesters who kidnap people to strip them of their augments and sell them we don't see that. It should have followed Blade Runners example and shown us everything. The last comment was made by Angry Joe in his review and I drew to the same conclusion and whole heartedly agree with what he said. Thankfully thought that is the only negative when it comes to the story.
As far is presentation goes the game looks and sounds fantastic. The soundtrack fits the futuristic theme quite well, the color palette consist mostly of gold and black, and the sound design in general all come together and fantastically emersed me into the games world. One small gripe I have with the graphics though is that facial animations are very stiff which doesn't do much for the wonderful looking game. Speaking of wonderful the backgrounds in the game look gorgeous and make the world all the more real. Also I forgot to mention voice acting so I'll do that now. All of the voice actors do an incredible job reading the scripteven Jensens voice actor although I found his voice to be a bit to raspy like Batmans but that is just a minor nitpick. Overall the game does incredibly well and stands up there is one of the best games I've played in a while which is why I'm glad to say Deus Ex Human Revolution earns an 8.5/10 it was worth the $60 dollar price line as it is but now that you can pick it up for $20 you'd be crazy not to pick it up.

Games commonly offer you a choice in whether you want to be good or bad. To go guns a blazing or to be a ghost seen by none. Often the way it is done is so obvious that the illusion of choice is broken. This is where this game shines. I was able to play the way I wanted to throughout. If I wanted to sneak around and crawl through grates to get through to the room I wanted I could. If I wanted to speak to someone and convince them to let me in, more often than not, I could. If I wanted to hack the door to let me in undetected I could. Those are only some of the ways that the developers  employ  in progressing through the game. There are some drawbacks however. During the bossfights you would have to exercise some sort of violence against your enemies. Otherwise, this game was a lot of fun. It wasn't just a polarizing good or bad story line but it felt like I could really choose my own path in this cyber punk world. This inlcludes the leveling system. No matter which way you go you'll find that there is no bad power. Although it's old, I'm glad I gave it a chance.

To start off, i have nearly 700 hours (or more) depending on how accurate steam stats are, on Paladins. This game has been one of my favorites ever since i heard about it. It was a fun, exciting, and FREE to play game with harmless cosmetic microtransactions. Honestly, i havnt had this much interest in a game since probably halo 2 or 3. Through my time playing ive spent probably around $100 on this game from buying the founders pack, account boosters, gems, and skins, which at the time was well worth it to support a game which i loved.
Then, the news broke, Patch OB64 was on its way. Now ive had some dissagreements with previous patches like anyone would, but OB64 came in at a whole new level. The backlash started during the live patch preview reveal, and has gained momentum ever since. The patch was pushed back a week further than they usually are to allow for Hirez to "listen to the community feedback". This was a joke. Even after every big content creator and the forums were flooded with "dont release this it will ruin the game" Hirez  released a statment that said they were commited to these changes.
For those unfamiliar with these changes, they include but are not limited to crazy broken champion skills, numbers on loadout cards that just got astronomically high, a change to the loadout system (which was working just fine imo), differences in loadouts across comp/casual play, rediculous grinding sytems (even if you have everything maxxed out before the patch goes live), and implementation of pay to win tactics.
It sickens me that i even have to write a review like this. I LOVED this game prior to the OB64 announcement, and trusted Hirez as a company who listened to its players. I felt like i always had a voice before this patch, but it was all turned upside down very quick. As i am writing this review, OB64 still has yet to have a release on the live servers but from what ive seen so far, the community cant do much to stop it. I hope that Hirez will learn from their mistakes and take the community input a little more seriously as time goes on. As of now, i reluctantly plan to quit and uninstall the game in its current state. I know for a fact that many others are doing the same. I have no doubt that ammendments will be made sometime in the future but untill then, myself, and the other 7,100 players who have signed the petition against OB64 via
will not support the game. Once Hirez realizes what theyve done, may be too late as a game like this revolves around its playerbase.
Yours truly,

BlazBlue: Calamity Trigger was ported over to the PC might be due to that the Games For Window Live version might be shutting down soon. But this was also done to see that if Arc System Works could port future titles to the PC. I'll cut to the chase right now. If you never played BlazBlue and you have a hunch for 2D Fighting games like Street Fighter then I highly reccomend BlazBlue: Calamity Trigger. Though if you already played this game before then there is no reason to go back into this port. But for Newcomers Calamity Trigger is Highly reccomened.
Developed by the people who made the wonderful Guilty Gear titles BlazBlue was basically the first real HD title to be devolped by Arcs. The game features 12 Characters all hand drawn and they look amazing. The fighting system uses four buttons and it easy to do stuff like quarter circle moves here and there. But if you really want to get most out of the game then practice you're combos well. Also I highly reccomened starting off with the beginner friendly characters like Ragna, Jin and Noel. Once you master thoes characters you can always move on to the other characters. As there is a steeper learning curve for the rest of cast like V-13, Haku-Men, Iron Tager, Litchi, Rachel and a few more. Also just about all of the characters play different from eachother as nobody has the same fighting style. Plus BlazBlue comes with a Super Deep storyline for a fighting game. It will keep you busy for quite sometime and the branching paths make everything awesome. The presentation is all anime style and if you're a fan of that you'll love the art. Music is also incredible with a Heavy Metal style soundtrack. The soundtrack for me is the biggest highlight of the game.
Also if there is one major nitpick with the PC version is that there is no online. Which is quite dissapointing for some of us to thoes who want to test there skills across the world. Hopefully a patch will come soon for an online. Overall BlazBlue: Calamity Trigger is a great fighting to really get into. Though if you already played this game before on consoles like Xbox 360 or Playstation 3 and the Windows version there isn't anything to make you head back to it. Plus the lack of online may turn some people off. But overall this a high quality fighting game that can sit and join the ranks on titles like Super Street Fighter IV: Arcade Edition and Mortal Kombat. If you never played the game support this games release and pray for future BlazBlue games  like Continuum Shift or if were ever lucky Chrono Phantasma... But lets we get more of these titles.

*If you're running windows 8.1 and game doesn't start!*
-Google, download, and install:  Microsoft Visual C++ 2005 Redistributable x64
-Go into Settings (move mouse into top right corner of screen), PC Info, Advanced Settings.
-Click "Settings" in Performance section.
-Click "Data Execution Prevention" Tab
-Make sure "Turn on DEP for all programs and services except those i select" is selected.
-Click "Add" and look for the executable file for the game and add it. Usually located in the in your C drive under something like "Program Files (x86)/Steam/Steam Apps/Common/BlazBlue Calamity Trigger.
-Click apply after adding the executable file to the list and you should be good to go. For extra measure, look for the executable file and run it as administrator.

To begin here is how I had the game working on WINDOWS 8.1 followd by my review.
Initialy I had trouble getting this to work. My solution:
When the FreeSpace Launcher starts, click 'setup' then 'Detect Available Cards' and ensure the 'Primary Display Driver' is selected. Try clicking 'Play FreeSpace' and see if it works. If this doesnt work you will probably have to restart.
If it didnt work repeat what you did then bring up 'Task Manager' (control,alt & delete) find 'FreeSpace Launcher' under name.  Right click on it and bring up 'Properties' then click on 'Compatibility' Tab at the top. Tick the box that says 'Run this program in compatibility Mode For:' and select Windows XP (Service Pack 3). Apply the settings and then click 'Play FreeSpace' on the Launcher.
For me this worked. If this didnt work then try running the Compatibility Troublshooter.

The Basics:
This game is a space sim - this means you pilot fighters or bombers in the theatre of space.
You CAN play this game with a mouse and keyboard, it will be improved with a joystick or gamepad but its more than playable without.
The game purchased on Steam includes the Expansion Pack 'Silent Threat'
I believe the game was released in 1998 although the graphics were amazing then they are obviously dated now. However not to the point of hampering my enjoyment.
A Classic. The game tells a truly gripping story of a desperate fight for survival. Every story needs a good antagonist and this is no exeption, a mysterious and ruthless enemy await you. What this game really shines at is it makes you feel super involved with intense against the odds battles.
New technologies arent just thrown at you theyre introduced intwined with the story and discussed in briefings everything feels like it had reason behind it.
The ship designs are nice, if not a little limited by the technology of the time.
The Controls are simple and easy to grasp however as i pointed out before will be improved if you have a joystick or gamepad.
The mission briefings are great and sound Authentic and the missions themselves offer enough variety and unpredictability to keep your attention. The whole game makes you feel involved & has a great storyline, a definate for the oldies that prefere a riveting story and great gameplay.
This game has been a favorite of mine since childhood. It has stood the test of time, meaning its still fun to play and the classic graphics style is not a distraction.
