Short version:
The story is amazing, the gameplay/interface is just outstanding (but you *need* a controller imo), the characters are well done, the voice acting is high quality, and to top it off the music is some of the best I've heard in a video game. In fact, I'd say the music is *the* best. Get this game. I think it's a must have experience for any gamer.
Long version (very basic plot info included):
Great setting for the story. You're basically fighting in an endless proxy war on a desolate Earth between AIs created by humans and robots created by alien invaders, except that neither humans nor aliens have shown themselves in hundreds of years. You play as a couple of the AIs fighting on the side of humanity against the evil mindless robots, but it soon becomes apparent that things aren't quite as you've been told when you're sent down to earth and start seeing things firsthand. There are many huge mysteries and plot reveals in the game (each more mindblowing and tragic than the last) as you work through all 3 playthroughs, yet the game still leaves just enough unanswered questions that leaves you thinking about it long after you have completed it.
The side quests are really well done and they add some perfect touches to the game. Aside from the first couple of "tutorial" quests, there are essentially no pointless collect a bunch of these things or kill a bunch of those dudes quests. They are all meaningful and really add to the richness of the story. Some are about funny little endeavors and ways in which the robots try to mimic humans (an underlying theme in the game; what does it mean to be human?) while others are heartbreaking tragedies that would be unique to an AI/robot.
This was my first Yoko Toru game but it's clear why people say his games are masterpieces. The story and characters are truly well done in this game. You can't help but feel for every single one of them. I even went back to play the first Nier in the middle of playing this one to get more of the history of this world because the game just left me craving that knowledge.
To elaborate on the battle a bit, it's all in real time, it runs smoothly and not clunky at all. You really have to practice this game if you want to get good enough to play in the harder modes though! The boss battles are also really fun and creative as well as challenging. This game is not super heavy on the combos compared to some other JRPGs, but it's still very fun to try and master the game and beat harder bosses on the more difficult modes. You still have to really work at it to play flawlessly.
Back to the music. It's not your typical video game music. It's better and more thought out than the music in most movies to be honest. Aside from being well done and good quality, it's packed with emotion, excitement, tragedy and I think you really feel what the creators want. It sets the mode for each situation or boss battle (some of which are tragic) just perfectly. Often I found myself going back to certain areas just to listen to a particular song. In the end I just put the soundtrack on my phone and it's my favorite one yet.
One problem: As far as I'm aware, the developers still haven't patched the game properly since releasing it for PC. You can't play it in full screen without downloading the fan made patch. On top of that, some computers also experience performance issues with this game. Personally, I downloaded the patch and never had a single performance issue or crash.
Other thoughts:
-Despite the less than top notch graphics that some people criticize, I still thought the game was quite beautiful. Some of the scenery was just amazing and works quite well with the themes in the game.
-No farming is necessary (at least not on hard mode)! The only time it comes up is when you are going for certain achievements and you can do those after beating the game in chapter select mode.
-For those who like to make choices that affect the outcome of the game, there isn't much of that. However, it's not that kind of game... Personally, I think that the story is good enough to where I don't care if I can change a bunch of outcomes. The writers are telling you a story and you're playing through it as it unravels. Though there are different many different endings which are great to play/watch.

Recommended generally for men - or anyone who likes cute anime girls attempting to be sexy - who wants to take a decent tour of different sights in Japan.  There's also a few bits of history as well, most of which would be suitable for folks who really don't know much about Japanese history.  The background music varies from great to muzak, depending on what location or scene you're at.
I will agree with the person who wrote that the protagonist was awed by some of the most basic technological things.  It may be that the technology shown has only recently caught up with us here in the States.  He also acts rather overly macho at some points and outright dumb at other points, even moreso than most of the male protagonists I've seen in other VN's.
One thing that I haven't seen a lot of mention of is when you are touring certain locations, there is a "Show Photo" button on the bottom right of the screen.  When you click on it, it will show you a photo of the area via Google Maps.  I thought that was really neat and was able to see a lot of photos of real places that awed me, especially the different shrines!
The two sisters themselves were written fairly well, although Akira's mood seemed to change quickly enough where I started wondering if she was bipolar.  The romance with younger sister Akira seemed a bit too forced and sudden, while the romance with the older sister Makoto was better-crafted IMHO.  The cute anime girls' "nude" and "panty" shots were more hilarious than erotic.  While it may not REALLY be an "All Ages" game per se, there's no nipple or nudity that would go beyond a "PG-13" rating if this were a movie.
I would recommend this as a light-hearted break from some of the more dramatic Visual Novels.  It's a quick story (I completed both scenarios in less than 4 hours) and it serves as an entertaining way to access some of the basic history of the more popular tourist areas of Japan.

In terms of length, quests, items, NPCs...Fallout 2 definitely is a step above the previous game. The only reason I have the amount of hours spent on this game is because I started over twice with the same character and build (I am playing this on my gaming laptop that runs Windows 8.1 and I have experienced the occasional corrupted save file). I have completed everything except the final end quest and have just been grinding to get to the max level of 99 so I can easily take on not just the final boss but all of the Enclave on the oil rig. Even though you can continue to play the game after the final quest and receive a book from Father Tully in New Reno that instantly increases all your skills to max % and gives you 10k xp per use.
Even with the mods installed, don't expect some up-to-date HD remaster with a new engine. It is all within the confines of the engine that the game comes with. It pretty much looks no different from the first Fallout graphics wise.
The characters and voice acting are top notch, especially for a game made in the 90s. The story and writing are what you expect from Interplay/Black Isle Studios, who would later create Fallout Van Buren aka the original upcoming Fallout 3 before Bethesda bought the franchise. Black Isle's members to include Chris Avellone would later found Obsidian, who made New Vegas (and another personal favorite RPG of mine: Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic 2 The Sith Lords). Hence the good writing and classic RPG elements. Some examples of the game's good characters and voice acting include: Sulik, Marcus, Myron, Lynette, Harold, Tandi, and Dornan. Those are just the talking heads as most NPCs are text only but if you like to read you can see the creativity behind the writing. I would rank Fallout 2 as the best (isometric) Fallout game.
Gameplay has not changed much from the first game. Still turn-based, relying on Action Points. At least you have a larger variety of weapons, armor, and perks. There are combat skills and weapons that are clearly superior to others however. Small Guns is the best for any beginning player, with the Gauss Rifle as the best weapon for you. Energy Weapons are nice once you already have your primary combat skill at a high enough percentage. The Pulse Rifle is the best energy weapon. In terms of close combat, the Mega Power Fist does the most damage and does not have the annoying knockback that costs Action Points, so consider the Unarmed skill. Make sure to aim for the eyes for max critical damage. The best 2 non-combat skills would definitely be Speech and Lockpick, so tag these 2 along with a combat skill for your 3 tagged skills. If you want maximum access to rooms, loot, and options to dialogue/quests, invest in Lockpick and Speech. Make sure to reload between fights if you use a weapon that consumes ammo or between turns if you have the AP. I play on Normal difficulty and it can be hard at the early levels. Beware of: Fire Geckos, Wanamingos, Deathclaws, Floaters, Centaurs, Mercenaries, Super Mutants, Robbers, and Enclave Patrols. If you have a high Luck, Outdoorsman skill, or related perks you can avoid random encounters entirely or run into Easter Eggs. The game is full of pop culture references to other franchises in the form of encounters, items, characters, dialog, etc. There are too many to list but Star Trek and Monty Python come to mind.
Due to the way the game is designed it can be annoying when clicking on things since everything is small on screen and of course the graphics are of limited resolution. Also, when you are behind a wall, it only makes it transparent in a circle around your character rather than making the whole wall transparent. For my birthday a couple weeks ago, I got a Steam controller and, almost as nice, $40 in Steam gift cards. Of course, the February Steam sale had just wound up, so my Wishlist went from everything on massive sale to nothing on sale, so I am still holding out for some good deals.
But I hooked the fancy Steam controller to my Windows PC and gave it a test drive. It's main claim to fame, as you can see from its picture, is that instead of a right joystick, it has something like a mousepad. You run your figure over it and the mouse pointer moves. There's a bunch of the usual buttons, including a couple on the inside bottom of the hand holds. It even has a gyroscope, like the Playstation Dual Shock. It feels good in my rather big hands and was pretty responsive.
But to be honest, I didn't really see the point after a bit. Even its biggest proponents, like GamerMuscle below:
says it works "almost as good as a keyboard and a mouse" in an FPS like Counter Strike. So why wouldn't I just use a keyboard and mouse? And for games that work with controllers, like say the Lara Croft games, the right joystick is hardly replaced very well by the mouse pad. The control is far more sporadic and hard to control, and I'd rather just use my wired Xbox controller. So what's the point?
But I found out the point when I used my birthday $50 Amazon gift card to pick up the
Now this is a nice piece of hardware with an obvious and single-minded devotion to do one thing and do it right - "mirror" your Steam PC experience on your TV. Plug it into my Ethernet network (wired works much better than wireless) and my home theater via HDMI, run Steam on a PC on the network, and boom - it finds Steam running and shows it on my 55" TV in Big Screen mode. Very nice.
But the Steam controller takes to all to another level. What makes it all possible, nay even exciting? The nearly limitless configurability of the Steam controller. There are all kinds of cool ways you can set it up, and use a custom setup for each game. So this makes it possible to play nearly any game with just the Steam controller, all wirelessly from the comfort of your couch. In this case, "nearly as good" becomes "this is way better", when you are settled into your couch, playing the game on the big screen.
I've tried a bunch of different games this way and have come away impressed. Luckily, most of the games I've tried have Community Templates that work pretty well. I've played games like Dirt 3 (a very fun rally game), The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing(a top down action RPG, a la Diablo 3), and even an old fashioned turn based RPG like Knights Of The Old Republic. They all work pretty well, and I haven't even tried to customize the control schemes much.
But, barring some fancy configuration (which is entirely possible - the config possibilites are amazing!), I am not sure the controller makes much sense at the computer. Keyboard and mouse, or the wired Xbox controller, still seem to be the way to go and the Steam Controller doesn't (yet?) replace either of them while I'm at my computer.
But if you combine it with a Steam Link, and sit back on your couch, then it makes a lot of sense. It works way better than trying to play with a mouse and keyboard on the couch (even a wireless one!), and it has configuration options that puts a normal Xbox controller to shame. And maybe, just maybe, with all the fancy configurations, it might even replace at least the Xbox controller on my computer and, more unlikely, the keyboard / mouse.
So I can't (yet) recommend the Controller for just computer playing. But if you use it with Steam Link (which I do highly recommend for its specific solution to a specific problem of playing Steam on your TV), man, it is just perfect. I'm going to give it a thumbs up, because it does work well in certain situations and I think the future is still very bright.

I want to describe more about this game to you, but I really can't go into too much detail without spoiling some good stuff for you. Here are some bullet points that played into my thumbs up review:
I kid you not, this story line had me going from "MEH RPG Overhyped bleh, to like, Woah, WTF is going on?".

Like I said before play this with a wired xbox 360 controller, also install the "FAR" mod as it will get rid of the annoying cursor that appears if you like to use borderless windowed mode. Link is here (
) I used the SKM from Github. NOTE THAT THE FAR MOD DOES NOT CHANGE ANYTHING GAMEPLAY WISE, IT JUST HELPS WITH PERFORMANCE ALOT.
My reasoning for you to use a controller is this:
It makes the dodge and counter mechanics easier. With the controller you press one button to dodge or move the joystick towards your enemy when they swing to counter / parry their attack when they swing at you. Also you're drone shooting is important as it can shoot down projectiles headed to you, this is on a bumper button and is easily held down when you need it.
Where as on the computer, the dodging is hotkeyed to double-tapping WASD (depending on direction of desired dodge) and can get annoying (It can be reassigned). There is a auto-hotkey script out there that can make a dedicated button a dodge button, so you infinitely dodge (Like holding CTRL). If you want to you can totally make it work with the Keyboard and mouse, but you have to tinker and work with the controls for quite a bit, which is why I suggest you use a controller so you don't get upset on that early on like I did initially.
I played this on a computer with an 1st gen  i7- 930 processor (2.8 Ghz) , 780 GTX, and 24 GB or Ram and it wasnt too bad of a experience, but your milage may vary. I see people on here complaining, but I didn't have much of an issue playing it vanilla the first time.
One thing I didn't like is the fact that there were lyrics to songs during town areas that threw me off because I was trying to read text, while at the same time listen to the music, I turned down the music a bit more to mitigate this though.
It has a weird part, you'll know it when you get to it.. It made me wonder about my purchase, but after you get past it, it makes more sense.
The other is that I don't get why the characters make the "Nnyygaahh" or "Gaahh" noise when they have a reaction to some things, it reminded me of Hank Hill's "BWwlllaaahhaa" Reaction to things. It didnt bother me, I just laughed at it alot.
Con rant over

For the price this is offered at, it is a must buy for beat em up lovers! Blazblue is a great fighting game that utilizes fast pace combo usage. Blazblue: Calamity Trigger, for those that don't already know (& most would know), is a fighting game that is basically a spiritual successor to Guilty Gear (series). All in all this game does have great music visuals, etc. In my opinion it does serve as a great alternative to other fighters, be it the Stret Fighter or MK series, if you're somewhat tired of those (not that they're bad by any means, but variety does help).
My issues with this game are relatively minor & can be largely overlooked. For starters, multiplayer is limited to local multiplayer, so if you have no one around that's willing to play, you're stuck playing against the AI. Secondly, as someone who predominately played fighters like the MK series, Street Fighter series, etc., & not so much the BlazBlue or Guilty Gear series, the learning curve seemed to be somewhat steep in terms of learning characters' mov lists. Lastly, & although I do not know if I should credit the game with this issue or it lies with my computer, but I did notice some slowdown. The fights' speed seemed akin to the pre-Turbo version of Street Fighter II. For the time being I'm giving Blazblue: Calamity Trigger the benefit of the doubt & placing the blame on my computer.
All in all, this game is fun, even with faults. Is it worth $9.99? Well the generic answer is yes, especially if you're a fighting game afficionado, a fan of Guilty Gear, and/or want alternatives/variety.

also goes for Fallout 2, which took everything that made Fallout great and made it bigger, better, more complex, allowing even more solutions to quests and dialogue checks. Here the history of the Fallout universe was fleshed out in ways that remain essential to this day. Whereas Fallout was shrouded in mystery and uncertainty, Fallout 2 explored the darkest corners of the post-nuclear world, unafraid to face what lurked in them. In fact it often laughs in the face of the most morbid and dark situations. It was a game for mature audiences in a decade when most games were still trying to be accessible to everyone.
The companions are one of the best improvements: whereas Fallout only had four companions and the interactions with them were very limited (mostly talking pack-mules), Fallout 2 offers a total of fourteen recruitable companions with great mechanics of interaction and combat control, which would resurface in Fallout: New Vegas with further refinement. In fact, the way companions work in Fallout 2 is the basis for the brilliant character development that New Vegas would offer many years later. Two of the companions even have their own talking heads, with some very decent facial animation for the technology of the time.
The possibility of rebuilding a nuclear-powered car is also a great improvement. Travelling in the wasteland can often be a nuisance, especially when you just want to get to your destination. With the Highwayman you can usually skip over encounters and get from A to B much faster. The trunk is also very useful to stash your loot. The best part is that it's not easy to get the car, not like when you get the first power armor in Fallout 4: it's not just handed to you, you have to work for it, do some quests, find ways to improve it and so on, which makes it much more rewarding when you finally hit the road.
While it may seem a bit silly at first, the saga of the Chosen One makes tribalism in the post-nuclear world very compelling and unique. On the surface, what starts as a very long fetch quest becomes in fact a saga that makes perfect sense in the grand scheme of the game, especially when you get to the Enclave Oil Rig. It's an indictment of the very foundation of the United States government, and this was five years before the invasion of Iraq.
It is also full of whacky moments and plot twists that later would be poorly imitated. From talking Deathclaws to Chinese computers; from a porn studio to a midget who call you a Mad Max wannabe; several instances of characters breaking the fourth wall, and so on. The combination of very dark and adult themes mixed with some very silly jokes is something very unique to this game: it includes an actual Easter egg as an item that does nothing at all.
This is not a game for everyone. Automobilista is the successor/upgrade to the underrated but great Game Stock Car Extreme. With it you get more content (all made to Reiza's great standards), a better menu than its predecessor, and new features to the ISI engine like track rubbering (in early stages) and tyre flatspotting!

Simple Review:
I gave one to my 8 year old daughter, who up till now did all her PC gaming with an XBOX 360 controller. Her initial response was, "It's kind of big".
We spent a day playing through all her favorite games (Castle Crashers, Dungeon Siege 3, Grow Home, Goat Simulator, and Risk of Rain) and no matter what kind of game it was she was able to play effortlessly with the Steam Controller. She even managed the 3D games better than what the dual analog sticks allowed her before.
At the end of it all she now prefers the Steam Controllers. I like them a lot, but I was worried they'd be too big of a jump (with the touchpads) for her but she needed no instruction and picked them up intuitively.
+1 to smart design that even an elementary school child can grasp and understand.

I've always, *always* had a terrible time using controllers. I've been a dyed-in-the-wool PC gamer since PC games became A Thing (before that, I used joysticks with my Atari system - that should date me sufficiently.) At my ripe age, learning2controller has always resulted in frustration and broken windows as I throw controllers through them. I bought the Steam Controller with the mad, naive hope that maybe... juuuust mayyyybe... I could learn how to use it.
And?
It's not bad. :) It's an ongoing process, but after about 8 or so hours using it with Subnautica, Minecraft, and a couple of other low-intensity games, I kind of like it. I still have to think about what I'm doing, especially if the game in question isn't really designed for controller support, but the right touchpad works better for me than another joystick has in the past.
I really like being able to quickly and easily download community-created configs, and changing things up wtihin them and saving my own is very simple. I still have a long way to go, but that's my issue, and not the hardware's.
It's comfortable to hold, too - the contours feel natural. The plastic isn't the highest quality, but neither is it the lowest. The buttons have good tactile feedback, and the haptic feedback is very configurable. I really love having two extra buttons on the bottom of the grips for things like jumping or crouching.
Good stuff - thank you, Steam!

From a person who hasn't played this type of strategy game in a long time, this is a lot of fun.
Scale: 1=despised 2=negative 3=could go either way 4=positive 5=loved
Game design: 4/5  It functions.  Things aren't polished, there's a lot of features that we hope to see included, and control limitations take a little getting used to, but it functions, and it's fun.  You play the aliens, invading from another planet, you fight humans, who are also invading from another planet, I guess.  Gather resources, build your base, trade up your inventory, explore, and conquer.  Some simple formulas done properly to give you great gameplay value.
Now the game has tutorials: personally I liked it better without them.  I liked being able just to play the game.  You got attacked in your base in the first 2 minutes of game play?  That's the tutorial.  Worked great for me.  Had some questions about what actions you should prioritize, but learning that is the bulk of the enjoyability of this type of strategy game, and it's not hard to figure out by experimentation.  So it's a great game if you actually like to learn while you play games rather than obliviously carrying out instructions and quests.
Tone: 4/5 Simple style, kind of cartoony.  I like that.  Night time is even kind of creepy the first couple times.  Kind of like first play through of Minecraft creepy, but less impending doom.  There's even hints of a developing story taking place.  I sure hope that gets implemented more in the future!
Personal skew: 2/5 I haven't played this type of game in a long time, and cartoon-y-ness doesn't ruin my emersion.  These are pros for me.  Beyond that you still have a stable game that will bring quite a bit of fun if you are into casual strategy.

A neat little rogue-lite brawler.  Lots and lots of achievement-type challenges to accomplish as you play, which in turn unlock new things in the game such as customizable heads, additional damage, or changed properties of certain attacks.  Lots of weapons and items to experiment with, and a nice mix of enemy types to fight.  The online co-op really makes it shine, though it's quite a challenge staying out of your partner's way at times, since friendly fire (while not damaging) can interrupt your friend's attacks and movement, or knock them off cliffs and kill them.
It's short for a rogue-lite, but long for a brawler.  Expect a successful playthrough on Normal to run you about an hour or more.  Good in short bursts.  Also I liked that there's equally many appearance options for both male and female characters, with no gameplay differences between them.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution isn't easy to fit into a specific genre. It could probably be best described as Stealth-Action-FPS-RPG. For it being such a genre mix, it's a brilliant game. The following points should elaborate why:
- The theme and story are unique (the original Deux Ex was pretty much a novelty when it comes to subject matter and setting). I especially like that there is not really a clear 'good guys' and 'bad guys' contrast, especially the in the end you are faced with fundamental ethical questions. The game offers both tragedy and humour which is always nice and refreshing.
- The game actually rewards you for being stealthy and not killing everything and everyone hostile you meet. If you don't set off the alarm, remain undetected for an entire segment, headshot people, or even only sedate them using non-lethal weapons, you get experience bonuses helping you to unlock upgrades quicker. The cover/stealth system works really well too, the game goes into 3rd person when in cover and remains 1st person when you are normally walking around.
- The voice acting is very solid to brilliant (the main character has about the sexiest sounding male voice ever).
- Cutscenes and scripted events do occur but not to the point where it feels that control is exaggeratingly taken away from the player. Also the cutscenes are (afaik?) not rendered with the in-game engine. Running everything on max settings @ 60fps, I have to say that the game itself actually looks better than the cutscenes, kek.
- For an RPG it is linear, but not incredibly linear by any means. The story is the same for everyone (with the exception of the end, expect a Mass Effect 3 kind of ending, but not quite as infuriating, don't worry), though the levels are often very open and offer several ways to the objective. On top of that, there's two fairly large hub areas that offer extensive free-roaming and looking for sidequests. The hubs are pretty much open-world-RPG-kind-of-open.
- The sidequests are not exactly numerous, but well written and diverse. There's not many, but at least all of them are good, no fillers to be seen.
- The dialogue system reminded me of the Mass Effect wheel. Different answers actually lead to different outcomes. Sometimes you might fail to reason with a person and the story may continue slightly differently or you could fail a sidequest.
Overall the game manages to marry together every important aspect of a videogame quite well; an interesting theme and story, a solid combat system, good stealth mechanics, convincing voice-acting, decent use of cutscenes and scripted events, looks and an amazing soundtrack (I actually DLed it to my phone and listen to it regularly). I would recommend this game to about everyone who has even the slightest interest in RPGs with a touch of shooter and stealth elements.

I've been a huge fan of the Dead Rising series ever since the first one hit the scene back in 2006 on Xbox 360 and though partaking of the zombie apocalypse has always been fun, it's never been this fun, or easy!!
Seriously, it's easy...WAY EASY.  Maybe not on Nightmare Mode (which I didn't do), but on one of the normal play modes with someone else (co-op) or kickin' it solo, DR3 is vastly easier than earlier installments in the series.  Why is that, well here are some examples: saving people is no longer the main focus of the story and though you can occasionally string along a survivor or two for assistance during a mission, most of the survivors you do save are merely trapped on top of a wrecked vehicle in random locations and you only need to A) kill the zeds in the immediate vicinity to save the survivor and B) you don't need to lead them back to a safehouse; the combo weapons are crazy awesome this time around, there are lots of them and you can even make super combo weapons by combining an already crafted weapon w/ another craftable item or additional combo weapon; the leveling system is still in effect and as you increase your skillset by unlocking new moves and abilities - namely increased inventory slots and health - you'll find that this time around your means of fighting back are not only better/more powerful but you can now fall from 50ft and lose only 1 health tick/bar...er...square.
Besides that above and despite the fact that the game world in DR3 is larger than both DR/DR2 combined, it's also never been easier to get around as there are many vehicles throughout the environment (and unlike in DR2, there's no need to save $1,000,000+ to buy a key to use some of them as money doesn't factor into DR3) and you can now make combo vehicles w/ added features/durability. Rollerhawg...nuff said! (ok, I can't help it: BEST VEHICLE IN A GAME EVER!!).
Sure, there are some rough edges w/ graphics at times and how certain objects are rendered/processed as the game plays out, but assuming you have some NASA hardware backed by military-grade networking capabilities to run DR3 smoothly w/ high settings, you'll find your zombie killing experience quite enjoyable.  The voice acting is pretty good, there's still a lot of humor (the banana hammock w/ a gringoe stache and pigtails combo + a 'massager' makes for an amusing time) and the psycho peeps you'll face are still....well, psycho of course. The DLC stories (the untold stories) are good too, though a little redundant if you do them back to back while doing all side missions therein.
If you're worried that you may not be able to play this game w/ your current PC setup, get it when it's on sale or you can always request a refund.  But if you're a Dead Rising fan, don't pass this one up!

I have to admit, when I bought this game I was expecting to be annoyed by some glaring issue that would have made it almost unplayable. Thankfully I was wrong and was treated to another solid entry in the Dead Rising franchise. If you're a fan the series or just want to blow off some steam killing thousands upon thousands of zombies then I can't recommend it enough. Just make sure your potato can run it mind you!
Dead Rising 3 is set in the post zombie outbreak city of Los Perdidos (Which I am convinced is just Los Angeles.) where we assume the control of one Nick Ramos. Nick is then presented with a tutorial and a couple of token introductory tasks that do a good job of teaching the player how to play in a relatively short time. After the tutorial you are given access to the city in all its destroyed, flaming, ruined, zombie-filled glory to explore as you see fit.
Some neckbeard guy gives our Nick little tips and leads on side missions over the radio, but really it's up to you as the player to decide how to use the six days you have before the city is nuked to oblivion. This is where you get to the meat and potatoes of the game, the environment and the range of tools at your disposal. Want to grab a gun and use it to kill some zombies? Sure, why not. How about a Katana or Machete? Great. How about duct taping those two blades together to make a twinblade style weapon with an awesome moveset, more damage and more durability? Oh yeah, combo weapons are back and better than ever. I could write a freaking bible on just how awesome most of them are, but you should really discover the joys of crafting these implements of death for yourself.
Unlike Chuck/Frank from DR2/OTR our boy Nick can craft combo weapons on the fly, no workbenches here! Another neat little addition to the crafting system is the combo vehicles. Combo. Vehicles. The first one is a motorcycle... WITH A STEAMROLLER AS ITS FRONT WHEEL! Not only that but it has a couple flamethrowers tacked onto the sides because why not? The combo vehicles are a great addition and really add another layer of depth to the game, especially in co-op mode.
Grab a buddy and you can double the fun. You can share your gear, mount vehicle turrets while your buddy drives, hit them in the face with what can only me described as Mjollnir... The possibilities are (almost) ENDLESS! Whats more is that any collectables found by one player will also unlock for the other no matter how far apart you are.
As a whole the game has plenty to offer and has enough replayability to have you come back from time to time. Be it leveling up, gathering collectables or just stress relief there's something for everyone... Who has some psychopathic tendancies.
Come for the zombies, stay for the... Well, zombies. I know I did!

World of Guns: Gun Disassembly. A simulation based around the assembly, disassembly, maintenance and operation of various types of firearms which allows the user to better understand the mechanics of firearms and teaches the user the proper method of stripping, disassembling and reassembling their firearm, as well as giving history and insight into the design and use of the gun. As a concept, it is a fantastic idea as it allows the casual gun interest to better understand, and therefor respect, the tool that they admire as well as allow the seasoned gun enthusiast or collector a means of virtually disassembling a firearm without risking damaging its real-life counterpart.
As a gun enthusiast and owner myself, I saw World of Guns: Gun Disassembly as the latter, a helpful tool. However, the sheer tedium of grinding one gun constantly to get to the next, only to grind that gun again, coupled with both the steep learning curve and steep price tag ($49.99 for "Lifetime Access", which grants access to all guns, structures, vehicles and skeletons) has put me off of this notion. While the potental for greatness is there, the severely misguided execution of World of Guns has left it floundering with the rest in a sea of shovelware and lost ideas.
Sadly, I must leave this simulation with a negative vote. I hope that, in the future, the developers of World of Guns will try to salvage this concept, as I firmly believe that it could be both a valuable tool for teaching the history of the gun as well as an invaluable tool in the workshop. But, until that day comes, this gets my thumbs down.
3/10. It could be something wonderful, but as of now it is simply shovelware

Okay, first things first. Blazblue is arguably my favorite fighting game ever. I've been a huge fan of the series since I first played this game on PS3. I currently own Blazblue Continuum Shift (EXTEND) on my PS Vita and it's one of my favorite games of all time. I am extremely excited to see this game released here on Steam!
However, I must be honest. As much as I love this game, this is a extremely straightforward port of the console versions. A Gamepad is a MUST to enjoy this game properly, as keyboard and mouse controls just don't work for fighting games of this sort. I am admittendly disappointed by the lack of online multiplayer. However, this version of the game does still support local co-op play. Perhaps even more impressive is the inclusion of the GAMES ORIGINAL SOUNDTRACK which is included with this Steam release. As Blazblue has one of the most impressive soundtracks in any video game, fighting or otherwise, this alone pretty much justifies the purchase unless you can track down the fairly elusive CD.
Blazblue is a traditional 2D Japanese fighting game with a emphasis on fast, dynamic combat and tactical strategy. The fighting is extremely dependent on precise timing and mastery of skills. There are several difficulty levels ranging from 'casual' to 'nightmarishly hard', and this allows players of all skill levels to jump in and enjoy playing the game. There is also a in-depth training mode which will walk you through each character's moveset and learn basic gameplay mechanics.
In addition, there is also a standard 'Arcade mode' in which you fight increasingly difficult opponents to win. A 'Story mode' which takes each character through their own unique storyline, and a 'verses' mode where you can challenge your friends in local co-op matches.
Blazblue: Calamity Trigger is a fantasic game and worthy of anyone's gaming collection. I recommend buying this edition if only for the elusive Offical soundtrack and it's a decent port of the console versions.
Highly recommended! (Unless you own one of the console versions...)

unfortunately, it is the original vanilla release of the game,
without online and without BGM in story-mode due to a bug.
With all that, is there any reason to buy this game?
If you haven't experienced the franchise, this is a cheap alternative.
The game is colorful and all around beautiful to look at,
the soundtrack is pure rocktastic bliss provided by Guilty Gear creator Daisuke Ishiwatari,
which you also get digitally with the steam release.
The gameplay is easy to pick up, much more so than its older sibling Guilty Gear
yet has plenty of depth to keep your attention.
The roster is, however small, largely unique within the world of fighting game archetypes,
and even when they follow specific archetypes, they always bring some fun tools to the table.
With online gone and the story-mode being somewhat broken,
your main timesink will go to the likes of training and arcade mode
(which shouldn't need explanation)
along with score-attack, a gauntlet of challenging opponents ending in a unique boss
that has to be beaten in one go or it's back to stage 1.
While you're better off buying the current newest incarnation,
Continuum Shift Extend if you want to seriously get into the series,
for this price, it's hardly a bad deal, just to get the unique series on the PC

Fallout 2 is a classic, a legend that stands amongst legends. This game is my go-to. I've owned probably 5 or 6 copies of it over the years, and whenever I find myself somewhere where Internet is scarce and my battery is a consideration, it never fails me. The equal of every great CPRG that came before it, and superior to most that came after it, this game has aged gracefully and still holds the charm it did when I first booted it up nearly 2 decades ago as a younger child.
You play as the Chosen One, a villager from a dying tribe who is sent on a quest to recover an ancient device rumored to turn dead wasteland into verdant fields: the Garden of Eden Creation Kit, or G.E.C.K. for short. This is not a new plot device, it is not terribly original to be the only man or woman in the world capable of saving your people/family/group. However, the
of this quest is what sets Fallout 2 apart, even from it's own successors.
You are given almost complete freedom to be anyone you want in this world. You can be a sociopathic killer, an opportunistic slaver, a drug-addled genius, or a savior to the common man and the tread upon. Your character, and how you are reacted to and perceived is entirely based on your choices.
As a top-down, or isometric, turn-based game, this is slower than most modern games. While dated by anyone's standards, the graphics serve their purpose with charm and readability; and more importantly it supports modern monitors, no patching required. There is a fan-made patch you can use that many will recommend, but I haven't tried it. Haven't felt I needed it.
There's next to no handholding, as the game will frequently murder you for taking on fights you couldn't handle, or frankly just for fun. RNG is a large factor here. However, the gameplay holds as true now as it did then. Plot your moves, mind your enemies, and bask in the glory of every hard-won battle - or at the very least, keep a recent save handy for those dire moments.
Enjoy ~

First off, ignore the 2H of playtime- I played this back in 2014 or so, when the launcher was a bit broken (wouldn't launch through Steam), and subsequently lost my account in the server wipe due to inactivity. With that said...
It's simply okay. The graphics are pleasing and the locations are interesting, but the combat is (in my opinion) rather boring, and the gameplay itself is repetitive. I wish it used a more "free form" combat system, like what you'd find in say, Avabel Online (mobile only), rather than the WoW/Xenoblade styled combat we've got. It got a bit grindy by the time I stopped playing, and I assume that only gets worse the further in the game you are.
It's optimized fairly well- I can't really talk about performance much because I'm using a very ill equipped machine, I had to stop playing in the city after the autumn area because of the frame rate being awful. No fault of the games, so I won't deduct points for that. For the machine it was played on with the graphical fidelity it carries, I'd say yeah, it's fairly well optimized, you'll want a decent CPU to play it though, as is the case with any MMO.
Overall, it's not a masterpiece, but it's free, and if you like anime art, there's no reason not to try it, unless you really hate combat systems like the one this carries. The aesthetic is honestly the main draw to it- the anime style it uses it quite nice, the rest of the game just kind of falls flat. Once again, at least it's free.

Well, after playing for 11 hours or so I feel I can give my early impression of the game.
Reiza have done an amazing job with an ageing graphics engine, it looks pretty good, better than stock car extreme and rFactor 1 (who's engine it's based on).
It runs at a high frame rate that you can limit in game, I have a 144hz refresh rate monitor so I limit it to that and it works well.
It drives very nicely and is a lot of fun, with the right car.
As it's from Reiza you get an awful lot of Brazilian tracks, which I'm not a huge fan of, prefering the classic European tracks, like Spa, Nurbergring, Hockenheim, Silverstone, etc.
The good news is that there are already some fantastic free tracks that have been produced, that are up to the standard of the publisher. These tracks, by Patrick Giranthon and his team, are first rate and look fantastic.
My only other gripe is that there are no GT3 cars, which are my favourites and far too many open wheelers, which I'm not keen on.
Having said that the modders have been busy and there's already a WTCC BMW to be downloaded free, which is an excellent drive.
If Reiza continue to update this game and release new content, and if the modders keep going I can see this game going from strength to strength.
One final word, the online is clunky (it was the last time I played). If this gets sorted that will be another plus point!

I'm enjoying this game very much. I had the previous game from Reiza Studios, Stock Car Extreme, and this game builds upon that game with more polish and more tracks, cars and the like. It's not a Forza or Project Cars type of game, with fantastic graphics. But the graphics are more than enough to support the racing and it also means it can run well on less than uber hardware.
The racing is very good. All the bells and whistles are there for setups. And there are a lot of options for control layouts. I use an X360 controller since I'm more of a causal racer and the game easily supports this. And the large number of different car classes means a player can find a number of different cars that appeal to you. And there is a whole range of assists so whether you are a newbie or a hardcore sim racer you can find the assist options that you prefer.
Finally, there is a healthy mod community already in place to support this game. There are already a zillion skins, several new cars and tracks and a bunch of other mods. And there is a good vetting system for these mods so you aren't downloading lots of dross hoping to find a bit of gold.

Isomer is an interesting mixture of surivial and basebuilding gameplay from games such as Dwarf Fortress combined with combat and exploration elements inspired by the Xcom series. The overall premise can be summed as reverse Xcom, you play as an alien force stumbling upon an already habited planet yet seeking to colonize never the less. Starting off with your humble dropship and ten workers, it is your job to survive and thrive in an hostile world. Overall in its inital steam release status, I'd say that Isomer is a very promising game. Currently I feel as though the foundations for a great base building and exploration are present though the content may be too barebones for some. So far I've noticed four diffrent unit classes, a wide array of generated structures for the player to explore and various different building blocks for the player to use. However the selection of middle and late game structures don't seem to be implemented. For example you can build your base to the extent of its layout with lights and lifts to different floors, but there are no doors present in the game nor any sizeable modules and things to fill up these rooms apart from soils to contain reasources.

I didn't play as long as I intended to, that being at least an hour, but I think I got a pretty good feel for the game.
Now, before I actually discuss the game, I would like the mention the fact that I played with different players, who all have said that the devs seem to be generally rude people. That said, I've not personally seen them, and this may be a case-by-case issue, but it seems a bit disappointing to see right off the bat.
In regards to the game, it does more wrong, than it does right.
Firstly, the combat in general feels...unfun. It doesn't seem as if you're fighting zombies, but instead as if you're fighting a group of people in GMod. Now, due to my short period of time before leaving a review, I didn't get around to playing PvP, but I would assume it's generally the same.
As well, the audio in the game is pretty bad, most notably the voice acting which consists of a total of maybe four lines, which also applies to the enemy bandits and friendly soldiers, who will constantly scream the same four lines time and time again.
The gun animations seem really high-quality, compared to the actual gameplay and other animation, which is both good and bad, due to the fact that I've managed to see numerous NPCs getting stuck in a T-pose while moving or trying to attack.
Overall, the game is okay, but it's not something I could recommend anyone play. If you're really in the mood for a good free to play zombie game, No More Room in Hell, or Zombie Panic Source are both very good choices and excel quite highly over this one.
Lastly, I see that a lot of the people leaving postive reviews are saying that "it's free to play so it's good", which is a pretty poor reason to suggest a game, seeing as there quite a bit of crappy F2P games on Steam.
Free is too high of a price.

Having only played the original old Deus Ex for a short bit,
and remembering it like it was "just another fps game",
i opened up Deus Ex: Human Revolution with low expectations.
I was positively surprised to say the least. The story of the game
is very well written, mixing in a lot of twists here and there, a lot
of them clearly very inspired by real world conspiracy theories.
Unlike most other games, even ones with well written stories,
this game doesn't just offer you a linear path from point A to B,
telling you a story a long the way. This game features optional
side quests, rewards and more. You can choose a lot of different
ways to complete everything as well. You can choose to go full
Rambo mode and just rush in shooting everything, or you can go
sneaky, even complete most of the game without "killing", by using
close combat, gas grenades, stun and tranquilizer guns and more.
What you choose will also have impact on how the game will continue
offering several different endings and twists in the story a long the way.
If i have to say something negative about this game there is a few
things to mention. Using stealth to complete the game is hard, very very
hard sometimes, which if you don't mind killing, will make you want to
go for the easier way and just shoot your way through, be aware of your
ammo though, as you will quickly run out and need to check every single
corpse, room etc, to keep gathering ammo. Also choose yours "augs"
wisely as some offer a lot of advantages over others. There is one very
annoying thing about the game in my opinion, the controls could be
better in certain areas. Like the game NOT having a option to switch
between hold/toggle crouch, was annoying me like crazy in the beginning.
I will highly recommend this game to anyone who likes a single player
FPS game with a deep and well written story. Especially if you also are
the type of person that likes conspiracy theories or is a critic of science.

Bizarre is a word that comes to mind when playing Fallout 2. Its a world both serious and very silly at the same time. The main quest is serious but the whole game is full of pop culture references and silly scenes, sex and drugs run rampant and it feel like almost everyone is a sneeze away from wanting to kill you.
I know this game is treated like a religion so people are going to hate me but I'm being honest despite the fact how someone can downvote this game while ignoring all peer pressure and being honest lol.
I Installed a restoration patch which added many things although I was there mainly for bug fixes. My strange story included giving children an orphanage to get them off the streets, sleeping with a mob leaders wife while dealing with mobster wars in an even more lawless city, getting someones spleen back which he lost in a bet, moving a plant to another garden so he could teach me how to beat a Radscorpion at chess and many many more but mostly just shooting annoying obnoxious people in the face. The combat is pretty much the same as Fallout 1 and for me that is no bad thing with a few new weapons added andthe gory deaths are still here.
I encountered many things in the world map such as knights looking for a holy hand grenade then right after meeting them again getting killed by a small rat despite their power armor, Darth Vadar and friends standing around chatting while Han Solo told me something there no match for a good blaster so gave me a blaster, a crashed ship with dead red shirts, a dead whale in the middle of the desert and a man guarding a bridge asking familiar questions, the Cafe of Broken Dreams and many more which you will probably recognise.
Amongst the things I didn't like is Fallout 2 has many quests but alot of them are not obvious and this game needs a guide/walkthough more than most as many are at least semi hidden and even when you get them there is no reminder in your log where you had to go/do what. Such things will effect new players more and it can be and get very confusing especially amongst its bloated game world. The same with items, there is no description how things work and what they do such as drugs and medical items and which items are just vendor trash. Once again this effects new players more because once you know you remember but there is no harm with an ingame description but I do understand games were different when this was made. With NPC's too Its so easy to say '' the wrong thing '' which more so than Fallout 1 can suddenly turn even whole towns hostile and likely result in a last save game reload. Skill checks are still here but like Fallout 1 they are '' invisible '' so you may not know when you are using them. This game is also difficult , more so than Fallout 1 and companions are almost as annoying.
Comparing to the later fallout games is hard because like the Fallout 1 they are so different especially the obvious Isometric vs First Person game worlds. When people ask me about this thing, my response is normally "Its interesting" Yes, it has its drawbacks but after using this thing for while now. I really like it.
In most of the reviews I've seen of the Steam Controller, this is one of the things people complained about. However I think that the build quality of the controller isn't too bad. Although the pretty much every button on it is very loud when pressed, not so loud its annoying, but loud enough for it to be picked up by my microphone about a 40cm away, especially the trackpads.
The thing that the Steam Controller does that no other controller can match, is customization. Every single button can be remapped to any button on a Xbox 360 controller or a keyboard, so you can use it anyway you like. Or you can use a configuration that someone else has made on the Steam Community, you can even take that configuration and change things to how you like it.
When you use it for the first time, it feels really weird, the trackpads just seem like they don't belong on a controller, but after a few weeks of using it, you do get used to it and it feels just as comfortable as a normal controller would. Since it can emulate a mouse, you can effortlessly play RTS games from the couch without using a mouse and keyboard.
The only SMALL problem about this is that you can only configure the controller in Steam Big Picture which for some may be a bigger problem than it is for me. I don't mind it, but it is annoying somtimes.
Overall, this is hands down, the best controller for the PC, as you are able to play not only games that have controller support, but those that don't and they feel as if they do as long as you map the buttons correctly. But you will have to learn how to use it. It will never be as accurate as a keyboard/mouse. It isn't designed to replace them, it compliments them.

The bad is that its not really superior to any of my current peripherals,  its just different. It definitely wont replace my keyboard and mouse for first person shooters. I suppose if this is your first and only controller it is not a bad choice,  but if you have already invested anything in your peripherals it probably wont be replacing anything you already use. The game itself is pretty simplistic, basically it's a prequel to the Grand Theft Auto franchise, showing what some future character may have been in his childhood. But for real, the character portrayed is named Jimmy Hopkins, Hopkins just transferred to Bullworth Academy, an American Private School which requires uniform (sucks right?)
The game is in just as much a style as the Grand Theft Auto franchise, which is to say, it's a carbon copy. The only difference in this regard is that many of the missions, weapons, and things to steal are not cars, mass amounts of cash, or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
The story starts off with your transfer and being introduced to the primary characters. Combat is simple, hold the lock-on button to auto block, and then punch the crap out of each other.
Since you're at a school it is expected of you to go to classes, these are optional, with some pretty cool but primarily cosmetic upgrades that come from them. Instead of a wanted meter you have a three sectional bar, which indicates in how much trouble you are, levels 1 and 2 are simply them not giving enough of a damn, they'll chase you, pinch your ear, and you can then proceed to hit them in the stomach, or step on their foot to get out of the situation, level three is the true danger, punch a girl or smaller student, and it's a crime against humanity, you're treated worse than Hitler in that very scenario.

The game itself is worth a buy when on sale, since the optimization is god awful, but managable. This game is enjoyable in an ambiance sort of thing, the music all fits together and combines well, the missions are interesting, and the plot, whilst light, is enjoyable even at its worst moments.

Short version:
Buy it if you prefer road racing sims to the more casual driving/racing games. Otherwise it's probably not for you. Also, no ovals currently.
Long version:
General
I'm no native Engish speaker. Automobilista (AMS) is Early Acces, but currently there is no racing sim that could be called a final product. So be aware that AMS and all the similar games are constantly changed, sometimes even introducing new bugs. I'm playing the game for quite a while, way before it came to Steam. The game is made by a small team and it seems that it's more about passion, than big money. It's not about being flashy, stylish etc., but about actual regulated car racing. No offense for NFS players, but this is the other end of the spectrum. It is true that AMS is based on rFactor 1, but it is much more than that.
Content
The game is rather obscure in this regard, but I personally like their picks. It started as a Brazilian Stock Car (which is a real thing) game, so the older content is Brazilian V8s and mostly Brazilian tracks. Over time they ventured into some popular and some less so areas, but most of the cars are quite different from each other. Many current games offer street cars, hypercars, GT3 and touring cars. AMS has Brazilian stock cars (60s, 80s and current), open wheel (old and new), fwd, rallycross, super trucks, and some more. Content is by no means mainstream. I didn't play much open wheel, but generally the cars feel authentic. I don't have any racing experience, but I'm driving probably before most Steam users were born. So yea, the cars feel really different. You sure don't drive the same a Formula Extreme and a Formula Vee. Night racing is supported, but no rain. Dynamic rubbering is on a Todo I think.
Force Feedback
I have a Thrustmaster T500 + TH8 H shifter, so your experience may vary, depending on the wheel you use. This may be the best part of the game. I have all the actual racing sims and my personal experience is that no current game feels near to AMS regarding FFB, especially the later builds. This may be subjective experience, but it seems that the bigger the publisher, the worse the FFB gets (kudos to Codies/Dirt Rally, which is a rare exception). If you have driving experience, in AMS you can actually feel what is happening with the car (Neils' magic). Some of the more popular titles (that I'm playing too) are laughable in this area.
AI
Don't expect human behavior (carnage in T1), but racing with this AI is probably the most you can get if you play no MP. In most current sims, AI is questionable and this one is I had the most human-like races with. Be honest, even in the better ones, the first two laps are miserable. Here you see cars passing each other, passing you. On the other side, I didn't see any human-like mistakes (which I only saw in R3E). I've also been ocassionally divebombed, but no crazy AI flying all over the road or all AI pulled on a string.
SP
The usual stuff. Training, race weekends and less usual, championships. There is no GT/AC/pCars like career. Championships are premade seasons for a car type. It is generally the same as rFactor1, except that the devs sometimes mess with the files and the championships don't really work, which is one of my main gripes with the game. For example in the current build, there are wrong (old) track names in the files and some series have 0 scoring. So without basic IT skills, you're doomed to wait for the devs.
MP
I only play that other game if I want actual MP racing without carnage, so I can't comment on this.
Visuals
Despite recently upgraded, visuals are a weak point. If you don't care about heat haze and sunrays, you'll be fine. But an AMS screenshot is like a photo of England on a regular day.

Sound
I find it that sound can get really subjective. I'm fine with sound in most racing sims.
Conclusion
More for people who appriciate the older racing sims (GTR2, GTL, GPL etc) than posting a screenshot of your purple Huayra.
PS I avoided mentionning other racing games where possible to avoid fanboys which unfortunately are a big chunk of racing sims/games communities.

I completed this game in 30 minutes alone, it was a bit difficult at first but after I got used to the controls and stacked up on a bunch of good items and familiars, the game became a breeze.
All the diseases I.. 'Contracted', were the exact same ♥♥♥♥♥disease' but sometimes they have a different effect, I often got myself killed on purpose just to get rid of the ugly effect it has on your character's appearance. Although I do admit this feature kept me amused for a good 5 minutes.
The game has a good amount of customization options, it lets you choose from 14 automatically unlocked male characters and 4 unlockable male characters, 9 female automatically unlocked characters and 3 unlockable female characters, and it also lets you choose from 19 automatically unlocked hats and 11 hats that are unlockable through these sort of.. Challenges. It's a shame there's no actual character customization though..
Classes work the same way as the customization options do, you unlock them through challenges/achievements. There's about 6 classes in the game, they don't have any major changes from one to another apart from perhaps a special ability or the ability to use magic. The combos stay the same, and you start with different items. But your controls sort of change.. For example, the pirate can't dash, instead he fires a cannon. Another example for the ninja, instead of evading normally, he will use a smokescreen. And the most unique one, which is the Battlemage, he can use four spells with four key combinations, for example using the evade + use buttons will conjure a magic barrier around your character. Quite a neat feature, but it's not really enough to keep me interested in this game.
Ah, forgot to mention something important. The multiplayer is practically dead, so if you don't have a friend who also owns the game and is willing to play it with you, the multiplayer is NON-EXISTENT.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
All in all, the game is good fun, but it's just way too short and doesn't do much to keep you interested in it.

Visually speaking, this game aint much to look at.. The nicest thing I can say about the art is that, at the very least, the developers have a good sense of the color wheel and this game avoids color palettes that are somehow 'off' in a way you can't quite put your finger on.
What's important here is the gameplay. What you see in the trailer is what you get. It's a brawler first and foremost, with randomly generated environments and permadeath. There are options for a "casual" mode which will just allow you to fight through to the end, but that's taking out the one thing that makes this game unique.
Unlike arcade games that are designed to eat your quarters, this games enemies all have patterns you can learn - the challenge comes from managing multiple enemies of different types at once. Every death feels like your fault. While it does have some more obtuse elements to it (such as potions with unidentifiable effects, items which will give you random curses or other ill effects), sessions are short and satisfying enough that it doesn't feel terrible. There's enough humor to be found in some of the ways an item or curse will change your character to balance things out, I think.
If you liked games such as Castle Crashers, Golden Axe, or any one of the dozen classic Konami beat em up games of the 90s, this game is the next logical evolution of that sort of game and I highly recommend it.
1.7 h into the game, and it's an excellent side scrolling hack and slash. :) Buy now!

Before I say anything, this was once a game I really enjoyed. With 387.2 hours on record as I write this I can say that as a game - Paladins is fine, even really good. But now they've introduced a new system that really seems to take alot of the skill out of the game. With the previous card collecting system people called it pay-to-win, but the fact is it really wasn't. In fact, it was only a little bit grindy, but now it really IS pay-to-win.
I think the best way to explain how is to compare it to another excellent game: Overwatch. In Overwatch there are no items that you need to collect, it is purely skill based. And this is more or less how Paladins used to be, but in the recent update (OB 64. something or rather, not really sure) they redesigned the card system. Where you used to collect the cards and then could upgrade and swap them willy-nilly within your builds, you now begin with 1 copy of every card >BUT< now cards have levels. Cards begin at level 1 and cap out at level 5. The problem with this is that players with higher leveled cards will always have a HUGE advantage. Imagine 2 players with the same skill level on the same champions facing off against each other. One has level 1 cards and one has level 5 cards; the player with the higher leveled cards with win almost ALWAYS. To make matters worse it takes a rediculous amount of time and/or money to level cards up. While fortunately players who have most of the cards will have there cards begin at level 3 this not only retracts hugely from the skill of the game but from the new player experience. I find it incredibly difficult to believe that most new players would stay at all with this new system as it puts them at an even greater disadvantage than they already would have been at.
Conclusively I will not play this game again until Hi-Res solves this problem (if that ever even happens).
I would not recommend picking this game up unless they have - thank you for reading.

Not only is it basically a grindathon if you rather not put money into microtransactions, but you must have a certain number of friends (which number increases the more you unlock.) in order to play the shooting range courses.. I can't believe I'm saying this, but I hope they make it a retail game soon, as that might remove the microtransaction and friend-needing element. The experience system is neat, as to challenge yourself to beat new difficulties in order to progress, but grinding does not equal challenge. It equals impatience and disinterest. And if you even try to repeat beaten game modes (Disassemble/Reassemble/Operate/Field Strip, etc.) the experience count you get for completion is laughable at best.
For operate, (COLT 1911.) I got 200 experience, repeated, it gives me a whopping 5. With the wallet-tease "IF YOU HAD A BOOSTER, YOU'D GET A WHOLE 12.5 EXTRA EXPERIENCE POINTS!!!!!111!!1oneoneoneeleveneleventy! JUST PAY US!" Having only played the original old Deus Ex for a short bit,
and remembering it like it was "just another fps game",
i opened up Deus Ex: Human Revolution with low expectations.
I was positively surprised to say the least. The story of the game
is very well written, mixing in a lot of twists here and there, a lot
of them clearly very inspired by real world conspiracy theories.
Unlike most other games, even ones with well written stories,
this game doesn't just offer you a linear path from point A to B,
telling you a story a long the way. This game features optional
side quests, rewards and more. You can choose a lot of different
ways to complete everything as well. You can choose to go full
Rambo mode and just rush in shooting everything, or you can go
sneaky, even complete most of the game without "killing", by using
close combat, gas grenades, stun and tranquilizer guns and more.
What you choose will also have impact on how the game will continue
offering several different endings and twists in the story a long the way.
If i have to say something negative about this game there is a few
things to mention. Using stealth to complete the game is hard, very very
hard sometimes, which if you don't mind killing, will make you want to
go for the easier way and just shoot your way through, be aware of your
ammo though, as you will quickly run out and need to check every single
corpse, room etc, to keep gathering ammo. Also choose yours "augs"
wisely as some offer a lot of advantages over others. There is one very
annoying thing about the game in my opinion, the controls could be
better in certain areas. Like the game NOT having a option to switch
between hold/toggle crouch, was annoying me like crazy in the beginning.
I will highly recommend this game to anyone who likes a single player
FPS game with a deep and well written story. Especially if you also are
the type of person that likes conspiracy theories or is a critic of science.

Whenever you play a MMO published by a Chinese or Korean corporation, you can expect certain aspects of the game and payment model to be different. Neverwinter is no exception. This game happens to be run by a Chinese corporation called Perfect World Entertainment. It is their "North American" division of Perfect World.
The big issues brought up by many North American and EU players is Pay2Win. Something that is rampant and very accepted and acceptable in Chinese, Korean, and SEA cultures among PC games. Neverwinter is an attempt to get away from some prevalent Pay2Win features otherwise present in their Chinese counter-parts and to a degree, has almost found a acceptable amount for NA players in their action games, such as Blacklight Retribution and especially Tourchlight. But these are exceptions to the rule, and they are not MMOs.
Neverwinter does have Pay2Win aspects, make no mistakes. Without paying any cash, it will require a player months to be on equal footing compare to what a paying customer can achieve in a week or two if they take their time.
These aren't the things I personally have an issue with the game though. Because, with the exception of the price of coalescent wards constantly on the rise, an item required to craft high level weapon and armor enchants, most things a player can attain in a few months play, if their okay with settling for rank 7 and 8, maybe rank 9 enchants, instead of rank 10s.
The issue I have with PWE is that forum discussions about the game among players almost exclusively happens on their official forums, which are heavily censored. Not surprising coming from a corporation that formed in Beijing, outside of China's Special Economic Zone(SEZ), their quasi-capitalist zones. Even though these areas aren't officially ran as communist zones, their strongest political party remains the communist party, and many North American and EU peoples would be unable to differentiate between the two because their are so many similarities to a full communist ran country.

I've had the controller about 3 weeks now. The controller works well. The buttons are responsive the battery life is reasonable. Some games like tf2 are already fully mapped for you. I have had problems with games that are already controller ready. Like skyrim does not accept keyboard mouse input while a controller is connected and controller support is active. So working around this problem is a little annoying because the interface for editing the active profile is slow and clunky and I have to look for the control like what does X do. So lets say X brings up the map, now knowing that I have to go from the controller bindings to keybinding to see what button on the keyboard brings up the map so I can place it in the same place on the SC profile for skyrim so we can have the profile properly labeled and ready for tweaks then to finally check if the title is viable to work with steam controller which for any title is not a solid yes or no answer it depends on the player, their skill putting together and working with a profile.
I know I can just download a profile that was put together by someone else but that tends to be disagreeable in the simple idea that I want the profile to resemble my own thought process and stand against my own trial and error. I have another idea, One that will not cost steam a penny, steam may actually make money doing this. Any game that has controller support and defaults to an xbox controller have a user just label the default profile properly take out the jumping back and forth between in game interface and steam profile interface when mapping. Steam would offer the task to users who are reputable, and in payment they would be offered A TF2 HAT. If the user accepts the assignment then they have a week to finish and submit or the opportunity goes to the next person in line. Do not try and tell me the hat is not enough I have people on my friends list that have preordered games that they didn't even like because it came with a TF2 hat and this was before the item market was announced in steam.
Next editing. It is really slow and needlessly redundant. One there are a few sets that I put in almost every profile one is skype controls the other is media controls. I have them set in almost every profile I use. Now setting them up is redundant I want to be able to set some partial presets to import parts of my other profiles into my current profile or direct import of my default or my own stock profile so that I don't have to set these defaults up every single time I pick up a new game with the profile. Another thing I am doing right now as I am reviewing this product is setting up a Profile for Civilizations 5. What I did in this profile is take advantage of the touch menu. The touch menu is a visual interface that pops up on top of the game featuring up to 16 buttons that you create and select a decal from a long irrelevant list of decals. Personally I would pay extra for relevant decals to go with the gaming title that I am playing nothing huge 50 cents a title get a few dozen game specific decals featuring commands commonly issued to your units.
The last point I want to make with setting up the profiles is when you invest a considerable amount of time on the drawing board setting up a profile to decide I want this group of buttons I set up on one side of the controller on the other side and vise versa. At the moment you have to set each button up again from scratch at the new location instead of a drag and drop feature. The same goes for the touch menu. I  want to keep that relatively organized to keep like commands next to each other so drag and drop is all too necessary.
Last problem dosbox based titles. They all run on the same exe file just slightly different address on the computer. The  controller at the moment does not activate dosbox profiles probably because the controller profile is activated by the exe file that has the front window or has the attention. One of 3 possible cheap fixes 1 is steam controller when using dosbox based game defaults to the last dosbox based profile that steam has launched. The other easy fix is to place a seperate file referencing the the appropriate profile in the same folder as the active exe file. The last fix is locking onto the profile based on the entire address of the exe file instead of just the name of the exe file.

Blazblue: Calamity Trigger is the first in the trilogy, and it shows.
For a proper review of Calamity TRigger, id recomend reading a different review than this one, as i will only be talking about the PC Port.
For a PC Port, Calamity Trigger does a decent job. They include some key features, such as a good amount of Resolution options, Anti Aliasing, Bloom and sound options. Its a sprite based fighting game, so there isnt really that much to change when it comes to the visual options.
The framerate is quite off though. My PC is not exactly top tier, but its definetly not low tier either. Mid tier, ive gotten drops to 45FPS which is really bad in a fighting game. Other than that, the game usually runs at a solid 60FPS.
The game also doesnt handle Alt+Tabbing out of the game that well, as ive seen the sprites bugging out by doing so. This can range from completely dissapearing  or the colours being completely off.
There is no online, though i personally dont feel this matters. Calamity Trigger is an old game, and the balance is VERY off. Multiple characters has 1 hit kill combos/setups, so going online you probably wouldnt be having that much of a good time.
The game does allow for Local 1v1, so if you want to play with friends, there is that option.
The Story is good. Its done in a Visual Novel style, and should take about 10-20 hours to go through, depending on how much of a completionist you are.
It does have "Supposed to lose" fights, so in a few fights you actually fail when you win. The game also has some fights which require a "Distortion Finish" which is basically requires you to win with a Super move. Both of these got changed in the later installments of the series, except for a select few matches where distortion/Astral finish was required.
Id say, if you buy this game, dont buy it for a Fighting Game solely. Buy it if you are interrested in the story of Blazblue and possibly want to see the rest of the games ported to PC. As a fan of the series, id say its worth it. You also get the soundtrack which is amazing. Its a mix between Instrumental Rock and Vocal remixed versions of the instrumental songs(Lyrics are in Japanese).
