Coming from a person who plays tower defense and strategy games quite a bit, the game is definitely on the harder side of the spectrum. You'll probably lose a lot at first, that's just the kind of game it is. If it stick with it though, you'll find that it has a surprising bit of depth to it.
Probably the most interesting thing about this game is that you're in charge of defending 4 seperate lanes simultaneously, so you'll constantly have to evaluate the defenses of each individual region to make sure that they're up for the task. Waves you beat in the starting section of the map will reappear in the other sections of the map at a delay of several waves, but each lane also has a different path, and some are set up to be easier or harder than others. It's kind of an interesting exercise in remembering how you beat certain waves and then adapting and reapplying that strategy to the other lanes.
Overall I would say that it's pretty interesting if you have the patience to deal with how unforgiving it can be at times.
The devs are also pretty active in the forums, so bonus points for that.

A hidden gem!
If you think you're getting another tower defense game by buying this game, you are going to be disappointed.
This game is really hard and very addictive. You have to perfect the layout of the towers and manage your economy to achieve higher waves.
At the begining you think you can overlook the economy and place some low level towers everywhere, but that won't get you nowhere. You have to master the tower upgrades and save money for bigger challenges as they increase fast.
Also, you play in four different landscapes at the same time and monsters will appear in 6 different spawn points at the same time, making it harder to just follow that one path. You have to be multi-task to nail them! And that's awesome! Thank God you can pause the game to think better the layout distribution.
The art design is pretty cool, giving it a feel of a board game. It reminds me of Storm The Castle. I don't know if they made it on purpose, but the reference is awesome. Some towers also make me remember Age of Empires; the tiles, any 90s RPG game like Final Fantasy.
The animations are pretty cool for an indie and specialy for a tower defense game. If you zoom in you can see the small details like war tattoos on the goblins and the attention to small details is something I like in a game.
I wonder if someone will get to wave 500 some day. Looking forward to checking the leaderboard in the future to see that.

At first glance this game might look like so many other TDs but it's USP is that there are actually four maps and you defend on all of them at the same time. Or at least you will if you can advance far enough into the game.
At the time of writing the best I've achieved is Wave 24 and defended on three of the maps at the same time.
The game can be brutal in it's difficulty at first but if you persist you can figure things out about optimal placement of towers and when to (or not) upgrade and buy mines to bolster your gold supply.
Also you can repair your castle in the centre of the map but there is a trade off between doing that and buying towers or upgrades. Tactically the game is quite deep for a TD game and initially trial and error will be the only way to learn.
If you get far enough into the game you get the chance to have a "second life" where you can start the level again if something goes wrong. I've been close to getting the second life but haven't quite achieved it yet. I suspect that it might be unlocked at Wave 25.
The dev is very open to suggestions on how the gameplay can be improved and is actually writing a strategy guide to aid players due to the brutal difficulty.
Despite the almost roguelike nature of the learning curve it keeps drawing me back to play it again just to see if I can get a bit farther in the game.
I bought it on release and paid £1.01 for it. It's much better than most TD games released in that price range and more addictive and enjoyable than most TD that cost five or six times that price.
If you like TD games you should buy it.

I'm going to be honest, I despised this game when I first played it. My attacks weren't doing♥♥♥♥♥♥ I was extremely confused on what to do, and hated how it felt. That was months ago, until recently. I sat down, read some tips and tricks and gave this game a shot. Now I've 70 hours in this game. It's a goddamn blast.
Pros:
-Interesting and well-developed plot: The more I got in, the more I wanted to see what was going on. The stroy hooked really hooked me in.
-Interesting locations: Many locations you visit always have some backstory around them and I gotta say, almost all of them are interesting and awesome to visit like the casino of New Reno with mobsters hanging around running the place or even
-Choices Galore: There are many choices to make in californian wasteland and many I never even knew about until my second playthrough. There's so much you could miss on one playthrough that it makes me want to do another just to see what the other way could have been.
-Dialogue and Writing: This game has the best writing in any fallout game hands down. There are many humerous moments that we come to love in fallout, but it knows when to be dark and disturbing. You'll want to talk to everyone just to see what they're gonna say. (Low intelligence runs are the funniest♥♥♥♥♥♥ever)
-Combat: This is a hit and miss for some. For me, it's a hit. When you sit down and understand what to do, the combat goes from something you may despise to something you won't mind at all.
Cons:
-Confusion: This game can be pretty confusing at times. Don't be afraid to pull up a walkthrough to help you out because while some quests are easy to do especially if you actually read what they want you to do, there are other quests where I just questioned Wtf am I supposed to do. Then when I do figure it out, I just think how tf was I supposed to know that.
-Useless perks: There are some perks in this game that I took on my first playthrough that I thought would be good, only later to find out how useless they are and pretty much ruin my run. Traps and Gambling are prime examples of perks that you're rarely ever use most of the time. Watch out what you pick. You could really bone your run if you choose booty perks.
Conclusion: This game may not be for everyone, but I urge you, stick with it. This is a kind of game I don't think we'll ever see today again. It's got laughs, it's got amazing writing, decent combat, some actual balls compared to newer fallouts (like being able to kill children and some of the subject matter) and it's just so damn interesting. Consider me a fallout 2 fan. This game rises as the best fallout game IMO.
PS: Get the restoration project mod too! It adds cut content back into the game that makes the journey even cooler. (Just be sure to follow a guide for that too if you get stuck) :)

I have mixed feelings about this one.
Without a doubt, it is over-hyped. It is definetly not a game that "revolutionizes the video game medium". But its merits are worth mentioning.
Visuals: 8/10
Beautiful graphics and dynamic lighting. Can sometimes look monotone in some places like the ruined city. Repetitive textures. Enemies especially can be visually repetitive.
Gameplay: 9/10
Satisfying hack'n slash. Cool looking combos, responsive dodge system, forgiving combat that only punishes the dumbest of mistakes. Large variety of gameplay that blends together well. Coupled with the excellent music, the experience is unmatched. Strafing a boss with pod gunfire while dodging projectiles is probably the most unforgetable moments in this game. It will not bore you. Even in the final playthrough, the game will still surprise you.
Exploration can feel alittle unrewarding. Loot besides weapons are uninteresting  and repetitive. The entire world is crammed into a relatively small space.
Music: 10/10, Implementation of said music: 7/10.
The transition between songs are often jarring, and poorly directed. Songs would end abrubtly with silence, then be replaced by a song with entirely different emotion, leading to a very bipolar experience.  In multiple scenes and battle moments, the music would imply certain undertones of emotion, but the actual contents of the plot lack these undertones, exentuating the shallowness of the actual plot. That being said, the soundtrack is perfection, there isnt a single mediocre piece in the entire game. The music alone is enough to justify playing this game.
Plot: 5/10
Ok, so this is where all my problems with the game lie.
The plot is a mess. The characters are relatively boring and the plot does nothing to try and portray them with any deep level of humanity or motivation. So when the time comes for the audience to feel empathy for them, it just falls flat. The way the game shows the emotions of each character is borderline cringe. Watching 2B cry for 30 seconds is not emotion inducing, it is  30 seconds of meaningless noise. The actions of each character are contradictory and often nonsense. Thematically, the story is all over the place, and fails to make any conclusive points on the themes. It felt to me like the creators of the game didn't really know what they were talking about so they left the game in vagueness.
OVERALL: 7/10
This game could have been a masterpiece. An actually meaningful plot coupled with the dynamic gameplay and presentation techniques would have easilly taken the spot for GOAT. Unfortunately, I value plot above anything else, if a game fails to give meaning to its existence, it is just that, meaningless.
Other notes:
Dont play this game expecting it to be what everyone has hyped it to be, you will probably be dissapointed.
PC port is pretty bad. You need decent hardware to run a playable FPS, download FAR and decrease you lighting settings to get max FPS. Keyboard and mouse controls are horrendous. Get a gamepad, or a PS3/4 controller to hook up to your PC.

Aura Kingdom is an MMO featuring an auto pathing system that makes the game so easy that you'll feel like its playing itself. Its easy to get to lvl 50 without having to read a single word. From my experience, all classes are so over powered in PVE that you'll find yourself pulling a group of 5 enemies of your level when you only have 20% Hp to start with and still win. I recommend this because its a nice game to play if you just want to keep your hands busy and not actually pay attention to anything. The game has a wide variety of classes, some that I've never seen in other games. All of the classes that I played have been fun, but the icing on the cake is that you can combine classes together at around level 40. The only time that I would say that I am ever really focused and enjoying the game is when I am soloing dungeons because its actually a challenge. The only problems I would say I have with the game is that the enemies don't follow you far enough to really pile up a group to attack. The most you will be fighting at any time is 5 or 6, but when you are this strong then you could probably take on half of the entire zone in 1 pull if I were allowed to do it. Additionally there are too many currencies in the game and it can be very repetitive to gain enough points do unlock 1 item.
Final conclusion. if you just want to press buttons and have things die in various flashes of light then go for it, plus there's a large selection of fun classes, but if you are looking for a deeper immersive experience then I would move along to something else.

Alright after playing for about an hour I think I can already say based on what I played so far. I had played the Original Brainbread Half-Life mod the past several months, although the the online community is long dead it was still enjoyable to play solo. It had an innovative blend of co-op objective FPS with RPG elements with and when I heard of a Steam  released sequel was in the works I was estatic and played Brainbread non-stop for the past few weeks before its release. With Brainbread 2 now out and after playing it for a bit although it currently lacks a lot of polish, it has a lot going for it. So I am going to go over what I liked and didn't like.
What I Liked:
- Many traditional elements from the first Brainbread have largely remained intact such as the FPS/RPG hybrid elements such as stat points and leveling up, the return of Fred who is pretty much Brainbread's equivalent to the Patriarch from Killing Floor, the "take too much damage and you become infected" mechanic, and even the cheap random enemy spawns from around the player's proximity. All while making the game feel fresh with (somewhat) refined gunplay and perks.
-GORE!!!! and lots of it, I loved how you can literally gib enemies in this game much like the first Brainbread in ways that would make Quentin Tarentino proud you can blow-off heads, arms, and legs which will turn zombies into crawlers and like in Black Mesa you will get blood all over your weapon to reflect the carnage you inflicted.
-Weapon Variety, the first game had a ton of weapons to use and they were lots of fun to use but they were all guns say for an axe which was F***ing useless and would only get you killed, but in this game although it does not have a lot of weapons currently, it added better emphasis on melee combat with more melee weapons including a bayonet, a hatchet, and even your own fists while retain the game's focus on gunplay by providing weapons with a generous amount of ammo.
- New game modes, along  with the basic "find briefcase and kill Fred" missions from the first game, Brainbread 2 brings new ways to play with a combination PvE and PvP based modes such as wave defense which reminds me of Codename
CURE's survival mode and even deathmatch which is the only non-zombie mode that pits human players against each other similar to Arena based shooters such as Quake and Jedi Knight.
What I Don't Like!
- The current Leveling system and how it works is F***ing stupid!!! What I mean is that when you are starting the game which most of you are. You'll notice that while starting the game you find yourself unable to use most of the game's weapons because your level is damn low and can only use a couple of the game's basic weapons such as the AKMS and M9A1 Pistol, and until you level up to a high enough level you are barred from ever using these weapons and this is a serious problem because you will at times find yourself in situations where you are surrounded by zombies in a room with weapons that could have saved you but you couldn't use because you're not at a high level this also gives the game an artificially steeper learning curve as you have to figure out what weapons you could and couldn't use at your current level. The first Brainbread had this but it was more lenient and strategy based because even at level 1 you have access to most of the game's weapons and only have to be concerned  with the inventory space, the gun's practicality and ammo pool, and playstyle and the only weapons you couldn't use were the game's Power weapons such as the Minigun and Sniper Rifle which were locked out for new players because they were overpowered and would've made the game too easy. Here, I just end up picking up weapons just because I could use them at my level and never had to consider the weapon's pros and cons which pretty much hurts much of the game's strategy elements and playability. So I ask the developers unless you are reserving this for Power Weapons, PLEASE GET RID OF THIS STUPID MECHANIC ASAP!!!
- Balancing Issues, the terrible level restrictions on weapons this is a symptom of how horribly unbalanced this game is and believe me it is so unbalanced that it can be nearly unplayable at times. First off the enemies, this game introduces human enemies, mainly bandits while great in concept it was poorly executed in it's current state these guys are armed to the teeth and take as much damage as the zombies, and since they can hit you at range they are a much bigger threat than the zombies and the fact that the game's leveling system prevents you from using most of the game's weapons you will find yourself at a huge disadvantage when going up against these guys and it makes Arena mode nearly unplayable. Another huge balancing issue is the Player controlled Zombies are too powerful, meaning that Zombified players can soak up a ton of damage without slowing down and kill you in one to two hits and because of how chaotic this game can be it is almost impossible to distinguish Friend or foe for human players yet for Zombie players, human players are marked meaning that Player zombies can get the jump on human players since they blend in so well especially since their nametags are visible for all players to see. Another problem is that players who get turned to zombies are stuck, in the First Brainbread, if you become a zombie, you can kill a certain amount of Humans and you can come back as a human on your next spawn, yet here I literally killed 30 humans in a row and I kept respawning as a zombie after I die. But that's not even the worst balancing issue in this game no, that goes to the game's horrific spawning system I am talking spawning that puts Call of Duty to shame, Too often I find myself literally respawning in hordes of enemies unarmed and naturally I was Screwed with a capital S what even worse is that you have a very limited amount of respawns so you pretty much get the idea of how games like this go with this kind of spawning system.

End rant
While it may sound I am ripping this game apart you'd be probably right. However, I also understand that the game literally came out today and is obviously going to have numerous bugs and balancing issues but despite all of that, I would still recommend this game, why? because like I said this was a very fun game it just lacks polish, and that why early access exists and why it is up to us, the community to make sure this game becomes the worthy sequel it was destined to be, so I encourage you to play this game and let the developers know what they need to fix.
Overall: In it's current state this game is a broken and unbalanced mess but beneth all of that it is an awesome game and I don't want it's final form to be anything like this because Free games like this are in such short supply and we need to make sure this game becomes the masterpiece it is set out to be. However, If you are looking for a more complete and refined free zombie game, go play No More Room in Hell , Codename CURE or go to Moddb and download the Original Brainbread.

Blazblue Calamity Trigger was a great game. I've spent more hours on BBCT than I have in Skullgirls & that's approaching 1000 before too long...
However, it must be noted this is the very first Blazblue (BB) game and there've been 2 full versions after. Currently, Blazblue Chhrono Phantasma is the game to play & there's been a campaign to get it on steam. After a week of the campaign, Blazblue CT (this game) magically appeared on steam. No advertising...no real announcements or nothing. So that has to mean something. Mind you, the game was already ported to PC a while ago, but it was 1-2 years after the original and the 2nd game had already come out, making it obsolete & furthermore, really effed up because of "Games for Windows Live" DRM.
In this new steam revision, they removed GFWL (THANK GOD), but at the time of this review, there's no netplay. You DO get all the DLC color palettes which are actually very cool, and the game runs VERY VERY SMOOTH at 60fps. Anyways, it might be good to get so you can familiarize yourself with the game and how the main characters work. And if nothing else, buy it to further the campaign to get more arc system works games on steam.

As a person who grew up with playing Neo Geo's King of Fighter I can say that I did enjoy playing this game. Something that BlazBlue lacks is a large selection of characters (there are 12 in total). Though, because of that, every single character has their own unique fighting style and personality. The pace of this game is just right and the characters are somewhat balanced once you get a grip of their combos/attacks. BlazBlue's soundtracks are also great, more than that; they're included when you buy this game!
This game features a story mode which requires you to play through all character's story to unlock more content. It's basically a visual novel. With that said, there are different paths you can take which leads to different endings.
Surprisingly the story of this game was quite deep (complex?) and far more what I've expected. It was quite entertaining and it did add a lot more value to the game. The voice acting for some characters however (like Ragna) was terrible, while others (Rachel) was really good.
And of course, there is an arcade mode as well!
If you're new to this genre, watch a gameplay of this game. That's probably the best way to find out if this is a game for you (there are no gameplay videos in the store page).
I personally don't really care about online mode, thus I did not take it inconsideration when I made this into one of my recommended games. As of now, there is no online mode.

Its a Facebook game thats somehow ended up on Steam. Because of its origin, and the fact that its free, unlocking stuff involves lot of grinding for experience points, which means assembling and disassembling same weapons over and over again. To unlock guns you only need XP, but for shooting range you need XP and you also got to send friend invites! Alternatively you can skip these requirements with credits, which can be earned with most difficult achievements, but even that can be skipped with, you guessed it, microtransactions! Buy credits or unlock stuff with real money.
But the question is, is it worth playing? The idea is really cool and if guns are your thing then yeah, go for it. The detail is excellent and it should satisfy the curiosity for those who want to know more on how guns work. However, lot of people will probably get turned off by the excessive amount of grinding and pay-2-unlock mechanics before they get to the guns they might actually be interested in. The game goes really anti-grind already after you've unlocked MP5, as the required experience to unlock the next guns keeps increasing and you earn less the amount of XP when you repeat old one's. I'd love to fool around with something like that Gatling Gun seen in the pictures, but I probably don't have time or patience to tear down the same bloody AK again, again and again, especially when I have better games to play which are actual full experiences.

It comes from a heavy heart that I do not recommend buying this controller.
I was a part of Valve's target audience, I believe. I wanted to use Big Picture and to begin using steam in the living room.
I believe Valve wanted to innovate the industry and push gaming forward in a small but significant way.
I just don't think they've succeeded quite yet.
Here are my main PROS:
I liked the PRESENTATION of the controller. The box it came in was sleek and minimalistic. The controller itself, just like I've seen in videos, looks pretty sexy with it's concave, rather than convex, controller design. Even the little bits like the battery slots for the controller seems very well thought out. The implementation of the controller seems very thoughtful and purposeful.
The TRACKPAD works fairly well in games that I would never have thought I would play on the couch. The precision is somewhat inbetween that of a regular controller and a desktop mouse. It allowed me to play Civ V, XCOM, and other casual games from the comfort of my couch. I needed to do A LOT OF TINKERING before I was able to get the controller to work as well as I wanted it to for shooter games (more on this later). The controller allowed me to play single player shooting games more accurately than regular controllers.
The SOFTWARE was quite impressive in features. It allowed me to customize any of the buttons I'd like. If I didn't like B to dodge in a game, I could easily remap it to X, or right button, what have you, using Big Picture. Also, the control configuration tool allowed me to map multiple mappings of the controller. For instance, I would have standard controller button scheme regularly, but if I pulled the right trigger I could have a secondary layout to remap keyboard commands (such as F5, F9, I, J, L, O, and otherwise common keyboard shortcuts). It really expanded the capability of the controller to become just as it wanted to be: both a keybord/mouse and controller.
Here are my CONS:
The SOFTWARE, though very high in features, has quite a learning curve to overcome. A lot of the features are left unexplained. There are examples of different layouts that other players have implemented themselves, but it takes a while to learn how to create a layout that works best for you. There is an amazing amount of features, but becoming familiar with them takes several hours of frustrating experimentation while all I wanted to do was play my game. It took me awhile to even recognize that there was a dual layout capability through button toggling, as well as a gyroscope function.
On SOFTWARE some more: Funny enough, Big Picture has a hard time recognizing the Steam Controller as one that is connected to my computer. I used to have another Logitech controller hooked up by USB, but even after disconnecting it, Big Picture either fails to recognize that I am using a STEAM controller that can use custom layouts. or fails to recognize the controller altogether. Sometimes, it was more useful to load up the game without Big Picture (on my computer). Oddly enough, I could access some of those custom layouts while playing without Big Picture although it isn't advertised to work this way.
On the TRACKPAD. Although the trackpad has higher precision than a controller, it does not substitute a keyboard and mouse. Games that require the crisp precision of a mouse simply cannot be played to the same accuracy. So, most online games like Team Fortress, CSGO, DOTA2 are all mostly an out. Also, while the track strives to improve accuracy, some games are not programmed well to implement the trackpad. For instance, a game may only accept inputs from a mouse/keyboard or a controller, but not both at the same time. So, programming keyboard shortcuts, or using the trackpad programmed to be a mouse, doesn't let you move using the left thumbstick to move since both keyboard/mouse and controller inputs are being put forth at the same time. With some modern games, this usually isn't a problem, but by enlarge a lot of the games I would like to enjoy suffer from this issue.
Some NEUTRAL points:
While the controller allows you to play non-controller games, most keyboard/mouse games are not very well designed to implement the Steam Controller. I listed a lot of casual games because the buttons required and the mouse accuracy isn't very stringent. Although it is a nice ability for me to play something like The Sims on my couch, it really doesn't work for things like Minecraft, Terraria, and other casual games. In short, I guess there are a lot of games I wish the controller worked well for, but it simply doesn't or doesn't as well as I'd like. Still, this isn't at the fault of Valve, but it does influence the decision to purchase the controller especially if I had a lot of older games.
The controller is wireless and quite reliable at that. I can be all over the room or even in the kitchen and it will register very well. Still, most other wireless controllers these days are able to do the same, so it's not too impressive.
TO SUM UP:
PROS:
+Presentation: Valve really wants this controller to appear new and sexy. It really does.
+Trackpad: It allowed me to play games that exclusively used the mouse while I was in the living room.
+Software: Has a high potential for customization and button layouts to get the most out of the controller.
CONS:
-Software: Because of its great number of features, there's quite a steep learning curve.
-Software: Big Picture doesn't recognize the steam controller very well, and there are other minor, yet still frustrating, hiccups.
-Trackpad: It's still not nearly as accurate or as intuitive as using a mouse, so competitive gaming is out. Also, I couldn't use the full potential of the controller on a lot of my games because of controller input issues.
NEUTRALS:
-Older Games: Some older games are just not fit for Steam Controller use.
-Wireless functionality: It's okay.
To wrap up: If you're curious, and you're the tech enthusiast, go for it. Make the purchase. But like the rest in the audience, you'll be in for quite a bit of learning, fun at first but frustrating by the end. Hurdles upon hurdles keep the Steam Controller from being a comfortable and seamless experience, and it seems a lot of the time the controller is fighting you, rather than letting you enjoy a novel experience.
It's interesting as a controller, but disappointing as "the" Steam Controller. I really hope that in a few years time, Big Picture and the software side of the Steam Controller will up the user experience to match the potential of its hardware counterpart.

the dead rising franchise has been a favorite of mine for years, it has pretty much everything you'd want in a video game. zombies, variety of weapons that can also be customizable, vehicles that can also be customizable, your own character that can also be very customizable when it comes to clothing and other aspects. the dead rising franchise has always been the type of game you can get a good laugh from, considering the humor the characters in previous dead rising games have, but in dead rising 3 they manage to but a little bit of everything, such as humor and some sad parts of the game. you get to make an emotional connection with the main character you play as, which is always good, weather you relate to him, or the story touches you, either way, the characters in the game aren't boring.
the story is a decent 16-20 hours of gameplay, yes, that is the main story, theirs also a variety of side missions throughout the entire game, you will always be running into things that will keep you busy regardless.
the game is a good port coming from the xbox one version, i've played through the game on xbox and just starting on pc. regardless of how good your pc is, the frame rate cap is unfortunately 30fps. theirs a way around this tho, simply go to where your deadrising3.exe file is located, make a text document called "user.ini" (without the quotes) proceed to go into the file and put "gmpcr_unlock_frame_rate = True" this will unlock the frame rate cap and the game will play much smoother and not feel like typical 30fps.
my final verdict is, anyone who enjoyed previous dead rising games on whichever console will love dead rising 3. even if you're new to the franchise, highly recommended to anyone who enjoys zombie games, but dead rising is so much different then any other, for its humorous feel, customizability, and story, the unique dead rising experience will keep you busy for hours.

When Bully arrived on PlayStation 2 a year-and-a-half ago, quite a number of people ignored it. After all, the next generation of gaming had begun. So it is likely that the majority of 360 owners never gave Rockstar's open-world angst-ridden game a shot. Good thing for second chances. Bully: Scholarship Edition polishes the graphics, adds a handful of new missions and delivers a unique and thoroughly charming experience on Xbox 360.
Though developed by Rockstar, makers of the Congressional-favorite Grand Theft Auto series, Bully is a T-rated game. There's no blood, no guns, no boosting of cars. Assault an officer of the law and you don't get a 6-star wanted rating -- you get busted. That doesn't mean there isn't plenty of mayhem (and violence) in Bully, just that it's not a GTA clone. Imagine if John Hughes made an open-world videogame starring John Bender, the thug from The Breakfast Club, and you should have a pretty good idea of the tone for Bully. This is an angst-filled game; a light-hearted simulation of the horrors of high school. And it's a lot of fun.
You play as Jimmy Hopkins, a 15-year-old delinquent who's been expelled from seven other schools. After his mother and latest step-father dump him in a corrupt boarding school just outside the town of Bullworth, Jimmy must find a way to go from social pariah to schoolyard hero. Bully takes us through Jimmy's first year at Bullworth Academy. It's a rough year as Jimmy must negotiate the social strata of the various cliques in school (bullies, nerds, jocks, preppies, greasers) and out of school (townies). There are classes to ditch, prefects and cops to avoid and an entire town to explore.
The first chapter of Bully is also the worst. If you pick up Scholarship Edition, don't be hasty to trade it back in after the first hour. The first chapter is your initiation into Bullworth Academy and as such, the gates of the school are locked. You're limited to school grounds, have almost no fighting combos, few weapons, and everyone hates your guts just because you're the new kid. Though befriended by the psychopathic Gary upon your arrival, the various cliques (including the nerds) would rather beat you senseless than give you the time of day. In fact, quite often you will be assaulted by bullies who start fights anytime they see you daring to walk down the halls towards class. This can interrupt and even ruin some missions, which becomes frustrating when just getting into the groove of a game. Be patient. Work through the first few hours and soon enough the gates of the Academy open up, the combat becomes more enjoyable and the bullies take your side.
Completing the main missions of Bully (which tally a considerable number) earn or lose the respect of certain cliques. This changes how they treat you on and off school grounds. Beyond this, each individual character also has a personal reaction to Jimmy. So while the nerds in general may love Jimmy, some will love him more than others. In fact, if you play your cards right, there's a mouth full of braces waiting to kiss you (whether you prefer girls or boys).

A shining example of Rockstar's ability to tackle, what seem like at the time, impossibly politcally incorrect subjects.  This game was originally released in 2006 on the PS2, and during that time was one of the games that shaped me as a person. Bully follows the life of Jimmy Hopkins, a by no means perfect teen, through his life at Bullworth Academy. He comes from broken home, with a mother who by no means cares for him, and a multitude of stepfathers. When Jimmy is introduced into the school he quickly learns that those who cannot physically stand up for themselves are tormented relentlessly, and that it is not only tolerated, but encouraged by the school. Jimmy is by no means a bully himself, but tries to establish himself as a sort of bringer of justice in the school, by systematically humilating the kids who needlessly bully others. This game was far ahead of it's time, it expertly tackled subjects that no other developer would dare undertake at the time, and in my opinion withstands the 8 years of aging. While the story is a very interesting social commentary on things like broken homes, and bullying, as the name implies, it's gameplay did not withstand the test of time in the same way it's story did. The game is essentially unplayable without a controller, is a godawful port in almost every way, and has very simplistic fighting mechanics. The game is capped at 30FPS, and when uncapped will break certain missions. The fighting essentially entails kick, block, punch, and while the additions of things like the slingshot or marbles can make it slightly more enjoyable, it's still pretty repitive. Overall I'd say it's worth it for the story and, as any good Rockstar game contains, great social commentary alone. Although if you're very gameplay centered I'd say wait for a sale.

I will start off by saying its about damn time that Arc Systems put a Blazblue game up onto Steam, as I am a HUGE fan of fighting games and Blazblue: Continuum Shift has easily become one of my favourite games of the current/last generation (Depends on when you are reading this). I'm going to admit now that I am a bit embarrassed for having gotten confused when I first picked up the sequel on my Xbox without having played the original, which led to a great deal of confusion.
Anyways, onto the actual review: the game plays fantastically although I seem to have some issues trying to pull off half-circle back, forward moves (Or 63214-6 attacks for you fighting game buffs) which isn't much of an issue when I am playing on my Xbox, however it has severly limited my combos and playstyle for this game since I would usually start off with a basic combo and finish off with a distortion (The equalivent of a super combo/edge attack/what have you) or vice-versa.
The story of Calamity Trigger is a bit tough to grasp at first as you'll need to play through each individual character's stories to figure just what the hell is going on in the game's universe. In short, the story is about a world that has begun building cities atop giant pillars called Hierarchical cities as the surface of the planet is covered in a thick smog of poo gas which will mutate you or kill you flat out. An oppressive police force known as the Novus Orbis Librarium (aka the N.O.L. or the Library) has taken control over the world using Ar Magus (Just think magic) and has been secretly building super weapons that look like young girls (Its Japanese, did you expect something else?) called "Prime Field Devices" our hero, a criminal called "Ragna the Bloodedge" ventures to the Hierachical city of Kagutsuchi to destroy the 13th Prime Field Device, however he has a huge bounty on his head and must fight several colourful enemies to continue his quest. AND THATS ONLY ONE STORY.
The characters are fairly balanced (Except Hakumen, that counter spamming, stun locking cheap S.O.B) and all have very unique styles that require lots of patience and timing to use correctly. I personally like the cast as they all have great personalities, stories, motives, and theres one character who is essentially a mentally stunted cat lady who is just too goddamn adorable for her own good. Plus the characters who have interactions in the story/arcade mode will have unique dialogue before, during and after a fight which really helps to give the player a strong understanding of just who the character are in their own world.
Personally, I think the sequel is much better (I main Hazama, and he is absent from CT) as it adds more characters, a larger story, more levels, and a few additional game modes (Depends on which version you are playing, original had Legion, Extend has Abyss). That being said, I am not saying that CT is a bad game at all, in fact I have praised it quite a bit to friends and I look forward to playing both Continuum Shift and Chronophantasma on Steam in the near future. If you are a fighting buff like myself, then you owe it to yourself to play the Blazblue series, but be warned that you may have to take a few visits to the wiki to figure out just what everything is in the game (Or watch the slightly amusing "Teach me Ms. Litchi!" series in the game).

So, BlazBlue. Never played the actual game until now, but I had Bang, Tager, Rachel, Noel, and Ragna for MUGEN, so I was curious to see where they were from. How is the game? Surprisingly good for a 2D 1v1 fighter. I never got into games like Mortal Combat and Street Fighter because they didn't seem very interesting. You didn't know much about the characters, they all looked the same, and they just seemed like something you would just play at a friends house.(note that not all of these statements are neccessarily true, because I never did play them) BlazBlue, however, focuses on only twelve characters, which is small for a fighting game roster in this day and age. Because of this, they all look different, all use different tactics, and all play differently, with a few extreme examples. You've got Ragna, the all-rounder and face of the game, a man who wears a trenchcoat-shaped cliche and wields a big sword, Noel, who uses dual pistols which behave unlike most pistols I've seen, V-13, which is somehow pronounced 'Nu', who animates eight floating blades for attack and defense, and Taokaka, a cat-person with massive claws and some truly impressive speed. These all use the same controls and are usable by pretty much everyone to good effect. But then you've got Akumen and Rachel, who play completely differently. Add to this variety a story mode for each character, and you've got something I didn't expect from this genre. Other than the story mode, there's a versus mode, training mode, Arcade mode, Score attack, and that's it.
The art design is consistently interesting, and all the stages are distinct from each other. Music is pretty good, but nothing standout. Gameplay wise, it's pretty balanced. A few characters have really powerful attacks that are balanced by their completely different playstyles, which lends the characters variety without making some of them overpowered.
Overall, it's a fun game, and it's only ten bucks. I recommend it.

It's hard not to recommend a game like this.  Being the sequel to one of the best computer RPGs ever created, it had very big shoes to fill, yet it managed to fill them.  It's a big adventure, with plenty of places to see and quests to complete.  And best of all, you can go about it pretty much any way you want.  Be it by trickery, stealth, or just plain violence, there are usually multiple solutions to any problem in the game.  Indeed, if you feel like it, you can kill
(yes, even the children) who literally or figuratively stands in your way.  It won't be easy, and there will usually be consequences, but it can be done.

However, the game is not very beginner friendly.  Those coming from Fallaout 3, New Vegas, and 4 will likely be frustrated to find themselves missing half or more of their attacks at early levels.  Not to mention the frequent encounters of 5+ enemies at a time while you're travelling, each of which takes a turn each round.  This can result in lengthy encounters which end badly for you.
If you stick with it, however, and pace yourself while also building your character to survive, these encounters will soon become a piece of cake, or a thing of the past altogether.
In all, a fantastic experience awaits you with Fallout 2, and if you have the time and patience for it, you'll in for a hell of a ride.
One final note: if you played New Vegas and found the "Wild Wasteland" jokes to be more annoying than funny, then take heed: this game's humor is like Wild Wasteland on jet.  Seriously.  You can't go ten minutes in this game without some character breaking the fourth wall, or making some pop-culture reference or other.  Some of them are really good, but if you're like me, you'll find yourself tired of them quickly

The Steam controller can be a bit of a mixed bag. With some games (such as Portal 2) it works absolutely great. It's a thousand times better than a more traditional controller (especially because aiming accurately is so much easier), while in other games it's more awkward than a traditional one (mainly due to a trackpad not always being a good substitute for a thumbstick). But when it works, it works beautifully. It still doesn't get exactly to the level of a mouse, but it's much closer to it than a traditional controller.
Being a rather different kind of controller, it takes a bit of time to fully get used to, but surprisingly not that long (especially if you are already adept at using a more traditional controller). For example, I decided to play Portal 2 through using Steam Controller to get used to it, and by about half of it I was already so fluent that it was actually a joy to play.
The positioning of some of the buttons feels awkward at first (especially the ABXY buttons), especially if used to a traditional controller, but one gets used to it quite fast. Also, being able to fully remap all buttons helps a lot.
The more I use the controller, the more I like it. It still can't replace the traditional controller in all games, but in a good portion of them it really does improve the gameplay experience.
Sometimes there are some software problems, but those are usually just temporary hiccups, until the next update is released.

tldr: a fantastic game held back by an abyssmal port.
Let me start by getting the game's (or rather the port's) shortcomings out of the way. In fullscreen, when set at 1080p the game renders at 900p, and doesn't hide the mouse cursor. Both of these issues can be fixed fairly easily with Borderless Gaming. There are a few minor LOD issues, you will often see items pop in to the environment before being obscured by a bush that was supposed to load in first but didn't. The worst offender, however, is definitely the mouse and keyboard support.
I know, I know, "what the hell are you doing playing a Platinum game with a keyboard you cretin". Rest assured I busted out a 360 controller and had absolutely no problems on that front, but if you're planning to use a keyboard and mouse you are in for an awkward time. Dodging, which is integral to the game and is accomplished in one button-press on a controller, requires you to *double tap* the sprint key. It is impossible to change this in-game, as dodge and sprint are set to the same key and cannot be separated. There is also an autorun funtion on keyboard which can get annoying quickly. To sum up - i had an easier time with Dark Souls on kb+m (managed to finish the game with kn+m due to lack of controller) than with Automata (gave up with kb+m withing the first few minutes).
With that out of the way, the game itself plays and sounds fantastic. The combat system is fluid and intuitive, and rewards up-close-and-personal dodge-and-strike playstyles. This is further supported by the plug-in chip system, which will allow you to customize your character to suit your own playstyle, from cautious laser spammer (cooldown reduction, long range attack) to reckless DPS cannon (heal on kill, heal on damage dealt) to unkillable facetank (various defense chips, health up). This is all topped off by the ability to set your companions combat style to a variety of settings, including "passive" to have them stay out of your way and not steal your kills. Throw in concise enemy telegraphing and satisfying dodge animations, and you're left a fun and rewarding combat system.
The game looks alright. It's pleasing to the eye but nothing special, though the character models are clearly made with love and attention. The graphics are, essentially, okay. Moving on.
What Automata lacks in graphics it makes up for with one of the best soundtracks I have heard in a while. The music reflects the atmosphere of the situation perfectly, ranging from relaxed guitar strumming in the resistance camp to the drawn out vocals of the desert to intense drumming and strings of the boss battles. Oh, and the Theme Park music. Ooooooh, the Theme Park music. The soundtrack is up there with my other favourites, Dishonored and Hyper Light Drifter.
To sum up: good game, bad port, great music, 2B's butt. Just make sure you have a controller.

Long story short, you should get this game for at least one of the three following reasons:
* The OST is included with the game. You'll be hard-pressed to find a legal copy of the OST that is this high-quality. Even the pirated copies aren't as good as this.

Personally, I'm getting it for all three reasons. Maybe one day we can play the current revisions of BlazBlue and Guilty Gear alongside our console brethren.

Alright, before I go any further... THIS VERSION DOES NOT HAVE ONLINE MODE, among a few otther features and fixes. If those are what you're here for, leave.
By itself, however, I find BlazBlue rather enjoyable. Design and concept are pretty interesting, the visuals are pretty good for their time, but come on-- a lot of people who think of fighting games tend to think of how it looks when you beat the living snot out of something, and this game delivers that out the wazoo. If you can stand the hardware demands and lack of online mode (among other things), it's a good game to play by itself or for whenever you feel like laying a smackdown.

One of the best fighting games out there, as can be expected from Arc System Works. This may be an outdated game, gameplay-wise (multiple new editions have come out since this one, with new characters, balance changes and continued story and such), but I think it's still worth getting the first game for the sake of the story mode. The story mode of this series is actually quite rich and detailed with a very thought out lore and world (rare for this genre) with very lovable and charming characters and funny situations, and in a gorgeous visual novel style. Other than that, there is arcade mode and versus with a very expansive gallery mode to collect for.
My favorite thing about BlazBlue other than the story mode is how unique each fighter plays. They are totally distinct from each other, and in more ways than your usual fighting game because of their Drives. Drives are a special ability each character has unique to them. For instance, one character's drive attacks steal a little bit of HP with each hit, and another's freezes them, and another controls a puppet, or pulls you in with magnetism, or summons flying swords out of thin air. Just awesome stuff, and it makes the characters so much fun to play as. This is a 4-button fighting game, with weak (A), medium (B), heavy (C) and drive (D) attacks. And last but not least, the taunt button! It's a really sophisticated combat system, and it's just outstanding. Also, the graphics and music and overall presentation of the game are just absolutely beautiful.
For $10, this is certainly worth the price, especially when that includes the amazing soundtrack. Hopefully this means the sequels get on Steam eventually too, as well as more from Arc System Works in general.
Unofortunately, this version of the game doesn't include online multiplayer, since it was sacrificed in order to get it here without Games for Windows Live. For me, that's a worthy trade-off, but for others it might not be. This is a fantastic game and I am so glad it has finally made it to Steam, but buyer beware.

I just finished my first read-through with Akira and I have to say I'm very pleased. This Visual Novel is short but sweet, and very educational. I will admit I'm a bit of a weeaboo and I've always been fascinated with Japan and wanted to visit someday. This VN really seems to capture the thrill of being a tourist and how it goes in the blink of an eye.
I found myself reading and being unable to stop. The story gracefully balances the relationship between the protagonist and the two girls who you stay with, while still telling the story of visiting Japan. It's great because you can choose where to sightsee, and while you can't see everything in one run-through, it makes you want to read it again! I really feel like I'm a little more prepared to visit actual Japan one day, and now I have an idea of what I'd like to see!
Anyways, the story is sweet and touching, and I felt a bit teary when it was time for my character to leave. I liked how they had a USD to yen converter in game to kind of give you an idea of what everything would cost too. And you learn about taking trains, which is hella important.
Anyways, this is a great VN for anyone who likes a bit of romance and wants to visit Japan someday. =)

'Go! Go! Nippon!' is an informative, charming and nicely illustrated story. A bit pricy for what you get, but still a great purchase. Get it when it's on sale.
7/10
The story itself is standard. You are a tourist from the west who's lifelong dream is to visit Japan. While he's there he'll be staying with two siblings who he, at first, assumes to be boys but he is later mistaken. It doesn't take long before he settles in, meets his hosts and sets out to see sights and taste food, with great travel advice along the way.
At first the characters, particularly the protagonist, seem like they would get on your nerves, but within about 10 minutes this is sorted out. At first the main character seems to be some kind of hermit, dropping his jaw at everything he sees, but shortly after his arrival he becomes a likeable, if a little bland, character. Nothing worth complaining about, but he's not exactly winning any awards. The two sisters who act as guides for the protagonist have far more personality than he does, and later on in the game you will get quite attached.
'Go! Go! Nippon!' is a great visual novel for those who are interested in visiting Japan. You can set the Dollars or Euros to Yen rate and as you purchase items in the game it will give you a realistic total of what it would cost like in real life. The two sisters guiding you around the various locations of the country have lots to say and you can learn a great deal about the history of both main and hidden-away tourist destinations.
In conclusion, a pleasant story that you should definitely pick up if you are interested in travelling in Japan. The advice and history you get throughout the game is awesome and unique. It is a little pricey for what you get, so I recommend waiting for a sale.

Dead Rising 3 is the best single-player action game I have ever played.  I am a big fan of the series, and this game improves on all the fun aspects of the previous two by leaps and bounds.
In the first two games, your time limits to get objectives done, or explore the world are very rushed.  Not as much in this game, you have tons of time to explore, do side missions and still stay on track for the main missions.
In Dead Rising 2 they introduced crafting.  I felt it was poor in that game, as you had to remember the recipes and the items required for craftables were scattered few and far between with many useless items.  In this game every item is useful and a component for a craftable.  The craftables are nicely catalogued and easily referenced, and usually item pairs are placed together around the world, so anytime you find one component for a craftable, you find the other right beside it.  All the craftables are much improved damage and fun, and it really improves this game greatly.  There are many overpowered items, but the great thing about this game is that no matter how OP something is, it only lasts a short while and then you're back to scavenging again!
The level-up system and RPG elements are pretty nice.  Granted it isn't full scale role playing game depth, but there is certainly a lot of options and unique customization for your character as you progress.
The graphics are just beautiful.  I have had no problems with optimization issues, crashes, or bugs.  There are so many zombie deaths and animations for each weapon; they didn't hold back on the gore and you can rip apart a zombie in many different and awesome ways.  It really makes killing each zombie fun and entertaining, and keeps it "fresh" every time you use a different weapon.
The story is so-so and the main character is a big woosy with no options to do anything evil or pick sides in a fight (which in an apocalypse should be an option).
All in all this game is amazing, and I give it an easy 9/10.  Super fun, super worth, high action, great graphics, fun gameplay that doesn't go stale.  Con: Woos-bag hero lol

I don't agree with the many professional reviews that compare this controller unfavorably to the XBox 360/One controller (or other O.G. controllers). It's a different animal. It's also an innovation.  It will take me a long time to master this device,  but I like the almost unlimited possibilities. You can program controller schemes, sensitivity ... anything you want, really. It's not ideal for fast-paced FPS, but it's better than a standard controller by a long shot. Certainly, it's great for any use case in which you want to mimic mouse and keyboard control without those devices. If you can only have one controller, get a PS3 or XBox 360. They work with most games. But if you want to play games controllers normally fail at, try this as a value-add. The fact I can play Fallout 4 the way I want to on my TV more than pays for the controller and Steam Link IMHO.

Like its predecessors, this Deus Ex follows the story of an augmented man, trying to save Megan Reed, his girlfriend, who was kidnapped in front of him.
To begin with, this game can be played the way you want : you prefer to be sneaky, and bring down silently this guard with a cool cut-scene (you can either kill or knock out), or even sneak into a highly protected place without touching a guard? Sure, you can, and is in my opinion the funniest way to play this game. As a bonus, every bosses in this game can be killed/knocked out while staying in the shadows. This way, you can even finish the whole game without firing a single bullet.
Or maybe do you prefer those frontal assaults, doing ♥♥♥♥♥ons of noises and killing every enemies on your way ? Well, you also can, thanks to the complete arsenal at your disposition, rewarding every play style, such as sniping targets from afar, or going all-in with that heavy rifle, along with a couple mines/grenades.
Whichever play style you choose, the levels are incredibly detailed, and often full of computers you can hack to discover secrets, hidden doors, stories about the background of the game, or even mails telling you that this guy went to the bar with some friends some days ago, giving life to the characters, even the minor ones. Exploration will also be highly rewarded, such as giving you alternate ways to take care of the bosses, unlocking some side quests, or providing more information on your surroundings. Additionally, there are ALWAYS more than one way to do something.
Also, it is important to say that your actions have consequences on the future of the game. Thus, if you let that guy live out of mercy he might come back to try to kill you once more. Or maybe will he help you, it's up to you to choose.
To achieve your objectives, you will be able to choose from a wide number of augmentations, helping you jump higher, fall from any height, immunising you to gas, making you tougher, able to see through walls, or even changing you into a master hacker.
Finally, as usual in the Deus Ex's, the devs make the player doubt, making him question the morality of his actions, and also raising quite a lot of philosophical questions related to the development of the human race.
A major problem about this game is that if you actually explore every levels carefully and unlock these secrets, you will quickly realise how easy it is to gain experience to level up your augmentations, thus making you able to get every augs in one single playthrough, which is kinda game breaking.
TL; DR: #buythisgame

Deus Ex, what a wonderful game in the series. It's funny because I got this game for the xbox from Eidos themselves, my dad worked in the anti-piract business and I never beat it on there. Then, I bought the game again, for the PC, never beat it, AND then I bought the Director's Cut and I waited a whole 8 months to play it, and I recently beat it
Deus Ex, is about a man named Adam Jensen, he's an ex-swat member, who is now a security guard for a big, augmentation corperation called Sarif Industries. In his line of work, he has two co-workers, Megan Reed, a scientist that has made a breakthrough in augmentations and Francis Pritchard, a computer person or whatever. Then, Sarif Industries was attacked by augmented spec ops, who kidnapped Megan and 4 other scientists. You were trying to save her, but in the process, you get gravely injured and have to get augmentations. After you get them, your mission is to find out what happened to Megan and her team and get them back.
This game was crafted so well, the gameplay was fluid, a FPS shooter mixed with an RPG styled level up system. You put points into augments to upgrade and make better and upgrade the ones that better suit your play style. Stealth or go head on. Mine was going head on, I hate stealth. This game had a various amount of weapons, grenades, abilities, etc. All were different in their own ways. The quest system was quite, course directed, besides the one or two side missions in each mission location. The interaction with people was fun, you could get information out of them or you could just go up to them and knock them out. I like doing that.
The DLC, Missing Link, comes with the Director's Cut, incorperated into the game, was absolutely horrible and was not needed. Who wants to know about the time he got all his augments stripped from him and he has to fight his way to get them back. It was really boring, a lot of running back and forth, and not to mention all the damn biometric scanners. I wish I could have chosen to play the DLC at the end. But, putting it, into the story, made somewhat of a difference. It does work well with the story, but honestly it wasn't what I was looking for in a Deus Ex DLC.
I know this is a shorter review than normal but, I'm not really feeling well, but this game was a masterpiece, this is the only Deus Ex game I've ever played, but I plan to play The Invisible Wars. But, for now, I loved this game, I can't believe I never finished it. I beat the game in about 15 hours, plus watched all the endings. So I give this game a 9.5/10 :D

TL;DR:
In my opinion this controller is a ergonomic disaster.
Coupled with some buttons needing quite some force to press, it makes it a very VERY unpleasant experience.
Longer story:
As I already said, this controller is a ergonomic disaster. The bumps at the bottom (which I assume are to lift your thumbs so that both touchpads are "easier" to use) are basically just in the way and don't allow you to "hold on" to the controller.
Further, this controller fells/is huuuuge (sidenote I don't have "small" hands but they aren't super big either)
So, coupled with the force you need to press some buttons (LB, RB and the ones at the bottom of the controller. Also that one joystick that's left) this makes it a real pain because you kinda push the controller out of your hand while pressing e.g. one of LB or RB.
So basically you end up pressing both hands towards the controller in order to keep it in place.
Than, LB and RB are super awkward to reach -> ergonomics again
Not a whole lot to say about.
Next up, the placement of X,Y,A,B.
Again, due to the ergonomic disaster and the bumps at the bottom I have to stretch my right thumb to its fullest to reach the
"X" button which I just can't get used to (doesn't matter how hard I try)
Also, LT and RT pretty much have no travel at all (and have a physical click at the end). Not sure what to think about that one.
It didn't annoy the crap out of me so I guess the lack of travel and the click are just fine.
So all in all I basically keep shifting the controller around my two hands in order to utilize/use all buttons and that's just plain wrong.
In the controllers "defense", I only tested it with Rocket League so far.
But as the controller failed so bad I didn't bother testing any other game (even though I was pumped to try it with e.g. Raise of the Tomb Raider). But as the controller is so uncomfortable to hold and use there is no reason for me to even try.
All in all I really can't recommend this controller BUT I hope valve is going to make another one that's basically smaller, needs less force for certain buttons to be pressed and removes those stupid bumps on the bottom so I can properly "hold" that thing.
Disclaimer:
1. I really really REALLY wanted this controller to be great but in my opinion it's very far away from that
2. I've only used xbox controllers (and a PS controller like a ~decade ago) BUT don't care about the brand or anything like that.
I'm happy with whatever you throw at me as long as I don't get literal cramps using it (which is the case with the steam controller after ~5 mins Rocket League)

My favorite free game on steam. Silly, fun arena shooter with butter smooth feel and familiar gametypes with nice twists.

I can imagine the beta must have been awesome with ability to create huge amount of different guns and loadouts, but as the game is now, it is still terrific. Weaponcrafting is cool, and it is great that there are plenty of different styles of play available.  If you play for a while you can unlock a competitive bunch of guns and equiptment. No need to pay. You can pay to level faster, or pimp out your character/s, if you like.
But the gameplay of the matches, especially all humans, is where this game shines.  The bots best gametype is Death Snatch; they are often too good aiming and stay close. Bots desperately need better pathing in other gametypes, especially Capture the Hammer. They are quite fun to beat up on though. Game could use some more maps, but the ones it has are fun and pretty, and make for fantastic multiplayer.    8.5/10

Vehicle Simulator is a great game that allows you to fly and drive a wide range of vehicles, including submarines, sailboats, aircraft, helicopters, cars, and RC quadcopters. The amount of DLC available for free on the internet for this game is vast, allowing for a wide range of scenarios on land, sea, or air.

What I like:
-Realistic sailboat controls, which I haven't seen in any other game.
-Highly unique vehicles available like flying boats and spacecraft all in a single game.
-Everything is customizable, and you can even design your own vehicles if you have the skill.
What I don't like:
-Although very difficult to get started with flying, once you get the hang of it, it's very fun.
-The graphics leave much to be desired.
-Many add-ons are from 3rd party sites, making me think twice about downloading a vehicle (although I haven't seen any malware yet.)
This game is for vehicle enthusiasts who enjoy taking leisurely adventures, or designers who want to drive their creations with total control of the stats. I was tired of seeing high priced simulators with expensive DLC, so having a game with unlimited options and a one-time price was very appealing.

This game is a tour guide of Tokyo and some parts of Kyoto presented in visual novel form. While staying true to aspects of its medium such as relationship routes and happy endings, it provides a comprehensive insight on various things related to travelling around Japan, such as means of getting around, conveniences like washrooms and credit card ATMs, the kinds of food offered in restaurants, besides of course meaningful descriptions on various places of interest that even I, a frequent traveler to Japan, would recommend visiting. This first edition may be somewhat outdated (the Tokyo Skytree is already fully operational, for example), but there is a 2015 edition to look forward to.
For a VN, it is rather short, and that contributes to the fact that plot progression may seem somewhat forced or rushed. Nevertheless I do think the writers pulled off a splendid job given the space they had to work with. I got to the endings with feelings of bittersweetness and warmth. It isn't unneccesarily complicated, there are no bad ends, and flags are automatically triggered based on the decisions made on the first three days, and beyond that there is minimal player agency so just sit back and enjoy the ride the rest of the way. Obviously since there are two girls, one would need to run through the game more than once in order to unlock all the endings (read = 2). Each of the storylines are distinctly different from one another, it's worth the extra playthrough.
One more thing to appreciate about the game is that learners of Japanese will find the game tremendously helpful as it presents Japanese text above the English, written in everyday conversational Japanese. Players who are studying the language will be able to grasp the nuances not found in written or scripted Japanese, and can rely on the English translation presented simultaneously to understand how native speakers communicate with each other.
Do pick up the game if you haven't already! 9/10

Charlie the Duck is a remake of a 1996 side-scrolling platformer with the same name and developer.
You can find a about over 10 minutes of gameplay with commentary here:

You control Charlie the Duck. The goal of the game is simple, progress through 3 Worlds, each make up of 3 stages and an additional boss stage.
Movement is simply left and right, with a jump. Some of the water that Charlie can swim on are portals to hidden areas - pressing down will take you to an addition zone on the stage so you can collect additional coins and diamonds. It is prudent to check all the water parts as I found some stages include multiple hidden zones.
You can play with keyboard or controller - but I found that sometimes while using the thumb stick to move on my xbox controller that Charlie would just keep walking in the direction I was pressing, even after releasing it. All I could do is put him up against an obstacle in the game and wait for it to stop. I have not had this problem with other games, so I do not believe it is an issue with my setup. Using the D-Pad on the controller to move seemed to avoid this problem.
I thought sound effects were fine, as was the music. The graphics are a 16 bit style, and the background is layered to give visual depth.
Gameplay wise, its an adequate platformer which (at my skill level) I found challenging enough. Thankfully when I died I could continue from the start of the world stage I reached. This was appreciated as I died A LOT on the 1st boss. But it does take away from the replayability of the game, I don't see myself playing it again after I have completed it.
I was torn on recommending this game. Gameplay wise its fine, but I feel the price at release is too high given the amount of content in the game. It took me a bit over 30 minutes to complete the 1st world. If that continues for the other 2, then I will be finished in an hour and a half. For $6.99, that is a limited amount of play considering I don't feel there is much replayability. If you are interested, I recommend waiting for a sale before picking it up, at a cheaper price I would recommending if platformers is your preferred game.
If you do decide to buy this game, just a tip for fighting the first boss (the fish). You need to jump on his eyes, closer to front of his body instead nearer to the spikes on his back to score a hit.

The modding community is active and very talented. Automobilista has been out in early access for less than a day and there is already an excellent track mod (Nurburgring)  as well as some skins and a couple hud mods. More are soon to follow.
Communication with the developers is excellent and they back what they sell. They are racing fans who made a great game.
I'm sure I could go on and on but If you want a realistic racing experience - one that gets you about as close as you can get to the real thing - buy this game.

tl;dr This game is genuinely a masterpiece of games as a storytelling platform. A game you will absolutely never forget and needs to be experienced to completion by absolutely everyone.
Nier distills the fantastic parts of all video games as a whole and presents an incredibly tight experience that polishes them all to a sheen. Consistently jumping styles of games within seconds of each other is no small feat, but feels seamless here. There's never a dull moment to be had -- the action is plentiful and the downtime is always a pleasure.
Incredible writing and a cast of characters that you will grow to love are here in spades. No one character is out of place or irrelevant. You'll be entirely invested in each character's desires that you'll celebrate and hurt with them.
A subtle progression system that slowly expands your repertoire that is simple to understand and addictive to continue leveling. Customizing became almost as fun as the fighting itself.
An incredibly beautiful story told over several acts that consistently improves after each playthrough. You'll want to come back each time, and every time raises the stakes and evolves the narrative that much further.
The only fault I can find in this game is the lackadaisical port. Do not expect a patch -- download the FAR plugin and follow a guide to get configured. A few minutes to tweak and experience this game is worth the trouble.
My personal game of the year, and a game that will remain on my personal favorites for as long as I live. A masterpiece. 10/10. A++. Play. This. Game.

This is a great cyberpunk RPG. I ended up beating this on console, but went and bought the directors cut on Steam because I liked it so much. The setting has a perfect dystopian feel, and the plot/characters/story aid in this. The music is superb. From the ambient free roam & combat music, to the rushing cut scene music, to the small things like "Welcome Home, Mr. Jensen" as the blinds in your apartment automatically raise and the cityscape is shown. In my opinion, the biggest selling point for a cyberpunk game is that it has to have the correct atmosphere for the entire game, and this does. From the two main city hubs, to the combat & infiltration missions, to the high-tech police station, to the bass throbbing golden night club you visit, to the "L.I.M.B" clinics (basically mini augmentation hospitals) every city/area/mission has the correct atmosphere. "High-tech and low-life" would describe it. I am looking forward to another play-through of this game, and also any sequels that will surely follow.

What can be said about this game? Hmm. Well the first thing you should know is that you shouldn't judge this game by its graphics. The post apocalyptic world many of the modern day gamers are used to seeing is rendered in 3D and significantly different in both story and atmosphere. This world seems almost filthy and bland by comparison.
But that's the trick of the matter. This game decieves you thinking its some lame top down RPG when it is actually one of the most immersive games *ever made*
In Fallout 2 your character creation really, really, matters. The way you design every stat and trait has ramifications that will help or hinder you throughout the game. People in the world really notice, and not in a stupid skyrim "I see you're a fair hand with a blade" generic line noticing either. You'll converse with them and they'll immediately notice if you are a dumb hulking brute or a sly sneaky sort. If you are handsome or ugly people will comment on it. Hookers will upcharge you if you are too ugly or simple. Murder or hurt enough people and the world hears about it, townspeople will run from you when you walk by, while criminals will nod respectfully as you pass. The way you make and play your character changes everything.
Lets just start with Intelligence. If your character is of average intelligence, you can proceed through most of the game normally. But should you have high intelligence many options open up when dealing with more intellectual people or subjects. You can figure out solutions to problems that a less intelligent character couldn't, to the point where some boss fights or enemies can be defeated with a simple dialog option because your character was smart enough to see through the problem.
The same goes for charisma. A charismatic character will be able to talk his way out of incredible situations. Heck, if you are persuasive enough you can sleep with a mob boss's wife and convince him you were just lost. You know, just lost, in her bedroom. There are places where you can talk down suicidal bombers or convince hard hearted racists against ghouls to change their ways and be more accepting.
Every single stat is like this. Stronger characters will be able to open doors and force their way through situations others can't. More perceptive characters will see hidden traps and doors to avoid enemies and change the way confrontations happen. Every type of character made will have unique ways to solve any problem and this feels *so* good.
Maybe you want to be a big stupid brute who is barely smart enough to speak but can kill anything with ease. Maybe you want to be the cocky sharpshooter who is perceptive, smart, and good with a gun but can't take much of a hit. Maybe you want to be completely crazy and give yourself 10 luck and the jinked perk so everyone around you dies in horrible catastrophic accidents while you walk away from huge explosions with minor cuts and scratches.
You can do all of these things. The limit is really your imagination. This game is massive in scope and provides hundreds of hours of content, and with the addition of bugfixes and additional content added from the folks at
who headed the Fallout Restoration Project, it becomes near a thousand hours of things to do in this game.
If you want a game that you can play a hundred times and come back a hundred and one times and STILL see something new, buy fallout 2. Its a fabulous product and my only regret is that Bethesda did not put as much care and love into future releases as this original team did into making this a work of beauty, despite its flawed exterior.

A cute, lighthearted read. You take on the role of a weeaboo finally visiting Japan, but--surprise!--your tour guides are two cute sisters (whose parents are conveniently away on business)! You do get romance options for the girls, and there's 1 ecchi pic of each, but there is no sex. It's fluff, not hentai. There's also a bilingual option for the game, so this is nice if you are learning Japanese. Visual only, no spoken dialogue, but the music is alright. Some funny moments (your protag somehow isn't familiar with wasabi!), some heartwarming moments (the end of Makoto's route). If you're looking for something serious or in-depth, look elsewhere. Good for what it aims to do . Seeing as it's very short (~5 or 6 hours for all dialogue options), I wouldn't recommend getting it unless it's on sale.

As a person whos followed the BlazBlue series on consoles (i.e ps3 and xbox360) this game brings back alot of nostalgia, however there are a few problems people might pick up on which i'll explain later. Now the bad points: if you was hoping for some good online fights well sadly this game doesn't have it, in the old ps3/Xbox version there was a online section so why its not here i do not know, so you are limited to having a friend round to play with you. Also not super relavent but the story mode has multiple paths in the game for each person that people might find annoying, such paths like multiple choice, ending a fight with a super or astral finish, or even just dying to the enemy itself.
Overall, its still a fun game to play if you like 2D fighters or like the old nostalgic fighting of BlazBlue, but as most people will put it, Its missing out the online part of the game.  I give this game 7/10. ^_^
