Short Version: Worth a buy.
Detailed Version: For a few minutes I couldn’t figure out how to get my damn PS3 controller working with the game (had to set it to XBox settings on DS3). That’s not a problem with the game however. As for how it works, it ran pretty responsively, and the command inputs were near-perfect. (Bang’s Astral is still ♥♥♥♥ing hard to pull off and I haven’t done it yet) Performance-wise in terms of FPS and lag, there was no delay, and any slowdowns the game might’ve experienced were due to the fact that I’m playing it on a crappy two year-old laptop. Otherwise, slowdowns were minimal, and they didn’t make the game unplayable. The Steam port of BBCT isn’t the best PC fighting game I’ve played, (better than how KOF13 ran but not as well as Skullgirls or Guilty Gear Isuka) but for 10 bucks it’s worth a shot if you’re a BlazBlue fan. And the one plus to Steam? If you buy it, you have it for GOOD. So if your computer dies and you need a new one, you can redownload BBCT on it free of charge.
And hey, if enough people buy this, that might convince Arksys to bring Continuum Shift and their other fighters to Steam. :D Here’s hoping for Chronophantasma and Persona 4 Arena as well.

I've owned Vehicle Simulator for a few years, and over that time I've grown very fond of it. Lately I've been starting to use it as a way to teach my friends how to fly simulators, and so far it's working well in that capacity.
Since most of those friends don't have joysticks or controllers, I've been learning to fly it with keyboard + mouse only in order to help them. The keyboard + mouse control in VS is surprisingly good, though helicopters are almost impossible to fly without a joystick.
The game supports TrackIR and various peripherals.
If you want a simulator that scratches many of the same itches as Microsoft Flight Sim or X-Plane without overwhelming complexity, Vehicle Simulator is worth a try.

Okay...so I've owned a SteamBox for close to a year now - I love it. I use a 360 controller, but I do have a wireless mouse & keyboard for titles that don't support a controller. The Steam controller replaces the need to use a mouse and keyboard for titles that you would expect, like city builders or turn-based strategy games, like the Anno series or XCom.
Unfortunately, the Steam controller's strength is also it's weakness: it's a handheld mouse & keyboard. On a 360/DuelShock controller, the right thumbstick controlles the camera, and on mouse, you use all the features of a mouse to control the camera. On the Steam controller, there's no thumbstick to pull back or move forward, or no mouse wheel to control zoom, so bringing up maps in open world games gives you no zoom option.
Also, since the right touchpad is basically a mouse, you have to constantly flick your thumb to control your view in 3rd & FPS's instead of moving continuously in a certain direction. For example, if I want to stand in one place and have the camera or myself spin around endlessly on a 360/DuelShock controller, I just move the thumbstick all the way to the left or right. However, on the Steam controller, my thumb is tracked, so once my thumb reaches across the touchpad, all motion stops, and I have to move my thumb from the beginning of the touchpad to the next to continue motion. Yes, you can tweek mouse sensitivity to correct this, but unfortunately, you sacrifice aiming accuracy in 3rd to first person aming.
There is no rumble pack, but there is a sort of feedback you can feel to know that stuff is happening. "Haptic feedback" they call it..like it's some common phrase people are supposed to know what it is. >_>
The design of the controller isn't good imo. Only the home button lights up and not the others (A,B,X, and Y). It would have been good to have the other buttons light up, not only for aesthetics, but so I can see  where the buttons are in my peripheral vision. Also, the A,B,X, and Y buttons are too small, and too far downward and away from your thumb. So it's a bit of an uncomfortable reach every time.
The bumper & trigger buttons are not only spaced too close together, but they're angled at an angle which not only makes no practical sense, but it's uncomfortable, and your finger knuckles might end up accidentally hitting the bumper buttons if you're a person with big hands, like me.
Quality wise, the controller feels cheap...the USB cable feels cheap. It looks like it'll fray in no time. It's not long either; so if you were planning on using it wired - forget it. The dongle (used to boost wireless signal) is unreasonably heavy for something so small. If you dropped it on someone's head from a second story window, not only will you ♥♥♥♥ them up pretty good, but you'll probably be charged with Assault With a Deadly Weapon if the law were to get involved.
So in summary:
Pros:
-  the controller is able to play mouse & keyboard only games.
- It's highly customizable.
-  has 80 hours of battery life.
- works seamlessly with Big Picture mode - easy texting/messaging via virtual keyboard.
Cons:
- always needs to be configured before playing a game.
- not for 3rd or FPS.
- Camera control is terrible.
- Uncomfortable to use due to design.
Would I recommend getting it? No, it's truly only an option for Steambox owners, not necessarily PC gamers in in general. I own a Steambox because I love the comfort of console gaming, but prefer the power and customization of a PC, so it's a great option for me.
Do I regret buying it? Absolutely not. Now I have a way to play keyboard & mouse games with a controller.﻿

Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Director's Cut (Spoiler Free Review)
I own both base Deus Ex: Human Revolution (DE:HR) and the Director's Cut version.  It was a game I enjoyed so much that I bought it twice.  I am reviewing the Director's Cut version since it appears to be the only version you can get anymore on steam.  Please read my full review but to cut to the chase, DE:HR was really the better game.  The only reason I am recommending the Director's Cut is the experience the game provides.
(Story)
"They say they saved me, but I'm not sure saved is the right word".  In the not too distant future, mankind has pushed the limits of human existence.  Prosthetics and biomedical engineering have reached unprecedented levels.  People can even freely choose to be "augmented", or have technology put into their body to give them some kind of edge or replace a lost limb.  Unfortunately, Adam Jensen (the character you embody) does not get to choose and is instead augmented in an effort to save his life.  As Chief of Security for a large biomedical firm, you are caught in between your allegiance to your business colleagues and the opposition who view your augs as unnatural.  Adam rubs elbows with politicians, gangsters, and everyone in between to uncover the culprit behind a violent act of espionage conducted against his employer.  Adam also investigates the death of his girlfriend all the while coming to terms with his new condition.  The Director's Cut version includes the Missing Link DLC, except it is inserted into the story in its logical place and you have to play thorugh it to beat the game.  While Missing Link does allow you to unlock and upgrade nearly every augmentation Adam has, it adds little to the main story and you only get the big reward once you finish it (and finishing it is a little tedious).
(Gameplay)
The game is first person with a third person cover mechanic.  Stealth, hacking, or a guns-blazing approach are all valid for combat and all are just as fun due to the variety when it comes to weapons and augmentations.  As you play, Adam gains XP which is used to upgrade his augmentations so there are RPG like elements, including an inventory.  You can literally play this game through without killing anyone, choosing to focus on exploration, social, and hacking type augs.  At various times, you will have to engage in dialogue and choose responses.  This is what makes the DE:HR experience: living with the decisions you make during a conversation, especially if you cost someone their life.  Players will face many a dilemma and that is what makes this game great.  Many side missions are optional but all feel relevant and some provide hefty rewards for the dedicated player.  The DLC will strip you of most your augmentations in an attempt to make you vulnerable and force stealth.  Director's Cut also adds several new weapons and different ways to defeat the game's bosses.
(Design)
As other reviewers mention, DE:HR had a unique look about it.  A golden haze shoruded certain environments and textures looked more detailed.  The game features several unique locales, all of which are industrial, futuristic, cosmopolitan, corporate type environments with their own flavor.  Attention was paid to each one and it is nice to just listen to NPC's converse with one another.  From the clothes to the interior design, the game oozes cyber punk.  Director's Cut by comparison looks noticeably different and not in a good way.  Textures were muddier in my experience and faces looked waxy.  I never had sound issues with either version of the game, though you may have to tweak the video settings.  The DLC has an interesting part where you are on a ship in a storm but this was my favorite part of it since the remainder is spent in closed quarters that feel gray.  The DLC has very little in the way of new dialogue and its characters are not as memorable as the main game's.
(Final Comments)
DE:HR is an excellent Deus Ex game with interesting characters and great design.  Gameplay can be clunky at times but is fun for the most part.  DE:HR is a contender for my favorite game of all time and I enjoyed every minute of it.  It's too bad you cannot buy the base DE:HR anymore through steam otherwise I'd recommend it.  Though it lacks the appearance of its predecessor, do not miss out on this extremely smart and highly relevant game.

Prior to the upcoming patch (OB64) and bugs, glitches, and balancing issues aside, the game itself is pretty fun. The levels for the most part are well made, the characters are fun to use, in-game items always spice the game up, and the cards adds more flavor to the game and make it more interesting. Out of all Hero Shooters out there, this COULD'VE been the very best.
However, here's the problem: The new upcoming card system stinks a lot. The current card system the game has is arguably already fine. You pick up 5 of them, adjust their levels, and go fourth. It's as simple as that and it what makes the game unique out of every Hero Shooters available as far as I know. The new card system, on the other hand, is not. If it's you're first time playing, every card you own will start at level one and if you're an old timer, it starts at 3. If you wish to increase their level, you have to unlock cards which is only restricted in chests, and this is when one of the main problem begins. As if RNG isn't enough, the only way to purchase chests is through either in-game currency or real life money and it takes time to get enough in-game currency to purchase chests ,as far as I'm concerned, so you know what that means, you either pay up to get better cards faster or suffer with how slow it takes to purchase chests.
Speaking of the new card system, another problem pops up. In ranked mode, all cards are set to level 3 by default and in casual, it's a free-for-all since a player whose cards are level 1 can face a player with level 2+ cards bringing in unfare advantages. There's plenty of problem that can be seen but one thing for sure, the freely adjustable card level, which people love by the way, is now gone. A system that makes it shine from its competitors is now dull. Even if all cards are now unlocked, it still sucks.
Overall, don't play the game (for now anyway). This new card system is very problematic that tarnishes a decent game. Even if they decided to cancel or backtrack, the damage has already been done. People's trust with the company Hi-Rez is now gone as if people weren't already mad at them because of Tribes a few years ago. I know this game is still in beta and that in its full release, some problems may be gone but we have now see how desperate this company has for money. This is not a good way to gain profit. This could be the last profitable game they ever have (until now anyway) unless for some reason, they managed to pull in some suckers on their new games or they learned from their mistakes which I doubt will happen anytime soon.

What can be said about this game? Hmm. Well the first thing you should know is that you shouldn't judge this game by its graphics. The post apocalyptic world many of the modern day gamers are used to seeing is rendered in 3D and significantly different in both story and atmosphere. This world seems almost filthy and bland by comparison.
But that's the trick of the matter. This game decieves you thinking its some lame top down RPG when it is actually one of the most immersive games *ever made*
In Fallout 2 your character creation really, really, matters. The way you design every stat and trait has ramifications that will help or hinder you throughout the game. People in the world really notice, and not in a stupid skyrim "I see you're a fair hand with a blade" generic line noticing either. You'll converse with them and they'll immediately notice if you are a dumb hulking brute or a sly sneaky sort. If you are handsome or ugly people will comment on it. Hookers will upcharge you if you are too ugly or simple. Murder or hurt enough people and the world hears about it, townspeople will run from you when you walk by, while criminals will nod respectfully as you pass. The way you make and play your character changes everything.
Lets just start with Intelligence. If your character is of average intelligence, you can proceed through most of the game normally. But should you have high intelligence many options open up when dealing with more intellectual people or subjects. You can figure out solutions to problems that a less intelligent character couldn't, to the point where some boss fights or enemies can be defeated with a simple dialog option because your character was smart enough to see through the problem.
The same goes for charisma. A charismatic character will be able to talk his way out of incredible situations. Heck, if you are persuasive enough you can sleep with a mob boss's wife and convince him you were just lost. You know, just lost, in her bedroom. There are places where you can talk down suicidal bombers or convince hard hearted racists against ghouls to change their ways and be more accepting.
Every single stat is like this. Stronger characters will be able to open doors and force their way through situations others can't. More perceptive characters will see hidden traps and doors to avoid enemies and change the way confrontations happen. Every type of character made will have unique ways to solve any problem and this feels *so* good.
Maybe you want to be a big stupid brute who is barely smart enough to speak but can kill anything with ease. Maybe you want to be the cocky sharpshooter who is perceptive, smart, and good with a gun but can't take much of a hit. Short version:
Very good open world zombie hack n' slash, brings together all the best features of the previous games without following their shortcomings. 9.5/10, Buy this game.
Long version:
Dead Rising 3 is a prime example of how game developers should make follow-up titles. All too often you see a direct sequel improve on the second, followed by a game that only barely changes the formula, sometimes ending in an endless regurgitation of the source game in various forms (Call of Duty, Battlefield, Halo, Borderlands, Resident Evil?). So far, Capcom has avoided doing this to the Dead Rising franchise. This game improves on Dead Rising 2 in a multitude of areas, and is definitely my favorite Dead Rising game.
Level Design in DR3 is improved by merging all the game's areas into one giant GTA-size map. This is a brilliant move, and eliminates loading screens (minus the ones for cutscenes) during gameplay, which improves on the immersion. The vehicles are much more varied, and are extremely useful in a map this size. The only downside to this is that many areas are unavoidably locked until a specific time in the storyline, although many things can still be discovered at any time.
Vehicles are much more varied, and are practically essential on a map this large, making them even more fun. Add to that new vehicle combinations, and you immediately get a game that definitely sets itself apart from GTA ripoffs. The way zombies realistically cling to and bounce off the vehicles is also awesome.
There are tons of combo weapons in the game, significantly more than the other two games. Unfortunately, you have to find and unlock every blueprint before you can craft the item; however, it really won't matter in the end because you only have to pick them up once (even online games count), and it is genuinely fun finding the blueprints. There is also a new skill that allows you to improve your crafting, which, once maxed, makes using desired combo weapons a breeze.
The skills menu is a new addition, with the previous games choosing which skills you acquired at every level (why didn't they think of this before?). This is a huge improvement, and allows a truly custom character during the first few playthroughs. Unfortunately(?), over time all players can just max out their characters on all skills.
Speaking of menus, this game has all the menus you would expect from a modern PC game. Unlike the previous titles, you have full control of graphical detail, voice communication, controls, etc. You might think this is an unspoken rule, but often ported games like this fall for this oversight.
Capcom brilliantly decided to split the game into two main game modes: Story and Hardcore.
Story is more relaxing, with no (visible) counting timer, and more time to complete all the side quests. I was able to easily get all sidequests and still have time to explore in story mode on my first playthrough. Additionally, you can save at any time (minus a few spots) by pausing the game. Auto-save is also enabled on this mode.
Hardcore is the difficulty anyone who played previous Dead Rising titles will remember. Tougher enemies, less player health, and the game is only saved when the player visits a bathroom or porta-potty. Players have less time than story mode, although plenty of time to simply rush the storyline. Additionally, due to the new skill system, once a player is fully maxed, even hardcore mode will not present much of a challenge.
Capcom really nailed it on this one, addressing every complaint I had with the previous title (on steam). The graphics are awesome, and I personally had no problem with performance on two separate computers. There are brief moments when the game will hiccup or crash, but no more than your average PC game (especially a port like this). I would definitely recommend this game as a purchase, especially if you can snag it during a sale like I did.
My only complaints:
The lead developer decided it was a good idea to make the DLC singleplayer only. The ENTIRE game is co-op, except for the DLC. I watched an interview where he was asked why, and responded with something about "enhancing the story experience". Honestly I view this as a lazy mistake, with co-op either being overseen, or simply dropped due to the difficulty. In my opinion, this game is much more fun with co-op, making the DLC relatively dull (also no outfits/clothing in the DLC, to 'enhance the experience'?). And who REALLY plays Dead Rising game for the story? I feel like the DLC was slapped on unfinished, when it could have been a legitimate addition to the rest of this gem.
Also,
The online co-op can sometimes have lots of issues between some players. Some online matches I play fine for hours, and others I crash out or disconnect every few minutes (keep in mind this is with people I am skyping just fine, so not internet issues).

This game is an experience, and I'm really glad I forced myself to complete it to the end. Definetely one of the smartest and unique ideas I have ever seen, some of whom involve the player, personally. Without spoiling anything, this game is a must-play if only for the story, a very deep journey through the minds of three different characters. The attachment, the emotion, the pacing, the twists, all come together in this 30 hour experience to form one incredibly gripping tale.
As for the gameplay, it suffers from very repetitive combat, especially the hacking sequences, which are very simplistic, boring and useless. The hack-and-slash is super fun at first, but will bore you after a while. What's done really well were the seamless transitions from 3D combat to a 2D side-scroller. To give you an idea, the best parts of the game occur about 20 hours in, after it forces you to complete the begining of the game twice. However, it really is worth it to see it through to the end, as it all culminates in a very intense and satisfying finale.

From an RPG standpoint, you have your usual boring sidequests (which are mostly fetchquests) and lots of combat customizations via plug-in chips that modify your attacks and shooting abilities. There is absolutely no armor customization, which I feel should've been added, but I was well satisfied with the hub world, the shops and the typical resource micromanagement of a role-playing game. Nier Automata perfectly demonstrates how the videogame medium can push the boundaries of storytelling further, if done well.

Definitely recommended, and no review will fully explain the scope of this game and what it entails. Don't miss this unique experience.

I bought the controller about a week ago. And I have been playing with it off and on, testing various genres of games and such. It's a replacement for the Xbox controller, with some games. But not all.
The sleek style is the most attractive to me. The touch pads were not what I was expecting. They feel like they are made from teflon, which gives it a very slick & slidy surface, at touch.
However, I'm not fond of the left pad. I imagine it's suppose to represent a d-pad button. But found that it needs a bit too much pressure to use as a straight up D-pad for older titles like platformers.
On games like Skyrim, it felt almost like a natural fit. As if the game was specifically made for this controller. Granted, depending on the many user created configs you choose, you will have to tinker around with both the controller, and the game configurations, before you get the right adjustments where it feels right.
Older titles like Quake and Serious Sam were a mess to control. It didn't matter what user configs I used. I just found it cumbersome to move the camera around normally, without it zig-zagging all over the place. Often, the vertical axis was to blame. I'm not sure if this is a mistake of the developers, or just a problem with old software.
But then using the controller for games like Doom and Duke Nukem 3D, with mouse looking turned off, made it playable.  It felt just as doable as playing these games on Xbox Arcade.
I also tested it out on Civ 5 and Simcity. For the most part, it was a fine transition for both games. No issues with control, or moving the cursor around. A minor complaint would be just having to adjust the mouse sensitivity, because out of the box, it feels like your jumping logs or something on a pond, with the cursor.
Terraria is another game I've tested. And well... your better off buying the PS4 version if you want to play it from your couch. That's just my opinion of course. I didn't like it much.
Non-Steam games can be a hit or miss with this sucker. It's doable of course. But you'll find yourself having to really doing some changing of things in order to get it work properly. Also I'm not sure if this is set in stone, but in order to use the controller on these games, you have to add the game to your library on Steam.
I'm not fond of having to use Big Picture mode for everything. I understand why they went this route. But as someone who primarily plays his game from a PC and not a couch, it's not needed in my opinion.
I was able to get some console emulators to work with it though. Although, I don't recommend using the controller for  Project64. You're better off sticking with an Xbox/PS controller for that.. or an actual N64 controller, is a better idea.
Now the question is would I recommend this controller to people? It depends on your willingness to adapt to it. I think if you come from using an Xbox or PS4 controller, you'll find adjusting to it fine. The only complaint I have is where Steam decided to put the XYAB buttons. They're placed where the right analog stick would be on an Xbox controller. That was the hardest learning curve for me to get over so far.
The saving grace for this thing would be having a left analog stick to go to. Thank God they included that, or else I wouldn't even bother with it.
Overall it's not a bad controller. It's just different. Some games will work fine. Others will probably be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to get right. And some just don't make the cut, in my book.  I believe where this thing will shine is when newer titles are built with the controller in mind. It has a lot of potential.

I'm writing this at a time where I'm very...let down..by Paladins. OB64.
Anyway, the pros... yeah, this was a fun kinda casual competetive hero shooter/moba. Overwatch clone? Sort of, but with enough identity to make it fun. Also the card system allowed for customization of your characters, much like the talent trees do in Heroes of the Storm.
The grind was there, but overall I earned enough gold and essence to get the stuff I wanted. I also spent some real money on a few packs, and a few cosmetics. It was worth it.
With OB64, they're essentially getting rid of casual queue, the one that most players play. They are changing the card system to introduce a *huge* grind wall, or you're forced to pay literally $1000+ to level your cards up to 5 by getting a crazy amount of duplicates from lootboxes.
If your cards aren't level 5, you're screwed. You'll get stomped without any real chance to fight back. An example:
Your Bob, his punch deals 500 damage with the level 1 card.
The enemy Bob, his punch deals 2500 damage with a level 5 card.
You struggle to deal damage. Enemy hits you twice and you're dead.
Bob has 2000 health by default with a level 1 card.
Enemy Bob has the card at level 5, boosting his health to 5000.
In short: There's no more balance. It's ruined. They created an unfair playing field. Casual/Quick Play queue is extremely crap and frustrating to play now. Ranked isn't for everyone, and even if you play it, all cards are level 3, no exception. More fair, but doesn't really offer any balance either.
Devs have said they *will* push this patch on december 13th.
My thoughts? With the extremely negative reception of this patch, I foresee many players leaving, or playing less. It looks to me like they want to end this game, and make as much last ditch effort money off it as they can, right near the holidays. Overall, Paladins seems to be going the way of Tribes: Ascend and Global Agenda, two other now-dead HiRez games. They registered a new IP for a sort of PUBG clone. We'll see if that'll work, I guess.
I dunno if the devs really want this change, or if the management is pushing this through. Either way, it's going to happen. Also, it's useless to voice your concern about it to the devs. It usually gets ignored. Heck, my post offering constructive criticism and suggestions on alternative ways to handle these changes were deleted for no reason at all. It was not offensive, not one bit. And yet, that gets deleted. I made a post about my post getting deleted: Also removed within 5 minutes. -.- If that's how kind concerned players are being treated, then forget it. Let your game die, then. >.>
My advice: Don't spend money on Paladins. Don't even bother playing it. It's sad, because I genuinely enjoyed the game, despite the many bugs. I would recommend you at least try it, if it wasn't going in this direction. I'd say..wait at least 'till summer 2018 to see how it has survived. I myself will be keeping an eye on it from a distance. But the Paladins team has lost my trust, and my respect, with both the game changes and their treatment of my offered assistance.
If you *really* want to play a PvP focused MOBA-ish game by HiRez, play Smite. It's been out of beta for years and relatively stable and played by millions. I've certainly enjoyed it since I started playing, and I'm nearing my third year of playing Smite. It's not perfect, but it's heading in a better direction than Paladins.
So sadly, no, I can't recommend this game to anyone. Not unless they fix all the crap they're breaking with OB64. No more lootboxes. No more grind2win or pay2win. No more unfair playing field. Fix the bugs. The random ending of matches, to name one. Or the voice/chat mute buttons no longer working. And a plethora of others.

For fans of the original title from 2000, this game is everything you could want and more. Without spoilers, the storyline was engrossing, weaving all the characters together into a network of conspiracy and intrigue. The time I needed to play through the game first-time was about 50 hours, so you're getting your $$'s worth in gaming content. The characters you encounter are memorable and unique in their own ways. (The Chinese still have bad voice-acting, but thats no negative). Social persuasion was a part of the interaction with key characters as well as in the storyline. I'll admit, some of the conversations to convince somebody got pretty intense; hearing what they have to say in response to your own.
The Combat is an interesting place to address. The mechanics are largely successful in allowing varied gameplay across the missions. If you want to stealth, there are ways to stealth. If you want to be Rambo, you can be Rambo (just expect a bit tougher experience). While going Rambo can get you through a mission, the game rewards the player for being "ghostly", or not detected by the enemy. The maps and locations gave many different approaches to get to an objective or in a firefight. Vents are sometimes seen in walls to allow the hiding of bodies or escaping from fight heat.
The vast array of augmentations allows the player to shape Adam Jensen into the character you feel comfortable playing as. One of the things I liked about the augmentation system is that it didn't force any down your throat. When you collect Praxis Kits for augmentation upgrades, you have the choice to apply them or not. An interesting game playthrough worth considering is a No-Aug run, where you never upgrade (out of the thoughts of Jensen's aug-opinions).
Overall, after completing the game myself, I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys story-driven gameplay and well-executed stealth mechanics. Combining engrossing storyline with gameplay mechanics and player-choice, I rate this game a 9.5/10.

Vehicle Simulator is, well, a vehicle simulator that was originally released in 2009 by Quality Simulations. Six years later, Vehicle Simulator has made its way on to Steam bringing all the original content as well as some free DLC packs which include some of the best mods which have been released for the game. Vehicle Simulator allows you to take control of aircraft, naval vehicles and cars in single player and multiplayer. I haven’t tried out the multiplayer and I’m not too sure how it actually works so this review is based entirely on the singleplayer portion of the game. It’s also worth mentioning that for aircraft I’ve played the game with a T-Flight HOTAS and for naval vehicles I used mouse & keyboard.
Full disclosure: A review copy was provided by the developer.
Being a six year old game, Vehicle Simulator obviously isn’t the best looking game. If you’re used to playing older games such as FSX (though FSX does look better than VS in my opinion) then it shouldn’t be too much of an issue for you but if you’re a bit of a graphics nut you might not enjoy it so much. The base game vehicles are all great, looking about as good as they can, given the game’s age, however the vehicles included in the add-on packs are very hit and miss, some of them look just as good as the base game vehicles with other ones looking pretty rough. Obviously, how good the add-on vehicles look hasn’t really got anything to do with the devs but since you will want mods to expand the library of vehicles in the game I feel it’s worth mentioning.
As with most simulators of this sort the main appeal of the game, in my eyes at least, is the free flight (or the equivalent for boats/cars) but VS does feature scenarios for you to try out, you can even make your own! The scenarios are usually pretty simple, such as fly from point A to point B but some of them are far more interesting such as cargo runs or mid-air engagements. Free flight is self-explanatory, you just fly (or boat, is that a verb?) around any area you wish at your own pace for the simple purpose of exploration!
VS has several different locations for you to explore, mainly in Southern Europe but there are a couple in the US and the Caribbean. Each location has its own scenarios, the number of scenarios depends on which location you’re looking at, with some having more than others. While the number of locations available in the base game with the free add-on packs isn’t particularly impressive (locations in particular, there are a reasonable amount of scenarios) there are plenty more to be downloaded from the VS add-on library website.
One of the really cool things about VS’ gameplay is that you can create and run scripts in the game, VS also includes three pre-made script scenarios and more are available as mods. If you know how to create them you really can do some cool things but the scenarios available are also pretty cool to watch, such as an F-86 taking down a little Cessna.
As with all simulators, the realism is incredibly important and while I’m no expert, VS feels reasonably realistic. The aerodynamics seem to be pretty good and for the most part aircraft handling felt about right for the size and mass of the aircraft in question. Naval vehicles also seemed pretty realistic to me but I know a lot less about boats and submarines than I know about planes and helicopters. Sound effects also contribute to a game’s realism, sadly VS’ sound effects are pretty hit and miss, with more misses than hits. While some of the sound effects, mainly the engine sounds for base game vehicles, sounded reasonably realistic other sound effects weren’t so great and I often found myself wondering what the sound effect I was hearing was actually supposed to be. For a couple of aircraft I also felt that the variation of sound effects depending on where the chase camera was positioned was off though that may be dependent on the mod-makers rather than the game itself. In some cases the engine sounds would completely cut out unless the camera was positioned directly behind the aircraft which of course, is not very realistic.
If you can look past its dated graphics, VS is a solid simulator with enough free add-ons to keep you entertained for quite a while. While the non-sale price is a little steep for what the game offers I’d say it’s well worth purchasing at 25% off or more.

Canis Canem Edit, Or Bully is a good game. It is Rockstar's most unappreciated game. It is brilliantly paced, has excellent writing, has surprisingly solid gameplay mechanics, looks decent for its age and has great characters and voice acting. It's splashed with Rockstar Games humour, and is more than mini-GTA.
However, the PC version is a poor port. The PC controls are a mess, so you need a a game controller to have effective control in all situations. It's also locked at 30 FPS by default, although there is a crack that removes the frame limiter, but to use this, you need another method of keeping the frame rate below 60FPS, or else it will run too fast.
And after all of that effort, if you have a new system, during some instances of running the game, it will stutter, and nothing can stop the stuttering other than restarting until you get lucky. My old system got had zero stutter after Patch 1.2, and the 60FPS fan patch, but my new, more powerful system almost always stutters, I have to restart and restart until it decides to not stutter. It can run with no stutter, but it's a matter of luck.
Because of this, I recommend buying it on console, specifically XBOX 360 or Wii for the additional content that is also on the PC version. This game is worth playing, but the efforts to optimise the game on PC are terrible. It's also on available on Xbox One through backwards compatibility.
This is a modern classic, but the awful porting drags the entire package down.

Too much innovation with not enough standarization. I grabbed this because I wanted something to replace the xbox 1 controller I use for my pc gaming, I also wanted to start playing a handful of games I've got which need a mouse/keyboard to play from my couch. Sadly the steam controller really fails at everything. For all of it's gimmicks it simply cannot replace a keyboard/mouse and it's a horrible controller placement. For GTA 5, ARK, The Division Beta, Vermintide, Watch Dogs and more I simply couldn't stand the Steam controller after about 15 minutes. Everything is un-intuitive, and the biggest screw up was putting the buttons where analog stick traditionally go and putting the touch pad where the buttons go. It's not JUST a matter of familiarity, which I'm sure it partly is, but it's a matter of accessability. Pressing A to jump on the steam controller is a stretch, awkward and slow compared to a classic design. Their placement isn't just different, it's inferior. As for the keyboard/mouse titles, like Dawn of War, Company of Heros and Natural Selection 2, it's a nightmare. It doesn't come close to matching the mouse for accuracy (especially when in mouse emulation mode) and while Valve tried to make the controller highly mappable, everything turns into button combos to try to make up for the lack of a keyboard with all of it's keys. The problem there in though is that instead of remembering a single key for a single action/ability/etc, you have to remember a combo, Hold Left of Dpad+A/B/X/Y. It might not sound like it, but it's slower and a lot more taxing to remember the different combos than to just use a keyboard. It's not as fast or percise as a keyboard. Again, in less than 15 minutes of trying for all those games I was forced to unplugged the controller and go back to the old mouse/keyboard combo.
Overall I'm sad and let down. From the reviews I thought this might be a good alternative to my current setup. Sadly though it's entirely useless. I can't find a single game where this is my preferred method of play other than ONE GAME. Elite Dangerous, which supports no controller, is without a doubt to me easier with this controller than anything else. The problem of course being Elite Dangerous is HORRIBLE, so ohwell.

I like the steam controller. It has positives and negatives.

2. Any game can use it.
Now i'll take about this in the negative side too. Here is what's positive. An game you want to play can use this whether you use it with the big picture mode or just as any other controller. It can work. It doesn't always, but it can.
3. Wireless
Not a giant positive but I thought I would mention it. Many controllers have wires that contrict the enjoyment. This does not have wires so I could freely move around. I know that there are a lot of wireless controllers before this one.

Negatives

Now the steam controller can be used with a lot of games, and then some are hard to work with. Certain games I've played required me to use big picture mode to actually get the controller working for them. I can't gripe too much about it but I would have like to just plug in the controller and then play any game.

Skullgirls (more on the control sceme of the game. It makes a very odd control layout with a controller)

In the end, it comes down to your thoughts. Do you play a lot of controller recommended games? Will you use this controller? Are you wanting to pay $50 for this? Think about what you would answer. I personally recommend it.

Been a console gamer since the atari days, recently made the jump to PC full time a few years ago and picked up one of these in January.
This controller is fantastic! The programability of this thing is way beyond my expectations.
you can customize just about every little aspect of every thing on this device.
With the "shift" function you can pretty much assign double duty to any part of the controller. you will have the primary function and then when you hold down the modifer that same part now can act in a different way.
Example: For my Star Citizen scheme I have the right pad as a mouse functionality but if I hold down the left grip it turns from mouse input to right analog stick input. In Doom 3 when I soft pull the left trigger and touch the left pad it will bring up a button pad to which I assigned the numbers corresponding to the key board numbers for directly selecting a weapon instead of having to cycle through the with the bumpers. I think you can assign up to 16 keys total on one button pad and each one can be assigned any key on the keyboard or mouse and you can double that by assigning the right pad as well.
The biggest hurdle if you are used to a traditional controller is re-training your muscle memory for a standord layout.
Next thing is how long it can take to customize to your specific liking, but once done you can save that configuration and it saves per game so when you launch that game next  time it will load up the config you have created.
Highly reccomended. May not be perfect for all scenarios but it's pretty damn good for must of them. Very happy with this controller. I have officially retired my 360 controller.

I was afraid that Fallout 2 might've been too outdated for me at first, that it wouldn't be entertaining or worth the time.
Oh boy I was wrong. I'd say it's the best Fallout game I've played so far (haven't played the first one yet but I'll get to that someday).
The combat feels satisfying and its turn-based gameplay seems to have aged well, though, it might be a bit slow at times and can be very punishing because of them lethal critical hits. But there's a lot of options to fiddle around with to personalize the type of experience you want, same goes with the game's great characterization system where you can create a lot of different builds.
Game's tough at the start but if you give it time and try to make some progress you'll surely get well rewarded, because of the loot you get after hard-fought battles feels worthy enough for you to want progress even further.
The dialogues are really well written too, there are a lot of different options you can choose from depending on what stats you invested in, which can lead to some really amusing conversations. For instance, high intelligence with the speech skill mostly provides with the most available options, but even low intelligence comes with unique dialogue or reactions from NPCs throughout the world.
Choices you make does actually feel like it has consequences, it also affect the game's ending to a large scale. So the replayability is there if you want to tackle the game with an entirely different approach.
The whole plot in this game is also a pretty thrilling experience the more progress you make, it's very gritty and has this dark atmosphere to it which I love. I also do think the game's soundtrack and visuals have a big impact on the game's atmosphere and that it's really well done.
I'm happy I decided to pick this game up, even bought it during a sale for a few dollars.
So money well spent I'd say. If you're a fan of the RPG genre you should definitely get this game, Fallout 2 is the classic RPG you wouldn't want to miss.

I hope I don't have to explain why I am stronger than Chris Redfield and still couldn't stop the zombies in time... All the clothes, blueprints, levelling, grinding, quests, looking for weapons, and clothes...
All the stores, every one having different outfits and almost every building having a collectible or a blueprint for a weapon or vehicle It takes the massive scale of gta or saints row and scales it down so it can give you more buildings and more rooms to access that look and feel like an actual setting. Liquor stores, toy shops and malls so strategecly placed to the point that you will always miss the trun to find the other stores. Quests that take you all around the map so many times. you start seeing garbage on the stret instead of zombies. They fall flat as long as you're prepared.
But even without the zombies. The overall setting and internal detail of the city give you a reason to go into every room, unlock every door,  run along rooftops, fight through the trash. I haven't felt this involved in a game since morrowind. Along your way to quests, you'll find reasons to get side tracked, get lost, and do other things aside from save the occasional survivor. (will not feel occasional if you don't do the sidequests) I feel like I am awaiting the empty feeling when I find everything, and do all of the things that need doing.
The options for creation and customization are unique and serve up the desired plate of diversity. light sabers, shoryukens, staves, football rockets, teddy bear turrets, scythes, hammers, blanka lightning, disco afros, mascot costumes sport outfits, It's a taste of everything from your typical saints row playthrough, albiet a little less, but in the same breath, the amount of internal detail makes it feels exponentially more immersive to play in as most of your time playing feels like a giant mall, you play on the street, go shopping, play on top of buildings, go to a resturaunt, jump through mansions, run through sewers. and all of it means something, the few locked doors to you offer things you can't find anywhere, so every quest has a little taste of looking elsewhere, finding clothes, blueprints, or picking up things you passed by, or died and couldn't find again, it's all worth your time to the point it feels like there's not really any zombies unless you're travelling. It's a fantastic feeling. The psychos, or side bosses, have their own thing going on, and are all different and fun to interact with.
If you take too long getting lost along the map, you can jump back chapters and do them faster, without looking for clothes or blueprints, because you retain them. Nut I honestly don't know If I would like what the game would feel like outside of the mindless exploration. It feels like you're the last person on earth and you can run amok and do and take whatever you want. I'm not sure I'm supposed to be enjoying that idea that much, but I do.
There are drawbacks, such as the cars going in reverse in the most painfully slow speed for like 6 seconds, or some cars getting stuck under other cars, allies being useless as always, The save system letting you down a lot, resulting in backtracking that is almost never as fruitful as the first time you did it, albiet faster. the fact maximum level and stats is easy to get to, and that certain weapons are so complicated to make that they are more useful to grab out of the closet or not use at all, and that you have to use mods to pull all of the unique hairs in the game from outfits to be used standalone.
The only reason I mashed all of the drawbacks together is because they don't linger for very long, You'll save more if you die or crash a lot, you'll stop carrying followers if they always die, And you'll stop holding onto super combo parts in hope they'll turn up. After that, It's litterally a serene stroll in good ol zombieland.
I hope people enjoy it as much as I do, also, it's co op, so force a friend to get it, and go kill zombies. And more importantly, Do everything else, and sort of kill zombies because you have to.

Been a console gamer since the atari days, recently made the jump to PC full time a few years ago and picked up one of these in January.
This controller is fantastic! The programability of this thing is way beyond my expectations.
you can customize just about every little aspect of every thing on this device.
With the "shift" function you can pretty much assign double duty to any part of the controller. you will have the primary function and then when you hold down the modifer that same part now can act in a different way.
Example: For my Star Citizen scheme I have the right pad as a mouse functionality but if I hold down the left grip it turns from mouse input to right analog stick input. In Doom 3 when I soft pull the left trigger and touch the left pad it will bring up a button pad to which I assigned the numbers corresponding to the key board numbers for directly selecting a weapon instead of having to cycle through the with the bumpers. I think you can assign up to 16 keys total on one button pad and each one can be assigned any key on the keyboard or mouse and you can double that by assigning the right pad as well.
The biggest hurdle if you are used to a traditional controller is re-training your muscle memory for a standord layout.
Next thing is how long it can take to customize to your specific liking, but once done you can save that configuration and it saves per game so when you launch that game next  time it will load up the config you have created.
Highly reccomended. May not be perfect for all scenarios but it's pretty damn good for must of them. Very happy with this controller. I have officially retired my 360 controller.

If you want a breakdown of its features and a list of games with little bits talking about how the controller worked for each one, you're not going to find it here. This review will cover much broader pros and cons of the controller as a device. I do not want to hear "why didnt you talk about the gyro" or "but its customization", that's now what this review is about.
With that out of the way lets talk about what it does and doesnt do.
Does it allow you to play games without controller support?
If the profile loads, yes.
Does it work with games that have native controller support?
If the profile loads, yes.
Why do I say "if the profile loads"?
Because steam will very frequently refuse to load a game's profile. Especiallyover the past month steam will outright refuse to load a game's profile and will instead load the "default" profile or sometimes my "desktop" profile. Restarting steam will sometimes fix it, othertimes im forced to give up.
Will it allow you to play non steam games?
Most of the time no. Steam's ability to run non steam games has gotten worse and worse since the controllers launch. Games that I used to play regularly through steam, no longer work at all and steam refuses to see them running after being launched. They supposedly fixed this by allowing steam to detect a running .exe and load the correct profile. This has not been the case for me at all, infact Its a fight to get even the desktop profile I made to load when I turn the controller on (again is a problem that is currently considered "Fixed" so I really have no hope of it getting better).
So what is this game controller good for if not for games?
The one thing I will say in favor of this controller is how amazing it is for controlling your PC without having to sit at a desk or controlling a HTPC without using a wireless mouse/keyboard. The trackpad is simply incredible and thanks to a recent update with one button press an onscreen keyboard pops up giving you full mouse and keyboard emulation. This is pretty much the only thing I use the controller for now. I use it to control my HTPC, and I also use it to navigate windows and launch games which I end up playing on my PS4 controller when im on the couch.
When the software and firmware matures im sure this controller will be a cheap and easy way to replace a traditional Xinput controller. But it's not there... not even close. In its current state the only thing it will replace is HTCP peripheral, and do a damn fine job at it!
So if you are looking to buy this as a controller replacment, I would advise againt it. Its simply not worth the headache. The customization is great; but in addition to its abysmal Uplay and Origin game support, I would prefer my stuff just work over fancy bells and whistles that only save me the trouble of downloading a different third party customization tool and using that to make custom profiles for my PS4 or 360 pads.
If you are looking to buy this for the ability to play games without native controller support, I would say wait till the software matures a bit. It is incredible being able to play classic games like Doom or Fallout with a controller and its just as cool playing something more modern that should never be able to be played with a controller like Guild Wars 2. Its not just scraping by like using Xpadder to make a mouse profile on your 360 pad, it works and feels great. But again this goes back to how poorly this thing works with non steam games. Simple .exes without launchers or clients to launch from seem to work just fine, but its a coin toss if it'll work with what will prob make a bulk of your non steam collection (Origin, Uplay, and MMOs with multiple launchers).
The only instance I can recommend this game is for use with an HTPC or if you simply wish to control a PC from anywhere but the desk. I mean this too, if this is your intended purpose for the steam controller, buy it right now. It easily destroyes even the best wireless mouse/keyboards simple because of its easy to use form factor. Ive handed this to people ranging from 8 to 65 and everyone was able to use it to control my PC after a moment of explaining what does what. Its impossible to explain how good it feels navigating windows (once it decides to load the correct profile) and how well designed the keyboard for it is.
Aside from that singular instance. I would steer clear of the Steam Controller. I bought this thing on launch, used it for hundreds of hours across dozens of games in every possible genre, and I absolutly loved it for the first few months I owned it. Hell I even wrote a positive glowing review. And while they added alot of cool new features, they have broken so many core features in the process that simply trying to use the controller for its intended purpose its nothing short of a battle. They keep claiming to fix things but I rarely see improvments, and a few things that just worked before (like loading the correct profiles) only started not working after the updates that claimed to fix them. I started out singing praise for this device, but as time went on, less and less of its features worked for me. As stated before if I want to even use it for my HTPC I have to make sure I full screen steam to get my desktop profile to load up. Its not the end of the world but its a pointless extra step I need to take to use this controller and valve's stance on the issue is its fixed. I want to like this controller again. Its great when it works but no full retail product should have this many issues. I paid for a finished product, not to be a tester for one.
To save some of you time, I personally do not care if "I dont have these issues". I do, and this is my review. If you really feel so compelled to defend the controller from people who arent so lucky write your own review.

Keeping my old rant to show that I was wrong and to not have to retype the original problems.    I relied on having a 'master config' for all games using the 'desktop configuration'.  X-input buttons for Desktop was specifically disabled in an update.  (ref. a Forum post of mine with a steam rep)  With that update other issues were presented.  Following some guided troubleshooting, the Beta client fixes my other problems.
I still cannot recommend the Steam controller now except two uses:
- Using a controller to play a game that does not support controllers and has more keys than normal controllers have buttons.
- Using a controller for precise FPS games. With some effort to configure the right pad to your preference, it can work really well for aiming.
There is certainly no longer a reason to buy more than one steam controller, I find that PS4 controllers with DS4Windows is much easier for the "pick-up and play" or "party" experience (even easier if you have 360 controllers).  X-input desktop mode used to provide that experience, making the Steam controller a good default choice, especially for games not executed by the client.  This usefulness has been disabled.  The official response about hooking to games sounds legit, but I still miss the option.

Mid 2017 Review----------------------
I have 4 of these things now.  And I want to love them and hope that they continue forever; because when they work, they are magical.....but that doesnt happen much anymore.
My biggest gripe....Going offline makes steam forget all your settings...even local ones. Nothing more frustrating than getting a group of people together, hooking things up, and then spending an hour trying to keep steam from giving them all the same default keyboard commands.  Then when you give up and go home, it all works again thanks to internet.  Every time I think that I've fixed this, the situation happens again.  Even if I save my configs to local....going offline resets to the default with no saved profiles available to choose.
They have become more useless than Razer products for anyone that games in places other than their hoome with constant internet.  Why can't I save at least 1 default profile to a controllers hardware?  Cant say memory space; 1GB xd cards are under .50 in places.
And even if you have ideal internet, I occasionally have issues where Steam just doesnt want to enable the changes I made.  Sometimes, it takes multiple savings and a restart to get a setting to stick.  Why?  It's all in the cloud.  Hell, if the internet is spotty, the configs sometimes wont let me bind gamepad buttons at all.  They just dont appear in the menu.
Unless you absolutely want to play certain keyboard heavy games with a controller,  just go and pickup some used 360 controllers and plug those in.  No hassle.  No lost settings.  Just sit down and game.
I'll probably change this back to a positive review when it's friendlier to people who travel often.  Or if they unbind them from Big Picture and have a driver setup like Logitech products.
Early 2016 Review--------------------------------

Recommendations:
Set Non-Steam games and emulators to run through Steam.
Set Big Picture mode to run in a window.  Solves many issues with games that don't like switching back and forth when changing control settings.
-Either create a shortcut to Steam or use one pinned to the taskbar.  R-click > "Properties" > "Shortcut" >
-set Target: "C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\Steam.exe" -windowed
-You can also add -tenfoot to always startup in Big Picture.
Learn to backup/install controller profiles manually.  Custom settings don't travel with your steam profile.

I've had this controller for about two/three months, initially I didn't like it, however I decided to wait it out - I thought with more updates and firmware updates it would improve, well there have been quite a few firmware updates and regular updates since then, and yes I am in the Steam Beta... Well I still don't like it and cannot recommend it.
I have not given up on this controller yet, I still hope in future it will get better; but there is no reason for me to use this controller over my existing PS4, Xbox One or Keyboard and Mouse... None, and I'm the intended market, someone who prefers controllers over Keyboard and Mouse and yet wants the precision and customisation options offered by Keyboard and Mouse.
I've spent a lot of time, energy and frustration trying to find configurations I like but none of them are are as good as using a regular controller or keyboard and mouse... I have spent significantly more time trying to get a good configuration for me than actually playing games with it. Every now and then I will pick a game, go off and try to find a good configuration - albeit creating my own, using community made ones and spend hours tweaking but I will always come to the same conclusion - I'm going back to PS4, Xbox One or Keyboard and Mouse
I'd say the biggest issue this controller has is the right trackpad; it does an
job at emulating an analog stick and it does an ok job an emulating a mouse - The controller works best when you can have everything but the right trackpad assigned to a gamepad and then you have the right trackpad assigned to a mouse - Unfortunately very few games have simultaneous keyboard and mouse support; even then it's ergonomic choices are still questionable.
The second issue I have with the controller is the position of the ABXY buttons, they are way too far away, I physically have to stretch my thumb to reach the X button and that isn't very comfortable. Note I do not have this issue with PS4 or Xbox One controllers.
I really wanted to like this controller, why wouldn't I? I spent £39 + Shipping so it's in my best interest to like something I purchased, but I simply cannot recommend anyone to pick this up; even with future firmware and updates I still don't think I will ever choose this over my PS4 controller, Xbox One controller or Keyboard and Mouse.
The Steam Controller is meant to be comfortable, like an XO and PS4 controller, it should allow you to sit-back and relax while offering the precision and customisation of Keyboard and Mouse... I feel it suceeds in none of these areas. It's no more precise than an Xbox One or PS4 controller (in many games I find it non-usable) and is even less comfortable.

Imagine you took all the Americana Juvinalia films (the Sandlot, Meatballs, Revenge of the Nerds, Porky's, A Christmas Story, etc), blended them into a fine paste and made a video game from it. That would be what Bully is.
I wish I could recommend it. I wish I could say its better because it's unique and can be a lot of fun, but it does get a bit stale by the middle of the game.
Gameplay wise, the missions are what you would guess. You egg houses, raid panties, french girls and all the stuff you'd expect from something of this genre. You learn different melee moves and you get ranged weapons, both of which are useful in many cases. There is a bit of variety in missions, but some of the missions are the same as in previous chapters, just with a difference of location and enemy.
Also, something really, really annoying: Sometimes if you fail a mission you will not get the chance to do it until the next day. I know the game has to punish you for failing, but I would have preferred to just restart the mission.
The story kind of wore on me after a while. I didn't really get attached to any of the characters because they wheeled them around like I was riding a rollercoaster past everyone in the school. I wasn't too thrilled that I had to go through all the factions pretty much doing the same types of missions in order to boost my reputation with them. There was a bit of predictability. I didn't really laugh as much as I would have expected from a comedy game. Though, the ending did get me super psyched and that made up for a lot of confusion during the middle of the game. It feels like you lose the purpose of the game near the middle.
The open world seems small at first glance, but it is designed excellently. There's a lot of nooks and crannies to get lost in. There's a few collectibles, but not the obscene amount that you see in most open world games.
The music is quite unique as well. The soundtrack is usually dominated by bass guitar with xylophone paired with celeste, which gives it a feel all its own. The problem is that some of the tracks aren't looped well and you'll be listening to 10 second clips stop then start again.
Also, in regards to the sound design, some of the dialogue, which is excellent, is drowned out by the sound effects and you'll frequently find yourself straining to listen.
I did run into one bug that caused the game to get stuck in a cutscene. I had to reload from an earlier point and that sucked.
I really want to recommend this game, but it has its share of problems. If you're looking for something different this isn't a terrible choice, but bear in mind that this game has a LOT of annoying issues.

Honestly, NIER: Automata is one of the best games I've ever played.  Definitely in my top five.  It's pretty much an improvement on the original NIER in almost every way, except the story itself, which I would say is ever-so-slightly better in the original NIER.  However, both stories are easily 10/10, so that's not saying much.
STORY (spoiler free):
So Automata takes place many thousands of years after the events of the original NIER.  Aliens have invaded and unleashed a seemingly endless army of machine lifeforms to annex the planet, pushing what little remains of humanity onto the moon.  Humanity, too few in numbers to initiate a counter attack of their own, rely on their androids to fight for them, launching a number of orbital bases to encircle the Earth, each holding the androids who would attempt to take back the planet.  Each attack, however, is met with defeat, as the machine lifeforms are too powerful and too numerous.  So both humanity and the already existing androids turn to a new breed of android soldiers called YoRHa, far more powerful than what came before, to finally end the war and take back Earth from the machines and their alien masters.  You play as two of these YoRHa androids: a battle model named 2B, and a scanner model named 9S.
The story is my type of convoluted, sci-fi awesomeness.  If you're a fan of books like "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" (AKA: the movie Blade Runner) or animes like "Neon Genesis Evangelion," "Ergo Proxy" and "Ghost in the Shell," this is going to be a real treat for you.
GAMEPLAY:
I can't really think of too many flaws with the gameplay.  From what I heard, the combat is not really as complex as some other Platinum games, like Bayonetta, but I had a fun time with it.  Automata, much like the original NIER, is an open world adventure game with RPG elements.  You follow a main storyline, while also taking on side quests along the way.  The side quests are admittedly a bit dull, but are very important, as they add to the overarching plot as well as character development for 2B and 9S.  Certain plot revelations will occur later on, which will be much more impactful depending on what side quests you did.
The difficulty is a bit of an oddity.  Other people have pointed it out, but Normal mode is a bit too easy, while Hard mode (at least at first) is way too punishing.  This doesn't really bother me all that much, but for other people who are looking for a happy medium, it sadly doesn't exist.  I would recommend playing the "tutorial" on Normal mode, and then switch to Hard mode after you reach your first save point.
MUSIC:
Just like the original NIER, it's amazing.  Nothing else needs to be said, really.
PORT:
This seems to be very hit-or-miss with people.  I think I'm one of the lucky ones who had little to no trouble getting this game to run on my PC using the FAR mod.  But other people have reported low fps and constant crashes.  If you don't have a PS4 and want to play this game, I would recommend buying it and then refunding it within two hours game time (the deadline for which you can refund a game on Steam) if it doesn't work properly.
OVERALL:
NIER: Automata is fantastic. I don't regret one penny I spent on it.  I beat this game several months ago, and not a day goes by when I don't think about it.
It's easily a 10/10.

Back in 2016 when this game came out I loved it, although like many, I had mixed feelings about the multiplayer. Coming back after update 6.66 to see how it fairs (along with what I missed in the dlc content) I was left plesantly surprised. I found myself really enjoying the directions that ID took with the multiplayer as it has really transformed into a game much like arena shooters of old. Firstly, weapon skill and trick shots have become a must, as the game isn't just about spamming a choke. Instead, you have to combo weapons with your quick switch to achieve near instant kills on an enemy, and ensure you have the upper hand in gunfights by collecting armor and health, not going in while damaged, or just generally only going in when you know you'll win the fight. You just kind of, run around in circles switch shotting with one of the many combos; rocketlauncher:shotgun, shotgun:super shotgun, sniper:shotgun, just to name a few. It seems like they addeed better mid range machine gun options as well, as the burst shot and lightning guns seem particularly effective to me, and the equipment choice in the loadout allows a lot of variety and strategy as it allows you to hold grenades or even what are essentially special abilities. For the hardcore complaining about the lack of weapon pick ups, the game actually has a much better system in my opinion, which limits these to certain weapons and demon runes, which really help to dictate those little combat zones without leaving fresh spawned players at a disadvantage. The only real issue I have with the multiplayer's current itteration, is the lack of key rebinding, as there is no number pad usage to switch weapons, and each action can only be bound once to keyboard, and once to mouse; i.e: weapon swap being bound to q by default; which is a minor gripe, but it takes some getting used to be honest. Anyways, I digress, I find myself enjoying this game enough that I'll be coming back to it periodically to get my fix off of overwatch. I think it's really enjoyable, and I reccomend any shooter fan to give the multiplayer a try and see if they enjoy it.
Multi-Player pros-
-fast paced
-skill based
-quick ttk, but low enough to react and make plays
-good map design
-load of content (dlc is free)
Multi-Player cons-
-key rebind feature is lacking
-small community
-poor reception upon launch

I did figure out the main plot at about the 10 minute point, but generally I very much enjoyed discovering another piece of the Fallout universe.

The overwhelmingly positive reviews others have left should convince anyone who hasn't played classic Fallout yet to change their ways, so I'm not even going to go into every aspect of the game.
As I've already mentioned, Fallout 2 is a lot more jokey than its predecessor, featuring a ghost, aliens, a super mutant magician, talking mole rats, Skynet, Mike Tyson, civil deathclaws, Tragic: The Garnering, scientologists named Juan Cruz and Vicki Goldman and the POTUS to name a few. If it's hard to imagine a story arc that incorporates all of these seamlessly then you're probably on to something. I can't say that all this humor is somehow bad though, just know that Fallout 1 and 2 are different and you may find the latter not quite what you would've expected.
I've read a few reviews that call Fallout 2 'slow' and being a total fanboy had to stop and think for a second to digest this criticism, but it's true. 2's story starts off really boring and I applaud any millennial that can sit through Arroyo and Klamath without deleting the game. Without using Cheat Engine or somesuch, shooting and missing a rat or gecko for the 23rd time really is for the dead-of-brain. But I swear from The Den and on the game improves by an order of magnitude with the high points coming in New Reno, which provides much to do in itself (like boxing and starring in porn) beside being a nexus for many quests from other towns.
A small annoyance I noticed during my female playthrough was that Fallout 2 is very obviously a game by guys, for guys. Male PCs get a whole extra ending for New Reno, can donate sperm to alleviate the inbreeding situation in Vault City and have dozens of extra pervy dialogue options to use compared to females who can at most suck D to save a few hundred caps here and there. Caps, by the way, which are infinite after you get to ~120% in gambling. Can't say I blame Black Isle too much though because if you think of how many people owned a computer in 1998, played games on it, had the intellectual capacity to grok RPGs and out of that tiny sliver of the population, how many were women, well... peddling encyclopedias at Bible study might have been a better business model than catering to girls with Fallout 2.
As customary with RPGs, save often and into different slots. I recommend always keeping around a save from the first second you arrive in a new marked location so you could replay it if need be.

To describe Nier properly, I'll start by speaking to the possible types of audience that this might attract.
If you're looking for Devil may Cry style combat depth and difficulty, this isn't quite it.
If you're looking for an actiony RPG, you've found a great one.
If you're looking for an expansive open world game with lots of varied side quests, this isn't quite it.
Nier Automata is much like its predecessors, highly story driven games with RPG elements and action combat.
Unlike the Drakengard games progression of strength is not only through leveling but largely through the plug-in chip system, which you might consider similar to say Materia in Final Fantasy 7 if Materia only granted status bonuses.
There are several weapons to find too of course but still, the bulk of your strength will come from how you set up your chip layouts. Every battle in the game can be made as hard or as easy as you like with these chips and the progression granted to you through them is thoroughly addictive.
I should warn new players that if they want to keep everything somewhat difficult that they should under no circumstances get their chips past +5. Anything past +5 gives you massive stat gains that utterly trivializes both fodder and bosses alike.
Very much like Drakengard on the other hand is the weapon progression, each weapon can be upgraded to level 4 and has a short story attached to it that is revealed as it is leveled. Unfortunately these weapons don't all have unique combos like in Drakengard but they do still have unique abilities, for example Spear of the Usurper can subjugate an enemy and make it fight for you, it also has a critical chance boost.
The soundtrack is both haunting and pleasant, the visuals are both bleak and rich.
The combat is relatively simple when you get down to it, one simply has to evade attacks and the window is quite generous. There is no such thing as an attack that can't be evaded and there's nothing to stop you from simply mashing the evade button.
The majority of your losses will be from new bosses where they send out a new attack and surprise you.
If you want difficulty right away, start with Hard immediately. Very Hard is a one shot mode so I don't recommend that unless you want to primarily spend your combat evading.
The story is what you'd expect from Yoko Taro. A relatively bleak story that asks you to question some deeper concept. The game is dripping in his usual techniques and it's always a joy to see.
If you're a fan of Drakengard or the original Nier this will be a massive improvement gameplay wise and cannot be missed.
Now to get on to the sidequests. They've never been the strong point of his games. They often result in escort missions, fetch quests, and general kill x y amount of times quests. That said the point of them is to add extra narrative and hammer home the questions the game is asking you to think about. On that note, they do it quite well and one should try to dabble in them a little bit at least.
Now I'll discuss the world. The world is absolutely open with no loading screens. However if you're looking for something the size of an Assassins Creed map or Skyrim, you'll be severely disappointed. No. Nier's world is much smaller and yet because of that, every single area in Nier Automata has a purpose. Every space has something to find or someone to talk to.
Finally let's describe the gameplay. As usual Yoko Taro and team have decided to go with several types of game play in one game.
You'll find a bullet hell style aerial combat, a bullet hell 2D shooter, side scrolling, and top down action. In addition of course to the default third person, free camera, action combat.
The latter two aren't really much different other than offering a different camera perspective. The former two are totally different on the other hand.
Unlike most bullet hells you do have the ability to destroy bullets, which is nice for those of us who don't like bullet hells, myself included. At least on normal these battles are simple enough.
Your chip setup actually can affect your performance in the aerial combat but not in the 2D bullet hell.
At least on normal, I found them easy enough to get through.
If you're a completionist you can expect at least 70+ hours.
If you're just here for the main story, it should clock in around 40 hours.
Overall, I enjoyed this game even more than I thought I would and that's coming from someone who leveled to max in Drakengard 1 and 2, found every single weapon and leveled them all to max, and completed every chapter.
It didn't feel as long as Drakengard but maybe that's a good thing, its ground combat though simple is very enjoyable so hunting for weapons never feels like a chore.
I highly recommend it to those looking for an action RPG to take up at least 40 hours of their time.
For anyone who insists on getting the best chips and all of the weapons, you can easily add another 30 hours to the game.
If you want to see all the side quests then I can't even imagine, I'd probably estimate that the game has 100+ hours of content for hardcore completionists.
