Bully on PS2 was one of my favourite games in the Rockstar catalogue back in the day, and so I was excited to get my hands on the Scholarship Edition which promised to bring the world of Bullworth Academy and its surrounding towns into glorious HD life. And whilst textures and draw distance have been improved, B:SE isn't without its issues.
The game is noticeably buggy, more so than the original and especially prevalent with the AI behaviour, particularly as you have a whole school's worth of NPCs running about. The new classes/minigames feel tacked on and are of poor quality, with the bonuses you gain in completing them utterly pointless. And call me vain, but I also dislike main character Jimmy Hopkins' new face; I mean, the kid wasn't exactly going to win any male model prizes back in 2006, but his makeover makes it seem like you're now controlling a middle-school aged Wayne Rooney who, in case you don't know, *definitely* isn't a looker. If you need to, give him a quick Google Image Search, and shield your eyes. One of the appeals of the original was saving up enough pocket money to buy new clothing for Jimmy, constantly dressing him up in just enough school uniform mixed with casual items so as to not get busted by prefects for violating the dress code, and so I don't think this demand for superficial consistency is too much of an ask.
Despite these complaints, I'd recommend B:SE for any newcomers who never had the chance to play it before. The game is full of charm and accompanied by a brilliant soundtrack, finding a great balance between Rockstar's GTA formula with just enough new ideas to make it seem like a fresh enough experience for both GTA fans as well as those who've begun to grow tired with that series. However if you've already played Bully before, there isn't enough here to live up to the nostalgia, and I'd recommend investing on the PSN version of the original instead. For all its muddy graphics and atrocious framerate, particularly when the outside-school environments open up, the game was perfectly balanced in its original incarnation, without the out of place classes and, certainly, with a much better designed main character.
7/10.

Tested on four desktops and a Microsoft Surface, ranging from an i5 to an i7 on the Intel side, and a 1100T on the AMD side.  Additionally tested with a Steamlink.  I'm looking at supporting this controller in software I'm working on.
On the same port that we see under 15-20ms press to response latency on Xbox and Playstation controllers, we're seeing 300ms plus press to response from the Steam controller when wired, and three to four times that when operating wirelessly, with the latest firmware.
As an example, Street Fighter IV was unplayable with this controller due to control latency.  Note: frame rate was above 60fps consistently, but the controller was lagging about a half second on Street Fighter IV.  I replaced it with the wired Joystick, a Q4, and that was fine from a latency standpoint on the same USB port, on the same computer.

The year is 2027. Human advancement has brought us to the level of self augmentation. Our evolution is at a crossroads.
Other than being one of the most visually stunning games released in 2011, this game presented an intriguing storyline and fantastic game mechanics. This is one of the few games where choice is an ever present option. The central storyline is pretty linear and though you are given the option to choose dialogue options in conversations, the outcome remains mostly the same. The biggest area of freedom is in your play style. You are able to choose between stealth, assault, or hacking as your main skillset and allowed crosscombine whatever augements you wish as you unlock more experience in the game.
The game itself is centered around a main character from Detroit, who much like Robocop is seriously injured and saved only by using technology and robotics to repair his broken form. Human revolutions is a dark game where the main character you control, Adam Jensen, can come off as anywhere from a business-like security manager trying to stay optimistic to the broken survivor who is as cold and unconcerned with other people as a machine.
The game plays like a atypical shooter where you have to choose between the right moments to sneak by enemies, ambush them quietly, or open up with gunfire and hunker down until they are all defeated. I would describe the game overall as a cyberpunk/noir style which is absolutely worth playing if you enjoy either genre.

I will start the review with the features that i liked. Firstly, the campaign missions in saints row 2 are interesting. The cutscenes that take place before and after the missions can be brutal, humiliating or funny. Also, the abilities that the players can acquire after fully completing the activities are really prominent and cool. Players can get abilities such as, infinite ammo for pistols,shotguns,assault rifles and sub machine guns. In addition, players can have the ability to run permanently if they fully complete a particular activity. In my personal opinion, activities like septic avenger,insurance fraud, fuzz and drug trafficking are really amazing. Personally, i enjoyed assembling all collectibles and discovering secret locations. However, the game has its own flaws and problems. The driving mechanics in saints row 2 are horrendous. It is really hard to drive any vehicle in this game. As a result, completing the trail blazing activity will be infuriating. Furthermore, the game has been poorly optimized for PC. The game has tendency to freeze and lag. These two things can take place anywhere and at anytime. The game can freeze or lag while the character walks in the safe house or drives a car or simply moves around a specific location. I also noticed that sometimes cars and people, that are in front of my character, have a tendency  disappear. Also, at one point in the game, during a chop shop activity, a random vehicle spawned over my vehicle. In some missions the enemy AI could have been improved. Sometimes some enemies just dont seem to react to the presence of the saints in their location until the saints start shooting at them. In contrast, the other enemies are engaged in combat against saints. Overall, i will give this game a 7/10.

A review for people who have never played SR2:
It's like GTA, except the controls are functional, combat is actually fun (holy crap, you can actually aim your guns in SR2!), and the main character is only as ugly as you want them to be, instead of just plain ugly like in GTA.
Content is huge, it's almost impossible to run out of things to do, ways to customize your character/crib, etc.
Now here's where i get controversial- SR2 is better than 3. BY FAR. There's more to do in 2 BY FAR, more character options in 2 BY FAR, a better story BY FAR. Even though the games take place in the same location, 2 just feels bigger somehow... probably because there's so much more to do, and enough variety therein.
That said, cons, yes it's one of the worst PC ports in gaming history, HOWEVER, don't let that deter you from enjoying the game, it IS fixable with mods, patches, and a lot of trial and error ingame menu tweaking, to the point that the issues it does have can be rendered relatively moot.

This is a wonderful example of a visual novel that serves a larger purpose than just telling an interactive story. Its multiple languages is a great learning tool for people who are currently trying to tackle written Japanese, something which is hard to get into for a lot of people due to its complexity. The gameplay is full of options, from choosing where you wish to go, to what you want to eat.
The characters in the game feel like real people, even though the game mainly focuses on telling you about Japanese customs and tourist spots, it uses the two female leads in a wonderful way. You will find yourself quickly getting attached to them.
It has a few lewd or "ecchi" scenes within, though they are short and usually caused by the protagonist screwing something up. If I have a single complaint about this game, it would be how those scenes were included even though I feel like it could have been fine without them.
The information provided and the potential for learning within the contents of this game are both huge in number and insanely varied. It's a great experience for any fans of Japan, especially those planning to make a trip to Japan some time soon, I highly reccomend you play it. The price is perfect for the time you get out of it.

I've been kind of tracking something that I feel is a persistent problem in the world of boardgames and even compiling what could be called case studies to support my position.
First of all, this is not a horrible product. You can play TTR with it. The interface is far from the worst of boardgame adaptations on the market, which is good considering the enormous well-deserved popularity of this modern classic. Compared to other tabletop adaptations, it's on the better end of the spectrum.
If that is enough to convince you to buy it, stop reading. Otherwise, unleash the kraken...
Boardgame companies see a lot of money in apps. Apps are easy sells. You get a mainline right into the special interests of millions of consumers. You get your stuff autosuggested BLAMMO right into their laps. They are relatively cheap to make (not for your average board game publisher, and the worlds couldn't be more different) and the ROI can be enormous. Compare $4-5 "profit" for a $60 board game to 25-50% on an $8 app, the former, on a good run, selling 5,000 copies, the latter, on a good run, selling 5,000 appstore purchases on a bad month.
On one hand, this is great. It means that boardgame designers, publishers, and distributors, the latter two of which are in a constant state of breaking even or going under, have capital to rest on. Better components, Better contracts for designers. Better games. Every betterer you can get.
In reality, boardgame publishers find themselves in a world they don't really get. This is apparent to me when I see fly-by-night developers make rather cheap looking, buggy iOS apps. As masterful game publisher do not necessarily make masterful computer game publishers, they often end up with pretty clunky, piecemeal games with 80% (good enough!) functionality.
This is not a PC game. This a almost an identical copy of the iOS app.  I have bought the iOS app, actually, twice. They made me buy it twice, because Apple introduced new architecture and phased out Game Center and whatever else the reasons for the first edition breaking were. I then bought it a third time, on Steam, which was really just me buying the right to play it on a large screen divorced from the iOS ARM64 nooselock. I also own the hard copy of TTR, as well as TTR Africa. Both of them I am donating to a distant gamer in need of games.  I am filing my divorce papers with Ticket to Ride.
I have looked over a couple dozen boardgame ports to Steam and to iOS. TTR gets maybe a 5/10. If you didin't get gauged like I did, maybe you'd like it more.
Talisman is perhaps in the top 3 boardgame adaptations. Sure, it has the usual cumbersome interface quirks (turn order and queing are a mess), but it was planned-- they thought ahead!. And it  works!  The art is... actually good! I have a lot of BG apps that DO NOT WORK.  At the bottom of the list is Scotland Yard.  Settlers of Catan is not too bad, but clumsy, the game has simultaneous turn mechanics, but this falls to pieces on the app. The network multiplayer is broken (for my friends and myself at least).

-- The reason I bring up these other games is that I think game buyers should draw a line in the sand. Don't call smartphone apps PC games. Stop selling them as PC games. Stop gauging your community's coffers with featureless copy-pastes of your Appstore catalogs. PC games are robust, they're big. Sell big games for big computers with features PC/mac/linux* users expect.
-- I know distribution deals are complex animals. Consider burning them all and integrating a more open source philosophy into  your products and franchises. Tabletop Simulator (or something like it) is kind of where I'm going with that.  Take inspiration from the bold move of WotC when they introduced the d20 system and more or less saved Dungeons and Dragons. Stop being motivated by  trademark control. Stop working with subpar dev teams that drop the product in a lake when the money runs out.
If you read this far, consider not buying any smart device >> Steam hoodwinks and ask for a better market.
* - As a newish Linux user. I always give a humble bow to any developer that makes a native port to my OS, thank you.

Great game, better than I expected. The pace isn't the mayhem-inducing spamfest of projectiles that it seemed to display itself as either. You'll be walking around with nobody in sight and it'll seem calm, then suddenly a laser starts frying you and you're now jumping and rolling while firing rockets at yourself in the hopes it kills them before you. The weapon system isn't as varying as I'd like but the balance, which makes most part combinations have the same dps, allows you to decide if you want a weapon that oneshots people but means you need to wait an hour to reload (aka. DON'T MISS) or if you want to send torrents of bullets towards your enemy that only do 1 damage. The system is based on your preference and that means that it isn't you that makes you good or bad, it's the weapons you make. I also love the ability to have medical guns that aren't just beams that stay on the target until they go out of sight or too far away, you can heal someone with a sniper rifle or bazooka. My healing choice is a gatling gun. My shotgun does more damage than my rocket launcher but requires point blank to deal it. IT'S COMPLETELY BALANCED. Except grenades. If you get caught in a 'nade blast and survive I will worship you. I swear, one well placed grenade can take an entire team down on capture point based modes. The levelling system isn't like others either, instead of instant levelling up to level 5 or something, it makes you play for those bonus blutes (The F2P currency of the game). That brings me to the currency. Like most F2P games, it has 2 currencies, money obtainable through gameplay and money purchasable (In some games it can also be found through being good and completing feats but Loadout's P2P currency is buy only). That's why it's sad that every piece of cosmetic itemry that this game lets you through on that gib-prone hunk of human steak is only obtainable through SpaceBux (The P2P currency). I do, like most, want my character to look dashingly handsome (Or in Loadout's case, like the guy that put your car window out last night and left beer bottles in your garden) but the game restricts this to people who pay. This creates an aura which makes me feel slightly like a noob. That is something I don't like being as I've already gotten good at the game with these 4/5 hours. And it isn't just a thing people feel like that pro players don't notice or point out, as I've pulled the angry face at noobs in other games plenty of times. Some TF2 servers even give F2P players tags to make them feel bad. I want to fit in without dishing out more of my money. Please Edge of Reality, add some cosmetics (Even if they're just really boring hats like a baseball cap or a sack of poop) so we can have SOME customization on our characters. Thanks.

tl dr - just play it, 10-/10, god-tier gameplay, god-tier soundtrack, god-tier story. It's not perfect, but it's amazing anyway. Amazing replay potential.
PC Port - As of December 2017 I had 0 issues with PC version, 0 crashes, stable 60 FPS, running as smoothly as one could wish for. However, the default keyboard controls are bad, the default dash/evade double-press is just bad design. Game will play better on a pad as it uses 10 combat buttons + movement buttons and it might be hard to bind it comfortably on a keyboard (if you have 2 button mouse with wheel, that's 10 buttons for your left hand - during fast combat, compared to 6 buttons + stick for left hand and 5 buttons + stick for right hand on a pad).
- while playing you are very likely to just stop and look around the world or feel glad you're going to revisit place X, because it looks awesome. Maybe it's not the most advanced graphics out there, but what it does it does
well. Water splashes / moving sand / bushes could use more work, but that's minor stuff - budget limitations.
- detailed smooth, fitting movement of characters with extra "fabulous" spins added to it just to prove how awesome their animations are. Pretty much the only bad animation that exists is when you walk into your sidekick - it gets dragged along like a physics ignoring doll, but that's a minor thing which happens only in 2D sections.
- Heroes Of Might And Magic 3 tier awesome soundtrack.
- This game is
to play. They made even walking around in this game fun. Jumping, running, riding animals, dashing just to see the cool animation and water splashing around, combat, progression, game is very fun and satisfactory to play. Guaranteed you'll spend plenty of time just dashing around in circles because it's so fun to do.
- The combat is pure gold. Easy to learn, very hard to master. You control your weapons, your gun, your special abilities, your dodge, and if that isn't engaging enough you can switch your weapons mid-attack to create new combos, switch your gun type and toggle between 3 special abilities while watching out for enemy attacks to dodge. If you want to go hardcore, you
go hardcore trying to control all of those things at once in this game. You can also go 'boring' "smash one attack button style" - it won't be very effective, but it will get the job done. Imho it's incredible that both hardcore gamers and newbie casuals can enjoy this combat system.
- saying anything would be a spoiler. This game will make you feel sadness. You will have "oh cmon game don't do this" moments. You will feel engaged with the story, when "urgent" main story quest will be ongoing you will ignore sidequests and rush towars the main quest. It's weird like that, games don't usually do this
.
- by game standards. A lot of people praise the story like it's the second coming of Christ, but imho it's overhyped. It's great, one of the best and absolutely god tier - by videogame standards. If you're new to Japanese sad stories, or new to philosophy, you'll probably get numerous "brainf**ks". It's a great, very engaging story. By videogame standards the story is a masterpiece. But just don't get too hyped about it, especially the ending. Outside the medium of videogames, I would give the story a solid 9-/10. Some minor plot holes and 'dumb moves'  just to make the story more dramatic (but those are camouflaged, which means the author was aware of them and wanted to make them less visible). Some minor plot twists  were very easy to see very early on. How the ending ties the story together is in my opinion underwhelming and a bit of a letdown, but it could be because the story until ending part was very good and had amazing potential. Also it doesn't really do anything new outside the medium of games. But cmon, it's 10/10 by games standards, can't expect it to also be 10/10 overall when compared to books and other mediums.
- You can pick from auto-play down to impossibru difficulty. On Easy you can adjust if the game will play for you, if you want some help, lots of help, or no help and just easy difficulty. This allows even the biggest casuals to progress and not get stuck, and as they get better remove the extra help. However, the difficulty spike between Normal and Hard is way, WAY too big. Also later on in the game Normal gets way too easy - it's very easy to kill a boss under 10 seconds with one cast of certain special ability - one shotting a boss shouldn't happen on any difficulty, but it could be the issue with "blender" (you'll know it once you see it) ability being
too overpowered when fully charged.
- boss fights are a weaker point of this game. They're not bad, just not as awesome as the rest of the game. Fights are fair, there are no cheap moves. For most bosses chances are you will be too focused on the story to pay attention to the "not as good" boss mechanics. It might sound weird but the boss fights not being so great seems like a minor thing in this game, as the "good stuff" lies elsewhere.

Whether or not you will enjoy this game....pretty much relies on what you think of 'budget' titles. For those of you that are unfamiliar with the term....it's basically a game that can't really compete with it's bigger budgeted cousins....which is why they are usually priced much lower. These titles aren't meant to be game changers....they are simply diversions to tide people over until something better comes along. If you find that these games are your cup of tea....then please allow me to elaborate on the game's mechanics further. In a nutshell....Ubersoldier 2 is pretty much a shoddy knock off of the classic 'Wolfenstein' franchise. You are here to kill occultist Nazis and nothing more. You will encounter a decent amount of weapons in your travels....but you can only carry five different types at one time. One of those weapon slots will consist of your sidearm....another slot is for your rifle....then machine gun....heavy weapon....and grenades. The game relies on many stapes of WWII themed combat games....which means you have the usual Kar98....MP-40....Thompson....Panzershreck....ect. You won't find much in the way of anything special when it comes to the weapons....but luckily you have some special abilities to help you out. One of those is a shield....which deflects bullets but    won't allow you shoot the enemy either....unless they pass right through it. If you score three headshots in a row or knife three enemys back to back....then you can unlock Ubersoldier abilites....which are both centered around your character being invulnerable for a short time....in which you can either score numerous head shots with ease....or just run up and stab enemies with no fear. For a budget title....the graphics aren't bad at all. In fact....this is probably the greatest looking poor man's shooter that I've come across yet. Yeah....that might sound like a bold statement....but keep in mind that I own dozens of FPS shooters....and I can name off quite a few of those that are just downright horrible to look at. The game even has some snazzy weather effects....so when you find yourself fighting in the rain....drops of water will actually splash across the screen. It's nothing ground-breaking....but it is a nice touch. The levels are varied....but rather linear. So if you are in the mood for some exploration....you won't find anything like that here. There is only a handful of enemy types however....and they love to utilize cheap tactics. They will shoot from cover....run away while firing....and vault over obstacles....which your character can do none of. Sometimes the game will place an enemy unit so that it will be in a prime position to kill you within seconds....but thankfully these are few and far between. Some of the enemies are armed with flamethrowers....which also act as tractor beams. If your character gets lit up by chance....you will not be given an opportunity to run away....so you will just have to roll the dice and see if you can get out of range before you are burnt to a crisp. The story sucks....but there are some really well done comic inspired cut scenes to keep you informed....but you will be wishing the rest of the game was that creative. The game has multiplayer....but no one is actually playing it. In the end....I would recommend this game....but only when you compared it to it's cost. Right now the game is way overpriced at $9.99. If you want to pick up this game....then do what I did....and  wait for one of the major STEAM sales to come around....so that you will only have to pay pennies on the dollar for it.

Admission time: I didn't get into Fallout until 3... and I don't like the older ones.
It's not the visuals - I'm a huge fan of Baldur's Gate and Divine Divinity, which it resembles from a visual perspective. It's fine, if not impressive.
It's not the writing. The word is definately Fallout, and it's awesome.
So... here's the problem...
IT'S SOOOOOOOO SLOW.
It's maddening. I really, really want to get into it, and explore the world, and delve into the earlier fallout games. I want to watch the step-by-step creation of a thing I love. I did the same thing for Saint's Row, and while 1&2 are pretty rough around the edges, they're still perfectly good games.
Fallout 1&2? Yeah, not so much. I'm not spoiled, I'm not too "modern" a gamer. I love turn based strategy games. I only want the visuals to be appropriate and not hideous, and these are well within that criteria.
But the interface is awkward, even taking into account the age of the game. The action is so slow that it's hard to call action...
And all of that keeps me from enjoying the rest of the game - which, I'm told, is awesome. It could be the best game ever, but I can't bear playing it through the initial quest, so I'll never know.
If you've got the patience of Job, I imagine you'll love it. If I hadn't played the Baldur's Gate games - which use the same engine, but move at a steady clip - I might love it, too... but holy crap, I just can't bear the awkward coupled with the slow.

I bought this product after researching its capabilities and I must say that I really like this controller. It's not meant to be used for every video game but its the best when you want to lay back and relax. What I like best about this controller is that you can use it outside of games, like browsing the internet or watching a move without having to get up(a steam engineer was probably watching a movie from his computer and thought "hey i really like how consoles let you lay in your bed and watch movies without getting up, why not do this for the PC?")
I use this extensively for casual games but i haven't tried it for games that let you control the camera.
What I really dislike about this though is that it only comes with one stick and I've been so used to having my thumbs on two sticks that sometimes it feels awkward. Another feature i dislike is that steam has to be on for certain features such as scrolling up/down on the left trackpad. Finally sometimes you have to reconnect the controller after it's been sitting unused for a while to reuse it.

You need to spend a LONG period with this controller. Then, after playing a few different games from your library, you'll say to yourself "SELF? HOW DID WE GO THIS LONG?" I've always loved mouse aiming, but hated Keyboards 8-way movement (Oh, you have a joystick now? EXACTLY what I wanted). The Touch Menu, while pretty dificult to set up the first time, eventually shows you that yes, you can indeed have your cake (couch-comfortability) and eat it, too (Mouse aiming and having up nto 16 buttons [Not incluidng mode shifitng {See? BIG learning curve, but once you learn it once, you're set FOREVER}] on a single controller)
Only real criticisms are that it's not rechargable (2 AA Batteries, but it allows for swapping rather than cabling yourself [A big deal if you like to play from the couch like me {CITIES SKYLINES IS AMAZING WITH THIS GAME. So is Darkest Dungeon, and Underrail. Yeah, this controller makes it all possible}] but that improves overall controller life (No propietary batteries, less chance of overcharging/etc).
Also, the controller was designed with Couch play in mind. So, I must ask... WHY IS THERE NO LITTLE HEADPHONE JACK ON THE BOTTOM? I have to use my PHONE to SKYPE my friends if I'm playing on my couch. PC it's no problem, since I'm a headphone jack away. I get that it would make the controller heavier/more costly, but if they made a Deluxe Edition or whatever, I'd buy it. No questions asked. This one will sit at the PC, that one at the couch. This was something I noticed 3-4 days into using it from my couch. Seems a silly thing to forget. If the Steam Machines are supposed to be Console-Killers (They won't be, not because of price or whatever, just that people can be turned off by thinking of how complex pc gaming can be [Because they are silly]) then you must MUST start putting headset jacks into the controller. Just a small plug under where the battery pop-off is now. Move that over a bit, give us headset support (Like a typical 2-in-1 heaset, like the iPhone has, or any heaphone with built in mic may have). So we can COUCH this controller like the baussss sauccceeee we are.
Other than that, I will literally never use anoter controller unless I'm forced to, the game is retro (Shovel Knight with NES Controller Boner Alert) or someone jacks this idea, and adds headphones or whatever.
Seriously. This controller will end all your woes. All of them. Worst case scenario, you can also use it to just watch porn while leaning back without having to reach up for your mouse.
So, it's really an investment either way.,

Buggy but fun, recommended.
You're a gangster, you do gangster stuff. Murder, theft, takeovers, grudges, mercy killing, revenge, and get paid. It ranges from silly and irreverant to somber and serious, from fun to infuriating.
Every activity has context: you're not just spraying poo from a septic truck, you're trying to lower property values to aid allies (by spraying poo from a septic truck); you're not just driving a four wheeler on fire to blow up everything, you're making statements to the enemies of your friends; you're not just hurling yourself into traffic, you're faking vehicular injuries to help a shady doctor make a ton of money. That context comes with voice acting and usually a cinematic. Each side activity, except racing, has up to six levels of increasing difficulty, and that's where they go wrong - some of them are insanely hard - nearly impossible without finding a trick or exploit.
Each area of the city has a unique flavor, with a list of cars and npcs that only spawn in certain districts. All of which matches the social and economic layout of the town.
The story has a lot of great moments, with three main paths that can be run in parallel or in series - the game accomodates both (and I've played both ways), but the narrative beats can be really odd if you're doing two or more story lines at the same time.
There are a ton of collectibles and unmarked side activities. Some are fun and interesting (hitman, chop shop), some are tedious and frustrating (collecting CDs, finding all Tagging locations), and some are silly and kind of pointless (streaking, flashing, ho-ing).
What upgrades a bad port of a very old game to worthwhile is the loving fan community that created (and still provides) numerous mods to fix bugs and tweak gameplay to your desires. There are mods to add even more customization options, replay missions, increase difficulty, decrease difficulty, and many more features.
If you want to see a GOOD sandbox style game then this is worth your time.
If you want to have fun wreaking havoc across a fictional city then this is a blast.

Before even attempting to review Minecraft: Story Mode – A Telltale Games Series I should probably come clean and admit I'm one of those weirdos who know nothing about Minecraft as global sandbox block building phenomena that had everyone's attention before sandbox survival became a trend in recent years. I never got into it and genre as a whole did not grab my attention. This is worth bringing up because I may have on my hands a rare example of where not being familiar with source material to at least some degree can be detrimental and because you're piecing together what's what as you go along for a spin-off game. How'd I do? Well, let's see.
First episode is actually free so anyone can check it out, but just in case – we follow Jesse as he, or she seeing as you can choose the gender and some skin/clothes colors at the beginning making for a strange character creation in a Telltale game, and his two friends Olivia and Axel, are preparing to embark for EnderCon. Major competition of some sort for builders and that seems to be a big thing in the world? Accompanying them is also Jesse's best friend, a pig named Reuben. We see humor and jabs aplenty in these first few minutes and honestly, minus the QTEs, this single instance of a tree house room neatly condenses a lot of what Minecraft Story Mode is all about. Needless to say and self-evident for every good narrative this is merely the opening and soon world finds itself in danger as new heroes step up to save it. You connect the dots.
Weirdest thing for me was definitely getting over the art style. Fans will think nothing of it and it does grow on you over time, but goddamn if that first episode didn't take some time to acclimate myself. Maybe it looks better if you're playing further away from your TV and not seated in front of the monitor? I can't say. Geometry is simple, but at the same time I can only guess that may be the appeal for fans of Minecraft proper. Especially in later episodes when developers clearly went for some ornate and impressive architectural layouts, and realized them with various blocks. This is actually even brought up for story and character reasons seeing as building things is often the go-to solution for our party, but I really wish it wasn't relegated to just button mashing QTE segments. In fact, that's something I'd like to get into next...
I've ranted against Telltale's tendency to phase out actual gameplay with each new “adventure game” they keep making, but in many aspects this might be the worst example yet simply because such overt actions which COULD be turned into something where the player has to think for himself are automated. Crafting is one element where you do have to get involved, but it comes down to simple “hey, these are the ingredients you conveniently find in the same room where the crafting table is and all you have to do is match the pattern”. Maybe I'm [unjustly] expecting more than what Telltale can and has delivered so far yet Minecraft Story Mode actively made me question if I'm even necessary for anything in the game or whether my role is to just be an observer. For all the formula variations employed across eight episodes this is something that remained a constant – too many cutscenes where you're maybe required to occasionally press a button or two.
And really, it's bringing up episodes that takes me to the worst offender in what is, in a summary, an above average production – filler. My god, this did not require eight episodes. Certainly not if you're going to make two filler that amounts to nothing. Well, technically you got trophies from them that you get to display in the final interactive sequence, but story wise episodes five and six could've been completely done away with. One is a self-contained story and arguably Ivor development vehicle depending on how you handle it, but the other one... well, rarely have I seen such a self-indulgence on display. I can only surmise these characters are famous Minecraft Youtubers/streamers or something that got an entire episode dedicated to not mere cameos but actual story invasion. Let's just say I could've done without that and less said the better. Thankfully, plot steers back to its second arc somewhat naturally after that and builds up to a surprisingly good finale. Might actually be one of the best in all of these games, to be perfectly honest.
I briefly mentioned graphics upstairs, but soundtrack department was much more consistently satisfying. You can read from episode intro vignettes that one composer got dropped after a certain episode and you can hear it, but tracks grounded me in what was going on. Might sound strange when you imagine things like characters dying and other dramatic events happening set against the backdrop of such blocky visuals, but presentation itself is not the problem. It's merely a sort of juxtaposition until your mind accepts what the eyes see. Soundtrack lends itself well to this and chirpy tunes eventually settle in.
Why am I still recommending it then after this kinda negative piece? Because of what I said above – it is still an above average game of its type that simply happens to have some blemishes here and there, large and small. If you're a Telltale fan you already know what to expect and if you were hesitant because of Minecraft, like I was, I still think you should give it a go.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a fairly simplistic take on the FPS RPG genre. There is a variety of weapons in this game, but only one model for each weapon, something that people may enjoy or dislike. Personally, I prefer it that way because it means I don't have to constantly compare the stats of one shotgun to another. Additionally, there is no crafting system in this game (something that is commonly found in RPGs) so you don't have to constantly modify weapons using various pieces you pick up along the way. Leveling up is also not an issue in this game, so you don't have to acquire a certain amount of experience to proceed to the next portion of the story. Side quests are completely optional, the best reward you'll earn from them is some Praxis's.
The augmentation customization is one of the coolest parts of this game. For those who aren't familiar with this game or any previous title in the Deus Ex series, you play as Adam Jensen, the head of security at Sarif Industries. Mr. Jensen is more or less part machine and part man, and as you progress, you will have the opportunity to customize the machine aspect of him, otherwise known as augments. The augments you upgrade depend on your preferable style of play. Do you like being stealthy? Going completely invisible and silently navigating corridors? Or would you rather battle your foes head on, ensuring that you take reduced damage when doing so? The choice is yours in Deus Ex.
The biggest issue I had with this game, and perhaps the only one, was the boss battles. Upon performing some brief research, I quickly discovered that many others share my opinion. For example, defeating the first boss felt entirely contradictory to the way I had been playing the game up until that point. The generally accepted form of combat in this game involves ducking behind various structures and objects, then proceeding to briefly expose yourself so as to eliminate your enemies. Well, I tried that style multiple times with the first boss, and to no avail. It appeared that it would require an unlimited supply of ammunition to take him down, something I obviously didn't possess. So I resorted to something I typically try to avoid when playing video games: help. After viewing a couple YouTube videos, I learned that I needed to throw barrels at him, something I hadn't even attempted to do prior to my confrontation with this boss. But I tried it out anyway, and it only took about 30 seconds to defeat him simply by throwing barrels at him. It was as if "Deus Ex: Human Revolution" had suddenly become "Deus Ex: Donkey Kong Revolution".
Overall however, this game is worth a playthrough. Yes, you have to endure 4 lackluster bosses, but in the grand scheme of things, it's a small price to pay. The story involves a fun conspiracy theory which I won't divulge for the sake of avoiding spoilers, but I will say that you will be forced to make some tough decisions that impact the game's ultimate outcome. 7/10 stars for Deus Ex, easily 9/10 with improved boss battles.

Rampage Knights is definetely a great game but I must say, it is not for everyone.
If you are into a game that pushes your sanity to the limit, then this is the game for you. Rampage Knights may seem like an easy and simple game at first glance but once the player/s starts getting into the higher difficulties the game becomes a lot more challenging. Rampage Knights is very unforgiving of your mistakes, especially in single player as you have no co-op partner to revive you. I, personally, like the way that the single player is balanced, while in co-op you have a partner to help you deal more damage and to revive eachother, you also have to share items, potions and make sure you don't end up "accidently" killing eachother. However, when playing in single player, you start off with an extra life and you don't need to share items (for all you hoarders) and worry about friendly fire.
When it comes to the downsides of Rampage Knights, I have very little to complain about. Probably one of the only complaints I actually care about is the slight lack of content. I feel there needs to be more adventure in the game, more story. At the moment the story lacks heavily in detail, so much so that you will usually forget the story half way through a run and not remember until you reach the end of the game (where it reminds you of the story).
To summarise, Rampage Knights is great for those looking for a challenge that will push them but not so much for those looking for an in-depth story. And to those who are buying/playing this game, good luck, you're going to need it ;)

Absolute kudos to the developers for a fine technical execution.
Unfortunately the gameplay is problematic - while the premise of the game, matched up with smooth gameplay, would make this game a clear winner, the handling is quite clunky - machine guns aren't accurate, fine, but when I got a rifle and could shoot enemies easily, I found it takes about three direct headshots to kill the average Nazi. My favorite controller is the Gamecube controller, which to many may sound like a terrible choice. All things considered, it's an antiquated controller by more modern standards. It does, however, have one thing that I've always wondered why no other controller, including Nintendo's products since, has ever included. Shoulder triggers with springs in them that allow for half press recognition. Sure, other triggers can recognize how much you're pressing down, but the Xbox and Playstation controllers don't have anything to really let the player recognize that the controller recognizes. That's honestly one of the most important things a controller needs to do. It needs to not only recognize the player's actions, but also assure the player their action has been recognized. Not just in game, but as the controller itself. When you press a button, there's a tactile feeling of it being pressed all the way down. When you move the stick, the spring under it gives tension and flicks back into place when you remove the stick. It's what gives the Wii Remote a floaty feeling when you try to use the gryo/motion controls as a control stick, it doesn't have any real way to assure the player their motions are working as they intend. So, the triggers, which have since the Xbox, become perhaps the most useful button additions in the last few generations of video gaming, have had an bit of ambiguity to them. Not the worst thing, but still, ambiguity is not what makes a controller great.
Then the Steam Controller. I opened the box in the post office because I was so excited to test it out. First thing I did, I pressed down on those shoulder triggers to give them a test. And I felt that click as I pulled it all the way down. That click and then that thud as I pressed it all the way down. Half clicks. When I let go, I heard that spring. It felt like the Gamecube controller. But better. When I turned the controller on, at first I was shocked by the sound the controller made, and then a bit disconcerted by the buzzing from the trackpads. (The haptic feedback makes a noise not unlike a stomach gurgle, but a feeling like it's a wheel with a ticker on it.) Took me only a moment to get used to the haptic feedback from them. They're adjustable to 4 different levels of feedback (Low, Med, High, Off), the left trackpad is slightly stronger than the right trackpad, and the overall use of the trackpads are pretty solid. It took only about 5 minutes of holding the controller to realize that the odd shape isn't a cooky design choice but a purposeful one. The outward facing handles are designed to keep your hands pushed up so your thumbs can more naturally use the trackpads. Anyone who has ever used a trackpad or a trackball in any capacity will understand how to use the trackpads pretty quickly. However, the haptic feedback doesn't end at the trackpads. The control stick also has customizable haptic feedback as well, giving you feedback when you're facing the stick in one of the 8 cardinal directions among others. Then, there's the moment I went from loving the Steam Controller to complete adoration. The haptic feedback on the triggers. They already had good half press recognition, but the haptic feedback adds yet another level of truly being able to recognize your actions, completely assuring you that the action you intended was in fact made.
However, as much as I wish to give an outstandingly glowing review of the product, there are a number of concerns to bring up. The first is something that I think is universal among those who have held the controller, the face button placement. Until you have the controller in your hands, you will not know just how awkwardly placed these buttons are. They're not terribly placed, and honestly, you won't be bothered by it too much, but considering that their placement on the controller had made me press the wrong button on more than one occasion, and I've only been playing with this controller for only a couple of days, they're enough of a nuisance to warrant it as a complaint. Another concern is the gyro in the controller. It isn't terrible, and probably better than most motion controls I've experienced, but I wouldn't say that this is the motion control that makes those like myself, who do not like motion controls, a motion control believer. However, those two concerns aren't something I have very ready solutions to. Perhaps adding haptic feedback to the gyro would add a more solid assurance of movement and changing the placement of the buttons would help, but those would require a whole new controller, which is rather drastic for two concerns that are rather minor all things considered. If the Xbox 360 Wireless controller lived its entire life with the worst DPad ever and very little complaint from it, then the Steam Controller can live with a strange face button placement and gyro controls that are only marginally better than other gyro controls. The concern with this device that can be changed, however, is the configurations of the device. The configuration of control schemes for each game is not very difficult, and infact is rather natural. The community suggested control layouts are often great to use, and configuring those layouts for yourself is easy. The only catch is that you can only do this in Big Picture Mode. There is no UI outside of Big Picture Mode to adjust the controller. This makes sense in a way, as the majority of people who would use this device are couch gaming with either the Steam Link or with a living room PC, but this does greatly hinder those who would like to use a controller at their desk and those who would like to use the controller for non Steam Games. If you are not in Big Picture Mode, you cannot configure a thing on your Steam Controller. What's worse is that Big Picture Mode then doesn't even support the use of the trackpads inside the menus, half defeating the purpose of forcing people to use Big Picture Mode with the Steam Controller. Obviously, Big Picture Mode will eventually work with the Steam Controller, but I'm more worried about there never being a companion app with the controller that would allow me to configure it outside of Big Picture Mode.
This was a rather long winded review of the device that I hoped touched on the majority of things about the Steam Controller. I've likely left something out, as the controller is a rather steep distance from all the other current generation controllers and has a lot of things differentiating from them. Chances are, those have been stated in other reviews, so as always, take those reviews in mind along with mine.
The short takeaway from the Steam Controller is this: It is perhaps the best controller I've ever had in my hand for assuring me that an action has been made, even if that action was accidental. I wouldn't recommend it for anyone who uses a gamepad for games already and want to make an easy conversion, but I would recommend it to anyone who is curious and willing to work with this controller. It may take some work, but any work put into it will likely come back to you. And as a final tagline, this game works great with XCom 2.

Short Visual Novel that doesn't provide a deep story line or much emotional attachment, but it is fun and educational. I have spent hours just wasting time with this game. You play a male character who, despite his life dream being travelling to Japan, has almost no knowledge of Japan or Japanese culture. It gets a little embarassing as he overreacts to things like ramen and trains, but if you can get through those there is a lot of historical information as well that I found interesting. It is not presented in a boring way either, was not too "lecture" like. Involves a kind of half-a**ed love story with your Japanese hosts, including a few gratuitous changing and nudity scenes, but the art is well done, the writing is easy to follow and flows pretty naturally.
I bought this game on sale after playing Katawa Shoujo for like the fifth thime and needing a new VN to get my mind off of it. It is totally different from Katawa Shoujo, but well made, so that it kept me interested and entertained for a few short hours.
I wouldn't pay more than a few dollars for it, I think I only paid 3, as it is short and not really involved. I love Visual Novels and reading sotries though, so while it was fun for me to pretend to be in Japan, if you are looking for interesting characters, or actual plot, go with a different game. If you just want to waste some time, have an interest in Japanese culture, or just feel like some cutesy graphics and a shallow-but-happy overall feeling, this game is pretty good.

This little visual novel might actually make you nostalgic if you ever been to Japan, or could be very informative if you're planning to visit. If you don't mind the ultra cheesy story that actually goes nowhere (but tries to), one perfectly dumb protagonist that goes to Japan while being clueless about everything. They tried to add a little fanservice and flavor by making you stay with two females but don't expect much besides decent amount of major tourist spots and japanese reading practice as a side option. Quite short, has cards, fun little cheesy visual novel as a snack.

My favorite controller is the Gamecube controller, which to many may sound like a terrible choice. All things considered, it's an antiquated controller by more modern standards. It does, however, have one thing that I've always wondered why no other controller, including Nintendo's products since, has ever included. Shoulder triggers with springs in them that allow for half press recognition. Sure, other triggers can recognize how much you're pressing down, but the Xbox and Playstation controllers don't have anything to really let the player recognize that the controller recognizes. That's honestly one of the most important things a controller needs to do. It needs to not only recognize the player's actions, but also assure the player their action has been recognized. Not just in game, but as the controller itself. When you press a button, there's a tactile feeling of it being pressed all the way down. When you move the stick, the spring under it gives tension and flicks back into place when you remove the stick. It's what gives the Wii Remote a floaty feeling when you try to use the gryo/motion controls as a control stick, it doesn't have any real way to assure the player their motions are working as they intend. So, the triggers, which have since the Xbox, become perhaps the most useful button additions in the last few generations of video gaming, have had an bit of ambiguity to them. Not the worst thing, but still, ambiguity is not what makes a controller great.
Then the Steam Controller. I opened the box in the post office because I was so excited to test it out. First thing I did, I pressed down on those shoulder triggers to give them a test. And I felt that click as I pulled it all the way down. That click and then that thud as I pressed it all the way down. Half clicks. When I let go, I heard that spring. It felt like the Gamecube controller. But better. When I turned the controller on, at first I was shocked by the sound the controller made, and then a bit disconcerted by the buzzing from the trackpads. (The haptic feedback makes a noise not unlike a stomach gurgle, but a feeling like it's a wheel with a ticker on it.) Took me only a moment to get used to the haptic feedback from them. They're adjustable to 4 different levels of feedback (Low, Med, High, Off), the left trackpad is slightly stronger than the right trackpad, and the overall use of the trackpads are pretty solid. It took only about 5 minutes of holding the controller to realize that the odd shape isn't a cooky design choice but a purposeful one. The outward facing handles are designed to keep your hands pushed up so your thumbs can more naturally use the trackpads. Anyone who has ever used a trackpad or a trackball in any capacity will understand how to use the trackpads pretty quickly. However, the haptic feedback doesn't end at the trackpads. The control stick also has customizable haptic feedback as well, giving you feedback when you're facing the stick in one of the 8 cardinal directions among others. Then, there's the moment I went from loving the Steam Controller to complete adoration. The haptic feedback on the triggers. They already had good half press recognition, but the haptic feedback adds yet another level of truly being able to recognize your actions, completely assuring you that the action you intended was in fact made.
However, as much as I wish to give an outstandingly glowing review of the product, there are a number of concerns to bring up. The first is something that I think is universal among those who have held the controller, the face button placement. Until you have the controller in your hands, you will not know just how awkwardly placed these buttons are. They're not terribly placed, and honestly, you won't be bothered by it too much, but considering that their placement on the controller had made me press the wrong button on more than one occasion, and I've only been playing with this controller for only a couple of days, they're enough of a nuisance to warrant it as a complaint. Another concern is the gyro in the controller. It isn't terrible, and probably better than most motion controls I've experienced, but I wouldn't say that this is the motion control that makes those like myself, who do not like motion controls, a motion control believer. However, those two concerns aren't something I have very ready solutions to. Perhaps adding haptic feedback to the gyro would add a more solid assurance of movement and changing the placement of the buttons would help, but those would require a whole new controller, which is rather drastic for two concerns that are rather minor all things considered. If the Xbox 360 Wireless controller lived its entire life with the worst DPad ever and very little complaint from it, then the Steam Controller can live with a strange face button placement and gyro controls that are only marginally better than other gyro controls. The concern with this device that can be changed, however, is the configurations of the device. The configuration of control schemes for each game is not very difficult, and infact is rather natural. The community suggested control layouts are often great to use, and configuring those layouts for yourself is easy. The only catch is that you can only do this in Big Picture Mode. There is no UI outside of Big Picture Mode to adjust the controller. This makes sense in a way, as the majority of people who would use this device are couch gaming with either the Steam Link or with a living room PC, but this does greatly hinder those who would like to use a controller at their desk and those who would like to use the controller for non Steam Games. If you are not in Big Picture Mode, you cannot configure a thing on your Steam Controller. What's worse is that Big Picture Mode then doesn't even support the use of the trackpads inside the menus, half defeating the purpose of forcing people to use Big Picture Mode with the Steam Controller. Obviously, Big Picture Mode will eventually work with the Steam Controller, but I'm more worried about there never being a companion app with the controller that would allow me to configure it outside of Big Picture Mode.
This was a rather long winded review of the device that I hoped touched on the majority of things about the Steam Controller. I've likely left something out, as the controller is a rather steep distance from all the other current generation controllers and has a lot of things differentiating from them. Chances are, those have been stated in other reviews, so as always, take those reviews in mind along with mine.
The short takeaway from the Steam Controller is this: It is perhaps the best controller I've ever had in my hand for assuring me that an action has been made, even if that action was accidental. I wouldn't recommend it for anyone who uses a gamepad for games already and want to make an easy conversion, but I would recommend it to anyone who is curious and willing to work with this controller. It may take some work, but any work put into it will likely come back to you. And as a final tagline, this game works great with XCom 2.

I'm one of these gamers that buys a lot of games, but tend not to finish many and plays only until the point at which I feel that I have gotten enough. I say this because Nier: Automata is one of the first games I have completed
and has taken a spot in my favourite games of all time. I will try to use spoiler tags where possible, however, if you've not played yet, it is definitely worth going in blind.
Nier: Automata is a wonderful fusion of hack and slash mechanics, a beautifully emrgent RPG and a bullet hell style shooter that plays with game mechanics throughout keeping gameplay fresh, interesting and intrinsicly linked to the story.
One of the best trick this game pulls to keep you sucked in even from the early game is to seamlessly switch from a front scrolling ship shooter, to a twin stick shooter, into a fully 3D movement fighting arena to a sidescrolling fighting game. I mean, this all happens in the prologue and really sets you up for the kind of adventure you're going to be having throughout.
One you get a hang of the combat, it's well paced, feels very kinetic and the animations are beautifully fluid. This stands true throughout
.
The one criticism I have is that sometimes, the combat is a little bit easy in the easier difficulties and downright punishing in ther harder difficulties. On top of that there is an abundance of helaing items to sustain you through so as long as you're not one-shot, then you're going to be ok.
When I say the artstyle and graphics are amazing, you better believe it! It's not the highest fidelity world you'll ever see in a video game, however. the design work that has gone into everything is a marvel to say thew least. There is nothing in this world that doesn't fit in and everything that exists seems to exist for a reason. The world constantly reshapes to the events that occur around it with you experiencing a different version of the game world in each segment of the game.
Oh. My. God.
The sound track is phenominal! I have never gone out and bought a games soundtrack after having played the game before, but when I saw that barely any of it was on Spotify, I bought the whole thing. The music pumps the atmosphere of the game all the way up to 11. The director and sound designers had to know the game inside out and understand how the player would be feeling, as this is hands down one of the best synced up sound tracks I have ever heard. Even after having played the game, the music evokes an emotional response upon hearing it.
There are many great examples of where the music exhances the game going quitet and solumn at the right points to add poiniency to what you have just experienced. My favourite examples of which are
but throughout the music perfectly matches the tone.
Having said what I have said so far, this game goes from being what seems to be a simple plot to being so deep and conveying a great message through not only the major plot beats but through how you play the game and the decisions you choose to make.
There are many games where your decision affects the outcome of the game but one of the best parts of the decisions in Nier: Automata is that those decisions sometimes don't affect the game, they just affect the player and how you feel about what you have said or done.
I have chosen to delete my save so that I can play the game again from start to finish through a new lens as after completion revelations, you are definitely going to want to experience it again to gain new meaning to what you have seen.
Final words: Please buy this game and try it out. There are very few truely different games out there and this one is a masterpiece!

Dead Rising 3 is very enjoyable for about 15 hours, or 3/4 of the game, but very quickly becomes repetitive towards the end, especially with the DLC's.
Dead Rising 3 follows the story of Nick Ramos, a mechanic who is trying to escape the zombified Los Perdidos with his friends. Along the way he uncovers a big goverment conspiracy, very much akin to the previous Dead Rising's. I didn't much care for Nick nor his friends, unlike the previous protagonists Frank West and Chuck Greene. Nick acts too much like a baby or freaks out way too much at any event. The story as a whole is pretty lackluster and very forgettable.

Dead Rising 3 plays very similar to the past installments, but with some welcomed features that make the game shine bright. Sprinting and evasive rolls give you much needed mobility to travel the large open world, and are a great addition. Nick, being a skilled mechanic, can now craft combo weapons on the go, leading to a much faster paced and enjoyable fighting experience. Combo vehicles are also a new addition, and while I mainly preferred only 2 or 3 of the list, it's fun to craft them whenever you see the right vehicles. The new combo weapons and vehicles provide the most amount of fun in the game, ranging from silly "massager" shooters to crowd clearing death scythe's. The city of Los Perdidos is filled with many events to keep you occupied. With over 200 collectable's to find, you can stay occupied for a long while just explorning and discovering many secrets. As you find the collectables or kill zombies, you level up and get new skills for Nick. I'd say this is where the game was the most fun, as every level up was exciting and I wanted to just keep killing zombies to keep leveling up. Once you are max level however, most of that excitement leaves, and I really didn't see any need to killing the zombies anymore.
While not the best graphics out there, Dead Rising 3 does it's job well enough. The overwhelming hordes of the undead are quite a graphical achievement however. Turning a corner and bumiping into a sea of several hundred zombies is both terrifying and exciting. The framerate stays pretty consistent with all the onscreen action, but there were several times when just too much was going on and the framerate dropped down to a crawl.

There really isn't anything to say about the sound for Dead Rising 3. It's not bad, but there wasn't anything good. Voice acting was a little bit awkward, but nothing to complain about.
While being an overall decent port, Dead Rising 3 had a lot of crashes and other poorly designed problems. The game crashed on me about 10 times in the time it took for me to beat it, but the checkpoint system thankfully kept most of my progress. It's highly reccommended that you play this game with a controller, as keyboard and mouse are really tough to play with. After I beat the game I went back to a chapter to finish collecting the collectables, but found out that several of them were locked behind doors that could only be unlocked by getting to a certain point, which I was unable to without having to go even further back. And unless I wanted to start completely over again, there was no way I would be able to get some achievements. Minor complaints, but it really started to irk me.
The 4 DLC for Dead Rising 3 were pretty bad and really repitive. Each DLC follows a new character and their story in Los Perdidos. The main story for each DLC last about 1-2 hours each, but they are all filled with even more collectables. The stories and characters are really boring and generic, and don't offer much in terms of enjoyment. The collectable's in each DLC were just too much for me, but for completionists expect to get your money's worth from them.

Frankly, this is the best game I have played in a very long time. Making it work on my machine was a bit of a pain, as it is using incredible amounts of RAM. Disabling every other service at start up did the trick though, and I can enjoy the game at a very good level of graphic details without too bad a frame rate. I love the user interface. I love the realism of the situations and the fact that the few mini games within the game (essentially the hacking part) feels not too forced and even relatively realistic. But the most important thing is that I love the story. It is compelling, well told (even if sometime a little bit easy to foresee) and the characters feel true and seem to have motivations and personality. Although the game is not technically a sandbox game, it feels nearly like one, because all the railroading from one city to another feels quite natural. All in all, an excellent game, but with a couple of technical issues (RAM usage, and some bugs).

Very fun game for it only being in beta. The game offers tight, easy controls and mechanics that newer players can grasp quickly, while also maintaining a difficultly curve in-game to help keep even verteran players on their toes. As for gameplay, there are many classes to choose from including Pirate, Battlemage, and Assassin, none of which feel alike which offers great varitey in play. All characters have both ups and downs, some have higher vitality and do more damage, while some have lower vitality, but have spells or special abilites to help them along. These characters are unlocked from completing achievements corresponding to the characters traits. For example, to unlock the Warlock class, there are 3 demon related achievements the player must accomplish before gaining access to the class. There are also many non-class oriented achievements in the game which once unlocked, give permanent stat boots to your characters. These not only insentivize different playstyles needed to unlock these achievements, but also give the player something to work towards. These stat boots arn't that powerful though, some of the most potent being a +10 Vitality or a +5% Crit Chance. The game also offers plently of variations of enemies and room configurations, all of which varying from run to run. The only drawback to this fun rogue-like is that there arn't that many items in the game. Once you get to your 50th or so run, you've seen most if not all of the items in the game. Although, this problem will most likely be addressed as the game continues it's progression throughout it's beta.
SUMMARY: Fun rogue-like with tight controls and both varied and interesting play. Better with co-op than singleplayer but still a great game! 11/10 Pls nerf Assassin class.

I've only played a few hours into the game so far so I can only offer a bit of insight right now.
The game's fun, plain and simple. Each weapon type has its own areas that they handle well and badly in as well as their own specialties.
Rockets can deal lots of damage if they hit directly or very close to an opponent plus there blast radius helps with crowd control. But, they're easy to dodge if you work your rolls right and don't travel in easily predictable paths of travel.
Beams are very accurate over long ranges, don't deal lots of damage though, but still being able to keep a beam right on your opponents even with evasive manuvers on their parts is deliciously fun! But as I already said, they don't deal a large ammount of damage and can only fire for so long before they overheat.
Solid projectile guns, bullets that is, are what I so far see as damage per second weapons. They fire lots of rounds quickly and depending on what parts you've equipted the current gun with they excell in dealing lots of damamge at close range and slightly less at areas in the medium ranges. Long ranges, hmm, you'll hit occasionally but don't go expecting to do much.
Pusles, honestly the first time I fired one of these I laughed my rear off! Who wouldn't when they fire a Pulse gun and iron spiked balls materialise out of them and slam into your opponents and stick there with a loud clang sound. And keep on clanging with ever step they take.
Then there's all the equipment that you can use, though your stuck with a simple grenade till you spend some blue points (research points which you earn leveling up) on more in the tech tree (remember that you also have trees for each of the weapon types to check out as well).
Personally the good, fun, run and gun with your own customized weapons style of gameplay along with the character affects that appear when you hit someone (or get hit yourself!) adds a nice affect to the game. Hit someone with a flame round? They survive? Well, easy to tell they survived a strong fire since they look nice and charcoled!
There are ways to heal yourself or others, you can heal yourself by finding the square boxes lying around the maps that are green, the ones that are yellow aren't active yet. Then there's special types of ammo and grenades that will heal you or your teammates (beam weapon with healing ammo and solid accuracy can be nice to have at your back). there's also buff ammos and such equipment, don't know much about buffs yet still very low in level myself.
Last, I've not run into anything I'd call OP or breaking in this game but for one thing: Run into a good solid player with standard equipment like your own and have a fun time and likely loose and maybe win depending on the situation like anything else you'd expect. Run into a solid player with solid upgraded equipment who knows how to use it and what your using yourself and expect to get your rear blown, shredded, spiked, electrocuted or burned off! Oh, or hammered off depending on the game mode.
Right now, I love playing this game and can laugh even when I get my rear handed to me (literally its still running!).
P.S. hope this helped even a little bit for anyone looking at this game that hasn't simply watched the trailer or has and is simply wondering about it.

Are you familiar with the term "so bad it's good"?  Like something that is just objectively not well made but is still for some reason incredibly enjoyable?  Ubersoldier II is like that.  It is so bad, so utterly horrible, so poorly made that it should never be played... but for some reason I loved nearly every second of it.
This game is the "Sharknado" of video games.  It is bad in nearly every aspect but still a fun romp.  The voice acting is so bad, the story is almost completely nonsensical, the cutscenes are laughably awful.  This being said, everytime there is any kind of story exposition I can't help but crack a smile and just enjoy it.  The gunplay itself is pretty bland, not horrible but nothing amazing.  You get some special powers that spice things up a little and are really fun the first few times you use them but pretty quickly get stale.  The level design is so so so so bad that sometimes when I was playing through the game I would get stuck running around in circles while trying to complete a level and would end up screaming WHY????? when I finally figure out how to progress.  But even navigating these bizarre levels was kind of fun in their own way.  It was like exploring some kind of weird post modern work of art.
Is this a good game?  Hell no.  Is this game worth playing?  Hell yes.  (maybe just get it when it's on sale)

Long Review: This is the first game I have officially bought form Steam out of my own pockets. And I have to say, it was definitely worth it. The game has a lot of puzzling aspects which could frustrate you, but eventually you'll realize where you went wrong and have the most hardcore facepalm momet you'd have. The style of gameplay really had me, it was different. A good kind of different. It threw in a lot of different genres into it, making it your open-world, RPG, bullethell hack-n-slash. How's that for a combo, huh? The story, oh my lord, it took you through a real ♥♥♥♥ing roller-coaster. It hits hard, no matter what ending it was. IT. HIT. HARD. That's all I'm gonna say *breaks down emotionally*. The graphics really had me. The motion effects, the lighting, collision effects, so much more to be had. If I had the chance to play this on ultra setting with 300fps on a 240hz monitor, you best believe I would die happily on the spot. The nerd-gasm would kill me. Overall, this game is definitely worth the price. If net-neutrality is bumming you out or League of Legends has taken it's toll on you for the day, then get this game. Trust me, it's worth it. Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~ is a visual novel about an awkward protagonist that finally realizes his lifelong dream of going to Japan. A very novel idea that was not given away at all from the title. AwkProtag says that he is going to be staying with two friends that he met over the internet while in Japan. Thinking they are male friends, he is very surprised to find that the friends that he has been talking to over the internet are actually cute Japanese girls! What's better is that the house they're going to stay in doesn't have any parents in it because of the convenient "emergency business trip" excuse that is so popular in these kinda stories. AwkProtag is now happy that he is staying with these girls, especially since they are both very attractive to him. Makoto is the older sibling with big breasts and a nice temperment. Akira is your typical flat-chested tsundere. There's literally no more depth to these characters, except for the fact that they know ridiculous amount of trivia of Japanese history/landmarks. Of course, you have the option of falling in love with either of these girls. For the first (and only) playthrough, I ended up with Makoto. I didn't enjoy this game really and was only fun for the sheer ridiculousness of AwkProtag and the scenarios that he would get into. Eventually AwkProtag goes home and that's the end of the story.
Also, this game has very liberal usage of elipses. Like, I'm talking whole dialogues where the only thing the characters say are ".........." to each other. Like, literally the use of these were so ridiculous that I couldn't take it anymore. I wanted to quit so bad. This was a hellish experience and something that will haunt me for the rest of my life. I wasted 5 hours playing this VN and all I have to show for it is .....................

Certain Characters will go into T poses after activating a ability or finishing a ability.

Let's get this out of the way early doors.  The game doesn't have a story or any real progression, other than your bank balance growing.  There aren't any upgrades and it does feel quite simplistic.  But what it lacks in depth it makes up for in nostalgia.
If you haven't ever been to the bookies during the 80s or 90s then you might want to avoid this one.  However, if you remember a time before the casino machines took over the high street then strap yourself in.
While the game may not look much from the screenshots, it does a decent job of recreating the tv screens and racing papers that were an essential part of a saturday afternoon.  The football section feels a bit tacked on to be honest but it does help add some variety.
The best part about the game is that you can just chill out, read through the form and pick a winner.  You then get to listen to some basic commentary in the bookies and if you don't win you can drown your sorrows in the pub next door.  The real challenge is trying to make your money last until your next giro gets cashed.
If you are looking for a deep immersive racing game then I would suggest Starters Orders. If you've had a long day at work and you just fancy trying your luck without the risk of losing any real money then this game is really relaxing and good simple fun.
A couple of suggestions for the dev.  Greyhound DLC would be nice.  A bit more of a tipping section in the newspaper with naps would be fun.
