I'm only guessing because I'm from the states...  Wish they would use the announcer calls for their starters orders races but I digress...  So yeah it's stupid, it's fun and weird but there is nothing like it.  If you like horse racing, then you should give this a go because there just isn't much out there for us.

Firstly I helped BETA test this and got the game for free. So take this as you like:
Where do I start? This is an odd game but is it any good?
First play after 10 mins got bored. Then I came back to it. Played for about 1/2 hour. Come back to it and played while having a late night drink... Until I realised that I was starting to really enjoy it... So I'm glad I stuck with it and here is my review:
Unashamedly harping back to the 1980's and revolving around a dirty 'bedsit' and a betting shop that features lot's of smoke and audio commentary. You receive unemployment benefits every two weeks and have to survive by gambling in the betting shop or playing the fruit machine in the pub. I have to say the fruit machine seems to be a tricky proposition for making money! The betting shop is the core of the game with a realistic sports simulation of horse racing and football (all 1980's style). The horse racing is by far the deeper and becomes very involving as the game progresses. The football side could do with some improvements.
The pub and beach are places to visit primarily when you are getting short of funds as they work on a kind of community chest system where you get random cards often giving you extra funds or food. You will spend most of your time in the betting shop.
There is little actual progression to the game apart from the Steam achievements but that kind of adds to the hopeless vibe of being stuck on benefits in some seaside town in the♥♥♥♥♥♥end of nowhere. Initially the monotony can be a bit off putting but after a while becomes kind of hypnotic. You can add your own music tracks which play back through the radio with an authentic crackly sound. The real fun for me comes with the thrill of choosing a horse and listening to the audio commentary. Audio commentary is unpredictable. It doesn't matter if your horse has not been mentioned you still cling to the hope that it will finish fast and be called on the winning line.
In summary it's a very original and unique game but not for everyone. It's like a little dirty, old fashioned alternate life I relive now and again on my PC. Why? I'm not sure, maybe nostalgia but I regularly feel compelled to play. All to a soundtrack of Depeche Mode and The Police! Recommended.

A very unique but simple 80's game that reflects gives a nice retro feeling and an old visual style. Most of the game is spent in the betting shop trying to win on the horses (and football once a week) to survive. On starting it feels a bit repetitive. And it is! But the game grew on me after a few quick sessions and the horse racing becomes quite engaging as time goes on. The pub and beach are just add-ons that serve to give you a possible funds boost should you run low on cash. That's about it really. It does have a nice 80's feel and I would recommend this with the proviso that you remember the 80's and old betting shops! LOL. It's just an odd game.
Anyway, in some way’s it feels like it has something to say around run down town centres and unemployment culture and the hopeless lives that used to (and probably still do) spend their day’s living this repetitive life. Maybe this game is some kind of cultural statement not normally seen in video games or maybe it’s just a simple game.
I read on the forums something about 'staring at a Lava lamp' but it feels more like a weird retro experience rather than a game if that makes sense. I suspect a large number of gamers just won't get it but I enjoy playing it albeit in brief sittings.  I think it has a lot of potential to be developed and expanded with a story and extra locations.

Steam isn't listing very many hours on my end, but I've been an avid fan of Aura Kingdom since shortly after OB was released several years ago. Since it's release, it has improved in so many ways, it's nearly breathtaking.
Many consider it "boring," or maybe "tedious," but I'd like them to say otherwise in any other online MMO. (Bear in mind I've also been a huge MMORPG fan since I was a wee one.) You adventure, you kill things, you enjoy the story, and you kill some more things. It's... an MMO.
But let's brush up on the other neat features they have, ye?
HOUSING. Lord, when this feature came out, I screamed in joy at my computer. It's unfortunately not as vast as Rift's "Dimensions," but it's housing nonetheless, something that many, many MMOs lack and I've always found to be a wonderful fluff feature of gaming. You craft your furniture and other things for your preset home and are able to place it anywhere you like.
CRAFTING! I personally hate the crafting system, but that may just be me. I hate crafting in most games.
CARD BATTLES! wut! You know all of those fancy new online games that take after Magic: the Gathering? Yeah buddy, AK has one, too.
There's so much more, too. Various currencies you can earn in-game to get neat stuff, like costumes and even mounts or epic gear is one of my favorite features in this game. There's achievements, which earn you stuff, too, and even adventure quests and the like you can do.
Lots of people also whine and moan about AK being pay-to-win, but in my many years of playing this game, I REALLY just don't see it. Shortcuts? Sure. What F2P MMO doesn't have that nowadays? But is it game-breaking? Far from. Far, far from. Honestly, the only thing I have spent my money on in this game are costumes and mounts, because my materialistic little heart just pines for pretty things all the time. Which, by the way, they have a tiered spender system which is AWESOME.
Definitely recommend anyone to this game that can get past the cutesy anime-style of the game. Looking for story? You got it. Looking for extensive gearing and stats? You got it. Looking for stunning costuming and mountage? You. Got. It.

I haven't scratched too much at this game, but after fifteen hours of play time I have to admit that the game has grown on me to the point of earning a positive review. I admit that I have widely ignored fabrication fishing outside of quests; haven't dappled in cooking, fortified or enhanced any of my gear or weapons; and really anything else beyond questing -- all of which would no doubt add to my level of enjoyment at some point or another. So here's a quick summary of my experience so far.
While not the most graphically advanced game, it's still a beautiful world with a variety of locations that you can unlock over time.
The display is a bit congested at first, but spending a moment to familiarize yourself with it solves that problem as you figure out what you prefer to have open.
The UI is a pain, so I chose to forfeit my Archer for a Brawler - someone who, at least in their description, seemed to have the ability to have some recover and decent damage - so that I didn't have to worry about moving around so much.
Switching was unnecessary though, as so long as you're using your abilities, you're dispatching enemies well before they put too much of a dent in your HP. My Brawler has a restoration ability that I haven't used at all since learning other offensive abilities with great synergy.
That being said, the combat is satisfying and gorgeous, but over time it does get grindy.
Speaking of grindy, the questing is incredibly easy. You interact more with the quest feed that you do the game, as it not only pathfinds for you, but performs the actions necessary too. That is, except for killing (x) amount of mobs. This is the kind of game you play in the background while doing something else. (Reading Aftermath: Empire's End, which I recommend.)
There are loads of pointless items all over the map, so it can be easy to load up your inventories quickly. At least quest=specific items will let you know that they are just that in their description. Management is doable.
Stats seem to rise and fall as you level up, which I haven't figured out why nor do I care to, because even so I'm still progressing swiftly through the game.
The passive abilities web is fantastic, allowing your to reach the edge of the web for amazing buffs in the early levels. I personally was able to secure a +10% crit chance with my weapons just for following, what, evasion? I foget. But it's amazing.
Eidolons are fun little companions that do notice if they're being neglected.
Boob physics is intense.
All in all it's a solid little game.

A surprisingly good game, and one that hasn't got near as much love as it deserves.  I went in without expectations on this and was very pleasantly surprised.  Word of warning though, this is not a survival horror as you would gather from the murky trailer and photos.  Rather it's more a psychological puzzler.  And a good puzzler at that!  As a whole most puzzles strike that very pleasing middle ground where it's not insultingly easy or hair-pullingly hard, and the puzzles move along at a very pleasing beat.
There's a neat, albeit minimal crafting system, which somehow manages not to come across as vestigial, and there is a pleasing buzz to get out of scouring the environments to gather the necessary materials to craft the item needed to progress.  Though this is only part of the gameplay.  Pretty soon the game introduces you to a handheld electromagnetic you control which opens up a whole new series of puzzle types, pushing boxes around, pulling yourself around platforms, or bouncing off magnetic surfaces.
The story is meted out in little audio clips, discarded documents, and the constant goading from the main antagonist over the intercom system, and while not stellar, definitely contains enough intrigue to keep you moving along.  However, the spoken word dialogue in particular could have done with more of an editor's touch, and the voice acting is a mixed bag altogether.  Some voiceovers are good, and others not so much.  The main antagonist sounds like the joker from the Arkham series, and while competently voiced, didn't really strike me as the right style for the type of character he was supposed to be.  But overall the audio doesn't distract too much to being an issue.
So overall, I definitely recommend you pick this up if you like a little bit of dread layered upon your puzzling games.

As you can see above I recommended this game, and if you want the quick notes scroll to the bottom of my review.
It’s always hard to figure out where to start with these. I suppose let’s start off by saying, if you’re going in expecting another indie jumpscare fest prepare to be surprised. That was my first impression with this game. There were a few jumpscares here and there, but mostly it was pure ambiance. But even this wasn’t particularly scary.
The Crow’s Eye is a “scary” puzzle game. It is reminiscent of older games where the simple objective was to get through the puzzle or solve this weird series of switches. Visually, it looks really good. For a new company they got a good team to work on this. Not to mention the soundtrack. I think that out of everything I loved the soundtrack the most. Most puzzles proved to be challenging and enjoyable. I applaud the main voice actor for William Holtwick. I enjoyed his voice work and thought he did well as did the voice actress for Evelynn O’Donnel. The storyline had an interesting start and had some good themes and ideas, however this is where my list of pros end.
The first problem I really ran into was lack of explanation. Don’t misunderstand me, there were plenty of control explanations and tips, but at certain puzzles you were given almost no indication of what to do. And yes I enjoy the good ol’ figure it out for yourself method. But even these at least give some hint. The first trouble I ran into was a series of six or seven switches. There was no hint, as far as I could find, as to what order you were supposed to pull them and I had to figure it out via trial and error.
The second issue I had was that there were a number of things that seemed to go nowhere. *Spoiler*
For instance, the worms. I ran into maybe three throughout the entire playthrough and I explored every nook and cranny I could find. I felt they really were unnecessary in such a small amount. Either add more or remove them in my opinion. The plot overall felt like it kind of teetered out in the end. Throughout the entirety of the playthrough it is hinted that experiments went on with people and something about the grafting of animal parts to people, however these are not seen till nearly the very end of the game and serve absolutely no purpose. And it turns out they were irrelevant as well to the experiments you are involved in. Speaking of petering out, we never truly discover what happens to Robert. He simply disappears and his notes end. Never stated what happened, if he was killed for his turning on the doctor or if he left, etc.
As it turns out, you’re involved in some sort of experiment where your father is hooked up to you and shown your death in a million different ways to exploit some sort of precogniscience he has gained via an experiment from some years previous through a vague experiment titled the “Philadelphia Project,” that is poorly explained in the end. And though you are hooked up to your dad mentally, it is never stated whether or not what you experienced was real. If it was, then there was absolutely *no* explanation as to what the hell was going on. If it was just a mental simulation than they should’ve stated.
The entire ending is an explanation going on for some minutes by the antagonist where he reveals why we went through this. It never really explains the strange symboled doors we sometimes saw or why we were randomly transported to trial rooms after entering a place. It really felt like we were all over the road plot wise and I felt that a good plot could have really cemented this game and made it great.
*Spoiler End*
The plot isn’t overall bad. It has a lot of potential and was interesting as well. I just wish they had explored more of the things they hinted at.
Something that was more of a pet peeve than anything major was that most of the “hidden areas” for the achievement were pretty much in your direct path and needed only a turn of the head to find or see.
Out of a list of five voice actors I enjoyed two of them, the two stated previously. I sort of like the voice for Benjamin, but disliked Robert’s. He felt like he was very forced emotionally.
I also felt the crafting system was very unnecessary. You really only craft like three or four items. The only ones you’ll continually craft are bandages with maybe three maps for the entire game and three sets of lockpicks. I just felt like this could have had either more done or been ripped completely and it wouldn’t have affected the gameplay at all.
Overall, I do recommend the game. It’s obvious the developers worked hard on the visuals and sounds and it shows...that they focused mainly on that. Its got a good price for a good amount of gameplay and I’d love to get my hands on that soundtrack.
Fun 3/5, Scary 1/5, Originality 3/5, Graphics 4/5, Maturity 4/5, Worth the Price? Yesish.

The Crow's Eye
PUBLISHER Nkidu Games, Inc
DEVELOPER 3D2 Entertainment
GENRE Puzzle/Psychological Horror
THE BASICS:
This is a first-person psychological horror game with puzzle and platforming elements. You don't have to worry about zombies lurking around every corner, nor all sorts of hideous beasts lurking for just the right moment to strike (though you will come across a few of those). You won't be going in guns blazing for this one, for your primary adversary – aside from the lunatic who put you here – is the old school itself.
You'll need to solve puzzles, starting from simple box/jumping puzzles to platforming while under the affects of adrenaline (here represented as a brief period of slowed time, during which you can jump much farther than usual), on up. The game has a basic crafting system, allowing you to make crude bandages, lockpicks, and more to get you through the game alive and (hopefully) still sane.
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
In 1966, renowned medical college Crowswood University was shut down after a number of unexplained disappearances took place there. Now, in 1966, you have been brought there as part of some bizarre experiment. Your goal is to survive and get back home. Bits and pieces of evidence, photos, documents, and recordings will help you to piece together exactly what happened there, as well as some of the University's dark secrets.
CONTROLS:
Mouse & slightly unusual Keyboard/WASD. Controller support is available (just hit any controller button to swap), but incomplete; on my XBONE controller, the d-pad was not usable. WASD to move, hold right-click to grab/throw items (plenty of delicate glass to smash!), E to interact, V to play recordings, F to toggle the map, TAB for inventory.
GRAPHICS:
Suitably creepy, and they can be maxed out even on a mid-range system. The environment feels like a decrepit, abandoned school facility that has been booby-trapped for your inconvenience. The dirty walls – which are festooned with some very odd paintings – are that sort of off-white color used to keep the inmates subdued in schools and in prisons.
SOUND:
The background music changes as needed to help establish tension. Solid voice work all around; a frightened professor has a tremor in her voice; your mad jailor has a distinct Mark Hamill's “Joker” feel to his ravings, etc.
OVERALL:
If you'd like to play Resident Evil without having to watch your back and blast zombies all of the time, this game could be right up your alley. Just the right price for the length, too.
SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS:
Moderate. Win 7 or better, 4GB RAM, Core i3/i5
REVIEW BY: Eric_Kei

Pros:
Good, subtly creepy atmosphere
Doesn't fall back on the tired crutch of “jump scares” to make the environment unsettling
The antagonist has a definite “Joker” feel to him

Gaining XP and/or (?) points will have you levelling up from time to time, at which time you'll be given upgrade points. You can pause the game at any time to unlock and upgrade attributes (damage, shot speed, shields, multi-tiered bonus modes, etc., and choose between bonus modes you've unlocked. Bonus modes will run for a specific time after activation, doing things such as giving you extra damage or slowing time as long as the bonus bar is reducing. This game has a lot of great things going for it, like consistent design, zero slowdown even under the craziest projectile load, and some seriously excellent sound.  The mazes are large and simplistic, and no level takes any real amount of problem solving to complete.  The neat tricks on offer - secret destroyable or passable walls, bonus exits etc - are used sparingly enough that the core gameplay is always front and centre.  It never feels like a weak game behind obscured by distracting tricks.  It is, I have to say, a real heap of fun, except...
It's too easy.  Powerups are generously awarded, not so fast that you fill all the gauges in a hurry, but fast enough that by level 20 most stages have become a cakewalk (and I'm playing on hard).  Even as new, bigger baddies are introduced (ooh, this vector circle's a different shade of purple, what does it do oh it's dead already) they're killed just as quickly.  It doesn't take more than the least amount of effort to keep from dying.  Boss fights are rare but never take two tries.  I'm 50 stages in (out of 80) and I've had to restart a stage maybe ten times, mostly in the first 20 levels.  I play a few rounds a few times a day but usually stop because it's just not exciting enough to keep going.
I wish I could wholeheartedly recommend this game, but it's got some issues.  I sympathize with the developer who has said it's not been anything approaching remotely profitable, and I suspect as a result the game's bugs will never be fixed.  Some powerup options cannot be selected, or sometimes they can depending on whether the game gifts one to you or if you earn it with experience points.  And sometimes not even then.  The game is always in-focus even if it's behind another application, so that it's always making noises as if you're hovering over a menu option.  It doesn't detect my gamepad, while every other game does.
If it were harder, if there were fewer enemies that were harder to kill, perhaps it wouldn't feel so inevitable that I'll beat it without dying 20 times.  It's a fantastic miasma of light and sound and I love that stuff to bits, but that thrill, that missing component that makes you want to keep coming back, just isn't quite there.

Owning this game is a weird mix of pure enjoyment and hatred. No matter how often it kicks the utter s*it out of me and makes me alt f4 in disgust, I just keep coming back and playing it.
Best way I can describe it is Binding Of Isaac but less f*cked up. You have permadeath, tons of random loot, some helpful, some put in just to laugh at your stupid face. It's got brawler like mechanics, you can swing enemies around giggling as you whack their skulls into rocks, trees, other enemies, or youir friends if you're in multiplayer. Then you can uppercut them into the air and basically Falcon punch them across the map. There's no real combo system, but it really doesn't need one. The combat does what it's meant to, without being overly complicated. The game is too fast pased and frantic to need combos.
The only real problems with it is the final boss is pathetic. It's a 3 stage fight. Stage one barely does anything. Stage 2 can't attack, and stage 3 doesn't take into account anything you have collected since it's a completely different game mode. Only time your items matter is when you get a certain few items that literally render all it's attacks useless.
The controls are very fluid and respond well. Out of all my deaths I've never once felt like it was due to s*itty controls or the game just being a d*ck. The game is very skill based and very fair. You never get curb stomped because the game felt like you had played enough, but because you decided to dodge away from the enemy, into another enemies axe blade, you idiot.
The game has a good risk - reward system. An example would be; there’s some armor you can find that slices off 20 life, and has the lowest armor rating in the game, only being able to block 3 hits when most are 4+. So why bother using it? Every kill you get regenerates its rating. Meaning you will not take damage as long as long as you keep killing, you can ensure you always have 1 - 3 armor points. It’s entirely based on your skill, and if you f*ck up you’ll be down armor and 20 life. If you’re good at evading and killing you’ll always have armor for those oh s*it moments.
The only time the  game feels unfair is on the later levels + difficulties. If you don't get the ability to fly over pits, there are times you just have to accept the death and restart, because some levels can be literally nothing but a massive pit, with spikes on almost every surface, against flying enemies. So if you can't levitate you're pretty much boned.
Runs are short, so the permadeath isn't a big deal like it was in Isaac. It usually takes me about 30 mins to go from spawn to final boss. With the randomized loot and level layouts, the runs never get tedious. Even the first area has some parts that can stomp you into the ground if you're not paying attention.
To summarize a bit:
Very frustrating but satisfying game. Get frustrated at all the deaths, then satisfied when you go up against hard enemies and turn their faces into mince with your now super good skills.
Interesting and creative items and other things. I once got a curse that made me take nonstop damage unless I was in combat, then a curse that made inanimate objects come to life and try kill me.
Controls are solid and very responsive. I've never had a moment where I was yelling at the screen for my character to move due to bad controls.
Final boss is pathetic, and once you know his 2 attacks he's utterly pointless, until you get to the final stage where you either get very good very fast, have a series of items that renders every attack ineffective, or die and restart.
It also has local and online co-op. No servers or anything, you have to invite people for the online thing. The co-op has a very interesting revive mechanic that involves ghosts and me floating about going "Wooo spooookkeeee" and p*ssing off my friend.

I gotta say I am starting to really love this controller.  What it is for me, is a way to play mouse/keyboard games on the comfort of the couch (streaming steam to a mini PC which is hooked up to my TV).  It also works as a great nav tool for Kodi etc.  The customizability alone is mind boggling, even to the point where you can use the analog stick to move around in a point-click move type game likes Diablo 3.  It does take a bit of getting used to, but if you are willing to spend the time to customize the controls, it can be a rewarding piece of gear for your PC-couch-gaming setup.

It feels well made and it works well. The triggers and extra buttons underneath all worked well.  It plugged in and off I went, though the start-up and shut-down noises are fairly annoying (I'll figure out how to turn them off at some point).
I like the idea of the touchpad but I've not used it enough as of yet, though it does allow more accurate 'look' than the traditional sticks.
All in all it feels like Valve are taking things forward and together with the steam link I bought and plugged into my main machine, I now have a pc upstairs and a "console" on the tv downstairs.

Firstly, it's not a Playstation or xbox controller, it's a PC controller.  With that in mind, it's slightly different to the aforementioned ones, so there's the ergonomics to get used to.  Once you have figured out to hold it and which buttons are where you then have to get your head round the fact that you're playing PC games with a controller, which means that it's never going to replicate being a mouse and keyboard.  What it does do though, is get very close to it.
The best part of it, for me, is the customisation - the possibilities are virtually endless and for a lot of games, there are custom configurations already uploaded that you can use or tweak to your own personal settings.
Steam has a lot of games - different types of games, and this controller goes a long way in being able to be a very good input device for many of them.  Some games in my library I still want to use the actual keyboard and mouse, but for others, I'm converted to using the controller.
Would i recommend it? Yes, for the price and customisation abilities, it's a no-brainer and it wins hands-down over plugging in a Playstation or xbox controller to the PC.  Would i ditch the keyboard and mouse? (er...?) No, there are always going to be games that you need that extra bit of sensitivity or many multiple function keys for.

On first use it was weird and clunky, but after a few hours of game play and switching up which games I was playing I was understanding the controller better. I think most major complaints are the product of expecting something to work perfectly with every game. Takes practice and the patience to design your own configurations. If you are looking to get a controller specifically for your computer I would highly recommend this over a traditional xbox or ps2 controller. The two extra triggers are extremely useful, but this by no means competes with a keyboard/mouse.

My review is going to be a bit longer than the others, sorry about that: I am this kind of person who writes walls of texts.
At first I was planning to write a long review that would deeply analyze how does Paladins compare to Overwatch, e.g. "Overwatch has way better graphics and lore, but graphics and lore don't bother me, both games have crappy balance (you can find tons of articles about both games), Paladins have way more interesting gamemodes (compare the boring Payload in Overwatch to the Siege in Paladins), lower time to kill, better average mobility, etc”. Actually, from my extremely subjective point of view,  Paladins wins against Overwatch as it is now. As it is before the OB64...
On December 13th a new update is gonna hit (and most likely kill) the game, with a system called "Cards Unbound", which is gonna turn Paladins, currently a free-to-play session-based FPS/MOBA game, into a pay2win MMORPG.
Here you can read more about that system's cryticism:
Don't forget to read the comments, they have some extra points raised.
Here you can sign a petition against it:

This is already signed by 6241 people as of 7. December 2017, which is around 1/3 of average amount of daily players for the last 30 days (according to Steam Charts:
. After just 6 days in!
I am lamenting, but not because I can't afford Overwatch -- I own it, but I just don't like the low TTK (time to kill), low mobility, poor optimization, and many more other to-be-improved aspects of the Blizzard game. Neither am I whining because I cannot afford to buy those powerful cards that are to be released and basically require you to pay or grind: I can afford them. But I just don’t want to pay for them.
Playing a pay2win game is unfair in any case. If you win, you cannot be proud of it, because there is a chance that you have won just because you have paid. If you lost, you can always just think that it happened because your opponents have bought better cards.
If I am going to play Paladins after this update, unless the concept of "Cards Unbound" changes, it is going to be ranked matches: they will not have they pay2win aspect, cards' level will be a fixed number, equal for everyone. However, I am not even sure about me playing ranked after OB64 as it is currently announced, for the following reasons:
1) People who don’t play ranked games, perhaps at all, and only play non-ranked matches, can get fed up with the upcoming pay-to-win chaos, and transfer to ranked games with their non-ranked mentality: for example, not playing to win, but rather playing for fun and for the sake of it, not caring much about the rest of the team, about coordination, picking the right characters for the current situation instead of the one you like to play most, etc. This will spoil the fun for many ranked players, who expect a lot of team cooperation to win. Of course, those unranked-thought guys will unlikely fit in the high-tier divisions like Diamond (top 16% players), but they will likely spoil low-tier ranked divisions like mine (Silver IV, something very low). I am, perhaps, low-skilled, but I am very deeply involved in team coordination, and expect other ranked players to be that way.
2) This is covered by the Reddit post, but some the balance of Paladins was largely based on the cards. If you drastically change them, you also harm many aspects of Paladins that make it a good game. Some cards that enhance movement abilities gonna get nerfed — means that mobility in general gets nerfed once again, and it is harder to escape when you think that it is time. DPS abilities’ cards are buffed — time to kill becomes lower again, healing is indirectly nerfed, tanky abilities with limited tanking HP pool are indirectly nerfed, DPS heroes are buffed. Some new abilities get introduced during the chaos of OB64 — there will be no testing environment for it. Etc, etc.
3) Also covered by the Reddit post, but the game will mostly lose its customization aspect, which I liked very much.
Overall, it makes Paladins five steps closer to the pew-pew shooters like Battlefield or Quake. Don’t get me wrong, they are awesome! But I liked Paladins for being different: after all, if I want some pew-pew gameplay, I can just play Serious Sam, Battlefield, or Quake.
This also makes Paladins 10 steps closer to a typical Asian MMO, with a typical grind2win and pay2win fests. While some gaming cultures consider pay2win something typical, any such mechanic alienates the game from the competitive genre.
I am very sad about it, but Hi-Rez, the developer of Paladins, seems to miss the events currently happening to EA and their recent “hit”, Star Wars: Battlefront II, that has lost billions of dollars for their lootboxes problem.
Another problem is that when the game has so many players, it is very hard to find friends to play with or get your players into this game. They will all learn about they Pay2Win hell that this place will become and likely decline the offer. After all, it will be a bit unfair to know about this and try to get someone to play Paladins.
I would be glad if they cancel this update, but I don’t believe in this. I will try to find my own place under the sun of this game.
Though, I strongly not recommend this game to anyone who is not deeply involved yet.
Yes, I understand that the game developers themselves are *likely* not the ones to be blamed: the executives are. But crap is still crap, no matter who is responsible for it.

You might be like me.  You got into gaming on Doom and Doom 2.  You played Quake and Quake 2.  You maybe skipped Q3 because DM only games... meh.  You got Doom 3 and while an excellent game, it was a little too survival horror.  This DOOM is probably what Doom 3 should've been.  It's fast paced intense combat.  I get headaches from clenching my teeth trying to back-peddle and shoot Hell Knights at the same time!
It's a bit over the top gory. When I first saw the glory kill thing I immediately put this game on my "don't bother" list with the latest Mortal Kombat.  Don't get me wrong, you shoot a demon in the head you want to see copious blood and bone right? RIGHT!  But it's this new trend of close up "let's pause the action so we can watch bones break and see individual blood drops hit the camera" thing I can't get behind.  But I'm happy to report the glory kill mechanic is completely optional and has the benefit of giving the player small amounts of health for doing them, and they really kind of add to the fast pace gameplay, even though they're semi-bullet-timey.
The thing I really love though is how fluid the game feels.  You glide from place to place, you can jump AND MANTLE to higher ledges, it's just very clean and smooth feeling.
There's also some great dark, though modest humor that harkens back to the good ol' days.  Like if you jump into a pit of fire, you slowly burn, fall to your knees, hands out in front of you, slowly burning and just as you sink down to die your hand slowly turns a thumbs up just before the "load" screen comes up.
There's also a bunch of RPG type upgrades to find/earn/get, changing the functions of your weaponry, upgrading your suit's ability and armor, not to mention playable Doom 1 levels using old textures just like you remember, but DOOM (4) monsters in place of the classic ones.
Once the level is cleared (or mostly cleared) I have just as much fun running around trying to mantle up everything seeking out every last secret area as I do fighting the monsters.  It's like two games in one.
I'm not much for public DM but I found I just had to try and it was presently surprised with how that all worked out.  Except, F that guy with the lighting gun.  Every kill I got was followed by a streak of lightning from behind and this guy running over my corpse!  Still fun though.
All that being said, I HIGHLY recommend this game for fans of the original.

I first played Deus Ex - Human Revolution when it was first released on the Xbox 360. I have to say, the game's replayability has not been diminished. While having an interaction/combat system similar to the Mass Effect series (conversation wheels, cover system), it manages to use this with a greatly expanded environment. Can't hack the door? Then shoot it down. Or mug the guard for the code. Or talk him into giving it to you. Or climb through the air vents, circumventing the door entirely. The augmentation system, the game's answer to RPG leveling, can make your character absolutely amazing, without ever making him overpowered. Don't want to fight through a room of soldiers? Hack their security system, turning turrets and robots against them. Or stick to the shadows, and hunt them down silently, Splinter Cell: Conviction style. Or just lob a grenade in there. The story is a well thought out 'detective - intrigue meets personal journey' plotline, with some classic conspiracy thrown in there, and a plethora of optional side-quests, set against a divisive ethical debate that you can interact with. All in all, a fantastic game, and the release of the Director's Cut, which bundles together a graphical rehaul with DLC and improved boss fights (allowing the same freedom of playstyle that the rest of the game offers), is simply the icing on the cake.
9.5/10 - Nothing's perfect; I never liked 'The Missing Link' DLC, and I thought that a more fleshed - out epilogue would have done the game good.

I originally played this game on console a few years ago, at the time it became my favourite game. I had to buy it on PC and I'm so happy that I did. The game's story is incredibly immersive, it's a believable not too distant future in which cybernetic augmentation has become common place and you play the role of one such augmented person. There are a wide range of skills which you can upgrade as the game progresses, a range of weapon choices and a multitude of side quests. Even if you try to rush the campaign it would likely take you well over 20 hours but once the story takes hold you'll find yourself completing every side quest you can find. The game is often stealth orientated but if you choose an all guns blazing approach is your choice to make in every situation. The Director's Cut is available, offering even more missions and options including stealth aspects to boss battles.
You can make choices as the game goes on and every choice matters, your skills will limit your choices too so depending how you upgrade will depend how the story plays out, offering multiple endings. Once you've finished the game, you can start again, choosing new skills and playing a different story. This is one game that will stick with you! If you enjoy a bit of gritty sci-fi and some very well designed free roaming levels with an in depth upgrade system, then this is the game for you!

I was concerned that Dead Rising 3 would suffer some loss of its quirky charm because Capcom Vancouver was developing it as opposed to a Japanese studio, but I was pleasantly surprised.

All in all, this game is a MUST have for any serious Dead Rising fan. Honestly this is even a compelling reason to buy an Xbox One if you're in to consoles. Luckily it had a PC port and that wasn't necessary. It was one of the better games I've played in recent years.

Rampage Knights was one of those games on a whim that a friend and I decided to chalk up to chance and give it a shot. I'd been hankering for a game that reminded me of the action-packed, responsive, game-play mechanics that were offered by games like Castle Crashers (as many people have already mentioned) and, while dated, extremely satisfying in this respect, Streets of Rage. I have to say, I'm very satisfied with the purchase! It satisfies that hunger for quick (or not so quick depending on your intentions for progression), gratification that comes with simple objectives yet satisfying the desire for the complexity that comes with character customization (both cosmetic and functional), character diversity (in class choice availability), and advancement (that comes with the numerous available power-ups, weapons, armor, and accessory choices). In many, many ways it exceeds all of the expectations that came from its predecessors.
The difficulty scales appropriately based on how far you've gotten in a single session, is adjustable based on your masochism (I kid slightly, but make no mistake, harder difficulties prove to be VERY challenging especially when playing cooperatively), and rewards you for your diligence and skill. You can very quickly find your patience dwindling faster when playing cooperatively as it can be very easy to set your friend off track with an accidental strike placed in their direction, or an unfortunate curse that involves a giant foot crashing down on your unsuspecting companion.
Dungeons seem randomized in a way that makes every experience fresh while still providing you familiarity in the general progression with each 'level' being the same theme as you continue your adventure, but the rooms you encounter can change drastically with whatever monster, items, or mini-boss/game events you encounter. I always find myself pleasantly surprised (or feeling dismal surprise) with new blessings or curses encountered in each playthrough. It's roguelike in almost every sense of the word - offering permadeath, procedural generation, and the plethora of available magical items that alter your character for good or bad. Not a true rougelike with turn-based business and emphasis on multi-session labyrinths, but close enough to scratch that itch if it's what you're hankering.
In all:
+ Procedurally generated areas that offer fresh diversity with every playthrough
+ Tons of items and artifacts to collect to enhance or hinder your character during your session
+ Fair difficulty scale that rewards skill over button bashing and sheer persistence
+ A number of character customizations that come from the start and from earning them along the way
+ Easy to pick up and put down with diverse schedules
+ Simple plot that gets right to the point and focuses on the journey itself and the mechanics that make it so enjoyable
+ Very responsive, action-oriented gameplay that make you feel in total control of victory or defeat
- Cooperative gameplay can be frustrating with included mechanics to not specifically damage your ally, but totally disrupt their movements and cause lethal consequences that are 'usually' completely accidental
- Up-combo-strikes seem to always result in painful enemy openings unless it's one-on-one
The negatives are a stretch too as they add a very tactful variation to the way this game can be played, so I likely wouldn't replace them. I've experienced 0 connectivity issues either (which is a relief), especially since I play with someone who currently lives on the other side of the world (literally).
Definitely recommend this game!

So while the wife and kid were taking a nap, I decided it was time to try out this horror game that I picked up the other day! At first glance I expected a game that was going to make me wake up the family with my childlike screaming and heavy breathing through dark and damp hallways. While this was the case in a few instances, overall the game did not have that scare factor that I had expected. (This is noted on the description of the game, that if you are looking for the surprise jumps and scares, you may be in the wrong place)
I believe that I had roughly 2 instances of being actually startled by something in the game. One was when I was nonchalantly grabbing a key and a work jumped on my screen(in game of course) and the other when an ominous tone came into my speakers randomly. 
Unfortunately this game, while interesting and somewhat addictive (until you get too frustrated to continue) does leave something to be desired. The storyline is a bit hard to follow with the addition of multiple characters over time, and the random creepy guy who seems like he is from the past, but is talking to me as I am playing. I would have loved at least a few scary things around some of the vents and corners, but I can't ask for that if that is not what they intended. 
The quest line, while somewhat linear, does bring into play a bit of guesswork, and not in a good way. This guesswork created a very frustrating 10-15 minutes of sitting there wondering what I missed and where I have been on my very basic map. 
Overall, I would recommend this game to someone who enjoys mysteries, doesn't harp too much on the quality of graphics, and the person who wants to play a horror game without really being terrified.

This game was reviewed using a code provided by the developers/publishers
The Crow’s Eye is a puzzle horror game, set against a backdrop of psychological terror.
Story:
The Crow’s Eye follows a man, who wakes up in what seems to be an abandoned university. You have amnesia and you’re not sure how you got there. You are soon greeted by a man called William Holtwick, a crazy scientist who puts you through increasingly dangerous puzzles. The goal is simple – survive and escape from the scientist.
Graphics:
When I booted up The Crow’s Eye, I instantly noticed the Bioshock influences and the more you play the more similarities you notice between the two games. Graphically The Crow’s Eye looks alright, it’s nothing too special. A lot of the textures are really low res which detract from the enjoyment, but for an indie game it’s really good looking.
Audio:
The sound effects in the game are all really good. It’s creepy at times, where you walk around and hear the sound of the floors creaking. The voice acting is alright for the most part – everyone does a great job, expect the person who does the voice of Holtwick. His voice sounds like a poor man’s Mark Hamill Joker.
Gameplay:
The Crow’s Eye is rather similar to Portal. Each level you are thrown into a map and you are free to explore all of it, but some of it is locked off by puzzles which you have to solve to get further into the game.
The first couple of puzzles are rather simple and not difficult whatsoever. Most of them boil down to common sense, which makes things sort of easy. Not to worry, though, if you’re looking for somewhat brain teasing puzzles, as the game gets progressively harder as you venture deeper into the university.
The Crow’s Eye also has some platforming segments, but most of them are incredibly easy and won’t give you a hard time. To help you, the game gives you adrenaline which slows down time and makes you jump further.
One of the weirdest aspects of The Crow’s Eye is the crafting system. Throughout the game you find items which let you craft all sorts of stuff, like medicine, maps and lock picks. In the end none of those things are useful, as there are no threats in the game to actually harm you; the only way you take damage is by either falling off a ledge or poisoning yourself.
Verdict:
The Crow’s Eye is a fun puzzle game, with a fantastic atmosphere and some really smart puzzles. For the price it’s going for, it’s a fun game and I think it’s worth playing through at least once if you enjoyed games like Bioshock and Portal.
Final Rating:
7/10
Pros:
+ Smart Puzzles
+ Great Atmosphere
Cons:
- Some minor bugs

Really solid and tight twin-stick action, with deviously crafted levels and RPG development mechanics. Anyone who's a fan of twin-stick shooters or action dungeon-crawlers owes it to themselves to play this.

Radiangames makes some of the best pure overhead shooters, period.  It's a shame that thus far only his latest is on Steam, many having started on XBLIG and a few (notably JoyJoy) making their way to tablet and mobile.
But damned if he didn't further refine the pure fun and pressure of the original Inferno.  The experience isn't simplified, but rather distilled: four guns, each the right tool for specific situations, four missiles, each likewise unique and providing more oomph at the cost of limited ammo (there's plenty to be found, but you still need to be careful not to shoot yourself dry in the middle of a firefight), and four triggerable powers suiting different playstyles.  You can focus your powerups on the missiles and guns you enjoy most, and the specific boosts can be chosen in any order (for example, one of the guns may have more damage, faster shots, or a stunning effect... rather than being arranged in a tree, you can pick which to get first, with the knowledge that the cost of getting a second, then the third is going to increase afterwards.)
Personally, I'd love to see more of his games arrive here, though for now I can at least strongly recommend this one.  Fun as heck.  :)

Don't go into this one thinking it's a super-complicated visual novel- there's not a whole lot of depth to this one; but at the same time, what's there is actually pretty decent.
You play a guy who's living his dream of taking a trip to Japan.  He's made arrangements to stay in the home of some people he met in a chatroom on the internet.  Expecting a pair of brothers, he's kind of shocked to find out they're actually sisters... and the story goes from there.  There are two endings- one where you fall for each sister (the sweet older girl, or the tsundere tomboy who can cook).  The only three choices that have any impact upon the storyline are choosing what three places out of six given you want to go sightseeing at.  Each sister knows about three specific sites, and the one you spend at least two days with is the girl you end up with.
There are other choices that don't matter as much, but if you're a completionist, you'll want to play through the game three times to make sure that you can see everything (because on the night you get to pick dinner, there are three different choices).  There's no possible way to lose the game- like I think I just made a bunch of you guys do- so I would say if you're just looking for a sweet story to warm your heart and bring a tear to your eye, invest in this one- when it's on sale.  If you pay any more then five bucks for it, you're paying too much for it.  There IS a bit in the way of content here- you walk in on one sister in the shower while she's wearing nothing more than a towel, and then the next day, you walk in on the other one in her underwear- but nothing more serious than that.
I got it as a gift, and I enjoyed it, but like I said- ten's too much for this.

Keep in mind that as of this writing, I have NOT played single-player, only online co-op.
+Levels are just random enough to stay fresh, while also remaining familiar enough that you can get better at clearing them faster and faster.
+Co-op is a blast. The first time you hit your buddy and blood spatters everywhere, there is a moment of nervous panic, until you realize he took no damage. If you are your friends are a bit trigger-happy, you'll survive (unless you get knocked into a pit).
+Wide variety of weapons, spells, consumables, buffs, debufs, and special events. After nearly six hours of playing, I would guess at least 50% of the loot and special rooms we found were encountered only once or twice.
+Progression is fun and implemented well. Though you lose everything when you get a game over, your accomplishments will earn you bonuses (and hats—lots of hats) which persist from run to run.
+Death in co-op games is handled really well. When you die, you become a ghost, capable of striking enemies for 1 damage. If your partner can manage to kill a certain number of enemies before dying himself, you'll return to life with all your gear intact.
-THE FOOT! OH GOD THE FOOT!
TL;DR
It's a brutally fun game to play with a buddy, good for a quick 20 minute dungeon crawl, or for a whole evening of tough battles and epic defeats.

Go! Go! Nippon! ~Squiggly Lines~ is probably the most known cheesy visual novel on steam. I'm talking about cheesy ones, not actually good ones.
You play as Randomerican, some otaku from america who has been interested in japan ever since he watched an anime. One day he finally gets the chance of his life and goes on a trip to japan where he can stay with two japanese friends he met over the internet. Upon arrival you notice how the hero barely cares, seeing how he was expecting the two friends to be males instead of females. In my honest opinion he should probably be more careful with his decisions or he might aswell would have gone to japan and never get back home. And to his luck, the two girls are home alone while you are staying at their place. What a cooiincideeence. We all know where this is going.
As you stay with your one week waifus you get to learn about japan and it's culture. Yay! This is actually not too bad of an idea, but the execution is not the best. At all. If the main character wasn't acting like the average tourist all the time (WOAH! A TRAIN!) the novel would be way more enjoyable. But on the other hand it might just be a better idea to just go to a nearby tourist office, grab a brochure about japan (if they have those, I don't visit those) and be done with it. But I guess this game has a story. Somehow?
During the game you get to make your own decisions. Sometimes. And instead of just being there like in Sakura Spirit they actually affect the ending. It adds at least some sort of diversity, but it's literally either love girl one or love girl two.
And don't forget, like every poorly translated anime visual novel, you get your daily dose of random fap material. Like really, the two moments where that happens have no relation to the story at all. It's just there to beg for your curiousity.
Ramen/10.

----- The problem with this version of DOOM is a simple word, “Satan”. -----
One of the most iconic features of DOOM was satanic icons on EVERYTHING in game. I personally like to compare this version of DOOM with the previous one DOOM 3 which released in Aug 2004 (same year as Unreal Tournament 2004).
What we had, was a great ambient sound, nice story line and rich textures of blood, satanic icons and dark gore. This mix provides a feeling of “despairs” and “trapped” in player which even now with all these new graphics on modern game engine, is a great joy of gaming to try. In another word, they made an advanced version of old DOOM ( 90`s), and update all features in a beautiful, artistic and well-done quality. After years, still players put comments on how to expand graphic quality by using new graphic cards over the game (hopefully someone take this serious for a patch.).
The new DOOM is poor. Very little signs and icons of Mephistopheles, ambient music and sounds are NOT a right match and choice. Creatures are mostly wild, not psycho. One the most advantage of DOOM, was and “is” the creatures animation and feelings. I`m not off to hunt wild creatures, I`m looking for DOOMed creatures !
But, play ability is pretty sexy when you play on ultra-violence mood. I like the upgrades and secrets, they look pretty modern. The only problem is with shotgun, it doesn’t feel like 90`s, even in DOOM 3 , shotgun was a big mess in my opinion.
I can suggest “this” DOOM for fun and good gaming, but if you are an old dude of DOOM, well … give a try and make hope for better one…. : ) ,,

Saints Row 2 is more or less what youd expect of a saints row game (if youd played 3/4 first), but not quite as batshit insane yet.
See, Saints Row started as a poor mans GTA and up until SR3 it still very much contained that in essence, though it probably got a little more eccentric than GTA ever did.
Youll often hear people saying that SR2 is the best saints row game, and rightfully so, but not because 3/4 are actually bad games or worse games, but because SR3 and 4 are really really not what saints row was, so for all intent they may as well be considered a different series altogether.
In the end, SR2 is an excellent game, with lots of dumb fun and a nice large and filled map to do whatever you want with. Couple that with a good price and its almost a must buy for those who havent had the experience yet.

Since there is no neutral voting option for Steam games, I will rate this game a 5 on a scale of 1-10. Not great but not terrible either. I will preface this by saying if you plan on playing though the Saint's Row franchise and have never played before, start with this game first. SR 2 is by far the worst of the series, as I will explain below. If you have played 3 and/or 4 first, this game will probably annoy you.
The Good: The story and gang mission/strongholds are well done, for the most part. The plotlines are gritty and brutal and  the mission mechanics are pretty easy to understand. Having to eliminate each gang one by one makes you really feel like a kingpin and that you are making the city your own criminal empire one block at a time. I only wish the other aspects of the game were as fun and rewarding.
The Bad: Activities and Diversions for the most part are horrible. You can tell in the future games, Volition made it a priority to improve this aspect of the gameplay. The rewards the ones in 2 give are just not worth the aggrevation of fully completing them unless you are determined to get the 100% completion. Quite a number of them suffer from the same problem, forcing you to travel from one end of the map to the other and not anywhere close to the area the icon marker is located. And after getting past level 3 of 6, the "challenge" is just enldess mob waves that clog up the screen.
The Meh: The controls for the most part are easy to get the hang of, but at times they are very clunky. The gps system while helpful at times, make you take a lot of ridiculous routes and sharp turns and almost always makes you go in the opposite direction of where you want to drive . The world itself is full of life, but I lost count of the amount of times another car just appears out of nowhere to run into you or makes some jackass turns. The pedestrians for some reason always run into the road to avoid danger rather than away from it, but running them over is a riot.
If you are a Saint's Row fan, you will probably want to play this as it features the best and most raw story of all the game series. For those who like the genre (Just Cause. GTA, etc), it has enough to keep you occupied, but this game's mechanics can get very irritating and are not as well done.

Seems like Eidos Montreal decided they could never equal or better the first game, and given the colossal mess that was DX2, they made DX3 a tribute to the first, instead of an independent prequel. The number of similarities to DX1 are overwhelming, and so many elements are copy-pasted that as a die-hard DX1 fan, it makes for a bittersweet experience; it's a reminiscent mashup of things most people love: DX1 + Batman + or other games, yet it lacks depth and originality.
Adam Jenson from DX3 and JC Denton from DX1. Same syllables in name. If that sounds like a silly similarity, relax, I'm just easing you in. The list is endless: [spoilers]
The original DX3 was orange/gold bearing a stark resemblance to a few iconic scenes from the movie The Dark Knight. They went overboard making the entire game resemble the theme of those scenes, but after backlash from critics and players, they ended up normalizing it in the Director's Cut edition. And it looks much better now. Even then, if you pay close attention to the Detroit music you will notice the famous intro theme to Batman TAS. Moreover, a lot of people have even commented that Adam Jenson talks like Batman.
The hacking mini-game is a refreshing change, Typhoon augmentation (even though it clashes with the timeline), tons of easter eggs, being able to holster your weapon. Overall the music is very cinematic and atmospheric, with cultural influences too, such as the zhong-hu instrument in "Hengsha LIMB Clinic." Another score I absolutely loved is "The Mole." Vending machines are finally made useful, environments are much more "fuller" than doors/vents on an empty canvass like in the original Deus Ex, different ammo takes up inventory space (instead of one kind of ammo for everything), which is a nice touch of realism. There is a lot of detail in the world, which makes the world immersive. Critical conversations actually require you to listen to the other person, analyze their personality, and at times even their body language, and facial expressions, which is brilliant.
But 13 years have passed since DX1 and the AI still says, "huh, what? nevermind I'm hearing things" after you drop something in front of their face and successfully hide. This AI mechanic was revolutionary when it was introduced in Thief but not many games since then have built upon that. I threw 5 cartons on top of several open cubicles at a police station and everyone only said, "what was that?" and got "suspicious." This even goes for sound. Takedowns don't alert an enemy standing 2 feet away, even when the person you're taking down lets out a muffled squeal. I felt that was weak, especially for a game based highly on stealth. Any alarmed state can be nullified if you simply "walk away" from the scene, which is so manipulative it becomes unfun, and I think it is an element largely influenced from the Batman-Arkham series. Of all the games whose AI they imitated, if only they would have sampled Metal Gear Solid; once there is a state of alarm it never reduces back to normalcy. Alas
DX1 broke boundaries, and was the actual "revolution" in the gaming world. DX3 feels like a revision of the first, and a safe recipe of things that all gamers would love. It's unfortunate that Warren Spector was excised from the DX3 project by Eidos Montreal. Silly how the world works. He made a mind-blowing blockbuster of a game (DX1), but DX2 fell short of that standard, therefore he was boycotted. Cruel, given that he was the main brain behind this whole series. Eidos played it safe when making this prequel, and I guess you can't blame them. Not everyone can improve on perfection, but many can merely honor or mimic it, which is exactly what they've resorted to. And it makes for an enjoyable experience.

It is undeniable how much of an impact Amnesia: The Dark Descent has had on the survival horror genre as a whole. I think it’s safe to say The Crows Eye would be very different, or perhaps wouldn’t even exist without it. Amnesia opened the floodgates, showing indies the horror genre could be so much more. The Crows Eye takes a page out of Amnesia’s blood soaked book and adds numerous unique twists of it’s own, focusing on the psychological terror of it all.
You follow the path of an unnamed protagonist trying to escape the university of Crowswood. Influences from Bioshock are also abundant with a crisp Art Deco user interface, and audio logs represented as tape-players scattered throughout. You’re soon introduced to the insanity of William Holtzwick, the man in charge of the university. He will guide you through the university accompanied by his disturbing cackles of joy as he tests your mental well-being. While this cliche inspired by many horror influences such as Saw can be tiresome, the voice acting is hard to fault. Sometimes it does feel a little bit over-done, but this it balanced out by the audio logs of the other characters who are counter-actively much less insane.
You will also come across many puzzles, some of which are solved by mere trial and error, others requiring much more thought. Unfortunately there is a jarring disconnect between the environment and many of the puzzles. After exploring an abandoned manor house, the first puzzle is occupied in an enormous room of towering pillars and floating boxes. While the game soon gives you a reasonable explanation for these floating boxes, I would be lying if I told you it didn’t ruin the atmosphere a bit.
In the context of the entire game, floating boxes are a minor quibble, The Crows Eye nails the atmosphere 99 percent of the time. It knows how to play off your expectations, my stomach sank with dread on the first occasion it gave me a healing item; “Why is this game giving me a bandage? What’s going to hurt me?”. The notes you are given offer just enough mystery; keeping you eager for more, while letting your imagination run wild. Thunder claps will sound in the distance, the sound of crows taking flight, constantly keeping you on the edge of your seat.
Many of the sounds are so subtle it’s hard to tell if something dreadful lies behind the corner or if it wasn’t coming from the game at all. This tension isn’t squandered by cheap jump-scares every 5 minutes either, there were times I was almost hoping for a monster to appear, only to relieve the knot that was forming in my stomach.
The further you venture into the unknown the more variety soon opens up. While many of the puzzles involve pulling levers and moving boxes, they are short and satisfying to ensure they don’t become too repetitive. The game is paced with a mixture of searching for items, soaking in the atmosphere, performing logic puzzles and some simple platforming puzzles. First person platforming is often a huge frustration in games, but very early on you are given a syringe of adrenaline used to slow down time. This mitigates any frustrations I would normally have towards this kind of platforming.
The story twists and turns drip feeding you just enough information to keep you going. Some might find the story horribly vague at first, but to me it felt justified; brilliantly simulating my own confusion if I was in that situation. Almost all the loose ends are tied up, however it feels somewhat rushed. It would be far more engaging for the player to make up their own mind, being directly told extinguishes a lot of the mystery for me.
Last but certainly not least, this is all brought together by a surely haunting original soundtrack. While the graphics are somewhat dated it was hard to be taken from the experience when the music adds such a huge level of emotional depth. Mostly composed of violins and piano, it distinctly sets each scene and consistently keeps tension high.
All in all 3D2 Entertainment have a made an enthralling psychological puzzle horror game, despite the cliche setting. It takes many of the tropes from the horror genre, but uses them sparingly to ensure your experience never feels cheap. Those looking for a gruesome horror game with a jump-scare around every corner will be disappointed. The Crows Eye lets your imagination do a lot of the work, enabling a much more psychological feeling of terror, rather than fight or flight. If that sounds like your kind of thing, I highly recommend it.
Rating - 8/10

I’ll start by stating very clearly that The Crow’s Eye is every other genre you can imagine, but definitely not Horror. In the several hours of playtime I have accumulated so far (and reached the end of the story), I wasn’t startled or scared by anything this game has thrown at me. No jump scares, no implied terror or even tension at the very least. You have to be aware of this and if you can come to terms with a relatively toothless “atmospheric horror” as it is being marketed, you might enjoy playing it. I sure did, despite the mislabeling. The game represents the Steam debut of its developer and I am pleased by their first project.
While I never make a habit out of spoiling the storyline or even subplots in any of the games I review, I can safely offer you some small but crucial details, which you may learn anyways within the first 30 minutes of actually playing The Crow’s Eye. The title is clearly linked to the location you’ll be assiduously exploring throughout the game: Crowswood University. I could draw several stylistic and plot similarities to BioShock 1. Rapture is also seemingly abandoned at first glance and things quickly take a turn for the worse as you arrive. Crowswood has William Holtwick as main antagonist. A mad and equally deadly scientist in the vein of Andrew Ryan.
Both aforementioned titles feature silent protagonists whose identities are only revealed near the end of their stories. I have finished the game and I can point out to story or visual style influences from gaming cult classics such as The Suffering series and the good ol’ Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth. In other words, you’re preparing for a very gripping storyline filled with challenges and unsettling characters.
Sadly, the graphical details cannot keep up the pace or level of polish, present within the gameplay mechanics. I am always pleased to see the Unity 5 Engine being stretched to its limits by ambitious developers, but the textures and assets used in The Crow’s Eye felt both overused and lacking in sufficient details. Even when running the game maxed out, the textures weren’t very crisp and their patterns could be found on all the game’s levels. Gameplay repetitiveness only gets exacerbated by the constant use of just a few assets.
Even more weird was the resolution option which never seemed to change as far as my screenshots were reporting. Screen resolution was thus unchanged and just the game objects were affected by the switch from 1920x1080 to 2560x1440 or 3840x2160 options. Frame rate was all over the place when running both the screen and object resolution at full 4K. Some performance tweaks or patches are quite mandatory in this case. Overall, the game does look decent but nowhere near as pretty as the standards for quality 3D indie titles in 2017 demand.
At least you’re in for a treat in the audio department. Top notch soundtrack, which can also be purchased separately on Steam and contains 33 tracks ranging in style from smooth jazz to eerie instrumentals. In-game use of the OST is spot on, as some level sections feature dream/nightmare sequences that make good use of songs not typically found  in titles within the  horror or thriller genres. The really pleasant surpise though, was the voice acting.
For a game in which you rarely interact directly with other characters, at least their spoken words shall guide, tease, mock and attempt to trick the protagonist in a skilled manner, from both the pronunciation and voice tone perspectives. Hearing Holtwick’s self-righteous drivel and incessant laughter throughout most levels, he reminded me of Mark Hamill and his brilliant performance as The Joker in the Arkham video games or the Batman animated series.
Pure 3D Puzzle Platformer with the occasional creepy atmosphere which I shall summarize as “3D Adventure”. Can’t really call it Horror since you’ll only witness 4 direct threats to your health during the entire playtime. Three of those potentially deadly instances contain some type of facehugger/bug that you need shake off your head through rapid movement of the mouse peripheral. The fourth and my favorite such tense moment involves, finding an antidote for your unexpected poisoning within the time frame of less than two minutes.
As you can imagine, such examples of unexpected action from a game that has you wandering countless rooms and corridors, provide well deserved distractions for a fairly repetitive core gameplay. The Crowswood University once hosted students of Medicine but now it’s a near literal ghost town. You’ll be constantly on a fetch quest for one object or another. A crafting system is implemented and thus you may combine various inventory items into, bandages, lockpicks, maps or a powerful electromagnet which will prove crucial to late game puzzle sections.
Even without a looming threat per se, the game does its best to offer a creepy ambience. It didn’t really click for me, but your mileage may vary.  The puzzles you’ll need to solve are intuitive and increase in difficulty as your character also descends ever closer to madness. Alas, I found them diversified enough and with just the right amount of challenge to boot. The presence of so many bandages and static save game stations, tricked me into thinking that this title might feature combat of some sort. That expectation never materialized, unfortunately.

The Crow’s Eye shares more of its gaming DNA to the Portal series than Silent Hill, for example. If you’re okay with that, the game can be quite entertaining albeit misleading from its current Steam Store description. You have no foes to face head-on and I won’t spoil you the ending, but suffice to say it offers a cliffhanger large enough that I expect a sequel eventually. And I do hope The Crow’s Eye fares well with its potential buyers and players. If you would judge the developer just from the perspective of a Steam newcomer, you would be impressed by what they achieved with their first and so far only, released project. For what it offers, I consider it more than decently priced.
+ Challenging puzzles.
+ Captivating storyline.
+ Excellent voice acting and soundtrack.
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements.
- Doesn’t quite live up to the promised “psychological terror”.
- Level design frequently requires backtracking.
- Underwhelming graphics.

It's a pretty interesting spooky adventure game. The graphics are pretty decent, but optimization is a little on the weak side. The voice acting is good. Puzzles are legitimately pretty decent. The entire game feels like a budget version of Resident Evil 7 honestly.
If you want to know more feel free to watch my YT video :)

or watch it here:
The game is set in a medical university. You don’t know who you are or why exactly you’re there, but a bizarre voice guides you over the radio. As you progress through the game, you explore and find letters and audio logs that shed some light on the disappearances that took place in the university decades before. The sense of mystery is always intriguing, but as the plot developed and more of the pieces came together, things got strange, and I felt indifferent about what I learned.
The gameplay starts off on the slow side with a lot of walking around, and exploring rooms to finding specific items you need to progress such as a key to unlock the door. I spent a lot of time waiting for something to happen, but I learned quickly that I could essentially throw all caution out the window. I admit that I was sort of bored with the gameplay early on, since it felt like a walking simulator without the immersion factor.
When I reached more puzzles, I became more interested in the game. The puzzles were definitely the highlight for me, but I wish there had been more. Some of the environmental puzzles require platforming skills; you also have a magnet tool, and an adrenaline booster. The adrenaline boost temporarily slows down the world around you, and let’s you jump further than you normally could. The magnet tool allows you to push and pull certain objects (including yourself).
The game took me a bit under 6 hours to complete while taking my time and trying to explore thoroughly. However, it’s not worth replaying the game to collect everything.
Ultimately, I’m pretty torn on the game. There were things I enjoyed, like the puzzles, and using the magnet tool and adrenaline ability. Then there were other things I didn’t like that resulted in a weak atmosphere, and lack of immersion. The Crow’s Eye is an ok game; it isn’t bad, but it doesn’t stand out as being that good either.

You're sitting alone in a sweaty back room of a club. Around you are 4 men wearing suits and oakleys. As you sit uncomfortably on the steel chair set in the middle of the room, you hear screams coming from the walls. You sweat harder, thinking what horrible demise awaits you, when a small, balding man walks in through between the men. He hands you a checklist, and you are confused as you read it. You sit and take in what you just witnessed, feeling the power rise inside of you, and walk out the door of the room, into the club. Go! Go! Nippon! is a short visual novel most likely intended to be more educational or at least to lend a somewhat idealised insight of a trip to Japan rather than to be a standalone story. The cast is downright minimal, CG usage sparse and quality of the writing quite basic. However, as much as its possible to reprimand its simplicity it can just as much be a positive note -- it feels as though this would make a neat little "My First VN".
The novelty of GGN! comes from its usage of a dual text box showing both English and original Japanese text. For anyone interested in learning or, perhaps more adequately, someone who has a moderate knowledge of the language it makes a nice reference point. If I had any criticism of this it was that it wasn't possible to hide one or the other languages on the fly (to practice reading and translating) and there was no option to enable furigana for the more complex/rare kanji to really make it stand out as a learning aid. A full AGTH-like interface such as the ability to hover individual words/kanji and see more detailed information would have really made it useful for this, although this could have been achieved manually by playing with a dictionary in hand.
The protagonist is very much meant to be a self-insert for the player: someone who wishes to visit Japan and knows odd bits of the history and customs through anime as well as a bit of study; punctuated in moments where some of their expectations get shot down when reality has been stretched by the fiction they know. The only real sense of disbelief here is that while they claim to have done a "little bit of study" on the language, they speak damn near fluently save for plot, learning or surprise. The two girls of the game -- Makoto and Akira -- are very much cardboard cutouts of standard anime personalities: the knowledgeable and understanding older sister and the tsundere, slightly tomboyish younger sister. As far as writing is concerned I cant really fault either of them as much as I cant really find much interesting or unique about them. Its almost clinical. The romance between either one of them feels rather contrived also. More dialog/choices during trips with them probably wouldve done well to blur this a bit.
Anyone who has been to Japan may find themselves relating or reminiscing with the protagonist, their mindset and any revelations they encounter (the teeming trains and scarcity of ATMs being mine) but, as I say, this VN is most likely intended for people who havent had the opportunity to visit and are willing to play a short VN on the subject as a form of self-tortu-- motivation.
Theres a number of VNs out there I can and would recommend to people not interested in Japan, anime or even the culture at all but (and this probably goes without saying) this is not one of them. It feels a cop-out to end a review like this, but if you even think youll like this game then you likely will. GGN! is very much a game built for people who would be interested in the first place. Theres no hidden gems here, just a VN thats so on the nose you may as well call it Pinocchio.

This controller is garbage.  I pre-ordered because I was excited by the concepts it embodies -- I thought it might be a genuine generational leap for controllers.  In short, this is not that.  This cheap and flimsy feeling controller is a symphony of bad design.  The trackpads are imprecise and provide insufficient feedback; the much-vaunted haptics don't solve this problem.  The face buttons are small and awkwardly placed, almost impossible to distinguish by touch.  The shoulder buttons are hard to reach given the shape of the controller, and the back panel buttons are positioned such that I'm constantly pressing them inadvertantly.  I've tried the controller with a variety of games from The Witcher 3 (a modern controller-friendly action RPG) to Sid Meier's Pirates! (a classic mouse-and-keyboard only sim) to XCOM2 (a modern strategy/tactics game with Steam controller support built in!).  All of them are terrible to play with this controller.
