This is easily one of the best games I have ever played in my life. It wasn't perfect (due to some bugs and glitches here and there), but otherwise, it was pretty damn close. May contain one minor spoiler.
The story itself was absolutely phenomenal. It was nice and deep, and explored a forbidden territory. Yeah, I suppose it can be a bit stereotypical where [Future Technology] is used by a government to militarize it and then [Religious] group/s riot and organize their own terrorist groups to fight it. We've seen it in many sci-fi games and movies. Regardless, the story was still very enjoyable and captivating, and it always kept me wanting more. I never skipped any of the cutscenes or cinematics, and I really liked the multiple endings at the end of the game. I also really enjoyed the side quests. They didn't contribute directly to the main story, but they showed how other people are being affected by it, such as certain girls being forced to get augmentations for their "job".
As far as gameplay goes, it reminds me a lot of Mass Effect, because of the conversation system (it looked almost identical) as well as the cover system. That's not a bad thing, though. Both of those things work very well with this game and let you pursue three main types of gameplays (though you can alter them as you go): Ghost, Pacifist, and Rambo (as I refer to them). Regardless of what you choose, the gameplay mechanics work well, hardly there is ever an issue with them, and there is just so much you can do in the game, such as hack terminals, or convince people to spill information, or stay in cover and kill enemies without them ever knowing where you are. The possibilities of what you do in the game are virtually limitless. It even has an open-world map that is divided into sections, so you can always explore it as you wish without having to be confined to tiny areas and be forced to do the main story missions, which is always a bonus for me.
The sound design was brilliant, too. The sound effects were decent, but the soundtrack was absolutely to die for. One of the best game soundtracks I have ever heard in my life. They never felt out of place; rather, they always complimented the gameplay, regardless of where you were, i.e. exploring the city, stuck in battle, watching a cinematic, or even just screwing around for fun. I will admit there were a few points where the soundtrack "froze" and was stuck in a tiny loop, but that was just a minor bug that was easily solved by just saving, restarting the game, and loading. A minor inconvenience, if you will.
All in all, this game was absolutely amazing. I'd easily give it a 9/10. It's a shame about the few bugs and glitches here and there, but again, they are minor inconveniences, and if you overlook them, this game is easily one of the best sci-fi games ever to be made. I honestly want to see more games made like this.

I dont often do reviews, though maybe I should just for fun. I've played a lot of games, tons and so I hope my opinion comes across as sensible, although a bit wordy.
Starting off I will address a few annoyances that I had. As mentioned many times over, alt tabbing from the game changes the game from fullscreen to window, and borderless window is not an option. This was rather irksome, especially since the game has been out for many months, I feel this could have been easily patched awhile ago but I got the impression this game will not ever receive any sort of patch support which kinda sucks. Another issue I had was random freezing in game. I can't recall anything specific setting it off but the screen would go white. After a few seconds I could hear the game resuming as normal however the screen was stuck on white, the only fix being to restart. Luckily after the third time I got the idea to check out my Geforce Experience App to see what they recommended settings wise. The only thing they had different was to change the texture filter up to 16x. To my amazement this actually resolved the freezing issue I had, so I would certainly suggest doing the same. As it's been stated everywhere, also make sure AA is off. Moving away from the bugs, the next issue that has been stated many times over is the 30 fps locked cinematics. They really do suck. Overall the game looks pretty great so when you head into a cutscene it can be disappointing. I would think that most people get excited for cutscenes in games as it's an opportunity for the visual team to really display their talent, I for one have always been a fan. Not the case in Nier.
Okay moving on:
By the time I got through the first playthrough, I felt... a little disappointed. I knew you had to play multiple times to get the full effect but still I was starting to wonder if things would improve. Luckily they did to a degree. The 2nd playthrough gives the game new depth as you get to explore the same things you just went through from a different perspective. It was enjoyable seeing context of conversations, opinions and feelings change. The third playthrough doesn't disappoint either as a whole. All 3 play throughs do seem to round out the experience making it seem more or less like a finished product and one that is decent. I will say though, some aspects of the game just really didn't do anything for me. I used only the weapons with the highest dps, and I had no incentive to do otherwise. The combat is enjoyable in it's own way, it's just not complicated. It doesn't require adaptation, once you get the gist of how things work you can pretty much steam roll everything. Unless you are playing on harder difficulties which would require more turtling/dodging. However you like to kill enemies, chip for it and you're done. Getting a different weapon or optimizing my chips just seemed fruitless, as it would not impact how I played, nor would it impact the results. So the gear/weapons aspect is kind of meh, nothing to really spend a whole lot of time worrying about. Which then left me wanting to complete the game, get all endings. I've done most of the side quests, and they are... okay. They really just seem like the usual stuff with a shade of game relevance. The only real appeal to the side quests is seeing if there is any morsel of interesting story, nothing mindblowing... just decent.
My opinion of the endings without spoilers.
I've gotten 25/26 endings, the only one remaining is the one that requires you to get all weapons and to get all of them maxed. Truth be told, not sure I'm going to get around to that. So as far as endings go A,B,C,D are alright. They definitely made me excited for what was in store with ending E and I have to be perfectly honest here. Ending E was super disappointing. I can't really explain further without spoiling anything but... I just feel like it was very bland. A "good" ending but no where close to satisfying, emotional or intriguing. It was empty and cliche and where I should be rejoicing, I was more like "meh, okay."
Bringing my thoughts to a conclusion, I would say the game is definitely enjoyable which may actually contrast a lot of points that I've made but there is a reason why I say this. The game gets you to at least think about this little realm of existence and it IS an interesting story. If you look into where this story comes from (Drakengard, and the previous Nier) you will find that this little world of lore is actually INSANE. Like I'm pretty sure the entirety of the lore (including previous games) has dragons, mages, magic, demons, robots, androids, aliens and a variety of soul related concepts. I mean, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥the whole story has EVERYTHING. It's interesting as it is something new and different from most everything else and the actual gameplay isn't too bad. It can be frustrating at times but overall I've played much worse. It's fun to engage in a story that doesn't involve humans for obvious reasons. Is it a masterpiece? No. I recently played Witcher 3 in it's entirety and THAT game is a masterpiece. My biggest complaint is actually the main ending, just didn't do it for me. Overall Nier is pretty aight, definitely worth a play but it's not groundbreaking.

It has the Dead Rising title but none of the charm. It's generic 3rd person zombie sandbox game with a bad story (while the Dead Rising games never had an amazing story, they at least felt interesting even if they were "campy") but by the end of the game I was disappointed. The game offers no challenge (having personally struggled with psychopaths in the 1st two games, the ones is this game were uninteresting and incredibly easy), combo weapons are locked behind collectable blueprints (no experimenting with the crafting like DR2) and the characters were very bland. Technically speaking it's the best looking of the series and zombie density is quite high and outside of the “special” zombies it’s tough to find any 2 zombies that look identical, but the performance issues ruin any technical achievement (I averaged around 30-40fps on medium-high settings with pretty decent hardware but beware the opening of the game is the toughest part on your machine). The DLC is even worse, the mini-campaigns take about an hour each if you just go through the main story, or if you want to waste time you can do some filler collectable quests (which offer no reward) and their supposed tie-in to main story is incredibly weak (although sadly some of characters you play as are more compelling than the main protagonist).
Is it fun? For a short while, but ultimately it gets repetitive too quickly and lacks anything that made the 1st two DR games standout. At the end there’s nothing memorable about this game and all of its cons heavily outweigh the few good things about this game. I purchased this for $20 during the summer sale and while I enjoyed some moments the game had to offer I wouldn't recommend this game even at that price.

This is the video game version of the popular board game
. The goal is to claim different train routes between major cities before your opponent can. The victor is the person who successfully claimed the most train routes (and blocked their opponent from claiming theirs) by the end of the game when one of the players has run out of train cars to place on the board.
The game has been adapted pretty well from the board game and streamlines the scoring system (a big bonus!). The game is really easy to pick up; with simplistic rules and turns mechanism, the game goes quickly and easily. If you've never played the board game, the tutorial is fast to play through and helps you quickly learn the rules of the game.
The game is fun and easy to play but don't expect it to hold your interest for hours on end. This is a great game for kids or train enthusiasts. It would make a nice birthday or Christmas present for PC-gaming kids, but it's probably honestly better and more fun to buy the board game for them.
The base game only comes with one, single map. The rest of the maps are DLC, and not in one big package. You have to buy individual DLC map packages to unlock all 4 areas. The base game is $10 and the DLC bundle is, as of the time I am writing this review, $29.31 (on a 30%-off sale). Even with the sale, $40 is too much to unlock all of the content of such a simple game. There are better games out there for $40 than a digital board game. You could buy the actual board game itself for a lower cost! (I'm aware that you can't buy all versions of the board game for less than $40, but you could at least have the actual hard copy to play with friends for less than the cost of the digital game.)
There is a fair amount of replayability, but I don't foresee myself putting enough time into the game to warrant the $10 base cost (for ONE MAP) or the full $40 to unlock everything. I just don't think it's worth the price for the low amount of time you're likely to get out of the game. If it was on a really good Steam sale, and you were planning to pick up the entire DLC bundle, then the game is probably worth the money. But at its current asking price I can't recommend it.

You don't have to play the first to play the second, as it only loosely makes references to events that occured in the first game. Additionaly the dialouge takes on a more darker tone rarely found in modern RPGS, and does not shy away from letting the player do pretty much anything they want within the boundaries of the gameworld and game engine.
Over the years, this game has held up extremely well in my view, and I would often find myself wanting to come back and experience it all over again. If you want to add more content to the game I highly suggest you try out MIBB's Megamod. If you wish to just have content cut from the original game restored, with a few added features, I suggest trying the Fallout 2 Restoration Project.
Closing: If you love the post-apocalyptic genre and crpgs, get this game.

One of the best RPGs ever created. Period. And probably best of post-apocalyptic games of all time.
Pros.
- Absolute freedom within a strictly linear plot (paradox?): you can finish your mission.. if you want. Or go somewhere to find something. Or kill anyone in sight. It's up to you. Playing this game is so much more fun than finishing it..
- Totally unpredictable random encounters (on first playthrough, but anyway): getting in the midlle of gangfight? check. saving innocent farmers from wildlife? check. saving innocent wildlife from some bad trappers? check, and don't mind if wildlife would try to eat you, it's just their way to say "thanks". getting one-hitted by gigant predatory lizard? check. finding an extremely OP weapon being level 2-3 right after you leave starting location? check, if you'll find a way to actually get your hands on that weapon without dying.
- Special encounters: no spoilers, you must find them all by yourself.
- You and only you choose how you would play: kill bad people and get praised by others (actually not), kill good people (and get your butt hunted for that), don't kill anyone ever (it's even possible to win the game that way, with only one exception), aimlessly wander around exploring, become a gangster (almost), help some people with their problems (or help other people with those problematic jerks). Your choice is only thing that matters.
- Side quests: they make up about 95% of all quests you'll get. Yes, you could finish the game and see about 5% of content only. But take one step aside from main quest - and a brave new world will open before you.
- Easter eggs: there are plenty. Nuff said. Go find them.
- Combat: totally unpredictable even on your 144 playthrough. Critical oneshot with a 7% chance to hit? Easy. Missing target with 95% hit chance while it's staying in front of you? Easy. Killing three random targets with minigun - out of five standing before you EXCEPT YOUR ACTUAL TARGET? Very easy. Killing yourself with a critical miss? Not that easy, but possible.
- You can actually kill these annoying little critters: yes, it's about kids. Name another game where you are allowed to do such horrible thing at last? No more immortal godly beings that wander around, annoy you and steal from your pockets. Be warned: people of wasteland won't like you for that (and your♥♥♥♥♥would be hunted).
Cons.
- Too much myths about cut content: there are some really beatifull things that didn't get to the final version. Maybe they existed, maybe not.
- Map: after 4-5 playthroughs you will get everywhere and find everything. Maybe sooner, maybe later, but that will happen. There are so much empty space on the map, so many lost opportunities to place something exciting.. not to mention that map from first game could've been added to second.
- Replayability dissapears after 50-60 times. Seriously, what else could you do when you've done everything possible?
Total score: 9.7/10. Almost perfect.

A little background on where my viewpoint comes from: I have not played Deus Ex Original nor Invisible War, and before this was a complete newbie to these sort of 'fps-stealth-rpg games'. Not a huge deal of experience in shooting games and almost none in stealth games (I find most rather frustrating). However, I found the theme rather intriguing. Without further ado:
A game I reccomend to the end of the earth, if you have any intrest in the issues presented by it (transhumansim). Picked this up for $5 on a Steam Sale, easily the best buy I've made in a long while. Very suitably atmospehric and well themed and it godamm manages to make those specs and a trenchcoat look cool.
The gameplay is also rather good, with a great mix of both shooting and stealth. The shooting is cover-based and stealth also involves hacking, etc. However, I don't think for somebody that has invested a lot of time into stealth or shooting games that they will find these aspects of the game incredible. Games like Dishunoured would outcompete it in stealth and many games would outcompete it in shooting. However, if you are someone with little experince in either like me, you will find both immensely satisfying and I'm sure even a stealth/shooting veteran could find some good elements. The stealth/shooting is by no means bad, it is actually very good, it just doesn't compete with games dedicated to these apects.
Deus Ex: Human Reveloution - A game with an amazing and immersive story, great world building and good stealth and shooting mechanics. My favourite "one time play" (i.e. not a MOBA of online FPS or the replayability of the like) to this date. No doubt.

It's a fascinating piece of tech, but I think the original vision of it was more promising than the thing actually turned out to be. This is supposed to bridge the gap between controllers and keyboard/mouse, but at the end of the day there is still a lot of fiddling around and troubleshooting involved with getting this thing to work how you want it to. PC gaming as usual, in other words.
For starters, using this controller causes Steam to crash all the freaking time. There are too many games that don't work with this even if you use the templates, and once again Valve is leaving it to the community to do their work for them. One can only pray that there are enough people who own this controller for there to be enough volunteers to take the time -- for every game on Steam -- to make sensible control setups. And that's the catch 22; I don't recommend buying this controller in its current state. There's a lot of crappy community bindings with no effort or cleverness put into them, and you can only even see these in Big Picture mode. The developers can make their own official bindings, but from my experience, those can be pretty bad too, and hardly any developers are making them in the first place.
There's a lot of features that have yet to be implemented, but it's improving and getting new additions at a steady enough pace as time goes by, so maybe someday this controller will be good and completely hassle-free like it was intended. It does have promising ideas. The ease of finding/using other people's bindings is cool. The touch pads, paddles, and binary/analog triggers are cool. I should not have to aim around with a damn gyroscope, but it's cool that that is there to explore and tinker with as well. The way you can type with it is pretty cool, but could be a lot better. The Bluetooth that just works is cool. What's not cool is how you HAVE to be in Big Picture mode to tinker with the bindings, and how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ the internet browser works with it -- it's not consistent at all.
Maybe Xpadder should just have a website to download community-made controller bindings for Playstation/Xbox controllers. PS4 controllers do have touchpads and motion sensing on them already, and I think it would be a better way of leaving out the guesswork. And it has an actual D-pad and two analog sticks. Most of the time, that's all you really want. The analog stick and face buttons are not very comfortable, being secondary to the touchpads. That touchpad on the left that's halfheartedly trying to be a D-pad is GARBAGE as a D-pad, it doesn't feel right at all, so I usually just use the analog stick. Even the touchpads don't work ideally as touchpads, since sometimes you gotta move your finger to the VERY EDGE of the circle.
Long story short, most of the time you really are better off just using a keyboard/mouse or a regular controller. There are MORE complications and fiddling around and troubleshooting, not less. That is too much time that could be spent playing the game with ol' reliable.

Perhaps I'm getting more cynical about my opinion of games as the years go by, or perhaps my interests in gaming have vastly changed, but I did not enjoy this game as much as I was hoping I would. When it came out, it looked great and I really wanted to play it, but now having beaten it, I can't help but leave a bit disappointed. This is an okay game, but I'm struggling to see what merits the crazy acclaim it has gotten. Don't get me wrong, this game is kind of  solid and somwhat enjoyable at times, but, in my opinion, the metacritic is quite high for this game. Graphically, this game look dated, older than it really is. Models look pretty bad for the most part, and it does not look as sharp as I imagined this game would. Gameplay is alright throughout, although hacking is more of gimmick and doesn't always seem to reward you appropriately at times (some times you just get side information via the emails, which are time consuming to read and boring in my opinion). There's a bit of open worldedness to the game at parts which is nice, and there are a number of side quests to find that are generally not that interesting.  Gunplay feels pretty lackluster but there are a number of choices of weapons (although your inventory will severely limit the number you can carry and ammo, so choose wisely). I thought that ammo was kind of scarce at times when it shouldn't have been, and the inclusion of ammo as a spot in the inventory really made managing the inventory space more difficult than it needed to be at times. The choice of some buttons for the gamepad is a bit odd, but no major qualms there. Storywise I did not find it captivating until the very end, and the use of the word captivating there is a bit of an overstatement. The message is clear: advancing technology too much is bad, to put it into plain terms. While I agree with this sentiment, it was fairly predicable that this would be the outcome and I probably would have enjoyed this more in my teen years, but I've seen the same thing done elsewhere and done better. Voice acting is nothing special, and Jensen isn't that fun to listen to since he's monotoned almost all game. Overall, while I didn't enjoy this game as much as the hype excited me, its not a terrible game by any means, but its just not worthy of the acclaim. Most people will probably enjoy this game, and I can't really say the same.  5/10

Absolutely phenomenal piece of gear. Has a few small cons, but overall, this is the best PC peripheral out there, better than any xbox or playstation controller. Before you read any review calling it "light" or "cheap feeling" know beforehand that they're objectively wrong. It has plenty of heft (moreso than a ps3/4/xbone/360 controller by 10-30%) and the controller doesn't creak or flex, the plastics feel just fine, and the build quality has held up to hundreds of hours of use so far and it still feels good as new. Battery life is great, I got over 100 hours out of one set of batteries. The haptic pads really do work well, with an INSANE amount of customization options that are very easy to do. It's actually easy and fun to set up a custom setup for your games, as every game has a working default made by other people that you can refine to suit your needs in seconds, from everything ranging from sensitivity, force of the haptic feedback, moving buttons around, it's all easy and simple and intuitive. Most games, even non-controller-supported ones have layouts that work perfectly straight away thanks to the open sourced nature of the software. It's very comfortable, I like a ps3 controller, but the way this controller is shaped so your thumbs are moved in and towards the pads is unbelievably natural and intuitive, and I don't get thumb cramps like I do after a huge session on other controllers. I can play FTL with no issues. I can be competitive in warframe. This is obviously not as absolutely precise as a mouse/keyboard, so don't expect it to do anything your mouse/keyboard can, but it's 80-85% as good, which is miles beyond a controller.
Consider this not as a mouse/keyboard replacement, but as a controller replacement, because it does that in every way, and even edges in and widens the scope of games accessible from a relaxed, couch-based gaming position.
The software is truly the thing that makes the steam controller stand out as light-years ahead of anything else on the market. Valve has set the new benchmark for customization. Period. No argument. You can set the haptic pads to emulate a joystick with a huge amount of weaks from dead zone to edge spinning, snap back speed, everything, to mouse emulating, with edge spinning, to trackball, where you can flick it and keep it spinning (which is genuinely cool as hell in 3rd person games like warframe. I get a lot of use out of the trackball with flicking and tapping to spin and stop the virtual ball) and everything in between. You can set up a button to work as a shift or control button, effectively doubling or tripling the number of buttons you have (the bumpers work great for this, in a game like mechwarrior with tons of keybinds, you can bind every weapon group you could dream of. I'm still experimenting with world of warcraft, and I'm up to 20 possible keybound spells along with my target changing and focus macros) And the crown jewel in the software is that no matter the game, if it's on steam, there is a playable controller setup created by players, and raised to the top of a list shown to you with number of people using it, so you can jump in on the most popular key setup and just play a game right away. If you don't like the setup entirely, pick another one, or if there's just one little thing you don't like (such as how fast the camera spins, that it uses a trackball instead of a mouse emulator, etc.) then changing it is a matter of seconds using a very intuitive menu system.
Typing on the controller works, but don't expect it to be usable in fast paced multiplayer scenarios. I really don't bother typing in warframe on it, it's just too slow, even with practice. It's good for inputing passwords and console commands, etc. or typing in steam chat, but if you are playing CSGO without a mic, just keep the keyboard handy for typing.
I have two small complaints. Firstly, the left haptic pad is not a good D-pad replacement. I feel like the left haptic pad is kind of pointlessly supplanted by the joystick, which just wasn't necessary. I'd have preferred a D pad in that joystick's location, because certain D-pad functions (such as the d-pad item switching in dark souls) are just not quite as intuitive as they are with real buttons, though this issue does go away after an hour or so of use, I would have just preferred two haptic pads, as they do such an absolutely incredible job of emulating a joystick that it's rendered kind of moot, since the haptic pad can do d-pad duties while the joystick cannot, you are usually forced into using the joystick anytime you need the additional buttons of the D pad. My second complaint is that there is no place on the controller to plug the dongle in to store it. This is actually my major complaint with the pad, as I like to use it both on my PC and on my laptop, and when I'm moving it, I have to be VERY careful to not lose the dongle. There are a bunch of ways that valve could have made a slot for the USB dongle, and it annoys me greatly that they didn't do this. Hopefully future iterations of the controller will add this in.
Overall, if you are a PC gamer, you owe it to yourself to have the first real, genuine piece of PC tech that blends the best of PC gaming with the best of console gaming. If you already have a controller like I did, the steam controller will open up a whole new world of games you previously didn't think were playable with a controller, and if you don't have a controller yet, don't even CONSIDER buying anything but the steam controller. The build quality is good, using the controller feels great, and the software is nothing short of unbelievable.
I hope I've covered this well enough. I'm not a valve fanboy, I only care about whether or not a product is good. In this situation, I genuinely can't sing the controller's praises enough.

Although for less intensive games (ie: Minecraft, Stonehearth, SkySaga, Terraria, oddly Just Cause 3) it works a lot better. Simply put: For each game, it's a hit-or-miss experience. First things first---I've seen a LOT of complaints about patches and such and video or crash issues without a 3rd party program to correct the issue. Not for me. Game has performed beautifully right off, but I am running a system set up for gaming. Intel i7 4.2 GHz with 32 gig ram and NVidia GeForce GTX 1080 graphics card with tons of memory as well. As for the game itself...There isnt much in the way of tutorials or instructions in-game which is frustrating. And the opening of the game most certainly needs tweaking. You must play the entire prologue WITHOUT being killed or else start completely over from the beginning. There are no save points. Suggest the first thing you do is set your difficulty level to "easy" until you get through this. After that you can save throughout the game. That's all the negatives I have. Once you can play the game with save points, it is mesmerizing. Story, action, visuals, all top notch. And the soundtrack is absolutely the best of any game I've ever played. After reading/watching all the stellar reviews of the game, I caved in during the sales and decided to give Nier a try. Conclusion- Underwhelming & Overated. I want to love the game, really tried I meant, its not a bad game, and I praise the dev for trying to create something new, but man this is not for me. Well here goes, some good, some bad, some are my general thought about the game.
-Fluid genre hopping. One minutes you're playing a 3rd Person Action-Adventure game, the next its a Side Scroller and suddently its a Top-Down. Uniquely done, and a nice trip down memory lane. You'll just have to get used to the camera, basically your worst enemy in the game.
-Bad, half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥PC port. You can expect the usual fps drops and stuttering, thank god there's a community patch/mod to address the issue but as of Nov 2017, there's still no fix from the dev yet. The game run at 60 fps while cutscene is in 30. Great control scheme using controller, you can even costumize it to your own liking, but for KBM, I have a 5 button mouse, can't bind anything to the thumb click.
-Story is decent at best, but can't be sure, there's multiple endings, just finished A and B, will update when I finish the all of the ending. There's some tear-jerking moments, and they tried selling it hard with music but I'm not feeling it. Maybe I'm just too old for anime style story telling.
-Lots and lots of invisible wall. Buildings in the game is full of holes, some you can enter, some you can't, even the big fat one, am I supposed to check every other hole in case I missed something? Same goes with ledge, Some you can jump on to, some you can't, even when you jumpe higher then the ledge and there's space for it. This feels sloppy.
-Side-quest=Chores. Some has good story attached behind it, but most are just fetch quest I don't really care about. Go to the marker, get this, fight the robots, come back, here's your reward.
TL/DR: Lots of untapped potential, bad PC port
Edit: Finished the game, all the main endings at least (A, B, C, D, and E), deligted by some big twist, but I'm standing by my opinion earlier. It's a preference thing I guess

This game is the rare breed of game know as "so bad its good." It's worth playing.
Scores:
Functionality/Playability: 4/10 Not so near broken mess
Gameplay: 7/10 Solid,but could have been so much better
Visuals: Don't really matter so rate how YOU want
Soundtrack: 3/10 Dull and uninteresting or out of place
Fun and Enjoyment: 8/10 (Seriously! Just trust me in my review)
Overall Score: 6/10 But really worth playing
The mechanics are pretty similar to a average fps, aside from a wierd default keybinding (try binding knife to space and sprint to shift and jump to e since you will rarely use it). The skill point system works well. melee gives you more points than headshots. If done correctly, you can finish a mission with 30+ skill points (the most I've ever gotten during a mission was 34) to spend on Health, Energy, Uber Shield, Emotion Time (crying and screaming while going on your invinsible murderous rampage) and Accuracy for the next mission. Helpful tip: max out accuracy ASAP! Your accuracy at the start of the game will be atrocious! Once you've done that, you'll be getting hundreds of headshot without even trying using automatic rifles and lmgs. Afterwards, upgrade everything else to your heart's contents (you won't have to worry about stasis shield unless your trying to become MLG with dope trick shots). Especially that emotion time! The SS or whatever will cower in fear as you slaughter their comrades while in tears crying like a baby (an invincible homicidal baby). The game's AI is.. interesting. They'll try to kill you but,, (for a better explaination, check out the gameplay from Inside Gaming on Youtube parts 1-4. You can go all the way to part 8 if you just want to watch Adam suffer while Bruce and James do their thing).
The cutscenes are interesting, but are often either confusing or just flat out make no sense. They may or may not make you question your sanity. The game explains what exactly is going on; so luckily, you won't have to play whatever garbage the first Ubersoldier might have been.
Lastly, the game's bosses (*SPOILER ALERT: Their are only four and you will be glad their are only four. Six if you count the two types of minis.)
Now, about the bosses (*NOT A SPOILER: JUST A HELPFUL TIP) The strategies you need to defeat them is simple for everyone of the except for phase three of the last boss. As James from Inside Gaming explains perfectly in part 6 of their gameplay on YouTube: "You just shoot 'em." No puzzles, no QTEs, or anything; just shoot 'em 'til they die. It may seem like its not working since their's NO INDICATOR OF ACTUAL DAMAGE (blood!) As Bruce pointed out after Adam defeated the first boss; even though every enemy you've fought beforehand has bled when you filled them with bullets and shrapnel. And its actually the only thing that works. Trust me and James. Its all that works so don't bother trying anything else!
Despite the game's bad (not quite terrible) functionality, the game is fun. I'm not sure how to explain it. It's just fun! Actually it might have something to do with feeling like a god when your emotion time kicks in from being a badass and start a murderous rampage during your temporary invinsibility. As well as watching the AI struggle to figure out how to kill you without killing themselves in a hilarious fashion. Like I said from the start of my review; this game is the rare breed known simply as: "Its so bad, its good."

What I liked about this game? The completely non-serious nature of the gameplay. Yes, sometimes I come up against really good teams, and I die every 30 seconds. But 3 seconds later, I respawn and do it again. That's a nice  break from all the other shooters that I've been playing lately, where it feels like Death is punished severely. Here, death is a minor setback. You don't lose your items, you don't 3 minutes of your life waiting for a round to end, you don't lose XP. It's just 3 seconds of frustration and then you're back to having fun. Ridiculous, brightly colored, graphically violent, bouncy, over the top obscene fun.
I also like that the micro-transactions aren't totally pay2win. You need weapon pieces to upgrade your guns, but weapon pieces are bought with "blutes," and blutes are earned by playing. It takes maybe 2-3 hours of play to unlock your next piece.
What I don't like? Some weapon makeups are blatantly better than others. There's nothing inherently wrong with that, but the problem comes from investing heavily into the tree for rocket launchers, only to find out that you kick♥♥♥♥♥with pulse weapons instead. But the preview mode only lets you test one tier above what you have, so you can't see how the top tier of equipment plays.
Also, The gun upgrades give you stats on what each bit does, but doesn't explain what each stat means. Reload and Damage are obvious, but what's the difference between Stability, Recoil, Aimed Accurace, and Hip Accuracy? And the flaming ammo gives you a higher damage output, but it doesn't tell you that it's a lower direct damage combined with a weak burn effect, to TOTAL higher. it's counter-intuitive, but it takes LONGER to kill someone in a direct fight that way.
None of that really matters once you find a favorite gun and get a few matches under your belt. You'll be having too much fun dodging, dipping, ducking, diving, and dodging your enemies bullets while you unload hot death that shreds the flesh from their bones.

- Totally unpredictable random encounters (on first playthrough, but anyway): getting in the midlle of gangfight? check. saving innocent farmers from wildlife? check. saving innocent wildlife from some bad trappers? check, and don't mind if wildlife would try to eat you, it's just their way to say "thanks". getting one-hitted by gigant predatory lizard? check. finding an extremely OP weapon being level 2-3 right after you leave starting location? check, if you'll find a way to actually get your hands on that weapon without dying.
- Special encounters: no spoilers, you must find them all by yourself.
- You and only you choose how you would play: kill bad people and get praised by others (actually not), kill good people (and get your butt hunted for that), don't kill anyone ever (it's even possible to win the game that way, with only one exception), aimlessly wander around exploring, become a gangster (almost), help some people with their problems (or help other people with those problematic jerks). Your choice is only thing that matters.
- Side quests: they make up about 95% of all quests you'll get. Yes, you could finish the game and see about 5% of content only. But take one step aside from main quest - and a brave new world will open before you.
- Easter eggs: there are plenty. Nuff said. Go find them.
- Combat: totally unpredictable even on your 144 playthrough. Critical oneshot with a 7% chance to hit? Easy. Missing target with 95% hit chance while it's staying in front of you? Easy. Killing three random targets with minigun - out of five standing before you EXCEPT YOUR ACTUAL TARGET? Very easy. Killing yourself with a critical miss? Not that easy, but possible.
- You can actually kill these annoying little critters: yes, it's about kids. Name another game where you are allowed to do such horrible thing at last? No more immortal godly beings that wander around, annoy you and steal from your pockets. Be warned: people of wasteland won't like you for that (and your♥♥♥♥♥would be hunted).
Cons.
- Too much myths about cut content: there are some really beatifull things that didn't get to the final version. Maybe they existed, maybe not.
- Map: after 4-5 playthroughs you will get everywhere and find everything. Maybe sooner, maybe later, but that will happen. There are so much empty space on the map, so many lost opportunities to place something exciting.. not to mention that map from first game could've been added to second.
- Replayability dissapears after 50-60 times. Seriously, what else could you do when you've done everything possible?
Total score: 9.7/10. Almost perfect.

+

~	Maybe I missed the prompt that told me what to with survivors (how to get rid of them to be specific) or they just don’t tell you. I accidentally dragged one into a bossfight where she of course died because I didn’t know that I had to deselect her at the whiteboard in a safehouse.
Cons:
-	The game crashed a couple times. Even forced me to reboot my PC twice.
-	Sometimes textures take long to load.
-	It’s dumbed down to appeal to the masses. I didn’t die once in the story. In DR1 and DR2 that was pretty much impossible to do.
-	You have way too much time. There was no feel of urgency at all. I finished the game on day 4 even though I completed all the side missions and psycho missions. Had I focused on the main missions I would’ve finished it on day 3 at the latest.
-	The collectables sometimes are a real pain in the #ss to find. More than once I found myself thinking “How the f#ck am I supposed to get up/over there?”
-	The vehicles are useless as sh%t. Fun yes but the fun lasts for about 2 minutes tops. Then they go boom.
-	It feels like there are less combo weapons than in DR2
-	The constantly getting grabbed by zombies. Every 10 seconds you have a Zed hanging on your #ss. So damn frustrating.
-	The constantly exploding sh!t right next to you. Maybe I was too blind to see it but somehow there was always stuff exploding right next to me and Nick hugging the street.
-	90% of the doors are locked and will only open if you do a side mission that is related to that place. I’d like to emphasize on one in particular where you have to protect a woman on a shopping trip and one store is locked. She simply kicks the door open… She can do that but Nick, who is at least one foot taller than her and bit more muscular, can’t? That’s b#llsh%t.
I guess that’s about it. I haven’t played the DLC’s yet but I probably will in the next few days and I’ll probably play this game in Coop where it’s hopefully more fun.

Well...
They plan on adding a new card system next patch, that will change the game dramatically.
This new system changes the game to the worse. It's a shame because the game is not bad at all.
Old system was - You get 5 default cards for every champion and have to unlock other cards or buy them with one of the in game currencies. It takes some time to unlock but you don't even need all of the cards for all of the champions. If you lucky then you'll get the ones you want from the chests that you get by leveling up and then buy some of the others that you are missing if you really want them and earned enough to buy them -which is not that long.
Even with the default cards and some of the better ones you can do well. Not all of the higher rarity cards are better than the default ones. I found myself using some of the lowest rarity cards on many champions even when I had higher rarity cards unlocked.
In this old system you have 12 points to assing to the 5 cards you choose for your loadout. Each card can be from level 1 to 4 and with each level the card's effect is better. So you have to choose which one you want to be stronger and it gives the game a lot of customization.
New system- All cards are unlocked for all of the champions and you no longer need to aquire them. No more 12 points that you assing to the cards, each card starts on level 1 other than a few that start on level 3. Cards that you already owned in the old system start on level 3. Max card level is 5.
That means that it's possible to have a full deck of level 5 cards, you don't have any point limit like with the old system.
You level those cards by collecting duplicates from a crate that has 4 drops and contains cards and cosmetics , and from a new champion specific crate that drops cards only (5 of them). The amount needed to level up the card to the next level increases every leevl up of the card. The only way of getting this crate is by leveling up the champion which take longer and longer every time you go up a level and at level ~10 it takes a long time. Anohter way is to do a 1st win of the day with each champion, which gives you 1 crate.
So...yeah it will take you a long time to get a card to level up especially the higher the level of the card is.
Newer players will have a harder time against older ones and will have to grind way more than with the old system.
ABout competetive - ALl cards are locked on lvl 3 no matter what level of the card was. Meaning that lvl 4-5 cards go back to 3 and lvl 1-2 cards will go up to lvl 3, That's good, it makes it fair for everyone, yeah. Problem is...you can't practice the champions and get used to them in casual anymore due to the difference there wil be between those 2 modes. Something that's possible in casual will not be possible in competetive.
You may do great in casual with level 5 cards, move on to competetive , play same character and something that you thought you that could do is not possible and this may be the reason for you doing badly.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Directors Cut fixes Deus Ex: Human Revolution and makes it one of the best games I've ever played.
It's hard to accurately state how much I love this version of Deus Ex. When Deus Ex: Human Revloution came out it was a stunning disappointment that only further cemented what a gem the original Deus Ex was. There was literally only ONE way to play. You could try to  play pacifist or hacker, but what was the point when bosses were bullet sponges and you had only one option to deal with them?  It RUINED the game.
Most reviews say that the most significant thing this version adds is that it weaves the DLC in to the main story. Nonsense. The most significant thing is the way the bosses were fixed. Although you can't talk your way out of boss fights, or take them non lethally, you do have optoins for how you do kill them. You don't have to focus on guns. You can focus on hacking, and hack a robot to do your killing for you.
The game feels more cohesive as a result, and the entire experience opens up. Add to that the blade runner aesthetic, good voice acting (better than the original Deus Ex at least) , and the cool story line and you have yourself a very memorable experience.
I do have a couple of issues with the game. I disliked the reused conversation animation and some of the textures looked low resolution despite my settings. Ultimately, these are nit picks. I emphatically recommend this game.
If it's under 25.00, buy it.

In OPUS, you spend most of your time moving a telescope around with WASD to locate Earth. You end up scanning a lot of planets before you find it. As the subtitle of the game is "The Day We Found Earth," I don't think it's too big of a spoiler to say you eventually locate it.
I found the gameplay to be a little unexciting, to be honest. You're initially given the zone (of which there are four in the game), the section (these are typically named), and the coordinates for the planet in question. These criteria are meant to guide your search. As the game proceeds, you're given less and less detail to guide you.
In-between searches, you're treated to a little bit of dialogue, mostly with an AI created to help you. However, I really never felt emotionally connected to anything that was happening. Your robot was created from the ground up to help a scientist, and the AI was created from the ground up to help your robot. So although the robot is aesthetically cute and throws little fits, you're really just witnessing two computers following their programming. Additionally, details given in the story make you question if it really matters if they find Earth at all. For me, at least, this was a recipe for disengagement.
My point

From the sounds of it, this was going to be very well suited to my interests in astronomy and robotics, but it turned out to warp both away from my expectations (Which I submit may merely be that my expectations were unfounded, but surely that's what makes a recommendation or lack thereof, I'd think)
I'd love to support it - hence the purchase on sale - but sadly it fell short.
Short answer:
Pros -
* Able to pursue a limited sense of astronomical pleasure
* Art is good in its minimal nature
* Had strong conceptual makings
Cons -
* A strong concept, but seemingly wasted for me
** One lacking an actual interest in Astronomy, but still having an interest in the stars may enjoy?
* Story was a trite in the sense of predictability, and also in the mother/child (whom happens to be a robot) relationship
* Robot was nearly insufferable in tone and writing, as well as other characters
* Game disallowed any sense of discovery, and forced one only down its preferred path
** Even so much as forcing the view back to the main room whenever panned, despite clear items of interest in other rooms which were still clickable if one fought the camera hard
** The achievements indicate they want you to explore, but the actual game mechanics act in direct opposition
A bit more data:
Specific issue with the story was the overplayed mother/child relationship with a non-standard child or mother, wherein the robot child was typical of the much proclaimed "terrible twos" variety, which I found nearly insufferable, honestly. Demanding, terse. Perhaps an attempt to craft an underdog that succeeds Deus Ex Machina? Whatever the impetus, it detracted heavily for me, when the game sounded quite compelling.
To that point, I liked the idea of glassing galaxies and stars of my own accord, eventually tracking down the long forgotten orb. To stand triumphant over mere witness of some select set of photons. The game, however, fought against this completely and sapped any sense of actual curiosity and discovery, to be funneled down the story line.
You MUST go to this point, it proclaimed, as it vomitted warnings, admonishing me for curious wonder at the art they had wrought for the Universe. Don't you want people to have a look at your work?
And given that idyllic wonder is the very essence of many an astronomical fantasy, this seemed to be at odds with the very audience I'd expect to be compelled (if only myself).
Furthermore, I made the choice labelled specifically to not have one's hand held, but it disallowed any sense of investigation and even forced the view back to the main room when trying to view the ship. Again, strange to me that you'd be so forcefully corralled from enjoying investigating the game.
Really I was hoping I could just sit and scan stars across the Universe, once it was shown to have telescope mechanics. Even if that meant clicking every one of the presumably hundreds of lights to get there, becauuse that's the joy of the journey.

Coming from the XBone and XB360 controllers, this one took me some time to get used to.  At first, I couldn't get over the fact that the buttons were so small and placed in, what I belived at the time, an awkward spot.  In fact, I was ready to put it on eBay after a week. However, after a couple of weeks of getting used to it, it is hands down (no pun) my go to for controllers on PC 99% of the time.  Everything about it, from the ergonomics to the customization makes it stand out from the other options.  I actually prefer the button sizes now to the larger buttons on the XBox controllers.
My only quibble is that it does make certain games harder to play not easier.  For example, NBA 2K series relies heavily on the right thumbstick for crossovers, spin moves, and even shot selection if you go that route. With this controller, it makes that near impossible.  So you do have to hang on to your old controller for a game like that, but otherwise, I have no desire to go back.
I knew it would be impressive with FPS, but what I wasn't counting on was how great it is with Third Person View games.  It really immerses you in the environment unlike the slightly jerky right analog stick ever could.  Try the Arkham series, Mordor, or Tomb Raider reboot when you get this.
In all, I would highly recommend this mouse to anyone on the fence.  9/10.

I want to be clear that I did not play the first Nier at any point because I've never owned a playstation or any of its increments. I also want to be clear that at first when I played this game I thought it rather enjoyable aside from its rather dull gameplay. It was only as time went on and I started to trudge through more of the story that I started to lose patience with the game and began to sincerely loath it. Allow me to elaborate:
I'm going to start with things that aren't spoilers obviously, such as the gameplay. At first it's not bad, if completely unchallenging. Some nice little hack&slash dodgy combat for people who want a short, stroll in the park kind of game. This only started to get annoying a bit later, when it became clear that in order to break the game you only have to install all the healing chips and nothing else and dodge around the arena any time you're in a modicum of danger. I only died once in this game, and it was to the first boss because I was unsure of how the game was supposed to work, and just to be clear, I was playing on the second hardest difficulty at the time. It only became infuriating when the game started to seem to think that its gameplay was quite difficult and deserving of a 10 minute long boss fight at the end where nothing is changed, it isn't any more difficult than any other boss, and it just dragged forever. If you continuously dodge in this game you are utterly invincible. No game with that as a mechanic can be any amount of difficult no matter what setting you're on.
There's a nice big paragraph for gameplay, now let's move on to enemies shall we?
Boring boring boring boring boring. There is little to no variety in the enemies that you face in this game. Don't get me wrong, there's some difference in the aesthetic of some enemies, but it's nothing more than one of the standard enemies putting on a little outfit most of the time, and even then, they're almost all just varieties of the same ball-headed robot. Not enough of a problem to tell you to give the game a pass alone, but pretty bad regardless.
Environment!
There are very few areas in this game, and they're all rather small to boot. In fact, the entire map is extremely small. They don't make much sense at all next to each other either, but in a good game this could be ignored.
Character design wooooooo.
The design of the characters is essentially the only redeeming factor of this game. I firmly believe that if this game didn't contain a character whose butt is super nice and plenty of beefcake as well, that nobody would bother defending it with the amount of fervor that they do.
Story... oh boy. Ooooh boy. This game's story is a train wreck and it is the primary reason why I utterly Hate this game.
Let me explain. Just so you know this is the part where the review starts to get spoilery.
At the very beginning of the game it drops some fascinating story threads that are meant to get you thinking. Who are the aliens? Why did they leave? How did they even get here? Is humanity still even a thing? All the messages are quite clearly prerecorded so probably not right? Are the machines really sentient or even that different from androids? All very fascinating and I immediately began to speculate on what it all meant and how it related to each other.
It's just too bad that literally everything I came up with was far, far better than what the game actually had in store. It goes for the most obvious, low hanging fruit twist there could possibly have been and seems to think that in doing so it was actually being clever. What, humanity doesn't exist and Yorha exists to cover it up? That's literally it? I gathered that much in the first thirty minutes of the game and at the end it acts like this is a big deal. What the heck?
I thought that perhaps the aliens hadn't ever existed and that maybe Androids were created by humanity first in our quest for sentient AI, only to be supplanted by them and that in their last moments they created the machines (Shoddy, utilitarian things) in a last ditch attempt to defeat the Androids. After all, we don't see aliens until about an hour in, so for that first hour it's practically screaming that something that involves the aliens not existing is going to be the twist.
After the aliens turned out to actually exist, (a thing I was quite disappointed about) I started thinking, hey, perhaps it was the Androids who were created by the aliens rather than the machines. After all, the Androids are clearly far more advanced, and why the hell would the faction created by terrestrial humans have a moon base, and an orbital platform as a base of operations for terrestrial action? Wouldn't it make far more sense for the aliens to have that? I started to think that androids were the true invading force and that perhaps they had supplanted the aliens as the invading force, hense why they're all dead (And why Adam and Eve look exactly like Androids rather than machines).
But no, those plot holes about how humanity builds orbital stations to fight interstellar aliens who overran them on earth, presumably who had some kind of interstellar fleet, never even comes up. Of course, by the very conclusion I was so utterly uninvested that it may have actually come up and I just missed it. A possibility I will not discount. All in all, I gave the game far more credit than it deserved as far as the overarching plot was concerned.
Now let me pick apart some smaller elements of the story, in order of least to greatest annoyance.
Throughout the game they kept throwing these philosophical phrases, names, and notions in a clear, cynical attempt to sound far deeper than it actually was. In truth, there was no philosophical bent to the game at all, it has no deeper meaning and just sort of throws all the elements of such on the floor like pieces of IKEA furniture that it never bothers to put together into something.
Throughout most of the game 9S insists that machines can't possibly have feelings or think at all. This is true even after he meets Pascal, who is actual proof of the contrary. It makes 9S come across as utterly moronic, when the game is trying its damndest to make him seem insanely intelligent, to the point that Yorha literally designs an entire type of android to counteract his supposed intelligence. It makes no sense how he could be so legendarily dense.
If the aliens came from space, it's a serious plot hole that not only are Androids more advanced, but that they also have an orbital base where supposedly the "aliens" can't get to them. I've mentioned this before but it's a serious plot hole and it really bothers me.
Does A2's character have any reason to exist aside from the fact that they had to kill 2B for the climax? Her only point is to fill the gap that 2B leaves without actually being 2B. Kinda lazy to me.
Do Adam and Eve have any reason to exist in the plot At All? Honestly, they come, they do essentially nothing, and then they leave. They just leave. Boom, dead. Their only point (Being generous) is to illustrate more pointedly how much machines want to act like humans, but that's done far better by all of the other machines in the game. Sheesh.
Several times in the game, 9S has to upload him and 2B away to the main base because they're about to be destroyed. If this is the case, why the hell don't they just keep running backups of themselves? Every day just spend a few minutes making a backup of yourself to activate upon your destruction. There is literally no reason why they couldn't do this. Hell, with any forethought, some of the more intelligent androids could have several backups spread throughout both the main orbital base and the surface itself.
And to finish, 9S' breakdown at the end is utterly contrived. I can't get very in depth about this because apparently there's a character limit to these reviews and I am rapidly approaching it, but honestly, his angsty self-destruction made me want to roll my eyes.

Well this was kind a train wreck comparing to the first one. Felt like a budget version of the first one which was not a triple-A product to begin with, but still like a B-class war movie with a bit of Wolfenstein and other old school shooters.
I was kind a surprised that the sequel even exists so I picked it from the last Steam Summer Sale for a couple bucks. It was fairly priced, like straight-to-video rental sequel, which Ubersoldier II suitably is with subpar production values and thin plotline.
The first one was not anything too special but it was fun to play as Neo against Nazis by stopping bullets and sending them back. It was a nice feature to have fighting against the telekinesis super soldiers and other UberNazis. Too bad that the sequel does remind me all of that, but does it way worse than the first one.
You play as an Allied Ubersoldier named Karl from the previous game. He must destroy the rest of the SS guys who still want to produce ubersoldiers, waste the rest of the world and rule the universe. With him travels one damsel in distress which you need to escort and protect time to time. Karl makes his way around the world from Europe to Africa to Himalayas but it’s more like kill bad guys while travelling from point A to point C via point B.
Action’s pace is slow in general. Even the car turret shooting scene at the beginning is slow as post-war trial. The shooting is sluggish but easy; enemies are easy to hit to the head which will award you an uberaccurate slow motion Ubersniper-perk if you manage to kill three enemies by a headshot in certain time. It’s easier than you think. The other way to turn into a slaughter machine is to stab people to death three times in a row. By that way you get a Berserk-perk which with you can kill people with one knife hit.
During these “emotions” player is completely invulnerable so it’s easy to waste battalions of soldiers in a few seconds. There’s no really a cool down to these abilities so you need just to kill next three people you come up after the Berserk or Ubersniper ends. It’s somewhat essential that player uses the knife and get headshots because they also bring experience points.
I just spent the points to prolong the Ubersniper and Berserk perks, more health and more accuracy. Because you can find health packs almost anywhere and while in berserk you get the health back while making your knife red.
The only real challenges are offered by the stupid telekinetic super soldiers and 10 feet ubersoldiers. They both nail you to the ground with their rocket launchers or mini tornados. But if you stay well covered and sink few headshots they’re just a couple minute obstacles.
Comparing the first encounter with the telekinesis guy was way more epic in the first one, the guy just appeared at the long dark road and started to fly stuff at you and it was like in a tornado all a sudden. In the sequel the guy just walks down the stairs in bright daylight and starts to fly sand at your eyes, such a disappointment.
Overall Ubersoldier II is not very uber. I was just uberbored while playing it. Even the normal fights had more adrenaline in them than boss fights. The makers were even ripping the design of the female elite soldiers from Return the Castle Wolfenstein. Comic styled cut scenes are not well made or the 3D-cinematic ones. Dialogue is cheesy and the studio members were probably playing the roles themselves. It’s playable, easily beaten in 4-5 hours, but it’s just a below average FPS and only worth when in -75% or up sale. 4/10
I sincerely hope that Steam gets the first one to the catalogue. That was uberfun.

Ubersoldier II is pretty much another generic linear first person shooter. All the guns operate more or less the same. The movement is Uberclunky. There is no auto-save during each level so if you die and didn't quicksave it, you get to start all over again. The story is Ubercomical, yet almost seems Uberserious at times. The graphics and textures are Uberugly even at HD resolutions.
You get XP during levels based on kill streaks to level up your Uberness which amounts to an Uberbullet shield, more health, additional accuracy, or longer Uberness. If you score 3 headshots in succession, your next headshot will rank you an Ubersniper granting you invincibility, unlimited ammo, and Uberaccuracy for a short time. If you score 3 melee kills in a row, your next melee kill will set you in a beserker rage where you just insta kill anyone that comes in contact with your knife. The skills are actually useful since there are endless hordes of Ubernazis that continue to spawn, sometimes even behind you in that last room you just cleared.
Overall, Ubersoldier II is an Ubercheesy first person shooter that pretty much Uberstinks. I only dropped six quarters on it, but I'm still trying to convince myself that it was money well spent.

Screencheat is damned clever. It is a fast-paced first person arena shooter in colorful maps where you are always watching the screen of every player, to find their position and murder them. There are several game modes, including death match, king of the hill, murder mystery, and others. Murder Mystery is like death match, except you are given a weapon to pick up and a target to kill -- and you only score if you accomplish killing that selected target with that specific weapon. The weapons are clever, too. Rifle revolver, exploding bear bomb, blunderbuss, brave knight charging on a children's makeshift horse-on-a-stick.
The only downside is the limited player-base. As of this writing, you can find a game, but it will take awhile and you will probably be the one who has to host it. This would be improved, if the developers didn't require you to leave the game and go back to a lobby in order to pick up new players (including those who are actively spectating you and may want to join). A smarter move would be to just fill the empty slots with new players as old players drop off. If not during a game or round, then in-between rounds. This oversight is frustrating.
As of this writing, Humble Bundle store has this game on sale for four copies for ten bucks. It is absolutely worth that. Even if you have to find a few people to play locally on a LAN with. This is a unique experience that should be tried.

Ticket to Ride is an adaptation of a popular board game, with the ability to play against AI, or local or online opponents. The board game has a pretty simple rule set that's easy to learn, and it has some good strategic complexity. I haven't been playing it for all that long, but I've definitely enjoyed what I've played so far.
I found the voice acting obnoxious and turned it off immediately. The music grates after a little while, but you can turn that off too. The game controls pretty well and shows a lot of useful information on screen. The menus are a bit clunky, and this actually makes it a little difficult to get in to the online game lobby.
But really, what matters is the gameplay, and Ticket to Ride has great gameplay. I had fun playing against AI and against humans, and there's tons of replay value. This game will definitely be worth it for board game enthusiasts at full price. I'd still recommend it to anyone that can appreciate a strategic, turn-based game. As for the DLC, it allows you to play on different maps, sometimes with different rules. If you like the base game, the expansions will add quite a bit

What was once a great game with layers of complexity, fun and exciting gameplay and an amazing community is turning into a shallow grindfest. The game has been progressively dumbed down during the latest patches (with many mobility skills nerfed and direct damage buffed), bugs are frequent and it doesn't look they will be fixed anytime soon. The devs seem hell-bent on churning out new content (champions, skins, etc) without taking a break to fix the bugs - some of which have been around for months or even a year. Expect drops, crashes, and bugs that mess with your rewards (bugged drops, etc). At this poins the daily quests are broken completely, so you won't even get your rewards for playing the game. Want to unlock stuff? You gotta pay. The final nail in the coffin is OB64 though. Once that patch hits, the game will turn into a proper sh*tfest. The complete overhaul of the cards system will not only remove the complexity that made the game stand out against OW (how you could tailor every champion's build to fit your playstyle) but will also make the game completely P2W. New players won't have a chance against those that have stronger decks - but prepared to either play insane amounts of time, or shell out thousands of bucks (no kidding) to unlock the cards you want. (Not to mention it will be based solely on RNG, so you won't even be able to choose the stuff you really want.) No, thank you.
It is really sad that it has come to this since I had immense fun with this game for months. (997 hours played in total.) It used to be a really fun (if somewhat buggy) experience with enough depth to keep it fresh on the long run. The champions are generally fun to use - that includes supports too -, the community is amazing, and the customization options made it so that I kept coming back again and again to try out new builds.
Hi-Rez dun goofed (it's not their first time - see Tribes for example), and I cannot fathom what they were thinking with the past few patches, and, especially, the upcoming one. I'm just sad for the devs that worked hard to bring us this game. I wanted it to work, but someone, somewhere, messed it all up with their stupid decisions.
Steer clear for now - even though this was once a great game, the good times are sadly over.

Saints Row 2 is my Favourite game of all time.
Taking place in the City of Stilwater, the game follows upon the ending of Saints Row 1, where the boat you were on exploded, you, being the then-appointed boss of the Third Street Saints, survived the explosion.
As you and the Boss are thrust into an unfamiliar world, you must rebuild the Saints from the ground up.
Honestly this game is everything to me, The characters are all incredibly real and believable, unike in 3 where everyone seems to have become a caricature of themselves. Each of the gangs feel incredibly real, and unique, Each gang controlls a set of territory and you gradually capture more and more land as the story progresses.
As I said, the gangs and the bosses all feel real, and you will learn to despise each and every one of them.
Character Customisation is great, Car Modification is expansive and vast, there are different clothes shops around in different locations which all sell different clothes.
The entire city has so many different locations that all build this big picture, like the University district, filled with young adult students going from place to place, some holding laundry, some on their laptops, some sitting together, to the slums where you'll find derros sitting on the streets smoking joints, or the high class rich area, filled with fancy cars and people in suits.
If I had one gripe about the game the port was pretty shonky, and apparently it doesn't work well for people? I've never had a problem playing the game myself but apparently it doesnt run for some people, theres a mod that does fix that however.
My main gripe is the vehicle controls, which are very jerky and hard to control, especially in missions where vehicle control is key. The mod "Gentlemen of the Row" fixes these issues but personally changes a bit too much of the game for me to like using it.
I'm sure someone else could've made a much more in-depth review of the game but I'm just here, saying that this is genuinely my favourite game of all time, and I'm actually gonna play it the second i'm done with this review.

Boring, text-only review below:
"Rampage Knights has been out on Steam for a couple of weeks now, and I only got around to playing it today. I spent a modest time with it and haven't explored its co-op mode, but have gone through enough of its single-player component to give a solid opinion on how it plays out. Here's what I think.
Developed by Rake in the Grass, an indie studio from the Czech Republic, Rampage Knights has one very clear inspiration not only in how it plays but in how it looks: famous XBLA indie hit Castle Crashers. If you've played The Behemoth's game, you'll feel right at home with Rampage Knights (or if you're more the oldschool sort, think Golden Axe).
You start off at a small encampment where you can customize your character: there are many bodies and heads, from lumberjack lookalikes to vikings and orcs, and hats (because who doesn't like hats?) to choose from, starting with a sizable collection that you increase as you complete challenges and perform certain tasks. While these are strictly cosmetic, you can also choose from six classes - each one playing different from one another - that you'll unlock as you progress in the game. Accompanying these are also a plethora of challenges and dozens of achievements.
You'll then head out into the randomly generated enchanted forest to recover your treasure, stolen from a mysterious fiend. There are multiple weapons to find, each with their own reach, damage and special attributes (such as freezing or dealing additional critical damage), along with four other types of item: a permanent item that allows you to perform a certain action, such as casting a spell or dealing additional damage, for mana; throwing weapons; spell scrolls; and consumable potions. Certain potions and interactions can yield negative things, such as getting the head of an ♥♥♥ or running uncontrollably.
You can chain combos to swivel foes around you, tossing them up and down, stomping on their heads and bowling them into other enemies. Combat is fluid and dynamic, with many combos to perform and different approaches required depending on what you're facing, but I couldn't help feeling that the visuals were too flattened, making it difficult for me to ascertain precisely where my character was. Variety comes in the form of enemies, who can go from simple skeletons who slice you with their swords to charging undead and fire-spitting dragons, but more often than not it's a matter of side-stepping when their attack prompt pops up and going back in for a few hits while they recover.
The game played well enough and has plenty of unlockables and extra content to keep you coming back to it, if only to get that cool extra hat or beat a tough challenge. It lacks the humor and story Castle Crashers had, shunning the linear experience in favor of a roguelike structure where you must begin from the start after dying a couple of times, and trading the leveling/skill system for more varied classes and single-run items. The boss fights are hard and the game itself has multiple difficulties you can unlock, and I can imagine from playing other co-op brawlers that the two-player multiplayer is even better. At the end of the day its a solid 2D brawler with plenty of progression elements and unlockables to keep you coming back to it."

Bully. It's GTA, but without blood and deadly weapons, and instead of playing as an adult man, you play as Jimmy Hopkins. A 15 year old kid who's aggressive and a fighter, but not truly malicious. He only gives people what they have coming to them.
Bully takes place in Bullworth, a town in New England. Your mom, well, Jimmy's mom, drops you off at Bullworth Academy. A boarding school. The school is full of bullies and corrupt teachers and it's up to you to put a stop to it.
The game's storyline will guide you through six chapters (There are 65 missions, the sixth chapter is an endless free-roam chapter, giving you the chance to complete non-storyline missions and to collect collectables.) Each of them takes place in a different weather season. The missions vary, it's never the same. One time you're cleaning a rat infested library and the next time you're helping a teacher escape from a psychiatric hospital. As Jimmy, your main goal is to bring peace to the school by helping and befriending the five school cliques: The Nerds, the Jocks, the Bullies and the Preppies.
Of course you'll have to go to class. These classes are: English, gym, geography, math (ew), music, shop, art, photography and biology. They are simple mini-games which become noticeably harder every time you attend them and make progress. You'll also have to deal with a time schedule. You can skip class, but you won't get any rewards if you do so and prefects will catch you if they see you outside of class.
Jimmy, your character, is highly customizable. You can buy clothes, change your hairstyle and more. You can even buy a bike, a go-kart or a scooter if you saved up enough cash. Money can be earned by either taking a paper route, doing missions for townies or students or by completing storyline missions.
You've got weapons. No, they are not guns and no you can't kill people. There's a super slingshot, you can use firecrackers, stink bombs, eggs, a bag of marbles, a bottle rocket launcher and so much more. You can also pick up one of the many objects around you (umbrella's, vases, bottles) and use them as a weapon.
Interacting with your fellow students is fun too. You can talk to them, give them presents, put them in trash bins, punch them in the face (aka bully them) and even kiss them. (This only applies to several girls and yes, you can kiss some guys too if you're into that.)
The game has a very impressive map size. You can explore the entire school, the school grounds, the town, a fully functional theme park, an industrial park and a few more awesome places. There are many collectables scattered around the map too.
Bully may be pretty good, but it's not perfect. The graphics are rather outdated, the sound isn't that amazing and you will have to deal with odd controls and some bugs. But don't worry! It doesn't kill the fun. Bully is an amazing game and there's much to do. And for only $14.99 - £9.99 - €9.99, it's certainly worth it.
Go buy it!
