I'm going to start by saying that I am a Founder who hasn't bought anything but the pack back in the day.
A quick TL;DR for the most of you: The next update can either make the game a 100% better, free Overwatch experience or it can be a slap to the face of those of us who have played up until this point. Below are my 6am thoughts on Paladins. What it is, was and could be soon as well as whatever else pops in to my head as I type.
The game used to be *almost* comparable to Overwatch in the ealier days of OB20' and OB30's. The game was buggy, fairly unbalanced and was overrun by the kinds of players that Overwatch had mostly weeded out by that stage. The people playing for kills in a game that didnt even have a Deathmatch mode.
As it stands right now, Paladins is far more enjoyable than Overwatch. There are, yes, bugs. That having been said, theres nothing outside of cosmetics that you can't earn in a reasonable amount of time just playing through the game. I've only put in 100 hours give or take and, as it stands, I'm missing a grand total of 3 cards. Two from Seris and one from Maeve. Basically, what I'm saying is that it's never been difficult to get a foothold in Paladins and start ripping up the asphault, so to speak. You may say that that's not good enough, considering that you unlock all characters in Overwatch when you buy the game, but this one here's Free to Play and honestly lacks the extreme sodium content of Overwatch for the most part. Characters actually have a bit of personality and it's just an overall friendlier experience.
With the newest patch, OB64, some rather drastic changes are coming to the card system. You'll have the base level of every card upon getting in to the game, but only the base level. Duplicate cards will level yours and increase the cards effects naturally. This means that long time player and/or anyone who sinks cash in to the game will have a moderate advantage over a F2P player. What the negative reviews aren't fessing up to, or being honest about, is how easy it is to earn chests (which will contain cards, that will be duplicates because you'll already have *all of the cards*) or that leveling up characters and geting First Win of the Days with each Champ will net you a Champ chest that will have cards for that specific character in it, that will again be duplicates. If you're a Warframe player, or a
player, or a LoLer, etc, etc, this grind won't likely be anything like what we're already used to.
There is one legitimate complaint that I have with OB64 and thats the VIP Tier system. On top of being able to purchase the 'Crystal' premium currency, Hi-Rez introduced a VIP subscription system and points which you can gain slowly by winning matches or purchase outright. As it is in OB63, VIP subscription isn't a huge deal because it's only acts as a booster and the points are only a secondary currency you can get with Crystals or Cash and exists just to pick up skins or to rent 'Golden weapons' which increase your earnings for a few days with individual characters. Sounds like a lot, but it's nothing that outright effects your in-match gameplay.
OB64 concerns me only because of a 'VIP Tier' System that's similar to the  Mobile MMO counterpart of the same name. By earning or purchasing VIP points you unlock EXP/Gold/Mastery/VIP Point earning bonuses and a discount to the VIP Point Store that ramp up the more VIP points you have. If this is just a permanent bonus that doesn't require you to have  VIP access active in order then that's fine. It'll reward long-time players with a few neat skins and some nice things in a way that says 'Hey, thanks for playing.' However, if these bonuses are tied to being a VIP access player, then it becomes a matter of 'Look at these nice things you've earned with your time, but can't have unless you fork over a few bucks.' and  that's not an acceptable way to treat the playerbase.
12/12/2017 marks the release date of OB64. If you're looking to get in, I suggest checking it out now, get  what cards you can. They'll be pushed to Level 3 of 5 retroactively Tuesday. See what you think of the game now, make your call next week.

I've been toying with whether or not to actually write this review because the game has been out for a long time and mostly everyone are either going to get it or skip it in favour of the crazier Saints Row 3 and 4 but I guess the sales are a good itme to write this considering the game is $2.50. If you want to know whether to get this game or not, I'd say yes. Here's my review, but please keep in mind this review is going to be pretty long, Saints Row 2 is one of my favourite games period.
Saints Row 2 is obviously the second game in the Saints Row series. While The Third and IV decided to make things as over the top and crazy as possible, 2, for the most part, is fairly grounded. The story is all about revenge and reclaiming what was once yours. Taking place five(?) years after the first Saints Row, your character wakes up in prison from a coma and kills their way to freedom and finds "their" city ruled by rival gangs. The Saints aren't the giants they were at the end of the first game, everything has fallen apart. From there, you embark on a jounrey across Stilwater, killing and maiming rival gang members as you take back the city you "deserve."
Now people are quick to say that Saints Row 2 on the PC is an awful port and I'd sit there and agree with you. It crashes, it runs like crap and there's a lot of clipping issues and whatnot. So why do I still want to reccomend this game? There's a mod that fixes all of those problems; Gentlemen of the Row. Download it. As well as perfomance fixes and whatnot, GOTR also has optional features you can include from DLC content (Only console releases got DLC) to extra clothing and weaponary such as a chainsaw launcher! Very awesome stuff.
In terms of the base game, Saints Row 2 is nowhere near as fluid as The Third and IV. Despite this, it still has a lot of charm. That may just be me wearing nostalgia goggles but everything in this game feels much more enjoyable than future games for a multitude of reasons. The activies are much more entertaining; ranging from spraying septic on everything in sight to dressing up as a cop to help record footage for a reality show known as FUZZ. Fight Club is also in this game and it's much better than the Fight Club in IV, which was terribly broken by the addition of super powers. While the story is much more grounded, the side activites is just as fun and rewarding as you'd expect from a Saints Row game. Awards for completing these activites range from unlimited sprint to reduced flame damage, etc. The radio in Saints Row 2 is also one of my favourites in the series, I love a majority of the soundtrack in this game and find myself listening to it more than my own Spotify. Not only is the music great but the DJs and callers are also funny to listen to and often leave me smirking in my seat.
Now the biggest thing I'll bring up is the city. Stilwater. It's just a much better environment then Steelport of The Third and IV. While Steelport only consisted of three districts (Factory, Suburb, Downtown), Stilwater is so much more than that. You have Little Shanghai, a prison island, a university, trailer park, underground shopping mall with visitable shops and so much more. The city is much more diverse and fun to explore, much more interesting then the industrial wasteland of Steelport that left me bored after five minutes. Concluding both the gameplay section and my discussion on the game's environment, Stilwater is home to several easter eggs and roughly 130 interiors. Some interiors are hidden while others may be stores. If you're into exploring aimlessly or looking for developer jokes, Saints Row 2's map is a perfect world to get lost in.
I already briefly covered the plot in my Overview but I'll go a bit more in depth here. However, I will not be dropping any spoilers for the sake of newcomers. Saints Row 2's story isn't perfect but it is interesting. Unlike 3 and 4 where you did missions in a linear order, this game allows you to choose your form of progression. You complete six Prologue missions and then you may choose which of the three gangs to attack first. If you get bored or want to take a break from that gang, you can switch to taking on a different gang. Once all three gangs are eliminated, you get a six or seven mission epilogue and there's even a hidden bonus mission that ties up some loose ends from the original Saints Row.
Wrapping up the plot discussion, I will state that the plot of this game is still pretty good. It doesn't have crazy set pieces like 3 and 4's skydiving out of a plane or going up against a giant soda can monster, it's much more serious and grounded outside of the activities but I like it. There are moments that will leave you speechless or perhaps even cry like me, the game has a lot more down to earth emotional scenes than three and four compared.
Saints Row 2 is the best game to come out of this series. I'm still a huge fan of the future games but this one is just the perfect mix of everything you'd want in a Saints Row. You have a dark and gritty story about revenge and betrayal, fun and over the top side content and a huge city to explore. With the most customization the series has to offer, you can turn lighthouses into penthouses, sports cars into...sports(ier) cars! What are you waiting for? The game is currently $2.50 at the time of this review, go get it! As long as you grab the Gentlemen of the Row mod, you should be able to run this game smoothly and will hopefuly have a great time.
I hope everyone enjoyed this review and if you couldn't be bothered reading due to how much I put into it, that's understandable. This game means a lot to me, shaping my musical tastes and giving me some fun times during high school so I thought it was time I gave this game the review it deserves. Thanks to those who have read this and I hope I managed to convince some people to try this game out. If I did, I wish you all the best and hope you enjoy!

I love this game.
The brawler combat is easy on the surface and feels very satisfying (except for trying to stomp crawlers, which needs a bigger hitbox).  However, it gets pretty hectic with lots of enemies so you need to predict and react to attacks/projectiles and kite away from swarms of enemies so you can fight them separately.  I am bad at video games and this game makes me feel like I'm not, because it pretty much always does what you want.  It's also very good at getting you a little further each time you play, and doesn't feel like a grind or hitting a dead end.  The more you play the more challenges you complete and the better your characters get.  The different classes of characters (though I haven't unlocked the warlock or battlemage yet) all feel fun and different, if maybe not balanced in strength.
The co-op is very entertaining, if a bit harder than the single player in my opinion (my girlfriend keeps knocking me over so I can't do anything in the middle of fights...).  It's sort of a half-way friendly fire system.  You can hit your partner and knock them down with your dash attack, but you don't damage them.  The loot is also "shared", so prepare for your friend to take everything and let you die.
The art style is fine, nothing feels out of place.  It's a cartoony game full of cartoony humor.  Controller support was pretty good, I was able to use a PS3 controller (emulating Xbox 360) and a Logitech Direct Input controller, both were recognized and mapped properly.  It'd be nice to have proper button remapping, but the default is pretty good (it can take a bit to get used to the item bar and learn how to use it).  Technical settings are adequate, not much to be said for a 2D game.  Full mouse and controller support in the menus.
Overall very good game that I keep wanting to play more.

I think the Steam controller is a must own for anyone who prefers to use gamepads. It won't replace the Xbox One controller as my default input device, but it is the perfect compliment piece. It perfectly fills in the gap where traditional controllers fail. First person shooters are awful with Xbox pads, be it 360 or XB One, but with the Steam controller, you get almost the same level of precision as you would from m&kb. I own hundreds of older games that lack controller support and using things like xpadder often would provide less than adequate results, but with the Steam controller those older games just work, no hassle, no messing with button mapping, just pick a preset and you're good to go. Honestly, for me, the only downside to the Steam controller is that if you have big fingers the face buttons are a bit too closely bunched and small. And on the flipside, if you have small hands, the controller may be too bulky and cumbersome.

GemBreak is a game full of surprises. Unfortunately, most of them are related to the physics, which is not what you would expect from a Peggle clone. The ball bouncing is so all over the place it's actually kind of funny. The devs tried to introduce refreshing ideas into the formula, and many of them could even work, but the wildly inaccurate ball action makes it impossible to take the game seriously. Too bad.

A fun & challenging pachinko/pinball style game with obvious similarities to Peggle, enjoyable physics & variety in level design.
My main reason to leave a comment is that I feel the 22% of negative reviews misrepresent the game. They all seem to be from peggle fans that are unhappy GemBreak isn't a precise clone of their favourite which isn't a good reason imo to downvote any game. If you might be one of these, watch the videos first to decide if you like the game play.
GemBreak kept me hooked while I was unlocking each of its one hundred stages & its addictive nature, variety & leaderboards keep me coming back for one more go, trying to get a higher score or unlock the remaining achievements. The launch price is more than fair & the dev is still working on the game which is a bonus.
It's also pretty much bug free. I encountered no game breaking bugs; in fact I only saw one minor cosmetic error - sometimes the counter of remaining gems doesn't decrease when a gem is destroyed, however it doesn't affect game play as GemBreak does seem to know how many gems actually remain. In any case I only saw this two or three times in about ten hours of play. That's good going for a game less than two months into release.

What can I say about Loadout? Well let me say it's like if Ratchet & Clank but just mixed it up with a hint of Borderlands insane gun combinations, but even that doesn't describe how insane and bloody this game is. It is a cartoony violent 3rd person shooter with Deathmatches, capture the flag (Jackhammer), take point, etc. This F2P is crazy and when you die, it makes me laugh alot.
If it's F2P there is the option of cash for power-ups and appearance. That doesn't bother me too much. But it does go way overboard on the cost of appearance...I could only afford 2-3 items in the outfitters (For about $20) but hey, appearance does nothing on the gameplay. The power-ups are great to rank up faster to unlock more upgrade for your guns.
You got your typical machine guns, rocket launchers, grenade launchers, your usual shooter stuff. But the best part is how you customize your weapons. You can put either poison, electric (tesla), or fire in your bullets.
If you're expecting a story out of Loadout, there isn't. It's just a bunch of space rednecks blowing up each other in space. There is only 3 characters: Axl, T-Bone, and Helga. But choosing any of them won't affect your gameplay. The atmosphere is like a desert, canyon, and space. I like it, it reminds me of Borderlands but more cartoony.
Bottom line: I recommend this game. 8/10

Wow, where to begin... I'm surprised this game has so many positive reviews.
Well, TL;DR: Bought game ~40% discounted. I completed one ending in a little over 9 hours, and I literally said "THANK ♥♥♥♥ING GOD" out loud when I saw the credits roll. I really did not enjoy this game, and my favorite moment was when it ended.
I'm going to try not to focus too much on the quality of the PC port, since that has already been beaten to death in the reviews. However, make no mistake, the PC port is pretty terrible. Just about everything other people have said in the reviews is true. But there are plenty of other reasons I would not recommend this game, on any platform.
Pros
====
- Tolerable graphics. They kinda look like PS3-era graphics (even though this was a PS4-era title). So, not the best, but not the worst.
- Mostly fluid player-controller. The movement and combat animations on the player are pretty good, and everything feels responsive, except there are several animations that lock down your controls a little too long when they probably shouldn't. Maybe this is "balance," but I just found it terribly annoying most of the time, especially when it would get me killed and I'd have to do the whole level over again.
- Combat is somewhat satisfying. Not quite as good as Metal Gear Rising: Revengence, Bayonetta, or other games with similar combat style, but it's one of the few halfway redeeming aspects of this game.
- Weapons effectively feel different from each other.
- Novel customization by being able to disable different parts of your HUD in exchange for more "power-up" slots.
- Choose between English and Japanese dialog. I like when they give the option. Both voice acting quality is about what you'd expect. Far from the best, but it's average for this type of game.
Cons
====
- The story is fairly lackluster. They try to get kinda deep with it by questioning "How are machines with complex AI different from humans if the AI experience emotions?", but it mostly falls flat. It's a subject matter that has been used over and over again so many times, and this doesn't bring much new to the table, nor does it even do what it does particularly well. This disappointed me, since I had heard the story richness was one of this game's strengths. I haven't played all the endings, but I honestly don't think I could bring myself to go back and play it again.
- I didn't care about any of the characters. I might have liked the story better if I actually cared what happened to the characters, but between the sporadic presence of voice acting vs. text-only vs. the pre-rendered low-resolution cutscenes, no lip movement vs. lip movement, lack of personality, and the "typical anime character" behavior all characters exhibit, it was just hard to find any of these characters believable or likeable.
- Most of your time spent will be running from place to place and then back out the way you came (or dying and having to replay entire levels). Yes, there's a "fast-travel," but half the time the locations to travel to for your current quest have conveniently been disabled by some "EMP" or some other BS that was clearly done just to pad out the quests, since pretty much all the secondary quests are fetch quests. So, you end up going to activate these transport locations, only to not be able to use them for one reason or another, so you have to essentially play entire areas over again for no reason. Then, a lot of quests end after traveling down a long dead-end path, like down a sewer tube, or a catwalk, or a canyon, so you have to back track through the entire level after you're done. And sometimes the enemies will have respawned by then. One of the characters even spouts a line about how it sucks to have to backtrack.
- Pretty much every boss is one of these: "Shoot and slash while dodging projectiles and melee attacks for about 10 minutes with no variation, and hope you don't die. Ah, he's finally dead. OH BUT WAIT, NO HE'S NOT; NEXT FORM. Whew but now he's dead... OH BUT WAIT A SECOND; HE'S BACK. And... now he's finally dead. Okay, finally I can save my game... NOPE THAT WASN'T EVEN HIS FINAL FORM. ♥♥♥♥. HOW LONG CAN THIS GO?!" It gets real old, real fast.
- The textures are really hit-or-miss quality. Some are great, some are atrociously low-res on structures right next to the player. This would be forgivable, except...
- The level design is pretty simple in most areas, and there's not a lot of detail to look at. There are a handful of decently made areas, but it mostly feels very bland.
- The camera is awful. There's lots of settings you can tweak, but it's really just fundamentally flawed. The game has a habit of not being able to decide what genre of game it wants to be. Sometimes it's like a sidescroller perspective, sometimes it's like a top-down twin-stick shooter perspective, sometimes it's a behind-the-player manual right-stick camera, sometimes it's automatically rotating camera, sometimes it's some strange mash-up of perspectives. This sounds like an interesting, novel concept, but it really just ends up being frustrating. Because it switches between all these so often, which all behave slightly different, and even sometimes change the attack styles of your weapons, it becomes a struggle to keep track of the player sometimes (especially when you've got 9S with you, who has a nearly identical silouhette), and you have to constantly context-switch your interpretation of the controls and whether or not you need to be controlling the camera yourself or the direction you're shooting or how your dodge is going to work. Also, be prepared to see a lot of grass directly in your face, because for many enemies, if you lock onto them in third person mode and don't then manually continue to adjust the camera pitch down, the camera runs into the ground where all the grass is, but the grass doesn't fade out or anything. Makes it nearly impossible to see. Tight spaces are also bad in the same way, as you might expect.
- The sound effects have the quality of sounding like they're from some freely-available 1000 stock sound pack, or something. The range of the quality of the different sounds is quite noticabe.
- The enemies all have about 2 or 3 different voice lines (with a cheesy "robot" filter applied over them) for each type, and they all scream them in your ear over and over and over and over.
- Some people say the music is good, but I found the numerous 30-second loops of mediocre orchestral music with people chanting and singing in every song particularly annoying. There was also very little middle ground between calm music and "OMG SO EPIC" music. It got pretty old, and it took impact away from any parts of the game that actually would have otherwise felt epic, but didn't. Maybe it's just not my style.
- The map is nearly useless. There's even an NPC in the game that agrees the map sucks, and basically tells you, "deal with it or don't use it."
- Invisible walls everywhere. Sometimes I could hardly tell where I was allowed to go, because you'd see an opening that looks like you could fit through, but there was an invisible wall stopping you, and there were no good visual clues to indicate what openings you could fit through. Then there'd be railings and such that you should easily be able to jump over to get around faster, but they'd be invisi-walled for no real technical reason. That, on top of the wacky perspectives, made traversing the world a chore most of the time.
So, I wouldn't recommend getting this game unless you REALLY like games similar to Metal Gear Rising: Revengence, Bayonetta, etc. AND it's highly discounted. Definitely don't pay $60 for this game. I'm glad I waited for a sale, and I still feel like I overpaid.

Ubersoldier is weird game where Eastern Europeans write games where the hero kills lots and lots of Nazis... and localizers tried to make it sound... American, ending up with a weird mess. But at its heart, it's about, well, killing bad guys with lots and lots of bullets. And that it does very well... but it's nothing we haven't seen before.
You play Karl Stolz, who escaped from the Ubersoldier program headed by a mad Nazi scientist (another videogame trope) who resurrect dead soldiers to make them perfect killing machines (duh). In the first game Karl destroyed the T-8 drug machine and killed the mad scientist, but the nightmare had not ended. The Resistance is still fighting Ubermacht, the secret Nazi unit responsible and there are rumors that the mad scientist is not dead, and there's an uberhenchman that's unstoppable... Thus the sequel.
The shooter itself is well made. There's no lean and blind-fire, but the physics and ragdoll effects are quite good. Throw a grenade and expect boxes and weapons blown all over the place. You are expected to use environment to your advantage. Shoot exploding barrels like grenades, use grenades to flush Nazis out of cover and headshot them. Use stun grenades to incapacitate them to knife them easier. So on and so forth. Enemies will do the same to you, but it's pretty old trope. The occasional mini-bosses, the snipers on window ledges, the ambush... it's typical designs, and you can almost SEE the trigger points before you hit them.
What separates this from most "shoot Nazi" games is the inclusion of two uber-modes... Ubersniper, and Berserker. If you score 3 headshots (quickly) and score a 4th within 60 seconds, you get "ubersniper", where time slows down and enemies are highlighted, giving you much easier headshots, which also adds to your uber-time. If you score 3 knife kills, and a 4th within 60 seconds, you get Berserker mode, which gets you invulnerability temporarily, so you can knife even more people.
Berserker mode trigger also gives you 10 XP while headshots give you 5, and subsequent ones only give 1 XP. The XP's can be used to upgrade your abilities, from health to accuracy, more Ubertime to other attributes, in a bit of RPG-likeness.
Graphics are good, and the game's not TOO difficult on easy mode, except near the end, where enemies ambush, use grenades a lot, and guard keypoints with non-stop firing MG42's (obviously not realistic), and backup with snipers that move around a lot. The end boss is even MORE stupid, as it is practically invulnerable to weapons. (sorta spoiler)
There is no "where to go next" nav marker, but the levels are NOT that hard to figure out. Though remember to qucksave, as autosave doesn't kick in often enough.
There are a couple problems, with the sole female protagonist, Maria (yes, it's a proper German name) portrayed as sexy (in some outfits you can see nipples behind the shirt) even in a warzone. And there were kisses here and there (with Karl, of course) and of course, focus on the more, uh... feminine parts when she's in the cutscene.
Cutscenes are drawn comic-book panel style, which are quite well done, but the voice-acting... Well, the German don't sound German... They sound American. And yes, they were shouting in English in bad accent. *sigh*
But it's a good shooter... Better than most "budget shooters" you find in the bargain bins. For $5, (or $2.50 on sale) you can't really miss.

OPUS: The Day We Found Earth, although a short game, was an enjoyable and relaxing experience of a game. Although there are not many characters, the story was charming.
You play as a small robot named Emeth who is currently in many years in the future, when humans have long left their planet of origin to live among the stars. By then, Earth has become a mysterious and little-known planet, treated as if mythical. After many years of genetic engineering, the human gene pool has been deteriorating, however, and the only way to save it is to find samples on Earth. Project Earth then started building and constructing the spaceship known as OPUS, and your goal as Emeth is to find Earth, somewhere in the galaxy.
OPUS: The Day We Found Earth was a charming and pleasant little game, with a lovely soundtrack, and with a nice story. The visuals were also pretty, and looking at all of the stars and planets was relaxing and thought-provoking for me. I would recommend this game to anyone who likes story-rich games, and relaxing games, as well as anyone who enjoys the idea of sci-fi stories. ^.^

You're told which star you are to scan -- so it's your job to navigate the telescope to that named sector and then to those given coordinates in that sector and scan a star in
area.  It'll usually find a planet and score it's likeness to Earth, and give you an opportunity to name the planet you discovered.
After every scan it returns to the spaceship view of the game where the story resumes (usually), or if not, you can return to the telescope to search for Earth around another star, or click on a few things around the ship gathering information and back story that way.
The graphics in the game I thought were very well done making it enjoyable to navigate the telescope across the night sky, but really, it's the story that shines in this game.

The game sells itself as a guidebook to Japan in the form of a visual novel. It is effective as an educational/informative tool to a point, but an actual guide book would be preferable as this is a somewhat limited and distracting format. At the least, some unfamiliar terms will be introduced, inviting further research on the part of the reader if they do want to make the investment of a trip to Japan later.
As an edutainment game in VN form, it accomplishes what it sets out to do. The plot is fairly weak and often takes a back seat to informative anecdotes, though the love story threads are very complimentary to grasping particular aspects of the culture. The protagonist is enough of a massive dork to elicit entertainment value, ironically or otherwise.
Production values, with regards to art and music, are all solid and with no major flaws. I question why the need was felt to include overt adult fanservice in this, as removing it would not affect the overall length in any major capacity.
I ended up enjoying this more than anticipated and find it recommendable as its own product. If you're interested in the culture of Japan, or like visual novels in general, you'll enjoy this. That said, it's worth acknowledging that it's not the most effective guidebook by any stretch of the imagination, and further reading is recommended; it has been catered to the VN-reading audience as an introduction, nothing more.

Nearly 20 years later and this remains my all-time favorite game. Its "go anywhere you want at any time" approach was something that most of the RPGs of its time were not doing. Sure Baldur's Gate had a big world, but it had a fairly linear path through it. Fallout 2 just set you loose to go wherever you want from the start. The more modern RPGs that share this approach (such as Bethesda's) are great, but they can't match the sheer scale that Fallout 2 had, even with almost 2 decades of advances.

For me, Fallout 2 is by far one of the greatest examples of how an RPG should be and the best Fallout game to date. Building upon the solid foundations that Fallout 1 set, the sequel does the typical 'bigger, longer, better' make-over while keeping true to it's roots. The beggining areas of the game are a perfect natural tutorial to new players and oozes with a rich atmosphere which acts as a perfect introduction to the game and keeps you coming back time and time again.
The original disk version was great, but with the version added on Steam the game works so much better with new machines, giving you less issues and higher resolutions.
I voted this game as Steam's 2016 Steam Award's 'Test of Time' nomination because of it's brilliant character and addicting gameplay that makes it an instant classic worthy of going back to at any point in time.

The original release was one of the best games of 2011, hands down. It has a deep, rich storyline and setting that fans of cyberpunk--from Blade Runner to Ghost in the Shell--will greatly appreciate. The gameplay is smooth and challenging, and players of games such as Metal Gear Solid, Mass Effect, Thief, and the original Deus Ex will find themselves right at home with this fantastic title.
With the Director's Cut, a few changes and additions have been made. The most notable of these are the inclusion of the DLC missions into the main campaign--the Missing Link is no longer a separate game--the improved boss fights, and the developer commentary. There were other minor changes, but many players may not notice these. The inclusion of the Missing Link chapter helps round out the storyline, as well as give the player the opportunity to redo his or her skill points, which was something missing from the original 2011 release.
The improved boss fights were appreciated, though the additional avenues of defeating the bosses will still take some quick thinking, or trial and error, to truly take advantage. For fans that want a more balanced approach to the game, where any style of play is rewarded, this is the edition to purchase.
Developer commentary in this version of the game is an interesting and valuable addition. It can be toggled on or off at the player's convenience, and many of the nodes offer intriguing insight into the minds of the game's creators. The only minor irritations with the commentary involve the nodes themselves. They are not always apparent in the game world, and once a node is playing it cannot be stopped without going into the main menu options and toggling the commentary off. Still, in spite of that minor oversight, the commentary is exciting to listen to and veteran players will appreciate it.
I highly recommend that new and old fans of Deus Ex: Human Revolution grab a copy of the Director's Cut.

DOOM was one of my favorite video games of 2016. More so than Doom 3, this game feels like a modern version of the classic Doom. It is insanely fast paced and offers more depth in gameplay than what appears on the surface. Each of many weapons allows for different strategies in battle and none of them feel useless (even the pistol which has the advantage of having infinite ammo). The enemies are menacing, aggressive and challenging, especially when in hordes. Just like the weapons, each demon requires different strategies and tactics of approach. Weapon modifications and abilities are simple additions that only compound the gameplay's depth. The campaign is where you will experience the best DOOM has to offer. The story is rather lackluster, but honestly, I'm glad there is a story at all. Multiplayer is really hit or miss. Some aspects of it are unique and fun while others are just average. Snap Map is great content creation tool and adds a lot of longevity to the game. It is like a never-ending supply of DLC from the community.
Overall, DOOM is great FPS for those that love fast-paced, action-packed, bloody and deep gameplay. Now that the DLC is free, multiplayer might become more appealing as well.

Doom (4) is a game about killing demons to genosidale levels, as you are human rage incarnate armed with futuristic lead throwers and electron flying blades (as in the models are gibbed when hit by the projectiles). It also has multiplayer and a level editor to help expand the lifetime of the game.
Objectively, the game runs well on my computer, getting well above 100 FPS on a 1050p screen with middle settings (I think). I perfer max resolution and FPS over graphic details. As for online, it works reasonably well on a 5 Mb down and 2 Mb up connection with 2 other heavy internet users, but I did see the other players teliport. I recommend being careful if you have a poor connection. The only problems I had was with the editor, named Snapmap. I did run into graphical glitches and a few crashes, but a simple restart fixed some of the problems. I think it needs an update next.
As for the subjective part, I find it a fun game. Like many good games, you can be quick if you pratice and it's not a fustrating endevor ether. Singleplayer has a lot of content, like a good range of weapons and equipment with upgrades that add more to the guns, and not simple upgrades. There are runes, which are passives, that can also be upgraded. All are done by doing certain things. There is a story, but like the older games, it not focused on a lot. Yet it does have some depth too.
For multiplayer, I am enjoying it more after the 6.66 update. Before I found the lack of control over the unlocks annoying. I would have to grind to get the parts I want, as they were randomly unlocked. Now, you can choose what parts you want. They also redid the rune mechanic to they operate like the single player runes, but tuned for multiplayer. there are runes with tracking however. They are not a huge problem though.
For the Snapmap, I find this rather weak. While people have done great things, the thing was built with the consoles' limitations in mind. So we can't get Nuts' level of enemies and maps have limited sizes. They did expand the limits, but it's  nowhere close the limits of the PC. It also means the game lacks the same modding support that the old games have. Now, I do see why they did not allow it. Many triple A games use more advanced methods that modders can't have, but I argue that they should. If the modders are given the ability, those who have the tech see the increased demand and can make deals for the modders, making the price cheaper for the devs in return. It may take awhile, but all good things come to those who wait. (sorry for the slight tangant).
I recommed this game, worst case is to wait for a sale.
EDIT: The game is huge, so it will take a while if you have a slow connection. Days even.

This game has a lot of promise but pulls it's punches pretty hard.
First, I will say what I like about Opus:
- The art and graphics are nice
- The characters are likable and interesting
- The gameplay, while minimalist and repetitive, doesn't outstay it's welcome.
Now we get to the meat of the problem, the story.
The setup is simple; You're the unseen narator on a spaceship trying to find humans ancesteral birthplace, Earth. The game centers around a childlike robot named Emith trying to complete the mission but also find out what happened to his beloved creator Doctor Lisa. Along the way he's teamed up with a motherly A.I. based on Lisa who is trying to help him with his mission as well as help Emith understand the world around him. The game does a wonderful job of "show don't tell" by giving you clues to the whereabouts of the Lisa since she's that she's clearly not on the ship. This isn't a a major spoiler since the game sets that fact up pretty quickly. And that's awesome, they don't try to go for the obvious plot twist and instead decides to let the story be about the A.I. help Emith understand and come to terms that Lisa is gone.
Without spoiling things too much; they really pull their punches at the end in a number of ways. I'm a sucker for tear-jerk moments and was expecting to be crying at the end but instead the game ends ambigiously without any sense of satisfaction or conclusion.
In an attempt to get some closer to the story I checked Wikipedia and later YouTube. All Wikipedia had was a blurb about the setting of the story, clearly written by the developers, that couldn't be found in game and YouTube only showed me the same ended I had achieved; meaning what I got is all there was.
In the end I can't recommend this game. It's short and simple with great visuals and music but the story and grindy gameplay just makes the whole experience not worth it.
If you get Opus in the dollar tier of a bundle and want to waste an hour, you could do worst but you could also do a hell of a lot better.

Launch a game and it will very likely have a reasonably intuitive default layout.
This device also works outside of steam. From your browser to Origin to Steam, to any application, I'd surmise, the Steam Controller simply works.


I mean, you can, however, a high performance mouse and keyboard will track circles around it, literally and figuratively, especially for FPS titles.
The Steam Troller excels at this, opening up a fresh and surprisingly natural way to control your favorite city builder, RTS, roguelike and miscellaneous titles. This experience is easily compounded by spending a little time mapping your controls.
The default control scheme is usually obvious and intuitive.
The controller configuaration interface through big picture mode makes this controller the most adaptable product on the market, imo. Map any key from your qwerty board, mouse or third party gamepad to any input on the device. Assign a second layer of custom controls to any input, activating the second tier by an input of your choosing. For example, I like to set my second tier to a full pull of the dual stage left trigger, leaving a soft pull open to another function or bypass. The directional pad, analog stick and mouse track pad can be set to emulate other types of inputs entirely. For example, set the second tier of the analog stick to act as a scroll wheel, vertical, horizontal, or circular. Export your control schemes to the community or browse other Steam user's control scheme ideas in a game specific manner.
These options enable you to create control schemes for complex, control saturated games such as Evochron Legacy or DayZ.
Anyone not exclusively gaming from a workstation should own a Steam Troller.
While the Steam Troller is not of poor design or build material, I would like to have felt a more rubberized, industrial grade material other products contain.  Most of this product is constructed of classic hard black plastic.
You can dim and even turn off the effing power indicator light! The last thing I want to see during vidya time is the glaring effing light from my input device stabbing me in the brain.
+ exceptional software, interface, versatility
+ ease of use, yet boundless options adapt to even the most complex niche
+ essential hardware for the evolving integration of living room PC gaming
+ feels familiar yet fresh and unique
- not going to replace your performance gaming mouse for competitive play
- build materials could have been more heavy duty
+/- larger than average design

I'm going to go with a fairly cautious recommendation on this game. Overall, I did have fun with the game, quite a lot at times, but any recommendation I would gives comes with a number of qualifiers, a terrible port job being the main concern. The actual gameplay of Dead Rising 3 is chaotic and fun as hell, almost rivaling the complete anarchy of a Saint's Row game and for that alone I think this game is worth playing. It's a good game to get on sale and enjoy over a weekend for a laugh.
I got respect for Capcom as a publisher/developer they tend to make games that play really well even if they don't always have the best writing. Which is the case with Dead Rising 3. The story is basically just a crutch to hang gameplay on so the narrative is nothing astounding but it serves its purpose. Though, I guess there are people out there who follow the Dead Rising storyline I am just not one of those people. In fact, this is the first Dead Rising game I ever played so I would keep that in mind for anyone who is a longtime fan of the franchise looking at this review. The games writing is just good enough to frame the situation which is fine, I guess.
Though one issue I did have with the writing was that it was very well, im just going to say it, mean-spirited at times. There seems to be quite a bit of the Adam Sandler school of comedy where some of the jokes are basically just point and laugh at this person that is different. Like a villain who is a grotesquely obese woman which is funny because... she is just really obese? or another woman who is funny because she just really looks like a man and is very muscular. There was even a really out of place implied sexual assault gag near the beginning of the game which wasn't really intended as a joke but the seriousness of threatening♥♥♥♥♥♥against a woman in the middle of something that had been so incredibly campy was just, well, weird. These things weren't insulting enough to make me want a quit or even made me angry, they were just kind of made me be like "Oh..." These portrayals are at least not made worse by a protagonist who is equally mean-spirited and shames them for their appearance at least. Nick is just a good kid who wants people to get along so we at least see them through the lens of someone somewhat decent.
The biggest issue, I would have to say this game suffers from is its performance. I saw a lot of people compare it to the infamous GTA IV port which is pretty accurate. So, I would basically say if you don't meet the recommended hardware speccs, I wouldn't recommend trying this game, well I guess you can always refund it now. Even with hardware far above the recommended level you will still notice framerate dips and texture popping so be warned. I never had any technical problems actually interfere with actual gameplay at least. framerate dips never got low enough to hinder reaction times which resulted in a death or anything. I also don't think the game crashed on me once. So, that's something at least. With the sheer number of animated npcs on the screen at any one time, it was amazing that the frames stayed at 30 sometimes which is the locked framerate btw. So, if locked framerates make you incredibly angry then stay way. Though it might be changeable if there is an .ini file that you can edit I just didn't care enough to look.
I think this game also performs badly not just because of it being a direct port but also that it was software developed for new hardware even from the start. This was a xbone launch title...  I'm not saying this just because some of the xbone reviews of this game also stated problems with texture pop-in but because you can tell this game by its map design was made in a way to hide its poor optimization.There are a lot of carefully laid out roadblocks and cars strewn across the roads so that you can't ever travel too quickly on them so the engine has time to draw in the detail on new areas, however that wasn't often enough since is still noticed a lot of pop-in The map is also arranged in a modular way so that it is 4 mini-hubs rather than one major area, to reduce how many assets would need to be loaded at one time.
But, to end on a positive, I have to say the gameplay is just so damn fun. It reminds me of what I love about Saint's Row where the sheer chaos and ludocrity of the gameplay situations translates into pure, unadulterated entertainment. I've heard a lot of people who are series fans complain about this game dumbing down for causal audiences by making crafting less demanding and being easier and allowing more time for sidequests, but as someone who has never played a DR game I think it is good fit for something this silly. Your mileage may vary of course. One of the things I like best about this game is that is exactly as long as it needs to be. The map is not unnecessarily huge it is just the right size it needs to be and detailed enough to be memorable and interesting. It's the kind of game you can pick up for a few hours and play to unwind from a day at work without having to invest to much in which has its own kind of value, for me at least, when so many of these new releases are huge content cows that could take up to 100 hours or so to fully complete. It's a fun, just as long as it needs to be, 10-14 hour game that is worth picking up when it goes on sale.

If you are looking for a game to play in a short break, Rampage Knights is yours.
The game itself is designed on a simple concept, you fight hordes of enemies through the stages to reach the final boss. However, the game adds several things to that, making your each run more dynamic.
SOLO gameplay is good, however, CO-OP gameplay will push the fun meter to its limit. Sometimes, the most troublesome enemy is your friend :D
Recommended for
gamers. However, if you are the type that do nothing, but gaming, thinking that the dynamic aspect will encourage you to play likes 5 hrs straight, this game might not be what you are looking for.
Still looking for more detailed, but spoiler-free review?, continue reading.
The art is nice, 2d cartoonish, not pixelated. Nothing special, but it fits the game really well.
Character looks funny, with some surprises here, and there. There are many different character, categorized into classes, but with different styles, equipments.
Audio, and other FX is well designed to fit the visual. Just a little something that I found several audio to be boring, lacking some BAM! factors, for my personal tastes though.
The combat is simple. You are limited to few movesets, and you will continue chaining them together until you lose or win each run. The game relies more on player skills.
You have several classes to play with. They have almost the same basic movesets. Each class has its own pros&cons, which will affect your playstyle.
For example; a big guy. He has bigger weapon, so longer range. He is buffed, more health, but slower, and he refuses to wear armor! the other guy, carrying a cannon on his back, so he can use it. he is faster than the big guy, however, he cannot wear boots!
You can pick up weapons, armors, accessories, relics, pets, enemies!!?, map props, consumables, and etc. to help yourself go further in each run.
There are some rogue-like elements here, which is enough to make the game interesting. Although you might be disappointed, if you are expecting fully randomized kind of game.
The game consist of several stages, and each stage consist of several maps connecting to one another. Each run will pick a number of maps from its available maps, then put it together as a stage, by connecting them with doors, or passages. They are not randomly generated. However, it offers some varieties, enough to keep the gameplay going.
Each map will randomly spawn-in enemies, chests, some map props, and some surprises. This can be ranged from an empty room to a tresure room fully pack with enemies, and traps.
The items you get during each stage is random, however, within the difficulty range, that it doesn't make you stream-rolled everything in your path, and they are not randomly generated, but pre-made items.
There are also many surprises, that you can find along the way. They can be good, bad, a little bit of both, or nothing ... really ... >w<
Oh, and don't worry, your hero will be reset in each run.
I think that the game is more enjoyable this way. The difficulty scales up a bit in CO-OP. more enemies, less loots (you have to share items)
If one of you is killed, your partner can revive you, as it suppose to in CO-OP games, or the dead you can even revive yourself (with the right condition, of course) ^^v
The game is friendly fire enabled, just a reaction hit though. Trust me, that's is more than enough to kill off your partner when things get messy.
One downside for the CO-OP ... you need good, fast, and stable connection for smooth gameplay. The lags can be extreme, which can result in very nasty way, and it affect both of you.

I never played the original games, so it's not possible for me to compare them. Purists will say it's not as good, those who prefer newer game will say it's better. But it doesn't matter whether the original doom was better or not, because this one, by itself, is completely worth your time and money.
If you wanted an old school "KILL THEM ALL" game, then DOOM is the game for you.
And for once, Bethesda was able to provide a game that doesn't need mods to be completely worth it (mods are not bad, it's just good to see that they can actually make a game that really doesn't require them for you to have the best possible experience).

NieR:Automata is an amazing, emotional experience and I liked it so much that I even played it on the PlayStation 4 after I beat it on the PC including the DLC.
It is an open world action RPG by Platinum Games and Square Enix with intense Hack’n Slash Battles and a fantastic story, which slowly unfolds itself during several playthroughs and over 30 hours. The main protagonist is YoRHa Unit 2B, however, she isn’t the only playable character. But I don’t want to tell too much about the story, since it is an important part of the game.
The music is simply terrific and it's so much fun to just explore the world while listening to the pleasant tunes. I found myself just staying there or riding an albino boar, enjoying the scenery and soundtrack a lot. The English dubbing is also very well done and not annoying at all, but you can switch to Japanese as well, if you like.
The game also features many great mechanics. Swords can be leveled up by collection the necessary parts and with the help of various plug-in chips you can not only improve your skills, but also add HUD elements. For example: You can get faster, do more damage with your swords, raise your health bar, display a mini map and much more. By killing enemies or as a purchase in shops you obtain lots of chips after a while to make the game way easier, but beware, if you die, you lose your entire chipset. So be quick and grab it from your dead android body, before it vanishes.
All together: I loved NieR:Automata. Play it. It’s worth it.

I'll start out by saying OB64 has a lot of good things going for it. Much needed balance changes to heroes like Vivian, removal of the essence currency, some dope♥♥♥♥♥cosmetics; more than we're used to, and new legendary cards for every champion. I know this is a whole lot more than we're used to in updates; these changes alone probably feel a bit overwhelming for some, and If this was all they intended to add/fix i'd understand and be totally cool with this patch. Then came the new card loadout system "cards unbound" is a complete joke that will kill this game and the community. No amount of polishing is going to make this turd anymore easier for us to swallow. Hi-Rez cannot hide from the glaring issues and criticism by delaying the update, pulling an EA and disabling microtransactions after it releases, and going as far to say "We remain committed to Cards Unbound and its core mechanics" because the flood of negative reviews, forum, and reddit posts aren't going away.  Hi-Rez's refusal to even talk to their enraged community is only pouring salt on the wound. The game and the player base is suffering, and if cards unbound sees the light of day both will be dead.
Why? What's so bad about cards unbound?
-The major problem with cards unbound is that it removes the old progression system in favor of RNG based progression through lootboxes. Lootboxes that will be purchasable with ingame currency, REAL MONEY, or by progressing in the game. You can also boost your chance at receiving certain cards and guarentee a legendary drop by paying extra premium currency. If this sounds familiar it's because EA tried to encourage the same Pay 2 Win environment in Battlefront 2. The backlash and outrage killed that game, and further damaged EA's finances and PR. This makes it all the more confusing as to why Hi-Rez would copy this system after it very blatantly failed with Battlefront 2.
-Aside from being Pay 2 Win it's also even worse and more boring than the old essence currency as you have to continuously get duplicates of cards to level them up and with at least 34 champions each with at least 20 cards of different rarities for each of those champions leveling them would be extremely difficult and boring. Getting a deck maxed without paying would likely take hundreds of hours unless you invest real money to speed that process up which is clearly what the developers intended.
-This will make the game very hostile towards new players. Hi-Rez outright lied in the patch notes when they say it was "even more free to play!" by giving us every card in the game from the start. What they fail to mention is that all these cards are at level 1 if you're just starting. Returning players will have all the cards they previously unlocked instantly boosted to level 3 so from the highest of GMs to the lowest of unrankeds if you played before this update you have an inherent advantage over new players. Even if they outmatch you in skill, or you outmatch them; they have that advtantage to you, and that's just not fun nor fair to new players.
-Your builds are trash now! Cards Unbound is supposed to encourage people to be more creative and have more freedom with their builds. Only as previously mentioned that can be highly dependant on RNG and a lot of builds and champions are actually getting screwed over by this. There exist many cards in the game that fit in well to the 12 point system in that you'd only take level 1 in the card to recieve one attribute that either doesn't need upgrading or can't be upgraded to add on to your build take Pip's Sturdy card for insance "Your gun no longer knocks you back and deals 25% less damage" This card works for Pip well at level 1 because no matter what level it is, it's going to stop knockback which is a lot less disorienting when you're in a fight. The self damage reduction is also appreciated, but has no real need to be upgraded beyond 25%. There exist cards like this in the game for multiple champions that with cards unbound will be utterly useless and cards unbound encourages you to max out and conform to the meta. It gives cards clear statistical advantages over others that didn't exist with the 12 point system. This applies to competitive too where everything is set to level 3. If you're being forced to level 3 and you've previously relied on your deck to be 4-4-2-1-1 its likely been screwed over as well. It's not as balanced as they think it is.
-Legendaries both new and old can become HELLA overpowered or HELLA underpowered with cards unbound. At level 5 Lex melts tanks, Jenos and Kinessa become the best flanks in the game, and Tyra's fire will kill you if you blink. Who on earth thought it was a good idea to make Legendary cards upgradable? This makes the game even more hostile for new players, and makes quick play nearly pointless to play as the chaos of level 5 legendaries makes playing it not only tedious but pointless as it can't accurately prepare you for competitive play. The new legendaries are cool in my personal opinion, but they should all be streamlined. Being able to level them up can make them way too over or under powered.
-Old players are being milked for their money. If you're planning on playing after cards unbound you might appreciate that they boosted all your currently owned cards to level 3. They aren't doing this out of the kindness of their hearts, but rather their interest in your money. After level 3 is becomes increasingly harder to level up to 4 and then 5. They're putting you in this spot so that you'll invest in buying more radiant chests and support, flank, damage, or frontline keys for your favorite heroes. The ordinary progression system makes earning the new "Champion chests" which gaurentee you unlocks for a certain champion; lets say your main, or one of your mains IMPOSSIBLE for returning players. Leveling up a hero after level 10 can take a frustratingly long time and it just gets higher and higher meaning after a certain point you'll stop naturally earning these chests and be forced to pray to the RNG gods in the radiant chests which you'll have to earn by playing a long♥♥♥♥♥time to level or a long♥♥♥♥♥time to grind enough gold for. That is... unless you buy the chests with real money and the keys that make it sliiiightly easier to gaurentee a drop for a specific champion along with it. Yes I do mean slightly. The keys only refer to a specific class. So if you want a card for seris and you buy a support key it could be a support you don't even play and have no intention to play, thus the chest and key and your money are wasted.
-Cards Unbound will undoubtly bring hundreds if not thousands of balance and bug concerns. The game is already buggy enough and unbalanced in its current state, why Hi-Rez would shoot itself in the foot by introducing a rework that will amplify these problems even more is a mystery to all. Keep in mind some of the bugs in the game now have existed since the game first went public like Pip's healing potion bug, when OB64 comes that's still going to be there, along with a plethora of new bugs and balance issues related to the new legendary cards. Hi-Rez has been and will continue to be inconsistent here.
-Cards Unbound is being worked on right now while I still can't get my dailies. The new daily quest system has been buggy af since it launched last patch and it's now been removed to be "fixed" only now, but in the meantime none of us are earning any crystals and rewards that we could maybe use on an upcoming big rework. That's definitely just a coincidence, and they're not only fixing it now as an excuse to bait us out of even more money when Cards Unbound goes live.

I, like many people (I assume), first heard about this game from the guys at Inside Gaming. It looked interesting, I must admit, and when the price temporarily dropped down to $1.25, I knew I had to have it in my game library.
This has got to be the one of the worst games I have ever played. To start with, for an FPS, the gunplay is surprisingly terrible. The guns have no real presence  and all of the sounds for them, from firing to reloading, are laughably stock. Each gun takes what feels like a year to reload (I'm sure you can see where that would get frustrating.) The graphics are extremely dated, even for a game that came out in 2008. It is also a Russian-made game. While this is not a bad thing, it does mean that it has had to be redubbed. The voice-overs are just unbearably atrocious. Everybody in it sounds uninterested in the current situation and when they should be yelling, they tend to do little more than talk in a high whisper. They are so bad that they make the acting in Just Cause 2 look like GTA V. The horrible voiceovers are not helped by the translated text, which so far has not had any spelling mistakes, but it is very convoluted to the point that you may need to reread certain sentences more than once.
The AI is something to be studied and talked about for many, many years in the future. Oftentimes I have seen enemy soldiers run into walls and not turn around. If they are not running into walls, they are throwing grenades at the ceiling and blowing themselves up. If they are not trying to commit suicide, they are making a beeline for you so they can continuously whack you in the face. To make combat a little more interesting (or maybe to distract you from the awfulness of literally every single gun), the developers have put a few "creative" features into the game. If you are taking too many bullets from all sides, you can put up your "UberShield", which will absorb incoming rounds and deflect them back at your enemies. It also, unfortunately, does not let you shoot back at them, as it collects your rounds and fires them when the shield runs out. In addition to this, there are the "UberSniper" and "Berzerker" modes, which make you immune to damage after 3 headshots and 3 knife kills, respectively. While all of these features may sound very interesting, they are not implemented into the game very well at all, and half of the time they just feel like a retread of other features from previous first person shooters.
The last thing I am going to talk about in this short essay of a review is the cutscenes. You remember cutscenes, don't you? The kind of ones that are either pre-rendered or made with the ingame engine? Well, if you don't like either of those, don't worry, Ubersoldier II has got you covered! Introducing the new and absolutely revolutionary comic-book cutscene! Watch as only 4 or 5 pictures are played continuously over bland dialogue. This has never been done in a game before, and I am sure that it is going to catch on with the AAA developers all over the world. (In all seriousness, the 4 or 5 pictures that they use in their cutscenes look hand-drawn, which at least took somebody some effort to make. Occasionally, they are drawn quite well, but not too often.)
It may sound like I am taking the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game. It might not deserve it, but oh boy is it such an easy target. It is definitely one of the worst games I can think of that came out in the last decade, something on par with Ride to Hell: Retribution. There are a couple of major differences between these games, though. Ubersoldier II has got plenty of soul, and a hell of a lot of heart, while Ride to Hell is as cruel and heartless as the Devil himself. When I play Ubersoldier, I at least get the sense that there was a team of people actually TRYING to make a good game. You know what, I think they actually might have succeeded.
In short: Is this a fun game?
Hell yes!

Overall the game is pretty average, but it's not bad. I can recommend it only as a bargain-bin buy. The graphics are decent, the game is linear, and parts can be frustrating. It'll appeal to fans of old school FPS. I thought it was better than Return to Castle Wolfenstein (2001), but not better than other WWII games like Medal of Honor: Allied Assault, Call of Duty (2003), Hidden & Dangerous, or Deadly Dozen. I finished it in just over 6 hours.

An enjoyable experience overall even if it's lacking in certain areas. You're OP1414, also known as Emeth, a small, childlike, robot who has been tasked with finding planet Earth by using a space telescope called 'OPUS.' This is what you'll find yourself doing for the most part of the game, searching amongst hundreds of stars for the location of humanity's first abode. While certainly a repetitive experience it can also be quite cathartic at times, as you do some stargazing to a very relaxing soundtrack, encountering alien planets, galaxies, and even supernovas.
Unfortunately, I found the concept was not developed to its full potential. What do I mean by that? After beating the game you unlock a new mission that has you tracking down the creators of Emeth's power armor through OPUS. I really enjoyed this short side-quest which had you play detective while teaching you a thing or two about light and space. I felt the game could've used more of these side-quests and that the characters should've been more reactive to Emeth's discoveries.
That brings us to my second point. Assisting Emeth in his search for Earth is a holographic AI named Lisa, modeled after the Doctor who created Emeth. Emeth is reluctant to accept the help of this "fake Doctor" at first but eventually they reach some sort of understanding, though their interaction is still quite limited. However, this prompts Emeth to ask a simple yet poignant question, where is the Doctor? I was really looking forward to solving this mystery, even if I felt the answer was fairly obvious. And yet, despite the fact that you find clues here and there hinting at what could have happened, you never get the full picture. At the very least I wasn't able to put the pieces of the puzzle together, leaving me clueless as to what happened to Emeth's beloved Doctor.
As a result, because AI Lisa and Emeth have very little interaction, and because the mystery of what happened to the Doctor is not resolved, I found that we didn't have enough (time and material) to bond with these characters. Furthermore, and I don't think I'm spoiling anything that the title of the game hasn't already spoiled, the game comes to an abrupt ending after you finish your mission, and it's an unsatisfying one at that. It's a shame because the ending could've been so much better if it had added a short scene with AI Lisa, rounding up the Doctor's fate at the same time.
I was also disappointed that something as simple as zooming out or having a space chart at hand wasn't available, what makes locating your objectives more time-consuming than necessary (there's a hint system though).
In the end, I'm afraid
didn't quite hit me emotionally as it did other players. While a beautiful game to play for a short while (it took me about 3 hours to complete), its narrative is a bit on the weak side, making the day I found Earth not as engaging as it could've been.
Recommended at a discount.

Alright, Valve finally added a way to configure and use the controller without big picture mode, so I guess it's time to add a review. I've been using it for a while now (Around two or three months), and I have to say this is without a doubt the best controller I have ever used. I won't go into the technical aspects, because quite frankly I'm not very knowledge about them, and I'm sure other people will be able to explain things better than I will. Instead, I'll list off all the games I have used it with, and share my experiences with each.
This was one of the first games I tried with the Steam Controller,  Previously, I had been playing Dark Souls exclusively with a 360 pad, since mouse control is really not much of an option. The Steam Controller performed marginally better than the 360 pad for a few reasons. I was just getting used to the touch pads, but they felt natural, and a bit smoother than the 360 joystics. The grips were the major difference here though, since I mapped both of them to sprint for easy access. This made rolling and sprinting so much easier than the 360 pad (Which wasn't even that bad), and it really made me appreciate the placement.
One of the few games I played that felt worse than using a mouse. It was way better than the 360 pad, but I've played so much of the game using a mouse that the controller felt very wrong, and I felt like I was imparing myself by using it. This is mostly due to how fast-paced the game is, and how much percision is needed for aiming. On top of that, there isn't a really good place to map the fire button since not every weapon is automatic, and using a mouse to click a bunch of times is better than using a controller. I also own a copy of the Vita version, which has similar problems with the controls, and feel the same way about them.
Another game that didn't work as well as I would have hoped. The problem wasn't really in the touchpads like I was expecting, but rather, it was in the sheer amount of controls an RTS needs. Maybe if I come across a better configuration in the future, or the devs add (Which is very unlikely) native steam support it would work well. For now, it's for lack of a better word; unplayable.
This is the game that made me start loving the controller. I had previously played SS2 a few times, with the mouse, but after playing through the entire game start to finish with the Steam Controller, I doubt I'd use the mouse again any time soon. System Shock 2 is a game that was previously impossible to play using any controller, but the Steam Controller has enough versitallity to be able to play it without compromise. The developer made configuration is pretty much the only one you need to use, and it works damn well. With the trackpad, I was still able to accurately and consistantly click on the tiny UI buttons (Which are hard enough as is with a mouse). The left hand pad was also used very well, and it made me start really liking the touch menu feature. Being able to visualize and easily click on the 1-9 keys was so much more useful than I had ever imagined, and something I pretty much never did on the keyboard since I never remembered which number was assigned to which gun. I highly reccomend anyone with a Steam Controller to go out and play this game. Hell, it should be bundled with the controller itself.
This was my first time using a non-steam game with the Steam Controller, and it wasn't nearly as bad as I was expecting it to be. Although there was no existing community configurations for me to use with the game, I just grabbed the config from System Shock 2 and modified it for the game (Which is uploaded and plublicly availible for the non-steam version). Aside from car controls being a bit difficult to map since this game wasn't a very good PC port, it unearthed another, small flaw with the controller. If the game is locked to 30fps, so will the touch menu. This isn't too bad, but using the touch menu felt a little bit laggier than it should have been. Other than that, the controller performed well with the game.
This one was a bit difficult to setup. I basically had to map the controls in dolphin to an Xbox 360 controller, and then map the steam controller to a 360 pad. I didn't play much (I've already beaten it), but it seemed to work well with the trilogy version. The regular gamecube version felt a bit off though, mostly from the aiming. I hope that Dolphin evenutally puts in native Steam Controller support, but for now, if you're looking to play mostly emulators, I'd pass.
The first and only game I played with native support, it went just as well as you would imagine. Not much to say about this game that hasn't been said in the above paragraphs.
This is the game that finally made me write a review. Although it was a bit of a hassle getting it to launch with the steam overlaty (Hint: run Steam as an administraitor), I was able to play it way better than I would have ever played it with a mouse. For reference, I'm pretty terrible at tactical/slow FPS games, and I much prefer games like Unreal Tournament. On top of that, S.T.A.L.K.E.R is not the easiest game, and it requires a lot of precision to do well. Like Saints Row 2, there weren't any community configurations for the non-steam version (I wish they combined the steam and non-steam versions), so I just imported the System Shock 2 config and went from there. It's another game that is actually impossible to play on a traditional controller, but I managed to map every single key in single player to the controller. Aiming felt very natural, and the touch menu made switching between weapons and other equipment very easy. As for the shooting itself, I was able to consistently place headshots once I got enough experience with the game, and I felt like I was doing better than I ever would with a mouse. Needless to say, I feel like I became better at FPS games because of it. Played start to finish with the Steam Controller, and had no prior experience with the game or series.
As you can probably tell, I quite liked the games that it worked well with. I tried out gyro for a bit because of everyone's reccomendations, but I really didn't like it much, and went back to trackball look soon after. Almost every issue i have with the controller I have is software related, and as time progresses it will get better and better (It already has since launch). I will point out though, that none of the above games are d-pad heavy, and I haven't actually tried any that were, so just bear that in mind.
TL;DR: It's good

SR2 is, hands down, the best game in the Saints Row franchise.
does it still have that GTA-but-tongue-in-cheek-knockoff quality that's been a hallmark of the series? of course. but it tempers the ridiculous nature of the series just enough to emphasize how ridiculous a lot of this stuff really is. as much of a fan as i am of whacking people with weaponized sex toys à la SR3, where is there to go when you've already got the satire/shock factor scale turned up to 11 right from the get go? SR2 makes you work for it a little more, and the payoff is, i would argue, far richer for it.
why is it, then, that i have magnitudes more play time in SR3 than SR2? because the PC port of this game is disapponting at best, absolutely atrocious at worst. unlike a lot of other reviewers, i wouldn't call it unplayable, exactly, but the concentration required in order to play it saps most--if not all--of the fun out of it. Saints Row is a series you pop in when you want to kinda mindlessly destroy a city and build up a criminal empire the likes of which has never been seen. hard to do that when you can't even take a corner in any car at any speed above "crawling."
i'll always recommend this game for people looking to get into the SR franchise, and thus can't give it a thumbs down. i'm a very strong believer in playing the series sequentially. but honestly? do yourself a favor: shell out $10-20 for a disc, get out your PS3 or Xbox 360, and play it on there. all the SR2 hilarity, none of the "why is it so hard to even move around" frustration.

Don't be fooled by my play time. I've at least beat DR3 5 times on Xbox One. It's a good game and a great port. Runs very smoothly with no hitching/stuttering, just make sure you've got a powerful enough rig. Make sure to use the 60 fps cap fix.
The actual game is a blast to play, however, I feel it has lost a lot of its charm compared to the original 2 Dead Rising's. The "massive" open world that was advertised is not so huge as one might think. The map is actually quite small. There is also tons of annoying roadblocks that get in your way, which I assume are placed to make the city feel bigger than it is. The open world is bland with almost no color, but that can be overlooked because of how fun it is.
The controls in this game are far superior than the previous titles. Crazy amount of zombies on screen. The combo weapons/vehicles you can build are ridiculously fun. Survivor AI is a absolute Godsend for anyone who has played the first two. Basically, everything has been upgraded. The only thing that hasn't been upgraded is the difficulty and psychopaths/bosses. This game is way too easy on the regular story mode. I miss the challenge of the older games. I recommed that you play this game on nightmare mode if you're a Dead Rising veteran, but it's still too easy imo. Bosses and psychopaths are not as memorable or difficult compared to the original Dead Rising (best one in the franchise). That was the most disappointing aspect of this game. Also, the story is ridicuously short if you don't do any of the side missons.
Even with the negatives, this game is still really fun to play. I recommend this to any zombie fan or Dead Rising veteran.

This is a game about going to Japan. As someone who visited Japan in the winter of 2010, I can say without a doubt that the game simulates the experience to a tee. In fact, one of my first experiences in Japan, and one of the earliest scenes in the game, was encountering the infamous “squirty” toilet, or a bidet as the locals call it. The first thing I do when I visit any hotel room is to examine the bathroom. I saw the toilet and was immediately awestruck by the array of buttons on a panel. I remember pressing a button with a water spout symbol, wondering what, if anything, would happen. And something happened indeed. From the middle of the toilet emerged a rod that sprayed water in an upward fashion: in the direction of my face. The experience was akin to drinking from a water fountain but much, much better, a truly wonderful sensation. Think of the hottest summer day in recent memory and remember uncapping that icy bottle of Poland Spring and pouring it all over yourself, no inhibition, nothing holding you back from such momentary release from the unrelenting heat. It was that good. I bring up this little anecdote because the game does that to you. It pulled from the deepest recesses of my memory the wonderful times I had in Japan. But it does something better. It brings you to Japan in the company of two girls  who host you in their own home. Compared to most games, the story is deep and the characters interesting.  However it's not a game, so I found myself instead comparing it to novels and films.  Compared to them it it is pretty shallow.  It held my attention mostly because I wanted to find out how it ended, and I found the conclusion unsatisfactory.

NVIDIA System? Buy.
