I purchased two copies of this game on release day, September 4, 2014, for myself and a friend. We stumbled through a collective 5 hours of trying to get it to run, over the course of a year since then, on and off. Our system specs are not at fault; twin HD6950 2gb's overclocked should be able to run this game at the bare minimum graphical settings at 800x600 resolution. An i5-2500k overclocked to 4.3ghz is not bottlenecking performance. My 250gb 840 EVO SSD isn't causing load issues.
The game was never optimized for PC, especially AMD. It wasn't at release, and not a single performance patch has been released since for AMD users.
The recent reviews page for this game is littered with similar complaints of poor PC optimization. The fact that almost a year has gone by and this game is still unplayable just isn't acceptable. I'm actually surprised Steam even offers it for sale any more.
All I want is my money back, in my Steam Wallet, so I can spend it on something else in the Steam Store for my best friend and I to enjoy, together.

While there are a few issues that plague the performance of ths game, a few registry fixes solved the majority of performance problems (be sure to turn on Triple Buffering in the options, and make sure if you're using an NVIDIA laptop card that your card is actually running the program, not your integrated graphics).
Deus Ex HR had a pretty big act to follow - the original game and Invisible War are often considered some of the best games of all time, up there with Half Life and System Shock 2, and there was certainly a lot of community pressure and anticipation to have this game live up to the exceptional standards its predecessors held.
Fortunatly, Human Revolution delievers the goods, and might even be the masterwork of the series.
By staying true to the classic game elements that made the original game great (choice of playstyle, multiple routes, deep storylines), DX:HR simply modernizes these tried and true mechanics to appeal to new and old audiences, while bringing deeper social commentary to the table. In the same vein as Blade Runner and GATTACA, modification of human ability, DNA mutation and cybernetics are all brought to a player's eye, raising questions about morality and survival in an honestly gripping and incredible experience that every gamer deserves to play.
This game surprised me - I thought it would be a lackluster spitirtual successor that would simply be a nostalgic cash-in. But like Just Cause 2 and Sleeping Dogs, Square Enix has once again proven itself to be the master of beautiful worlds that are not only engaging to explore, but fun to interact with. DX:HR warrents many playthroughs, if only to explore the dozens of carefully planned out ways to engage opponents, and discover new pieces of lore that satisfy and surprise whenever read.
The shortcomings of this game are very few, the obvious being the poor optimization that can plague performance without manual correction. If anyone is having issues with performance, I suggest this solution as a first attempt to allieviate any problems.
In short, one of the best games of this generation, and one of the best games of all time.

This is a anime MMORPG.
You are a anime teen that gets a eidalon to help you save the world, but be carefull for if you fall into darkness then your mind will slip and you will become a mindless monster.
The characters looks too much alike since there is not a rich character design pool.
There is a 3 character limit for a server, but it can be expected. There is a delete character limit per day.
You can only be a human male or female and there are no beards or wrinkles. You only have 1 starting area.
There is a auto-walk-to-quest thing in this game so you should not be able to get lost. Daily quests, mini quests, dungeons with solo exist and forced party dungeons that you will need others to complete.
You can pick between 4 eidalons in the start of the game. Eidalons are mosters that will help you in fights and they have alot of speech bubbles that will ask you about new friends and stuff going on. You can feed your eidalon with experiance and things that can give your eidalon better stats. Eidalons can be bought and be found in the quests. The eidalons can be sent out on quests that lasts 10 min and that will give you a item, but it will cost them some energy. You can give the eidalons more enegy back by asking them questions and getting to know them.
The people does not seem to be online or sosial so if you are not entering the game with friends then it is going to be a kind of lonly experience. The party and group finding isen't userfriendly for people that has not joined the game with friends. NPCs look alike, so you will see the same npc skin with different names.
Your character can have 3 different classes when you get to a high level. The extra classes can give you some extra skills that can help you.
This is my honest opinions of the classes untill level 15:
Bard is a support hero that is boring as all hell. With a Green and Red music meter.
Dualist is a single target dps class that is fancy to use and kind of fun.
Ranger is a ranged dps class. As this class a player actually talked to me and someone added her to the guild for no reason.
Ravager is a melee dps/tank class that has a Rage-Meter and that is fun in a fighting-for-you-life kind of way. I didn't noticed that I was level 14 at first cause it felt so much more fun then almost all of the other previous classes.
Reaper is a ranged dps/summoner class that can summon 3 demons out of 5 at a time to help kill the enemys. Not that much fun and the rotation is too slow so that you are autoattacking alot of the time.
Shonobi is a ranged dps class that can summon a shadow person that seems to be a neko or something. You can summon 2 different once by attacking, but only 1 of them comes out and leaves after a short while. You do look fancy using this class and you kill creatures effectivly but it was not my ally.
Ronin is a melee dps class that has a soul-meter. You can charge up it to use storm mode to use storm abilitys but you need to fight to recharge the soul-meter. The attack from it was kind of cool and it fits to take down enemy groupes infront of you.
Gunslinger is a ranged dps class with some traps. You have 4 spesial shots that seems to be randomized. It takes about 7 seconds to reload the spesial bullets. This is a class that is hard to fight single targets with cause some of the skills have alot of aggro.
Brawler is a melee dps class. This is a fast, intens and fun fighter. It has a small heal and is intense to use.
Grenadier is a ranged dps aoe class. This is a slow, aoe, damage dealer that can summon a machinegun to help, even has a frost grenade.
Wizard is a ranged dps class. This is a complicated one to use since it has a spell sync that you need to get some damage out of the spells with a spamable one, a healing one and a upgrader to 1 of your 4 elements.
Guardian is a melee tank class. You have a shield that can take the hits and later a skill that can reflect and protect you. Shield bash for the stun.
Holy Sword is a melee dmg/aoe/semi-tank class. You have a claymore and the light to kill enemys in an aoe. You have a Divine-Energy-Meter that automaticly fill that will make your skills do more damage for 1 attack, then recharge. Has skills that close gaps.
Sorcerer is a ranged dps support class. You have a book and deal damage with spells, even some support skills. You have a Dark-Magic-Meter that is filled by some of your spells and it can have up to 3 spells. The spells can be casted with a higher effect and it seems random what you got.
This character lasted until level 32 before I could not stand it anymore.
The grenader is a ranged dps that was kind of op. I just mean it cause I defeated people 11 levels over me by using the stun shot and the frost grenade + have the turret up right before the dual starts.
This is not the best or worst MMORPG out there. It is kind of mediocer in my opinion. So if you like having alot of classes to pick from and being only humans with eidalons that can help you fight and you have friends playing with you then this might be a game for you.
Have fun, enjoy and cuddle your eidalon :)

DOOM was one of my favorite video games of 2016. More so than Doom 3, this game feels like a modern version of the classic Doom. It is insanely fast paced and offers more depth in gameplay than what appears on the surface. Each of many weapons allows for different strategies in battle and none of them feel useless (even the pistol which has the advantage of having infinite ammo). The enemies are menacing, aggressive and challenging, especially when in hordes. Just like the weapons, each demon requires different strategies and tactics of approach. Weapon modifications and abilities are simple additions that only compound the gameplay's depth. The campaign is where you will experience the best DOOM has to offer. The story is rather lackluster, but honestly, I'm glad there is a story at all. Multiplayer is really hit or miss. Some aspects of it are unique and fun while others are just average. Snap Map is great content creation tool and adds a lot of longevity to the game. It is like a never-ending supply of DLC from the community.
Overall, DOOM is great FPS for those that love fast-paced, action-packed, bloody and deep gameplay. Now that the DLC is free, multiplayer might become more appealing as well.

Doom (4) is a game about killing demons to genosidale levels, as you are human rage incarnate armed with futuristic lead throwers and electron flying blades (as in the models are gibbed when hit by the projectiles). It also has multiplayer and a level editor to help expand the lifetime of the game.
Objectively, the game runs well on my computer, getting well above 100 FPS on a 1050p screen with middle settings (I think). I perfer max resolution and FPS over graphic details. As for online, it works reasonably well on a 5 Mb down and 2 Mb up connection with 2 other heavy internet users, but I did see the other players teliport. I recommend being careful if you have a poor connection. The only problems I had was with the editor, named Snapmap. I did run into graphical glitches and a few crashes, but a simple restart fixed some of the problems. I think it needs an update next.
As for the subjective part, I find it a fun game. Like many good games, you can be quick if you pratice and it's not a fustrating endevor ether. Singleplayer has a lot of content, like a good range of weapons and equipment with upgrades that add more to the guns, and not simple upgrades. There are runes, which are passives, that can also be upgraded. All are done by doing certain things. There is a story, but like the older games, it not focused on a lot. Yet it does have some depth too.
For multiplayer, I am enjoying it more after the 6.66 update. Before I found the lack of control over the unlocks annoying. I would have to grind to get the parts I want, as they were randomly unlocked. Now, you can choose what parts you want. They also redid the rune mechanic to they operate like the single player runes, but tuned for multiplayer. there are runes with tracking however. They are not a huge problem though.
For the Snapmap, I find this rather weak. While people have done great things, the thing was built with the consoles' limitations in mind. So we can't get Nuts' level of enemies and maps have limited sizes. They did expand the limits, but it's  nowhere close the limits of the PC. It also means the game lacks the same modding support that the old games have. Now, I do see why they did not allow it. Many triple A games use more advanced methods that modders can't have, but I argue that they should. If the modders are given the ability, those who have the tech see the increased demand and can make deals for the modders, making the price cheaper for the devs in return. It may take awhile, but all good things come to those who wait. (sorry for the slight tangant).
I recommed this game, worst case is to wait for a sale.
EDIT: The game is huge, so it will take a while if you have a slow connection. Days even.

I love this device, even if there are a few minor annoyances or adjustments to make.
I feel like the soft press of the trigger buttons takes a bit too much force to comfortably hold down with ease, or press quickly without going to the second stage. Similarly, it can be tricky to full press while holding down other buttom combinations, however, these are highly configurable with deadzone settings and the like. Using them gets better as you adjust.
Extremely useful. I like to put things like sprint or crouch toggle here. Can be easy to accidentally press when doing other things.
The right trackpad, or rather, lack of a right analog stick makes twin-stick shooters a bit more difficult with this! You've been warned.
They work quite well, although as mentioned in the cons, can be a bit unresponsive to slow small initial movements. There are ways to work around this, but I do wish I could make it more sensitive at the center, and a bit less sensitie at the edge. Trackball emulation is great. Really nails the 'flick' feel while retaining the regular movement while held down.
Great, but I feel the indentation could be slightly deeper. I suppose that's the tradeoff for letting it function as a trackpad among other things as well. I often don't use it as a D-Pad, but for a secondary analog stick movement option, or something of the like. If I do use it as a D-pad, or button pad, the ability to configure size and position of buttons can make it as easy or harder as desired to get a button press in.
Not super long, so it pulls easy and well, but also not very wide. However, I still find it is very easy to make small movements with it as needed. It could perhaps have a wider cap.
Like the trackpad, it may be initially unresponsive, made a bit worse by the initialization coming in after the delay in initialization of the trackpad. (Keep in mind this only applies to when you try to do very very fine movements. Otherwise, they work very well, keeping you aware of your positioning and giving you a subtle or strong feedback as needed.
A bit small, a bit out of the way, not quite ideal. They are very solid feeling, though, and you can adjust to their position and usage.
There is an absolutely insane amount of button presses you can achieve with a modifier or two present. There is an insane amount of options for what any button or pad or stick will do, even, allowing you to play however you want.
It is fairly easy to customize your controller, or shop around for the configurations of others. Or, you can shop around for a good starting point of another's configuraton, then fine-tune it yourself. Still, if you crack open the menus and take a good hard look at all the options available, you can almost always make something better than the community options that will work perfectly for you.
I've achieved as much in Torchlight 2, where the top configuration mainly was only good for melee characters, and I felt lacking in some buttons or awkward to use some others.
Regardless, the ability to have a different configuration for every game, as well as a desktop specific configuration, and have a library of community configurations is actually a great innovation and convenience feature. Beats the hell out of configuring in x360ce. Bonus points: You can have multiple configurations for the same game.

Navigating the menus with the controller is a bit awkward, but probably ideal, as you won't get the infographic details you will with the controller, for example with the adjustment of scrolling angle on the trackpads to match the angle of movements of your thumbs. (Awesome feature, btw.) You can also navigate with your mouse, and then fine-tune specific details with the controller.
There ARE a lot of menus to go through if you really want to fine tune everything, but for most things you want to have to define 60 buttons and 40 advanced features. Also, as you learn your average needs (say for sensitivity) it gets pretty easy to breeze through it all.
Having to enter BPM to configure this controller really isn't all that bad. You spend perhaps 5 minutes tops doing an exhaustive configuration, and you're done. The problem comes when fine-tuning while ingame. Alt tab, re-open BPM...wait...etc.

The steam controller takes some getting used to, but it makes total sense as to why it was designed this way. I kept trying to hold it the way I would hold a 360 controller, which didn't make sense, as the controller is designed to be held it's own way to get you acquainted with the dual touch pads. It was much more precise when I held it correctly.
The controller has one joystick with two touch pads, a, b, x, and y buttons, gyro control, click triggers (like gamecube controller), two grip buttons, and left and right bumpers/shoulder buttons. The touch pads act as the right stick, mouse, keyboard buttons and way too much more... No, that's not a bad thing. The other controls are standard/what you would see on most controllers for consoles and such, but here's the fun part; every single control is customizable. I honestly can't say that enough.
As for game compatibility, I have yet to see a game this doesn't work on....
If you want to get this for streaming games to your TV, this is definitely what you need. It's good for playing games on pc, yes. But it won't completely replace your mouse and keyboard.

Go! Go! Nippon! is a visual novel about a guy from an ambiguous country that takes a sightseeing tour around Japan (mostly Tokyo) with the help of two Japanese girls. This game is a bit of an oddity. There's actually very little gameplay here; you make roughly five choices throughout the whole experience.
Most of this novel consists of an animated, factual tour guide of Japanese hot spots, complete with history lessons. I found it pretty interesting, if a little dry at times. It was pretty neat to see Shibuya, which I remember from two other games I've played (The World Ends With You and SMT: Devil Survivor). This game tries really hard to capture the feel of everyday events in Tokyo, and it was cool to see all of these things described in great detail and in a way that points out things that foreigners would find unique.
You might also expect some romance from this description, and if so, you'd be correct. The places you visit determine which girl accompanies you, and you end up with the one that accompanied you the most. I only played through once, and I saw a little over half the content. The romance plot is not that interesting and ends before it really blooms. I kind of wish it was left out, especially the more, well, risque images. (Ecchi, I think. Not quite hentai.)
So basically, if you're looking for a fun game, this isn't one. This is a visual novel about being a tourist in Japan stapled to a romantic manga story. It only took me about 90 minutes to get through one playthrough, so it's a pretty quick experience. All in all, if you can enjoy a visual novel and you have some interest in Japan, I can recommend this. Not at $10, though... wait for a Steam sale. If my description didn't sound interesting to you, then this simply isn't for you and it won't be worth your time or money.

Cute, but little more than that, unfortunately. OPUS is an hour and a half of moving a cursor around a map and pressing space on the brightest spot in the region the game points you to. Doing so rewards you with some generic drawings of a handful of planet types and other cosmic structures, but there are seemingly none to find outside of those required for the story or side quests. Since the story also takes you to every interesting megastructure on the map, there's really very little to explore. In spite of this, one achievement requires scanning 1,000 planets, which is at least 10-20 times more than what's necessary to complete a full game, and 950 of them will just be "Similarity: Low"
The story is competent, but unambitious. It's obvious where you'll end up within 5 minutes, and the attempts to tug at your emotions along the way feel cheap and predictable.
It's better than the vast majority of mobile ports out there, but unfortunately that just means it's inoffensively trite rather than a wallet leech.

Anyway, the point of the game is that you’re a robot in space who’s goal is to locate earth.  You’ve got a computer that is finding things for you that “might be it?” but instead of just showing you it gives you obscure directions around a starscape to click on a specific star.  This is the game play, so if you’re into looking at pretty starscapes and listening to music you may be good to go.
Who should play:  anyone who loved mining planets in Mass Effect 2
Who should not play:   (on steam, anyway) anyone who owns a smart phone, who should check it out there instead.

Opus The Day We Found Earth is an excellent casual, story rich, atmospheric (in its own way !) point and click type adventure game. Which should take at a maximum of one hour to complete in the story mode. However there is another mode. Here in this review I shall try not to spoil the fun for new players. So beware its a heart renching story of belonging and despair. So read on at your own risk.
You start off as a robot tasked by his master with one goal ,to find Earth from a sea of stars, accross the galaxy, with your telescope. Your name is Emeth, your masters name is Lisa. You go through this emotional turmoil of betrayal as you only see Lisa at the beginning of the mission and than not so much. You do every thing to find her, but you keep missing her.Your only chance to be reacquinted is to find Earth save mankind and complete the mission. You have to find Earth because the human gene pool is dwindling and it must locate that familiar old planet to save itself. You are helped in this task by a hologram of Lisa, and their interaction is quiet entertaining. Will you ever find Earth, will you ever find the real Lisa, only time will tell.
The game play is smooth as most of the time youre given coordinates, to find new planets with a telescope. Which is neat and innovative. Every time you locate a coordiante you get rewarded as the story moves forward. The music is melodious enough to keep you going. Graphics are cartoony but smooth finish. There are many pros to this game and relatively no cons but to name a few:-
PROS
+Good and engaging storyline
+Rethymic music
+Low oprice
+Nice smooth finish  rendered graphics

CONS
-Linear storyline (but not rigid)
-No strategy
All in all its a 7/10 game for over all presentation and specially because it doesnt have any known bugs, definitely worth the money.

Some of the newer Fallout games can be described, much like newer Elder Scrolls games, with that old line of "wide as an ocean, shallow as a puddle." While Fallout 1 could be described about as wide and deep as a lake, Fallout 2 can be more accurately be portrayed as wide as the Great Lakes and about as deep as the Marianas trench. There is a nice amount of stuff to do in this game, maybe not as much exploring to do as some of the newer "rpgs" of the same series, but the main advantage this game has over those is that there are soooooo many different ways to handle all the situations in the game, and unlike Fallout 1 where many skill were little more than useless, Fallout 2 makes pretty much any character build viable. Dialogue options are completely different for characters with varying degreees of intelligence, playing a female character opens many doors, you can difuse many, many situations with a golden tongue and shoot your way out of anything that you actually have the skill for, you can sneak or be loud, you can walk up to a guy and shoot him or set up an elaborate system of events in order to make stuff look like an accident- the list goes on. There is so much to do in just over a gigabyte of space that this game takes up. And while the graphics and controls might not be for everyone, the writing stands up if not exceeds the quality of modern writing in video games. This game is a MUST for any fan of more vintage video games, and the same goes to any fan of in-depth RPGs. Absolutely amazing game and up there as one of the best games of all time.

I just finished it for the first time after 6 hours of gameplay. Maybe I'm just a bad player but I'd rather take that as proof, that this game is a good challenge for everybody. Now that i finished it will i stop playing? Hell no! After finishing the game on normal mode you unlock new difficulties which present an even greater challenge that I'm delighted to accept. Why?
Pros:
Easy to grasp but really fun fighting mechanics that still present you with enough variety
Different classes with fairly different playstyles
Randomize Item drops and Rooms will make every run feel slightly different
Is the game perfect? I don't think so.
Cons:
Sometimes you just feel cheated when you have really bad luck (Lucking at you curse rooms!)
Some classes can feel really weak if you don't get any drops that fit them (for example playing battlemage and getting nothing to improve magic)
If you are really lucky the run can end up being actually too easy (But don't worry...that's a really rare occasion)
All in all: Everyone who likes rogue-likes AND likes brawlers should definetly get this little gem. And if you are not sure about wether this speaks to you, I'd still recommend getting it, because you can probably still find some fun in the coop and 12 Euros are really not that much for so much fun.

I kept trying to hold it the way I would hold a 360 controller, which didn't make sense, as the controller is designed to be held it's own way to get you acquainted with the dual touch pads. It was much more precise when I held it correctly.
The controller has one joystick with two touch pads, a, b, x, and y buttons, gyro control, click triggers (like gamecube controller), two grip buttons, and left and right bumpers/shoulder buttons. The touch pads act as the right stick, mouse, keyboard buttons and way too much more... No, that's not a bad thing. The other controls are standard/what you would see on most controllers for consoles and such, but here's the fun part; every single control is customizable. I honestly can't say that enough.
As for game compatibility, I have yet to see a game this doesn't work on....
If you want to get this for streaming games to your TV, this is definitely what you need. It's good for playing games on pc, yes. But it won't completely replace your mouse and keyboard.

It's ok, though Big Picture mode is glitchy, often crashes, and the controller often doesn't work properly with it.  Not always easy to find (or manually create) decent controller layouts.
Oh, and even if the controller is plugged in, it still uses batteries. It was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥when I thought my controller was broken because it wouldn't function even when it was plugged into my PC.
The track pad is nice at times, but this won't replace your standard gaming controller.
I'd call it a $20 value.

One of the best games of the decade and probably the best reboot of all time.
Unlike Doom 3, this one is MUCH closer to the original games and a much better reboot than Doom 3 ever was. All the weapons and almost all of the enemies from Doom1&2 return (along with a few new ones!) and while for the most part they're implemented in ways you'd expect, Doom 2016 brings some fresh ideas to the table. All weapons now have 3 firing modes, enemies have new looks, attacks and patterns, you can find upgrades for your guns (most of which are fantastic, but a few are kinda meh) and even for Doomguy himself, secrets now reward you with unlockable extras & upgrade points and even the story is good! You now also have an excellent 3D map, which nullifies all chances of the player ever getting lost even without any upgrades.
One of the most fun new additions is how much more vertical Doom has become (with one level being a giant tower you have to climb and it's extremely fun). You can jump (!) and climb ledges (!!) and that's not only used for platforming, but it is also used extensively in combat! Surrounded by imps? A Pinky is charging at you? Why dodge when you can climb higher! It adds countless ways to aproach the combat of the game, especially when not two levels look the same. Every level throws something different at you and the game never loses steam. Unlike Doom 3, the boss battles are outstanding and very difficult.
But this is Doom, I hear you say! It's good that they nailed the gameplay and look of Doom with some new ideas, but what about the violence and gore that Doom is so well known for? And what about Hell? There was barely any Hell in Doom 3! And did you say that the story is GOOD in DOOM?! Slow down, friend, we'll get to those very soon... Sit back and relax, there's still much to be told.
Doom 2016 makes Mortal Kombat look kid-friendly. It's got blood and guts all over the place, you can pull off Fatalities on ALL the enemies (Yes, ALL of them!) and they're actually different depending on what part of the body you target! And yes, they're GORY as hell! The chainsaw might be my favorite weapon in the game, I cannot describe how satisfying it is to cut up demons while their insides are being sprayed all over the place and I hear the glorious sounds of flesh being sliced and bone being crushed. Hands down, the best chainsaw ever. Even when you merely shoot down enemies, the game still feels the need to spread Kill Bill levels of blood everywhere.
As for Hell, there are several long Hell levels! It doesn't just look or feel like Hell, it IS Hell! You're in the home of the demons, so now they're extra♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ which make the Hell levels among the hardest in the game. They're also a welcome change of appearance, and feature much more asymetrical level design than the UAC levels. The music also changes to creepy ambience and chants for when you're not fighting.
Speaking of music, Mick Gordon is GOD. His music enhances the game in so many ways and a lot of his songs feature melodies from older Doom games! Even when you just listen to it, you know it wouldn't fit any other game but Doom and that's what makes it so good.
Before I mentioned that even the story is good and yeah, it's surprisingly good. The game gives you just enough exposition to keep you going without ever placing the story over the gameplay. For more exposition, you can find hidden items which unlock logbook entries Metroid Prime-style, giving you info on the enemies and the backstory of the game.
Now that they made all the multiplayer DLC free it's better than ever! Multiplayer was pretty fun from what I played, although there weren't many players. Snapmap is also pretty fun, although I can't imagine it will replace Doom WADs.
All in all, it's an extension and an improvement over the classic Doom formula. A must-buy and a testament to how reboots SHOULD be done.

All the stars.

.Story.
OPUS is presented in an alternate reality where humans have advanced to the point that they live among the stars. You are Emeth, a robot created in order to use the telescope aboard OPUS, a space ship bearing a team of scientists tasked with finding Earth, the planet from which humanity originated.
The search is fueled by the approaching extinction of the human race: the gene pool is deteriorating due to years of genetic engineering and the only way to reverse the damages is to locate the oldest source of our genes on Earth.
There’s a real-life lesson to be learned here.
When you first start the game, you are presented with a cutscene detailing the mission, the two scientists who are tasked with it, and Emeth, the robot created by one of the scientists to keep on searching long after she is gone. Then, Emeth wakes up after having been powered off for who knows how long and it’s up to you to find out what happened to your human companions as well as to find Earth.
.Gameplay.
You control the telescope of the OPUS with WASD, moving the point of view around the screen in order to scan stars and other such celestial bodies with the space bar. Alternatively, you can use your mouse to click and drag around the stars and also to hit the scan bar, totally removing the need for your keyboard.  I personally preferred the keyboard approach.
When you first start, the ship is dark and underpowered. You pass time by searching for planets—your purpose—and bit by bit the ship will power up, giving you access to its innards.
The majority of your playthrough will be spent this way, though once you start discovering planets and unlocking different rooms aboard the OPUS, you’ll be able to explore the ship point-and-click style. Clicking around the ship will give you bits of information regarding the story as well as points of interest to search for with the telescope.
Finding main objectives is rewarded by a cut scene that tells the story of Emeth as he keeps his promise to his creator, Doctor Lisa. Rinse, wash, repeat, until the game ends.
.Atmosphere.
At the very beginning of the game, you’re advised that the game is better played with headphones. This is true. The music for OPUS is, haunting, wondrous, soothing, chill, atmospheric—it’s perfect for this sort of game. Period. Its presence instills a sense of wonder as you pan around the universe, stargazing, and collecting important scientific data.
The graphics are cutesy and brightly-coloured. The stars themselves are lovely to look at and the occasional swirls of colours against the inky backdrop of space are truly marvelous.
.Longevity.
This is the one place the game falls flat.
If you’re blazing through without reading anything, I estimate that OPUS could take you somewhere around 45 minutes to complete. My playthrough took roughly 2 hours, though maybe 20 minutes of that was spent enjoying the soundtrack and tooling aimlessly about the stars rather than trying to find Earth.
The side objectives add to your play time and you CAN spend time scanning each and every speck of light in the universe if you so choose to, but that doesn’t erase the fact that the core gameplay lasts anywhere from an hour to three—depending on how quickly you read and locate objectives. The two difficulties play into that:
- Story will give you hints after some time has passed.
-Normal won’t give you hints.
That’s the only difference between the two. The hints are simply arrows that point you in the correct direction, so they don’t exactly hold your hand.
.Pros and Cons.
.Bottom line.
OPUS: The Day We Found Earth is one of those experiences that you want other people to at least try out. I can’t recommend it enough. If you’re looking for a sweet story, buy this. If you’re looking for a peaceful game to enjoy during your down time, buy this. If you like space in the slightest, buy this. It does a fantastic job of instilling a sense of wonder that I associate with anything so awe-inspiring as
Wait until OPUS gets a bit of a price cut or buy it outright (preferably bundled with the soundtrack). Either way, you won’t regret the purchase.
An endearing and simple little game revolving around finding stars and planets.

Who knew looking for planets through a telescope could be this intense and emotional?
The core mechanic is simple, but it has enough variety to remain interesting, while the story lends the activity increasing urgency.  The characters likewise are simple but likeable enough.
While I found the experience engaging throughout, there does not seem to be quite enough meat to justify the full price.  Multiple playthroughs may provide additional rewards, but I don't think I will feel compelled enough to repeat it.
The devs set out to create something different, and they definitely achieved that goal.  If you are looking for an engaging, short story experience with a simple fun mechanic, OPUS is an easy recommend on sale.

10/10. Confidently. A true masterpiece, Yoko Taro has mastered of the artform of game design. In 100 years (maybe less) when there actually is a civil rights movement for robots, or possibly after robots take over, they will study this game in school like we study literature.
Let me back up that hyperbole for you. This is the most thematically cohesive game, or work of art that I've ever experienced. I can listen to the soundtrack and remember exactly where I was when I heard that song, what crazy, unexpected thing I was doing at the time. It's not so much the execution of each individual piece, but how they all fit together just so perfectly. The soundtrack is simply incredible, and you can visit a jukebox in the game and hear 4-7 different versions of all 41 (I think) tracks, including different instrumental and vocal versions as well as 8-bit versions of some songs.
I know I'm only 9 hours in when I'm writing this review, and I haven't even beaten the game once, let alone seen all FIVE of it's endings, but it just continues to surprise and delight me and raise and subvert my expectations at EVERY TURN. It's masterful. I just finished the most emotional experience in all of my 30+ years of gaming, a battle that left me weeping so hard I had to turn the game off, and it came out of nowhere. An escort mission, of all things. I just can't not recommend this game to everyone. This is what I want to spend my money on as a gamer, not loot box cash-grabs from EA. When I think about the power that gamers have to make change in the industry, and how committed we are to voting with our wallets, I'm proud to have spent my money on this.
On top of all of that the game is a pure joy to play. Movement around the world is fluid, and the combat is intuitive. The combat is a mix of hack and slash and bullet hell shooting, but it never feels repetitive because everything is constantly changing around you and weird stuff keeps happening out of nowhere. When I play this game I'm constantly saying "whoa, what is happening now!?" I was fighting a boss and making very nervous noises while I tried to avoid it's attacks and my girlfriend was wondering what the hell was wrong with me, but all she had to do was look at the screen to know.
I can't stop gushing on about this game, because the execution is just exemplary. When I think back on some single player games that I remember most fondly: Uncharted, FFVIII, Metal Gear Solid, Last of Us, they don't stick in my memory like NieR: Automata does. I know I've played it much more recently, but it's because of how harmoniously all of my senses are engaged by N:A that I remember my experience so vividly. I remember fighting an endless swarm of low level robots, feeling overwhelmed like I was about to lose, and then all of the robots started chanting something and forming one big robot, and the chanting transitioned perfectly into the boss music...stuff like that you don't forget easily.
Yoko Taro put so much thought and effort into this game, the least I can do is recommend it to everyone.

Robotpencil has what I'd call the "show, don't tell" approach to casual academia.
At a gorgeously low price for $4, you get about 45 minutes worth of lectures and demos - which really equals out to 15 minutes lecture, 30 minutes demo. The commentary is crisp (the dedicated demo is silent but otherwise fully commented without any awkward breaks), and while the streaming itself is prone to the usual downfalls of Steam's video player you'll still be able to squeeze 1080p out of it if you really want.
The art is all industry quality, which is plain nice to look at, and every bullet point and major area is followed up by a fairly in depth visual example. Shows you why it works and tells more than the commentary does.
For the commentary itself: I do want to emphasize that it is casual. You're not going to be getting the in depth, meticulous Scott Robertson-tier dissection including specular maps and all that jazz, it'll walk you through the 101 side of things with prac over theory.
Absolutely worth it, if you've already got enough of a grasp on the fundamentals to not be badgering everyone for their brushes. Otherwise I can see you being a little frustrated that Robotpencil doesn't "slow down" to show you every little meaningless thing.
At $4 it's a steal. Recommended to anyone who thinks they'll get anything out of this.

Deus Ex Human Revolution is a great game - a great game with an awful last act, one that brings down the rest of the game with it.  The DLC was "okay", but not essential by any stretch of the imagination.
The Director's Cut is a mess.
First of all, the performance. In the original, standalone game, there were initially some performance issues - periodic frame hiccups when the game streams area data if you were lucky, low framerate across the board if you weren't.  They fixed this, and the standalone game runs beautifully now.  The Directors Cut is not based on the most recent version, like you would expect.  The awful framerate and obnoxious frame hiccups are back, and it doesn't look like Squeenix has any intention of fixing this.
There are some registry settings you can change to make the performance "better", but if you've already got the original version (which is, sadly, no longer sold), there's virtually no reason to bother with the Director's Cut.  All the Director's Cut does is cram the game, the pre-order garbage, and the DLC together haphazardly, and gives you a few more options against the bosses.  The latter addition is very much welcome, as you can actually focus on a non-combat build if you'd like now, but the former makes the concept of a "build" even more laughably irrelevant.
The original game had this problem where, after a certain point, you're so stocked with abilities that there is nothing off limits to you.  A bad fighter isn't forced to hack - because you're a killing machine.  And a bad hacker isn't forced to fight - because you're a hax0r par excellence.  Plus you can jump around and throw dumpsters and go invisible.  It defeats the purpose of the game's open-ended design, where your ability choices will be helpful in some situations and a liability in others, so that you try and find a way to avoid those disadvantageous situations.
Since they duct taped the DLC on, this problem is even worse.  Yes, you still lose all your equipment and abilities at the start of the DLC, but at the end you get all your equipment back and a load of praxis equalling the amount you entered the DLC area with, meaning by the end of the game you're completely maxed out.  It makes the Singapore area a joke, and it makes the final area...  well, the final area is completely worthless any way you slice it.
Deus Ex Human Revolution is one of the better big budget AAA games of the last several years - it has its issues, but it's definitely worth playing.  The Director's Cut is not.  Avoid.

Latest update has caused a non-Steam game (FIFA 16) to no longer work correctly when using Steam controller. Before the update it was working OK.
Delivery was expensive (cost not apparent up front) and took a long time. I was surprised to see that this was because the product was dispatched from elsewhere in Europe. This is an atypical way of doing business, because usually the outlay of bringing a product into a country is considered to be a cost of doing business, and included in the product price.
Overall shipping costs added 20% to the advertised product price. I assumed that I was paying for fast delivery, and if I had known that shipping costs were so high because the controller was coming from another country I would not have purchased it at this time.
The controller itself functions ok, but has quite a plastic and amateur feel to it, almost as if it is still a protoype device.
The ergomonics of the controller could have been significantly improved with just a few adjustments. The most significant problem is the positioning of the YBAX buttons.
Using these buttons requires a different hand position to using the haptic pad, making transition between the two inputs awkward. For example you will see on an XBOX 360 controller that the D-pad is raised to avoid this problem of shifting your whole palm while transitioning between the left analogue stick and the D-pad.
Additionally, it is possible to touch the outside of the haptic pad when pressing either the Y or B buttons (even with little thumbs like mine), causing erroneous controller inputs.
One final frustration with these buttons is that they are very small and close together.
If these buttons were raised up (like an XBOX360 controller D-pad), or made larger and more spread out, these issue could have very easily been avoided.

This controller completly makes sense when paired with a steam link or living room steam machine. Compliments perfectly a normal xbox controller and together allow you to play almost any game provided you can read the text on your TV from your couch.

While it's currently on offer at 40% with the purchase of Xcom 2, and with how great it feels, I would recommend it as £20.99 seems like a reasonable price to pay on something that seems like a non-traditional controller.

My qualifications: I have been a PC gamer since the Wolfenstine 3d. I've owned just about every console except the PS3 or a Wii/WiiU. I game instead of sleep. I have a gaming problem.
The STeam Controller:
The heft of the controller is the first thing I noticed. It's good. It's not original XBOX heavy, but also not Xbox 360 comfortable. It isn't light, small, and fragile feeling like a PS4 controller. It is comfortable and feels sturdy.
The trigger buttons seem oddly placed, at first. The bumpers are where the triggers feel like they should be, so your hand has to shift up in a unnatural angle to be able to easily reach both triggers and shoulder buttons. This leaves the underside buttons on the bottom of the controller in less contact with your fingers. Those underside buttons feel like the flimsiest part of the device, but I like the idea of them being there. I think SCUF and the new Xbox controller do these types or triggers better.
The face buttons are smaller, and are a long reach from where a PS4 or XBO controller has taught you to expect them. With all the features on the Steam controller, you may not need to reach them as much, but they still seem distant. They are decent buttons when you have to use them. They get the job done, and I don't feel like I can break them through normal use.

The left thumbstick is perfect. I have really nothing else to add regarding this.
There are two touchpads on the face and they are huge. One has a D-Pad-like cross in the middle, the other is smooth. While holding it, powered off, they feel flimsy, floppy, and loose. The center click motion on both is unnatural and if you have to use it as a mouse button click, the motion will likely cause you to mis-click. However, powerred on, the tactile feedback of these touchpads is amazing. It reminds me of the old iPod scroll wheel that didn't really scroll, but it felt like it did. You can thumb the pad quickly like a trackball, and the feedback will tickle and slow down like friction on a real trackball. As you move across the surface, it gives feedback, and you have a sensation of true distance under your thumb that provides some kind of lizard-braid confirmation of motion. If the controller was good in any other area, this would be the thing that made it great.
Thumbstick aside, the problem is, the controller is not good in any other area. It's a mediocre controller with one really good gimmick. It's not a better controller than an XBO or PS4, and it's not a better interface than a mouse and keyboard. This hybrid aims for the best of both worlds, and really isn't good at either.
The configuration tool is really well done, and I like the idea that you can make complex mode combinations, like Left Trigger + A = Action1, Left Trigger + B = Action2. It's a great method to add extra functionality to the limited number of buttons - a complaint of controllers since forever. I recommend you try several different user configs and tweak them to what feels natural for you. I think with practice and the right config, someone could learn to make this an adequate replacement for a real controller, or a mouse and keyboard when they are sitting on their couch playing Portal 2.
Summary:
The controller is ok if you don't have a better alternative. It will work in a pinch, but it will never dethrone other methods of interface. I got it on sale, and cashed in extra Steam Wallet funds, so I didn't pay full price. It's adequate for what I paid for it, but I would not willingly pay $49.99 for it, or recommend it to anyone at that price.

Bet you know the deal already, right? Catchy product name, the female protagonist, tough police woman with the duty to clear the city from punks, mobsters and even demons eventually? A semi-open world game in a 3d, from the time when the games were looking much better in the 2d? A game where you running through the streets and climbing over the rooftops, driving cars, kicking punks in the balls, arresting them afterwards?
Oh, c'mon, either you've come there by some nostalgia link, like a video talking about noticeable 3d open world projects before GTA 3... Or you just liked the name of the game, right?
Well, in that second case, I urge you to look the other way, please. Yeah, sure, Urban Chaos looks not bad for a 1998 year product. There are surely the whole lot of a fun gameplay, with completing police missions, occasional beating & arresting simple pedestrians "just in case", et cetera, et cetera. 2 buttons combat is actually working, almost the same as in the Sleeping dogs. Same with the driving - with an exception that you can't change the car you're driving while you're in it. "Tanner, you're a slow pluck" - we all heard that thousands of times, but believe me, our heroine here, Darci Stern, is slower and clumsier.
Now, we're finally coming to the actual question: is it worth any actual gameplay interest now? Well, hardly. Being one of the first doesn't make you the best, obviously. While there are surely a lot of fun around, all is going to waste, as the controls just really bad and irresponsive. At least they were for me, and when I was trying to perform something fast, holding 3-4 buttons at the same time, the game just got stuck. Guess I'm not that manly anymore, striving through the really bad controls to see the good out of the game. But, Oni, a Bungie underrated gem, was blamed for the bad controls as well by some people, and how they were wrong! Maybe it's only my whining, if you're really into old games, maybe you'll like it. Don't look at videos, try the controls for yourself!
Me? I'll stick with Heavy Metal FAKK 2, Oni and Rune. And GTA 3, as it certainly better in all but the fact you're need to play for a criminal. But, I have True Crime Streets of LA, and that's already another league. Too bad so many of those named games were deleted from Steam...

If you liked the first Deus Ex you will definitely love Human Revolution. Acting as a prequel to the first game in the series and taking obvious inspiration from classic cyberpunk movies like RoboCop, you play as ex-SWAT Adam Jensen who ends up unraveling a conspiracy behind the death of a team of scientists that were on the brink of revealing one of the biggest breakthroughs in science yet, one that could potentially merge man and machine for good. Though little does he know that his trip down the proverbial rabbithole has barely begun.
The game is very much a seamless blend of stealth and action and like the first game leaves how you play the game entirely up to the player. You can sneak your way in, you can hack your way in or hell, grab a gun and kill everyone in your path. It's all up to you.
I highly recommend checking out the Director's Cut if you're a big fan of Human Revolution or haven't played it yet. The added developer commentary, DLC integration, and not to mention the improved boss fights makes this the definitive version of the game in my opinion. The boss fights was one of the biggest gripes with the game and this version adds far more tactical options to them for players who use different playstyles. It also helps that the graphics look far better in this version since the yellow filter is more toned down allowing for more colour variation. I also wanna mention the addition of a New Game+ mode that makes replaying the game on harder difficulties a bit more fun and achievable.
Well made game imo.

This is a must buy game for anyone into First Person stealth games. I garantee you that if you liked any of the old Thief games, the subtle path of Deus Ex: Human Revolution is for you. With good controls and a good camera (due to first person perspective) this a fun game to play as well, with no real issues programmer wise to bug you.
Though you can chose the way you play (guns blazing vs. putting evryone asleep - and variations of these), I've found in my play-throughs that this game really excells when played as a sneaky, humanistic protagonist.
It is true the boss fights in the first version of this game are rather jarring for anyone who has a stealth build, but the extra paths offered in the Director's Cut more than make up for this.
The way Missing Link is worked into this Director's Cut is rather good, though not great. It's a nice extra and the story told in this expansion is rather good, whilst playing you are rather aware of it being extra content compared to the core game.

This game is a dungeon crawling brawler with roguelike elements such as permanent death and random generation. And I have to say, it's really damn good.
Random generation is pretty well done. I've been playing for 40 hours now and I still see new rooms often, and new items every now and then.
Controls are pretty good and responsive and the game plays great even on keyboard.
Combat is very enjoyable. You can slash with basic attacks, you can uppercut the enemy which will have you beat him up in the air and then smash him onto the ground. You can also grab an enemy and spin him around (dealing damage to nearby enemies ) and then throw him into a wall, another enemy or even into a pit which will instantly kill him. It's a pretty good move for crowd control. You can also charge into enemies and use dodge-roll to avoid their attacks.
You can also use magic if you pick up certain items.
There's a pretty decent amount of items in the game as well. Different weapons, boots, armors, belts and all kinds of accessories.
Weapons will not only have different damage but a lot of them have different attributes to them. So the game isn't just about finding the weapon with highest stats, you'll have some hard choices to make. Will you for example keep the weapon that deals extra damage when fighting multiple enemies at the same time or will you pick one that occasionally freezes enemies while hitting them?
Also some weapons have shorter range while others longer. You'll also have to take that into account.
There are a lot of breakable objects in the game. Destroying them can drop gold or food, even potions if you're lucky.
There's a decent amount of special rooms in the game. Some are different kinds of shops, some are vaults with lots of chests, then there are several mini-game rooms such as wheel of fortune and playing cards with the devil.
You can also customize your character in the camp before starting a run by picking different head and hats. Some heads change your body as well so you can for example be troll, ogre, demon or cyborg. Some of those have to be unlocked though.
Overall the game is really fun and quite hard. Singleplayer is great and I'm sure multiplayer is even more fun. There are 4 difficulties so if you want more challenge than normal has to offer you can play on hard and if you're a masochist you can try insane.
Definitely a game I would recommend to anyone who likes brawlers and games with roguelike elements.

I purchased a Steam Controller expecting the software customization to be great and the controller hardware to be terrible.  The software while tied to Steam and Big Picture Mode works great.  The customization options are amazingly thorough and offer just about every possible adjustment or button layout you could ask for.
After around 30 hours of use here is my two cents.
The hardware portion is not terrible and actually quite nice.  The controller feels solidly built and while it doesn't feel cheap it doesn't feel as polished and 'premium' as some of the console controllers.  The XYBA buttons are a little close together and placed far enough in that it takes some getting used to pushing the correct buttons.  The triggers and shoulder buttons feel wonderful and the two-stage triggers are a great addition and open an insane amount of customization options.    I find myself accidentally pressing the two rear buttons periodically but the more I use the controller the less it happens.
This controller is not for people who will try to use it for two hours and then give up and claim it's terrible.  This controller requires a couple days of use and some good community profiles or your own custom profiles setup to your liking to really come alive.  Once you become used to the ergonomics and button placement it becomes quite a pleasure to use.  Over the last few months Valve has pushed firmware and software updates that continue to expand the customization options and features.  This software just keeps getting better and better.
TL;DR:  Good hardware, great software that is continually evolving, requires a couple days to get used to.  100% worth the time.

Did you like the board game of the same name? If so, you'll love this, as it replicates its mechanics precisely. As an added bonus, it also keeps track of the fiddly bits so you don't have to do so.
If you've never played the boardgame, this is a rail baron simulation. You are dealt 5 destination cards, and must keep at least three. Each turn, you can select train cards (which are colored; some lines require a specific color, though there is a more difficult to find wild card), lay track or draw new destinations. If you complete a line between the two destinations indicate on a card, then you receive the value posted on the card. Longer routes, if completed, generate more points. Additionally, laying track also gets you points, even if it doesn't complete a line. Holding destination cards in your hand when the game ends means you lose the point value on those cards.
I've only played this with the AI. So while it isn't as fun as playing with your friends, the AI is more available (but only has an option for three AIs; the board game allows for six players IIRC).
Anyway, a nifty game. The DLC replicates the maps found in the variety of versions sold by the boardgame's owner.
If you want to be robber baron, this is your ticket.

I paid for this game.  Actually I paid for 4 copies of this game.  I bought them so our whole family could play together on our Linux computers.  They suddenly dropped support and now we can't play the game.  NOT happy!

It's a great game, and lots of fun, but around the beginning of 2017, the developers decided they would just drop support for Linux for TTR, so now it's unavailable despite having PAID FOR this game to play on Linux.

Lots of people are not reccomending the game for port reasons and the fact that linux support has been removed seemingly without warning. Not a good move, IMO.
That being said, for Windows machines, this version of Ticket to Ride seems to work just fine. I haven't encounted any frustrating or game-breaking bugs, but then again I only really ever play it in the singleplayer mode. It's certainly faster than playing the analog version of the game. The Europe map plays better than the standard one and can be found at a pretty reasonable price during sales.
I'd say the strongest point of this version is to act as a singleplayer variant and to help learn and/or teach the game. It took me forever to understand the tunneling mechanic and the ferries system on the Europe board, but having an interactive version helps a lot.

‘Ticket to Ride’ can be a little intimidating at first, especially for people who haven’t played any tabletop game before. I’ve tried the traditional edition as well and I definitely prefer the digital one, let alone for the fact you have the board right in front of you every time, not having to look at it from the upside down nor any other angle.
There’s a nice selection of maps, though mostly sold as DLCs. Thankfully, prices are reasonable, even more so while on sale. Game runs smoothly and has a decent tutorial. After getting to know all the rules and a little bit of practice you will find yourself beating bots with moderate effort from your side. Getting achievements is completely different story, though.
Haven’t competed against real people in online modes much but from what I gather the game ran smoothly then as well and was even more enjoyable. If you want to start your adventure with tabletop games, I think digital version of ‘Ticket to Ride’ is a great one to help you with that. 7/10

a Sci-fi Indie Adventure game that will have you exploring, and seeing, the stars differently. I found Opus today, and of course played until I’d 100%ed the game. Though there are 31 achievies, they all come pretty normally through the story. By the time I’d finished the story, I had surveyed over 500 stars, which is the achievement just before the highest of 1000. But, I still had to locate a final supernova and a moon of one of the planets, along with the last 500 stars to survey, so that final count took a little grinding.
Story rich in a tantalizing and sentimental mystery, you are immersed in this charming tale of dreams, or goals. The title comes from the Latin phrase “Magnum Opus,” or “Great Work.” You start in a spaceship as a robot named Emeth. I’m totally unsure if that name comes from some Easter egg, or maybe it’s an acronym. But, two scientists are aboard with you and they are searching for the planet Earth, which was the origin of the human race, according to myth. They are growing doubtful they’ll find it, if it ever really existed, before they are too late to save mankind. The story presupposes that the gene pool has decayed to the point that survival is not expected. They need to return to Earth to collect more of their original genes. The robot is motivated by the female scientist to continue searching, despite the growing pessimism of the male scientist who is aboard with them. Then a power outage occurs, Lisa and the other scientist disappear, and a hologram of Lisa guides or assists Emeth in his search to find the missing planet Earth.
Opus takes a single game mechanic that is also present in the new Stellaris, by Paradox Studios, and does it even better. Lisa, the female protagonist, has programmed Emeth to operate Opus’s telescope. Opus is the large ship they are inside. When you turn on the telescope, you are gazing at the stars and you are able to scan in search of habitable planets matching the characteristics of Earth. Meanwhile, the hud overhead displays tabs for your target coordinates, target section/sector, target zone, & filters needed. Just beneath the display of tabs is a button for the Earth Locator, which functions to guide you to each of your missions and sub-missions, target planets & stars to explore.
The Earth Locator gives you clues to help you locate where the target star will be. You watch the display on your telescope and follow the degrees of rotation to calculate where you are, and where you need to be to find the target. This is comparable to flying an airplane by Instrument Flight Readings (IFR.) But, if you pay attention to the tabs at the top, each one lights up or turns off as you enter a zone or sector matching the description for your target, making it possible to just pilot “by the seat of your pants” as they say in Visual Flight Readings (VFR,) or flying by sight. If all the tabs are lit up, then you’ve found the right area. Also, a hint button will appear far right that will point you in the general direction, and you won’t find it too difficult.
Other than the comparison to Stellaris in the way you explore the stars, I find this game reminded me very much of Firewatch. In Firewatch you were given realistic navigation tools to find your way around a map of the forest. Opus does likewise, but you’re searching through the galaxy. Also, Opus has an immersive mystery story much like Firewatch. And, it keeps you engaged until you finish the game.

There are very few games I can remember playing that have drawn me in to the point of not wishing to touch another game before finishing it. OPUS: The Day We Found Earth not only had my attention from start to finish, but the only game I have played through without stopping, regardless of it's short length. The story in this game is truely a gem. You take the role of Emeth, a robot designed to hunt for the now mythically lost-to-the-ages Earth aided by a motherly shipboard AI, meanwhile unravelling a mystery the OPUS ship is hiding from you. Your character is endearingly simplistic, but matures bit by bit as the dual plots entwine.
The gameplay is focused and tuned for the length of the game. Yes, this is a short game, maybe only two hours, but remains fresh with new mechanics added that are quickly mastered before another layer is added on top. Playing on the upper difficulty does require you to utilize the systems available to you, and your ability to start recognizing the stars and nebula you gaze up at. The music is wonderfully crafted to the atmosphere of the game, both grandiose and subtle as needed. The art is charming and lively, vividly able to express the emotions of the characters. Overall, Team Signal has done a great job on this title, and it's worth taking an evening to sit down and enjoy.

is an atmospheric story-driven game, with elements that make it partly a visual novel.
You play as Emeth, a childlike robot who has been given the tasking of finding the long forgotten planet Earth. This is essentially the premise of the game and the story it follows. Playing as Emeth is unique in the sense that whilst you are controlling him, you are looking at him more from the perspective of LISA (an AI version of your creator,
). I don't want to ruin this for you by delving into it too much, but to put it simply: you are always ahead of Emeth, but this surprisingly never faults the story and actually adds more emotion to the game. This story aspect is definitely the strongest of the game and to fans of story-driven games, the intriguing characters and atmospheric story would provide an enjoyable playthrough.
On the other hand, the gameplay may disappoint some. The game tries to have unique gameplay aspects, which in some sense it does, but it starts to become repetitive at some point (which is especially not good for a game that requires around 2 hours to complete). The effort to try and stop this happening is displayed through the mostly little dialogue that interrupts you each time you discover a new star, which quickly becomes annoying. A breif explanation as to what this gameplay is like would be that it's almost similar to a hidden-object game, just with very little emphasis on the 'hidden' part. A positive towards the gameplay would be the fact that it still provides a somewhat relaxing experience, but despite this, without the engaging story the game would have barely anything to stand on.
Visually,
provides some really great art, something that would definitely be required to make the game a true stargazing experience.
Much like the artstyle, OPUS also provides some really good music that soothes the ears and suits each moment of the game.
Now for what is the biggest reason this game receives negative reviews: the price. To be honest, they have a point. For 8.99 USD, 2 hours of gameplay is quite overpriced and most probably not worth it. You can see the attempt to try to increase that time by adding in a tedious achievement that will probably bore you more than anything whilst trying to reach it.
✔ Mostly relaxing gameplay
✔ Engaging story
✔ Great artsyle
✔ Great music
✘ Repetitive gameplay
✘ Overpriced

I'm not the greatest at reviewing games, so I'll do my usual gabber/rant.
THIS GAME, *was* my childhood. I spent countless hours playing and replaying this game, and it was the greatest!
I remember coming home from school many times and asking to play this game, I was legitimately excited to play this. So when I discovered earlier today that this game is on sale for £1.24, how could I refuse?!
In the many hours playing this game as a child I eventually found some pretty game breaking bugs like being immune to fire with a pistol equipped. Or when you back to a wall, tap forward, back to the wall again without moving forward or back, tap forward again and suddenly you're at the top of the building. Can legit finish the jumper mission in about less than 30 seconds using that glitch. And can't figure out how to get to that enemy on the top of the building? Have no fear! The backing-into-a-wall-to-get-to-the-top-of-the-building bug is here!
Bugs aside, the game still runs like a dream, for its time the combat is really smooth, movement handles well on both foot and vehicle (once you adjust to the unorthidox control scheme). The max resolution however is only 1024 x 768~, which is fine for a 16 year old game, it meant that when I tried to stream it I just had to capture the game via monitor recording, rather than window/game capture, but it was no biggy. The voice acting is superb for its time too, there are a lot of old games with awful voice acting *cough* Resident Evil *cough* that make you cringe at every scene with dialogue, but not with this game.
So to conclude:
Urban Chaos, a hidden gem that time forgot, sadly ahead of its time, I have still yet to meet a person who has actually heard, let alone played this game (it was released a full 2 years before the likes of GTA 3). Dated graphics and sound but great voice acting.
So that aside I give this game a solid 8/10, would definitely recommend - especially with it being £1.24 for the next couple days.

I've been a Dead Rising fan since the original game, and so when it was announced for PC. I was really excited. After having spent a little over 35 hours with the game, here is my take of the game:
Pros
+There is a lot of content here. You will not be running out of things to do. I am still working on trying to achieve 100% in the game and this is not enough counting me going through the DLC of which there are more missions and characters to play as.
+No loading screens while you are running around town. This is perhaps one of my favorite improvements from previous Dead Rising games as the frequent loading screens killed a lot of enjoyment for me in Dead Rising 1 and 2.
+Los Perdidos is an interesting enough locale that is filled with collectables. There is literally so much to do and collect, so if you are into this, this is a good thing.
+Survivor AI is much better this time around. I do not feel like you have to babysit these individuals as much. Add it in with the fact that you can even summon AI to help out out or to take them out of the world when they are not needed is even better.
+The newly expanded crafting system is better than what we had in Dead Rising 2. There are so many combinations of weapons that it becomes pretty exciting to try out new weapons. I also appreciated the fact that it is much easier to craft  items on the go as you do not have to find a specific work bench to do it. With that said, there were a few weapons that seemed to have too many variations (I am thinking about the toy bear here).
+Having the option to select a more relaxed game versus the traditional timed setting. Dead Rising 1 and 2 instilled tension into players by having a strict time limit in which you would frequently have to rush from objective to objective (making detours to pick up items or survivors). While some loved this, others lamented the fact that it was too strict for their taste. Now, we have a choice. You can select "normal mode" which is a much more forgiving setting for players. If you want to go and find all items within the main story, this is definitely the setting to start off with. With that said, you do not have unlimited time here, it just ticks down even more slowly than the alternative "Nightmare mode" which is more in line with what previous games had.
+Powerups are actually useful. I've played games like this in the past which had questionable upgrades for each character, but in this game, most powerups are actually useful and add something to the game.
+Number of zombies. I was not sure whether to put this as a pro or a con. There are more zombies here than in any other Dead Rising title which is a great thing. The only possible negative here is that it could severly impact performance for some PC users.
+Your progress carries over when you start a new game or replay a chapter. This is in line with the other Dead Rising titles. As a result, you are given an incentive to level up over the course of the game.
Cons
-Terrible story. Complaining about a terrible story in a Dead Rising game is like complaining about the lack of shooting mechanics in a TellTale game, but I was hoping that Capcom could have given us something more than what we have here. Definitely the weakest of the trilogy.
-Forgettable main character. Nick Ramos is the least interesting protagonist out of the main series. Nick is a bit more vulnerable than Frank or Chuck, but, unfortunately, this was a wasted opportunity as we do not see much of a progression in his character over time (albeit it is not as bad as say Jason Brody from Far Cry 3).
-Traveling around the map can be quite annoying. You have to contend with roadblocks which make traveling around a bit of a pain. I understand why Capcom put these in there (they state that it had to do with having to include a ton of zombies), but honestly I would rather have less zombies and free access to the main roadways.
-If you revisit certain chapters, the only thing that carries over is the time at which you started the chapter. This does not sound like a big deal, but when you busted your butt to unlock most of the doors around the map and you revisit a chapter later, you will find all of the doors locked again which can be frustrating to say the least. Another example is that the PP trials you completed will also be reset which is a major pain.
-Performance issues. I have had this game crash on me a few times (not sure why). Having said this, on my rig I have gotten decent performance without any issues with regards to framerate, even in high density areas.
-DLC takes place in the same environment as the main game. This makes playing through the DLC a drag as I spent enough time in Los Perdidos in the main game. Perhaps they could have tried to change things up a bit by doing a smaller locale.
-Psychopaths are even less interesting this time around. I understand that psychopaths have never been the game's strengths, but this time around, they are even less memorable than the ones we fought in the previous Dead Rising games, which gets me to my last con.
-Tone is inconsistent. After beating the game, I was a bit confused as to what Capcom was trying to achieve. They seemed to want to go for a darker tone this time around, but, then again, you have to deal with survivors that have pretty dumb motivations (wanting to make a porno with zombies for example) and then you have these weird psychopath battles which could have been a bit darker, but they seem to be used for comedic relief. In my view, the game could have benefited from a more consistent tone in that sense (although this criticism could be levied to some extent against the other games in the series).
I can recommend this game to fans of the franchise. I started feeling franchise fatigue with this particular title, so I have no desire to put anymore time into this game, but I realize that this could be to my own gaming tastes changing rather than an issue with this game in particular.
Thanks for reading!

Don't expect a regular controller when you buy this, it takes a while to grow on you.

1. Hated needing or using any "console controller" on the PC the last 20+ years.
2. Happily bought 2 Steam Controllers.
Not perfect for kb/mouse users, but close as they've ever come.

Things to know if you're considering one:
1: This is not intended to be a replacement for a traditional gamepad. It's a replacment for a gamepad along with a keyboard and mouse, and because of that, it is a very, very different experience than pretty much any other controller.
2: This is not something you can just pick up the first time and use proficiently, and there is a bit of a learning curve, especially if you've spent several years playing with a standard gamepad. Nothing too severe, it's just a matter of getting a feel for how to move your thumbs and commit it to muscle memory.
3: The vast majority of games do not have full Steam Controller support right out of the box, and even those that do often require a bit of adjustment and fiddling. There's a great community doing great work, but there's enough work involved that it almost becomes a hobby in and of itself.
4: It's also surprisingly loud. The excellent haptic feedback is a big part of how it is able to work as well as it does, and as long as you have your thumbs on one or both of the pads, the motors will be going, letting off a kind of low, creaky groan. On top of that, the buttons and triggers, while solid, are 1980's mechanical keyboard loud, and you can often hear them even over headphones.

What it all boils down to is as long as you have a bit of patience and are willing to put in the work, the Steam Controller will consistently amaze you with how versatile it winds up being. This isn't great because of what it does, it's great because of what you can make it do.
