Don't be scared of it this is wonderful device, different for sure. But different can change the world given a chance.
It's certainly not just pick up and play but that also makes it so much more than it could have been.
This is one of the most complex and configurable device you are ever likely to come across. And as such it's not I'm afraid for everyone.
Love for the steam controller does not come easy. But like all things worth having, it's worth fighting for.
You could spend many hours(and I have) Setting up your your perfect configuration for every game in your steam library. But that's not for everyone as we all know...there are better ways to spend your hard earned time.
So as luck would have it there is a strong and growing number of community minded controller owners. Who are working day and night to make your choice easy.
If your favourite game needs a particular configuration, chances are someone has already uploaded it to the steam cloud. One press of a button to flash it to your controller and your good to go.
So there you have it what once was scary has been tamed, why wouldn't you want the best of all worlds!

The controller itself is very functional, the hardware is nice and responsive and the configs available for games are a great idea, as well as really easy to tweak.
What lets it down is the software side of things. I understand to some degree why functionality is tied to big picture mode and to the steam client itself but if you want to get it to work with anything outside of steam, it's a royal pain in the backside.
I'll heartily recommend it to anyone who plans to use it exclusively for steam stuff. It's great in rocket league for example. I've even played civ V on it and it felt pretty natural. If you're looking for something for emulators or stuff outside of steam i'd say go for a console controller of your choice.
Right now, the software and out-of-steam support for the pad needs vastly improving. When that side of things changes i will gladly switch this review to a 'Yes'.

Go! Go! Nippon! was the first title that MangaGamer published on Steam, and me being a vivid VN player and Japanese Studies student, I instantly felt the need to get this game. At first, this seemed like a perfect start for Visual Novels to appear on Steam, especially after other titles like Analogue and its sequel, Hate Plus. But after going through all of it, I'm not sure whether this is worth your time.
This game feels more like a kinetic visual novel, with choices that don't really make a difference. You can go through the whole story without saving a single time, but because of forced branching you'll have to go through it twice (blind choices however). Basically, the estimate as given by the VNDB is correct (2 to 10 hours). Is paying 10 dollars worth this gameplay time? Up to you to decide. The characters are quite stereotypical but on the other hand, you can enter your own name, which might be quite to your liking. I just wished that they also showed the Japanese price (instead of just your own currency) when buying something, since you most likely will be carrying only Japanese yen with you while you travel.
So why do I not recommend this game? Basically, I found it a bit too short for my liking (at least Europeans tend to travel for at least 2 weeks when going this far abroad), but there's something that was bugging me more. The translation quality. I found it very lacking and so did other friends of mine who are proficient at Japanese. I made several screenshots that show obvious grammatical mistakes that usually only beginners would make. Since this game is actually giving both the Japanese and the English text, it's supposed to be aimed for Japanese language learners (you would have no other reason otherwise), but this definitely backfires instead.
Another thing is that the game is already quite dated. While the game released on Steam this February, it was first released in September 2011. At one point of the story, they're talking about the Tokyo Skytree, which was yet to be opened on the time of the release, but it's one of the most popular tourist attractions nowadays. I also felt like they're not talking enough about the typical spots too. Not a single word about Tokyo Disneyland and Tokyo Disney Sea, and even the 109 building at the Shibuya Scramble Crossing. Kinkaku-ji was greatly praised, but no word of it's counterpart, Ginkaku-ji.
If you feel like you might go to Japan for the first time someday, with Tokyo as main destination, and love to have some nice fantasy about it beforehand, pick it up if you think it's worth the money. If you're already studying Japanese, chances are you know most of it already, and this will make you kind of annoyed at some times. The main protagonist is a know-all when it comes to Japanese, but is a complete blockhead when it comes to the culture. It's also feels incomplete, so if you want a great guide...Just buy an actual guidebook. Or else...Just find some Japanese tour guides in real life. It's not that hard if you look for backpacker or couchsurf sites out there.

Ticket to Ride is another great board game that has made the transition to a digital platform.
The adaptation has been done well and remains true to the original board game.
The background music can get a little tedious and get on your nerves after a while, but that can easily be turned down or off.
There are many options for gameplay, including single player v’s AI, online multiplayer, local multiplayer (providing all players are on the same network/wifi) and even a pass and play.  You can play against people across different platforms (PC, Android, & iOS) but with recent updates Linux support has been withdrawn which has contributed to a multitude of negative reviews from understandably annoyed players.
Overall the game itself is quick and simple to learn, yet varied and challenging enough to keep you coming back to play more.  It is easy enough to understand the game mechanics and the game achieves a good balance between skill and luck.  The UI is simple and easy to understand, allowing you to follow everything happening in the game.  With the various DLC’s now available, they allow you to keep the game fresh and pose new challenges to maintain interest.
Overall this was a great a board game that is arguably just as good as a digital version (providing you are running it on a platform that is still supported)

Bully is a game made by Rockstar, the development studio behind the Grand Theft Auto series. One of the many differences with GTA and this game is that instead of having deadly weapons you'll get weapons to prank and bully every kid in the block, the violent is toned-down too which is quite understandable since the game is set in a school setting.
The game takes place at the fictional New England boarding school, Bullworth Academy and tells the story of mischievous 15-year-old Jimmy Hopkins as he goes through the hilarity and awkwardness of adolescence. Beat the jocks at dodge ball, play pranks on the preppies, save the nerds, kiss the girl and ultimately navigate the social hierarchy in the worst school around.
Bully is divided between six chapters and many different missions which takes place in certain weather season much like Mafia II. As Jimmy Hopskins, a 15 year old mean bully, you are free to roam around the school or complete your classes like what normal student do or do what you do best, skip class and bully.

Bully: Scholarship Edition
+ A really fun open world game, where you play as a bully named Jimmy Hopkins. You can learn some really cool fight moves, use slingshots, stink bombs, itching powder, spud guns and throw eggs at people..there's many, many more items than that. This game has a comical and serious feel to it which is great.
+ The storyline is interesting and you get to interact with the stereotypical school groups, such as jocks, preps and nerds.
+ You can attend school throughout the game or skip it, but there's numerous activities to complete in each class, many of which are enjoyable. There are a lot of small errands to complete and collectibles to find.
+ I liked the style of the graphics. Even though they are not amazing for the time period, they're nice.
- The map size feels adequate when playing, but it takes a moment to realise it's quite small, especially for a Rockstar game. This is where Bully could have been improved. A bigger map, with even more to do and see. The exploration in this game is fine, but it could be enhanced.
- Lack of quality side missions. You can participate in errands, but they don't have any plot background and the rewards aren't exactly useful. Bully: Scholarship Edition would benefit from deeper story-based distractions and side missions, extending the gameplay time. Which leads me to my final point.
- The game is fairly short, it took me approximately 25 hours to finish which I suppose isn't too bad, but it's not quite long enough for an open world game.
Overall Score: 7.5/10
Bully: Scholarship Edition is awesome fun. It's a game that has been largely forgotten with time, but definitely worth picking up.

Remember GTA 3? I do. You wanna know something people don't often remember? Urban Chaos. And i don't see why. It's a sort of spiritual predescessor to it, in an odd way.
It looks alright for 1999 i suppose. Horrid by today's standards, but for the time, it looks decent. The draw distance is alright overall, my only major problem with it graphically is that it's always night. There's ONE mission that takes place during the day; otherwise, it's nighttime. It's my only complaint i can give for the game graphically that isn't caused by the time it was released.
Controls are a bit odd to get used to at first, but they work. Your character has Quasi-Tank Controls. While you CAN turn while moving, it's extremely finicky, and most of the time you're better stopping, turning and then moving. The fighting controls are okay, you've got your basic punching and kicking, and the "special moves" (grapples and the like) are simply performed by hitting a particular direction while punching or kicking. It auto locks on to enemies for you, and shooting is as simple as hitting the punch button with a gun out locked on to an enemy. My only problem with the controls comes with vehicles; they control terribly. There's very little real grasp of physics with them, and while they don't nessescarily use the tank controls, sometimes when you stop the game will behave like you DO, and your car will be locked in place for no reason for a couple of seconds before being able to move again. Considering how fast your sprint is however, generally you shouldn't need a car.
The levels are fairly expansive, and lend each mission a sort of Open-World vibe. There's secrets hidden around, optional objectives, stat boosts, weapon caches and all sorts of other stuff just begging for you to go off the beaten path to find. It can be a bit distracting from your main goal at times, but overall i feel like it helps the game quite a lot, it makes it go from what would've been a barebones linear Third Person Shooter with a decent melee combat system, to a rather open, fun to explore Quasi-Sandbox game.
Despite the minor flaws, i really can't see why this game isn't remembered better. If it's on sale pick it up; these day's a bloody Potato could probably run it with no issue, and it's fairly enjoyable.
EDIT: Of note though, apparently the game is extremely finicky on 64bit systems. Some it'll work on, some it doesn't. If you have a 64bit system, buy it at your own risk.

Speaking as someone who had never played this game before, I really can't find anything to recommend about it. Maybe it played better on consoles back when it first came out, but unless you have some deep nostalgia for it, I suggest you give it a pass. Any enjoyment I might have derived from this game was lost in the numerous design and control issues.
I've never been a fan of tank controls, but in conjunction with an unruly camera with no mouse support and combat that demands immediate reaction it becomes extremely frustrating. The melee system allows you to perform combos, but you never will, because it's faster to just grapple the enemy and cuff him while he's on the ground. Guns have to be locked onto an enemy to hit, and trying to get locked onto the right enemy in the heat of battle while having to keep constantly on the move to evade enemies' bullets is no easy task. There are just too many annoyances in the combat to delve into all of them; getting caught in 'melee mode' so it becomes impossible to flee, enemies constantly sliding to knock you down the instant they get close, the list goes on.
On top of the combat issues, some of the game's mechanics only serve to compound the problem. There's no map, so it becomes an ordeal to navigate to several of your objectives, especially when the only way there is via a convoluted route across the rooftops that starts nowhere near the objective itself. There are no checkpoints and no way to save mid-mission, but many missions are way too long for such a handicap, especially considering that you'll also have to redo any side events or collectibles you got if you die. The story is pretty bare bones and towards the end takes on a supernatural element that goes completely unexplained.
Unless you've got a history with this game it's really not worth your time or money, even if it's dirt cheap.

The best rpg I've ever played, bar none. Usually such grand claims for old classics are
attributed to the rose tinted glasses of nostalgia, except in my case I totally missed
the game when it first came out, raising my nose at the notion of turn-based rpg combat.
What I fool I was!
I played Fallout 2 for the first time more than 10 years after its release, long after the likes of
rpgs like Diablo 2, Morrowind, Oblivion, Icewind Dale and Neverwinter Nights. And yet Fallout 2
quickly became my favorite.
pros:
+ Incredible atmosphere, due to a believable and very well realized post apocalyptic wasteland
made all the more powerful by the superb soundtrack.
+ Robust and diverse character leveling system in which you are spoiled for choice most of the time.
Far less constricted compared to something like Neverwinter Nights.
+ Satisfying and brutal combat with excellent sound and visual effects.
+ Huge, but manageable world to explore with loads of interesting locations and people to interact with.
+ Very good replay value, with multiple ways to complete quests, and some quests being mutually exclusive. Also,
the restoration project adds tons of content which is perfect for a 2nd playthrough.
+ Fun easter eggs, of which there are quite a few.
cons:
- Starts slow and can be a little annoying the first hour or so while you are still dependent on your spear and ammo is sparse (unless you're going for a melee character).
- Can get quite difficult.

Platypus is a nice little claymation game in which you pilot a small green military jet, with the aim of shooting down hordes of alien spaceships that appear before you (and behind you, as the case may be).
(I'm guessing that they are alien spaceships, but they could just be from a futuristic Earth civilisation. Who knows? Not me, that's for sure.)
The game mechanics are not very much different from a wide range of similar games, but the claymation style gives it a sort of cuteness which is easy on the eye, being somewhat visually amusing.
Whilst the game is simple in its concept, it gets harder as you level up.
When you blow up some bigger enemy vessels you can collect the large stars they leave behind, which will give you better weapons.
Or they might drop fruit (bananas, cherries, etc.), which you can collect for bonus points.
In the higher levels you have to fight harder enemies: huge motherships, fixed gun emplacements, train-mounted guns, and more.
Whilst you can fly right down to the ground and take no damage by doing so, you might be in for a surprise in a later level when you crash into a ground-level fuel tank.
So, be careful with what you're doing.
Platypus is not a spectacular game, but it's a bit of fun.
With its claymation style, I imagine that it could be quite a good game for children.

OPUS is a wonderful experience, and I highly recommend it. The story isn't flawless, but it did succeed in nearly bringing me to tears, which is still something only a few games have accomplished - and it achieved that in under an hour and a half. If you're not someone who inherently hates iOS ports, you'll find something to love in OPUS.
That being said, I'm much better at writing criticisms, and I do have a major gripe with the game. When starting the story, you are prompted to choose between "Normal Mode" and an easier "Story Mode": Normal Mode promises to hold your hand less, while Story Mode promises to carry you through the story as painlessly as possible. So I chose Normal Mode, of course, but then it never actually felt like the game let my hand go. The story progresses by scanning specific planets, which the game points you directly towards - it points you to a general area where the star can be found, and the star is always the brightest one there. Even when those areas become larger, the game provides you a means to narrow the search down to a handful yet again, meaning you can realistically complete the game without ever scanning a "wrong" system, even on your first playthrough.
As soon as you scan one planet, you are immediately told where the next one is. First, this raises a lot of serious questions about the plot - how did they ever have trouble finding Earthlike planets when they're so helpfully mapped out for you? But even purely as a gameplay mechanic, I believe it genuinely detracted from my experience. More than anything, it actively discouraged me from exploring the actual map: the characters are constantly pattering about how they desperately need to scan the next planet, and the next planet is always right in front of you, so what kind of jerk would make them wait so you can go look for that supernova you just found out about? It also makes the whole scanning mechanic seem completely pointless; if you ever scan an incorrect planet, you feel like you've only wasted your time (more on that in a moment). I would have much preferred a mechanic where you would be told an even broader area to scan in, and you would need to randomly scan planets in the area to find clues to the next candidate - a reason to actually make you want to look around. As it stands, by the time the story gets to the "we're now desperate so we need to look fast" section, I didn't really feel much pressure, since I had felt pressured to rush the story scans from the very beginning.
And about scans being pointless: why on Earth is there an achievement for scanning 1000 systems? As mentioned, you'll probably get through the story with barely over 25 scans, and extra scans up to that points were already a waste of time; what's the point in asking players to sit around for 2.5 hours clicking on star after star, just so they can see the "that's not Earth, stupid" message pop up hundreds of times? I really wish developers would stop adding achievements that may as well read "do a boring and repetitive task over and over and over for us."
Closing statements on OPUS: Did you miss the first paragraph? Go buy OPUS, it's a beautiful, if brief, title. I only criticize it so much because I'm an obnoxious prick, and I believe giving games a free pass on critique just because they're indie or because they're iOS ports is fairly patronising.

Developers or Moderators deleted forum post which contained feedback and feature requests I thought would be beneficial to making gameplay more interesting.
This is the first time I've had this happen. Maybe it was a mistake, I can't say. But as I get the impression they do not appreciate user feedback, I cannot recommend the game on that alone. However even if that wasn't the case, in my suggestions I brought up several things that impact this game in a negitive way.
This game has a pretty solid story. But the pacing it terrible.
You play a small robot looking for earth. You search for it by aligning your telescope using the mouse or keyboard to grid coordinates or a general "In this area kinda", type instructions given to you by the computer.
You scan stars in the area you think the match is in until you find a planet that is a high percentage match of earth, but is not really earth.
You do this over and over again, with little variation in play, in between each star, you are shown a view of the ship and read through some dialogue, mostly about how the robot misses it's friend.
Your character appears in multiple locations on the ship as you progress and unlock new areas. However, these areas serve no other purpose in the game besides a different background to read more dialogue.
I felt like there are so many missed opportunities that would have made this a great game.
For example, incorporating zoom and focus into the telescope. Piloting the ship and repositioning it. Really, by the 10th planet that wasn't earth, I was really feeling antsy and begging for the game to give me some other task to do.
Bestowed upon you about 1/3rd through the game, is a computer aided locator, which lights up on average 3-5 possible stars that are the one you need to scan. This actually made the game even less fun because it removed difficulty from gameplay instead of increasing it.
Towards the end, you are given one new mechanic. It consists of a filter, which shows something similar to IR light when looking at space. The game has you use this about 3 times total before the end of the game and tells you when you need to use it.
Really I understand wanting a story based game and a casual experience. But in my opinion the dialogue felt more like it took me out of the experience more than made me hopeful to hear more story. This is mainly because you listen to more dialogue in the game after EVERY SCAN of an earthlike planet. Which means about once every 2 minutes. Most of this dialogue is not worth interrupting the player, showing the ship, and going through more dialogue.
This filler dialogue should be spaced out and for the non essential stuff, it should happen while you are looking for things and during scanning.
Once you finish the story. You unlock Normal mode. Where you can spend time clicking on random stars and scanning them. All gameplay functions in both Story and Normal Mode are as follows: Pan Up/Down/Left/Right, Filter On/Off, Scan.
This gameplay mode offers you nothing new, other than to continue scanning the 100,000,000 star systems in the game and naming them. Literally the most feedback the game offers is a random percentage of how close that planet is to earth, a picture, and a description of why it doesn't support life or isn't like earth. Once you finish the story I don't see much point in playing in normal because at the core, it just isn't varied enough to be fun.
I think this had so much potential. I am sad to see parts of this game that just have a failed execution. I hope the developers rethink some of the mechanics and make the experience a bit more captivating and varied. All the foundations are there. If they do I'll be sure to change my review.
Currently however, this plays more like a visual novel with a hidden object mini-game. That would be the best way to go into this I think.
I will give the game credit though. It does have a really nice graphical feel. Soothing music. A unique direction and above all, it's got a lot of heart. But for the reasons above, that heart just isn't enough for me. I would give it shot if scanning the sky in the game in a casual and very basic fasion sounds fun to you, but I think that after the story you'll probably never touch it again. That is what bums me out because this has an opportunity to be something really special.

Imma try to be as clear and polite as I can.
TL;DR: I'd've recommended the game a patch or two ago. I was really into how they handled the card system and it was overall pretty solid. Now that the card system is being handled based on card quantity, and therefore purchase amount, I just cannot. Furthermore, the decision to limit the effects to quickplay only means I, who hasn't put much money into this game and refuses to play comp, will be affected. No. I do not recommend you play Paladins. At least for the next few patches.
I'm not big into MP games. The few that I play, I play for about a week, stop playing them for a month and then I play them again. I'm trying to say that I've been with Paladins for quite a while even if my overall playtime doesn't reflect it. I rarely or never play comp. I've always felt like that's where the animosity is, which I get. It's competitive, you're playing to win. Unfortunately that ain't how I go about things. I play games because I enjoy games, and I don't really care about winning. Not too much. I haven't spent much on Paladins. About 20-30 bucks. Mostly to get a few skins I thought looked nice and little else.
Now, just as I was about to go in again, I notice that the essence system's gone. That now, card levels depend on how many copies of them you have instead of being able to adjust a card's level to fit a specific loadout. Now, that bothers me. To no end. I tend to have 2-3 loadouts with every character I play (usually 2 of each class, so around 20 total loadouts), and with this new card leveling method, I expect about 2 or 3 of ALL the loadouts I've got to be of any use since many of them relied heavily on rare cards that I purchased though essence and never got in a chest. Meaning those rare cards will now be Lvl 1 regardless of the level they had in my pre-patch loadout. Meaning the effect those cards have in my playstyle is minimal, meaning that I've gotten used to a certain set of playstyles that may very well be inconsequential now. Meaning a lot of the time I spent getting those cards to begin with went down the drain in one patch. Pretty irksome.
On top of that, these changes will only be influential in Quickplay, which just so happens to be what I play the most because I don't really like to play comp. And it's also what new players will play and will only be able to play 'till they're level 13 or unlock a set number of heroes. And it's also what folks that just got a new hero and wanna try it out play. What i'm getting at is that these changes should not affect quickplay. Not that I'm saying that they should affect competitive, because they shouldn't either.
These changes shouldn't have been made in the first place.
Hi-Rez probably won't read this. They were the ones that made the changes to begin with, so I doubt they care about what some randy in the internet says. That said, I'd like you, whoever you are, to take a second to consider whether what I just said makes sense or not. If it does, then my recommendation to you is to not play this game. If it doesn't, then my recommendation to you remains the same. Do not play this game.
At least until these changes have been reverted.

A year and a half or so ago, I would have given this game a thumbs-up.
Sadly, that's not the case now.
From a table-top player of the game, it does fulfill that need for a single player version of the game with AI.
The AI is usually on it's game, and can provide challenges just like a human opponent.
But what merits a negative review if the game is so pitch perfect for an electronic version?
The interface. The backend. With the update that came out that year/year and a half ago, the aspects of the game
that were controllable by the player were rendered completely and utterly useless.
No longer can we select player colour, or the player avatar. Completely locked out.
Want to turn off the irritating and mind-numbing music? Good luck. That too doesn't function correctly.
Now Kris, you may ask... did you try uninstalling the game and reinstalling?
Yes, several times. With a reboot, cleaning the registry, all the temp files, complete rip and reinstalls. Nothing.
As I said, I did several times, each time with a different tack, trying to force something to reset in the hopes that
I could restore functionality.
Even a complete uninstall, removal of ALL files, cleaning the registry of entries, a complete reboot, and a ful reinstall did NOTHING.
And apparently, I'm not alone with this issue. Posts in the Steam Forums and on the DoW forums point out these issues.
And what is done about it? NOTHING.
Oh, we did get new content though, so it's not abandonware.
If you want to buy the game, please do. It's a wonderful translation of the board game and has infinite replay value.
Just be forewarned that you can't do anything other than play it, as I've explained above.

Bully is a game made by Rockstar, the development studio behind the Grand Theft Auto series. One of the many differences with GTA and this game is that instead of having deadly weapons you'll get weapons to prank and bully every kid in the block, the violent is toned-down too which is quite understandable since the game is set in a school setting.
The game takes place at the fictional New England boarding school, Bullworth Academy and tells the story of mischievous 15-year-old Jimmy Hopkins as he goes through the hilarity and awkwardness of adolescence. Beat the jocks at dodge ball, play pranks on the preppies, save the nerds, kiss the girl and ultimately navigate the social hierarchy in the worst school around.
Bully is divided between six chapters and many different missions which takes place in certain weather season much like Mafia II. As Jimmy Hopskins, a 15 year old mean bully, you are free to roam around the school or complete your classes like what normal student do or do what you do best, skip class and bully.
There is no denying that the game is a console port but a well-made one. The controls is a bit weird but you'll get to it eventually once you get used to them. The game is a bit repititive but that's just a minor problem I had with the game.

Bully: Scholarship Edition
+ A really fun open world game, where you play as a bully named Jimmy Hopkins. You can learn some really cool fight moves, use slingshots, stink bombs, itching powder, spud guns and throw eggs at people..there's many, many more items than that. This game has a comical and serious feel to it which is great.
+ The storyline is interesting and you get to interact with the stereotypical school groups, such as jocks, preps and nerds.
+ You can attend school throughout the game or skip it, but there's numerous activities to complete in each class, many of which are enjoyable. There are a lot of small errands to complete and collectibles to find.
+ I liked the style of the graphics. Even though they are not amazing for the time period, they're nice.
- The map size feels adequate when playing, but it takes a moment to realise it's quite small, especially for a Rockstar game. This is where Bully could have been improved. A bigger map, with even more to do and see. The exploration in this game is fine, but it could be enhanced.
- Lack of quality side missions. You can participate in errands, but they don't have any plot background and the rewards aren't exactly useful. Bully: Scholarship Edition would benefit from deeper story-based distractions and side missions, extending the gameplay time. Which leads me to my final point.
- The game is fairly short, it took me approximately 25 hours to finish which I suppose isn't too bad, but it's not quite long enough for an open world game.
Overall Score: 7.5/10
Bully: Scholarship Edition is awesome fun. It's a game that has been largely forgotten with time, but definitely worth picking up.

My rating: roughly 4/10
-    Seeing that I used to play this and it is now lost, bought this on sale.
-    Cleared the whole game on hard, continued a few times but I'm done with the game.
-    Reminds me how Shooter and Bullet hell are different genres.
-    I like Autogun. Bullet hell games influence.
-    Art: musics, graphics, sounds, atmosphere.
-    Increase point item value by shooting it.
-    Special weapons can be kept on screen when there's no need to collect right away.
-    Manual firing is much stronger than auto firing. Imagine rockets fired at machinegun rate.
-    Difficulty. This is not about the game being too hard or easy, but somehow stage 2 seems to be the hardest and stage 3 the second, With all the blending background and hard-to-detect mini bullets.
-    Enemies come from behind without sign. No problem for me, but this is a casual game.
-    Stages don't end with just last enemy or boss defeated, but also a set amount of time passed. Such a waste of special weapons.
-    You can select any stage to start after you've beaten it once. Meaning you can skip harder stages and still finish the game.
-    Final score is affected by current score, credits left and not lives left.
-    Past stages are replayable. -> Credits are grindable. -> Score are grindable
-    Leaderboard. There is no need for it, seriously. Difficulty gives no bonus and they all share one leaderboard and score is grindable. The game is not that competitive, so this board is just a decoration.
-    This game is not so bad as I liked it as a kid. But there's really nothing much for moderate (or higher) gamers to look forward to.

Where to start? Firstly, if you're expecting a good story... Then you got it. This game does a very good job at keeping you at suspense and then giving you little hints as to the happenings of the world around your characters. The two main protagonists in this game are very humorous and reminds me highly of Wall-E and EVA from the movie Wall-E.
The gameplay is simple but it works very well. You won't get confused at it too much and there's always a little 'Hint' button to direct you in the general direction of the area you need to check out although that might be due to Story mode and not the other mode.
The music amplifies the gameplay experience a lot. It's a HUGE difference to be able to play this game with the music and without it. It really set the atmosphere and assisted in the narrative of the game as well.
Now the game isn't really too long, around 2-3 hours in one entire session until you reach the end. Double that if you play the other mode as well to find all the collectibles and other scraps of the story.
In fact I'd say this game would be criminal to charge me so much for such a short game but I forgive it. Why? The story affected me, the music affected me, and those were the goals of the developers as they have stated themselves. They achieved that goal with me and thus, I'd say my money was well spent. I even bought the soundtrack.
And the ending is one of those endings that you'll love but wish there were more.

This shooter breaks a lot of rules: lewd humor and over-the-top gore in a garish package. While some may say that it has a lot in common with TF2, it couldn't be further from the mark. Loadout offers only one player class, but the diversity in playstyles comes from customized unlockables for weapons. The third-person view benefits the gameplay well, so you can admire your own character's hats, while still having good situational awareness. Your opponents are as fast and sized the same as you are, so  one must develop a healty relationship with the lunge action in order to evade incoming fire.
Unlike other "free-to-play" titles, this one is not "pay-to-win". The only thing money affects is your character's attire (cosmetic only) and how quickly you earn xp (honestly, if you play the game enough, it doesn't matter). This means that any player can unlock any weapon modification, and build the 'loadout' of his or her choosing without spending a cent of real-world money. I, for one, hope that this business model takes off, and I urge others with an interest in shooters of any kind to take the time to download and try this game.

Ever felt like watching anime isn’t enough insight to what it’s actually like to visit Japan? Well enter your name, step into the shoes of the ultimate otaku stereotype and experience what it’s like to trick two young girls into letting you stay with them while you take in the sights of Japan.
The story revolves around spending a week in Japan and selecting one of several areas available to go visit. One of the girls you stay with will escort you to the area to narrate information about the location and sometimes get up to “wacky” escapades while there. While I can concede I didn’t know a lot of the stuff that was brought up, for me personally It was met with an “oh~” or “huh…”. Maybe the writers thought this was all way more interesting that I did or I’m just emotionally repressed (I am English afterall), but the protagonist takes any small piece of information and exclaims that it’s the most amazing thing he’s ever heard… Usually followed by a variation on “Only in Japan…”. This and the awkward dating sim parts really let the game down, because while funny the first few times, it permeates every day of the game and just becomes tiresome. Whether the writers honestly thought all tourists are like this, either through imagination or personal experience (fanboys *can* be creepy), I got really bored of reading it.
One of the neat touches in the game is that the dialogue prints out in japanese as well as english, so if you're learning the language you can follow along without having to manually switch between languages, or use a translation program. If aimed at people actually interested in learning the language or after ideas for places to visit during a trip, then the game actually does a pretty good job at achieving its goal. Sadly, the seedy, awkward dating sim side story going on that really detracts from that and seems to overtake the guide aspect as the focal point.
At first I didn't even actually believe this was going to have a dating aspect to it. Aside from the protagonist being creepy enough to send any sane girl fleeing in terror, it just doesn't really feel like the romance takes a natural progression. The whole premise of the game is that he's there just to take in the sights and be a humble little tourist, but after a few days he starts inner monologues about which sister he prefers and "choosing" between them (because that's how true love works). This gives the game a really sinister vibe to it; that he’s there under false pretences to try and get together with one of the girls.
Visual novels pretty much live and die by the quality of their story and/or characters, and on this front Go! Go! Nippon! is either going to bring mirth or migraines. The protagonist is established at the typical otaku right from the get go, completely at awe at everything Japan has to offer, including its toilets. The two girls have a few instances that make them tolerable, but their fawning over this abomination of a person cancels any of that out. Why they don’t throw him out onto the streets when he “accidentally” walks in on them in various states of undress really irked me.
Yes, the game goes there.
The game doesn’t exactly push any boundaries in the world of visual novels; it’s a standard character portraits and text boxes affair. It does keep track of the amount of money spent during the trip, though I never worked out why, money isn’t a finite resource in the game and doesn’t seem to influence any of the activities. Each day you get to choose which location you visit, and depending on where it is will influence which of the girls accompanies you. This in turn seems to affect the dating sim aspect; in that the girl you spent the most time with is the girl that’d like you. Outside of that, while you do get dialogue options you have very little influence on the story.
Maybe the game is intended to be tongue-in-cheek, certainly at times it seems that way, but similarly at other times it felt like it was to be taken deadly seriously. It's a goofy little game that doesn't really tell the most fascinating story (you can pretty much guess what the entire game's going to be after the opening scene), and in terms of player interaction, it's pretty limited. I did have some fun with it, even if it was just seeing what holes the main character would dig himself into and how completely dumbfounded he seemed to be by the world at large.

Cons: Just one -  only few choices. All other things are almost perfect. You can learn so much about Japan. It's impossible to remember all those things by playing this game only once. BTW, you can even turn on google maps to see locations "in real life" by pressing one button. And this ending... Damn... It's so emotional.  I want "second trip to Japan..." 9/10.

I wish my only options weren't thumbs up or thumbs down, because I'd give this game 3 out of 5 stars: not bad, fun in a lot of ways, but could have been better too.
First off, the minimum system requirements are way off. Though I own this game now, I started playing it on a freeplay weekend, and just for fun I tried it on a dual-core Pentium Extreme Edition (3.73GHz, 2M L2 cache). It runs like a charm on here, despite the quad-core i5 (2.4GHz, 6M L2 cache) processor Steam claims is a bare minimum for this game. Granted, it's paired with a 700-series GTX Titan, and we all know that it's the graphics card that does the heavy lifting in modern games. Still, I never would have even taken a chance and bought this game due to its nominal quad-core requirement, had I not tried it on a freeplay weekend first; Steam, I get that you don't want people complaining because they bought games that their systems can't possibly handle, but you're hurting your sales by overspecing the minimum system requirements. Amusingly, you actually *recommend* a quad-core i7 3.77GHz for this game, and for the life of me I don't understand how or why you think it's at all pertinent.
Now on to the game itself. Checkpoints. Really?! Yeah, I'm about to go into this crazy-hard area in which I know I have a good chance of dying, but if I do die then oh well I guess I'll just have to repeat the half-hour I've spent getting here since the last checkpoint. I mean, it's not as if I have a job, a house to maintain/repair, pets to take care of, friends or family I might like to see, a gym membership, or any other hobbies whatsoever besides playing this game. I have games from the 90s that allow me to save anywhere/anytime, that additionally allow me to restart the level (using a quiet autosave that the game handles in the background) in case things go catastrophically wrong. Is this 1995 or 2017? Am I playing a console or a PC? There's no excuse for this.
The graphics in this game are quite amazing. I've experimented at different resolutions, and things even look stunning at 1024x768, due to the miraculous shadings and reflections. The gore that accompanies melee ("glory") kills would impress a mortician or ER doctor with its realism.
For the most part, I actually do like this game; the first two hours felt a bit uninspired, but it definitely picked up impressively after that. This checkpoint thing is beyond ridiculous, though, considering that I'M NOT AN UNEMPLOYED TEENAGER LIVING IN MOM'S BASEMENT AND DON'T HAVE TIME TO REPEAT 30+ MINUTES OF GAME TIME EVERY TIME SOMETHING CATCHES ME OFF-GUARD OR I MISS A JUMP.

OPUS is a short and sweet experience - about 2.5 hours for my completionist run, just right.
The core gameplay mechanic is a simple but unique mix of "find the hidden object" and map memorization, of all things. You operate a futuristic space telescope and are tasked with finding a series of planets and other astronomical objects given only a very incomplete skymap, some cryptic hints, and a couple of magic decoder keyring-style tools.
This might sound monotonous, but there is sufficient variety and the game had a well balanced difficulty ramp. More importantly, I was always highly motivated to find each new planet in order to unlock the next chapter of the story. The plot and setting form the core of this game - if not that unique or groundbreaking, it was still very touching and well written. You start out with the goal of (re)discovering the long lost planet Earth in order to save a distant future version of humanity, but this cliched opening quickly gives way to more personal motivations. The story and characterizations are revealed through a combination of dialog, found artifacts, and flashbacks - once again, quite sparse but effective at letting you fill in the details of what happened in the past.
Some technical issues were my only real complaints. On my Surface Pro 3, the cinematics were inexplicably very choppy (probably less than 5 frames per second for what I assume would be a 24fps movie); in addition, there was an alarmingly high number of typos - "hybernation", missing prepositions, incorrect plurals, etc. But they don't detract heavily from a well worthwhile experience.

A fun beat 'em up with some modern gaming elements thrown in that make for a unique and enjoyable experience.
The combat, while not overly complex, feels good and has just enough moves to make it interesting.  The controls are easy to grasp and feel tight enough that you'll be rolling around and dash attacking with wreckless abandon in no time.  And while the levels are linear (fitting with the beat 'em up genre), the randomized layout, enemies and loot help to keep it from becoming too repetitive too quickly.
While I don't think it has the sheer volume of special items that Binding of Isaac has, it does have a bit of that same feel with certain items altering your character's appearance and granting special abilities.  There is a nice mix of different weapons, items, potions and spells that can be found randomly that will keep you looking for more.
However, the game is surprisingly hard, at least initially, but not in an artificial way.  The game will generally give you warning when enemies are about to attack.  You really have to pay attention and know when to dodge or otherwise avoid being hit.  One lapse of concentration can also cause you to accidentally roll off a cliff or miss a jump and leave you falling to your death.

I've only played the game for a few hours with a friend, but I can say that it was well worth the price of admission. Great Roguelike-game with many aspects resembling that of the Binding of Isaac, with the difficulty of Dark Souls (yeah I went there). There are six classes, five of which must be unlocked, and are all rather unique in set ups and play styles, all of which is not without its own pro's and con's (save for the Adventurer class). Playing co-op allows for some fun synergies and the ability to revive one another by killing a certain amount of enemies, making the pressure both intense and fun. Single player is also do-able as enemies are less in number and bosses with less health, alongside having two lives unlike co-op, plus the fact that items you find are all yours for the taking.
Pro's:
*Multiple levels of difficulty in a game where even the lower setting can kick your teeth in.
*Very Rogue-like being that items empower the way you play on top of a combat system that focuses on your ability to be aware of your surroundings.
*Random generation in all areas, yet each area has unique aspects that are retainned.
*Replayability is very high; lots of achievements that makes you feel like a giddy 12-year old playing CoD for the first time.
*(Co-op only) Bosses are excellently designed so that dead players can revive (kind of a must-play to see the value in).
Meh~:
*Co-op is much more fun than singleplayer, but take of that what you will.
*The difficulty is extreme; every hit counts, may or may not appeal to most. (Perm-Death on all but lowest difficulty).
*Friendly-Fire when playing Co-op; does not do damage but annoyingly knocks one another around. Hard to avoid.
Cons:
*No true customization of characters; you're given a list of pre-made characters of males and females (though less female costumes).
*Items tend to be seen multiple times; you can actually get an item, find it again, and have it stack, though most of the time it's a weapon you've already passed on.
*Some runs can be very imbalanced due to room generation and the types of monsters spawning (example: you can play through an area with all little enemies, or meet a room with all giants, or even not find any worthwhile treasures at all.
*Hitboxes can be very annoying and frustrating; jumping well-over enemies to be hit anyway really sucks, the game is very roll oriented since most enemies that you ignore will spam you with projectiles.
*(Co-op only) HE. KEEPS. TAKING. MY. SH*T.

One of the best games of the decade and probably the best reboot of all time.
Unlike Doom 3, this one is MUCH closer to the original games and a much better reboot than Doom 3 ever was. All the weapons and almost all of the enemies from Doom1&2 return (along with a few new ones!) and while for the most part they're implemented in ways you'd expect, Doom 2016 brings some fresh ideas to the table. All weapons now have 3 firing modes, enemies have new looks, attacks and patterns, you can find upgrades for your guns (most of which are fantastic, but a few are kinda meh) and even for Doomguy himself, secrets now reward you with unlockable extras & upgrade points and even the story is good! You now also have an excellent 3D map, which nullifies all chances of the player ever getting lost even without any upgrades.
One of the most fun new additions is how much more vertical Doom has become (with one level being a giant tower you have to climb and it's extremely fun). You can jump (!) and climb ledges (!!) and that's not only used for platforming, but it is also used extensively in combat! Surrounded by imps? A Pinky is charging at you? Why dodge when you can climb higher! It adds countless ways to aproach the combat of the game, especially when not two levels look the same. Every level throws something different at you and the game never loses steam. Unlike Doom 3, the boss battles are outstanding and very difficult.
But this is Doom, I hear you say! It's good that they nailed the gameplay and look of Doom with some new ideas, but what about the violence and gore that Doom is so well known for? And what about Hell? There was barely any Hell in Doom 3! And did you say that the story is GOOD in DOOM?! Slow down, friend, we'll get to those very soon... Sit back and relax, there's still much to be told.
Doom 2016 makes Mortal Kombat look kid-friendly. It's got blood and guts all over the place, you can pull off Fatalities on ALL the enemies (Yes, ALL of them!) and they're actually different depending on what part of the body you target! And yes, they're GORY as hell! The chainsaw might be my favorite weapon in the game, I cannot describe how satisfying it is to cut up demons while their insides are being sprayed all over the place and I hear the glorious sounds of flesh being sliced and bone being crushed. Hands down, the best chainsaw ever. Even when you merely shoot down enemies, the game still feels the need to spread Kill Bill levels of blood everywhere.
As for Hell, there are several long Hell levels! It doesn't just look or feel like Hell, it IS Hell! You're in the home of the demons, so now they're extra♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ which make the Hell levels among the hardest in the game. They're also a welcome change of appearance, and feature much more asymetrical level design than the UAC levels. The music also changes to creepy ambience and chants for when you're not fighting.
Speaking of music, Mick Gordon is GOD. His music enhances the game in so many ways and a lot of his songs feature melodies from older Doom games! Even when you just listen to it, you know it wouldn't fit any other game but Doom and that's what makes it so good.
Before I mentioned that even the story is good and yeah, it's surprisingly good. The game gives you just enough exposition to keep you going without ever placing the story over the gameplay. For more exposition, you can find hidden items which unlock logbook entries Metroid Prime-style, giving you info on the enemies and the backstory of the game.
Now that they made all the multiplayer DLC free it's better than ever! Multiplayer was pretty fun from what I played, although there weren't many players. Snapmap is also pretty fun, although I can't imagine it will replace Doom WADs.
All in all, it's an extension and an improvement over the classic Doom formula. A must-buy and a testament to how reboots SHOULD be done.

If there is one word that best describes Deus Ex: Human Revolution, it would be choices. During the game you will be making a lot of them. Early in the game you have limited inventory space and you have to decide what you want to take with you and what you leave behind. You cannot take everything with you, no matter how hard you try. You have to decide early on which play style best suits you, which type of weapons you want to use for that play style, how much ammo you take with you for each weapon, which grenades and mines you want to use, and the list goes on. Inventory management is not unusual in Human Revolution, you will be doing a lot of it. In many games this would be considered a bad thing, players want to play a game after all, not manage the inventory all the time. But in Human Revolution it is part of what gives it its soul, choices. One tip though, invest in the Carrying Capacity augmentations early on, you will thank yourself for it later on.
And here we come to another important part with the choices you make, praxis kits and upgrading your augmentations. For example, you can decide to invest heavily in the hacking augmentations and use security measures like turrets and robots against their owners. Or you could go the route of stealth and silence, waiting for the right moment to take out the unsuspecting guard, using lethal or non lethal takedowns or a variety of weaponry. You can also choose to take a more direct approach, investing in armor and resistances, like a flash suppressant, which protects against concussion grenades. For the combat lovers among us, there is also an augmentation called the Typhoon Explosive System, which expels fragmentation grenades outward, ideal for taking out groups (and bosses).
There are also upgrades to find for the weapons you can use. The basic pistol for example, can be upgraded with a laser sight, silencer, armor piercing kit, reload speed upgrades, ammo capacity, rate of fire and damage upgrades. Yet another way to diversify your game and play the way you want.
An augmentation called C.A.S.I.E., which gives you a psychological profile during conversations, and gives you the option to persuade people your way, is another way to approach certain situations. The outcome of such a conversation can really influence how you play the game. Early on in Detroit, you are sent to the morgue of the local police station, by your boss David Sarif, to retrieve a data chip from a dead hacker. At the lobby you meet an old colleague, Wayne Haas. You ask him for a favor and if you can talk your way past him, you can move freely through the police station. If not however, you have to sneak your way into the building and the officers present will shoot you on sight, they do not ask questions first! Please note however, that the C.A.S.I.E. augmentation is not needed for a successful persuasion, it just makes it easier.
Human Revolution always gives you multiple solutions to achieve a certain goal and herein lies its greatest strength. In Lower Hengsha, you have to investigate the former hideout of a hacker called Windmill. It is protected by Belltower personnel, a private military company. You could try to enter through the front door of the complex, but this is also the path of heavy resistance, a path that a combat oriented player could choose. You could also try to get to the apartment via the roof and make your way down, a path more likely chosen by a stealth oriented player. This does not mean however that a stealth oriented player cannot enter through the front door, you most certainly can, it just takes more patience. Even after multiple playthroughs I am still not sure if I have seen all possible entry ways.
The story and world of Human Revolution is conveyed through conversations, emails and datapads. For example, during your first mission at the Milwaukee Junction factory, where the production of the Typhoon system is planned, you can read a lot of emails from the employees working there. While it is in no way necessary to do so, you can achieve your goals by skipping it, it does help to flesh out the game world. It is recommended for the first time playthrough to read as much as you can or want.
The graphics are not amazing, but functional. The developer, Eidos Montreal, wanted to evoke a modern renaissance look, to further emphasize the point that humanity is at a crossroads. They mostly succeeded in doing so. One thing you will notice is the NPC models and how many of them look alike. This is a recurring point throughout the game but especially in the hub cities of Detroit and Lower Hengsha. Nixxes Software has done an excellent job porting the game to PC. The game has all the graphical options you would expect from modern titles, including a FOV slider. It runs well, even on average gaming rigs. I did have an issue with camera stuttering, but after looking for a solution on
, was able to fix it. The sounds, same as the graphics, are not special but good enough. Sound does play a crucial role with stealth though, make too much noise and the guards will come to investigate the spot where they heard something. The game has a few memorable soundtracks, especially the main theme Icarus, the main menu track, and the excellent track Everybody Lies.
So who is this game aimed at? To answer that question you must remember that this is a game with brains. It is in no way easy going, even on normal difficulty. You can play it as a shooter, as long as you use cover all the time and move around. But it really shines as a stealth action game. You get extra experience bonuses for achieving your main goals without being detected (Ghost) and without any alarms going off (Smooth Operator). Deus Ex: Human Revolution offers a great stealth experience and if you approach it in that way, you will really enjoy it!

For a free to play game, I wasn't really expecting that much from this but boy was I in for a surprise...
Here are my reasons for recommending this game:
Story:
-The main storyline is intricate and interesting meaning you always want to know what happens next with the constant plot twists and never-ending mystery. Especially with no voice actors whatsoever, I feel that it adds a new perspective to how you view the story and lets your imagination do the work for you.
Leveling and Skilltree System:
- Leveling in this game to me isn't that difficult and will be easy for those who are new to the game. This is because you need only follow the main questline. However, at later levels at 55-60+, the Exp requirement is stepped up a notch. In addition, the skilltree system is complex in its structure but simple to navigate and understand in a short amount of time.
Graphics:
- The graphics are surprisingly good. Great detail on the character models, weapons, VFX and terrain. This added detail always compliments a well-layed storyline. (Play on medium+ for maximum effect).
Premium Currency (Known as Aeria Points):
- As always, you get the temptation of paying real money to get an edge in the game. The payment system in AK is supported through steam as well as their online store. The one major advantage of paying for premium currency is that the amount that you spend in a month goes towards a loyalty feature that gives you rewards at certain milestones. As these milestones increase, the rewards get better and better. I haven't personally bought any but if you are, I would recommend the online store as it gives you bonus AP.
Side note:
For anyone who was permanently banned, the main reason for this is that you probably bought gold from a third party for a cheap amount of cash but you haven't realised that it is against the Terms of Service that they stick to 24/7. If anything other than this reason, then try to contact them directly. So, I wouldn't advise buying in-game currency from any third party sites whatsoever, as there is pretty much a 100% chance that your account will get permanently banned.
In conclusion, if anyone likes the following in a game, then I fully recommend you to download and install this game:
- Good & Immersive Story
- Great Graphics
- Extensive Leveling & Complex Skill System
- Option to use IRL money to buy yourself an advantage
- Kind & Friendly Player Community
- Anime based Character Models
- Wide Variety of Costumes to wear
- Quest Grinding
- And of course that you like Fantasy MMORPGs with PVE & PVP elements!

I was initially very sceptical of this controller, and to be fair I only use it for games like XCOM 2 (which has an official Firaxis config) The Sims 4 (Pain to stream, but it can be done) and any other non twitch style game.  For those purposes it actually feels surprisingly natural.  It almost doesn't feel like a mouse and keyboard emulation but rather it's own periferal (not flighty like xpadder).  The only recomendation I would make to the developers is to add a functionality to open the keyboard without using the steam overlay.
I can't vouch for shooters or fighting games as I would rather use a traditional controller anyways, but I think it's awesome for what I use it for.

There's no in between so say I MAY recommend this controller. It's either yes or no, but I would say I could recommend it based only on what your needs are for a wireless PC controller. The button placement is pretty weird and I much prefer the 360 contoller over this, BUT for strategy games etc it's by far the best option aside from M+KB. There is some button latency/lag and on occasion it can be the difference of winning or losing which sucks but it usually an issue with most wireless devices. Build quality is average, nothing horrible but not great either. It feels like a $30 controller not $50.

The Steam Controller won't be like any controller you've used before. It will take a lot of time to get used to it and you might get frustrated sometimes attempting to use. I believe that it is worth it.  The controller is highly customizable and can be used to play any Steam game, whether it has controller support or not. You can create your own custom controls for all of your games and save them under your Steam account and even change the sounds the controller makes when you power it on or off. Overall, I would give this a controller a 9/10, only because I still prefer to use a different controller or just a keyboard and mouse for FPS games.

First:
THIS GAME WAS NOT ABANDONED FOR PS4. IGNORE ALL REVIEWS THAT SAY THIS. THE PS4 VERSION WAS ESSENTIALLY A PUBLIC BETA OF 5.0 AND WAS A BIT TOO P2W SO THE DEVS DECIDED TO NOT RUIN THE PC VERSION BY ADDING IT TO IT. BOTH GAMES REMAIN UN-UPDATED NOW
Loadout is a beatiful game, with an amazing art-style, combat, and weapon customization.
So it is very painfull for me that I have to say this but... Loadout is dead, and the twitching is stopping.
Why/how is it dead? i hear you ask, well here is my version of the storyline:
Part 1, all was going well- Loadout was alive and kicking, youtubers including Pewdiepie and Nerdcubed were reccomending it, the devs had an amazing F2P model, and the game just had straight up STYLE! But, we never knew what was going to come
Part 2, a villian emerges- The devs had given us a few hints on a big update called 5.0, with a few nods at cyro, beta maps and maybe even a PS4 release!
Part 3, PS4- The PS4 version had been announced and released, so had a beta game for 5.0, the hype was real
Part 4, something fishy- The 5.0 beta had also come across with some news that when it was implemented, all progress would be wiped, scaring off quite a few players, doubled with the extremely controversial 5.0 P2W system that was seen in the beta, which postponed the update
Part 5, death awaits- The PC version of Loadout was untouched for months, and numbers of players dwindled, yet the PS4 had news of a large update in the future
Part 6, RIP- ALL BUT TWO of the devs at EOR had been fired, and the *last* large update had come out for loadout, and you guessed it, it was for PS4. BUT DON'T WORRY! PC got an update aswell... that changed damage on some barrels by 1-2%. Meanwhile the PS4 had just been given a new gamemode, maps, (it even had a new character) and taunts, but PC, is dead. The chance of a revival is slim (again 2 devs people) but if that day comes, I will be waiting.
Part 7, hope- I PERSONALLY hope that Loadout is `on hold` from the devs, while they make more small ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game ports etc. (like they did before loadout) to make some more money, they then will return to Loadout (the game "they wanted to play") and revive it, by porting over the PS4 stuff adding the 5.0 campaign etc. and cyro+ beta maps. But again, this is just me hoping. If it does die I will use my life savings to buy it from the devs and revive it :P
Remember:
Loadout will only die, when the players die
Oh, and this IS NOT P2W you can only buy cosmetics, yeah you can buy X2 boosters, but they don't really effect anything at all- you play for a tiny amount of time and you can customise the gun you want, halfing the (few games) worth of time doesn't make a difference, and for level boosters... levels mean NOTHING. Felt like I had to put this in as this is the biggest turn-off from F2P games.
Edit:
I made this a positive review as Loadout is -bottom line- a good game.
The extremely sad thing about Loadout is that it didn't die from the devs being greedy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s or through it aging badly... it died from the devs being too passionate about their game. They wanted everyone to play it, hence F2P, and made THE BEST F2P model I have ever seen, as they didn't want to give an advantage to other players who paid more. They then tried to push the game to console and realised that they ran out of money. I once saw someone say "Fool me once etc." about this game, but if anything, Loadout shows how much EOR care about their games. "Fool me once" should be used to describe Overkill software for treating their audience like wallets, not for EOR (yes their CEO might not be amazing at buisiness decisions) but they DO care. I love you Loadout :(
Edit:
It was just revealed on the forums that they actually ran out of money before the PS4 version, and a publisher gave them an injection of money if they made a PS4 version. So they didn't even leave to PS4 as a last resort, they never even intended to leave PC. Damn.

Pros:

Great little co-op roguelike brawler.  Online co-op works pretty well, with just a couple of lag spikes so far in my 4 hours of online play.  A few things could be tweaked in my opinion, such as not being able to knock your teammate over with friendly fire - they don't take damage, but they can be knocked over which can lead to bad things.
This game is fairly challenging, but you will get better as you learn monster attack patterns and make use of ranged attacks, throwables, and the terrain.  Casual difficulty does not seem to really lower the actually difficulty, it just lets you restart the current level if you die versus starting at the beginning of the game.
There is some cheapness in the game which I wish would go away.  My friend in co-op says he cannot see the red circle that appears to tell you where the Mighty Foot will strike when I have the curse, so he has no good way of dodging it.  Having large monsters that can jump diagonally and strike so quickly is surprising...you can adapt to it, but their agility seems odd considering their size.  Minions that randomly strike the area around you should not attack exploding barrels - that just sucks.  Also when you have the magic carpet and the mighty foot curse, I think you should have the red circle overlay the carpet so you can tell when the foot will strike.
Also I feel the sound levels are too high in this game.  I have to turn sound to 5% and music to 0% to hear my friend over steam voice chat (and yes my receive volume in voice chat is cranked to max).
That sounds like a lot of complaints, but even in light of the 'cheap' difficulty, my friend and I are having a blast.  We bought the two pack on sale for $15 and will probably get a good 10+ hours out of it.  Not a bad deal.  The art style is enjoyable, there are lots of humorous moments, the random level elements and drops make each run unique, and there is a good balance of challenge versus fun.  It's not quite up to Castle Crashers, but it's a great time with a buddy.

I wish my only options weren't thumbs up or thumbs down, because I'd give this game 3 out of 5 stars: not bad, fun in a lot of ways, but could have been better too.
First off, the minimum system requirements are way off. Though I own this game now, I started playing it on a freeplay weekend, and just for fun I tried it on a dual-core Pentium Extreme Edition (3.73GHz, 2M L2 cache). It runs like a charm on here, despite the quad-core i5 (2.4GHz, 6M L2 cache) processor Steam claims is a bare minimum for this game. Granted, it's paired with a 700-series GTX Titan, and we all know that it's the graphics card that does the heavy lifting in modern games. Still, I never would have even taken a chance and bought this game due to its nominal quad-core requirement, had I not tried it on a freeplay weekend first; Steam, I get that you don't want people complaining because they bought games that their systems can't possibly handle, but you're hurting your sales by overspecing the minimum system requirements. Amusingly, you actually *recommend* a quad-core i7 3.77GHz for this game, and for the life of me I don't understand how or why you think it's at all pertinent.
Now on to the game itself. Checkpoints. Really?! Yeah, I'm about to go into this crazy-hard area in which I know I have a good chance of dying, but if I do die then oh well I guess I'll just have to repeat the half-hour I've spent getting here since the last checkpoint. I mean, it's not as if I have a job, a house to maintain/repair, pets to take care of, friends or family I might like to see, a gym membership, or any other hobbies whatsoever besides playing this game. I have games from the 90s that allow me to save anywhere/anytime, that additionally allow me to restart the level (using a quiet autosave that the game handles in the background) in case things go catastrophically wrong. Is this 1995 or 2017? Am I playing a console or a PC? There's no excuse for this.
The graphics in this game are quite amazing. I've experimented at different resolutions, and things even look stunning at 1024x768, due to the miraculous shadings and reflections. The gore that accompanies melee ("glory") kills would impress a mortician or ER doctor with its realism.
For the most part, I actually do like this game; the first two hours felt a bit uninspired, but it definitely picked up impressively after that. This checkpoint thing is beyond ridiculous, though, considering that I'M NOT AN UNEMPLOYED TEENAGER LIVING IN MOM'S BASEMENT AND DON'T HAVE TIME TO REPEAT 30+ MINUTES OF GAME TIME EVERY TIME SOMETHING CATCHES ME OFF-GUARD OR I MISS A JUMP.

Words cannot describe how much I love this game and I have lost count of how many times I have played it from beginning to end.
Even though the game is ridiculously bugged and in many ways flawed (in its original form**); the gritty grainy charm, the uncompromising dialogue and gory pixilated body explosions on a critical hit or by using a massive enough gun are just unparalleled, even when compared to the more modern instalments of the franchise.
The retro pop-50s, hilariously grotesque depiction of a post-apocalyptic future is iconic and unmatched, it creates a post-eschatological environment that is equally gruesome as it is enjoyable.
With that said, I love all of the other iterations of the game universe including those done by Bethesda, even Fallout 4, but none of them really compare to Fallout 2, only New Vegas comes close.
I cherish my adventures with Sulik and his dialogue with his nose-bone, I laugh every time I buff John Cassidy in the heat of battle but forget his heart condition leading to his demise and of course the possibility of being reunited with Dogmeat from Fallout 1.
I also love that you can make a character with such a low intelligence score that virtually all dialogue is impossible (as you are more or less unable to speak) and yet, you can complete the game in a meaningful way.
I will be playing this game again and again, and force my children to do that same.
And if they refuse, I will disown them.
This game is indeed; a kiss to build a dream on..
** This is a review of the original game, not Bethesda’s polished version.

When I first saw a playthrough of Episode 1 of this game, I thought it wasn't very appealing - the humor seemed off, it didn't seem to have a story or characters that were that interesting. It was on sale recently, and I picked it up cause I enjoy Telltale, and I found that I had sadly misjudged this game.
When the game starts up, your character is a simple young man/woman, all they hope for is to win a contest with their friends and perhaps meet a hero of theirs if they win. As most adventures do, things get more complicated.
I won't spoil what happens specifically, but the game really takes off in the latter bits of Episode 1, and from there the story gets better and better.
It makes great use of the Minecraft game physics/world, and players of the game will appreciate the attention to detail.
This game is also very "family-friendly" compared to most other Telltale games of late, so if you have any kids wanting to play it, it has a rare minor swear word, but nothing you wouldn't hear in most movies. The humor and dialogue is good though, this isn't something an adult will really have issues with.
The story itself is actually pretty good. There's a main story arc, and it ends at a certain episode and after that, each episode is sort of a self-contained story. In my view, those stories were stronger and more interesting than the main one. I began to get more into the game, and the characters grow on you, of course. The "Adventure Pass" is worth it, but I'd wait for a sale on everything regardless.
There's a few minor glitches that I experienced - dialogue being cut off or not being heard at all. The familiar "X will remember that" glitching so you see just a "?" or "!" instead (which didn't last too long, and fixed itself).
The writing is fine, it's not as strong as other Telltale games, but as I said, this had a more family-friendly game experience in mind, and so it reflects that. Sometimes a character would state the obvious, or the humor would come off a bit too "nice", at first that was a bit off for me, but it gets better as the episodes go on.
In the end, this was a good Telltale game and I'd buy this with the Adventure Pass on sale, which in total is around $10-11. I got about 14 hours out of the game, which is me talking to most everyone, looking around etc; That's a pretty good deal. I am looking forward to playing Season 2 when it's lowered in price a bit.

- Cool Items! I really enjoyed messing around with the different vehicles and stunt jumps. While there aren't a huge number of weapons in the game, you usually have 4-5 choices per weapon class to use.
- Missions are fun! For a lot of games like SR2 missions can get tedious, but I never got that feeling for this game. The SR series doesn't take itself very seriously, but I felt like the character development was solid and I felt invested in the characters.
- Car customisation is solid. I always liked this aspect in SR2. It was just something fun to do if you didn't want to do missions. Just customise a car and drive around the map :)
Cons:
- Audio Bug. Sometimes when my computer is heating up and my CPU is working decently hard, the audio in the game is the first to go. It will crackle in and out, or just sections of it will stop working, like the ambience will keep going, but my gunshot sounds will go silent for a few seconds, then cut back in. I fixed this by simply shutting the game down and restarting it after a few minutes. If you have an advanced rig, I don't think the audio bug will be a problem.
- Mission Bugs. There are only a few mission bugs in this whole game, but I wanted to make them known. They're just problems in the port of the game. I solved all mission bugs by consulting Google when they arose.
- The "Respect" System. The Respect System (for those that don't know) is used in SR2 to make sure that the player can't just do all the missions at once, and it forces the player to explore the map and its various environments by killing enemy gang members, doing stunt jumps, etc. Sometimes this can get tedious, especially later in the game when you are on the brink of a climactic event and have to go grind for respect levels. I understand it was implemented in good taste, but it can get tedious.
Hope this informed some of y'all about this game. Overall grade: 9/10. Got it for free in April 2017 through the Steam Store. Lots of replay value for its price!

OPUS is a heart touching journey that you would remember for a long time!
This is my second playthrough of the game. I got the game first on Android and immediately loved it. It is not a game you can pull out of your pocket and play for 5 minutes. It is a game you need to leave yourself alone, put on your headphones, and immerse into the world.
The music is just AMAZING! Especially at the ending, I can still feel it resonates from deep of my heart. The story is very touching and well arranged. Compared with the first mobile version I played, all the story moment is now fully and nicely animated, which is something I want badly. Super happy I played it again on PC.
Also as a side effect of knowing the story beforehand, now all the items in the spaceship carry different meanings, not only the background story but also hints here and there. I'm surprised to find out the pictures on the wall, Lisa's notes and books, the name of stars and planets discovered by Lisa now all make sense. More deeply the game is full of metaphors. If you read carefully, the name and symbols for each zone and sections, the default name of the stars, the room background in the spaceship are all meaningful! I'll stop here rather than spoil it. But really, these are the stuff you would probably only find out in a second round.
I always prefer a condensed awesome and meaningful experience than long mediocre hours, and OPUS hit right in my sweet spot. Would love to see more games like this coming from this studio!
