I'll say first that I've been a supporter for the original OPUS on mobile, so I am very glad to see the game got released on Steam with various enhancements, and willing to play and finish it again on my PC.
From a PC game point of view, you might feel like it is just a twist on the hidden-object genre, with some memorization elements. And if you'd bother to check a little bit more you'll also find out the game last no longer than 2 hrs for average players. But in fact that's exactly part the point of this game:
For a novel, fresh experience & gameplay in games, you don't absolutely need 50hrs of play time or super innovative, convoluted, unseen or complex mechanics to achieve those. There are all kinds of interesting short and interesting games in the indie scene right now that you won't regret paying 5 or 10 bucks on them. For 90 ~ 120 minutes of the gameplay, OPUS provides a quite touching, and even deep, philosophical experience, if you know what you are looking at.
I am an avid space-themed media junkie, so the astronomical side of OPUS also highly interests me. But there's a thin layer of somewhat deceiving sugarcoat there, if I may say so. The scientific detail or the accuracy of terms and descriptions in the game sometimes doesn't add-up, even though improvements have already been made since the mobile version. But again, that's not really the point.
I am going to boldly claim that the game's astronomical / science aspect is only there to support it's narrative, just like Interstellar (YES, THAT CHRIS NOLAN MOVIE) -- even more, the central idea of OPUS can actually draw a few parallel comparison from Interstellar directly.
You know right from the beginning of the game, that hundred of thousands years into the distant future, human race has somehow forgotten its origin, and Earth has long become a myth. And one important character in game totally doesn't believe there is even an Earth at all. Just like in Interstellar, the general public has long "disapprove" the idea that human has been to the Moon and beyond, and no one believe in any of those grand idea anymore.
Of course, I am not really claiming that a small indie team can produce something that really rivals a worldly-acclaimed award-winning Hollywood movie, nor does it take as serious an approach to science as the Nolan film to cover its philosophical / spiritual ideas, but it's already an effort very rarely seen in games, in my opinion.
To say anything more about the narrative or story about OPUS would be a huge spoiler for the game itself, so I'll stop here. I only hope that my review can help you look into the game a little bit more, before you start nitpicking its problems. The game is not expensive, it will not cost you a lot of time and energy, the gameplay is smooth and I think the difficulty curve is just right for this kind of experience. So by all means try it out for yourself!

Take the rogue-like element of The Binding of Isaac, the combat and style of Golden Axe, add the humour of Castle Crashers and you get this wonderful game!
For me, Rampage Knights ticks all the right boxes.
+ Very enjoyable combat. I really like swinging and throwing enemies around and stomping those nasty skeletons on their faces. Sometimes it is a little bit too easy to bash enemies into a pit, but it's a valid tactic I guess.
+ The thing I enjoyed most about BoI was the random item combinations you end up with. Rampage Knights has less items, but there are still a lot of interesting combinations to be made. In one playthrough I got a curse that summoned explosive barrels in every room; luckily I found an item that made me immune to explosions. I really enjoy it if a game allows you to use a seemingly negative effect (such as a curse) as a positive thing.
+ Nice bit of humour, silly animations, goofy characters.
+ The game can be difficult, but it is never really unfair. If you die, it's your own fault - you can do better next time and learn to avoid that damage.
The only downside I can think of is that there isn't any global progression over all your playthroughs. You can unlock some new classes, but that's it. A nice mechanic that a lot of rogue-likes (BoI, Rogue Legacy) have is that you slowly build up your progress every time you die, unlocking new stuff, which slightly increases your chance of a succesful run. Rampage Knights just puts you back to square one every time, but I guess it works for this game.
I finished the game in about 10 hours, but I definitely want to play this some more with a friend in local coop.
The developers also wrote on the forums that they will release more content for free later on.

In Fallout 2, you're a tribal with nothing else other than a spear, fighting giant ants. It shouldn't be a big deal for players who are used to it, but I've seen people complaining about dying way too much at the beginning of Fallout 2 (and guess what, a lot of them never even played the first one!). I think I've played and finished this game more than enough to say that I loved it, and I still do, as I enjoy playing it from time to time, and try some different cool builds. It saddens me to have to Not Recommend this game, but I have done so for a couple of reasons.
1) This is the first TellTale game that adds an extra "Pass" to an already purchased season. Though The Walking Dead had 400 Days, it didn't involve any characters from the first season and set up some characters for the second. In this case, it was acceptable (barely). Here you have "Season 1" but you also have the 'Adventure Pass" which adds 3 extra episodes to the 5 included with the Season Pass. To me this is dishonest as it isn't a Season Pass at all. Imagine you bought Season 1 of whatever show, say It's Always Sunny in Philidelphia which is 8 episodes, but the Blu-Ray you buy only has 5 and you have to buy the extra 3 separately in a "Comedy Pass"
2) There are a LOT of technical issues that creep up. More than I have ever experienced in a Telltale game. From Text not matching what is being said to dialog that is cut off mid-sentence, to the information bubbles not showing any information other than a ! or a ? and choices that aren't even displayed at the end.
Obviously these things don't stop you from completing the game, but they definately impede in the enjoyment. For me anyway and considering how many of these things TellTale has done, it's disheartening to see so many stupid issues that shouldn't be there. I hope this isn't a sign that Telltale think they're too big to polish their games like happens to too many great developers. This is why I went with Not Recommended. Sorry Telltale, try better next time.

I find this controller a viable option for most games. But also I'm not one to play many FPS. so most of my games don't require quick pinpoint accuracy with fast paced action. I do own a few of these titles which i've tried on the controller, and will explain.
So the best way to compair this controller is to the xbone controller. So as you know, there's many titles out there that simply don't support controllers. this is defiently where the steam controller can work. it has the ability to map any button to anything, along with the triggers to be mapped to alternate mappings kinda like a mode shift with all the buttons able to be mapped to a diffrent set of keys, or atleast that's my understanding. (something i havn't needed to play around with yet) and the triggers on the steam controller suport turbo aswell. these are all features, you simply can't get on the xbox one controller, without a 3rd party application.
Now in the messaging friend in big piture mode the steam controller has a unique layout, where you can use both touch pads to select charrecters and type a message, fairly quickly. xbone controller has no support for this, so it can be rather convient when you're loungin' as a couch potato, and you friend requiers your attention. I can say that i get around 10-15 WPM on the steam controller. it also is able to have full control over my PC. i found i could launch games with a launcher even with the controller and apply settings using the right touch pad as a mouse. and right trigger as a left click. now done with the UI part.
let's talk about a game that does support the xbone controller and also using the steam controller. i'll discuss a game i enjoy, it's a rogue-lite title named Ziggurat. in this game it's aiming style is simmular to unreal torniment. with the xbone controller i found i had to use a clumbsy aiming style using the analog sticks with adjusting my charracters movement to assist in a more percise airm. with the steam controller i found i had more of a pricise aim, as it also gave me feedback on how fast my thumb was moving on the sensor with strange "clicks" but the feedback felt natural, and good. this allowed a much easier transition from keyboard and mouse to controller. now i didn't have the same fast and accurate percision is i did with the mouse. but it wasn't bad either. and it wasn't hard to get used to the touchpads either. you can compair the sensor of the touchpad like that on a laptop. but, it also comes with that feedback which i find it helps gadge how fast my charactor would spin the direction i'm applying. i can also say this for many other games. but, where i feel the steam controller really comes into a nice nitche for me, is RTS's. i've been playing some titles such as Galatic Civilazations III with this controller. and found i actually prefer it this way. in a enviornment where i can lounge on the sofa, bag of munchies at my side. and just get lost in strategic gameplay. it also opens the enviornmet more to a sorta social gameplay. my roomate sometimes will join me, and we'll debate on inproper and proper moves to take. plans of action. and even this allows him to enjoy the pc side some. as he's strictly all 'bout consol. in these ways i've found the steam controller amazing. and he's been easily able to make this jump from a xbone controller to a steam controller. i could keep going on about the pros of this controller. but that'd be a rather long review. so...
In conclusion: It's not for those fastpaced games with FPS elements. I find it far more suitable for RTS's, indie, and top downs.

My previous review felt really bloated so here's a simpler one.
The steam controller shines in its configurability, BUT, that's sometimes very difficult to plan out - I had to diagram layouts for some of my games.But it's not too big an issue thanks to community configs you can try which are pretty sweet.
You have to go into big picture mode to use custom configs for your games, BUT, if hitting the steam button on your controller is too much of a hassle, you can map a default configuration for the controller to use in desktop mode, such as when you just want to just use it as an xbox gamepad.
Speaking of gamepads, you have to hold the Steam controller more broadly, in order to comfortably reach the controls. Gripping it tightly like an Xbox/PS controller doesn't work too well.
The haptic feedback is a nice touch when using the touchpads. However, when i did turn on rumble emulation for a game, my controller felt/sounded like something was broken. Haptic feedback's fine though...maybe it was just an issue with Bioshock Remastered though.

We've all been there, playing GoldenEye or Halo multiplayer in split-screen and looking at our buddy's screen for an easy kill. It's an impossible temptation and something that everyone has done no matter how much they might deny it. Well, just like everything else that happens in the gaming world now, someone made a game about exactly that. And it's actually pretty fun, and even took steps to persist past the inevitable death of its multiplayer scene.
Screencheat is a multiplayer FPS where everyone is invisible. That would be a pretty decent hook for a shooter but it's actually in service to another gimmick, that you have to look at your opponents' screens to figure out where they are. Whether playing local or online matches the game plays in split-screen, showing you what all of your opponents are seeing at all times. Using this information you have to line up your shots to dispatch unseen adversaries, and also keep them from using your own view against you.
Everything in Screencheat is designed to support this gimmick, from the weapons to the levels themselves. Each arena is small enough for the maximum of four players to be constantly tripping over each other, and every part of it is painted in a different bright color to make it easy to figure out what part you're looking at. The game modes share this intelligence of design, like the King of the Hill mode having very small capture zones that light up with the color of the player occuping them. There are some really crazy ones that make use of the premise, like the Clue-inspired Murder Mystery where you have to kill a specific person with a specific weapon.
The weapons deserve special mention for being creative and perfect for this kind of game. There are no pickups or unlocks, just an entire library of a dozen or so armaments to choose from between lives. You've got familiar guns like a blunderbuss and a beam cannon, clever additions like ricocheting energy balls and the line launcher from Dead Space, and crazy options like exploding teddy bears and a wooden horse you can run people over with. My personal favorite is a spiked ball the size of a moon that rockets out a short way, and then blasts back towards its point of origin with terrifying speed.
All weapons have infinite ammo and are one-hit kills, as there is no health or healing to be found in Screencheat. In fact, you won't find any sort of pickups in the game at all, which is a bit of a mixed blessing. On the one hand, it keeps the action focused entirely on finding and annihilation your hidden opposition. But on the other, it cuts out a lot of the tactics that keep other multiplayer games fresh, and in doing so kind of relegates itself to more of a novelty than a shooter you can really dig into. It feels like the developers thought otherwise, since you can level your profile up through matches to unlock... stuff for your profile? I have no idea why you would bother, because this game makes a great diversion with your friends and not much else.
Even if you did want to become a Screencheat grandmaster, the online multiplayer is all but dead anyway. There's between zero and one servers up at any given time, even on weekends with the allure of double profile XP. Normally that would be enough for a thumbs down from me but the developers smartly added bots in one of their last updates, and they're clever enough to make matches worth playing solo. Like I said, it's not much more than a novelty but it's a quality one that's sure to have you hooting at getting run down by wooden horses or crushed by flying balls. Not every game has to be a cornerstone of your library, and Screencheat makes a great little break from more serious or deeper shooters.

In the short amount of time I have played this (at time of writing), I have loved every second of the experience that this game gives. Pros:

Cons:
-A little difficult to pick up, as you'll probably be staring at your own screen and not at the other players screens
-Weapons have no explanation to them other than their names, leading to you probably killing yourself to find out what the weapons do
-Might be left incapacitated from the amount of laughter that will be had
I most certainly recommend this as a party game or a game to play by yourself when you need a quick game that will incite a lot of joy and laughter. Go out, enjoy this and have fun Screencheating!

OB64 will add P2W gameplay that will make you forget about the EA and Battlefront 2 fiasco. I invested somewherein the ~$150-$200 range into this game as I felt it was worth it for development even though the chests were overly expensive and direct purchases were hard to come by.

This game is unique and, in my opinion, still holds up to this day if you get used to how it plays. No other game made me genuinely laugh out loud at a conversation that I had with an NPC, and text based, too. This game has some of the best writing you will ever see in any RPG that you have played before, and most importantly, it is addictively fun; not Fallout 4's shoot and loot fun, but more questing and talking fun. Fallout 2 is one of those unique, special games that makes you always think twice about every little decision that you make. The world is fully tailored to your actions, and you rarely decide to kill someone because it can have disastrous consequences on the story or immediate situation. Although almost all of the quests are linear, most of the endings to the quests have some form of choice that lets the outcome fall into your favor (or maybe not, which is the beauty of this game). You truly feel like you're in a post-apocalyptic world; everything in this game is HARD, difficulty wise, and brutal, atmosphere wise.
So, do I recommend this game? Yes, but only if you think you have the patience to play it. Combat can be exceedingly slow at some times, and the first 2 hours of the story can feel a bit more boring than the rest of the 46 hours playing the game. If you are looking for a hard, gritty game full of choices with a story tailored to you and a very rewarding ending, look no further than Fallout 2.

I got a steam controller for Christmas and I have logged around 100-200 hours on it so far. Initially, I was a little worried that I wouldn't like it as the default configuration was often less than perfect. Since that time, the community mappings have improved dramatically. I have also developed a feel for how I want the controller set up for various games. At this point I don't even want to bother with my keyboard and mouse! I don't think that this model will be a console killer, but it is perfect for PC junkies that want to rock the couch. It takes the kind of person who wants to fiddle with all the switches and push all the buttons to really make good use of this controller with unsupported games. That said, I have tried to play FPSs with a xbox controller and I'm certain that people thought I was drunk or 11 years old; once I got the hang of the steam controller, I feel like I'm playing at 90-100% of what I can with a keyboard and mouse.
Pros:
Extreme configurability
Living room comfort
Sharp, precise control
Cons:
High learning curve
Not ready for console junkies who expect a uniform experience
TLDR; I love this thing. Get one.

As a fan of Dead Rising and Dead Rising 2, I was sceptical of this game being set in an open world environment. I was also sceptical when other players were reporting performance issues and how the setting and psychopaths were quite bland.
Despite my scepticism, I went ahead and bought this game, anyway to form my own opinion on it and honestly it was a lot better than what I was expecting.
In essence, it's basically the same as the first 2 Dead Risings. Despite being in an open-world city, it's pretty similar to the Mall/Casino from the other 2 games. Each area is distinct, much like the different casinos in Dead Rising 2. The characters, I'd say, are on par with the other 2 games, as well. The psychopaths all have their own unique gimmicks, similar to psychopaths in previous games.
There are plenty of nods to the other games in the franchise, too, such as the Frank West trophies dotted around the map and although you can get way without playing Dead Rising 1 and 2, the storyline in this game is very much part of the same World with references and cross overs to previous games at various points.
The game improves upon many things which were annoying about the other Dead Rising games. Namely the ability to construct combo weapons anywhere so long as you're carrying the parts. I barely used Combo Weapons in Dead Rising 2 but I found myself building almost every one in Dead Rising 3. Mainly because of the ease and because each plan I found had the components needed to build it close by.
As you collect weapons and build combo weapons, they're added to your armoury, too, which can be accessed in one of the many safe houses dotted around the map. This makes accessing combo weapons a lot easier than before. I found myself relying on the Katana in older games, but in this one, I was happy to try out the fantastic combo weapons available.
A similar thing happens with style items, too. As you equip a style item, it's added to your wardrobe which is again available in your safe house. So if you want to put that favourite pair of jeans back on, you don't need to go to the store you found them in to do so.
Also, you can now finally save via the Pause menu! Books don't take up inventory space and certain large weapons (namely the chainsaw and IEDs) can be carried around in your inventory instead of being dropped. Oh and yes, there are achievements for the 50,000+ zombie deaths to unlock, but unlike previous versions (at least on the PS3/360 versions), these are continuously earned regardless of which play through you're on. No more play throughs where you spend time running over zombies in the underground!
There are some performance issues for sure, but I imagine these are caused by the huge amount of zombies on screen at any given moment (I recall getting a combo kill of 300+ zombies by detonating a combo weapon bomb in an area) and also the fact that there aren't any loading screens any more when you want to go to a new area.
As a fan of the franchise, I really enjoyed it and recommend it to anyone who loved the first 2 games. I'm sure this game will not be liked by all, even by some fans of the franchise, but overall, it's worth checking out. At least in my opinion.

The new card system might be giving us whatever we need right from the get go with all the cards, but with the new system, we can no longer use + or - to customize our loadouts and the strength of our cards will be based around RNG since we can't get to level 5 without getting duplicates.
Are we supposed to have Pride and Accomplishment for the duplicate cards that we get now?
Aside from that, it seems that we'll be able to get all our cards in our loadout to level 5 so long as we were able to get enough duplicates for it. This might appear good, but it actually removes a huge part of what made the loadout system good: balancing Pros and Cons, as well as opportunity costs. Now, people could go into quickplay and have all cards at level 5 so long as they have the duplicates for it, and in Competitive, everyone only have cards at level 3 with no variation. Everyone will become uniform, and those who have grinded long enough will have a drastically huge unfair advantage over those who only have level 1 cards.
The problem here is the very core of their proposal is what is broken. No matter how much they adjust its stats, if the core is broken, it can't be fixed. The root of the problem of this system is that it ties your progression to RNG, and it gives you innate advantages over other people. Before, everyone had 12 points -- no more, no less. With the new system, new players would have 5 points, current players would probably have around 15 points, while those who will be able to survive the awful grind for level 5 cards will be able to get a whopping 25 points. With the old system, everyone had 12 points. It's just that people who were able to grind the cards have a more versatile kit since they have a wider access to cards, but their cards are no better in terms of effectiveness than the cards of new players. Now, new players with 5 points can potentially go against an experienced player with 25 points
Before, it was fun trying to distribute 12 points into 5 cards. Because of this, you had to make a good loadout for various scenarios. For example, I have an Inara build that has one focused for walls, another one focused for warder's field, and another one for damage reduction. Now, since all cards can be at level 5 at the same time, everyone will just use level 5s. I have a Terminus build with long distance jumps for use with his stun legendary, a defensive build for cramped maps where mobility isn't that needed, a ranged build which allows me to play Terminus as a Ranged burst finisher, etc. etc.
If you truly want to make the game fun for both casual and competitive players, here's what you need to do:
Remove Essence as you've already planned
Give us all the cards as you've already planned
Maintain the current loadout system as it was already in the game
Don't ♥♥♥♥ UP a great loadout system that is very fun to tweak with its customizability due to the Pros and Cons of distributing 12 points to 5 cards and making a card loadout for various scenarios. The current system allows Casual players to just use the Default deck or pull one off straight from a person on the leaderboard, and Dedicated players can tweak their decks on their own. The new system would just reward people who have grinded more and have more level 5 cards for Casual, while the new system would just make Ranked a homogenous mess with everyone having the same loadout card levels without any personal tweak to it.
Don't ♥♥♥♥ UP Casual. The idea of having no point limits for Casual Mode is absurd. I understand Casual is less serious than Ranked, but it was still serious and could be used for practicing for Ranked. With the coming Casual changes, it would just reward people who have gotten more level 5 cards too much and having all cards at level 5 would actually break the loadouts. Heck, even Overwatch made a separate No-Limits mode for their absurdities. Once again, Keep Casual Casual and don't turn it into the abomination that it will become.
With the old system, I could spend hours tweaking and theorizing with all the permutations of the loadouts, researching loadouts that would fit my playstyle and my playstyle alone. Of course, one could easily just grab one from the leaderboard, but actually, that's the beauty of the old system. It allowed for both casual and dedicated play.
You don't care for cards? Well just go ahead and use the default one or grab one from the leaderboards and be done with it.
Want to tweak and micromanage your loadouts to the point that you're treating it like a mini-Armored Core? Well you can do that as well!
With the new system, it punishes both players old and new alike; new players for not having enough level 3 or level 5 cards, and old players by limiting their customization options.
What Hi-Rez is doing now simply hiding the grind by making the all cards APPEAR to be accessible to all, but actually shift the grind to making the cards actually as optimized as possible at level 5.
PS: To people saying it's not Pay 2 Win since you can't buy Radiant Chests with crystals anymore, think again and please don't swallow the lies Hi-Rez is shoving onto us. Hi-Rez already stated that they are planning to make Radiant Chests buyable again if not on OB 65, then in the near future. Also, even if one can't buy Radiant Chests directly, Radiant Chests which will be used in the new card levelling up system are acquirable through gold, and gold can be acquired FASTER through Account Boosters, VIP Status, and Golden Weapons. It might not be outright pay 2 win, but it is an Indirect pay to win through this painful Pay to Progress Faster method that gives a lot more advantages to those with levelled cards. Pay to Progress Faster might not be that bad at first glance, but it only takes one glance to find out that Pay to Progress faster is almost just as bad. Just look at World of Tanks' model wherein Premium Players get access to increased experience and credit gain allowing them to drastically lessen the amount of matches wherein they would have to fight with a "Stock" or "Unupgraded" tank. In WoT, fully upgraded tanks are placed in the same match making as stock tanks. Paladins will share the same bleak future if we don't stop this from being implemented. Take note: I said bleak future. I'm not saying it's dead or dying; I'm saying if it continues down this path, it will be.

This WAS an awesome game but I just don't see a future for it now. Even if they scrap the Cards Unbound system, Hi-Rez have lost my faith by showing they would even consider such a blatant cash grab.
I stopped spending money on this game a few months back when the smaller cash grabs started filtering into the game and things like bug fixes dropped off massively (OB 61 patch just literally didn't work and the overall quality dropped so much).
Other microtransaction systems were added, such as chest keys that would guarantee a legendary card to drop from chests. It all became clear why, with the announcement of the Cards Unbound system in the OB64 patch.
Currently every champion has 3 legendaries (34 characters, 102 total) and these have a massive affect on their capabilities. Up to OB63 if you got a legendary, which are very rare drops from chests, then that would be it, you now have that legendary working at 100%.
With the new system, you have to level up legendaries from 1 to 5 requiring unboxing 10 duplicates total. Bearing in mind, they are already rare drops, there will be approximately 680 other cards that can drop from these chests, so the only vaguely reliable way would be buying the keys, with real money (on top of buying the chest with either in game currency or in future, real money) that guarantee a legendary drop. However these keys are role specific (frontline, support, flank and damage), rather than champion specific, so you could still end up getting legendaries for champs you don't play. The ability to buy the exact card you want has been completely removed and replaced with pure grind and RNG.
On top of this, they are giving every champion a 4th legendary (just in case levelling up 102 wasn't enough) and no doubt even older players (who will get every legendary they currently own set to level 3) will have to level these up from level 1.
These changes are only supposed to affect the more casual game mode. The fact is, many newer players will get bored of being destroyed, due to having lower level cards and will have to move to the ranked mode (a mode where card levels will be set to 3 for everyone) in order to get fairer games. Of course, this will ruin the competitive mode as it fills with people who have little idea how to play the game mode or their champion. On top of this there will be nowhere to test decks before you go to ranked play.
All in all, it comes across as one last cash grab before burying the game.

I never tried, and probably never will, the original Minecraft game. But I did enjoy this game.
While there are many things that I disliked, the gameplay and story were both pretty enjoying most of the time. Not mindblowing like other TellTalle titles, but interesting nonetheless.
TT shows us that they can make a game out of anything. Like who ever thought a Minecraft story game could ever be possible?
The best experience I had was in the third and fourth episodes, in the first and second ones I didn't really enjoy the story too much, and the last episode really felt like a filler. The story should've ended in the fourth episode, for reasons I can't discuss because I don't want to include spoilers. Tho I did enjoy the last episode as well.
It took me a while to get used to the pixelated art, childish style of dialogues and the building theme, but I really think it was worth my time.
It is clear that this title is mostly for the younger audience, and, obviously, for the Minecraft fans. While, as a Minecraft fan, you will certainly love this and appreciate the references and the way they've build the story inside that universe, I do also think that this can also be played and enjoyed by the other types of players, but it'd be not as exciting and entertaining as other TT titles.
What I most of all didn't like were the dialogues and the way the characters reacted most of the time. The lack of "harsh" sentences and reactions in dialogues. But that's clearly because it is directed to a younger audience.
Overall, I enjoyed my playthrough and, to my surprise, I ended up liking the story and caring a little for the characters. If I'd have to compare this to the other titles released by TT after the first TWD, this would probably be the last I recommend, not including TWD:Michonne since that I wouldn't recommend at all. But I would still recommend this nonetheless.

There are, in the games, few places happier to spend time than in a visual novel writer’s head.  It is a head where the wild things grow, twisting and spreading like vines, like fingers, and taking us in their captive embrace. Over the last three decades these wild things have laid siege to us even as they have mutated.  An acclaimed example is 999: Nine Hours, Nine Persons, Nine Doors, where nearly every action and dialogue choice can lead to entirely new branching paths and endings. Each path only reveals certain aspects of the overall storyline and it is only after uncovering all the possible different paths and outcomes through multiple playthroughs that everything comes together to form a coherent well-written story.  There have even been role-playing video games that feature visual novel style elements. A well-known example in the West is Lost Odyssey, a role-playing video game that features a series of visual novel style flashback sequences called "A Thousand Years of Dreams", which were well received in the West.  From the meta-cinematic masterpiece that is Deadly premenition to the anguished distortions and surrealism of Persona visual novels have dominated gaming.
OVERDRIVE invites us fans to visit the bewitched boulevards, stunning shrines and sleepless cities of their home Japan in their first triple A title to publish on steam and one of the first games to truly be deserved to be called art!  I have so much to tell you about this game but as he Good Witch of the North says, it’s always best to start at the beginning and, so, once upon a time, Makoto, a English Literature major and her younger sister  Akira recieve a stranger(that's you buddy) they met in a chatroom from another country into their home for a week while their parents are out.  There are opportunities for *sightseeing* if you know what I mean but what makes this game so great is it's a return to the great visual novel tradition.  This juxtaposed with the edutainment of learning glorious nippons traditions, culture truly make you feel connected with both the modern and historical nippon through it's characters.
Owning 1300 video games in my life this is the one I am most proud of owning so I highly encourage you to take that first trip to Japan.

Now the steam controller, just from about 3 hours of usage, is something I can already tell was worth it.
First I'm going to talk about the controller itself. The thing feels well made, and has nice quality buttons, trackpads, and overall feel to the controller. I didn't realize how much I'd like haptic feedback until I tried out this controller with it, and boy does it feel good. You also have the choice between plugging it in with an included micro usb cable, or using it wirelessly with the included adapter.
Next I'm going to talk about the Controller editor within Steam Big Picture mode. Best way to describe big picture mode's editor is buggy. Some games the editor won't even load, other games it won't save your settings if you edit them mid game, other times steam fully crashes after editing, making you restart steam, and then rarely, it all works just fine even though you expect all of that. It's unfortunate that Valve's own editor for this is so buggy, but when it does work (which it's about 50/50 for working the 1st time or running into a bug), the editor is so powerful. You can have the controller mimic an Xinput (xbox one or 360 controller), have the controller mimic a keyboard and mouse, or even use the gyroscope as a steering wheel for racing games or something. Anything can be bound to any controller button via Valve's editor. I'm also a bit bummed that the editor is only available if you use the steam Big Picture mode.
Overall, when the editor works, the controller is amazing, and I still recommend it, even with it's buggy editor, as the editor is just (fingers crossed, knock on wood, etc.) going to get more improvement and bug fixes as the steam controller gets more sales and more popular.
8/10 (9.5/10 if the editor was bug free)
Pros:
Nice feeling in my hands (just the right size for slightly larger than average hands)
really nice buttons
(When it works) Really Nice editor
Cons:
Buggy Editor, that's only usable in Steam Big Picture Mode.
In Conclusion, I would recommend it, after a few more updates to the editor.

I have no experience with consoles at all. I'm 110% PC gamer. So this review reflects my point of view, experiences without any reference or comparison to anything even close this what this controller is.
I love it. Some games where harder to get into then others. The seemingly unlimited options of configuration is really breathtaking. The overall feel to it is nice. I haven't any thumb fatigue as I see many reviews tell. It's comfortable holding. It does have a little bit of learning curve, but for me it talked to me really fast. Only 1 game took quite some time to learn. All games where I have to pin point with the mouse, FPS games alike, works surprisingly good, especially with they gyro. I will personally never ever play such game with it. But thats my personal preference speaking.
Equal games alike, as mention above, but with a relaxed phase, I enjoy to sit back and relax using the controller. Some games where mouse it not involved in, it's perfect for the controller, much better then keyboard and mouse.
Games I've tested and likes are: Minecraft, Elite:Dangerous, Rocket League, Brawlhalla, Burnout Paradise, Sonic & All-stars, Sonic Generation, just to name a few, gives you a general idea of what games it works good for.
Games I've tested and didn't like: Killing Floor 2, Firefall, Trove, Team Fortress 2, Killing Floor, I guess you can see the pattern here. This was the games I would never use a controller for, since the mouse is far more superior.
Again, this is from a fully fledged PC gamer with no experience or reference from consol or controller at all. My opinion is as neutral it possibly can get, and I like the controller a lot. However, I do experience the Y,X,B,A is a tiny bit too tiny (no pun intended). So that would be the only con.

Honestly, there are just too many things to say about how awesome this controller is. But I'll keep it rather short as I don't have a great deal of time to type everything out.
It takes a bit of getting used to, for sure. The shape and the trackpads especially. Some games will be a lot easier to play than others, as well. First-Person shooters, I find, are still very difficult to play with this controller, but I /am/ slowly getting more and more used to it. But that's about it for anything negative about the controller.
The gyro and fully programmable buttons make using the controller for pretty much anything SUPER easy and convenient. Games that might have needed a controller to be played can be played, and anything you can think of that had no controller support can easily be set up to work. Point and click, RTS, old FPS, etc, etc. Very convenient to play such games from the comfort of your couch. Even other games that you'd think should have controller support are made all the better. Undertale, for example, doesn't have controller support. But with the Steam Controller, you can just kick back and play it.
As a small note as well, the most recent firmware update (that must've come out in the past couple days or so) added in some pretty neat things. For starters, they finally added in the built-in configurations for the controller. This being so you can just take it elsewhere, like a friend's place, and still have all your configurations because they get loaded into the controller. Another cool thing this last firmware update added is the ability to change the sound the controller makes when being turned on and off. I had no idea the controller was even able to make some basic musical chimes. It's really nice.
As an end rating for the Steam Controller, based on my own experience with it, I'd give it a 9/10 rating, for sure. This controller is so great.

I love these claymation games.  Nux is fantastically quirky, and Platypus does not disappoint.  Although there is only one method of play in this one (side-scrolling shooter,) it's varied enough that it does not lose its appeal as you play.  The bonus items for weapon upgrades are nicely varied, the game tracks your score percentages per section, and some of the bigger ships that you destroy will drop bonus points... in the form of FRUIT that you need to collect before they fall off of the screen. lol~
You start off with four lives, and two credits.  When you lose your four lives, you can continue by using one of your credits, which gives you four lives again... Of course your score resets when you continue, but the game will save the highest score you gain for the leaderboard.
It also looks like a second person can join in and play with you, as there was something on the screen that said to press a button to join.
Platypus doesn't seem to be controller-compatible, but using the mouse to play gives you plenty of maneuverability.  There's no click-click-click, either; just hold down the left mouse button to shoot continuously.
There are weather balloons that float across the background giving you hints such as, "Shoot the stars to change weapons," and "Special bonus for passive resistance!"  Hah!  Try not shooting anything and live through it, I dare you!  If you die even once, it ruins your "passive resistance" because you'll usually take something out with you, and you'll get NO bonus. ;D
Platypus is yet another delightful arcade game by Idigicon, and I've happily added Platypus II to my wishlist.
Great game for casual play.

Ahh, Platypus. This game has some nostalgia for me. Played this game as a kid and thoroughly enjoyed it.
Options: Nothing much to do with this. Sound and music have an on and off button, no scroll bar or something to make it better. The game itself is really loud, so I have to turn it down in the windows sound panel to play this game at comfortable levels of hearing. There is a 2 player option! Either player can use a keyboard, mouse, or joystick. All you have to do it click through it to find your preference. Game pad is not an option, sorry peasants.
Gameplay: You pilot an easily destructible aerial vehicle in a horizontal scrolling game filled with bad guys of various types that you need to destroy. You actually get freedom of choice, if you choose a "non-violent resistance" as the game hints at you in the first level in the back ground, you will get a bonus. But, I've found this to be somewhat difficult, so I don't do it.
You can die very easily in this game, if you are hit once, you are dead. And you respawn with however many lives you have left. So, if you're into that sort of thing. There you go. You also get rewarded with lives as you earn a certain amount of points.
There are 4 different types of weapons. These will be dropped from the orange colored enemy's. you have to kill all of them for them to drop a star. There's the default weapon which fires slowly, but works fine and you can defend yourself easily with it, at least in the first levels. As you advance on, the enemy's get more difficult. The second is a 4 shot spread. The third is a very fast rapid fire of your default weapon. My I highly recommend using this whenever possible. It's fast, and it kills fast. Which is what you need. The fourth is this weird wave type weapon. It's like your shooting a right bracket at the enemy that goes only the length of Justin Bieber's♥♥♥♥♥♥in front of your craft before it magically disappears. I do not recommend using this. The fourth and final weapon is... red rockets. These are cool, but I don't use them. They take their sweet time to exit your craft and launch off into the enemy's direction. And these aren't heat seeking or anything amazing like that. They just fly straight.
Graphics: Everything is in clay-mation. And I got to say, they did a darn good job. I really like the art style. Mainly because I was raised with it. Movies like Wallace and Gromit really helped with that. Other than that, there is a rolling background as you continue flying to your destination, which as it shows in the world selection screen is a big boss at the very end.
I've never beat the game unfortunately, but it is a lot of fun if you want something for fun just to play.
This isen't a bad game, but don't pay any money for it. It plays like something my dad made for me when I was young. On his Tandy 1000. .... 25 years ago.

This is a very simple shooter all done in clay. It really reminds me of the neverhood in that there's abstract shapes and everything is not super smooth. 5 weapon icons, including a 4 way shot. (Weak but can hit multiple enemies at once), rapid fire shot (my favorite. Doesn't have a scatter effect but does take down enemies quick), a wave (can hit multiple enemies at once but kinda weak.) a rocket (much better if you have the sidearms too. They scatter and it can be tough to hit enemies), and a laser. (Also passes through enemies. Pretty strong, but rare.) You can pick up two sidearms to triple your firing power of whatever weapon you have active, and there's a 2x score multiplier. You get additional ships fairly easily in game, but it's one hit and you're destroyed. This is not a bullethell shooter, and even if you've played games like tyrian 2000, you'll probably find this one on the fairly easy side.
Pros:
1: Very cool artstyle.
2: I like some of the effects. Level 1 has a long train boss for you to destroy. Level 3 has a volcano that rains rocks and coins. Level 4 is a polluted city.
3: The music. I can identify the level 1 music as a commodore 64 remix of Comic Bakery with a splash of Jurassic Park NES level 1 music.
4: Picking up same colored powerup icons extends the time you can use the weapon.
Cons:
1: When you die if you have anything special like the sidearms, you lose them. This can make things like the bosses challenging when you're given sidearms and rockets to shoot the boss with.
2: No real upgrade system to speak of, or even a in game shop of any kind. Once the time runs out, you lose your special weapon
It's worth picking up if it's on sale.

Alright this is my first serious review I am gonna write, any others or any past ones I have wrote were either jokes or poorly done.  This time I have taken the time to actually write a half decent one, so bear with me please.  Also if you do not feel like reading that much then feel free to jump to the summary below.
The story in this Dead Rising takes place 72 hours after the Los Pardidos outbreak.  You play as Nick, a mechanic who is joined by several other survivors.  Your goal is to not only survive, but also learn the truth of what really happened and what really caused this outbreak.  The story is actually really nice, and worth paying attention to, especially if you have played any of the previous installments.  The story loves to reference the previous games, it also references the two side games which were Xbox 360 Exclusives, although if you have not played any of the games then they will drop hints on what happened, so you do not have to worry too much.  How the story is presented is pretty good as well,  not the greatest but it works and it is good enough.  Nothing really stood out in terms of voice acting or pacing.
While fighting in Los Pardidos, you have a variety of weapons to choose from, from a traffic cone to even a battle axe!  Although what seems to be the main focus of the game is not only the combo weapons, but the combo vehicles.  The combo weapons are actually REALLY fun to use and have way more variety than Dead Rising 2, and the combo vehicles are also a huge plus, giving you 10 in total.  There are some combo weapons that are not that great but you can't be perfect, especially if there are over ONE HUNDRED! Also the fact that you can make the combo weapons on the fly, and the fact that now there is attribute points actually improves the game quite a bit, no longer do you randomly get skills by leveling up or need to find a maintenance room anymore, but now you can play the game however you wish without any restraints. Control wise the game is very nice, it is highly recommended that you play with a controller though.  The controls for keyboard and mouse could be better however, but fully playable, I had no problems with them at all and it was my preferred method of playing the game.   You also have Xbox 360 Gamepad support, so keep that in mind if you don't like the keyboard and mouse controls.  If you are used to Dead Rising 2's PC controls, you better start forgetting them because the control scheme is very different in this game!
Content wise this game is DEFINITELY worth the money.   After fully completing the game, getting all the collectables, and beating all four episodes of Untold Stories of Los Pardidos, I have logged around 60 hours into the game.  The base game alone took me 20 hours with side missions and getting most of the collectables.  If you were to play the game and breeze through it, like I have during nightmare mode, it will take you around 6-7 hours, more if you go after the side quests, which are highly recommended for leveling up.  In the PC version of the game you also get all four episodes of Untold Stories of Los Pardidos, which has you take on the perspective of four other people before, during, and after the main story.  You also get Nightmare mode, which makes the game harder and gives you less time during the main story.  When playing through the Untold Stories, I highly recommend you play it after the main story, and you play them all in nightmare mode however, because your character stats do carry over no matter what mode you play in.  There is plenty of game play here for you, even if you pay the $49.99 price tag, you will definitely get your monies worth.
During this review I have been very positive, and for a good reason, it is a great game!  Then... there is optimization.  From what a lot of people say, this game is a terrible port from the console, and sadly most of that is true.  The Dead Rising series has always had terrible ports on the PC, including 2.  Dead Rising 2 wasn't capped at 30FPS but the options menu was a joke and it wasn't very well optimized.  Dead Rising 3 however does have a great options menu.  You have plenty of options to choose from, from shadows, to texture quality, to even anti-aliasing, unlike the second game where you can only change the zombie quality and shadow quality.  The game IS capped at 30FPS, although Capcom did say that you can easily disable that via a .ini file, although they said it was highly discouraged and they said to do it at your own risk.  I myself have not done this.  I can run the game at the High Settings preset using a GTX 750ti and a AMD FX 4130 at around 25-30FPS, although sometimes it dips to 22 in some cases.  If you do not care about the cap, then optimization shouldn't bother you if you have a good enough rig to handle it.  When you are reading the system requirements for the game, keep in mind Capcom had this game optimized for 30FPS, and not 60.  Overall if you do not mind the game being at 30fps and having some dips depending on your settings, you are good to go.
This is a great game!  I highly recommend it to anybody who loves zombie games, and anybody who loves Dead Rising especially. The story is great and will be sure to entertain you, especially at the end. The gameplay is solid and there are plenty of options when it comes to controls.  Content wise the game is amazing, you will have plenty of hours in the game to either play the main story, do side quests, or just kill zombies!  Optimization could be better, having it be capped at 30FPS, but if you can work around that you are good as long as you got the rig to support the game.  Overall, it is worth the purchase, even if you pay full price!
If you can pick it up during a sale, it is 100% recommended by me.

I had only played the Europe map for the table top game before buying this on Steam and the game on Steam is incredible. I have had no technical issues whatsoever. I play this with my dad and brother, who live half way across the country, and we have a great time.
There are quite a few maps and each map has different rules, scoring, music, bonuses, and the look of train cards. There are stocks for one map, tunnel and/or ferry routes for others, longest train bonuses for others, bonuses for traveling from one country to another, single, double, and triple routes for others, and so on. New maps are also consistently being released. The game has high replayability; every game is different; all the maps have different strategies; you can play online, with friends or against the computer, and all maps have many different strategies to win. For example, do I go for the longest train? Do I go for the most completed routes? Do I go for routes quickly to start the game or do I stockpile many cards and then unleash several turns worth of completed routes? Do I complete several long routes or go for shorter routes? Do I try and block opponents from completing routes? Do I try and at least stall them from completing routes? Do I pick cards or complete a route? Do I choose a locomotive? Do I pick up cards without knowing what they are?
The AI can also be quite challenging to play against as well as completing achievements. It can be easy to spend several hours playing before you realize you have done so. I can't wait to see what new maps are introduced. DLC is affordable and different in several ways from any previous map.

This game offers the sort of irony, satire and dialogue that the best this era of storytelling has to offer. The punchlines offer more than generic slapstick found in a lot of sandbox games. I played this game almost daily for quite some time and while the F2P model and beta allowed the game's minor issues to coast by fairly unnoticed, recent changes and additions have garnered my attention.
The game is unbalanced in almost every aspect, up to and including which side of the map you start on can sway the game.
Champions are diverse but HiRez insists of making spammy assault rifle champs. You can definitely see where their design crew decided to stop trying as hard. The power creep is real as well. Newer champions are almost better in every way as opposed to the old, compare champs like Fernando and Terminus, both frontlines (tanks) Fernando has a shield that is based on damage (and duration without the legendary card) which is easily dispatched by new champions with absurd damage output. Then you have Terminus, who has a absorb cone that he can turn off and on at will and makes him practically impervious, then when you successfully outdance his cone and kill him, he explodes (which is an auto-kill to most champs without some form of getaway). This is just one example but the incredible difference between champs is noticeable to the point where in ranked, you get harassed for even playing certain champs.
Speaking of ranked. I didn't play in that puddle for too long, but from what I saw it was as toxic and horrible as other well established games. The matchmaking is unbalanced to the point where it almost just seems like it throws you in a spot that's open regardless of who else is in the map. I've had games where I couldn't even poke my head out without getting blown away instantly. Then you find out that your team is full of players that are very new to the game while your opponents are all Gold ranked or higher players with hundreds of hours on their hero.
HiRez also does very little in the way of moderating their game, a game they are pushing for E-sports crowd. Aimbotters and cheaters run rampant in this game, and for the most part are easy to spot given the games death-recap and PotG moments where these champs are constantly flipping around spamming attacks that land 100% of the time. It is possible to still win when facing an aimbotter, which is nice, but it requires the whole team to work together (see toxic community)
Sadly HiRez is falling for the allure of pay to win in their game, pushing loot boxes and upgrade cards in exchange for slogging through the game or giving them money for a chance to get what you want.
The game has a lot of flavor and potential but HiRez's focus on manipulative marketing and lack of proper balancing or community support has all but killed the game for me. I'm sure some will disagree but I, for one, am done with Paladins and HiRez all together.
TL;DR Good game in theory but developer needs to fix the problems that are there instead of making more and/or worse.

So after a month of use, I have come to opinion of the controller: I love it*
*Well, for certain situations, in fact only in one situation.  When paired with my Steam Link away from my computer.  In that scenario, yes, the Steam Controller is great.  I can play pretty much any game and even deal with the little launch windows without having to get up and use the mouse I keep attached to the Link.
However, in front of the computer, there's little point in this device.  I'll assume 99% of PC gamers who keep their PCs in a "computer room" of sorts already have a mouse and keyboard.  And many already invested in a controller (be it Xbox or some other).  In that situation, there's little point in this device.  You already have all the tools you need to play games.
As for the controller itself, I was never much of a console guy, so it doesn't feel "weird" to me.  I love the mouse like touchpad.  I could never aim right with a thumbstick in an FPS style game and although not as good as a mouse, it's still pretty damn good.  My only issue is the grip buttons.  Sometimes I old onto the controller too hard and I end up pressing one of them, and in one game they're set to be the quick save and load buttons.  Ouch.  But that's an easy fix to have them unassigned.
So if you want to play your PC games away from a PC using a Steam Link (or Machine I guess), then you'd want this along for the ride.  However, if you're playing in front of the PC, I'd give it a pass, you don't need it.

Almost instantly I thought the steam controller was brilliant and it's immediately become my go-to controller.
This thing is comfortable and fits my hands very well, although, it is quite big so smaller hands might struggle with it. The layout and the addition of the backplate buttons are fantastic.
That said it takes a little while getting used to it and it's better doing some things than others. FPS titles will always be superior with KB/Mouse for example, but if it's just casual gameplay this will do the job. 3rd person RPG titles I've found this to work like a dream and it seems great at general browsing of the web in conjunction with the Link too.
There's still a few little quibbles I've got with it; there's a learning curve and takes time to grasp and the triggers are a touch sensitive for my liking. I'm not entirely conviced by build quality either; whilst I haven't experienced any problems with it, it doesn't seem as solid as say, the XBOX controller for example.
It's a bit of a 'jack of all trades, master of none' type thing. It will never replace dedicated peripherals for certain genre's of games (steering wheel, flight stick etc etc) but that applies to all controllers. The difference here is that the steam controller has the added bonus of KB/Mouse emulation and endless configurability.
Overall a wholelly recommended product.

If you love games like Double Dragon, Streets of Rage, Final Fight, etc., this game is for you. The game levels are randomized on each play through, and there are plenty of monsters, and other enemies in your way.
Rampage Knights has plenty of random items to keep things fresh. Your characters have four equip slots for things you'll find on your way to the end. The slots are for Magic, projectiles, magic scrolls, and potions, one per type.
There is a lot of fun to be had with the fighting in this game. Although I wish there was a higher variation of attacks the characters can perform, I feel the developers made up for it by making sure that you'll die by your mistakes alone.
There is a dodge button (which you should get used to fast!) and moves that can help even the playing field when you're surrounded. You're able to pick up enemies when they've fallen and throw them, and swing an enemy which effectively hurts any others nearby. An aerial combo can also be performed.
I have a good time playing this in single player, but its the co-op that makes this game shine. Your attacks hit your co-op buddy, but won't take health away from them. I had a pretty fun time communicating with the people I played with to make sure our flashy attacks wouldn't mess the other up in the process (No ones perfect, I admit I've kicked people into pitfalls to their death a few times).
There is local and online co-op offered, as of this moment you can only play with a Steam friend online. No server menu or matchmaking. I had no trouble with lag whatsoever, but the people I've played with live about an hour drive away from me tops. Your experience may differ.
All in all, I think this is a game well worth your money, especially if you have someone to play with. Give it a try!

A candidate for a HOG classic on the rise!
Enable the Hidden Object scenes in the Options section and then you're in for a real treat in this game.
While HOG usually have paper thin storylines (or thinner) that serve as an excuse to show nice HO scenes and some puzzles, the mood is often set to be pretty with fluttering butterflies, lots of sparkles and other pretties - THIS game has an unusual attention on the mood setting, and it is not pretty! Eerie, creepy and a glint in the blood pool - that is what this game is about. You cannot die (I think), there's no (true) jump scares and you don't need to be trigger happy (awww) - this is a casual game with HO containing a slight twist from the typical bunch. But the execution is good and the playlength I got out of it was very good (approx 5 hours).
Usually I have little to no interest in the game diary, which most HO games provides in an attempt to do 'story', but here it made sense to follow the diary to get a fuller picture of the story. Yes - I actually had an interest in the story and the game lore ('lore' may be a bit of a stretch for a HOG, but... it does make sense for this game). Seeing that this is only the first installment of a trilogy, I can only hope that the developer Goblinz maintains the standard: Good story (a rarety in HOG), good mood setting and good play length (I'll be really cross if the two following parts are rushed with shorter play time).
Does that mean this game does not contain bugs/oddities? No, I noticed a few bugs/oddities here and there, some where the progression felt a bit crude, others were inconsistent in gui, but no show stoppers. The most obvious in that department was a rather stiff moving (and looking) main character, but that is HOG as we know them :)
If you like HOG and you enjoy a creepy mood and story, then definitely pick this one up. In my book True Fear: Forsaken souls is a rising classic when it comes to HO in combination with story and mood.... not that there are much competition with regard to story (in general: HO+story... *giggles*) and mood setting, but I digress.

I bought it in the sale. Here's my review:
Overview:
-Gameplay is varied and jumps between action and bullet storm with some basic RPG and platforming elements mixed in.
-Story is OK (I'm only a few hours in).
-Androids are cute.
-Chip system allows you to configure the player character with boosts and skills, which is neat.
-Combat system is lacking but not too bad, you can buy different weapons to equip and mix things up.
-Death is handled like Darksouls, You have to recover your dropped chips and gear from your own corpse.
-Various Post apocalyptic environments to explore (though there isn't really much to them from what I've seen).
-Music is very good, it's actually one of my favourite things about the game. Even if you don't get the game, I highly recommend checking out the soundtrack.
Things to note:
1. It runs ok in cutscenes but gets MAJOR framerate and slowdown issues in most gameplay areas.
2. There are also resolution issues
3. Kaldaien's mod for this game is a MUST, it allows you to configure more settings and fixes the frame rate issues. Look it up and check out videos of people running it on youtube!
4. With the mod it becomes passable (for me), however it's a shame it can't be experienced at higher or 'intended' quality settings at this point in time.
5. There is one particular area with flowing water which is ROUGH.
6. It is unlikely to be patched in the near future. If you have a PS4 I suggest buying it on that instead.
My score after modding: 7/10 (it is unplayable for me without mods)

NieR: Automata can be perceived in multiple ways. It’s an interactive anime, a surprising RPG and a solid action game with a bit of shoot’em up on the side. We never  get to see these elements coming together in a single game which is an impressive feat on its own, but having them almost proportionally equal in quality and seamlessly transitioning is something else entirely.
This was a great gaming experience from the very start to the very end and I mean that literally. Even the end credits oozed some sort of hipstery awesomeness hiding a deeper meaning and choices that tie within the entire story concept. It’s almost as if this game never wanted to let the players get bored always changing for their benefits. Listening to Yoko Taro’s recent interview I know this was an intentional hard work trying to push an evolutionary leap on the overused design framework of today’s video games.
It’s hard to look over this review and not question my own objectivity which has been a driving force for my writing. Is this really an objective review or a love letter to a game that I now hold close to my heart? I can’t answer my own question so I’ll let time settle out the dust over this deeply troubled generation of gaming promising to look back on NieR: Automata when the time is right to judge if it was a strike during a weak moment or part of the generation defining games joining the ranks of cult classics.
Pros:
+ Engaging and captivating story
+ Intelligently written quests
+ Supports multiple playthroughs with new content and different outcomes
+ A convolution of multiple genres with seamless transitioning
+ Frenetic and spectacular combat system
+ Surreal music
+ Artistic direction
+ A rather complex progression system
Cons:
- Dated graphics
- Controls with mouse & keyboard
- The game world is too small for the narrative’s scope
- Optimization problems

WARNING, WALL OF TEXT AHEAD.
If you don't want to read what I have to say, or don't have time,
TL;DR: Upcoming update ruins a solid game, and may not kill the game for the current fan base, but will definitely deter newer players from enjoying this game, which will eventually result in it's death as it slowly runs out of players.
This game is solid, having several unique features setting it apart from its competition. One of the most significant of these features is their card and loadout system, where you are given a cap of 12 points to use however you may like on 5 cards, and one legendary card that modifies one of your character's abilities very significantly.
For example, 1x level 4 card, 2 x level 3 cards, and 2x level 1 cards.
This adds to 12 levels in 5 cards, along with one of the legendary cards that are available for the character.
The cards are unboxed in chests, which you get for leveling up characters and your account level. The cards can be disenchanted, in a similar way to some CCGs (hearthstone, duelyst, etc.) and this "dust" can be used to make other cards.
This is a good system. Not perfect, but I have had no significant complaints in 140 hours about this system.
In my 140 hours of playing, I have gotten to enjoy and learn to play reasonably well 8 characters.
Of these 8 characters I have never unboxed a legendary card for any of them, let alone one that I want. The same goes for the more common cards for these characters, I disenchant cards I have from characters I don't play, and use this to let me make my build that I like for each of these characters.
Some people dislike this system, and want the return of the gold purchase of cards that was in place before essence.
My reply to that is I wasn't playing at that point in time, but it doesn't seem like an awful system either, and I am open to that replacing the essence system.
Now Hirez, the developers of Paladins, in their infinite wisdom, are getting rid of the essence system in favour of having 5 cards, which can be up to level 5 (incredibly powerful) but must be repeatedly unboxed from chests to level up.
They are asking me to unbox a legendary card 10 times from chests to be able to use it to it's full potential. 10.
In 140 hours of play, I have never even unboxed 1 for a champion I play.
For common cards they ask that you unbox a measly 42 duplicates for the maximum level.
No.
Do note that every player gets the level 1 of each card, but at level 1 cards are garbage and useless, so this means nothing, additionally, they say that each card you already own will be raised to level 3, which my rebuttal is, this may appease some players, but there are more ways to kill a game than lose it's current fanbase. When you release this update it will make it impossible for newer players to enjoy playing this game, being matched against players who have played longer, giving them the advantage of experience, as well as just flat out having higher leveled cards. Being matched against others better than yourself isn't inherently bad, it is how we improve. But being matched against other players gives us nothing to study or learn to improve our own gameplay. New players will hate this new system, and even if everyone currently playing the game were okay with this update, it would still die as a result.
Also note that this only applies to casual matchmaking, which is what I play, as I only have around one other person at any given time to play this game with.
In Ranked, they do not use this system, instead opting for letting people pick 5 cards that are level 3.
They do not have to level these up, and if they have the card above that level it is mediated to level 3, making ranked an even playing field. Except it already was, each player having 12 points to use in their loadout, to choose how they want to make their build.
This update marks a loss of freedom to choose your own build in a way that lets you maximise some benefits, or choose a more even point distribution in your build. It makes each build incredibly more generic and will end up in even more people just using the same build as some professional player, which they were hoping to remedy with this patch.
This ranked system opens up another issue with OB64, they claim they want something for people to work towards,
however this update will make chests almost entirely useless for competitive-only players. What do they stand to gain from chests? cards they don't need and a few cosmetics.
Hirez, Please do not go through with this update. If you must get rid of the essence system, replace it with the original gold purchase system.

This is one of my favourite games, I enjoy the gameplay more than almost any online game I have played. But I couldn't stand by and watch Hirez burn this game into the ground too. Don't do it Hirez. You have something special here, don't kill it, listen to your community.

A small town GTA-like game about an increadibly aggressive but at the same time noble boy at the Bullworth Academy. It surely is not a perfect game, but still worth playing in my oppinion, because of its unique scenario and storyline. If you want to try it, pick it up at a sale, it is often available at very low prices.
Overall the story was nice, very unrealistic at times, but still nice. It features some very odd humor and a highly stereotypical view at US school environments. The mission design seemed to me to be a lot easier on the player than the GTA 3 and IV series of games (which were frustratingly hard and unforgiving at times). I think of this as a mostly positive thing, but some missions like most of the races just felt a bit too easy. The game has five story chapters including a lot of separate missions and additionally has a bunch of minigames called classes which can be accessed at specific day times or are forced upon you if the school agents catch you while classes are running. Most of these classes were quite OK and revolve around pressing the right buttons when signalled or dragging icons to marked places. One of the classes on the other hand was so hard that I skipped it all along after three retries.
The game was first released in 2006 and was ported to PC in 2008, a few months before GTA IV was released. The graphics level more resembles GTA San Andreas than GTA IV and looks quite ugly by 2013 standards. There are also quite a lot of rendering and texture glitches and a 30 frames per second limit in the PC version. The latter can be solved by a modified executable file (check the Steam guides) which works mostly fine but breaks one mission. Even if the PC port was overly hungry for resources (I do not know, but most Rockstar ports are) this didn't affect me much anymore because the game ran very smooth on the highest settings on hardware from 2013.
I cannot state much about the keyboard/mouse control scheme, which other commentators stated to be horrific (which would resemble the situation of the GTA 3 and IV series ports) because I played the game with an Xbox 360 wireless controller through the PC adapter. Played with the controller the game's handling didn't feel so bad, but could have been done a bit better at times. The combat, even though there were quite a lot of moves to be acquired throughout the game, most of the times felt quite annoying. The vehicle mechanics like skateboard, bikes and go-carts didn't feel bad at all.

If ARMA and Minecraft had a child, which was then raised by wolves, Nomad would be the result.
Spend hours building a base whilst dealing with tedious tasks like "stay hydrated" and "manage inventory". Forage the ruins of small towns for supplies. Run across the map to find the tools you need to maintain your shelter. Then get killed by a twelve year old cosplaying the Punisher - and respawn on the beach, a good six minute run from home.
Built in Unity, this is an impressive technical achievement. Fully synchronized server-client simulation makes the game more latency-tolerant, albeit with an increased ping time. The game features a startling array of character customization and powerful (but frustrating) construction.
It's easy to lose hours to the game simply mining or cutting down wood. Building impressive structures requires innovative thought - it's quite easy to hit the building height cap, but can be worked around.
During my play in Nomad, I built a tower, and then a bigger tower, and then a wall that stretched for miles. Over time, all buildings take damage, everything returning to ruins if not upkept.
A game of existential angst.

It's an alternative option to your traditional keyboard or controller. That unfortunately doesn't make it better. A lot of people say "oh you get used to it" and the like but even when you do you realize how inferior it makes your gameplay become. I can imagine it's not an issue for slow/casual games/gamers, but for those in PVP situations where every movement needs to be exact, the steam controllers has trouble.
Every game has some sort of "popular" control setting that people "rate up". These aren't always the best. I get how some people can say "oh you can just create your own!" but that is a special kind of person who will sit down for every 50-100+ games they have on steam and configure the controls for each and every one that has steam controller compatability.
The steam controller is something you get better at as you continue usage, but not to the point where you become better than those using a 360 or xb1 controller. The touchpad, no matter what people say, will always be inferior to the actual sticks. Unless you're precise as hell 100% of the time, you'll be losing those PVP deathmatchs, or other similar scenarios.
One positive that I will include is that it's good for desktop browsing. Again, not as great as a mouse but it's an alternative option. Although in this case, browsing is fairly casual so it doesn't really matter what device you pick up to move your cursor around.
Overall, I would only reccomend to casual gamers who play casual games. If you're looking for an advantage when it comes to "skill" in gaming or "becoming better" at PVP, you're looking in the wrong place.

I wasn't expecting a whole lot going into this as an adult playing a game targeted toward kids. That being said, I was really pleasantly surprised with the product I got.
The Minecraft aesthetic lends itself surprisingly well to a narrative-based game. The set pieces were pretty gorgeous and nice to look at. The action sequences were numerous and exciting. The story, though very grandiose, was surpisingly interesting and kept me very keen to keep playing. The dialogue wasn't incredible, but it is a kid's game and the voice acting was fantastic enough that it didn't even matter.
The game has the usual Telltale fare of graphical glitches, TONS of typos, poor facial animation, and abysmal lip syncing. This issues can really shatter the immersion fast, along with the constant references and YouTuber cameos. All that in mind, I can still recommend this game as a family-friendly and unexpectedly enjoyable romp.

After completing it, I have to say that it's just not a good game. Every single puzzle just hands you the solution, and the QTEs they added to keep the players paying attention in cutscenes have such generous reaction windows that they may as well just not have a fail state at all. The story is so terrible that you'd think they pulled words out of a hat and strung them together, though I really can't blame the writers, given that they had to create the entire thing from scratch. The characters are flat and all have the depth of a kiddie pool, the dialogue is terrible, and devolves from semi-coherent in the first four episodes to a character spouting a pop culture reference every other line. The only redeeming qualities this series has come in the performances of the voice actors, excepting Patton Oswalt, who can't really muster the range of emotions that the writers tried to give Jesse.
All this being said, I thoroughly enjoyed watching this dumpster fire burn, as the insanity of the plot just kept ramping up, with episode 6 being nothing but laughs (though I doubt this is what the writers intended). It's worth picking up if you can get it at a massive discount or in some sort of bundle. Still a terrible game, though.
