As of v0.6 (although I'm sure most of the points will remain true even after the game's released):
Rampage Knights is 2d brawler with some roguelike elements.
And what’s the most important part of the brawlers? Combat. It has to be fun and it has to be varied enough or you’ll get bored really quick.
Rampage Knights do not have a lot of combat variety in terms of possible actions - you can do 6 basic attacks: normal, jump attack, charged (and charged directional), uppercut and carousel. And that’s it. If it was just a plain brawler, that’d get boring very quick.
But Rampage Knights is not your simple brawler. First of all, it has crazy number of different pickups - from throwable weapons that do massive damage, but no always available, to a large variety of potions that can make stronger, curse you, turn your head into♥♥♥♥♥(I kid you not) or do all of that at once. How about some large foot curse that causes a large foot (pretty literal, yep) to stomp your location with a small delay every dozen of seconds? Can be a pain in♥♥♥♥♥ but can be damn useful too!
In addition to usable pickups you have different weapons and gear. Those are a bit more rare and you’ll usually have to fight a mini-boss to get them. But they as well can change the way the game plays quite a lot since all gear has special props, and weapons have attack arcs, speed and delays. You have to know how to use this stuff to survive.
Enemy variety is pretty decent - you usually have 2 to 5 types of enemies per specific level. It gets really hard when enemies start to combine with each other - getting those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ archers behind knights with shield can be damn hard!
Levels are usually 5 to 10 randomly generated rooms (think Binding of Isaac rooms) made to murder you. Not that long, if you are good you can beat a level in ~5 mins or so. Again, according to devs the full campaign run should take about 45-50 mins. I wasn’t able to finish 3rd level, let alone the campaign - that stuff is quite hard :D
And all of that is accompanied by permadeath. Once you are dead, you have to start again from the very beginning. And you’ll go through the same levels, but with different rooms, different loot, different buffs and curses.
It’s pretty damn fun! And works equally good with keyboard and controller.
Downsides right now:
- No meta-progression, but according to description texts in camp - it’s definitely coming
- No local co-op (which would be perfect for this game)
- No proper resolution options, only fullscreen toggle (which might be problem for some setups I imagine)
- No way to rebind controller buttons (but that’s a minor one, default controller layout works pretty well)
You can watch a bit more in-depth look at the game here:

Traveling home with a bag full of treasure from their latest adventure the heroes are set upon by an evil warlock, overpowered by his dark magic and waking up hours later they find everything gone. Time to seek out this demon to regain your loot and pride!
Rampage Knights starts you in a village with access to several NPCs, some unavailable but the ones active gave appearance changes, alternate hats and choice of classes. Combinations ranged from wild-bearded vikings to leprechauns in space helmets (all visual changes only). Class options were Adventurer (no pros or cons), Barbarian (+strength, +HP, +better weapon -slower movement -no armour), Pirate(+parrot +bottle of rum +regen while drunk -no shoes) and Assassin (+faster movement +double jump +throwing weapons +assassinate finishing move -lower hp). There was also a challenge NPC (kill X quests) which didn't seem to be functional.
While the game is randomized you will move through select zones, each containing different enemies and alternate themes. Some areas you can make a beeline for the exit while others lock you in until completion of mini objectives or slaughtering everything onscreen. Enemy loot is gold primarily but also drop all manner of items (armour, weapons and 1-time use) so it's worth your while to be clearing rooms, including static structures which often surprise you with nice treasures.
Controls were playable and completely remappable with both gamepad or keyboard/mouse, but I would highly suggest a gamepad as it did feel much more natural. Game supports solo and co-op online play and while I didn't have a chance to test multiplayer yet, I'm sure it would only be more enjoyable. Soundtrack was upbeat and fitting though it could use a little more variety. Maybe I just didn't make it far enough yet. :)
If you enjoy things like Castle Crashers + Binding of Isaac and looking for a new fix, this is probably the game for you. With most of the content in place other then bosses, there is plenty to keep you going after "one more round".  Look forward to seeing future updates and easily recommended to fans of the genre or games I mentioned. Cheers.

I have always loved the Dead rising series. (even though i started with DR2 instead of 1) but i have got to say, i played this for .. 2 hours? and i can see an abundance of flaws in the game.
Initially i loved the cinematic, but it was a lil choppy. (it should not be my com's issue)
then gameplay started and it was kind of smooth.. kind of. and thats where the problems happened.
I played DR2 and it was good, so im using that as reference to my critique.
One more thing, this is all default settings(for key bindings) so i recommend to change it as you see fit.
Picking up items:
It is really REALLY difficult. Both DR2 and DR3 has this problem, you look at the item you want to pick up but it picks up everything else in its path but the item you want. and worst of all if you are full of items, you drop every item back on the floor near you.
DR2 allows you to throw most of the items except things that has ammo(ie. guns and bows.)
DR3 has really weird wonky throw accessibility? sometimes 'right click = aim' so  its natural to think most of the time throw is equated to left click. however, sometimes it is middle click due to this new function it just makes it really unnatural. (it could probably im used to using two fingers on the mouse therefore using the wheel click function is just weird.) Also, you can 'drop' items but like i mentioned, throwing is easier and especially when the zombies just keep coming and you have no time to look at your character drop and pick up multiple times just for one quest item/normal item.
Controller ports:
When i read reviews of this game on steam i see that most of the people are really annoyed with bad ports so i didnt think much of it as i never actually experienced porting issues, but yeah it is bad. just not good.
Glitch:
I fell through the map multiple times and it just was annoying as hell. walking to an area and i got bumped by a zombie, next thing i know, i fell through the floor. found an item near a corner, picked it up, fell through the map. walking up the stairs, fell below the stairs and into oblivion. (you get the gist)
Camera:
the camera angles.. omg dont get me started. it just.. flails around like a kid wanting chocolate even after he had 5 already. you are near a wall and suddenly the camera zooms so close to the back of your head i feel like i can see the hair pixels then i have no peripheral view of my surroundings. it happens whenever you get too close to a wall then the camera suddenly spazzes or when you have some counter with your back facing it. or car or anything that the camera cannot be placed to follow you behind like a balloon tied to your neck.

The combat is very fluid, both the hack-'n-slash and the shooting parts are awesome and each character plays differently than the others (2B uses the triangle button to do strong attacks and combos, while 9S uses it to hack into the enemy and make you play a shoot 'em up section to destroy the enemy from the inside. Obviously, you'll note that I played this version of Doom for only a couple hours, so take what I have to say as you will. However, I also played the original Doom (90s Doom) when it came out.
I think that this modern DOOM is trying to rely on players' nostalgic memories of the original game, in the story, setting, appearance of the Marine armor, and other elements.
Unfortunately for me, I've changed a lot since I played the first DOOM, and what worked then doesn't work for me now. The campaign story is that humanity opened up a gate to "Hell" (the Judeo-Christian one,
) on Mars for some reason (I guess because it's red [[*ahem*orange]] already, oh, I mean a transdimension rift, blah blah) and now literal "demons" are popping out and killing people and setting up bizarre death monuments composed of limbs and viscera and junk. This is like something out of a B-movie. As an Atheist, a curmudgeonly skeptic and a life-long science-fiction fan, it's hard for me to swallow the story. It's silly and hokey and turns me off every time I hear the base's passive computer warn me about the presence of "demons" in an area. Really? Demons and Hell aren't scientific, they aren't sci-fi. It's just a weird juxtaposition if you think about it. I know there was that Event Horizon movie, that was also silly without meaning to be silly.
Although 90s Doom took place in the same setting, it had more of a cool Gothic aesthetic and didn't seem to throw the Hell thing in your face as much. The chronology I linked earlier agrees with that statement.
The gameplay itself is mediocre. It's not riveting for 2017. Not reloading is another unrealistic element that not only is unnecessary, it also removes suspense. The game isn't particularly scary. All the blood on the walls and corpses look cheesy and aren't relatable or believable enough to make me feel scared. The music is too noisy and busy to actually add atmosphere. It's the kind of music that should be played at a monster truck rally. Quake had this same problem but was more fun.
I briefly, briefly played the team deathmatch. The map I was on didn't look good, all that fake hell-flesh and bones, more cheese factor. It was very convoluted in spatial layout, and I ended up getting killed and not knowing where it came from, so kind of annoying.
Overall, I don't think this game would be worth 30 bucks. If you like simplified FPS play, then go for it, but if you want something more in depth in a more hard sci-fi atmosphere, like System Shock (1994), then you might be bored.

This is a funky piece of kit! There is absolutely nothing like it out there. I've only used mine for a few hours. And honestly, once I figured out the various quirks and configuration settings, I was having a blast. This controller gives you the organic feel of an analog stick with the speed and organic precision of a trackpad for aiming/looking. Really getting into a zone with this requires overcoming years of built in muscle memory- no previous input device has required us to operate a touchpad with a thumb. But once you find the right control scheme, things start to click magnificently. I'm faster with a KB+M combo, but that old standby suddenly feels limited, binary, and artificial.
The Steam Controller is a strange beast. It doesn't do much of anything particularly *better* than other mice, trackpads and controllers. But it absolutely can give you the best of both words, if you have the patience to get to know it.
TL;DR: Buy it if you want a controller but think analog sticks kind of suck for aiming/looking.

-------------------------------------------------------
If you want one controller that does everything, get this. If you already have a gamepad, joystick, wheel, etc and a comfy way of playing from your couch with a mouse and keyboard, it's not essential.

This is my all time favorite single player game. I highly suggest buying it, even for the full price.
First I will start with the cons:
- Gameplay is generic hack 'n slash, but doesnt feel too repetative as it is still rewarding to kill stuff
- Harder modes only really give enemies morre health and you take more damage. (Although some bosses spit out more bullets and have a slightly different attack pattern)
-Getting new weapons doesnt feel that rewarding because they all feel like they do the same or weaker damage then the default starting weapons (this changes for level 4 weapons because they all have special "unique" abilities)
-Hacking is repetative and made for a controller. For mouse / keyboard you have to use the arrow keys and wasd and you have a very short amount of time to move your hand from the mouse to the arrow keys to make it work.
-Areas are diverse but feel a bit forced. e.g. a desert next to a lush forest. It gives the game variety but doesnt really make much sense from a story or world building perspective.
Next, the pros:
[No real Spoilers]
- Story. Holy **** the story is so good. The creator, Yoko Taro is a bit of an oddball. He likes to focus more on how a game make the player
rather than gameplay or  mechanics. This game is the sequel to the game 'Nier' (2010), but it also stands alone as a game by itself. There are definetly references to 'Nier' in this game, but it is purely for the fans of that game and you can enjoy this game without knowing any of the lore.
The story was written backwards. This means Taro came up with the full story, then took away parts of it until there was very little left. This is how much you know at the start of the game. As it continues, he reveals more and more of the story. The first playthrough reveals a basic plot and if you just play games for the action and gameplay, you could probably stop ther and feel satisfied. However if you enjoy story based games, you will be left with a feeling like there is something missing and there must be more.
The third playthrough however, is where the game really comes to a climax, and Yoko Taro's genius is revealed. If you like movies/games/shows that make you cry, then you will love (hate?) this game.
You really have to play for yourself to understand what I am talking about, and I suggest stop reading reviews and just buy it already. Don't look up any spoilers, just buy it.
- Graphics: Alright enough with the story. The graphics in this game are amazing. When i first got to the ruined city,
I said woah out loud. The mix of a city scape and nature is hardely a new idea, but Nier: Automata pulls it off so well, it is the best I have seen. The only other game that has made me very impressed was probably FFXIII when it first came out.
- Music: This game has amazing music. It provides a perfect ambiance and heats up at just the right times. I usually barely notice music in games, but for Nier: Automata, it was one of the reasons why this game can get so emotional. It is perfectly times and perfectly fits the current mood of the game.
- Characters: The characters stay with you long after you close the game. Enough said.
- Smoothness: This game runs no problem on my beast of a computer, but I can understand why it may not run as well on a lower end one. I literally can only tell that this was made for console first and PC second because of the issues with hacking and not being able to use the mouse, but other than that it is a perfect port(?).
- Cinematography: Nier: Automata makes amazing use of the tools games have now for camera work and implements it flawlessly into the game. Whether its flying a mecha gunship in Top-Down 2D bullet hell shooter, a 3D, third person free camera, or 2D sidescroller, Nier implements it fantastically and none of the transitions feel forced. It makes sense with the game and gameplay at the time. I only with that the cutscenes were more interactive. (i.e. First play through ending)
All in all, Nier: Automata is easily my all time, favorite video game. It made me feel in a way that no game ever has, and no other games have come close since. Literally all other games feel so shallow when compared to this one, and it gives me hope for video games as a storytelling medium that has largly been untapped up until this point. If you are on the fence about playing this game, ask yourself what you are looking for in a game. Do you only play fast pace multiplayer FPS? This game is probably not for you. But if you enjoyed games like Journey, Final Fantasy, and other story driven games, then this is the game for you. It is easily worth the $80 price tag, but if you are lucky enough to get it on sale, then go for it!

I'll start off this review by saying that Saints Row 2 as a game is pretty good, but as a port, it is arguably the worst I have played. The game itself is fun and is especially good in Co-op, but the performance issues I have encountered let down the entire experience, to the point I cannot recommend the game on PC unless it is either free, or you don't mind low frame rates or glitches.
Pro's:
+ Despite the crude humor, the story was pretty enjoyable. It won't win awards for storytelling, but it was decent enough to keep me playing.
+ The shooting mechanics felt good with the games ragdoll effects making gunplay very satisfying.
+ The numerous activities located around the city are both diverse and fun to play, though some activities are better than others.
+ A brilliant game for Co-op, the game provides a great time for more than one player.
Con's:
- The animations for the game are pretty lackluster and at times stiff. Being an older game, this is more of a nitpick than a legitimate con.
- The AI at times could be infuriating, with my own gang members running me over on multiple occasions.
- The main missions are locked behind an arbitrary reputation points system that artificially increases the games length.
- Performance issues were rife and glitches commonplace. Having played the Xbox 360 version in the past, it caught me offguard that this game runs better on a seventh gen console than a high end PC. At times when playing the game, I wondered if I had a toaster connected to my motherboard rather than a GTX 1080 Ti, though a quick look under the desk at my PC, disproved that theory on multiple occasions. Taking into account the Saints Row series considerable following, I would have thought the development team would have polished up the port, but that's evidently not going to happen. As for the glitches, objects clipping into the environment comprised a good portion of my visual experience. The NPC's kept popping in right in front of me, even with draw distance on full. Many a time when driving round the city, an NPC would spawn in the car with me.
Overall, the game itself is good, with many promising attributes, however the optimisation is at times pitiful. The console versions of Saints Row 2 are no doubt going to be regarded as cult classics, but the PC ports many issues leave it destined for permanent mediocrity.

A fun anime mmorpg, but the cons outweigh the pros sadly. I played up to level 30ish with the Guardian class. Not entirely F2P, but most components can be played without irl money.
6/10
Pros:
- Cooking and Fishing minigames are a nice addition and feel refreshing imo
- Always a fan of anime visuals for both monsters and people/NPCs
- Environments are pretty
- You can solo quests that require dungeon instances.
- Tons of available quests throughout the world. Some include "sneaking" instances which was surprising to me.
Cons:
- Camera is clunky. Mouse cursor is not locked to game window.
- Quests are too easy. You can click and your character will automatically run to quest givers, preventing exploration of levels.
- Combat feels too easy. (or at least for Guardian class.) No mana or stamina encourages spamming buttons.
- Certain quests require you to have irl cash on hand (cannot go F2P, but fortunately they are mainly side-quests)
- Skill tree and mastery make little difference.
- Eidolons pop-up too frequently, interrupting gameplay. (I haven't found a way to turn off eidolen notifications)
- Cutscenes of just white text on a black background breaks immersion.
Very nice to look at, very fun to play, and very addicting! I'm generally not a big fan of MMO's, but this one is an exception!

My experience with Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~ was a rollercoaster of a ride. I learned a lot about Japan and the ways of the Japanese people. I appreciate the art and music that gently portrayed the calm and serene atmosphere in the Japanese cities and buildings that the story took place. The templates used for the characters did not feel outdated or stale which contributed to the overrall storyline in a positive way. It almost felt like I was there.
I started off my adventure with choosing my name. I chose the clever and witty name of "Onii-chan," which I have heard so many times in other Japanese mediums. An interesting design mechanism that the developers implemented was that all text in the story that was referring to me added "Onii-chan". This enveloped as I felt like I was in the game. I can't believe the level of immersion that this game has presented to the market.
This game presented a twisted and joking tone right off the bat, as I was plunged into thinking I was going to "hang out with my bros" in Japan, which I had previously met in an online chat room. The developers even provided sillhouettes of said bros. Well I was in for a surprise when a young girl appeared before me and presented herself as the "bro" I was waiting for. Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~ threw a curve ball in my visual novel experience that I was not expecting, but was pleasantly surprising.
When I started my journey, the game's text was presented in English, which was midly disappointing to me. The reason I decided to order Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~ was due to recent Japanese animations (anime) that I have been watching, such as my favorite, Boko No Pico. Well, the game developers in their infinite visual novel wisdom decided to have all characters talk in Japanese. Although the game can be read in English, a Japanese alternative was displayed on top in a separate box. I have been wanting to learn Japanese because of the Japanese animations I have been watching, and this novel has definitely helped me.
Character development has enriched the way I view myself as a person, and the world around me. The main character started his experience in Japan with a viewpoint that things would be the same as in his home country of The United States of America. He was met with the surprise that even the most simple things were not the same as what he expected. One example would be that simple things such as toilets are completely different (which led to an uncomfortable but humorous encounter which I still find myself chuckling about). There was also a separate event that happened, where the main character thought that the world outside was dangerous at night like in the United States. Well soon after he realized that it was extremely safe, against what he had grown up knowing. After playing Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~, I look at things at different angles and learned to question the world around me.
Overall, this game was a cultural masterpiece that helped me envision Japan, which I have been wanting to do for quite some time now. I would recommend anyone that has even the most slight interest of Japanese culture to try this visual novel. It has given me insight into the Japanese culture, and provided wonderful, humorous, and witty dialect the entire adventure.

Games have always had the ability to educate and bridge cultural gaps but I’ve never encountered a game that specifically tried to culturally educate. Through the language of moè anime and visual novels Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~ attempts to educate the player about what a real trip to Japan might entail. The big question is whether the language they are using will get in the way of that educational potential.
The game opens with our hero (you!) not being able to get any sleep on the plane. At the airport he is greeted by two beautiful young women who will serve as his friends and tour guides throughout his trip. The dialogue, character tropes and story contrivances will be pretty familiar to anyone who’s watched an anime romance or played another dating focused visual novel.
The gameplay choices are pretty light, even by visual novel standards. You choose which districts of Tokyo to visit which determines which of the two girls you’ll spend your time with which determines the ending you’ll get. Production values are average. The still pictures are well drawn, however, a few times you’ll be forced to look at a picture of sky and imagine what should be happening. If you’re looking for a lot of branching paths, higher production values or even just a fleshed out plot you’ll have to look elsewhere.
Still, the trips themselves are enjoyable. Having the vocabulary and activities that make up a trip to Japan explained through two characters interacting is much more fun than reading a guidebook. The information is nicely highlighted and kept in a sightseeing album available from the main menu. The amount of money each activity costs being displayed in American dollars or Euros at the top of the screen (provided you have put in the exchange rate at the beginning of the game) helps make the information easy to digest. Speaking as someone who’s visited Japan before this was a nice review of activities I might enjoy again or I missed the first time.
While the medium of a visual novel will attract otaku and people already interested in Japan, the medium’s quirks will probably turn off anyone else. Some scenes, particularly the ecchi (or sexual, perverted) scenes, seem like they’re pandering to their audience. Even though the game is short (about an hour a half for the first playthrough) it still feels like some things could have been left on the cutting room floor.
Despite these problems I can’t help but come away liking Go! Go! Nippon! I not only had a good time but I learned something too. That’s not always something I can say for games. If you’re looking for a short little excursion to a foreign culture from the comfort of your computer give Go! Go! Nippon! a look.

Ticket to Ride does not want you to leave.  Ticket to Ride wants you to stay... forever.
Okay, a little overdramatic.  But I've had this game since the original version, and while the original version had its issues, the new one is just awful.
First, I do like the timer idea.  It keeps one person from holding up the game.  It's great... when it works.
When it doesn't work, one player accidentally gets disconnected from the game, does not get replaced with a bot, and then forces the entire board to wait as their would-be time slowly ticks down.  Want to leave?  Sure... provided you don't want to reflect negatively on your karma score.  If you want to keep your karma (or, heaven forbid, keep playing), you have to stay there until the bot comes in.  Woe if this happens at the beginning of a game and the timer is set to fifteen minutes.  Hope you have other things you can do.
I have also had the timer count down when it wasn't my turn.  I have twice had one player accidentally get disconnected from the game, causing a massive chain where everyone got kicked out.  Just when I'd gotten some decent tickets, too, dammit.
Graphically, the game will continue to highlight the cities of tickets I didn't keep.  After I complete a route, the board remains darkened.  The time continues to count down while it shows me what routes I finished.  Little stuff that, while not game breaking, is very irritating and shouldn't be happening for a game that's been around this long.
There is no report bug option in the settings for individual games, nor one I can find to report players while in a game.  Report after the game?  The forum button for Days of Wonder doesn't work.
Oh, and the kicker?  Neither does the exit game button.  You are here... forever.  And if you do manage to leave, it sends you a message that you have a turn waiting.  Even if you have clearly finished all of your games.
If these issues are fixed, I would happily and heartily recommend this game... it's a one of my all-time favorites.  But while this buggy, time-wasting version is active, I think I'll just have to break out my tabletop copy of the game.
ETA: As of March 19th, I can exit the game.  Sweet escape!  Unfortunately, others are still having the problem, and the rest of the gameplay issues are still broken.  Sigh...
EETA: April 24th, after the newest update: still having graphical glitches and Steam notifying me I had an unfinished game after it was clearly over.  At least I didn't get kicked out the online game this time.
EEETA: After the June update... nope.  Still having graphical bugs and just got kicked out of the game due to sync issues.  Again. Keep trying, Days of Wonder.

This is a casual point-and-click HOPA (Hidden Object Puzzle Adventure) game. It is the first installment in a trilogy. If you like the genre and you like creepy stories, you are pretty much guaranteed to like this game.
For the rest of the world: the thing that makes this game stand out is the story line. It isn't just the story itself, but the way it unfolds. It delivers a spook factor without resorting to gimmicks or gore. There is also a clever humor in the details (for example, at one point there is a book called Emblem Furniture: Where to Buy It, because no one actually owns a drawer that you lock by removing a piece of its carved surface)
The game comes from a very small indipendent developer. The second installment in the trilogy has been delayed, literally, years. But the hype hasn't died down. There is a large devoted following that is willing to do crazy things like repurchase the game on Steam simply to support the small operation (even though the developer warns that there is nothing to warant the re-purchase). That should give you an idea of how special this game is.
If you are looking for a big budget horror game, you'll probably be disappointed. But if you are looking for a well-crafted, casual, spooky experience for a rainy afternoon, look no further.

When I heard people raving that True Fear is a truly scary hidden object game, I chuckled a bit as I added it to my basket of electronic goodies.  I've played "scary" HOGs before, and they're usually no more frightening than a child's campfire story.  So when I finally got around to firing the game up, I'd done so  expecting little more than a mildly amusing spooky tale with decent adventure-lite gameplay that would at least satisfy my craving for HOGgy goodness.   What I got was something more.  Much, much more.
Before I delve into the review, one must ask the question, how can a game elicit a fearful response from the player when the threat of death is completely absent?  This same question is often brought up with many horror point and click adventure titles, some of which have managed to sufficiently unnerve me; and I will tell you this, the horrors of a man's heart is far more terrifying than a monster that wants nothing more than to eat you.
As appearances go, True Fear may look like your standard HOG, but is in essence a very solid point and click adventure title, provided you play on Expert with no hints, skips or highlighted areas.  Yes, there are hidden object scenes (quite difficult ones, actually), but you can toggle between them and simplified adventure puzzles where you use items in the scene to ultimately retrieve the tool you'll need.  These alternate puzzles help keep with the adventure feel of the game, something hidden object scenes often interrupt (a common complaint among HOPA critics).
Outside of the in-game environments, the CGI movies are fairly high quality.  While the graphics won't hold a candle to any triple A game we've seen in the last 15 years (or even most indies), for a HOPA they're quite impressive.  What's even more impressive is how the action is framed, utilizing camera techniques drawn from horror films to instill fear and unease.  Sound, pacing and music all give these scenes a cinematic feel, even if the characters move a bit stiffly with limited facial expression.  How you present the material makes all the difference in the world.
The best gameplay and graphics mean little without a compelling narrative to pull you in, and this is where True Fear shines.  The way the mystery unfolds with each reveal leading to more questions as details build to an even greater mystery, it keeps you digging.  The first in a three part series, I have several suspicions as to what happened, but only scraps of proof to back my theories.  In the end, I could be totally wrong, but puzzling out the story is part of what makes the game so damn enjoyable.  And that story is even darker and more twisted than I expected.
Of particular note are the bonus materials that open upon completion of the main story.  Aside from the bonus chapter, which I absolutely suggest playing through as it oozes creepiness while adding a ton of clues to the overall storyline, you'll want to look through the developer's extras for interesting insights into how the game was made as well as things that were cut for story-related purposes.  This is one of the few times I've felt the bonuses are indeed worth looking through.
Have I interested you in the game yet?  True Fear is in its own league, transcending the genre in storytelling and presentation while at the same time remaining grounded in familiar conventions that dedicated fans so love.  If you were ever mildly interested in hidden object games, this is a great title to wet your feet in.  As for HOG and adventure game veterans, it's a MUST play!  You have been warned...

I used to use my Xbox one controller for my PC gaming...then i thought to myself... "I need to upgrade",,,so i got the steam controller.
At first glance the controller is HUGE compared to other controllers such as the PS4 and XBOX controllers. but after holding it firmly in my hands i knew the size was PERFECT!
The amount of customizations and key mappings you can do with this controller is unbelievable, i found it really easy to play ALL my steam games with this controller...even those who dont happen to have CONTROLLER SUPPORT! and with the recent update i was able to play ALL my games...not just those on steam (all i had to do was add the game as a non-steam game, then start mapping from there!).
The only problem i encountered was the size of the buttons on the controller....being a person who used an xbox controller i was used to LARGER a,b,x and y buttons...so i found that a bit "bothering" at first....but then i got used to it.
The second downfall was that the touch pads make a clicking sound as you move your fingers across them...this sound is really low and nearly impossible to hear unless you are in a completly silent room.
I really like this controller and i would recommend it for people who want it for their games...unless they are shooters (i still can't handle this controller with shooter games like PAYDAY 2 and Borderlands, but my friends have it figured out and actually perfer it over mouse and keyboard...)

I'm way over the recommended specs across the board. Still, this game runs terribly. The load times are long, the cut scenes are choppy, when I stop moving forward my character always takes an extra step, combat is a mess. It's a shame, because I love the Dead Rising series, but at this point I've spent more time trying to optimize the graphics than actually playing the game. I was planning on upgrading my RAM anyways, and hopefully that helps, but it's so bad I honestly doubt it. I probably won't be able to play this game until I buy another new computer some years from now.
Bottom line: Understand you're gambling with your money if you buy this game.
Update: I found a low specs patch that loads through a program called Ragnos1997 Client. It plays the game through a windowed screen, so I changed my desktop background to black, put all my desktop icons behind the window, and hid my taskbar. I'm playing on a 32 inch TV screen, so the window is actually a little bigger then my old laptop's screen. The quality of graphics is obviously downgraded, and pick up items and some objects literally materialize (think Star Trek teleportation) when you get within about 25 in game feet. The load times are just as long, the cut scenes are a lot better, but most importantly I can actually play. I still wouldn't recommend the game, but if you already have it I highly recommend the low specs patch.

I'd want to recommend this game, but I'm just too disappointed. I still play it once in a while, and maybe you should
it. But the game does not hold up or live to the promise of "goldeneye/halo with mandatory screencheating".
I don't want to just bash this game, as it's fast easy fun every now and then.
Positives:
+ General idea. I played a lot 4 player splitscreen Halo:CE in my teens. First we played with "screencheating enabled". You could tell who took a sniper and where he is looking at. Then we moved to splitting the 32 inch tv with a blanket so only teammate is visible, but you could still cheat by listening... And I kinda miss those days.
+ Color coding the areas. The game divides maps to four or more areas with distinct colored walls and floor. So you can see if the player is in blue area, red/yellow cross or something similar.
+ Weapon diversity. There are melee weapons, wallhacking weapons, grenade launcher, etc. with quite a different feel and gameplay.
So sounds great, right? Well... here are where the game falls apart and differs from what
were:
- Every single weapon is a one shot kill. The weapon balance is... well, there is none. With some weapons, you can just spam, with some you just hope to get lucky, with some you can almost never hit (almost 0 kills with wallhacker) and the basic blunderbuss is really easy to hit from close to moderate distances
- You can start with any weapon. But only one. So you don't want to use situational weapons, or you change weapons just to get away from the game feeling "samey". There are no ammo either, so you don't really have any reason to go for the candelight melee weapon (hobby horse is still cool).
- The last two problems create another: There are no pickups. No armor, no weapons, no health, no powerups - Which means that in the basic game modes, there are no areas the players would pursue and where players would regularly meet. Which also means no one camps - and the screencheating is perfect counter for camping.
- The game is almost as fast as Quake III... how on earth should you keep track of more than one player? You peek upper player screen, quickly check your own, and when you check your opponents screen again, he is on the other side of the map.
Can you spot the problem? The game is too fast, without any chokepoints on maps and all weapons being one hit kill. Poeple just keep running from place to place, if they can see even a hint of right color on the opponents screen, shoot and pray the one shot weapon will hit.
If you are looking for something like avoiding proximity bombs you saw your peer to use, lure your opponent to use his last bullet while he's camping and you can see him pointing the corner, or shooting your pal through the floor while trying to get to the overpowered sniper rifle (which spawns only for one player to use)...
Screencheat is not that game, and that is a real shame.

Human Revolution is an absolutely MUST HAVE title! I'm pretty sure that I can't put to words everything that I love about this game but I'll do my best, as usual.
It's set in the same universe as the first game, and though having played the first one is not required, recognizing some music and character references was a rewarding experience to me.
I finished this game three times : first when It came out, then a pacifist playthrough at maximum difficulty, and another just so I could listen to developer commentary.
Visually speaking, the game is unique, the art fits, character concepts and environment design sucks you into the game and the famous orange-ish theme only adds to the it's identity, once in a while you have to revisit a map, but the story events change the way it plays, so I can't say the scenarios are repetitive. I also have not found any bugs related to graphics.
Gameplay is a mix of first and third person shooting with cover and rpg elements. From stealth takedowns, advancing through enemies cloaked, shooting tranquilizing darts, to hardcore combat with a variety of firearms, explosives and scenarios elements to use at your advantage, the combat in this game couldn't be better, it's as if the game says " hey, choose one of these, and do it your way! ". It will often give you choices, for example : at the first mission, you could go straight to the objctive, or try to rescue the hostages among the way, an option speaking of wich, has more then one way to be accomplished. It's one of those games where you're given freedom inside a linear level path, and this is called replay value!
There is an Augment system, each time you gain a level or buy a praxis kit, you can upgrade something that might have a huge impact on gameplay : reaching higher places you otherwise wouldn't be able to, skipping a set of enemies by going invisible, breaking through walls and moving heavy objects to reveal shortcuts and rewards, it encourages you to play again and again in different ways and once you finish the game, you enter NG+ with all the previous augments you had.
The story is well written, I won't spoil anything, the plot makes you want to search for answer at all moments so expect twists, also, there are four distinct endings depending on your choices, and in case you can't get enough of it, hit the wiki for more Deus Ex universe.

Ticket To Ride has always been one of my favourite board games, so I decided to get the PC version, too (including all DLCs). As a player, you have to build railways between different cities, according to the route tickets that you drew at the start of the game. It's a great game that, at its core, has a lot of replay value thanks to all the different routes you can play and the different maps and other game mechanics it offers. As a bonus, the art is great too, giving you that awesome industrial/steampunkish vibe that goes so well with... well, with the whole train theme.
+ It takes less time to set up than the board game and plays pretty fast
+ You can play solo, with Steam friends, or even just with online strangers
+ You still get to enjoy the art
+ It's a fun, strategic game
+ It's a lot cheaper than the actual board game
- Absolutely horrendous AI. I won a game where the AI had a score of -1...
- It's a buggy and unstable game, especially in multiplayer
- The UI is messy and it's difficult to find what you need
- The DLCs are kind of expensive, especially compared to the main game
- No inclusion of my personal favourite DLC for Europe, 1912
- The background music and the ambient noises are terrible and tend to ignore the fact that you put them on low volume
I really wanted to recommend this, mainly because I love the actual board game so much. However, this is a buggy and unstable game; even as someone who loves playing solo, the AI is just not smart or strong enough to offer me an actual, somewhat intelligent challenge (instead of juist randomly building railways wherever it can). I only play it for brief periods of time when I'm a little bored or looking to pass the time with something really simple.
So nope. You're probably better off playing an older Ticket to Ride version, or just setting up the actual board game.

Something you have to keep in mind with this controller is that it's not supposed to be a competitor to an xbox or a playstation controller, and that it is its own seperate thing. On that note, I would personally recommend this controller for anyone who doesn't already have a controller to play PC games with, and even if you do, I'd recommend giving this thing a go. It works really well for both games that require accuracy (Half-Life 2, TF2, ect), as well as games that are more controller-oriented, like Rocket League. It also works really well for games that require a mouse to play (at least in their current state), such as Kerbal Space Program. Please note, this controller isn't gonna replace your keyboard and mouse in terms of accuracy, but for what it's worth, it's a really nice controller. It's well built, doesn't really feel cheap, and overall has a really nice build quality to it. It also has an AMAZING battery lifetime (uses 2x AA batteries, and comes with a pair). But wait, you don't want to use batteries? Just use the included microUSB cable (or your own cable if you prefer) and you're all set.
On that note, I'd give this controller a 9.5/10. Works really well with games built for controllers, as well as games built for KB/M. Oh, and it's cheaper then a new xbone/ps4 controller off the bat.

I want to like it, I really do. They put so much work into it, and it's got some really interesting features, and the concept is noble...being able to play M&K games on a television? It's the perfect hybrid/bridge between PC gaming and Console gaming, right?! Sadly...this is not going to bridge that gap. It's not awful. The first time you plug it in and try to play with it? You WILL think it's awful. It's not, it just has an insanely high learning curve. I spent days following youtube video guides on how to calibrate it. That whole "Oh just download a profile from the internet! You won't need to calibrate!" aspect of it? That very rarely works. Either the profiles won't load, or they just weren't right for my tastes. The good news is, the controller has an awesomely deep set of custom settings so you can eventually fiddle around enough to find something you like, hopefully. But at the end of the day, this thing is to M&K and Gamepad as a spork is to a spoon and fork. It combines all the features of both, with the functionality of neither. The trackpad is just not good enough for anything first-person. It's sub-par compared to an analog stick, and downright awful compared to a mouse. The trackpad is where every other controller in history has put the face buttons, and the face buttons are disastrously placed where another analog stick would/should be. They're really awkward to reach with any sort of accuracy whatsoever. The paddles underneath sounded like a GREAT idea! Hey, cool, more buttons = more functionality, right? Yeah I don't know about you, but I grip my controller when things get intense or challenging. Now I can't, lest I accidentally pull the paddle and jump or whatever I have keyed to it. Very inconvenient. If you bought one, this thing is not unsalvageable. I'm sure it's great for slower games like RTS or turn based roguelikes and things like that. And I managed to get it....functional?...for other games. I played halfway through Portal 2 to see if maybe I could train myself and re-learn how to play. It kind of worked, but at the end of the day there is absolutely zero reason that I would ever choose this thing over a standard XBox controller if I felt like playing in Big Picture mode.

If you have ever heard of a place called "Japan", you probably already know all of the things this game will try to teach you.

Visual Novel, Manga, Anime (not really)
Adventure, Comedy, Harem (a little bit), Romance (almost a little bit), Eechi (third a little bit)
Our protagonist is a fan of Japanese anime and games. He makes friends with some Japanese people on the internet, and decides to stay with them for a week.
Thrilled by the prospect of a week's sightseeing in Japan, he touches down in the airport, only to discover that his new friends -- "Makoto" and "Akira" -- are actually a pair of attractive young sisters!
After their introductions, the protagonist arrives at their house to learn that no one else is there.
"Um... where are your parents?"
"Our parents were called out of town for two weeks on urgent business."
(In other words, the only ones in the house will be Makoto, Akira, and I?)
(How is that going to work!?)
The local culture has some surprises in store on your first night there, but you'll soon head out on the town! Enjoy the date-like atmosphere as Makoto and Akira take you on a tour of famous sites. You'll marvel at the beauty and history of Japanese culture, fill up on local delicacies, and even share some thrilling moments with the girls!
The week you spend in Japan will certainly be memorable!
First of all, imagine you are visiting Japan that you never been there before, meet the two lovely young sisters (Makoto and Akira), and seeing wierd stuff. You came to heaven. You feel like girls are attracting to you. Oh noes!
Moving on, you are playing as a protagonist, which means you. There is no such thing as a gameplay. It's like Visual Novel or Manga you are reading on the computer. You interact things when you're about to make a choices. There are no right or wrong for this part of the story. It just focuses the plot of the story you are visiting in Japan places and culture.
Overall, I feel that this game seems to be like reading the book, imagining to have a relax or nothing to do. Even if I'm not visiting or in Japan, one day, I would go there sometimes (if I have enough money to travel. =P) I actually understand what I learn some Japanese culture, and language (a bit). There are no such things like scores, FPS, Strategy, or anything. Although, I'm a biggest Japanese Anime Otaku fan. xD
If you feel bored and don't want to play any other type of the games or you are the biggest fan of the anime, then this might be useful for you to relax (and content material =P).

Last Played: Mar 2014
Pros: +Graphics still scale nicely to higher-end GPUs +Good voice acting +Nice, if trite story
Cons: -Bugs are common and some are serious –Lots of lethal options for guards, few non-lethal
I had high hopes for this game when I bought it: reading about the awesome story, the killer graphics, the variety of ways to achieve objectives. Within the first few hours, I knew I liked, but would never love this game. It is true, the graphics scale very nicely on the PC version, competitive with current releases (though the pre-rendered video looks crappy when these sequences trigger). Voice acting is quite good, and the story is interesting in a reimagining-the-classic-world-domination-plot kind of way.
Unfortunately, that isn’t enough to compensate for some serious shortcomings. Within the first few hours I had a loading screen that looked funny – I wasn’t bothered until the loading screen went away and the patterning on the walls was so messed up that I couldn’t tell walls apart from holes and fell to my death trying to get back. Re-loaded: the walls were all bright yellow and I still couldn’t tell what was going on. Kept trying with different save files and eventually restarted the software to get a correct load (fortunately I didn’t have to restart the game or I would have put this down and never touched it again). After that I saved my game A LOT more frequently just in case, which was annoying, to say the least. Other bugs range from story-line critical to merely annoying. For example, some quests and sub-quests do not update, so you have to find the next part manually (particularly annoying in large, multilevel maps). Alternatively, you will frequently find than one or more character models in a “takedown” move are wholly or partially invisible. Of particular note is the game’s annoying fickleness when it comes to knocking out/killing opponents. The pacifist achievement and the “best” game endings are dependent on killing no guards, instead knocking them out. If you are very dedicated to this outcome, you will have to get close enough to check EVERY BODY because takedowns and tranquilizers will sometimes kill rather than stun your opponent. There is no way to predict when this will happen, and reading the on screen experience pop-ups does not always help (sometimes will read “merciful soul” for a knock out, but the body is marked dead). This also refers to another problem: the game encourages non-lethal force but provides few methods to pursue it. You are given 10 lethal weapons, plus grenades, explosives, hackable robots/turrets, and lethal takedowns, but non-lethal is limited to 2 guns, gas grenades, and non-lethal takedowns. Using the same (only non-lethal long-range) gun the entire game is boring, and shows a lack of creativity on the part of the developer.
In the end, I don’t regret spending $7.50 on this game, but it certainly doesn’t live up to the glowing reviews you see here.

Well what is there to say about this game?
This game is a digital version of the classic board game with the same name.
All that you have to do in this game is to build train tracs by collecting "cart-cards" of a specific colour to build a train of the tracs. For example, if i want to build a train between Copenhagen and Stockholm and there is 3 squares with a purple colour you need 3 purple cards to build on it.
To win you need the most points in the game,
1  cart=1 point
2 carts=2 points
3 carts=4 points
4 carts=7 points
5 carts=10 points
6 carts=15 points.
But you can also get points by completing routes like Copenhagen to Rome. There's two kinds of routes, short distance (normaly worth 5-10 points) and long distance (worth up to 21 points).
In the end you can also get bonus points by either building the longest route, completing the most routes or by doing both.

Works great for me on Windows 10, with all DLC.  I loved the game on Xbox 360, but it only had the 1910 and Europe editions, and no discounts on DLC.  Steam has all the DLC, and the package price was good.  I was hesitant to at first because of all the negative reviews about the cross-platform consistent interface, crashes, and DLC recognition issues.  But I gave in and bought the base game first, and it worked great (on my Alienware Alpha with Windows 10).  Then I bought the complete DLC pack, which installed on its own, and was recognized just fine when I checked.  The shop doesn't offer to sell me them, and they all can be selected and will allow the button to say "Play".
The new interface works good for me (on my 47" TV).  I was very used to the Xbox 360 version, which I am guessing was the same as the old interface people refer to on Steam.  But I did find the interface to work well, intuitively, and more quickly.  Anyone who knows how to play should be just fine.  In fact, the play flows faster than the Xbox 360 version, which was a surprise to me because I expected the worst after all the negative comments about the new UI.  The text might be a little small in some cases if viewing on a small screen, but it is the same on tablets and is perfectly fine on a large TV.  The words don't really matter anyway, you can get the gist from the large graphics and colors.
I only wish it had controller support.  The mouse works fine and intuitively.  I had just expected it to work with a controller like the Xbox 360 version.  It would be easier for multiple local players if each have their own controller (like the 360).  But it works just fine.  I ended up getting a 2nd copy for someone else to play with me via Online, and that solved that problem :) .

I want to like it, I really do. They put so much work into it, and it's got some really interesting features, and the concept is noble...being able to play M&K games on a television? It's the perfect hybrid/bridge between PC gaming and Console gaming, right?! Sadly...this is not going to bridge that gap. It's not awful. The first time you plug it in and try to play with it? You WILL think it's awful. It's not, it just has an insanely high learning curve. I spent days following youtube video guides on how to calibrate it. That whole "Oh just download a profile from the internet! You won't need to calibrate!" aspect of it? That very rarely works. Either the profiles won't load, or they just weren't right for my tastes. The good news is, the controller has an awesomely deep set of custom settings so you can eventually fiddle around enough to find something you like, hopefully. But at the end of the day, this thing is to M&K and Gamepad as a spork is to a spoon and fork. It combines all the features of both, with the functionality of neither. The trackpad is just not good enough for anything first-person. It's sub-par compared to an analog stick, and downright awful compared to a mouse. The trackpad is where every other controller in history has put the face buttons, and the face buttons are disastrously placed where another analog stick would/should be. They're really awkward to reach with any sort of accuracy whatsoever. The paddles underneath sounded like a GREAT idea! Hey, cool, more buttons = more functionality, right? I've been using this for a month now, I have to say it's an incredible device. As games appear recognise it as a keyboard and mouse, it allows one to play retro games with the controller; it is a joy to play the original Tomb Raider games with a controller, without having to purchase additonal software to get a regular controller working.
However, the Steam Controller experience really differs, based on the genre and type of game one is playing. Sidescrollers like Broforce or Risk of Rain are a joy to play, as are games like Total War or Civilization.
However, of all the genres I've played, FPS and over-the-shoulder games, such as Metal Gear Solid V, Rise of the Tomb Raider, Mad Max, Grand Theft Auto V, or Dead Space, are very uncomfortable to play on it. No matter what I do, I can't find a comfortable setting for them. Aiming takes a while, accuracy is very difficult, and I ultimately get killed before I can even take aim. I have to switch to my Xbox One controller or keyboard and mouse when I want to play such games.
The gyro setting, to me, is utterly useless aswell. You have to prop up your controller to use it, and aiming with it is so fiddly, it's pointless. Unless you have a driving sim and want a cheap solution to not purchasing a wheel.
So, in general, I do recommend it. It's very good for playing old games and certain genres. However, it is imperfect; in my experience, FPS and over-the-shoulder third person games do not interact well with it.

NieR: Automata is my clear Game of the Year of 2017, even though it's not quite AAA level in terms of technical polish.
This creativity and bravery to do something new is what the industry needs, it's far from being perfect, but compared to the budget these people were on, what's been achieved here is crazy impressive.
Pros:
- Creative design that make you rethink the limits of storytelling in video games. This isn't just a cinematic experience, the core game mechanics themselves are tailored to make you experience the story of the characters, in a way no other medium could possibly achieve, other than video games.
- Great action, probably the best combat system Platinum has done at this point. Great free flowing movement and combos, that will take some time - and a lot of fun - to master. No quicktime events ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, the combat is manual, you control what your character does.
- An RPG system that puts most streamlined AAA titles to shame, great costumization (gameplay, not visual), that really allows you to build your character to fit your own playstyle.
- Incredible story with great characters, crazy emotional load, huge, shocking plot twists that make you change the way you look at what you already played through repeatedly. Seriously, you keep thinking ok, this is it,♥♥♥♥♥♥surely can't get any more real than this, but the game's just written so well, it keeps surprising you all the way, you truly haven't seen anything until you complete the 5 main endings (which takes 3 playthroughs, oh yeah, the first 3 playthroughs are all different too, the game doesn't end after just finishing the first one). Add to all this a deep, meaningful theme delving into questions about the world and what it's like to be human - which you'll absolutely love if you're into that sort of stuff (the experience is still epic even if you're not though).
Cons:
- The big one: technical issues. The vanilla PC port is playable by all means, but honestly,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ It won't get an official fix either, since Square Enix won't give the funds to Platinum to actually fix it, they just don't care anymore. However, there's an amazing community made fix available on Steam (FAR mod), that fixes the issues of the port for most people. K&M controls work great btw, so at least that's not an issue.
- Graphics aren't what you'd expect in a 2017 game. The characters and the effects look great, but other than that it's not impressive.
- The open world can be pretty empty and dull at times, which fits the theme of the game but still not ideal. Exploring is only kept fun thanks to the great movement and combat system.
It's definitely worth a buy imo, even though Square Enix is trash, the director Yoko Taro and the other great people at Platinum deserve the support. Who knows, maybe next time they'll get a bigger budget and can do something this epic with AAA worthy technical polish.

TL;DR Below.
I love the BIT.TRIP series but for many reasons this title failed to satsify my rhythmic needs. The music compared to the runner series, Beat series, and Core, seems to be all beat/bass and no melody (In my opinion). There is no exact or specific time you're required to collect dots which kind of defeats the purpose of a rhythm game. The game is by no means horrible, but it does not fit into the category of rhythm games.
There is also no indication or anything that notifies the player that they're near the next phase, near nether, or shows them their total score... why may I ask? The BIT.TRIP Runner series had it, so did the Beat series, why not Void?
As for controls, BIT.TRIP Void is the one title in the series where you are not required to tap a certain key to the beat of the music. Instead, you are required to MOVE in order to collect the beat, regardless of whether it is to the music. This makes the whole concept of "rhythm" obsolete, as you are not required to collect a dot in time to the beat of the music. (There is no consistency). The game doesn't allow you to choose how you control your orb. It's fixed on keys. Being a rhythm game, precision is a vital component. There are times in the game where getting a dot requires you to be pinpoint accurate. Not being able to fluently move is a big no-no for rhythm games where you are able to move freely. Even just a tap of a key can cause you to overshoot ending your combo and possibly even sending you into the nether... how would you know? There's no health bar!
Being able to use the mouse would've definitely turned the tables around, although it wouldn't help with the musical aspect of the game.
Long story short, BIT.TRIP Void isn't a horrible game, but for a rhythmic game, it does a horrible job trying to accomplish what it set out to achieve. It is tagged as "Rhythmic" but I would not call it that at all, but rather survival. I find myself focusing more on surviving than enjoying the music as I cannot or can barely hear it. Since the game doesn't require you to pick up dots on a constant beat, you can just run around picking up black orbs that are in safe reach regardless of listening to the actual music. I would not call this rhythmic as there is no rhythm you're creating. As opposed to the other series, where you HAVE to be rhythmic in order to successful pass the levels.
TL;DR: Interesting game, but bad controls and no engaging rhythmic music that actually requires you to be rhythmic.
In my honest opinion, just get the other titles, they are way better and are actually rhythmic.

The objective is to collect certain beats and to avoid other ones, by pressing the space bar you "cash" in your points and shrink the void sphere. Sometimes challenges conclude before one is officially over and the controls reset before you even know it, it's a little problem but not a big deal.
The music of this game does not play if you aren't doing very well, you just hear a repetitive beat over and over, if you do poorly, you go down to this zone where you collect beats which are worth no points and you try not to die. I STRONGLY advise you to play this game with a controller since very frequently you need to move diagonally across the screen faster than you anticipate. The PC version is probably the worst port of the game and can be very frustrating without a controller.
I only recommend this game because it isn't bad, it's the controls and especially the challenges, they are very messed up. Buy it if you have a controller or if the game is less than its current price.

Saints Row 2 is a pure GTA3 clone, there is no way around it. If you like GTA, please ignore my negative rating and just buy the game, I'm sure you will have a great time. However, I'm one of those few(?) people that don’t really like the GTA series (well, I only played the first two iterations on PS2, I can’t comment on whatever was released afterwards).
It’s not that I don’t like open world games, I spend way too many hours in Skyrim and Fallout for example, those are absolutely my favorite games on the PS3. I don’t really know why the GTA type of games never captivated me. I couldn’t get any satisfaction from the games at all, most of the time it just got on my nerves. The same is true for Saints Row 2.
I really tried to like the game, I did my best, gave it more then a few chances, you’ll notice I have around 10 hours of play before I gave up.
I do feel like they try to put in some interesting storylines into the game, the problem is that you cannot just play through these stories. No, you first have to build up respect. Respect is gained by completing silly, stupid, mind-numbing mini games (car races, beat up shop owners, all kinds of fraud, …) and they are just no fun. The cars in the game are all rubbish (this is the same for GTA), fighting is clunky as well, basically the controls are bad. It doesn’t help that no mater how you configure your Steam Controller, the controls stay horrible.
The overall feel of the game is a bit dated, ofcourse it’s a game from 2009, but there are many older games which still have tight controls and are a joy to play even today. One thing that is good about this game is the soundtrack. It’s not even the type of music I prefer (mostly Hip-Hop), but it’s just good.
On SteamOS/Linux you’ll also bump into bugs and oh so many slowdowns (for no reason), frame rate drops etc. And this is on a killer i5 / Nvidia 1060 setup which runs games like Mad Max in highest detail without a hitch.
I hear the next games in the installment are better, as they are no longer just a GTA clone, but something that stands on it’s own and doesn’t take itself so seriously. My hopes are higher for those games. Ofcourse, if you are a Linux gamer and want a GTA-type of game, this is basically your only option for now.

I wasn't expecting much going into this game, but a friend got me interested and I picked it up day one. I can safely say this game has far exceeded my expectations. There's much to love here. The combat is fluid and fun, the game is absolutely beautiful to look at, and the story is quite deep and delves into many darker themes that the game itself with advertising didn't show. I was really surprised at this, and also surprised at the blend of genres. Things like sidescrollers, bullet hell shooters, etc, make an appearance in this game at certain sections. I was also very surprised at how long the game was. There's multiple endings to find and other characters to play as, each adding new story and new combat elements, so it stays fresh for the duration you're playing. It's in my opinion also highly replayable, there's a lot of side things the game offers that you can discover that add on to the lore and help build the world, which I found to be very nice, even if some of the quests seem pretty generic.
Only negative I really have for it is performance. I have an AMD card and the game would crash 5 minutes in. I had to roll back to previous drivers to even play the game without crashing. That was very irritating and it's a shame no more work is going to be done to improve the game's performance. Luckily it was worth going through for this game, but it's still no excuse and should be mentioned.
I can highly recommend this game to anyone who is looking for something with a very good story, fun gameplay, and amazing graphics. Whatever you think of it now, I promise it will surprise you more than you think it would. It's worth every second I put into it and I hope my opinion helps influence one's decision in picking up what I would consider a strong contender for GOTY.

The steam controller was a nice surprise for me. I got it in a bundle with the steam link and I expected the controller to be pure crap but... I was wrong... VERY WRONG.
I think I had lowered my expectations so much that when I accually started using it I was plesantly surprised. I expected the trackpad to be really bad and the positions of the trackpad to be really straining however I found that the trackpads were very comfortable for my thumbs and they worked really well, think of the trackpads as a good trackpad on a laptop. One problem I do have with the positions of the buttons is that it is quite straining to use the joystick due to the position. While I don't have a problem with the button positions surprisingly it is a problem for me with the joystick.
One of the biggest advantages with the steam controller compared to a normal controller is the fact that you can use the entire thing on the desktop (including keyboard). This is really good for when I am using the Steam Link because I can just sit back and relax while using mouse and keyboard.
Now on to something a little more mixed in my opinion, compatibility. One thing you have to know before going out and getting a steam controller is that you are going to be spending a lot of time configuring controls for games. While you can get most control presets from the community and some game companies already have presets you most likely have to change a few things in the settings especially in the trackpad area. Alot of presets have trackpad mode enabled which in my opinion can be really annoying and I would really reccommend turning it off for most games because it basically treats the trackpad like it's a trackball so when you flick on the trackpad the mouse will continue to move like if you flicked a trackball. While this can be useful in some things it can be annoying. Another problem (and this isn't the controllers fault) is when games are forced to use controller modes if the controller is being used (fallout 4 is an example of this) This means that you have to use mouse-like joystick which can be very hit and miss with games. On FO4 it accually works pretty well if you spend a little bit of time configuring it however in games like GTAV it just dosent seem to work very well no matter what I do (luckily you can use mouse mode with a few problems though). Overall compatibilty isn't too bad... It's not perfect but it is very good considering that there is no actual built-in compatibility with games. Another positive thing to mention about the controller are the grip buttons. These buttons can be SUPER useful when having to do things like reloading and I find them quite to use in Euro Truck simulator 2 for the indicators, I really hope grip buttons become more of a common thing with future controllers (instead of £120 xbone eilete controllers XD).
Now on to my worst problem with the controller. Luckily this is a software problem and not a hardware problem. I have experenced many problems with steam crashing while using the steam controller. Crashing in the steam client, crashing while using the keyboard in the desktop forcing me to get back to my computer and quit big picture etc. -_- No matter it is in beta still.
Overall I would reccommend this controller as more of a secondray controller instead of the main controller. It is not going to replace mouse + keyboard or controller it's too much of a middle ground product to be that but it is a real pleasure to use it once you get used to it, while the plastic dosen't really feel that premium I feel the costs have been used on buttons and haptics since the buttons and haptics are really satisfying and all the buttons (apart from the Y X A B buttons) feel very mechanical feeling and the haptics really help with that. If you have £40 lying around I would really recommend getting but just don't go rushing out for it.

The steam controller is great, I tried it for a variety of different games, and it is very versatile and will work for almost any genre, and it is very fun to type with. It is very fun to customize your controls, and you can rebind the buttons to make them do pretty much anything. The customizability is great, it is very fun to use, and using it is an overall good expeirence
However while the steam controller itself is amazing, but it does have one major downside; big picture mode.
Big picture mode is terrible, and very annoying, it is not good, it is not cooperative, and by all means IT SHOULD NOT BE A REQUIREMENT TO USE THE BASIC FEATURES OF THIS HARDWARE. It is so irritating, but luckily if you have already set up bindings on your controller (using big picture mode), you can play games without it, however that does not change the fact that it completely relys on it. To make it even worse, the second you turn on your steam controller in big picture mode, your mouse and keyboard stop functioning properly (your mouse in particular), it disables your mouse and makes you use the controller. Big picture mode also comes with plenty of bugs, but I will not go into those (some involve computer and steam crashes, and ect.). Now this could be bareable because as soon as you have your bindings on your games you are free to play them without big picture mode, but there is one thing that is a bit of a pet peeve of mine;
You are not able to turn your controller off without big picture mode, which is a huge pain, especially when you accidentally turn it on.

However, if the steam controller can become fully functional without big picture mode, or if they can somehow fix big picture mode to make it a better experience, then I will give this controller my full recommendation.

I'm in the category of people who wanted to like it but always felt that it would be awkward and imprecise. I picked it up to satisfy that expectation so in that regard I wasn't disappointed.
My big concern prior to purchase was the sacrifice of its d-pad to add a thumbstick, which felt like an admittance that a trackpad couldn't replace it. As there remain no affordable natively-supported PC controllers with good d-pads this was a big opportunity cost. The added indent to the left trackpad was an insufficient compromise; they simply aren't noticeable enough when playing the kind of games that expect the precise high-speed input of a d-pad's core function.
Annoyingly the trackpads
perform a thumbstick's input very well, so the controller pointlessly doubles up on one input type at the cost of another which could have been genuinely useful. The troubling possibility is that this change was made in response to pre-release complaints of no thumbstick; if true this means a marketing decision diminished the quality of the final product.
I like the trackpads (comfortable and accurate), triggers (easy to use and dual-purpose) and grips (useful for toggles). I dislike the thumbstick (convex without grip) and face buttons (small and difficult to reach). I utterly
the bumpers that are astonishingly difficult and actually a little painful to press even once, let alone repeatedly as some games require.
The shape of the controller is questionable; the lower end of the hand grips curve
into your palms, requiring those of us without giant hands to move them around the side of the controller, particularly to reach the face buttons. There seems to be no hardware inside that part of the grips so this is baffling design.
The inputs are incredibly customisable, which is not as amazing as it sounds. Any game that is best played with a controller has already been designed to use one, so often that customisation ends up being to replicate existing design (where possible given the above deficiencies). For games which are not designed for a controller - ergo, the keyboard/mouse combination - any controller will always be at a disadvantage.
The customisation has certain limitations for things that would have been useful. For instance, turbo cannot be assigned to an individual face button - it is either every face button or none of them. I'm not sure if these are oversights or deliberate countermeasures to cheating, but it means another opportunity for the Steam Controller to have something over the more dedicated alternatives is lost.
The controller also needs Steam's Big Picture mode to be active, which is not a good thing at all. Big Picture is not well laid-out and an unpleasant experience which significantly affects system performance to the detriment of gameplay. Amusingly the controller's missing d-pad means it is also uncomfortable to navigate the confusing menu layout with the thumbstick. The configuration menu itself is well laid-out though I think I'd prefer an ability to calibrate buffers and dead-zones in-game rather than repeated trial-and-error with countless sliders.
Overall, the Steam Controller is marketed as being an all-in-one solution for gaming in your lounge when a keyboard is not to hand. After trying to find another purpose for it, I'm forced to conclude that is possibly the only situation in which it the best option.
